name: Tipaza
description: Founded by the Phoenecians as a small trading port, Tipasa was recolonized several times over the centuries, with the Romans, paleochristians, and Byzantines all making their mark on the city. These many remodelings make Tipasa "one of the most extraordinary archaeological complexes of the Maghreb" - especially high praise considering it's coming from UNESCO. Spread across three hills overlooking the sea, walking through the site you'll find everything from pre-Roman necropolises, Roman ruins including a forum, thermal baths, and a theater, and Christian remains, like one of Algeria's largest Byzantine basilicas and a cemetery. If you need any further convincing about Tipasa's historic weight, it even inspired Albert Camus to write a poem - a legacy immortalized by a monument to the writer.

name: Gurye
description: With its picturesque landscapes and serene atmosphere, Gurye is a rural haven that beckons travelers seeking natural beauty and cultural experiences. During the spring and autumn seasons, Gurye transforms into a hiker's paradise, attracting outdoor enthusiasts from all around. The county hosts a series of captivating festivals, including the renowned Sansuyu Flower Festival in mid-March, when the hillsides are adorned with the vibrant hues of cornelian cherry blossoms. One of Gurye's hidden gems is the Ssangsanjae, an antique house that artfully blends the essence of hanok architecture, a traditional Korean courtyard, and a serene Korean garden. Another enchanting attraction is the Thousand Juniper Forest, where rows of juniper trees create a captivating garden setting. Visitors can enjoy the calming ambiance and even relax at the garden's quaint café, savoring the tranquil surroundings.

name: Ephesus
description: Founded by Greek colonists in the 10th century BC, Ephesus passed under Greek, Persian, Roman, Byzantine and, ultimately Ottoman rule over its 11,000 year history. At its height, Ephesus was a bustling port, one of the largest cities in Asia Minor, and home to some of the finest monuments of the ancient world. Most notably, the Temple of Artemis - one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Inhabited until the 15th century, today this UNESCO World Heritage Site presents an unparalleled snapshot of Hellenistic, Roman Imperial and early Christian cultures despite 80% of the city remaining unexcavated. Walking the ancient Roman roads, you'll find terraced houses with mosaic floors, intricately decorated gates, a bounty of bathhouses, and several temples, including the foundations of the Temple of Artemis. The famed two-story library with its columns and sculptures, and 25,000-seat theatre put the city's size and status into perspective.

name: Pereira
description: While the Spanish had attempted to settle the area as early as 1540, Pereira wasn't successfully founded until 1863. The 20th century saw the settlement swell as settlers established coffee, sugarcane, and cattle farms in the fertile soil. Today, Pereira is the largest city in Colombia's coffee-growing region, and as an economic center, is faster-paced than the usual tourist destinations. That doesn't mean visitors can't find some respite in its elegant cathedral with its colorful tiled floor, and ornate wooden ceiling. Of course, there's also a Simon Bolivar square where you can find vendors, street-food, performers, and a statue of the national hero - except in Pereira he's shirtless atop his horse like a Greek god. The plaza, or one of the city's countless cafes, would be a great place to try Colombia's most famous export: coffee. This is often sweetened with local, unrefined cane sugar known as "panela".

name: Rijeka
description: Rijeka is Croatia's third largest city and the the largest city of the Kvarner region. It hosts many festivals and is home to the largest and most popular carnival in Croatia. Rijeka also has a rich and colorful history. It has been ruled by many different countries and empires throughout the years. The best place to discover Rijeka's history is in its many museums feautring extensive exhibitions. The city center is adorned with ornate Austro-Hungarian style buildings. It also houses the City Tower, Roman Arch, Church of St. Vitus, and the National Theater. Far above the city is the Trsat Castle. This 13th century fortress offers a perfect view of Rijeka. The city is also a popular destination for swimmers, with many swim spots located near the city center.

name: Chiclayo
description: The city of Chiclayo is a fascinating combination of cultures; the fourth largest city in the country as well as the commercial and financial capital of Northern Peru, it sits at the confluence of ancient civilizations and modern post-colonial values. Visitors can browse the bustling Mercado Central and Mercado Modelo (the latter of which contains in a famed "witch market," where shoppers can peruse a selection of occult and spell-casting props). History buffs will appreciate the Republican-era architecture of the Municipal Palace and the Cathedral of Chiclayo, both located near the city's main park. Be sure to bring a hat or sunscreen, as shade is hard to find in this ever-sunny desert landscape!

name: Bratislava
description: Following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia at the end of 1992, Bratislava became the capital of the new Slovak Republic and immediately began to transform itself into the popular metropolis that it is today. The city undeniably justifies its position as the political, cultural and economic center of Slovakia and is home to numerous theaters, museums, galleries, concert halls, cinemas, and foreign cultural institutions. History and culture lovers can explore Bratislava Old Town, often referred to as a "Mini-Vienna on the Danube" with its plazas, museums, baroque and gothic palaces while sampling the cafes and the many ethnically diverse restaurants. This exuberant and energetic multicultural city comfortably caters to every taste through its large range of historical and modern attractions and should be high on every travelers "to do" list.

name: Blumenau
description: Blumenau, nestled in the picturesque Itajaí Valley of Santa Catarina State, Southern Brazil, is a captivating city with a unique cultural blend. Strolling through downtown Blumenau between April and December unveils charming German-style architecture and a welcoming atmosphere. However, brace yourself for the scorching summer heat. The city's hilly terrain offers both challenges and breathtaking views, with well-maintained sidewalks downtown. Landmarks like the Aldo Pereira de Andrade Bridge, affectionately known as the "Ponte de Ferro," offer spectacular vistas. The Blumenau Municipal City Hall, a German-style gem, stands as one of the city's most beautiful buildings. The German Village (Vila Germânica) showcases traditional houses selling everything from souvenirs to delectable hot dogs. The Oktoberfest, the second-largest beer festival globally, transforms Blumenau into a lively celebration of German culture, attracting over a million tourists annually.

name: Yuma, AZ
description: Long settled by Native Americans because it offered a safe place to cross the Colorado River, Yuma was developed by Europeans for the very same reason. During the gold rush, this crossing made Yuma the gateway to California, which allowed the town to flourish. It was also a bastion of law in the Wild Wild West, with the territorial prison being built on the banks of the Colorado River in 1876. The prison, as well as the old U.S. Army Quartermaster Depot and other buildings in the Colorado River State Historic Park are some of the oldest in Arizona and offer a multifaceted look at life in the Old West. The Yuma Historic Downtown isn't quite as old as its name implies, having been rebuilt following a massive flood in 1916, but it still has that atmosphere of days gone by.

name: Campos do Jordao
description: At 1,628 meters (5,341 ft) above sea level, Campos do Jordão holds the title of highest city in Brazil, and is a popular holiday retreat for the country's well-to-do. Befittingly, the architecture of Campos do Jordão draws inspiration from traditional European alpine architecture, making it one of the most unique cities in the country. The downtown is packed with bars, restaurants, and shops all housed in colorful half-timbered chalets. Be sure to take the time to tour the Boa Vista Palace (Wed-Sun 10AM-5PM). Built in 1964 as the winter estate of the then Governor of the State of São Paulo, Adhemar de Barros, this 3000-square-meter chateau is filled with thousands of pieces of furniture, paintings, and objects d'arte. The tour is free, and done on a first-come, first-serve basis.

name: Debrecen
description: Settled in the middle ages following the Hungarian conquest, the city grew in stature when many of the surrounding villages were abandoned during the Mongol invasion. The city never built a castle for defense, and so relied on diplomacy to resolve tensions during the Ottoman era, often shifting their allegiances. By the 19th century the city had become a cultural center, and was made the temporary capital in 1849 when the Hungarian revolutionary government relocated there. Today, visitors can simply walk through the scenic center of Hungary's second largest for a healthy dose of culture. The central square is faced with one of the city's most important landmarks - the Reformed Great Church, where Hungary proclaimed independence. Nearby, the eclectic Deri Museum has diverse collection, with everything from paintings by Mihály Munkácsy to an Egyptian exhibition.

name: Kitakyushu
description: Since the Meiji Era, Kitakyushu has been a pivotal industrial center on the island, bridging the gap between Kyushu and Honshu. It thrives as a center for history and art, with landmarks such as Kokura Castle showcasing Japanese customs through time. The meticulously restored stronghold proudly symbolizes the city, nestled in Katsuyama Park and sharing its domain with the Kokura Castle Japanese Garden and revered Yasaka Shrine. In spring, the park's hundreds of cherry trees create a stunning spectacle during the sakura season. Moji Port, with its historical edifices from the late 19th century, was designated a "special trade port" in 1889, lauded for coal exports and its proximity to China. The port's prosperity led to the establishment of western-style buildings housing financial institutions and merchant companies. The area encompasses the Idemitsu Museum of Arts and the Mojiko Retro Observation Room, which affords panoramic vistas of Moji Port, Shimonoseki, and the Kanmon Straits.

name: Creel
description: For those seeking authentic Mexican souvenirs and a chance to explore the local Rarámuri indigenous culture, Creel is a vibrant town and geological wonderland. Discover a variety of traditional handicrafts that reflect the rich heritage of the Rarámuri people at Artesanías Misión, and pick up some coveted artwork. Just 11 kilometers from Creel lies the renowned Valle de los Monjes (Valley of the Monks), named after its captivating rock formations resembling monks - but for more intriguing rock formations closer to town, the Valle de las Ranas and Valle de los Hongos showcase stones with uncanny resemblances to frogs and mushrooms. For relaxation seekers, the Recohuata Hot Springs, situated 22 kilometers from Creel in the Tararecua Canyon, offer a tranquil escape amidst picturesque natural surroundings. Nearby, Lake Arareko, just 10 kilometers from Creel, boasts a serene U-shaped body of water surrounded by pine trees and home to various wildlife. Visitors can enjoy picnics and even rowing on the lake.

name: Mineral del Monte
description: After the Conquistador subjugation of Mexico, geologists discovered valuable minerals, especially silver, in the area around Mineral del Monte. It is conservatively estimated that 6% of the world's silver mined since 1500AD originated here. Initially Ameraindian and African slaves were put to work but in later years problems with flooding and inefficiencies caused a steep decline in production. Then the Cornish arrived, bringing expert skills and equipment fresh from the British Industrial Revolution, revitalising the silver mining industry for the next century. Allow two hours for a tour of the informative Mine Acosta museum to learn more. Cornish influence is clearly visible - many older houses have sloping roofs and high chimneys, the beautiful church in the town square has one English style tower, and there's an elegant English cemetery (Panteon Inglés). Their lasting legacy however is the Cornish pasty, albeit a cocktail version with dozens of different flavours, and some producers have taken their products nationwide.

name: Giant's Causeway
description: As you approach the Giant's Causeway, a UNESCO World Heritage site, the sight of over 40,000 interlocking basalt columns rising from the sea is nothing short of mesmerizing. Each stone seems meticulously placed, creating a natural staircase leading into the ocean. The site's dramatic scenery, combined with the rhythmic crashing of the waves, offers a truly magical experience. According to Irish folklore, the Giant's Causeway was built by the legendary giant Finn McCool to cross the sea to Scotland. This myth adds a layer of enchantment to the already captivating landscape, making it a destination rich in both natural and cultural heritage. The surrounding area of the Causeway Coast boasts scenic walking trails, offering panoramic views of the rugged coastline and the sparkling Atlantic. Visitors can explore the cliffs, hidden coves, and lush green hills that frame this geological wonder. The state-of-the-art visitor center provides insightful exhibitions and guided tours, enriching your understanding of the site's geological significance and mythical stories.

name: Ait Benhaddou
description: Situated on a caravan trail, Ait Benhaddou was known as the 'door to the desert'. While the buildings only date back to the 17th century, the structures and construction techniques are identical to those used centuries earlier. The compact living quarters, narrow windows, and community spaces including a mosque, public square, fortification, and loft at the top of the village illustrate the traditional earthen constructions of communities around the Atlas Mountains. Inside some of the buildings you can see traditional artefacts, while others now serve as storefronts for hawkers. Opting for a guided tour is a good idea to better understand kasbah culture, and learn about the many movies that have been filmed here.

name: Salinas Grandes
description: Just like tango, the Andes, or carne asada, Salinas Grandes is one thing that defines Argentina. These salt flats are so big they stretch over both Salta and Jujuy provinces, with an overall area of over 80 square meters, its white desert about 200 miles wide. The Salinas are visited by thousands of tourists yearly because of its unreal scenery – the never ending, snow-like ground with turquoise pools, often separated from the clear blue sky by the colorful Andes, can easily make you feel you are visiting another planet. The area has two seasons – wet and dry; the latter will turn the ground into a giant mirror, since a layer of water sits on top of the flats. It will be a crime not to take tons of photos at this natural wonder and capture an adventure of a lifetime! There are a few things to consider before the visit. Salinas Grandes are located about 11 thousand feet above sea level, and altitude sickness can be challenging, so bring coca leaves and take it slow and easy once you get out of the car. Sunglasses and a wind jacket are also necessities since the sun can be blinding and the area – quite chilly. Although there are no admission fees or opening times, the Salinas do not have too many facilities but occasional portapotties and food and souvenir stalls. Lastly, the road to the flats is scenic, but take nausea pills just to be safe.

name: Messina
description: Founded by the ancient Greeks in the 8th century BC, Messina's had a rough history- it was butchered by ancient pirates, has been ravaged by multiple major earthquakes and tsunamis, and was devastated during World War II. However, the friendly inhabitants always bounced back. Today, visitors can enjoy the atmosphere at the city's piazza, which is dominated by the beautiful Cathedral - a restoration of the 12th century Norman church that was destroyed during World War II. The elegant belltower was likewise restored, and houses an astounding astronomical clock that comes to life everyday at noon. Visitors can admire the cathedral from the 16th century Orione fountain, and elegant creation by one of Michelangelo's students. At the Regional Museum, visitors will find some exceptional cultural and artistic treasures, including works by Caravaggio. Be sure to make time to enjoy some of the city's signature cuisine - they're renowned for their pastries and ice-cream, and of course, seafood, particularly swordfish.

name: Centro Ceremonial Otomi
description: While it may look like an archaeological site from another planet, the Centro Ceremonial Otomi was only built in the 1980s after Otomi elders sought to create a space where they could preserve and promote their culture. Built on a mountain known as the Cerro La Catedral, the complex is spread over several plazas, each with its own purpose and significance. The Plaza of the Colossus is named after a giant figure of Tahaay, the lord messenger of fire and life, which is followed by the Plaza del Sagitario. This main plaza, surrounded by 45 enormous sculptures, is home to the 7-columned Assembly Hall. At the apex are twelve silos, each representing a generation of Otomis. Just a year after its completion, the unique complex was featured prominently in the James Bond film "License to Kill", and has been attracting Bond fans ever since.

name: Sejong
description: The legacy of the fourth king of the Joseon Dynasty is deeply ingrained in the identity of Sejong. Seamlessly weaving together tradition, innovation, and serenity, this city will leave a lasting impression. The city proudly houses the Sejong National Library, a captivating and bustling hub for students and scholars adjacent to a gorgeous lake. As the leading smart city in Korea, Sejong embraces innovation, harmonizing it with breathtaking sights like cherry blossoms that captivate photographers and seekers of tranquility alike. The city is a haven of beauty with countless libraries, statues, landmarks, and parks, inviting exploration of its cultural richness. Cherry blossom paths add romance to the city, with the Jocheon, Buyong, and Reservoir Cherry Blossom paths offering an enchanting experience during the blooming season. For culinary enthusiasts, Sejong's diverse offerings include side dishes, dumplings, stews, and more, representing authentic Korean flavors amid the city's vibrant dining scene.

name: Burgas
description: Despite the area having been settled for 5000 years, modern Burgas only developed in the 19th century. Since then it's maintained its role as the country's main port, and one of the largest transport hubs. Because of this, most tourists just think of it as a transit point, forgetting that it's also a resort town in its own right. On the clean, pedestrianized streets, you'll find some charming buildings dating back to the 19th century, like the Archaeological Museum, where you can discover the area's ancient history. Of course, if you'd prefer to spend your time outdoors, you can always walk the huge Sea Gardens, take a stroll along the T-shaped pier, or hit the beach.

name: Milestones Museum
description: Opened in 2000 by the Duke of Edinburgh, the Milestones Museum preserves Hampshire's social, retail, and industrial heritage by bringing the Victorian era and the 1930s to life through streets, buildings, shops and vehicles. A wonderful collections of vehicles, toys, household appliances, and authentic room sets show how homes developed through the 20th century. As you explore the museum's streets, you can experience days gone by first hand as you buy a 2oz ration of sweets with your old penny, or site down at the local pub. A free audio guide completes the experience, with the audio commentary giving context to your adventures. Please note: the museum is closed on Mondays. For more information, please visit milestonesmuseum.org.uk

name: Kairouan
description: Founded in the 7th century by the Umayyadss, Kairouan quickly established itself as a premier center for Islamic learning. At its heart is the Great Mosque, the oldest in North Africa, which dates back to the founding of the city. This masterpiece of Islamic architecture was where the horseshoe arch was first used in the Islamic world, and its scholars helped it achieve a status comparable to that of the University of Paris in the Middle Ages. While not as large, Kairouan Mosque of the Three Doors presents the oldest surviving sculpted facade of Muslim art. The Barber's Mosque was built in the 17th century atop the tomb of one of the prophet Muhammed's companions, and is filled with vibrant tile decorations. While these landmarks are draws in themselves, the entire UNESCO-listed medina is an enchanting place to explore, where traditional houses and zaouias beckon to photographers and sightseers with their ornate doors and shuttered balconies.

name: Hail
description: Ha'il, the capital and largest city of Ha'il Province, is located in the northern part of Saudi Arabia. In ancient times, the city was a well-known stop on caravan routes, catering to pilgrims, and it still maintains a reputation for its friendly locals. Ha'il's landmarks include its three castles. The A'arif Fort, a 200-year-old mud castle perched on a hill, overlooks the city and offers a stunning viewpoint. The Barzan Palace, a grand 19th-century structure, is famous for its magnificence. Lastly, the third and youngest castle, the Qishlah Fortress, was constructed in the city center during the 1940s when Prince Abdul-Aziz bin Musa'ad Al Saud held office in Ha'il Province. Other attractions include the Al Rajhi Mosque, renowned for its lush interior. Nowadays, the city is an agricultural hub famous for the production of dates and other fruits, so make sure to stop by one of the local markets to savor some.

name: Redwood National Park, CA
description: Redwood National Park (and adjacent state parks), preserves one of America's most precious ecosystems. The famous California redwoods were nearly logged to extinction in the 1800s, with an estimated 90% of the original redwoods having been cut down. 45% of the remaining old-growth redwood forest is now preserved within this National Park. Reaching over 350-feet-tall and living for over 1,500 years, walking among the Coast Redwoods is an unforgettable California experience (and movie buffs will also enjoy knowing that Jurassic Park 2 was filmed among the living fossils in Fern Canyon). The ancient forest eventually peters out at the coast, where tectonic activity lifted up the very sea floor millions of years ago.

name: Coquimbo
description: Coquimbo, a coastal city in Chile's Elqui province, boasts a vibrant blend of history, culture, and natural beauty. With the Pacific Ocean tempering the climate, Coquimbo is a popular summer retreat, with mild temperatures throughout the year. The city boasts a long coastline with beautiful beaches, making it an ideal destination for sunbathing, swimming, and various water sports. La Herradura, Totoralillo, Las Tacas, Morrillos, Playa Blanca, Puerto Velero, and Tongoy are some of the popular beaches. A visit to Coquimbo's fish market is a must for seafood lovers. You can savor the freshest catch of the day, including a variety of fish and shellfish. Try local specialties like churrasco marinera, a fried fish sandwich served with pebre (a Chilean condiment). Take a stroll through the colorful Barrio Inglés neighborhood, adorned with painted murals that depict the history of the English and European settlers who once lived in Coquimbo. The pastel-painted wooden houses, many with balconies and unique figurines, add to the area's charm. Coquimbo, with its captivating blend of history, culture, and coastal beauty, invites exploration from coast to coast.

name: Montefrio
description: Originally a Moorish stronghold, with a strategic position and commanding views, Montefrio became one of the premier Moorish frontier fortresses in the 15th century. The citadel was even believed to have been designed by the same architect in charge of the magnificent Alhambra. However, by the end of the century it was recaptured by the Christians and destroyed. In its place, a church was erected, which, incorporates elements from Mudéjar, Gothic and Renaissance architecture. Please note: the castle is only open from 11:00-14:00, and closed on Mondays. Slightly down the hill is the Iglesia de la Encarnación, a unique neo-classical structure with a huge domed roof, compliments of the acclaimed architect Ventura Rodríguez. Just outside of town is the La Peña de los Gitanos, a 6-square-kilometer plot that contained over 100 dolmens, some dating back to 5000 BC, along with a post-Roman-ruin and Visigoth necropolis.

name: Hopetoun House
description: Completed in 1701, Hopetoun House's first occupant was a 16 year old Charles Hope. A few decades later, the house was greatly extended by William Adam, and its interiors completed by his sons John and Robert. Since the 19th century, the manor has been a stately Scottish fixture, serving as the site of King George IV's departure following his visit to Scotland, the knighting Captain Adam Ferguson and Henry Raeburn, and the home of the Duke of Sandringham in the BBC show 'Outlander'. Within the manor, visitors can admire some of the most grandiose interiors Scotland has to offer, with opulent gilding, classical motifs, and intricate carving and ceiling painting. The grand State apartments showcase the lavish lifestyles of the 18th century elite. Surrounding the manor is a 150 acre English-style landscape park where visitors visitors can enjoy a quiet walk, and maybe spy the resident deer. For more information, please visit hopetoun.co.uk

name: Sisi
description: Standing in sharp contrast to the bustling tourist hubs, Sissi is charming village where that has preserved its traditional way of life. The heart of the village is its port, which teems with fishing boats, and you'll likely find local fishermen at work while their wives clean the day's catch. Explore the narrow streets, adorned with colorful doors, before sitting down at one of the many renowned tavernas, which serve up some of the best seafood on the island. The village's sheltered location makes it an ideal base for exploring local beaches, such as the main Boufos Beach as well as smaller and more secluded spots like Avlaki, Kalimera Kriti and Limani being perfect for families with young children. In addition to its natural beauty, Sissi offers a range of hiking and biking trails, as well as excellent birdwatching opportunities, thanks to the many rare bird species that call the area home. For those who want to delve into the region's rich history, the Monastery of Agios Georgios and the Malian Palace Archaeological Site are just a short distance away.

name: Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park
description: Located just a short distance from the ocean, Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park showcases the unspoiled, primeval majesty of redwood trees. Visitors to Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park can immerse themselves in a range of outdoor activities. The pristine Smith River, California's longest free-flowing river, beckons with opportunities for fishing, snorkeling, and kayaking. Scenic drives along Howland Hill Road and campfire programs at Jedediah Smith Campground provide a taste of history and relaxation. Hikers can explore 20 miles of trails that wind through lush rainforests. The rich diversity of wildlife within the park includes black bears, deer, coyotes, bobcats, mountain lions, skunks, foxes, beavers, river otters, squirrels, and chipmunks. Bird enthusiasts can spot majestic creatures such as Bald Eagles, Spotted Owls, Pileated Woodpeckers, and Marbled Murrelets. Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park remains a sanctuary of nature's wonders, safeguarding the legacy of these ancient giants.

name: Lichtenstein Castle
description: This Neo-Gothic castle was built in 1840-1842 based on the novel 'Lichtenstein' by Wilhelm Hauff after the original castle built in 1200 was destroyed several times and eventually lapsed into ruin. The castle complex comprises other nineteenth-century buildings, a chapel, a large garden and the romantic courtyard. The bedchambers of the count reflect the opulent grandeur of the period when the castle was built while the well-preserved weapons and artifacts tell the castle's history as a hunting lodge. What the castle lacks in size, it more than makes up for with its superb views of the valley, dotted with long-extinct volcanoes that are now covered in lush greenery. This not so well known castle is the ideal location for those who fancy a spot of sight-seeing without the hordes of tourists that can sometimes be found at the more popular castles. There is also a castle restaurant for those in need of refreshment.

name: Gualaceo
description: Gualaceo existed as a pre-Incan settlement, but after the area was conquered by the Spanish, the original town was destroyed, and Gualaceo reduced to a mining camp. It took over 200 years for the population to grow enough that Gualaceo was even recognized as a parish, and it remains an off-the radar settlement to this day despite being one of the largest cities in the region. That is, unless you're looking for a traditional woven Ikat. Recognized for preserving the "Cultural Heritage of the Nation", artisans from the surrounding area produce traditional shawls the same way their ancestors did, and exhibit their wares in the bustling Sunday market, where local produce, food, and even traditional medicine can also be found. The rest of the week, a smaller number of vendors sell food and handicrafts in the pleasant man square across the street from the charming church, and the riverside park is a pleasant place to stroll.

name: Albarracin
description: Once the capital of a Moorish kingdom, Albarracín was a self-governing mini-state between 1167 and 1300 when it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Aragon and fell into obscurity. Today, the town looks like it's been lost in time, and is still surrounded by its medieval fortified walls. The oldest section was built in the 10th century by the Moors, while the newest are from the Reconquest. Albarracín's precipitous position make for some steep streets, but it's worth the legwork to explore the narrow alleys on the way to the Plaza Mayor. Here, you can enjoy stupendous views of the river valley below from the Town Hall. The 16th century El Salvador Cathedral is connected to the old Episcopal Palace, which now houses the Diocese Museum, where you can admire a valuable collection of flamenco tapestries.

name: Archaeological park Stobi
description: Stobi was founded as an ancient Paeonian settlement before being conquered by Philip V around 217 BC. Under the Romans, Stobi grew to become the provincial capital, and was even visited by Emperor Theodosius I in 388. The city's decline began when it was sacked by the Ostrogoth King Theodoric in 479, a powerful earthquake in 518, and finally the Avaro-Slavic invasions in the 6th century. Today, Stobi is the largest archaeological site in Macedonia - 25 ruins have been unearthed, and it's still slowly being excavated by archaeologists. The first and largest ruin you see is the 1st century theater, with a 4th-century Episcopal Basilica nearby. Believed to be the first church in Macedonia, you can still see beautifully preserved mosaics and early Christian frescoes. Other highlights include the Theodisian Palace and House of Psalms, which both sport stupendous mosaic floors, Roman House with its 1st century frescoes.

name: Brighton
description: Settled since the Bronze Age, the Brighton of today was born from the 18th century hydrotherapy fad. As a growing number of visitors flocked to the town to bathe and drink its seawater, Brighton recreated itself as a resort town. After the Prince of Wales built a palace here, and railway access put the city in easy reach of London, Brighton underwent an explosion of development. Built in an Indo-Arabic style, the Prince's 18th century Royal Pavilion is one of the most amazing buildings in the country, and its interior is an unbridled display of extravagance from the peak of the British Empire. The town's famous pier, built in 1899, is a 2.5 acre carnival, combining fun, games, and history. For many Londoners, the main draw is the waterfront, where you can relax on the colorful pebble beach, take a spin on the ferris wheel, or ride the oldest operational electric railway in the world. If all the fun has you feeling peckish, fear not - Brighton has one of the most vibrant food scenes in the country!

name: Eltham Palace
description: Given to King Edward II in 1305, Eltham Palace would serve as a royal residence until the 17th century when it was destroyed during the English Civil War. In the 1930s, Stephen Courtauld purchased the estate, and built one of the world's finest Art Deco homes on the site. Visitors can experience the glamorous decor that once entertain socialites and politicians, nobles and artists in what was the cutting edge of Swedish design. Even the bathrooms of this refined home are breathtaking, with one rendered in glittering gold. Courtauld also had the original great hall restored, preserving the intricate woodwork of the country's 3rd largest hammer-beam roof. In the palace's 19 acre grounds, visitors are treated to the Rock Garden, with its series of pools and cascades running down to the moat, which is crossed by London's oldest working bridge. The sunken rose garden preserves Virginia Courtauld's passion for roses.

name: Lindos
description: At the heart of Lindos lies the magnificent Acropolis, a hilltop citadel dating back to antiquity. Here, visitors can wander among the ancient ruins, including the Temple of Athena Lindia, and marvel at panoramic views of the surrounding turquoise waters and rugged coastline. The Acropolis is a testament to Lindos' rich history and is a must-visit for history enthusiasts and photography enthusiasts alike. In addition to its archaeological wonders, Lindos boasts a labyrinth of narrow cobblestone streets lined with traditional tavernas, boutique shops, and quaint cafes. Visitors can meander through the town's charming alleyways, admiring the whitewashed houses adorned with colorful bougainvillea and bougainvillea. Don't miss the opportunity to explore the historic Captain's Houses, elegant mansions dating back to the island's maritime heyday.

name: Chignahuapan
description: Designated by the Mexican government as a magical town to bring investment to facilitate an excellent tourist experience, Chignahuapan comes closest as a magical town in its definition. Located in the depths of the jungle, the morning mist unveils a picturesque town with slopes on the side, fruit trees surrounding the limits, coffee plantations, waterfalls, and a lagoon. You can marvel at the sheer beauty of the town's surroundings, or take a walk to marvel at the facades, or chow down on some local grub at the kiosks in the centre. To add to the magic, you can find thermal baths that are said to employ healing properties.

name: Corvin castle
description: Built by John Hunyadi, regent of the Kingdom of Hungary, in the 15th century to replace an older keep, the castle had 3 main sections surrounded by towers. It's said the prison tower also had a bear pit to dispose of any unnecessary prisoners. Following his death, the castle quickly declined, and wasn't restored until the 17th century. Taking some artistic liberties, the castle was restored to reflect what the 'ideal' Gothic castle, making for a more fanciful facade. Today, visitors can enjoy the well preserved architectural details, the sumptuous Knights' Hall, inner courtyards, and rooms filled with medieval art and artefacts. There's also a separate torture museum for those who want to learn about the many possible ways Vlad the Impaler could have been driven made while he was supposedly imprisoned here.

name: Cane Garden Bay
description: Cane Garden Bay presents a plethora of opportunities for relaxation and exploration, where visitors can bask in the warm Caribbean sun, take leisurely strolls along the shore, or partake in thrilling water sports such as snorkeling, paddleboarding, and sailing. Dive beneath the surface to discover an underwater wonderland teeming with colorful marine life, or simply unwind on the shore and enjoy the rhythmic melody of the waves. As the day unfolds into evening, Cane Garden Bay transforms into a lively hub of activity, with beachside bars and restaurants offering tantalizing cuisine and refreshing tropical cocktails. Live music fills the air, creating a festive ambiance perfect for mingling with locals and fellow travelers alike, or simply soaking in the vibrant energy of this coastal paradise.

name: Hidalgo del Parral
description: Parral is known for its prosperous silver mining history, home to one of the world's longest continuously operating mines spanning a remarkable 345 years. Take a visit to the tourist office to receive information about exploring the mine and ascending the mirador (lookout) for panoramic views of the town's surroundings. Visit El Palacio de Alvarado, a splendid mansion once owned by one of the town's most influential families. This family's fortune, derived from the La Palmilla silver mine, was so substantial that they once offered to pay off the nation's external debt. Today, this palace serves as a museum and cultural center, retaining much of its original European-made furnishings. Parral also hosts the Francisco Villa Museum, housed in a historic building close to the site where Villa was assassinated in 1923. Every July, the town commemorates this event with a reenactment. Casa Stallforth, once a luxurious palace, showcases exquisite baroque architecture and is adorned with Nordic mythology figures.

name: Las Piedrotas
description: While many say the huge stones of Las Piedrotas were left exposed by centuries of erosion, some locals argue they are meteorites - for how else could such a strange landscape form? The stones' extraterrestrial origin is also the basis for the belief that a reinvigorating energy envelopes the site. Regardless of their origins and paranormal powers, the behemoth boulders surrounded by cow pastures provide a beautiful place for a stroll, with some boulders bearing carvings made by prehispanic tribes. For the more nimble, they've become a destination for rock scrambling. The largest of the two formations are even connected by a zipline, which offers a dose of adrenaline for a mere M$150.

name: Krka National Park
description: Situated along the Krka River in Central Dalmatia, Krka National Park's lakes and waterfalls make it the ideal spot for swimming and exploring nature. More than half of the Krka River is part of the national park, which includes the majority of the river lakes and two waterfall systems - Roski Slap and Skradinski Buk. There are over 222 bird species and 17 fish species to spot in the area. Along with its abundant wildlife, Krka also houses an ethnographic museum, the Visovac Monastery, and many caves and ruins. The nature trails and wooden bridges make it easy to navigate the park while enjoying the nature scenery.

name: DRUPA Interactive Chocolate Museum
description: Starting with the trees of their organic cocoa farm, the DRUPA Interactive Chocolate Museum takes visitors through the history and production of Mexico's most influential export. Though audio-visual presentations and displays of real production equipment, visitors to the museum will learn about each stage of the chocolate-making process in an immersive, multi-sensory experience - you'll even be able to taste a cocoa drink made from the beans. Afterwards, you can get your hands on the finished choco-product in the chocolaterie, or enjoy a more substantial lunch before indulging your sweet-tooth. Entry costs 275 pesos per person.

name: Manizales
description: Established in 1849 by settlers from Neira and Salamina, Manizales lost most of its historic sights when it was ravaged by two major earthquakes and a fire. But as one of the main hubs of Colombia's Coffee Triangle, coffee is of course the main attraction. The best place to look for some local brew is on Carrera 23, which is lined with shops, restaurants, cafes, and squares. The cathedral, while relatively modern, is well worth a visit for its list of accolades - it's the tallest in Colombia, is one of only two churches in Colombia with a canopy, and offers the opportunity to climb to the top of its tower on a guided tour. Situated at over 2,000 meters, Manizales has some great views, and none beat the El Chipre Viewpoint. The 360 skywalk will get your heart pumping even more than the strong coffee.

name: Quillabamba
description: Located in the higher jungle area of the province of Cusco, this small town sleeps in the clouds. This jungle town runs on agriculture, specifically coffee, cacao, tea, and coco. The Urumba river flows through Quillabamba providing a source of gold and other earth minerals. Do as the locals do and head to the Plaza de Armas to relax in the sun and enjoy the sleepy culture of this agricultural town.

name: Bejaia
description: Bejaia was founded on the ancient Carthaginian port of Saldae, and thanks to its Mediterranean climate, has remained a busy market town is famous for its olive oil and wine for over 2,000 years. Watched over by the soaring Yemma Gouraya mountain, which was once the burial place of the patron saint of the city. Take a stroll through the old town, Bordj Moussa, browsing the shops offering olive oil, wine, and traditional Kabylian crafts before heading to the famous for Spanish fort. Built in the 16th century, this historic bastion now serves as a museum exhibiting Roman and Hafsid era artifacts, as well as a collection of birds and insects from all over Africa, and paintings by Maurice Boitel, on loan from the museum of Algiers. If you're lucky enough to be visiting in July, the city becomes even more lively with the Djoua Festival where traditional meals, concerts, crafts shops and many other activities showcasing the city's culture

name: Bustamante
description: Just north of Monterrey, Bustamante has been termed a "Pueblo Magico" for its undeniably magical qualities. The most alluring attraction of the town is the "Cañón Ojo de Agua Bustamante", or "Eye of Water". This natural spring features crystal clear water, tinged a brilliant blue from the minerals it contains. Enter for around 250 pesos and enjoy a barbeque at one of the facilities. Bustamante is also home to Ojo de Agua El Mezcalito, a stunning blue lagoon, and Cascada El Salto, a gorgeous waterfall. Stick around in the main town for one of the biggest events, Fiesta Patronal, on 12 December. The streets fill with music, dancing, colorful decorations, traditional food stalls and carnival games. Bustamante is also home to the International Festival of Balloons and Kites in August, bringing hot air balloon rides, kite-flying competitions, live music and more to the festive town. You'll have no problem finding bakeries on every corner selling the famous Bustamante bread to nibble on while you enjoy the relaxed atmosphere.

name: Lawas
description: Lawas exudes a sense of tranquility and peace, offering a pleasant stopover for travelers in Sarawak. It serves as a gateway to the highlands of Ba'Kelalan, renowned for its ecotourism opportunities, and is also home to fishing villages such as Punang and Awat Awat, where visitors can experience the authentic coastal lifestyle. The heart of Lawas lies along the Lawas River, which attracts visitors from Brunei during weekends, and the Medan Niaga Lawas, an open-air market. Visit the bustling hub where locals gather to purchase fresh produce, traditional handicrafts, local delicacies, and live poultry on Saturdays. Lawas invites travelers to experience its serene beauty, embrace ecotourism adventures, and discover the hidden gems that make this frontier town a distinctive destination in Sarawak.

name: Nyungwe National Park
description: South west of Rwanda, the Nyungwe National Park sprawls across an elevated ridge that divides the Nile and the Congo in an impressive display of bamboo, swamps, rainforest, grassland and bogs. Spend your visit to the park atop the Canopy Walkway, suspended over a steep wooded valley. A small stream gently flows below as groups of the amusing Ruwenzori colobus, with white bushy tufts emerging from their cheeks, clamor through leafy overhangs. The easily photographable primates are one among 85 species of mammal, along with 310 birds, 32 amphibians and 38 reptiles - most of which are endemic to the area. Surround yourself in pure nature, walk up to the gushing Isumo waterfall and pass picnic sites in East Africa's largest tract of montane rainforest.

name: Medjugorje
description: The village of Medjugorje is located in the southern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, close to the Croatian border. The small parish is made up of five villages, where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared to six people in 1981. Apparition Hill, a religious mecca, is the site where the first apparitions of the Virgin Mary were documented. The rocky path up to high hill gives way to a serene statue of Our Lady and a cross. It's a place where many come to reflect and pray. Visitors also gather at St. James Church for daily mass. Medjugorje is visited by million of pilgrims each year who hope to find inner peace and strength through reflection and prayer.

name: Hakone
description: For those seeking a break from Tokyo, Hakone is one of the most popular destinations of choice for tourists and locals alike. Explore the Hakone Kuzuryu Forest, a nature park lining the eastern waterfront of Lake Ashi, or take a trip to Hakone Gora Park for beautiful spring and fall-time colors. Take a dip in an Onsen, a traditional Japanese hot spring, and relax before or after your trip to Owakudani where Mount Fuji is in full view.. The Hakone Shrine and Heiwa no Torii along the shore of Lake Ashi dates back to the year 757, having since been relocated to its current location in 1667, and is an ideal destination for reflection and taking in history. Visit the Hakone Open Air Museum with its brilliant Picasso collection and the "Woods of Net", full of colorful hand-knit nets that will entrance children and adults alike.

name: Lake Neusiedl
description: Covering 315 km2, Lake Neusiedl is the largest lake in Central Europe that doesn't feed into the ocean. With a maximum depth of only 1.5 meters, the lake waters warm quickly in the summer, making it a godsend for beach-starved Austrians who flock to Neusiedl for boating and windsurfing. While the eastern shore offers the best beaches, the thick reeds on the western shore are home to nearly 300 species of bird, attracting birdwatchers from around the country. The reeds are encircled by a flat cycling track, making them a destination for pedal-heads as well. It's also worth stopping in one of the lake towns to sample the local wines produced in the surrounding vineyards.

name: Jaen
description: Beginning as a center for Arab caravans, the city was an important as a stronghold during the Reconquest. Today, it has returned to its trade-roots as the "Olive Oil Capital of the World". High above the city, the Moorish Citadel still stands, and offers visitors stupendous views of the city and Guadalquivir valley. At the heart of the city, the 16th century Santa Iglesia Cathedral dominates the whitewashed houses. Housed within its monumental Renaissance facade with a Gothic frieze is the Holy Veil, which according to tradition was used by Saint Veronica to wash Christ's face. The entire interior is a work of art, with the sacristy, the chapter room, the choir, and the main chapel being particularly impressive. As the city is famous for its olive oil, it would be a shame not to sample some, along with the local gastronomy, and there are plenty of options around the cathedral.

name: Groznjan
description: Groznjan is a small Croatian town where there is inspiration around every corner and the majority of its occupants are Italian. This truly creative town is infused with art galleries, summer music academies, dance and drama workshops, and humble peace activists. Throughout the summer there a multitude of music festivals with a jungle full of classical and jazz instruments in every hand. Simply by walking through the old town you will find a number of exhibitions, wine tastings, and a zest for life. Come visit this town in the heart of Istria, just a few kilometers away from the sea and soak in all of Groznjan's culture.

name: Senj
description: Senj is a pre-historic town with a background of over three thousand years, watching the fall and rise of countless empires. Although conquered by many, much of the Romans influence still stands today. The Romans left behind an aqueduct and many temples dedicated to their Gods and Goddess. Senj's most famous feature and symbol is the Nehaj Fortress. Built over the remains of churches and houses that lingered outside of the city walls in 1558, the Nehaj Fortress has survived centuries of war. Today it is a museum, housing weapons and clothing of the time, but its most notable component is a toilet dangling over the edge!

name: Pembroke
description: Situated in the Northern Region of Malta, Pembroke has evolved into an attractive and verdant residential town, adorned with historic significance and a stunning coastline. Its buildings date back to the Knights of the Order of St John and the British era, with two watchtowers erected by the Knights still proudly standing guard on the picturesque Pembroke coast. A military base encompassing fortifications and barracks was built between 1859 and 1899. Exploring the town, admire the Clockwise of Pembroke built in 1903, which stands as a well-known symbol of the town. The Pembroke Ranges continue to serve as training facilities for the Armed Forces of Malta, making the town a must-see destination of military and history buffs. The remarkable Harq Hamiem cave features unique geological formations and a deep freshwater lake for outdoor enthusiasts. With its blend of history, natural beauty and proximity to Malta's nightlife hub, Paceville, Valletta offers visitors a captivating experience in the Northern Region of the island.

name: Beja
description: Inhabited since the Bronze Age, Beja became the region's capital under Roman rule in the 1st century. Rising sharply out of the fertile plains, the town is crowned with a 14th century castle, which was built on the site of a Roman fort. While the castle is mostly ruins, visitors can still scale its 36 meter keep for fantastic views of the village below. Huddled against the castle walls is the 4th century church of Santo Amaro. One of the few remaining Visigothic churches in the country, it houses one of the premier collections of Visigothic artefacts. The former Convent of Our Lady of the Conception, a late-Gothic structure with Manueline and Moorish elements now houses the Museum of Queen Eleanor. Here visitors can marvel at both the ecclisiastic elements, and an important collection of Flemish, Spanish and Portuguese paintings from the 15th to the 18th centuries.

name: Al Lith
description: Al Lith, a captivating city on the shores of the Red Sea, lies to the southwest of the revered Mecca. The Jabal Al-Lith island near the mainland emerges as a beacon of natural beauty and allure, fast gaining recognition among both local Saudis and international visitors drawn by the charms of the Red Sea. This island boasts a diverse landscape of sandy shores and elevated mountains, surrounded by scattered mangroves. Optimal visiting months between March and June coincide with the congregation of whale sharks along the coast. A short boat ride of around 35 minutes from the mainland transports visitors to this haven. With charming white sandy beaches and breathtaking sunsets, Jabal Al-Lith Island offers an ideal tropical escape.

name: Ashdod
description: First mentioned in the 17th century BC, Ashdod has been destroyed and rebuilt countless times over the centuries as it passed from the Philistines, Israelites, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Crusaders, and Ottoman Turks. The modern city was founded in 1956 near the site of the ancient settlement, eventually encompassing it and a neighboring ancient village. Little remains of the ancient city, but head up to Jonah's Hill and you'll get a taste of its ancient importance - it's said that the Biblical Jonah was buried as evidenced by a now-destroyed tomb. The Corinne Mamane Museum of Philistine Culture exhibits artefacts uncovered here that showcase when Ashdod was one of the five main Philistine cities. The other main draw is Ashdod's beach, which is nearly the size of Tel Aviv's but only sees 1/10th the number of visitors and is watched over by a ruined ancient fortress.

name: Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal Park
address.city: Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal Park
description: Studley Royal Park is centered around the 12th century Fountains Abbey, which was one of the largest and wealthiest monasteries in England by the time of its dissolution in 1539. Over the centuries other noble buildings were added to the perfectly sculpted landscape, such as the Jacobean Fountains Hall, and masterful neo-Gothic St Mary's church. Today, visitors can walk through the remains of the massive abbey while learning about life as a monk with the free audio guide, before exploring the water gardens and deer park, and admiring the 10 other historic buildings scattered throughout the 800 acre estate. For more information, please visit https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/fountains-abbey-and-studley-royal-water-garden

name: Conca dei Marini
description: The ancient village of Conca dei Marini could date from as far back as the 8th century BC. For the next 2000 years, it would serve as a port and trading base, finally transitioning into a fishing village and holiday destination. Less-known than many other towns on the Amalfi Coast, Conca dei Marini has maintained its laid-back character and sleepy atmosphere. Stretched out along a small bay, the village is all white houses and villas and terraced gardens tumbling down the cliff to the sea. There's still some bastions of history as well, like the 16th century defensive tower and 14th century Convent of St Rosa (the birthplace of sfogliatella). Just outside of town is the town's most famous attraction: the Grotta dello Smeraldo. This partially submerged karst cave boasts some beautiful formations and water in a magical emerald green (and an underwater nativity scene!).

name: Cananea
description: Discover Cananea, where the echoes of mining history resonate through the picturesque landscape. Long before the city's establishment, indigenous Pima and Opata peoples called this region home. It was the arrival of Spanish explorers and Jesuit missionaries in the 1760s that transformed the area into a thriving mining hub. Cananea's story is deeply intertwined with copper, earning it the title "City of Copper." Here, you'll find one of the world's largest open-pit copper mines, a testament to centuries of mineral extraction. Take a mine tour, visit the Greene mansion, stroll through the historic downtown district, or enjoy the natural beauty of Cananea Nature Park and Reserve on your visit to this enchanting city.

name: Malacca
description: Malacca was founded around 1400 by Iskandar Shah, the last Raja of present day Singapore. Because of its strategic position and exceptional facilities, Malacca quickly became one of the most important ports in the region, though this period of prosperity ended in 1511 when the city was conquered by the Portuguese. This change in leadership threw the region into turmoil, and though the city would come under Dutch and British rule in the following centuries, it never reached the same level of importance. This slowdown ended up being a cultural boon for the city, as 500 years of multicultural history have been preserved. The heart of the city is the 'Red Square', a series of 17th century Dutch buildings that are believed to be the oldest of their kind in the east. Visitors will also find the remains of a 16th century Portuguese fort, and a wide variety of cultural monuments, from a floating Mosque, to temples from several different religions on Harmony Street.

name: Portsmouth, NH
description: When it was first settled in 1630, Portsmouth was originally named Strawbery Banke for the abundant wild strawberries that grew in the area. It quickly became a successful shipbuilding town, and in more recent years, one of New England's best getaways. The Colonial, Georgian and Federal style buildings are downright enchanting, especially since many are now home to cute cafes and shops. If you have any interest in history and architecture, don't miss the Strawbery Banke Museum. Explore 32 antique buildings in New Hampshire's oldest neighborhood while guides in period dress share how the early settlers lived. If you can't get enough house museums, stop by the grand Georgian mansion that once belonged to Governor John Langdon. For some maritime history, step aboard the USS Albacore, the prototype for modern US submarines, or tour the Portsmouth Harbor Lighthouse.

name: Grazalema
description: The immaculately-kept cobbled streets of Grazalema are lined with whitewashed houses set amongst a backdrop of stunning mountains, with the village being dominated by the magnificent rocky outcrop known as Peñon Grande. In the heart of the Sierra de Grazalema Natural Park, this well-preserved and restored village was once the recipient of the National Tourism Award for the Beautification and Improvement of Spanish Towns, and its historic quarter has the Property of Cultural Interest designation. In addition to it scenic beauty, Grazalema has much to offer, including a wide range of attractions for rural and nature tourism; traditional crafts, including a Traditional Textile Museum; the 18th-century Nuestra Señora de la Aurora Church, in Baroque style; and the Encaminación Parish from the 17th-19th centuries. Whether your goal is a relaxing stroll, a lesson on Spanish culture and history, or the perfect photo opportunity, Grazalema makes for the perfect destination.

name: Bletchley Park
address.addr1: The Mansion, Bletchley Park, Sherwood Dr, Bletchley, Milton Keynes MK3 6EB, UK
description: During World War II, Bletchley Park was home to the Government Code and Cypher School (GC&CS), the top-secret organization responsible for cracking the Enigma and even more complicated Lorenz cipher thanks to great minds like Alan Turing. Today, the "Ultra" intelligence base of operations is open to the public as a museum to show how thousands of dedicated thinkers shortened the war by years. A collection of several buildings, including a beautiful brick mansion, Bletchley Park's exhibits showcase a collection of mind-boggling cipher machines like the Enigma and Lorenz, as well as the technology used to crack them, like the famous Bombe, as well as the groundbreaking Colossus. Alongside these are the stories of the Allied codebreakers, the codebreaking process, and Bletchley's effects on the War. For more information, please visit bletchleypark.org.uk

name: Fredrikstad
description: Fredrikstad was founded in 1567 as a replacement for the town of Sarpsborg, 15km further up the Glomma river, after it was razed to the ground by the Swedish Army. This former industrial town is famed for the warmth of it's welcome, as well as being one of the sunniest places in Norway. The heavily fortified old town section, The Gamlebyen, built according to Dutch architectural techniques, contains high earthen ramparts and wide water-filled moats situated in a star-shape to better maximise firing coverage for cannons. The Gamlebyen is probably Northern Europe's best preserved fortified town, and forms the beating heart of Fredrikstad. Although you can still locate the odd cannon here and there, it is now a haven for shopping, cafe culture, and markets year round. Art galleries and museums are plentiful here, and the walls old fortifications nowadays makes for a relaxing stroll, and maybe a picnic.

name: Paradise Cave
description: Only discovered in 2005, Paradise Cave was given its befitting name by the British spelunkers who first plumbed its 31 km passageway, and emerged gobstruck by spectacular stalactites and stalagmites within. To reach the cave, visitors can opt for a rather long hike through the jungle, or pay for an electric buggy ride right to the entrance. The main tour brings visitors 1 kilometer into the cave, where stairs and paths bring you through chambers that can reach up to to 72 m in height. When the light falls on the formations like the Galaxy Waterfall and the Moon Rabbit, it's easy to see why the first explorers were so smitten with the cave.

name: Erbalunga
description: Erbalunga sits on the tiny peninsula of Cap Corse, jutting out onto the turquoise water of the Tyrrhenian Sea. Connected by steep roads and lush maquis, the village's stone-walled houses are built directly on the harbor, with balconies often dropping right over the water's edge. It has a rich history, with the geographer Ptolemy calling it the "sacred promontory" before it became a major exporter of wine and olive oil in the 11th century. During the 1930's, artists began flocking to Erbalunga, allured by its beautiful landscape and fishing boats poised in the harbor. In the streets of the old town, explore a tree-lined square with townhouses and cafes, and in the peripheral streets, ancient stone houses and small cottages. Explore the ruins of a Genoese tower at the tips of the peninsula or stop to admire the Church of St Erasmus, patron saint of sailors.

name: Armenia
description: Armenia was originally founded in 1889 as "Villa Holguín", but changed its name in the early 20th century in solidarity with the Armenian genocide victims. The Armenia rapidly expanded as one of the country's main coffee producers, but a major earthquake in 1999 destroyed much of the city, and it never quite recovered. While that means there are no historic monuments to seek out, the friendly, laid-back locals and village-like atmosphere make hunting for the perfect cafe a pleasant experience in itself (hint: they're all good). For a bit of local history, it's well worth visiting the Museo del Oro Quimbaya to see the work of pre-Columbian goldsmiths, as well as ceramics and ceremonial items. At the Quindio Botanical Gardens, you can immerse yourself in the lush ecology of the Coffee Triangle and learn about the background and use of native species on a guided tour of the lush jungle.

name: Rocamadour
description: In 1166, a perfectly preserved body was found in a nook in a cliff. Locals declared that it must be the remains of Saint Zacchaeus, the tax collector who was hugged by Jesus 1100 years earlier. The site became a place of pilgrimage with a large religious complex springing up on the cliff, and the town growing below as more pilgrims came. Sitting atop a 150 meter cliff, the castle ramparts offer visitors stupendous views of the valley below. The Basilica of Saint-Sauveur and the crypt Saint-Amadour, where visitors will find medieval frescoes and beautiful stained glass, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites on the way to Santiago de Compostela. However, the jewel of the sanctuary is the 9th century Black Virgin, housed in one of the 7 chapels built in the hollow of the rock.

name: Tredegar House
description: Tredegar House began as a grand stone building in the 15th century that hosted the likes of King Charles I. 200 years later, William Morgan, a relative of the infamous Captain Morgan, had Tredegar rebuilt as an even grander red brick country house - a rare construction material at the time. Today, Tredegar offers visitors a barrier-free look into the lives of one of Wales' grandest families. Here, visitors can marvel at the rich 17th century rooms, which are crowned by the stupendous Gilt Room, which is glistening in gold. In the 1930s bedrooms, visitors will learn about the eccentric Evan Morgan, who kept a boxing kangaroo and foul-mouthed parrot. Down stair, the kitchens and servant's quarters give a look at what it took to keep the house running. Outside, visitors can enjoy a pleasant walk through the manor's distinctive gardens, or stroll into the park to sit by the lake. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/tredegar-house

name: Umag
description: Known to tennis fans as a stop on the ATP world tour, Umag is a town with a history unlike any other. After its sister settlement was destroyed by pirates in the 9th century, Umag grew in importance and over the years was ruled by the Byzantines, the Venetians, the French, the Austrians, and Italians. Visitors can sip wine while soaking in unhindered views of the Adriatic, before diving into back into the towns history. Start downtown with the iconic Church of the Assumption of St. Mary, with its iconic unfinished façade, at low-tide you can see the remnants of Sipar, the town destroyed by pirates, or take a short trip to the ancient Roman Villa Tiola.

name: Cenote Miguel Colorado
description: Surrounded by a private nature reserve, the Cenote Miguel Colorado is the focal point of an eco-activity center. The deep green water is surrounded by 80-foot-high cliffs, which provide an exciting starting point for a zip-line across the sinkhole. Visitors can also paddle around in a kayak, or just swim in the cool waters. There's a slew of optional activities as well, such as hiking trails, a bat cave, and a crocodile-filled lake that can be enjoyed for an additional fee.

name: Ayolas
description: The quiet fishing village of Ayolas rests on the banks of the Parana River and offers visitors an opportunity to relax on its public beaches or take a dip in the pristine waters. Stop by the Atinguy Wildlife Refuge which is dedicated to wildlife conservation. Afterwards, take a tour of the Yacyretá Dam to learn about its environmental efforts and impact (don't miss a chance to see the fish elevator!). To learn more about the town's history, visit the Historical and Environmental Museum of Yacyreta (Museo Histórico Ambiental). Make sure to double-check the opening hours and available tours to ensure you get the most out of the Dam and museum. Yacyretá Dam: Tours for purchase on Monday to Sunday in three shifts: 8:30 AM, 10:00 AM, and 2:00 PM. This circuit lasts approximately 90 minutes. Historical and Environmental Museum Hours: Monday to Sunday, 7:00 AM to 3:30 PM.

name: Palencia
description: Settled since pre-Roman times, the city of Palencia was relatively unimportant for centuries. It wasn't until Christianity returned to the city in the 10th century that it began to thrive, eventually becoming a royal residence and home to Spain's first University. Today, the city is home to one of the greatest concentrations of Romanesque architecture in Europe, rewarding visitors for simply walking through its historic streets. However, the city's main site has to be the Gothic Cathedral, lovingly referred to as the 'unknown beauty'. Spanning the entirety of the Gothic movement, visitors can delight in the many reliefs that fill the church, the plateresque reredos, and the retablo by Queen Isabella of Castile's court painter. The church museum contains works by painters such as El Greco and Zurbaran.

name: Dinan
description: In the 9th century, monks settled on the banks of the Rance river, and 200 years later, the town of Dinan developed around their priory. In the 13th century, Dinan became a ducal town, which greatly benefited its development and surrounded it with the 3 kilometres of ramparts that still survive today. The town, having survived World War II unscathed still looks much as it did in the Middle Ages. The pretty cobbled streets, home to over 100 half-timbered houses, along with sturdy stone structures are an attraction in themselves where visitors can lose themselves in history. The town's 12th century Basilica of St. Saviour was never completed as planned, but still manages to exhibit a unique combination of Byzantine, Persian, and Romanesque influences. While walking the medieval ramparts gives a great view of the town and countryside, from April to September, the 15th century Clock Tower provides an even better vantage.

name: Kohunlich
description: Kohunlich was first settled around 200 BC and abandoned by the 14th century. Though the site's original name has been lost in time, it's believed that it was an important stopping point on the southern trade routes. Today, the site is over 20 acres of dense jungle dotted with captivating ruins. Right at the entrance, visitors are greeted by the noble's residential area and the monumental acropolis. Heading further into the jungle, you'll be treated to more temple ruins and the calls of howler monkeys until you arrive at the most impressive monument: the Temple of the Masks. Built between the 4th and 7th centuries, the main stairway of this 10-meter-tall pyramid is flanked with intricate masks of the Sun God Kin'ich Ahau, each larger than a man! Located slightly away from the main sites, a walk through the jungle will bring you to the elite residential area, where palaces and high-ranking tombs were built atop a platform.

name: Agios Nikolaos
description: Agios Nikolaos (or "Ag Nik" as the visiting Brits like to call it) is an ancient town where you'll find a little bit of everything. At its heart is Lake Voulismeni, where the goddesses Athena and Artemis are said to have bathed. Today, this little harbor is lined with colorful houses, bars, and restaurants, and is perfect for strolling or taking in the view. Also right on the lake is the The Folk Art Museum of Agios Nikolaos, where you can see traditional furniture, handmade textiles, and pottery. If you'd prefer to dive deeper into the area's history, head to the archaeological museum, which exhibits artifacts from the region, including the gold-wreathed skull of an ancient athlete. Then there are the many works of street art, historic churches, and pleasant beaches, which can easily fill a day of exploration.

name: Orebro
description: In the heart of Sweden, between Stockholm and Gothenburg, Örebro is one of the most scenic cities in Sweden. The majestic Örebro Castle dates back to the 14th century and serves as a museum and cultural center, where visitors can explore medieval architecture while looking over the city. The Wadköping Open Air Museum showcases traditional Swedish buildings from the 18th and 19th century, with craft workshops and charming traditional handicrafts to take home. The city is surrounded by beautiful nature and outdoor recreation opportunities, with nature reserves, pristine parks and stunning lakes for hiking, biking and fishing, including the popular Nature Reserve of Kilsbergen. Örebro is known for its thriving arts and music scene, where there'll never be a dull moment or empty street - the Live at Heart music festival attracts thousands of visitors from all over the world in September and events always spill onto the sidewalks.

name: Burgos
description: When King Alfonso III the Great of León reconquered the region in the 9th century, he built several castles and the region came to be known as Castile, the "land of castles". In 884, Diego Rodríguez "Porcelos", count of Castile, gathered the inhabitants of the countryside into one fortified village - Burgos. Construction on Our Lady of Burgos, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, began in the 13th century, and took over 200 years to complete. As such, the entire history of Gothic art is summed up in its superb architecture and its unique collection of works of art, including paintings, choir stalls, reredos, tombs and stained-glass windows. While the gothic cathedral is the most prominent, the streets are littered many other religious monuments, such as Cartuja de Miraflores with its gold altarpiece, or the Monastery of Las Huelgas. And don't miss out on the restaurants dishing out Burgos' exquisite cuisine.

name: Chain Bridge Honey Farm
description: The Chain Bridge Honey Farm was started by beekeeping advisor William Selby Robson in 1948. The Robsons gradually expanded the honey farm, and now have 2000 hives to produce everything bee-related, from honey to soap. At the visitor center you can learn about bees and their behavior, as well as the many products of the beehive including honey, wax and propolis. There's even an observation hive where you can watch a live colony of bees behind glass. All of the exhibit information is hand written by expert calligrapher Dorien Irving, while the walls of the are adorned with intricate murals by artist Tony Johnson, which give the visitor center a very friendly and personal atmosphere. Also on the farm is Stephen Robson's collection of vintage vehicles, which includes rare Lanz Bulldog tractors and a gentleman's caravan. A double-decker bus even serves as a cafe where you can enjoy all manner of honey-laden goodies. For more information, please visit chainbridgehoney.com

name: Iximche
description: Iximche was founded by the Mayan Kaqchikel tribe in the 12th century. In the 14th century, after a falling out with their allies, it was made the capital of their kingdom. 100 years later, after the arrival of the conquistadors, Kaqchikel allied with the Spanish and Iximche briefly served as the first capital of Guatemala. However, after this alliance was broken, the Kaqchikel abandoned the city, and the Spanish set it ablaze. Today, the ruins are a well-preserved nugget of local Mayan culture. Visitors can enjoy pyramid-temples, palaces, a ceremonial area, and and even two Mesoamerican ball-courts in a more easy-to-manage package. There's even a tree at the back of the site where the locals still perform Mayan rituals. As this this site was so important to the local tribe, most of the visitors here are actually indigenous Maya. The signs are only in Spanish or Kaqchike, so it's recommended you hire an English speaking guide if you'd like a more in-depth explanation of the site. Of course, you can soak in the historic atmosphere and peer at the artefacts exhibited in the small museum.

name: Szentendre
description: Inhabited since the 9th century, Szentendre was a rather small and unimportant settlement for much of its history, in fact, during a time in the 17th century, just a single family lived here. However, massive migrations of Serbs, and later, Dalmations, revitalized the town. The comfortable, provincial lifestyle just outside of Budapest began attracting artists in the early 20th century - a tradition that's carried over to today. Visitors can now enjoy the charming, colorful buildings and countless art galleries that make up the town, which is punctuated by seven church towers, each representing a different denomination and era. There are several interesting museums in town, such as the National Wine Museum, Marzipan Museum, and Dobos Confectionary Museum. However, for those interested in traditional Hungarian culture, the open-air Ethnographic Museum (or Skanzen) is the largest in Hungary, having collected 340 historic rural buildings from every region and filled them with thousands of traditional objects.

name: Kuldiga
description: First mentioned in 1242, Kuldīga did well for itself as a member of the Hanseatic League, but its golden age came in the 17th century when it was one of the capitals of the Duchy of Courland. Amazingly, the town escaped much of the destruction wrought by the Baltics tumultuous history, leaving it with the only preserved 17th to 18th century ensemble left in the Baltic states. Today, visitors are free to explore the charming cobbled streets and admire the historic homes, all topped with red tiles. The Kuldiga District Museum, housed in a charming building said to have been the Russian Pavilion at the 1900 World's Fair, showcases rotating exhibits on the ground and second floors, while the first floor is fully furnished as a wealthy turn of the century home, attended by costumed staff. The nearby Venta Rapid is the widest in Europe and a popular bathing spot among locals.

name: Cenote Hubiku
description: Located in a cavern with a large opening in its dome, Cenote Hubiku combines the mystique of swimming in a cave with the comforts of sunlight. The cavern's moss-covered walls, the hanging vines, and the deep turquoise of the water make for a marvelous natural spectacle. The circular pool is nearly 150 feet deep, and its waters a refreshingly brisk 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which has made it a popular attraction for locals and tour groups alike. The facilities here make the cenote more like an underground swimming pool, with showers to rinse off in before you get in the water, bathrooms, a restaurant, and souvenir stalls.

name: Santarem
description: Settled since the Iron Age, Santarem was an administrative center for Julius Caesar, a Moorish cultural center, a favored retreat for Christian royalty, and planning location for many of Portugal's expeditions to the New World. While the city has since lost its political importance, the cobbled streets of the Old Town have reminders of its former greatness. One of the standout monuments is the Church of the Grace, which along with being a wonderful piece of Gothic architecture, displays the tombs of Pedro de Meneses, the first governor of Ceuta, and Pedro Álvares Cabral, the navigator who discovered Brazil. The Museu Diocesano, housed in the 17th century Jesuit College attached to the Cathedral exhibits collection of artwork dating back to the 13th century. Overlooking the city and the Tagus is the Jardim das Portas do Sol - a pleasant garden that had been fortified since the 8th century BC.

name: Portoroz
description: The town's spa traditions date all the way back to the 13th century when Benedictine monks used the healing seawater to treat illnesses. Today, Portoroz is home to six wellness spas and resorts to enjoy and relax in all year round. If the weather is right, visitors can also swim in the Mediterranean Sea, which can reach temperatures up to 31 degrees celsius. Travelers of all ages come to revel in the town's well-maintained beaches, nature park, and elegant, modern architecture.
