name: Leipzig
description: Since the fall of the Berlin wall in 1989, Leipzig has experienced a fresh lease of life. With a thriving cultural scene, high standard of living and plentiful green spaces, the largest city in Saxony should not be overlooked! The historic downtown area of Leipzig boasts buildings ranging in style from renaissance to baroque to promoterism (an architectural style unique to Austria and Germany) and has many sites of historical interest. The most famous of these is St Nicholas Church, which played an important role in the 1989 peaceful protests against communist rule. As well as a varied history, Leipzig is also a city of culture. It has a strong musical tradition which is highlighted through the famous Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra and Leipzig Opera house. Meanwhile art-lovers can choose from a number of galleries and museums including Leipzig Museum of Fine Arts, the Ethnography Museum, Applied Arts Museum, and Musical Instrument Museum.

name: Skradin
description: While there's nothing left of the original Roman settlement, the ancient town of Skradin still offers plenty of old world charm. The quiet cobbled streets are lined with traditional houses, some still pockmarked from the Homeland War in the 1990s. The 18th century Baroque Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary stands on the foundation of the old cathedral, which was destroyed by the Turks. Its pipe organ is registered as part of the national cultural heritage. Skradin's iconic clock tower from 1872 was built on the nearest cliff, rather than right next to the church as is customary. However, the locals might be most proud of their Skradinski Rižot, or 12-hour Risotto, which was featured on Anthony Bourdain's 'No Reservations'. Since it really does take 12 hours to prepare, you should make advance reservations to experience this unique dish.

name: Victoria
description: Victoria in Seychelles, the capital city of this Indian Ocean archipelago, is a captivating blend of Creole charm, tropical allure, and vibrant island life. The city's focal point is the iconic clock tower, a historical landmark that stands proudly as a symbol of Seychelles' colonial past. Surrounding the tower, the Sir Selwyn Selwyn-Clarke Market bursts with the lively energy of locals and showcases an array of exotic fruits, spices, and handicrafts, providing a sensory feast for visitors. Victoria embraces its cultural diversity, evident in its architecture, cuisine, and festivals. The city is home to vibrant Creole houses, French colonial buildings, and lively street markets where the aroma of traditional Seychellois dishes fills the air. The annual Carnaval International de Victoria, a celebration of cultural unity, music, and dance, exemplifies the city's lively spirit. Nature enthusiasts find solace in the heart of Victoria at the enchanting Jardin des Roi, a botanical garden that houses an impressive collection of endemic flora. For panoramic views of the city and its surrounding islands, the Signal Mountain offers a rewarding hike and a breathtaking vantage point.

name: Porto Alegre
description: Located on the shores of the Logoa dos Patos, Porto Alegre was established in 1752 by 60 Azorean couples. Since then, it's grown into one of Brazil's largest cities, thanks to its key position at the junction of five rivers, but the European heritage of its residents is still clearly visible, especially at 17 meter high Monument to the Azoreans. Conscientious planning efforts have managed to preserve many of the city's historic monuments, such as the 18th century Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady Mother of God and elegant City Hall. You can even catch a movie in a converted, early 20th century power plant. Porto Alegre progressive politics have spawned a vibrant arts and culture scene, embodied by the great museums, and thriving LGBT community.

name: Medellin
description: Founded in the 17th century, Medellin's rich cultural history was overshadowed by the rampant violence of the late 20th century, when Pablo Escobar had the run of the city. Fortunately, public transit and other major public works projects have transformed "the deadliest city in the world" into "the most innovative" in a few short years. Today, Medellin's parks and plazas delight visitors and locals alike. The most famous is the Plaza Botero, where you'll find 23 statues by Medellin's most renowned artist, and several museums, including the striking Gothic Revival Rafael Uribe Uribe Palace of Culture. The surrounding Old Quarter is dotted with churches, but the more adventurous might want to head to Comuna 13. Once the most dangerous district in the world's most dangerous city, it's now a destination for street art aficionados and one of Medellin's greatest success stories where you can wander by yourself (during the day), or join a guided tour.

name: Newstead Abbey
description: Founded by Augustinian monks in 1170, the original Newstead Abbey was destroyed by order of Henry VIII in 1539. Rather than let the king's men take the abbey's treasures, the monks threw them into the lake. In 1540, the Byron family came into possession of the lands and created a gorgeous country home with beautiful landscaped gardens. While the poet Byron was famously 'mad, bad and dangerous to know', having buried his beloved dog in a giant tomb on the Abbey's grounds, his great uncle, the 5th Lord William 'the Wicked' Byron, was violently eccentric. He killed his neighbor over an argument over whose estate had better hunting, and built to follies from which to shoots at servants as they held mock naval battles for his enjoyment. Today, the abbey interiors let visitors experience Victorian room settings, including the poet's private apartments, while the beautiful 300 acre parkland and formal gardens provide a perfect place to relax.

name: Akhaltsikhe
description: Akhaltsikhe is a quaint city nestled in the southwest of Georgia. Struggling to pronounce the name? No sweat! Just remember it translates to 'New Fortress' in Georgian, the name given to the city because of its main attraction, the Akhaltsikhe (Rabati) Castle. This colossal fortress, located in the city's old quarter, is the emblem of Akhaltsikhe. There's no contesting the star of the city; the castle's impressive silhouette reigns supreme over the landscape. While the primary structures of the castle were erected in the 12th, 16th, and 19th centuries, its roots stretch back to the 9th century. One of the standout features is the Ahmediyye Mosque with its shimmering golden dome, a remnant from the 1500s when the Ottomans seized Akhaltsikhe and established it as the residence for the pasha. But that's not all there is to see - gardens, terraced walkways, an Orthodox church, fountains, archways, and towering fortifications abound. Some visitors liken the castle to a Disney creation. So, could we claim Akhaltsikhe as the Georgian Disneyland, or is that a leap too far? It's up to you to decide!

name: Cefalu
description: Founded by the ancient Greeks, Cefalu was originally an agricultural settlement. In the 12th century, King Roger II of Sicily shaped the town as it stands today, having it moved to the shore to take advantage of the excellent harbour, and had the Byzantine-style cathedral built. Today, the cathedral is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that preserves the town's unique Byzantine, Arabic, and Christian heritage be combining all three styles in its beautiful mosaics and elegant architecture. After admiring the cathedral, visitors can work their way down through the medieval alleys to the picturesque harbour. En route are several historic landmarks, such as a 16th century bath house, and part of a huge 13th-century palace. In the Museo Mandralisca, a relatively small collection showcases the town's rich history through artefacts like a 4th century BC vase decorated with a fishmonger chopping a tuna.

name: White Temple
description: Wat Rong Khun was designed by visual artist and painter Chalermchai Kositpipat, and is unique in both color and execution. The entire building is stark white to signify Buddha's purity, while the pieces of glass that adorn it symbolize Buddha's wisdom and teachings. The entire temple is rife with symbolism and mythology, from the statues of countless reaching hands that symbolise unrestrained desire, to the "gate of heaven", guarded Death and Rahu. Intermixed with the Thai architecture and Buddhist imagery are pop-icons like Hello Kitty and Harry Potter. Kositpipat is still working on the temple complex, and is planning to construct a hall to enshrine Buddhist relics, a meditation hall, monks living quarters, and an art gallery without the assistance of major donors.

name: Guarapuava
description: Nestled in the heart of Parana state's mid-south, Guarapuava stands as the largest municipality in the region, a vibrant city with a rich tapestry of history and modernity. Founded in 1810, Guarapuava's roots trace back to the pioneering Tropeiros, whose diverse backgrounds from Poland, Italy, and Germany shaped the city's unique identity. The anniversary, celebrated on December 9, marks the start of colonization and showcases the city's enduring spirit. Guarapuava's elevated terrain, standing at 1120 m, offers not only a picturesque landscape but also a vibrant cultural scene. The city takes pride in its high-level athletes, excelling in sports like shooting, cycling, football, and kickboxing. Visitors to Guarapuava can explore its historical landmarks, from the captivating Cathedral of Our Lady of Bethlehem to the enchanting Lake of Tears and the enthralling Park Lake. The city's commitment to preserving its cultural heritage is evident in attractions like the Municipal Museum of Viscount Guarapuava and the Jordan Recreation Park.

name: Moulay Idriss
description: Moulay Idriss is the burial site of the great-grandson of the prophet Muhammed, who came to Morocco in the 6th century. His tomb was rebuilt and renovated by Moulay Ismail in the late 17 or early 18th century, and its sacred significance meant that non-Muslims weren't allowed into the town until 1912 (and are still not allowed to enter the tomb). It wasn't until 2005 that the current King of Morocco, Muhammed VI, issued a decree permitting non-Muslims to stay overnight in the town. Because of its historic inaccessibility, the holy town is still a relaxing place to explore compared to the country's main tourist destinations. Wandering the winding roads through the historic center, you're sure to discover brightly painted passageways, traditional architecture, and intricate mosaics. The Moulay Idriss mosque has the only cylindrical minaret in Morocco, and was built using stones from the nearby Roman ruins of Volubilis, and is covered with verses from the quran.

address.addr1: Mote Rd, Ivy Hatch, Sevenoaks TN15 0NT, UK
description: Built in the 14th century, the moated manor house of Ightham Mote had passed through the upper echelons of English society. In 1953, the manor was purchased by the American Charles Henry Robinson, who chanced upon the property listing after having fallen in love with the estate when he was stationed nearby during World War II. Inside, each room represents a different era, giving visitors insight into the needs and lives of the various owners, such as the many representations of King Henry VIII and his wife, the Victorian billiard room with its door to the moat, the monumental Tudor fireplace with family emblems, or the New England style library and eagle-motif bedroom. The manor also has what is probably the world's only landmark dog kennel - a Victorian style house made for a Saint Bernard. For more information, please visit https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ightham-mote

name: Vlore
description: Founded as a Greek colony in the 6th century BC, the ancient port of Vlore is the epicenter of the nation's pride, and dissent against oppression. In the 16th century, they welcomed the Jews fleeing the Iberian Peninsula, while in 1912, Vlore was where Albania declared independence from the Ottoman Empire, and briefly served as the nation's capital. While Vlore Bay, the largest and deepest in the country is popular among beach-goers, the city has plenty of monuments and museums to discover. The Museum of Independence was the country's first museum, and is dedicated to the birth of the nation. Vlore's 16th century Muradije Mosque is the country's last remaining building made by the famous architect Sinan the Great. And, be sure to try the city's distinctive cuisine, which, thanks to its unique geographic position, means fresh seafood, and rustic pastoral dishes are both local specialties.

name: Gyeongju
description: Known as "the museum without walls," Gyeongju boasts a plethora of archaeological sites and cultural treasures from the Silla era, making it a top destination for history enthusiasts and tourists alike. Designated as UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Seokguram grotto, Bulguksa temple, Gyeongju Historic Areas, and Yangdong Folk Village preserve the essence of this ancient kingdom and draw visitors from around the world. The city itself exudes a laid-back atmosphere, offering parks, villages, and cafes for relaxation and contemplation. Woljeonggyo Bridge, the largest wooden bridge in South Korea, captivates with its beauty, turning into a magical golden spectacle when illuminated at night. The Gyeongju National Museum is a treasure trove for those eager to delve into the cultural heritage of Silla. A highlight of any visit to Gyeongju is exploring the Daereungwon Tomb Complex, home to 23 ancient tombs, including the renowned Cheonmachong Tomb. With its cultural significance, captivating historic sites, and serene surroundings, Gyeongju stands as a timeless testament to Korea's splendid past

name: Baracoa
description: Spanish conquistador Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded Baracoa in 1511 as Spain's first settlement in Cuba and their original capitol. However Baracoa's remote location left it an isolated port that specialized in blackmarket dealings. After contraband dealings dried up, Baracoa turned into a humble agricultural town that was only accessible by sea until the 1960. But it's precisely this perfect combination of rich history, stunning natural surroundings, and isolation that has made Baracoa Cuba's most atmospheric town. Walk the narrow, cobbled streets from Fort La Punta to the Matachín Fortress, and you'll find elegant mansions and colorful churches, including the Cathedral where Enriqueta Faber, a French woman who passed herself off as a man so she could be a doctor, and married a local heiress in 1819. Be sure to head up to the Seboruco Castle, for the best view in town. If you're staying a bit longer, look just outside of town for blissful beaches, and one of Cuba's most important national parks.

name: Ansbach
description: Founded by a group of peasant families in the 7th century, in the 14th century, Ansbach became the seat of the Hohenzollern Dynasty, and would continue to receive noble attention for the next 500 years. While this spurred the construction of some beautiful historic buildings such as the St. Johannis Church, the Residenz Palace is the pinnacle of Ansbach's noble splendor. Inside, visitors can marvel at its richly furnished rooms, such as the cavernous banquet hall, or the 'Tiled Hall', fitted with around 2,800 tiles from the local manufactory. The town also has a dark side - such as the werewolf that killed many of the town's children in the 17th century, and the enigmatic Kaspar Hauser, who claimed to have been raised in a dark cell before moving to Ansbach, where he was fatally stabbed in the palace's manicured gardens. Kaspar, and more of the town's rich history, is all covered at the Margrave Museum.

name: Fatima
description: This small agricultural town owes its fame to three shepherd children who, in 1917, saw monthly visions of the Virgin Mary in the Cova da Iria pasture, the last of which brought an estimated 70,000 pilgrims. Today, the site is marked by the Basílica de Fátima, where pilgrims come on the 13th of every month to honor the Virgin and her young visionaries. On the 100th anniversary of the event, Pope Francis canonized 2 of the children who died during the Spanish Flu pandemic. Today the village's main landmarks revolve around the event, and visiting the Sanctuary built on the site of Cova da Iria, or the homes of the children is an interesting experience even for non-believers.

name: Ljubljana
description: Wedged between Austria and Italy, Ljubljana is small in surface area but large in terms of hospitality and quality of life. It was awarded the "Green Capital of Europe" for 2016. The city features a plethora of theaters, museums, and galleries and is home to one of the oldest philharmonic orchestras in the world. Stop by the Ljubljana Castle to check the marvelous view from its Tower and walk the Three Bridges over the Ljubljanica River into Old City. Traffic is restricted in the city center, leaving the banks of the river free for pedestrians and cyclists. With a name (according to one theory) meaning "beloved", how could you not love it?

name: Mahdia
description: Mahdia originated as the Roman city Aphrodisium, which was later known as Africa. Along with (possibly) giving its name to the entire continent, the was notably the first capital of the Fatimid dynasty, who would go on to rule Egypt and Syria. The city's strategic location made it a frequent target for attack over the centuries, though its robust fortifications allowed many of its historic monuments to survive to this day. The historic medina, situated on a promontory, is accessed via the monumental Skifa Kahla ("black gate"). Built in 916, the gate is attached to the town museum for those looking to learn more about its rich history. The medina is lined with charming, traditional buildings, and its souks are an excellent place to haggle over some of the town's famed textiles. Mahdia's Great Mosque, built in the 10th century, is a fascinating architectural anomaly, being inspired by Roman temples rather than traditional Islamic architecture.

name: Tubingen
description: First mentioned in the 13th century, the establishment of Eberhard Karls University by Duke Eberhard im Bart of Württemberg in 1477 made Tübingen one of the most influential places of learning in the Holy Roman Empire. One of the oldest universities in Central Europe, the University is an integral part of the city's identity - the 12th century castle that birthed the town is now a part of the college campus. After admiring the historic architecture, visitors can head into the museum to learn more about its history. Visitors can also head to the Market Square to to enjoy a cup of coffee and admire the distinctive architecture of the City Hall and the surrounding buildings. The Collegiate Church, built towards the end of the 15th century was one of the first to convert to to Martin Luther's protestant church, and houses some exceptional sculptures.

name: Bogor City
description: Bogor was once the capital of the great Sunda Kingdom during the Middle Ages and now features an array of historical landmarks and gorgeous landscapes to explore. It bears the fitting nickname of the "Rainy City" due its frequent rain showers, even during the dry season. The climate contributes to the lush greenery and vibrant flora that grace the city, such as the renowned Botanical Garden. One of the oldest and largest in the world, it offers a haven of beauty and tranquility across 87 hectares and features meticulously manicured gardens, colorful flowers, serene ponds with water lilies, and even an orchid garden housed in a glasshouse. Visit the presidential palace, known as the Bogor Palace, which has witnessed significant events in Indonesia's pre- and post-independence era. Marvel at the palace's grandeur and enjoy the surrounding park, where around 250 deer freely graze and can be fed. With its historical palace and magnificent botanical garden, Bogor presents a captivating destination for travelers seeking to immerse themselves in the beauty of West Java.

name: Jamestown, NY
description: Through the 20th century, Jamestown, NY, was best known for producing goods like the crescent wrench, and the automatic lever voting machine, and a whole lot of furniture. But in 1911, it also produced an icon: Lucille Ball. If you love Lucy, the Lucy-Desi Museum is a destination in itself. See memorabilia, awards, costumes, and even complete set recreations! Step into Lucy and Ricky Ricardo`s New York City apartment, their Hollywood hotel suite, and try your hand on the interactive Vitamatavegamin line. In 2018, the First Couple of Comedy's museum birthed the National Comedy Center. Here you'll find an incomparable archive donated by some of the country's greatest comedians ranging from Johnny Carson to George Carlin. Time Magazine even named it one of the best places to visit on the entire planet. To see the city's industrial heritage take a stroll down the Jamestown River Walk.

name: Trebic
description: Trebic has experienced a new lease of life after two of its most historic sites were awarded UNESCO World Heritage status. The Basilica of St. Procopius began as a monastery in the 12th century and helped establish Trebic as a thriving market town. It's since undergone various remodels, with today's impressive structure coming from alterations in the early 1700s. One particular feature that stands out is a rare example of a ten-part rose window. Trebic's Jewish Quarter is one of the best-preserved and largest Jewish Ghettos in Europe. All the original inhabitants were deported and sent to concentration camps in WW2, with only ten managing to return after the war. While many of the buildings in the area are now owned by non-Jewish residents, the Quarter still contains two synagogues and an ancient Jewish cemetery as an act of memorial.

name: Munster
description: Well established by 793, when Charlemagne sent out Ludger as a missionary to evangelise the region, Münster has been an important hub for centuries. In 1534, the Anabaptists took control of the city, claimed all property, burned all books except the Bible, and required all citizens be naked. When, the town was recaptured in 1535, the Anabaptists were tortured to death, and their corpses displayed in the metal baskets hanging from St. Lambert's Church. The 13th century St. Paul's Cathedral has an astronomical clock that plays a Glockenspiel tune at noon. The city's most notable landmark is the 14th century, Gothic Town Hall, where the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648 - part of which is on display inside, along with portraits of the participants. For something more modern, the Pablo Picasso Museum of Graphic Art, is devoted exclusively to the graphic works of Pablo Picasso, and his contemporaries.

name: Daegu
description: Daegu, officially known as the Daegu Metropolitan City, holds remarkable sights of the Palgongsan and Apsan mountains, along with historical treasures from the Silla period and the Joseon Dynasty. For a glimpse of Daegu's beautiful nature, take a visit to Duryu Park, also home to the towering Daegu Tower that stands as one of South Korea's tallest observation towers. The Osaek Fountain, believed to contain mineral water with healing properties, captivates visitors, while Duryu Library, Daeseongsa Temple, and Geumyongsa Temple enrich the park's offerings. Cherry blossoms in full bloom make spring the peak season, and the lush landscape features over 133 species of trees and plants. For more insight into Daegu's spiritual history, visit the sacred Buinsa Temple, dating back to the 7th century. Gyesan Catholic Church, a Romanesque-Gothic masterpiece founded in 1900, stands as the only remaining building from that era, featuring exquisite stained glass windows and pinnacles. Daegu's allure extends beyond its historical and natural wonders, as the city hosts a myriad of lively festivals throughout the year. The Dongseongno festival, Palgongsan maple festival, and Biseulsan azalea festival are among the vibrant celebrations that attract tourists and offer an unforgettable experience of the city's cultural vibrancy.

name: Marsaxlokk
description: Marsaxlokk bursts with seaside beauty, renowned for its traditional Maltese fishing fleet. The luzzu boats that line the harbor have been a part of the local heritage since the early 20th century, adorned with vivid colors and eye-catching motifs that have become an iconic symbol of Malta. Witness their beauty firsthand in Marsaxlokk, also known for its bustling market that takes place along the seafront. Throughout the week it's a vibrant tourist market with local crafts, souvenirs and traditional delicacies, and on Sundays it transforms into a large fish market full of fresh seafood. Enjoy leisurely walks along the coast and harbor, or the sandy beaches of Ballut ta' Marsaxlokk and Marsaxlokk Strand to soak up the sun. In the heart of Marsaxlokk you'll find the Parish Church of Our Lady of Pompei, a 19th-century Roman Catholic church located in the main square. The town's blend of vibrant markets, colorful fishing boats and coastal beauty makes it a captivating destination on the Maltese archipelago.

name: Ranau
description: Renau is celebrated for its magnificent view of Mount Kinabalu and abundance of highland vegetables, and is also a living memory of the atrocities of World War II. Ranau's prominent attraction is Kinabalu Park, recognized by UNESCO as a Center of Plant Diversity for Southeast Asia, and showcases a remarkable array of flora and fauna. For a moment of reflection, visit the Last Prisoner of War Camp and Memorial Kenipir, which pays tribute to the Australian and British servicemen who suffered during the Sandakan-Ranau Death Marches in World War II. The memorial stands as a somber reminder of the atrocities committed during that period, and many people have since taken the journey along the Death March route. A favorite pit-stop for both locals and tourists alike is Pekan Nabalu, packed with food and handicraft stalls where you can sample fresh farm produce and traditional condiments. The lookout point offers a magnificent view of Mount Kinabalu, creating a memorable photo opportunity. Ranau holds a special place in the hearts of the Kadazan-Dusun community, as it is considered to be the original home of their ancestors—just a short distance away is the site believed to have housed the first Kadazan-Dusun settlers, marking a significant historical and cultural landmark.

name: Kundasang
description: Kundasang sits along the bank of the Kundasang River in the cradle of Mount Kinabalu—Malaysia's tallest mountain—and is often referred to as the "New Zealand of Borneo'' due to the terrain's similarities with the country. The town captures the essence of the region, with its famous vegetable market which operates daily and showcases a variety of fresh produce, local food, and handicrafts at affordable prices. Stop by the Desa Dairy Farm for the opportunity to interact with farm animals and sample fresh milk, cheese, and yogurt ice cream. The Spring Garden enchants visitors with its year-round blooming flowers and stunning views of Mount Kinabalu, while the Sabah Tea Garden invites guests to savor tea flavors, explore the lush tea plantation, and witness the tea-making process. Stop by the Kundasang War Memorial to pay tribute to the fallen soldiers and local heroes who played a significant role during World War II, finding a moment of reflection in the serene surroundings.

name: Amersfoort
description: First mentioned in the 11th century, Amersfoort held the regional court of the Bishops of Utrecht, flourishing under their patronage. The city's first, 14th century wall was demolished to make room for new houses - its original location is still marked by Muurhuizen (Wallhouses) Street. The 15th century replacement gave birth to Amersfoort's most iconic monument: the Koppelpoort, a combined land and water gate. From here, a network of cobbled streets and serene canals work their way to the city's market square, which is lined with shops, cafes, and restaurants. Watching over the Hof is the 98 meter tall Onze-Lieve Vrouwetoren, the late-Gothic tower of a 14th century church that was accidentally destroyed in the 1900s. Art lovers won't want to miss the house where Piet Mondrian was born, which is now a museum about the artist's life and work, and even has an exhibition of artists he influenced.

name: Granada
description: Originally a thriving indigenous settlement, in 1524 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba renamed the city Granada, establishing the first European city in mainland America. Despite being attacked by pirates multiple times, Granada continued to thrive as trade center, and today is the third oldest European settlement in the Americas. Among travellers, Granada is revered for its colonial architecture, exhibiting both Baroque and Moorish influences, and making the city feel like a tropical Spain. The Calle la Calzada is a pedestrian street lined with cafes, restaurants, and shops, where you can immerse yourself in local life. From here, it's a short walk to see Granada's impressive churches: the Cathedral Iglesia Guadalupe, Iglesia la Merced, and the yellow Catedral de Granada.

name: Gdansk
description: While Gdańsk's thousand-year history makes it one of the oldest cities in the country, the Polish consciousness knows it as where World War II started, and where the fall of Communism in Central Europe began. Gdańsk's unique history has left it with a distinctive cultural identity, and the unusual mixture of architecture and museums to match. In the Old Town, visitors are treated to narrow cobbled streets and historic thoroughfares lined with beautiful Baroque homes, Art Nouveau villas, and plenty of decidedly un-Polish styles made by wealthy merchants. Towering over the city is the 15th century St. Mary's Church, the largest red-brick church in the world. Along with its beautiful architecture, visitors can learn about the city's history in its many museums, from the fine art on display at the National Museum, to the lives of citizens over the centuries at to History Museum, to its seafaring tradition at the Maritime Museum.

name: Khon Kaen
description: Khon Kaen was founded in the 18th century, but its skyline is decidedly more modern, with skyscrapers and sleek malls popping up around its beautiful temples.. The heart of the city is the Bueng Kaen Nakhon lake, which is surrounded by a pleasant park and even has a waterfront temple. Another unique temple is the white, gold, and blue Wat Thung Setthi which is filled with white statues, while the 9-story Phra Mahathat Kaen Nakhon royal temple houses distinctive artwork and artefacts on each floor. For those looking to delve deeper into the city's past, stop by the Khon Kaen National Museum which exhibits pieces dating back to the pre-history, including the skeleton of a "New Stone Age" man.

name: La Vega
description: Founded in 1495 at the foot of a fort built by Christopher Columbus the previous year, La Vega was the first gold boom town in the Dominican Republic, and for a time, one of the largest and most important European settlements in the Western Hemisphere. Unfortunately, an earthquake in 1564 cut La Vega's glory days short, and the city had to be rebuilt on the bank of the Camú River. Today, you can still see the remnants of this original settlement, including parts of the fort and other building foundations at the Pueblo Viejo National Park. Within La Vega proper, the main draw is the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, which has an unusual "modernist castle" design. But what Vega is best known for is its colorful Carnival - a tradition dating back to 1520. For the entire month of February the city is an explosion of vibrant costumes, live music, and festivities, which attract more than a half-million visitors.

name: Tarija
description: In the picturesque heart of Bolivia lies the captivating city of Tarija. Lose yourself in the winding streets of the historic center, where every corner reveals a new story of the city's past. Tarija is renowned for its esteemed winemaking tradition, offering a taste of Bolivia's finest wines amidst picturesque vineyards. Delight in wine tastings and tours, where each sip tells a story of passion and craftsmanship. Beyond its vineyards, Tarija boasts breathtaking landscapes, from rolling hills to tranquil rivers, beckoning outdoor enthusiasts and nature lovers alike. Experience the warmth of Tarija's hospitality as you immerse yourself in its cultural festivals and celebrations, where traditional music and dance fill the air with joy.

name: Carlisle
description: Carlisle was one of the strongest British settlements by the time the Romans arrived and used the town to serve the forts on the nearby Hadrian's Wall. Just a stone's throw from the Scottish border, Carlisle was an important military stronghold through the Middle Ages, changing hands several times, its castle even being used to imprison Mary, Queen of Scots. The Industrial Revolution saw Carlisle transform into a major mill and railway town, and the region's cultural and commercial center. Today, the city is still guarded by its 11th century castle, where you can tour its imposing fortifications, view the 'licking-stones' where prisoners got their water, or step into Cumbria's Museum of Military Life to learn the 300-year history of the region's regiments. Afterwards, head to the Cathedral, where you can still see elements from its 12th century origins alongside, 14th century stained-glass windows and star-painted ceiling, and the exceptional 16th century Flemish Brougham Triptych.

name: Gran Cenote
description: Like the tens of thousands of other cenotes in the Yucatan, the Gran Cenote formed thousands of years ago when erosion caused its limestone cave formation to collapse. To the indigenous people, these natural wonders were holy places seen as entrances to the underworld. To us regular folks, they're some of the Yucatan's most beautiful natural attractions. The Gran Cenote is actually a collapsed tunnel system, meaning there are multiple caverns you can swim in. The impossible clear water (you have to shower before going in to keep it from being contaminated) isn't just refreshing - it's home to plenty of little turtles you can spot if you rent snorkel equipment. After having a swim, you can relax on the wooden platforms and soak in the beautiful scenery.

name: Sartene
description: Described by novelist Prosper Merimee as "the most Corsican of Corsican towns", look no further than Sartène for a true gateway to the past. This humble town, with its austere structures dating back to the 16th century, rises from a granite hillside in front of a mountainous backdrop. Whilst built by the Genoese as an inland sanctuary from coastal pirate raids, Sartène chronicles a bloody history of banditry and alleyway duels, including a feud between two prominent families of the town in the early 19th century. Explore the labyrinthine streets of the old town for yourself, ducking under arches and following mysterious staircases, before heading to the more vibrant part of town. Place Porta is a tree-lined square of cafes, bars and Saturday morning markets, containing the 16th century home of the Genoese governor, Hôtel de Ville. Stop at one of the many butchers, delicatessens or greengrocers for a range of cured meats, cheeses or chestnut-flour bread to tantalize your taste buds.

name: Herculaneum Archaeological Area
description: A sister site to Pompeii, Herculaneum was founded around the 6th century BC. By the time it was destroyed, had blossomed into a wealthy town with a population of around 4,000. The pyroclastic surge that killed its inhabitants, and left the city buried under 16-25 meters of rock, also carbonized wood, and other organic material, perfectly preserving it. Much of the ancient city lies under the modern suburb of Ercolano, so it remains unexcavated. Even so, the preserved houses revealed wooden lofts, wine racks, and bed frames, offering an intimate look into ancient Roman life. A walkthrough shows not only the well-preserved buildings but also stunning mosaics, ancient advertisements, and even fossilized remains of the city's unfortunate inhabitants. Please note: tickets are not included in the stop price.

name: Boumalne Dades
description: While there are no written records of when Boumalne Dades was founded, it's believed to have been settled in the 15th century by exiles from the Reconquest of Spain. Shortly after, a Jewish community arrived and built the Tiylit Castle, a striking ruin standing atop a rocky outcrop on the outskirts of town. Having been built by the French in the 1930s, the town kasbah isn't an ancient monument, but a symbol of foreign authority, colonization, and the suffering of the local people forced to build it. One of the reasons Boumalne Dades matches the surrounding landscape so well is that many buildings in town are made from traditional adobe, and even the modern concrete buildings are painted to match this earthy color. In April and May, the entire area is blanketed in fragrant roses, with nearby Kelàa Megouna holding a festival dedicated to the blossoms.

name: Yungay
description: Nestled in the mountain ridges just 15 km from Peru's highest peak, Yungay has kept it's spirit in the face of tragedy. In May 1970, the Ancash earthquake devastated Yungay. Caused by an unstable portion of glacial ice, the resulting landslide tumbled down to Yungay, covering the majority of the town in soil, and ultimately 20,000 people perished. The government immediately declared the covered town a gravesite, which to this day, has not been excavated. People travel from all over to pay their respects to the lost lives of Yungay, as there is also a lovely Cathedral that now sits on the mass cemetery.

name: Speightstown
description: Speightstown, the second largest city in Barbados, lies on the northwest coast in the parish of Saint Peter. Named after William Speight, a member of Barbados' first parliament and landowner of the city's grounds, this port city is also known as "Little Bristol" because of its historical trade connections to Bristol, UK. Visitors can immerse themselves in Barbados' rich history and culture, exploring its colonial architecture, art galleries, and vibrant local markets. Today, the city's marina is full of yachts, and its pristine beaches are a magnet for sun-seekers. Key attractions include the 19th-century Arlington House, which has been transformed into a museum chronicling the area's history, and the Saint Peter's Parish Church. For a genuine local experience, Speightstown boasts a plethora of pubs and restaurants. Although it's a peaceful retreat compared to the bustling capital, a visit to Speightstown promises to be a memorable detour!

name: Veria
description: Settled since around 1000 BC, Veria was the second most important city of the Macedon Empire, hosted Olympic-style games during the Hellenistic Era, and an important place of worship under the Romans. Saint Paul the Apostle visited the city in the 1st century, an even recorded in the Bible, and his the podium is a landmark within the city to this day. The 11th century Old Cathedral is filled with medieval artwork, but it's just one of the many Byzantine churches in the city, which earned it the nickname 'Little Jerusalem'. Visitors can also head to the 19th century Jewish quarter, where the stately homes still bear Hebrew inscriptions. However, the city's greatest cultural treasure is also the oldest. In the Aigai-Vergina Museum, the treasures of the Temenid dynasty, the house of Alexander the Great, are on display in their golden glory, giving visitors some context for their visit to the UNESCO-listed tombs.

name: Asan
description: Asan has become renowned for its rejuvenating hot spring experiences that draw visitors seeking relaxation and wellness. Among the city's highlights is the Asan Spavis, a contemporary hot spring destination with snow sledding and traditional spa treatments. For those seeking a touch of Europe in Korea, the Blue Crystal Village offers a taste of Santorini, Greece, with its picturesque Mediterranean village situated in Tangjeong-myeon. The village's white walls and blue roofs evoke a sense of exotic landscapes, providing a unique architectural experience. History enthusiasts will find Hyeonchungsa Shrine a captivating destination. Built in 1706, this shrine honors General Lee Sun-Shin (1545-1598) and houses some of Korea's official national treasures, including Sun-Shin's diary and long sword. Asan also boasts the Onyang Folk Museum, the largest folklore museum in Korea. The museum showcases architectural installations of traditional Korean homes and housewares, allowing visitors to immerse themselves in the country's rich cultural heritage.

name: Ulm
description: The city has featured year-on-year in 'The Top 100 Sights in Germany' awarded annually by the German Tourist Board, which comes as no surprise to anyone familiar with this quirky municipality. Ulm is particularly famous for two things — the first is that it is the birthplace of Albert Einstein and the second is that it is home to the tallest church steeple (530 feet) in the world today. Known as the 'Finger of God', the city's most prominent building reaches endlessly into the sky while the square it stands on provides visitors with a dazzling mix of historical and modern architecture. If that's not enough, a short walk away is the pretty-as-a-picture town hall, with its ornate astronomical clock. The town hall stands in magnificent contrast right next to the contemporary glass pyramid housing Ulm's public library, providing the perfect fusion of old and new that makes this city so appealing.

name: Papallacta
description: At 3,300 meters above sea level in the Andes, Papallacta is Ecuador's highest town. Papallacta has more than a dozen hot springs, thermally heated by the nearby Antisana Volcano. At such high altitude expect fog and cool temperatures during your visit, making the hot springs a welcome retreat to warm up (though you can dive in the freezing plunge pools, if you dare!). The most popular is Las Termas de Papallacta, with eight pools in a range of sizes and temperature. Set amongst beautiful gardens and natural rock formations in the Andean forest it offers spa treatments for a truly relaxing experience. And did you know that a spell in the thermal baths can burn as many calories as a 30 minute walk!? If you build up an appetite, local trout farmers supply the surrounding eateries with the cold-water fish where it is cooked up in a variety of ways for a delicious feast.

name: Viljandi
description: Founded as an earthen stronghold in the 12th century, Viljandi took 100 years to develop into a permanent settlement. The city flourished for a time, even joining the Hanseatic League, but wars in the 17th and 18th century all but destroyed the town. Today, the town is one of the most charming in all of Estonia. The quaint wooden houses, blend in perfectly with the beautiful natural surroundings, allowing visitors to step back to a simpler time. At the edge of the forest, visitors will find the ruins of the Livonian castle, the order's first foothold in Estonia, which is now a sprawling park. Home to the Viljandi Culture Academy, the town is a focal point of Estonian culture, which peaks in July when it hosts the country's largest folk music festival.

name: Great Falls Park
description: The site of the Potomac Great Falls, a beautiful series of major cascades that total up to 76 feet. For expert kayakers and whitewater boaters, this is the perfect place for you! For another discovery mission, the park has 24 kilometres of hiking trails that traverse streams, rivers and reservoirs. For a historical opportunity, visit the Potowmack Canal, a canal George Washington funded; making it the first canal in the USA that used locks. Go climbing on the Great Falls climbing area, where you can see Native American Petroglyphs while taking a scenic rock-climbing excursion over the Difficult Run, another river area.

name: Vinh Moc Tunnels
description: The Vinh Moc Tunnels were created by the people of this small fishing village when the American military, thinking they were aiding the North Vietnamese, began bombing the area. Between 1966 and 1972, the US dropped an estimated 9,000 tons of bombs on the area - an average of 7 tons of ordinance per person. By the end of the war, the tunnel complex grew to include wells, kitchens, individual housing, and medical areas, while preventing even a single casualty. Today, a guided tour brings visitors into this essentially unchanged underground village, which, while still cramped, is decidedly more comfortable that the Viet Cong's infamous military tunnels. At the on-site museum, you can see photos and relics to get a clearer picture of life underground.

name: Tallinn
description: The medieval city of Tallinn flourished for centuries thanks to its strategic position, leaving it filled with many lavish churches and refined merchant houses. In the heart of Tallinn's UNESCO protected Old Town, visitors will find the beautiful Town Hall Square, dominated by its gorgeous Gothic Town Hall. Among the many historic buildings lining the square is Europe's oldest continuously-operating pharmacy, which houses a museum dedicated to its 600 year history. Around half of the city's medieval town wall and its towers have survived, allowing visitors the opportunity to stroll the ramparts or scale the towers for stupendous views of the city. Dominating the city us the medieval castle, which now houses the Estonian parliament, and two of its most opulent churches - St. Alexander Nevsky Cathedral and the Cathedral of Saint Mary the Virgin.

name: Barrington Court
description: Built in the mid-16th century, Barrington Court changed hands for centuries, eventually becoming a tenant farm in 1745. Poorly maintained, the Tudor manor fell into disrepair until it was discovered by the National Trust and acquired as one of their first buildings in 1907. Architect Alfred Hoare Powell was brought in to restore the manor - a massive undertaking that taught the National Trust a valuable lesson about the intensive work involved in repairing and maintaining country houses. Today, the manor is open for visitors to explore, and though most rooms are starkly furnished, the focal point is the fine wood panelling and intricate design elements, such as Dutch bath tiles imported from Belgium and the exquisitely carved fireplace mantels. Outside, visitors can enjoy the greenery of the kitchen garden, which provides fresh produce for the on-site restaurant, a pleasant walk along the moat, the vibrant colors of the walled rose and iris garden, or a stroll through the orchard. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/barrington-court

name: Mandeville
description: Mandeville is a slow-paced, laid-back city surrounded by lush green hills and located in the central part of the island. Once the country's economic hub, this charming town is now a popular destination for retired Jamaicans who have returned from abroad, attracted by the high standard of living and tranquil environment. When in Mandeville, take time to enjoy the city's architecture, many of the buildings being an example of the 19th-century Georgian style in Jamaican interpretation such as the Mandeville Court House or Manchester Parish Church, but many of the residential buildings, too. Mandeville is home to several parks and gardens, the most prominent being Mrs Carmen Stephenson's Garden, one of the best-maintained in Jamaica. Golf enthusiasts can perfect their swing at the Manchester Golf Club, the first golf course in the Caribbean, founded in 1868. Lastly, be sure to pay a visit to the historic Mandeville Hotel to dine and drink. Mandeville is often described as the town for the " newlyweds or the nearly deads," but that is a good thing: the visitors can recharge and soak in its peacefulness.

name: Celaya
description: Founded in 1571, Celaya played an important role in 19th-century Mexican history when it changed hands several times during Mexico's struggle for independence from Spain. Despite having a turbulent past, today Celaya is attracting visitors seeking out relaxation and break from the crowds of big cities. Stroll through the historic downtown, admire elegant neoclassical Temple of Carmen. This simple church brings together a variety of techniques and styles and it's the only one of its kind in the world. Take a picture of Bola de Agua, the iconic symbol of the city and visit Museum of Mummies with 59 naturally preserved bodies from a cholera outbreak that hit Guanajuato way back in 1833. Before you leave, don't forget to taste Cajeta, traditional caramel based sweets made with goat's milk and Mexicans favorite!

name: Durango
description: Durango has a distinct Western flair with many residents closely associated with cattle culture and decked out in cowboy boots and hats. In addition to historical ties to battles and broncos, many contemporary Western films were shot on location in this desert landscape. An old film set has even been converted into an Old West Town that regularly puts on Western-inspired performances each day and serves as an amusement park of sorts. Learn about the town's wild past at Museo Francisco Villa or explore the historic downtown, the largest in Northern Mexico, which is dominated by the Neoclassical cathedral. You can even scale the cathedral's bell tower for a bird's-eye-view of the surrounding historic buildings.

name: Caesarea
description: Caesarea was founded under Herod the Great around 10 BC, and would grow into the Roman provincial capital. The city was destroyed and rebuilt on multiple occasions through the Middle Ages before being abandoned in 1265. After this, Caesaria wasn't resettled until 1884 when a small group of Bosnian immigrants built a fishing village on the site. Today, the real draw is the excavated and partly restored archaeological site, which is one of the most attractive in the country. Here, you can stroll a Byzantine street, admire a Crusader-era church, marvel at the 10,000-seat Herodian Amphitheatre, and see Israel's oldest Roman theatre all backed by the sound of crashing waves. On the pier, you'll find multimedia exhibits detailing ancient Caesarea's history. Divers can also swim through the ancient city's sunken remains - the world's only underwater museum! Call the Caesarea Dive Club (04-6265898) in advance.

name: Segesta
description: Founded by Sicily's indigenous Elymian tribe, Segesta was Hellenized quite early on, which had a profound effect on its culture. In times of strife, the city often turned to its strong Greek contacts, such as Athens and Carthage, and though it was allied with the famous Greek King and General Pyrrhus, it peacefully surrendered to Rome in 260 BC. After the fall of the Empire, Segesta was destroyed by the Vandals and deserted. In the Middle Ages, the strategic hilltop position was briefly used by the Muslims during the Norman period before being abandoned for good in the 13th century. Today, visitors can admire the magnificent Doric temple with its 36 columns, which was erected between 430 and 420 BC. Visitors can also hike, or take a bus, farther up the hill to the Greek theatre, which was partially carved directly in the mountain and offers amazing views of the countryside and the temple.

name: Jeonju
description: Jeonju is a city like no other, bringing an authentic South Korean experience to its traditional villages. A visit to Jeonju Hanok Village is a must, with around 700 hanok houses densely populating the area. Immerse yourself in history by exploring sites related to King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, the founder of the Joseon Dynasty. The Royal Portrait Museum enshrines his portrait, and the Jaman Mural Village captivates visitors with its warm and emotional murals, reflecting the lives of Korean War refugees. Being designated as a UNESCO city of gastronomy in 2012, Jeonju is a food lover's paradise. Explore the renowned Nambu Market, a bustling hub selling groceries, hot dishes, and colorful fruits and vegetables for over two centuries. For nature enthusiasts, a short 5-minute climb up to Omodae Viewpoint rewards you with stunning vistas of the idyllic Hanok Village. Jeonju's blend of gastronomy, history, and culture creates an enchanting destination, inviting travelers to explore its captivating heritage and indulge in the delightful flavors that make this city truly exceptional.

name: Macas
description: Originally known as "Sevilla del Ora", Macas was founded as a Dominican missionary outpost in the 16th century. It quickly became a thriving trading post, and later, affluent gold mining center. The town's mines were so prosperous that they became the target of violent attacks and had to be abandoned for the safety of the area's inhabitants. Now a busy commercial hub, the city's main landmark is the colorful cathedral with its even-more-vibrant stained glass windows.The Museo Arqueológico y Cultural de Morona Santiago in the top floor of the Casa de la Cultura has an excellent collection of Shuar artefacts, including feather adornments, headdresses made of animal heads, blowpipes, basketwork, and even a replica of a shrunken head. This museum gives a great bit of background if you plan on heading into the jungle to visit the Shuar and Achuar indigenous groups.

name: Aberdeen
description: Settled for at least 8,000 years, Aberdeen flourished as a fishing and trading settlement, though its position made it a frequent target for both Scottish and English forces. In the 18th century, the city began quarrying granite, which was used in constructing the city's buildings until the 20th century when the quarry closed. In the Old Town, you can admire the charming cobbled streets, the stunning 15th century fortified Cathedral, where the city's first University was founded in 1495, and some award-winning gardens. A stroll along the mile-long Union Street lets you experience Aberdeen's distinctive glimmer en route way to its other defining feature: the sea. First stop by the city's Maritime Museum to learn about the city's history with the sea, from fishing to oil, then head down to the colorful fishing quarter at the waterfront, keeping an eye out for urban dolphins along the way.

name: St Edward's Church
address.addr1: 2 Crossways House the Square, Stow-on-the-Wold, Cheltenham GL54 1AB, UK
description: Founded in the 11th century, St. Edward's Church was expanded and remodelled through the 15th century, with further additional renovations made during the Victorian era. On March 21st, 1646, the Battle of Stow saw Royalist and Parliamentary forces face off in the last major battle of the English Civil War. After the battle, the victorious Parliamentarians housed the 1,000 royalist prisoners in the church. Today, visitors will find a memorial to the battle, and to the fallen soldiers of World War I and II. Throughout the church, visitors will find reminders of its long history, from the 13th century columns and arches 15th century bell tower, to the Rubens-esque crucifixion painted by Gaspar de Crayer and the Victorian stained glass windows. However, for most visitors, the most striking feature is the North Porch, which is flanked by a pair of yew trees, and said to have been Tolkien's inspiration for the Doors of Durin.

name: Limassol
description: Limassol was an inconsequential market town until 1191, when Richard the Lion-Heart landed here, married Berengaria of Navarre, and claimed the island for the Anglo-Normans. The city enjoyed a few centuries of prosperity, but fell into decline following the Ottoman invasion of 1570, and only had 150 inhabitants by 1815. Like much of Cyprus, the British administration revitalized the city, and today, it's the second-largest on the island and the chief port of the Republic of Cyprus. While Limassol is known as the "party capital" of Cyprus, with sandy beaches giving way to countless bars and nightclubs, there are still quiet corners to discover. Next to the Old Port, Limassol Cast, which Richard I was wed, now houses an interesting archaeological museum, and the surrounding streets are dotted with restaurants and shops housed in historic buildings. Saripolou Square in particular is the best place to stop to refuel.

name: Zamora
description: Nestled on the banks of the River Duero, entrance to the city is gained over the medieval Stone Bridge, giving visitors a taste of what's to come. Throughout the Middle Ages the city withstood sieges and assaults, thanks to its triple defensive ring, of which, the first wall almost entirely preserved. Dominating the skyline, the Castle and the Cathedral wow visitors from near and afar. Surrounded by a scenic park, the fortress of Moorish origin still preserves its Keep, gate and moat. The 12th century Cathedral beside it is roofed with flakes of stone, in Byzantine style, while its accompanying Romanesque tower dates from the 13th century. The narrow, cobbled streets leading to the Plaza Mayor, are lined with Romanesque churches, while the 15th century Palace of the Counts of Alba de Aliste is a jewel of Renaissance architecture.

name: Six Flags New England
description: Six Flags New England has been a destination for thrill seekers for over a century. Its first rollercoaster, the Giant Dip, was installed in 1912, which sent this 19th century picnic grove on the path to becoming a full-blown amusement park. Today, it's filled with scream-inducing rides like the iconic Superman, one of the world's largest steel coasters, an throwbacks like the wooden Thunderbolt, the oldest running roller coaster in any Six Flags Park. If you're visiting with children, there's plenty of kid-friendly rides to keep them entertained. And in the summer, you can cool off while keeping your blood pumping at the Hurricane Harbor water park.

description: This mysterious Basaltic Prisms of Santa Maria Regla were formed millions of years ago from cooling lava, after which, a river developed in the hilly region above. Today, water rushes from the San Antonio Dam and down the the prismatic ravine, creating a truly unique waterfall. Stairs, walkways, and bridges have been added to make it easier to explore the site, and view the amazing basalt columns (locally known as the Alcholoya) from every angle. Nearby are two 18th century haciendas (large landed estates), Santa Maria Regla and San Miguel Regla, considered the biggest in the world!

name: Castries
description: Castries, the vibrant capital of Saint Lucia, beckons with its enticing blend of tropical charm, historic richness, and captivating landscapes. Tourists are drawn to Castries not only for its idyllic climate but also for its wealth of historic sites and landmarks. The Saint Lucia National Museum, nestled in the heart of the city, showcases a fascinating collection of artifacts unraveling the island's unique history and culture. A leisurely stroll through Derek Walcott Square, a popular gathering spot named after the Nobel Prize-winning poet, and a visit to the 18th-century Fort Charlotte atop a hill, offering panoramic views, add layers to the city's allure. Nature enthusiasts can explore nearby trails like the Botanical Gardens Nature Trail and the La Toc Beach Trail, providing an immersive experience in the lush surroundings. The bustling Castries Market, the largest in Saint Lucia, offers a vibrant tapestry of fresh produce and local goods, adding a lively touch to the city.

name: Zacatlan
description: Located 2,000 metres above sea level, the consistent climate and the ideal soil make Zacatlan the perfect agricultural area. The city is literally surrounded by fruit trees; wild and farmed. During the blooming season, the city air becomes overrun with the sweet scents of the different fruit trees. What's more? This fertile town's plaza may seem like a regular main square… until you look at the flower clock, maintained by a local clock company and made with flowers. If you have a pollen allergy, or sensitive to smells, there are many great indoor activities in this city. Take a look inside the municipal palace of the city, with its Neoclassical architecture adorning the interior. The restored Franciscan monastery, founded in 1567, contains beautiful murals depicting daily Spanish and Indigenous scenes. Other than its fruits and history, this city is also famed for its affinity to hobbies, most notably tinkering. Centenario Clocks is the first clock factory in Latin America. It is still in operation today, and its clocks have been placed in city squares all around the country and the region. Attend the Apple Fair, which is a grand display of this city's apple industry, where they have food, dance and a pageant to crown an Apple Queen.

name: Branson, MO
description: Beginning as a general store and post office, Branson, MO, quickly became a magnet for vacationers and quickly grew into a Midwest entertainment hub. With dozens of theaters and attractions, there's plenty to keep you busy, whether you're visiting for a few hours or a few days. One of the stars of Branson is Dolly Parton's Stampede, where you'll be treated to a horseback spectacular, AND a four course meal! If you're not able to catch a show, you can still see the stars at the Hollywood Wax Museum. Or head to the Titanic Museum to be transported out of the Midwest, and into history. With a half-scale replica of both the ship, and the iceberg that downed it, and over 400 pre-discovery artifacts, it brings the story of the Titanic to life. If you're looking for something more relaxing, just head to the Mount Pleasant Winery to unwind with some fine wines.

name: Riohacha
description: Once home to a large population of indigenous people, Riohacha was founded in 1535by the German conquistador Nikolaus Federmann. The coast's waters proved to be rich with pearls, and during colonial times the city had a booming pearl industry - which also attracted marauding pirates. Despite its long history, much of the city is modern development, though there are still a handful of historic buildings, like the house where Gabriel Garcia Marquez was conceived, and the pretty stone cathedral. The city's heritage is better preserved by its brightly-colored handicrafts, which are still largely influenced by the pre-Columbian Wayuu culture. If you need a hat or vibrantly colored bag, you can head to the Nuevo Market are just keep an eye out for street vendors. The city's main attraction is its 5 kilometer-long beach, which has a palm-shaded promenade running its length, and a pier from 1937 jutting offshore.

name: Oberammergau
description: In 1663, the little Bavarian village of Oberammergau asked God to stop the Bubonic plague outbreak ravaging Europe, and in return, they would put on a play depicting the life of Jesus in perpetuity. By July, the plague had loosened its grip, and in 1634 the people of Oberammergau upheld their end of the bargain and produced their first Passionsspiele - and have repeated it every year that ends with a 0 ever since. Today, the play draws hundreds of thousands of visitors to the town - with an estimated 500,000 coming for the 2020 performance. Even if you're not in town for the performance, Oberammergau is a mecca for mural lovers. The Bavarian Baroque tradition originated here with Franz Seraph Zwinck, and nearly every building is beautifully decorated in this style. Woodcarving is another of the town's traditional crafts, and the Oberammergau Museum has a collection of historical wood carvings on the second floor.

name: Guachimontones
description: Guachimontones was erected in the Teuchitlán tradition and is the perfect display of the traditional, tiered circular pyramid construction. The final result resembles a colossal beehive or towering layered cake. Guachimontones was excavated and reconstructed with an accompanying Interpretive Center to encourage visitors to the site to learn about the lost Teuchitlán culture. The pyramid itself is quite memorable with a blanket of grass climbing high up the stone steps. Visitors can expect somewhat of a challenging hike with steep inclines on the way to the pyramid. It is recommended to wear sturdy shoes and bring along water to stay hydrated. Check out Guachimontones and see where this ancient society worshipped their gods!

name: Mulhouse
description: First mentioned in the 12th century, Mulhouse didn't become a part of France until the 18th century. Around this time, the city's textile industry began to take off, transforming the border town into one of France's leading fabric producers. Today, the compact historic center is perfect for exploring, with beautiful half-timbered houses and colorfully decorated Renaissance structures at every turn. At the Place de la Reunion, visitors can admire the neo-Gothic Temple of Saint-Etienne, which still bears the stained glass windows from the 12th century church that once stood on the site, and the pharmacy, which has been in operation since the 17th century. The ornately decorated 16th century Town Hall now houses the local history museum. There are several other museums in the city, ranging from the National Car Museum, to the Musée de l'impression sur étoffes, which celebrates to city's textile industry.

name: Nazareth
description: For much of history, Nazareth was a shunned backwater. The birthplace of Mary, and home to Jesus for years, it was directly belittled in the New Testament. Despite its importance to Christianity, the town itself owes much of its identity to the Ottomans. Today, the Old Town is famous among Israelis for its Arabic market, and its streets are lined with Ottoman-style buildings made from rough stone, with many signs written in Arabic to cater to the predominantly Muslim population. While this is a unique sight in Israel, it's the Christian monuments that attract droves of tourists and pilgrims, the Pope included. First among these is the massive Church of the Annunciation, the largest church in the Middle East, which stands atop the grotto where Mary was told she would become the mother of the Son of God. Next door is the more humble Church of St. Joseph, which stands atop the former home of the Holy Family.

name: Jurmala
description: The city of Jūrmala is actually a string of historic fishing villages that caught the eye of wealthy landowners in the 18th century, who began building their own villas to relax in. After the Napoleonic Wars, Russian officers brought Jūrmala to the attention of the country's upper class, establishing a tradition that passed on to high-ranking Communist officials, and modern tycoons and oligarchs. Jūrmala's main drag, a 1 km long pedestrian street known as Jomas iela, is lined with historic wooden buildings, with a few modern developments, that now house boutiques, cafes, and restaurants. Alternatively, visitors can opt for a stroll along the 33 kilometer white sand beach, or the wooden seaside boardwalk. Preserving the local heritage, the Jurmala Open-Air Museum exhibits a traditional fishing homestead, historic anchors and boats, as well as Latvia's largest rope collection, which is on display in the hands-on rope-twisting workshop.

name: Bellinzona
description: The ancient Romans saw the defensive advantage the natural landscape in this valley provided and erected a frontier post, which was later expanded by the Lombards, and ultimately made into a heavily fortified Milanese town, controlling access to the Alps from the South. The heavy Italian influence has left its mark on the city, such as the neo-Classical theatre. The picturesque streets and squares are filled with decadent patrician homes and beautiful churches. Yet it is the city's triple fortifications that are the most arresting. One of only 12 UNESCO World Heritage sites in Switzerland, they are some of the best preserved fortifications in the country. The Castelgrande is the oldest and mightiest, and offers breathtaking views of the Old Town and surrounding area, as well as a museum covering the history of Bellinzona.

name: Rheinsberg
description: In the 18th century, Frederick the Great acquired an older estate, and had it renovated and expanded, laying the foundations for the Rheinsberg Palace as it stands today. Frederick described his time at the palace as the "happiest of his life", but had to leave when he ascended to the throne. He passed the estate to his brother Henry, who reshaped the castle and garden in the Classical style, and filled the estate with art. Set on the water, visitors can stroll the castle's sprawling park to admire its facade, and the beautiful surroundings. The lavish interiors preserve both Frederik and Henry's aesthetics, with the beautifully decorated rooms housing period furniture, lavish fixtures, and of course, an impressive art collection. The castle is also home to the Rheinsberg Music Academy and the chamber opera Schloss Rheinsberg, which occasionally perform on-site, and the Kurt Tucholsky Literature Museum, dedicated to the life and work of the famous social critic.

name: Heckington Windmill
description: Heckington Windmill was built in 1830 as a standard five-sailed windmill, with the 8-sail system being added at the end of the 19th century. The mill stopped working in 1946, and it wasn't restored for 40 years. In 1992, Heckington Windmill played a key role in a Guinness World Record for the fastest produced loaf of bread, letting local bakers take wheat from the field to the table in just 21 minutes! Today, visitors can explore the mill's six floors to learn about every aspect of milling, from the parts of a grain of wheat, to the mechanics behind the mill mechanism. Please note that the stairs between floors are very steep and narrow, so can be difficult for those with mobility issues. Even if you can't make it up the stairs, the mill's ground floor houses a visitor center, and there's a charming tea room in the miller's house, and an on-site brewery. For more information, please visit heckingtonwindmill.org.uk

name: Cascada de la Tzararacua
description: Mainly composed of volcanic rock, Cascada de la Tzararacua was formed with almost artistic precision by Mother Nature. This last frontier of the River Cupatitzio punctuates its long journey by making a dramatic descent down the wondrous red cliffs into the pools below. A memorable excursion for nature lovers and curious travelers alike, the 579 step hike through 45 hectares of Oak Pine forest showcases the sanctuary the falls have provided for flora and fauna as well as the mammals tracing up and down its viny cliffs. For the travelers not up for a hike, the trail can alternatively be made by horseback.

name: Kranj
description: Kranj is the capital of the Gorenjska region and is situated between two alpine rivers - Sava and Kokra. The city is an old Roman settlement, illustrating Gothic and Baroque architecture. Many Slovenes have contributed to Kranj's development, most notably the famous poet France Presern. The preserved old town is known for its medieval skyline shaped by city walls, a castle, and church towers. The old town has been protected as a cultural monument since 1983. It features a plethora of historical monuments, modern art spaces, and museums. There are also many bars, shops, and theaters to explore in this picturesque town.

name: Linz
description: Since ancient times, Linz has primarily been known as a transport and administrative centre. But in recent years, the city has embraced new technologies to startling effect and become a member of UNESCO's Creative Cities Network as a city of media arts. In few other central European cities does the past sit so well with the contemporary. To get a sense of the past climb the Postlingberg hill to the 18th Century Pilgrimage Church, enjoying the views of the city and the Danube as you go. Down on the south side of the river is the dazzling glass oval of the Brucknerhouse, built to commemorate Linzian composer Anton Bruckner. And just a couple of hundred metres away is the Lentos Art Museum, an ultra-modernist but ineffably stylish building, glowing a hot summer-sky-blue, pink, red, or violet at night, houses a huge and absorbing collection of modernist painting, sculpture and object art.

name: Kortrijk
description: Located near the French border, Kortrijk began as a Gallo-Roman town, making it one of the oldest settlements in Belgium. Starting from the car-free city center, the early-Gothic townhall, which visitors can tour to see its stunning interior. Nearby, the UNESCO-listed belfry. The city's St. Martin's Collegiate Church dates back to the 1300s, while the Our Lady's Church is 100 years older. The list of interesting sights continues with another UNESCO-protected sight, the St. Elizabeth Beguinage. All these monuments and much more create an unrepeatable experience and charm of Kortrijk, a city that's still waiting to be fully appreciated.

name: Cunha
description: Surrounded by rolling hills, sleepy Cunha is a far cry from the bustle of São Paulo. Here, you'll still see the occasional vaquero clip-clopping along the cobbled streets on horseback, and you'll definitely see colorful Volkswagen Beetles parked in front of the pastel houses on every street. It's estimated that there's a bug for every 17 people in Cunha. Between the slow pace of life, quaint churches and and historic cars, exploring Cunha definitely feels like you've been transported back in time. If you want to support the local economy (and need a souvenir), be sure to stop by the Casa do Artesão (Craftsman House), for some handmade ceramics. If you'd rather your visit focus on views of the countryside, head to the low-key O Lavandário lavender farm. It's not like the sprawling fields you see on Instagram, but it's a great place to take in the views and maybe grab a bite at the cafe.

name: Blair Castle and Hercules Gardens
description: Founded in the 13th century, Blair Castle and Hercules Gardens have been home to 19 generations of Stewarts and Murrays of Atholl. Over its long history, the castle has been visited by notable figures including Mary Queen of Scots, Viscount Dundee, Bonnie Prince Charlie, and Queen Victoria, who granted permission to Duke Murray to found the Atholl Highlanders - Europe's last (legal) private army. Today, over 30 historic rooms exhibit period furnishings, family portraits, landscape paintings, weapons and armour, and lavish decorations for a full serving of Scottish culture. A walk through the nine acre walled garden brings visitors past fruit trees and vegetable, a Chinese bridge and Gothic folly, and a path lined with both contemporary and 18th Century sculptures. In a quiet grove, visitors will find the second tallest tree in Britain, and the ruins of St Brides Kirk, the final resting place of Jacobite leader Bonnie Dundee. For more information, please visit blair-castle.co.uk

name: ZSL Whipsnade Zoo
description: The ZSL Whipsnade Zoo opened in 1931 after Sir Peter Chalmers Mitchell visited the Bronx Zoological Park, making it the first easily accessible open zoo in Europe. From its humble beginnings with two Lady Amherst's pheasants, a golden pheasant, and five red junglefowl, the zoo has grown to house nearly 4000 animals from nearly 200 different species in a 600 acre park. Visitors can see lions, tigers, elephants, and giraffes in huge outdoor enclosures, and even hop aboard a safari bus. Dedicated to conservation and education, the zoo hosts keeper talks and animal displays so visitors can learn how the playful Red Panda adapted to life in the Himalayas, or how hippos evolved in Africa. For more information, please visit zsl.org/zsl-whipsnade-zoo

name: Caltagirone
description: Settled since prehistoric times, Caltagirone literally means 'Castle of Jars' in Arabic for its 11th century Arabic castle and long-time pottery tradition. In 1630, nearly the entire city was destroyed by an earthquake and rebuilt in the Baroque style. This exceptional ensemble of extravagant architecture earned the town a place on the UNESCO list. Today, the town is unique in Sicily thanks to its ceramic-adorned architecture, which is highlighted by the 142 steps of the Scalinata di Santa Maria del Monte, where the upright of each step is decorated with colorful ceramic tiles. The tiled steps are also the centerpiece of celebrations throughout the year, seeing them covered in an enormous floral display at the end of May, and flickering candles on July 24th and 25th. But the steps aren't the only attraction - the entire town is bursting with beautiful churches, palaces, and shops, rewarding visitors for exploring its narrow streets.

name: Assisi
description: This scenic village has seen its share of saints. In 1208, St. Francis founded his eponymous order here, and St. Clare, and Saint Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows were also born here. Originally a Roman settlement, remnants of their empire are still visible, such as the city walls, the forum, which has been transformed into the Piazza del Comune, and the Temple of Minerva, which has maintained its original facade, even though was transformed into the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in 1539. The massive complex that can be seen from miles away is the Sanctuary of Assisi. One of the oldest Gothic churches left in Italy, and the final resting place of St. Francis, its interior rivals many museums, with frescoes by Cimabue, Giotto, Simone Martini and Pietro Lorenzetti.

name: Vientiane
description: Likely founded as a Khmer settlement in the 9th century, Vientiane was an important administrative city, but wasn't made the capital of Lan Xang until the 16th century, and between 1707 and 1779 it was even the center of its own kingdom. Like the rest of Laos, Vientiane was colonized by the French in the 19th century, and left with a tangible Franco-feel, particularly with its wide boulevards, cafe culture, and wine shops - they even have their own Arc de Triomphe that you can scale for great views of the city! In the heart of the city, French colonial villas have been transformed into upscale restaurants, boutiques, hotels, and, in the case of the French governor's mansion, the National History Museum. Saffron robed monks are a common sight, and of the city's many temples, the fortress-like, gilded, That Luang is the holiest site in the country.

name: Guadalajara
description: In the past Guadalajara was known for its tradition, conservatism, and Catholicism, while nowadays it is increasingly progressive, to the point where it's become famed for its gay scene. The city's broad, palm-lined avenues are blessed with an abundance of cafes, bars, and restaurants, while on weekends they are filled with free concerts and vibrant street markets. Don't miss the local specialties, such as carne en su jugo or torta ahogada, washed down with tejuino (fermented corn drink). Cultural attractions are many, from shopping in the colourful and pedestrianised Tlaquepaque area, to the beautiful twin-towered 17th century Basilica of Zapopan, to passionate football matches hosted by either Chivas or Atlas (and preferably a match between them!). Of the many historic buildings you can see the huge hospital complex of Hospicio Cabañas, built in 1791, is one of oldest and largest in the Americas, as well as being a UNESCO site.
