name: Guayaquil
description: Guayaquil was founded by the Spanish in 1538 on the site of a native village, and has since grown into the largest city in Ecuador, and one of the main Pacific ports in South America. Its heritage is still visible in the colorful colonial buildings of the Las Peñas district, particularly in the hillside enclave of Cerro Santa Ana, which takes a trying 444 steps to summit. The Parque Histórico offers a look into different elements of Ecuadorean heritage and includes an open air zoo with native fauna, an early 20th century settlement, and agricultural area. However, the real soul of the city is the Malecón 2000 - Guayaquil's waterfront promenade where you'll find everything from gardens to the Museum of Anthropology and Contemporary Art, and South America's largest Ferris wheel. If you're hungry, you can get some fresh local seafood from one of the many food markets.

name: Shikotsukoonsen
description: Nestled within the breathtaking landscapes of Shikotsu-Toya National Park, Shikotsukoonsen's allure lies in its pristine and little-developed surroundings. Lake Shikotsuko and the nearby Lake Toyako, both born from ancient volcanic activity, set the stage for an enchanting journey into Hokkaido's pristine beauty. Here, high-class ryokans, restaurants, and souvenir stores line the lakefront, creating a harmonious blend of luxury and nature. Dominating the horizon is Mount Tarumae, a majestic yet active volcano offering a thrilling ascent. At the northern shores of the lake, Marukoma Onsen stands as a haven of relaxation. This ryokan's unique hot spring baths, open to all, are situated along the lake shore, allowing an exchange between the pools' warm waters and the cool lake. With gender-segregated conventional hot spring pools, Marukoma Onsen offers a rejuvenating experience amid the natural splendor.

name: Playa Delfines
description: Playa Delfines (sometimes called El Mirador) has the crystal-clear waters and white sand beaches you expect in Cancun. It is conveniently located near many major hotels, but it is not overshadowed by the tall buildings like many other beaches - perfect for tanning! It is popular for surfing due to the strong winds, but they also make this beach more dangerous than many others. Lifeguards are posted and they use a flag system to indicate danger levels, so be aware of your surroundings during your visit. El Mirador, or the lookout point, is the perfect spot to capture spectacular sunsets with a panoramic view of the sky, sand, and waves. Time your visit for the early evening for the wide range of warm hues in the sky that play well off of the blue sea.

name: Sankt Wolfgang
description: Dating back to the early Middle Ages, Sankt Wolfgang became pilgrimage site after the canonization of the eponymous saint. At first, its waterfront church drew visitors looking for blessings, but after being rebuilt in the 14th century, it became renowned for its art collection. The interior of the seemingly simple structure is completely covered in Baroque frescoes and stucco, and houses a collection of amazing altars. The most well known is the 15th century Pacher Altar, a masterpiece of Gothic art, and the only preserved piece by Michael Pacher. However, the largest and grandest is the angel-covered Baroque double altar. After admiring these exceptional pieces, visitors can take a leisurely stroll along Sankt Wolfgang's waterfront to soak in its stunning natural beauty.

name: Jaco
description: Revel in this tropical jungle on Costa Rica's Pacific coastline. A relatively young and thriving community, Jaco was only founded in 1965 and has since been recognized as one of National Geographic's 'Top Ten Adventure Trips'! Start your adventure by delving into the town's backdrop of rich, green wilderness; best experienced through the Rainforest Adventures' network of ziplines, high ropes, and the revered tree-top tram - the 'Tranopy'. Once you're back on the forest floor, experience the magic of the Butterfly Garden and witness some of Costa Rica's most colorful wildlife! If you've still not had your fill of the forest, you can hike to the Pura Vida Gardens or to the impressive Catarata Bijagual waterfall, one of the tallest waterfalls in Costa Rica. For even more adventure, ATV and 4x4 tours will take you deeper into the jungle. When morning comes, head to the beach! Surf schools hold classes for all abilities; even the most inexperienced will get their chance to ride a gnarly wave. Climb to the El Miro ruins to see all the action from above. This panoramic vista will be the envy of everyone back home. As the sun sets, kick back and relax at Jaco's exotic beach bars or gaze across the horizon from horseback, along this 2.5-mile (4 km) stretch of volcanic coastline.

name: Covadonga
description: In 722 AD, king Pelayo led his Christian army to victory over the Muslims in Covadonga. Christianity's first victory over the ruling Arabs, many attribute the battle as the start of the 700-year effort to expel the Muslims from the Iberian peninsula. Today, Covadonga is a place of worship and pilgrimage for the people of Asturias. The 18th century basilica, built in neo-Romanesque style, houses some beautiful artwork. The almost-mythical cave, accessed via a staircase is home to a statue of La Santina, the tomb of king Pelayo, and that of king Alfonso I. The spring flowing from the cave feeds a fountain with seven spouts. Regardless of faith, visitors can enjoy the peaceful setting and natural beauty of this complex dedicated to one of the major turning points in European history.

name: Olvera
description: There has been much debate over the origins of this town, which is situated at the tip of the "White Towns Route"—a series of towns and large villages in Southern Spain known for their whitewashed walls. Some think the city was established around the time of the Celts, while archaeological evidence, including evidence found in the castle foundation, suggests the existence of a Roman settlement. No matter the origins, one thing is certain: Olvera is teeming with history. Visitors can explore the Neoclassical Parish of Our Lady of the Incarnation, built in 1822; the Arab Castle, constructed at the end of the 12th century on a strategic rock giving it the ability to communicate with other nearby castles through signals; the Moorish Wall, supported by seven buttresses; and the Villa District, whose streets will bring you back to a time some 700 years ago.

name: Chartwell
address.addr1: Chartwell, Mapleton Rd, Westerham TN16 1PS, UK
description: Chartwell estate solidified itself in English history in 1922 when it was purchased by Winston Churchill. Here, he obsessed over landscaping and painting, fought against German rearmament, raised his family, and recovered from his stroke. In 1946, Churchill's financial problems almost forced him to sell Chartwell, but Lord Camrose and a group of Churchill's friends raised funds allowing the National Trust to buy the house - provided the Churchills retain a life-tenancy. Today, visitors can make their way through Churchills' home for a look at his private life, and see the collection of gifts he received. An avid painter, Churchill's studio is covered floor-to-ceiling with the world's largest collection of the statesman's artwork. Visitors can also enjoy a pleasant walk through Chartwell's grounds, enjoying the view that convinced Churchill to buy the house, and even sit on the very chair he used to spend hours on in quiet contemplation, feeding his beloved fish. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/chartwell

name: Kutaisi
description: Nestled along the Rioni River, Kutaisi's laid-back aura is an appealing introduction to Georgian life. Throughout centuries, Kutaisi has been strategically important to several kingdoms and empires, and still is one of Georgia's most populated cities. Explore the city's diverse tapestry of centuries-old monuments, stunning natural scenery, and striking architecture. Treat your taste buds to delectable local cuisine and bask in the renowned Georgian hospitality. The city's symbol, the 11th-century Bagrati Cathedral, stands as a testament to Georgia's unity and prosperity. Other attractions include the Kutaisi Synagogue, art nouveau designs, the quirky Colchis Fountain, and even vibrant street art. Don't miss the colorful Green Bazaar, a bustling market bursting with sights, sounds, and smells. Close by, UNESCO-listed Gelati Monastery and Sataplia Cave with its dinosaur footprints await your discovery.

name: Kaunas
description: Established around the 10th century, Kaunas was an important medieval trade center, even joining the Hanseatic League in the 15th century. Over its long history, Kaunas was a prized property, and as such avoided much of the destruction that befell other cities. During the interwar period, it served as the capital of Lithuania, causing a cultural Renaissance. Today, visitors can admire the countless Art Deco and National Romanticism architecture, tree-lined boulevards, and charming cafes that earned the city the nickname 'Little Paris', UNESCO Recognition, and the title of European City of Culture. In the heart of the Old Town, the Town Hall Square is an airy plaza where visitors can relax, and admire the 16th century town hall and 18th century church. For a bit of history found nowhere else in the world, Kaunas is home to the Devil Museum, which houses 2,000 depictions of the devil from all over the world.

name: Auckland
description: Auckland at first seems like a contradiction - is it a skyscraper paradise, or a hub for the nature-loving? Good news for you: it's both! Visit the famous One Tree Hill for a panorama of the surrounding city and its historic monument to the Maori people. If you're looking for views, however, look no further than Sky Tower: the tallest structure in the Southern Hemisphere, with a stunning observation deck. Culture-lovers are also in luck - stop by the Wallace Arts Center for a constantly-rotating collection, or the Auckland Museum for Maori artefacts and Pacific natural history.

name: Hamilton
description: New Zealand's largest inland city, Hamilton is a lively town with a youthful, dynamic and innovative population thanks to its many student residents. The country's longest river is the focal point as it runs through the city; enjoy it on one of the cities many scenic riverside walking trails. On the south of the bank is the horticultural haven, Hamilton Gardens, the cities most visited attraction, which challenges the average botanical garden with extravagant displays in numerous themed plots. From China to England, Japan to Italy, the 50 hectare attraction tells a historical story of culture and civilizations expressed through garden design. Further along the riverbank is the Waikato Museum, with an extensive arts display across 13 galleries, and a vast range of exhibitions aimed to educate visitors about the heritage and culture of the Waikato region. Cosmopolitan Hamilton is packed with restaurants, quirky cafes and bars for those looking to leave the city refreshed!

name: Nis
description: One of the oldest cities in Europe, Niš was founded by the Romans in 279 BC. Over the centuries, the city was also ruled by the Ottomans, and during WWII, the Nazis. Today, visitors can still find Roman ruins in the 18th century Ottoman. The Ottomans also left behind the gruesome Skull Tower, a structure filled with the skulls of Serbian rebels. More chilling however is the Red Cross concentration camp, which held over 35,000 people. It was the site of the first successful breakout from a concentration camp, which resulted in the execution of 1,100 prisoners. Today, prisoners barracks has been turned into a museum. A tour the second floor shows where important political prisoners were held, complete with engravings on to the walls, and the original barbed wire lined floors that inmates were forced to sleep on as a form of punishment.

name: Mercedes
description: While Mercedes was officially founded in 1788, this town has had colonial significance since 1520. Mercedes was the site of the first step towards independence from Spain, which is why its coat of arms bears the slogan "our country started here." Standing on the banks of the Negro River, Mercedes is the perfect destination for fishing, nautical sports and other outdoor activities, and the riverfront promenade offers a pleasant place to stroll, taking in the river views and many statues. Alternatively, you can admire the beautiful 18th-century cathedral on the Plaza Independencia and the surrounding colonial architecture. This lively city is also home to the Museo Paleontologico Alejandro Berro which has an extensive fossil collection, including a very well preserved glyptodon, which is an extinct type of armadillo nearly the size of a Volkswagen beetle!

name: Lod
description: First mentioned in the 15th century BC, Lod was an important Judean town up through the early Christian period. The birthplace of St. George, the Crusaders built a cathedral here in the dragon-slayer's honor, which was transformed into a mosque once Lod came under Muslim rule. Up until the 1948 war, the city's population was almost entirely Muslim, and today, it's one of the few places in Israel that still has a large Arabic community. Lod's Great Mosque stands as a symbol of this mixed community, being one of the best-preserved Crusader churches in Israel, where both medieval Christian and Muslim inscriptions can be seen. The city's most precious historic monument are the intricate Byzantine mosaics which are among the largest and finest in the country.

name: Tepoztlan
description: As pleasant as Tepoztlan is, with its informative Carlos Pellicer archaeological museum and UNESCO site of Dominico de la Natividad (16th convent turned art gallery), most people who arrive here are interested in one thing only - walking in the footsteps of Aztec pilgrims up to the dizzying heights of the Temple of Tepoztēcatl which looms amongst the crags. Tepoztēcatl was the Aztec god of fertility and pulque, an alcoholic beverage made from fermented agave sap. The temple was important enough to draw devoted followers of this god to this pre-Colombian town from as far away as modern day Guatemala. The walk is steep and a round trip, which encompasses dense forests, interesting rock formations, and stunning waterfalls, will take around 2 hours. The toil is worth it though for the small but perfectly formed pyramid at the end, and of course that amazing god-like view of the world below.

name: Sant Josep de sa Talaia
description: In the foothills of Sa Talaia, the tallest mountain on Ibiza, Sant Josep de Sa Talaia - otherwise known as San José - manifests Ibiza's island lifestyle. Locals outnumber tourists in this charming village, which offers vast mountain views and direct access to the undulating ocean spilling from its coastline. In the cobbled alleyways you'll find an excellent choice of restaurants, cocktail bars, local butchers and patisseries. The San José Church boasts a wide portico and is unique in its exceptional height compared to other villages in Ibiza, hosting wonderful artwork and interior design inside. As the bells of the belfry ring through the streets, wander through the traditional Saturday markets where over 20 stalls offer organic products. In Sant Josep de Sa Talaia, you can truly live like a local.

name: Archanes
description: Located in a mountain basin, 380 meters up the Giouchtas mountains, Archanes is a pleasant agricultural town with a surprisingly rich history. Archaeological excavations have found the village has been inhabited for 5,000 years, and served as the summer palace for the Kings of Knossos. While most of the archaeological sites are still being excavated and are closed to the public, the village's Minoan, Byzantine and Folklore museums offer great opportunities to see some of the artifacts that have been uncovered. But Archanes' main attraction is its olive oil and wine. Sit down at a taverna in the square for some local cuisine accompanied by wine and rakia, or visit one of the nearby wineries. In the summer, you can even help harvest grapes as part of the Archanes Farmer Festival celebration.

name: Enna
description: Settled since the 14th century BC, Enna's position atop a large plateau surrounded by cliffs made it one of the most well-defended settlements of the ancient world, said to have only ever been taken through treachery. Visitors can still get a glimpse of the city's martial past at the Castello di Lombardia, one of the most important examples of military architecture in Sicily, which now hosts cultural events in its inner courtyard. Enna's Cathedral, a UNESCO Place of Peace, is an extravagant mix of architectural and artistic styles, filled with amazing woodwork, stupendous stuccoes, and even Classical ruins at the base of the pulpit. Visitors can also get a look at the cathedral's many sacred treasures, including vestments and jewelry, at the Alessi Museum. Nearby, there's also an archaeological museum showcasing a wide range of regional artifacts. (please note: as of January 2025, the castle is closed for renovations but is still viewable from the outside)

name: Teotihuacan
description: Founded around 200 BC, Teotihuacan rapidly grew into the largest and most influential city in Mesoamerica. At its peak, it was home to over 100,000 people (with some estimates as high as 250,000), thousands of buildings, and had conquered multiple Mayan city-states. And then, it collapsed in the 7th or 8th century, and had been long-abandoned when the Aztecs found it in the 13th century. Today, Teotihuacan is one of the most impressive and enigmatic archaeological sites in the world, with the 65-meter-tall Pyramid of the Sun (the 3rd largest in the world), 43-meter-tall Pyramid of the Moon, and a number of smaller temples lining the Avenue of the Dead at the heart of the city. Between the two main pyramids, you'll find the Palace Museum of Quetzalpapálotl - a 6th century complex with intricate carvings and murals. While you can explore Teotihuacan on your own, for more in-depth insights, you can also arrange a guided tour.

name: Santa Barbara, CA
description: Santa Barbara began as a Spanish military outpost and mission, but has since transformed into one of California's prime coastal cities. The perfect weather, beautiful scenery, and charming buildings has earned it the nickname "The American Riviera". Just pay a visit to the Refugio State Beach or Lookout Park (from where you can see the famous Channel Islands National Park) to get a taste of the natural beauty that has enticed visitors from around the world. In the city proper, you'll find charming, red-roofed Spanish-style houses. While many of these are from the early-20th century, the Old Mission Santa Barbara dates back to the original Spanish settlement and is the state's prettiest, while the El Cuartel adobe at the presidio is the second oldest surviving building in the state. Of course, as the poster child for the California good life, the city is filled with excellent shops and dining - especially if seafood is your thing!

name: Dammam
description: Known for its green parks, inviting waterfronts and sandy beaches, Dammam makes for an enchanting capital city of the Eastern Province and promises a vibrant atmosphere year-round. Even in winter, when temperatures average in the low 20's celsius, the city remains enjoyable for visitors. The city is gaining recognition as an arts, sports and entertainment hub, housing Saudi Arabia's first street-art exhibition in Al Khobar's Bayoonya district, along with various cultural centers and museums such as SCITECH and the Taybeen, Alfelwah and Aljowharah museums. Visit the iconic landmark of the King Abdulaziz Center for World Culture, also known as Ithra, which symbolizes Saudi Arabia's cultural renaissance. With its striking monolithic design, the sprawling complex accommodates a theater, library, cinema, galleries and a museum. Stroll through the bustling Share Al Hob souq, where traders, performers and street musicians create a vibrant atmosphere in the marketplace and showcase the best of Dammam's cultural experiences.

name: Rosslyn Chapel
description: Founded in the mid-15th century, Rosslyn Chapel is an artistic masterpiece, with nearly every surface completely covered in intricate carvings, but it's the strange symbolism that's been captivating curious minds for centuries. One father-son duo believe the hundreds of intricately carved stone boxes protruding from the pillars represent the patterns formed by vibrating powder. There are also over 110 carvings of "Green Men", which might represent pagan deities, and shapes are said to be corn, even though Columbus hadn't yet set sail for the New World. Then there's the famed 'Apprentice Pillar', a masterfully carved column said to have been made by an apprentice mason who was murdered by his master in a fit of jealousy - as punishment the master's face was carved in the opposite wall to forever gave upon his apprentice's handiwork. However, the juiciest mystery is the chapel's mysterious crypt and the secret Templar treasure, which could be anything from Jesus' head to the original Scottish Crown Jewels.

name: Zikhron Ya'akov
description: Zichron Yaakov was founded in 1882 by a group of 100 Jewish pioneers from Romania. The rocky slopes of Mount Carmel proved difficult to farm, and beset by an outbreak of malaria, many abandoned the settlement within the first year. Fortunately, French-Jewish philanthropist and winemaker Baron Edmond James de Rothschild stopped here during his visit to Israel and found the hill offered superb wine-growing properties. He established a winery, and revitalized Zichron Yaakov as a winemaking town. Today, the main street preserves many of the original buildings, with the First Aliyah Museum telling the town's origin story. Aside from the relaxing atmosphere, the main draw is a visit to the famed Carmel Winery - the oldest and largest in Israel. On the outskirts of town are the beautiful (and free!) Ramat HaNadiv gardens, made in honor of Baron Rothschild, and centered around the crypt of the Baron and his wife.

name: Treviso
description: Treviso's international airport gives visitors the opportunity to explore Venice, the famous city on water, but Treviso is an underrated town waiting to be discovered. Rebuilt from nearly nothing after the second World War, there is still much to see and do in this town. Its maze-like streets, cobblestoned alleys, and arched walkways induce delight in every nook and cranny. While finding your way around, make sure to visit the former church turned museum: Museo di Santa Caterina. This museum has vivid colors, magnificent cloisters, and beautiful frescoes. If sipping bubbly is more your style, then I'm sure you already know that Treviso is known as the original homeland of Prosecco. Prosecco can be found everywhere and is ready for tasting in plenty of varieties. We suggest sampling a glass with some dessert tiramisu, as it's often disputed that tiramisu was first created in Treviso. Confirmed or not, a trip to Italy isn't complete without a delectable treat and a glass of wine.

name: Kuang Si Falls
description: The Kuang Si Waterfalls are not only the largest cascades in the region, but the focal-point of an enchanting ecological area. A jungle river rolls down three tiers before plummeting 50 meters over the main fall and into a bright blue-green pool. For many, the beautiful travertine pools set amidst the lush tropical jungle aren't just eye-candy - they're stunning swimming holes. Along with this striking spectacle, the area around Kuang Si Falls encourages visitors to take a deeper interest in nature, with a butterfly farm and bear rescue center based nearby.

name: Seitan Limania
description: Crete might have plenty of beautiful locations, but Seitan Limania wins the title of "Crete's most Instagrammable beach". Located close to the city of Chania, its uniquely shaped canyons, turquoise water and white sand are guaranteed to make your social media friends jealous. But enough about the looks: the water at this beach is calm and shallow, which is good for a relaxed, safe swim, but since the canyons prevent the water from warming up, it might end up being quite chilly. If you're lucky, you might even meet the local goats – the occasional visitors at Seitan Limania (hey, goats like relaxing on a beach too!). Be aware that the descent to the beach is quite steep, and it is best to put on a trusty pair of sneakers for the walk downhill.

name: Butrint
description: Occupied from 50,000 BC up to the 19th century, Butrint has been the site of a Greek colony, a Roman city and a bishopric. From 800 BC the site was a Greek "polis", with a large theatre that still stands today. In 44 BC, the Romans expanded the settlement considerably and built an aqueduct across the Vivari Channel. By the 5th century AD, Christians gained control of the territory and added fortifications and structures of their own, such as a 6th-century basilica. The city was ultimately abandoned in the late Middle Ages after marshes formed in the area. Today, site is a collection of ruins representing the different periods in the city's development, and a paradise for fans of ancient architecture.

name: Cafayate
description: Hey you, wine lover! If you decided to visit Argentina just for the wine – no judgment here. You have to promise one thing though: visit Cafayate, a town located over 5 thousand feet above sea level in Calchaquíes valleys- where some of the best and original wines in Argentina are produced. While the white Torrontes is the crown jewel, there are some well-known types of reds that are honorable mentions, such as the local Cabernet Sauvignon or Malbec. Cafayate, a charming and tranquil city in itself, is surrounded by deserts and mountains, which make for a dramatic and picturesque landscape. But back to wine: Cafayate has wineries for every taste and budget, and many wine cellars around the town offer free tours (thank us later for the tip!) Pair a glass of your wine of choice with goat cheese, or, if you're feeling adventurous, get wine in a cone or wine-flavored ice cream – but please don't offer it to your children, they should enjoy regular ice cream from any of the town's numerous ice cream shops. Important note: it is not recommended to visit Cafayate during bad weather, especially during or right after heavy rain.

name: Altotting
description: The little town of Altotting has always been closely tied to the nobility and the church - the first buildings in the area were a Carolingian royal palace here, and later, in the 9th century, a Benedictine monastery. In the 15th century, the town became one of the most popular pilgrimage sites in Germany after news spread that a 3-year-old local boy who had drowned in the river was revived when his distraught mother placed him in front of the statue of the Virgin Mary at the town chapel's high altar. The chapel altarpiece is an amazing example of goldsmithing, depicting key figures from Christianity in gold and colored enamel. Also kept in the chapel are the hearts of King Ludwig II of Bavaria, the builder of Neuschwanstein castle, as well as his father's and grandfather's.

name: Schliersee
description: In 778, five brothers of Bavarian nobility stumbled across the wild plains and nurturing lake, thus beginning the story of Schliersee. Today more than 6,500 people live in Schliersee, with a lively center and a cheerful marketplace. A visit to the Bayern region wouldn't be complete without alcohol. Grab your purse and taste some delicious whisky at the Slyrs Distillery. Schliersee has grown popular for its winter activities, a perfect location for skiing and touring the winter sport museum. Don't forget to also visit the Markus Wasmeir open-air museum and take a short walk to Josefsthaler Waterfall to immerse yourself in mists of water splashing your face.

name: Szeged
description: With the highest number of sunny days throughout the year, Szegard is a popular family friendly destination. A top place to beat the heat is at the amazing indoor water theme park called Napfenyfurdo Aquapolis. Even in the winter, there is plenty of other indoor adventures at the hotels and spas that focus solely on wellness! Once you're fully pampered by the salt baths and the like, wander the city and admire the National Theater, the Grof Palace, and the Interactive Science Knowledgestore. Prefer the outdoors? Spend your time at Dom Square, the Erzsébet Park or walking along the River Marcos.

name: Iquique
description: The Chilean city of Iquique is often compared to Miami in the U.S. because of its laid-back atmosphere. Nestled in the heart of the Atacama Desert at Chile's northernmost point, this frequently overlooked destination offers a unique port city experience. Many visitors gravitate to beaches like Playa Cavancha for sunbathing or to take leisurely strolls along the boardwalk, especially during sunset. Beyond basking in the sun and admiring breathtaking sunsets, there's a plenty of fresh seafood delicacies waiting to be savored. Given its proximity to the ocean, a trip to the fish market is an absolute must. Both locals and tourists make their way to Caleta Riquelme, Iquique's fish market, to find everything from crabs and fish to shrimp and sea urchins. Downtown Iquique boasts a charming plaza, picturesque streets like Calle Baquedano, and a vibrant Central Market. As you wander, be on the lookout for evocative, politically-charged street art and graffiti.

name: Cuicocha
description: Laguna Cuicocha was created by a massive volcanic eruption about 3100 years ago, which formed a water-filled caldera, and four islands. Literally meaning "lake of guinea pigs", its named for the shape of the largest island, which is said to resemble one of these important animals. A hiking trails works its way around the rim of the lake, offering fantastic views of this picturesque formation.

name: Ponferrada
description: Beginning as a Roman citadel to guard their largest gold mining operation, Ponferrada became a major staging point on the Way of St. James in the Middle Ages. In the 12th century, King Fernando II of León put the settlement in the hands of the Knights Templar, who built a mighty castle to protect the town and passing pilgrims. To this day, the fortress stands watch over the town and invites visitors to step into the world of the Templars. In the old quarter below, you can find some beautiful Renaissance monuments like the clock tower, and in the Plaza de la Encina, the elegant Basilica de la Encina with its baroque tower. One of the town's architectural gems is the Church of Santo Tomás de las Ollas on the outskirts of town. This amazing 10th century Mozarab temple harmoniously blends Christian and Moorish architecture.

name: Lucca
description: Lucca is a relatively flat city with roads open to everyone: cars, pedestrians, bicycles, and scooters alike. Although open, priority is given to pedestrians, making Lucca a walk-friendly city. Its impressive walls that surround the heart of the city are well maintained and fully intact. Despite the many years of calm that have rendered the Renaissance-era walls useless, it has now been repurposed. The entire circle is a pedestrian walkway surrounded by an outer lying stretch of green. The pedestrian promenade makes it ideal to see all of Lucca's major gems from above. Once you get back on solid ground, be sure to visit the Duomo di San Martino, the Basilica di San Frediano, and traces of the amphitheatre in Piazza dell'Anfiteatro.

name: Fethiye
description: Fethiye was founded in late antiquity as Telmessos, a major Lycian city famed for its school of diviners, who attracted the likes of King Croesus and Alexander the Great. In 1958, the city was devastated by an earthquake, and it's since been reborn as one of Turkey's premier holiday destinations on the Mediterranean, and is now a hub for Turkish yacht cruises, and a favoured home base for beach-goers. While it's hard to tear your eyes away from the coast and its pretty islands, history lovers will want to head toward the cliffs behind the town. Here you'll find ancient Lycian rock tombs carved into the cliff face. And there are more free-standing tombs scattered throughout town, including one right in front of the governor's office. The Fethiye Museum is also worth a visit for its surprisingly extensive collection of artefacts dating back to Antiquity.

name: Ban Gioc - Detian Falls
description: Ban Gioc Waterfall is one of the most impressive and best known waterfalls in Vietnam, and at 300 meters wide, they're the broadest in the country. The falls are part of the Quay Son River, which flows from China through a serene rural landscape backed by soaring karst peaks. Before visiting the three-tiered cascade you'll first need to purchase a police permit (200,000d for up to 10 people) from the station beside the falls. Once you're officially cleared, you can watch the falls from afar, or pay to ride a bamboo raft close enough to feel the spray on your face. Nearby is the Nguom Ngao Cave, which is often called the most beautiful in Vietnam for its many stupendous formations made even more impressive thanks to dramatic lighting (we'd recommend adding 90 minutes to your stop to visit these as well).

name: Linlithgow Palace
description: Originally a 12th century royal manor, Linlithgow Palace was the favoured residence of the Scottish crown starting with King James I. King James III, IV, V, and VI continuing construction on the castle during their reigns. In 1745, Bonnie Prince Charlie briefly visited the palace on his way south - an occasion marked by making the palace fountain flow with wine. A few months later, the Duke of Cumberland and his troops stayed in the palace as they chased Bonnie Prince Charlie back north, leaving the palace ablaze on their departure. Today, the castle still stands how the English left it - a roofless, partial-ruin. Walking the halls, visitors can admire elegant architecture, such as the oriel windows of the king's and queen's bedchambers, while learning about the private lives of Scottish royalty through informative signs. Visitors can also scale Queen Margaret's Bower for stupendous views over the peel and loch.

name: Zapopan
description: The second largest city in Jalisco, Zapopan is an up-and-coming metropolis with its rich historical sites with religious significance as well as its world-class shopping malls. The Basilica of Our Lady of Zapopan is one of the most visited sanctuaries in Mexico preserving a wooden Virgin of medieval origin. A notable visitor of the Basilica being Pope John Paul II. For our travelers looking for an ecological escape, there is El Diente rock, an impressive peak overlooking the natural landscape for miles on end. Zapopan has an extensive collection of cultural opportunities in the form of art galleries, murals and museums in its arsenal worthy of visiting. These include the Museo de Arte de Zapopan, Museo de Caceria Albarran, and the Municipal Cultural Centre. Zapopan with its collection of cultural, historical and natural wonders is most definitely a sight not worth missing out on!

name: Ystad
description: Ystad is a small coastal town located in the southernmost part of Sweden, known for its well-preserved medieval center, charming cobblestone streets, and recognisable cultural exports. It's home to the Ystad Studios, where the popular Swedish detective series "Wallander" was filmed. Fans of the show can take a guided tour of the filming locations and learn more about the series' production. You'll notice, wandering through the streets, that the architecture is unlike most of the rest of Sweden - this is due to its Danish influence, when Ystad belonged to Denmark until 1658. The result is a colorful town bursting with half-timbered houses, with some buildings dating back to the 15th century. Stora Östergatan is the place to go for the town's shops, cafes and restaurants, or if history takes your fancy, visit the Sofiero Castle or Ystads Theater. The ABBA Museum is dedicated to the biggest pop group to come out of Sweden and is a great stop for some musical entertainment.

name: Hue
description: Hue was the historic seat of the Nguyễn lords, who controlled all of Vietnam from 1802 to 1945, and made the city their imperial capital. Hue was devastated during the Vietnam War, being bombed by the Americans, while the Communists massacred thousands in what's been called the 'largest atrocity of the war'. Despite this, Hue's pride and culture persisted, and today the city is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its distinctive identity. At its heart, the Imperial City, a vast walled complex that was once home to the Vietnamese Emperors - they even have their own 'Forbidden City'. Artefacts from this era, ranging from traditional garments to artwork are on display at the Hue Museum of Royal Antiquities. Hue also has its own distinct cuisine, which shouldn't be missed, be it at a themed royal banquet, or one of the 50 varieties of sweet soup.

name: Asilah
description: Founded in the 8th or 9th century, Asilah was conquered by the Portuguese in the late 15th century, and the Spanish 100 years later, which has has left a distinctive Iberian influence on the town. While the Portuguese coastal fort is the most glaring example, step into one of the town's traditional restaurants and you'll see paella and tapas, with a heavy focus on fresh seafood. Wandering the streets, you'll be treated to intricate mashrabiya (oriel) windows and vibrantly painted walls, doors, and window frames. Those in the know know that this fishing village is actually one of Morocco's cultural meccas thanks to two local friends inviting artists to repaint the medina walls in 1978. This has since turned into the International Cultural Moussem of Asilah, a summer festival that attracts 100,000 people and transforms the town into an open-air museum.

name: Senlis
description: Dating back to the Romans, Senlis is still partially surrounded by the defensive wall they built in the 3rd century. However, the town's golden age came in the Middle Ages, when it was home to the monarchs of France, peaking in the 12th and 13th centuries. Today, the town is filled with reminders of its rich past, most prominently, the imposing Gothic cathedral. Built in the 12th Century, the soaring 78 m tower took another century to complete, and is considered one of the most beautiful in the country. Opposite the cathedral are the ruins of the 12th century castle, which are now a unique garden. Among the town's many other historic monuments, visitors can enjoy a stroll along the ancient Roman walls, or head to the 12th century Raoul de Vermandois, which now houses the Museum of Art and Archaeology, to learn about the town's rich history through art, religious objects, and ancient artefacts.

name: Tilcara
description: Nestled in the Quebrada de Humahuaca valley, surrounded by the Altiplano and Sub-Andean foothills, Tilcara has been inhabited for at least 10,000 years. These rugged mountains create a dramatic backdrop for the town where colorful indigenous traditions thrive. If you're visiting in August, you'll be able to see this first hand in the annual festival dedicated to the Incan goddess Pachamama. But no matter when you visit, you'll want to explore the ruins of Pucará de Tilcara. Built in the 12th century by the Omaguaca tribe, this pre-Hispanic hilltop fortification's strategic location offered panoramic views of the valley, giving inhabitants plenty of time to prepare for any approaching enemies. Now, it offers visitors one of the best vistas in northern Argentina. Along with walking among the historic dwellings, there's a small museum on site where you can learn how this indigenous tribe lived while the small botanical garden showcases the region's indigenous flora.

name: Kitzbuhel - Kirchberg
description: The resort annually hosts the World Cup ski race in the winter while in the summer months the town braces itself for the arrival of Europe's glitterati to attend the Austrian Tennis Open. This spectacular valley town is mostly pedestrianized in the center, which makes for ideal sightseeing and browsing the up-market shops and the winding, cobblestone streets that ooze charm and elegance. To make the most of any visit to Kitzbuhel, then the town ideally needs to be viewed from high in order to appreciate its stunning Alpine setting. Take the Hahnenkamm cable car, relax and enjoy the eye-popping views as it ascends to the station at the top of the mountain where there is the James Bond-esque world famous Restaurant Hochkitzbühel. The restaurant is renowned for its cuisine and not only provides an excellent choice of stopover for lunch but offers views of Kitzbuhel to die for, whether from inside the restaurant or outside on the terrace.

name: Mechelen
description: Settled since the Gallo-Roman era, Mechelen was given town rights in the 14th century, which started a rivalry with Antwerp that would last for the next 600 years. Over its long history, it was home to the likes of Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and Anne Boleyn, and today is the seat of Belgium's archbishop. The charming marketplatz is surrounded by beautiful baroque buildings and dominated by the UNESCO-listed Gothic cathedral. Visitors can brave the tower's 500 steps for stupendous views of the city, or just enjoy the church's exceptional artwork, which includes paintings by van Dyck and Rubens. The nearby town hall has cleverly combined the old council hall, cloth hall, and UNESCO-listed belfry into one building. The third UNESCO site is the charming Groot Begijnhof - a neighborhood built between the 13th and 16th centuries expressly to provide a community for religious women.

name: Cenote Yokdzonot
description: With a diameter of 40 meters, Cenote Yokdzonot is one of the largest in the Yucatan. Surrounded by lush jungle, the roots of ancient trees hang over the 18-meter-high walls of this "open" cenote, creating a waterfall of wood. Unlike many cenotes, the area around Yokdzonot hasn't been built up. Rather, two women from the local community laid each stone in the walking path and cut the wooden railings by hand to preserve the site's natural beauty. They only buildings here are the palapa-roofed bathrooms and a small restaurant cooking traditional local food. As usual with cenotes, don't use sunblock or bug repellent before getting in the water!

name: Arica
description: Founded by the Spanish in the 16th century, Arica was the main port for sending Bolivian silver back to Spain. In 1868, a massive earthquake leveled nearly the entire city, but it was rebuilt, and thanks to its strategic position, still serves as a free port for Bolivia and major transportation and trade hub. Along with being one of the cheapest cities in Chile, the main draw here is its nearly endless sunshine and long, sandy beaches. History and culture lovers will want to make time to visit the neoclassical San Marcos Cathedral - it was built by the Eiffel company, and along with a colorful, asymmetric facade, has some beautiful stained glass windows. The other main landmark is "El Morro", a 130-meter-tall outcrop that dominates the city skyline. Visitors who take the short hike to the top are rewarded with stunning panoramic views, and a small but interesting Weapons Museum.

name: Mecca
description: Often referred to as the birthplace of Islam, Mecca is an extremely holy city which receives millions of Muslim pilgrims every year for Hajj. Mecca boasts the world's largest mosque, the Masjid Al-Haram, with its immense 160,000 square yards of floor space capable of accommodating up to 1.2 million worshippers simultaneously. The Kaaba, a monumental stone structure at the heart of the Masjid Al-Haram, is encompassed by a black curtain called the Kiswah, adorned with inscriptions marking its historical repairs. The city offers a plethora of other holy sites to explore, including the Makkah Museum, Masjid Al Jinn, Jannat al-Mu'alla Cemetery, Mount Arafat, Mina Tented City, Jamarat Bridge, and Jabal Al Nour. The striking Abraj Al Bait Towers, also known as the Clock Towers, comprise a complex of skyscrapers housing the Makkah Royal Clock Tower, home to the Fairmont Makkah hotel. Please note that non-Muslims cannot enter or pass through Mecca. Identification may be required upon entry, and attempting to enter as a non-Muslim can result in penalties.

name: Sakakah
description: Nestled at the edge of the Nafud Desert, Sakaka is a vibrant city renowned for its rich heritage, housing the Qal'at Al-Rajajil archaeological site, where ancient stone pillars stand as silent witnesses to history. Agriculture thrives here, with date palms, wheat, and sorghum dominating the local economy. Sakaka's desert climate yields blazing summers and mild winters, creating an inviting atmosphere for travelers seeking authentic Arabian encounters. Among its attractions, the Al Jouf Archaeological Museum presents artifacts tracing the region's past. The 18th-century Qasr Marid Castle welcomes visitors into its storied halls, and the Al Khuraybat Heritage Village offers a glimpse into traditional Saudi life. Al Hazm Fort, a 17th-century marvel, showcases unique architecture and stands as a testament to the past's military might. The Ajyal Agricultural Park flourishes with lush gardens, serene lakes, and tranquil walking trails. With its historical treasures and desert allure, Sakaka welcomes explorers seeking a blend of heritage, culture, and scenic landscapes.

name: Girona
description: Settled by the ancient Iberians, the city was desired by every major empire in the Iberian Peninsula, undergoing twenty-five sieges and being captured seven times throughout its history. Today, its fortified walls are still standing, offering visitors the opportunity to walk around nearly the entire Old Quarter. Maybe even more imposing than the fortifications is the monumental Cathedral. A late Gothic structure built on foundations dating back to the Romans, it has the second largest nave in the world behind St. Peter's Basilica. The Cathedral museum has the 12th century Tapestry of Creation on display, a piece which has been compared to the Bayeux Tapestry for its historical importance. Perhaps the city's most distinctive site is its Jewish quarter, which solidified in the 1100s, and developed for the next 300 years, becoming one of the largest in Spain.

name: The Historic Dockyard Chatham
address.addr1: Main Gate Rd, Chatham ME4 4UY, UK
description: Founded in the 16th century, Chatham Dockyard was at the forefront of shipbuilding, industrial, and architectural technology for the Royal Navy until its closure in 1984. Today, 80 acres of the dockyard's 18th century historic core have been perfectly preserved, making it the world's largest and most complete dockyard from the Age of Sail. Visitors can experience Britain's maritime heritage among the 100 preserved buildings, including the working Victorian ropery, the dockyard railway, historic lifeboats, and the combined collections of 2 national museums. There are also three historic warships on preserved here, which are floating museums in themselves. Visitors can work their way through the cramped corridors of a diesel powered submarines, step aboard a World War II destroyer, or explore a Victorian sloop to learn about the lives of sailors in three different eras.

name: Villahermosa
description: Villahermosa was founded in 1564, and in less than 50 years it was named a city by King Felipe II, and given the coat of arms that still identifies the state of Tabasco. Despite its age, the city remained relatively undeveloped until the 20th century, and it wasn't until oil was discovered in the 1970s that Villahermosa truly became a "modern" city. The search for oil uncovered a nearby pre-Columbian Olmec site, now known as the La Venta Archaeological Park. While many of the monuments here remain unrestored, the site's massive carvings, altars, and mosaic floors offer a fascinating look at the Olmec cultural capital. The Museo de Historia de Tabasco in the town square is also worth a visit for both the artefacts on display and the beautiful Gothic and Moorish style building which is covered in decorative tiles.

name: Aswan
description: During the days of the pharaohs, Aswan marked the southern border of Ancient Egypt. An important trade and garrison town, every dynasty exacted their tolls on ships passing up the Nile here. Aswan was famed for its granite quarries, which supplied the blocks for the pyramids and other ancient monuments throughout Egypt. Even today, you can see an unfinished obelisk that would have been the largest single piece of stone ever hewn, had it not cracked. At the exceptional Nubian Museum, you'll find artifacts from the Kingdom of Kush, as well as documentation of UNESCO's amazing project to save the nearby Philae Temple and Abu Simbel from the lake created by the dam. The city's main attraction is Elephantine Island, where you'll find colorful Nubian villages, the ruins of Answan's most ancient settlement, and a museum exhibiting artefacts from the pre-Roman era.

name: Nuremberg
description: It's worth visiting Nuremberg just to see the Schöner Brunnen, or "Beautiful Fountain". Situated in the main market square next to the town hall, it rises 19 metres from its octagonal basin, a progressively narrowing, gilded Gothic spire ringed at its base with forty painted allegorical stone figures. It's a good idea to ascend higher than 19 metres by visiting Nuremberg Castle, former home of the Imperial regalia and popular pit-stop for Imperial rulers. The observation platform atop its Sinwell Tower offers panoramic views of the city, while its Deep Well in the outer wall has spectacular views down to its rock-hewn roots 47 meters below. The house of Nuremberg's most famous artistic son, Albrecht Dűrer, provides insights into his life and art, while the Germanische Nationalmuseum has some of his most important works. The Frauenkirche, the Church of Our Lady, is another major draw with its Männleinlaufen, a sculptural mechanical clock and glockenspiel.

name: Myddelton House Gardens
address.addr1: Myddelton House Gardens, Enfield EN2 9HG, UK
description: Between 1865 and 1954, Myddelton House Gardens were the domain of Edward Augustus Bowles, one of Britain's most famous self-taught gardeners, artists, and expert botanists. Bowles dedicated much of his life to transforming the gardens, filling them with exotic plants. Today, visitors can enjoy the colorful 'Alpine Meadow', or discover unusual plants in the 'Lunatic Asylum'. There's also a serene beautiful carp lake, and a Victorian conservatory, divided into climatic zones. In the house museum, visitors can learn about the creator and see his eclectic collection of treasured artefacts, including a piece from the original St. Paul's Cathedral. For more information, please visit visitleevalley.org.uk/en/content/cms/nature/gardens-heritage/myddelton-house-gardens

name: Liepaja
description: Founded by the Livonian Order in the 13th century, Liepāja remained a relatively small settlement the late 1800s, when Tsar Alexander III deepened the harbour and built a massive naval port. In the 20th century, the city was home to the first Baltic fleet of Soviet submarines, and a major military base. Today, Liepāja is fascinatingly incongruous. The port city is also home to one of the country's most beautiful Blue Flag beaches. Visitors will be able to admire elegant timber houses and Art Nouveau masterpieces, and explore the pragmatic remains of the former military port, or see the world's largest mechanical organ in the beautiful Baroque Holy Trinity Cathedral. While exploring the streets, visitors are sure to notice the many fresh fish stalls - the city's famous for its fresh seafood, particularly cod, so be sure to give some a try.

name: Val'Quirico
description: Val'Quirico was a thriving hacienda up through the 19th century, but after its heyday, it was converted into a private club, which eventually failed. Seeing the opportunity to create a tourist attraction, the property was transformed into a medieval village modeled after those in Tuscany. Now, Val'Quirico is filled with bars and restaurants offering international cuisine, live entertainment, and boutique shops so domestic and international tourists alike can get a little taste of Italy in Mexico.

name: Carmen Tower
description: Tragedy struck the town of Tlalpujahua in the early morning hours of May 27, 1937 with only Carmen Tower, the remnant of an old church, as the sole survivor. The stone structure looms above what used to be a prosperous mining town home to thousands. After a heavy rainfall one night, the town's derelict dam collapsed to induce a devastating mudslide that buried the entire area. Surviving villagers were never able to recover many belongings and had to wade through heaps of mud to hunt for family and friends. Today, visitors tread lightly over ground where houses once stood to reach Carmen Tower - look closely and original details from streets and buildings can be seen.

name: Quatre Bornes
description: Quatre Bornes, nestled in the heart of Mauritius, offers visitors a delightful blend of bustling markets, cultural richness, and natural beauty. At the heart of Quatre Bornes lies its colorful and bustling market, where the sights, sounds, and aromas create an intoxicating sensory experience. Here, visitors can wander through stalls brimming with exotic fruits, spices, textiles, and handicrafts, engaging in the lively banter of vendors and locals. Beyond its markets, Quatre Bornes is home to a diverse array of cultural attractions and landmarks. The town's rich heritage is evident in its charming colonial architecture, with historic buildings offering glimpses into Mauritius' past. Visitors can explore the Eureka House, a beautifully preserved Creole mansion, or take a leisurely stroll through the Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Botanical Garden, where lush greenery and vibrant blooms provide a tranquil escape. For those seeking outdoor adventures, Quatre Bornes is surrounded by natural wonders waiting to be discovered. Nearby, the Tamarind Falls beckon with their cascading waters and lush surroundings, offering hiking trails and breathtaking viewpoints for intrepid explorers.

name: Altun Ha
description: Founded around 200 BC, Altun Ha developed into a major trade center before being abandoned around 1000 AD. Despite its stones being used to build the nearby village of Rockstone Pond, Altun Ha wasn't brought to the attention of archaeologists until 1963 when villagers unearthed a massive jade amulet. Since then, Altun Ha has been restored into one of the most iconic Mayan sites in Belize. Though "only" two ceremonial plazas have been excavated, they share nearly 500 structures between them. Plaza A is dominated by the "Temple of the Green Tomb". Plaza B is home to Belize's best-known Mayan temple: the 17-meter-tall "Temple of the Masonry Altars". Along with being the main ceremonial site, the temple served as the mausoleum for Altun Ha's high priests. One tomb provided the single most precious Mayan artefact ever found in Belize: a six-inch high solid jade carving of the head of the Maya Sun God, KinichAhau.

name: Kiel
description: Founded in the 13th century, Kiel was a Danish property until it was annexed by Prussia in 1866. Built in a fjord, the port was one of the traditional homes of the German Navy's Baltic fleet, which was mercilessly bombarded during World War II. Today, the best way to experience the city is a walk along its waterfront promenade, where visitors can watch the constant flow of ships transporting goods, or ferrying people from Scandinavia. The walk bring visitors past rows of boathouses, and the Heimholtz Centre for Ocean Research, which has an outdoor seal aquarium. During the last week of June, the Kiel Regatta attracts sailors from around the world, and over 100 historic vessels. Throughout the year, it's possible to step inside a decommissioned U-Boat. For visitors who can't get enough of the maritime flavor, be sure to try the local delicacy Kieler Sprotte: a whole smoked fish presented in a wooden box.

name: El Tuito
description: If you're in search of a traditional village with welcoming locals and small town charm, look no further than Tuito. Tuito's main plaza houses a cultural center where history about the town, old photos and vintage maps are on display for all to see. Step outside and see the photos come to life! Brightly colored buildings and brilliant murals breathe life into this corner of the world. Festivals throughout the year add excitement and energy and reinforce the town's sense of community.

name: Umluj
description: With pristine beaches, vibrant coral reefs, and captivating marine life, Umluj is a haven for those enamored with the outdoors. The allure of Umluj's turquoise-hued Red Sea beach is undeniable. The crystal-clear waters, untainted by river discharge, offer a stunning backdrop for both relaxation and exploration. White sands, shadowed by graceful palm trees, invite visitors to bask in the sun's warmth or cool off with a swim. Snorkeling and diving opportunities abound, revealing the coral reefs' intricate beauty and more than 1200 fish species, some unique to the region. Venture further to Jabal Hassan islands for an underwater spectacle of fringing reefs that grow along the shores. These intricate formations host over 300 coral species, creating a tapestry of shapes and colors. As you immerse yourself in Umluj's coastal beauty, you'll find a harmonious blend of Arabian hospitality and breathtaking marine vistas. Whether lounging on pristine beaches, marveling at vibrant coral, or tracing the steps of ancient civilizations, Umluj promises an unforgettable escape into nature's wonders.

name: Velenje
description: The town of Velenje is located in the center of Salek Valley, with the Kamnik-Savinja Alps and Pohorje Mountains on either side. A Slovenian town like no other, Velenje was built as a concept for healthy living in a socialistic society. The youthful capital is largely undiscovered by tourists. Velenje offers a unique underground adventure with its very own coal mining museum. It's also a city of opportunity, hosting over 1,500 events each year. Don't miss the Velenje Castle; it's considered one of Slovenia's best kept secrets!

name: Biskra
description: Hugging the northern boundaries of the Sahara Desert, Biskra was a popular spa town during Roman times, and underwent a cultural renaissance at the end of the 19th century. Oscar Wilde, Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald, Karl Marx, and Henri Matisse are among the many artists and intellectuals who flocked here for inspiration. Biskra is the setting of key sections of André Gide's 1902 novel The Immoralist, and Matisse's Blue Nude (Souvenir de Biskra) was finished here in 1907. And thanks to its subtropical desert climate, Biskra remains a popular winter resort destination. Head to the city's old town, where brick buildings, influenced by Roman, Arab, Turkish and French cultures, are interspersed with date palms and fruit trees.

name: Yeongwol
description: Beyond its picturesque natural beauty, Yeongwol boasts a rich history dating back to the Joseon era, with several important sites worth visiting. The Jeongneung Royal Tombs house the tomb of King Danjong, the 6th Joseon King, and the Cheongpyeong area boasts the largest pine grove in Korea, where King Danjong once resided before his untimely demise at the age of 17. In addition to its historical significance, Yeongwol houses a plethora of art galleries and museums. The Muksan Art Gallery exhibits paintings portraying the scenic landscapes of Yeongwol throughout the year, while the Yeongwol International Museum of Contemporary Art showcases sculptures from around the world. The Museum of Manbong Buddhist Art honors Buddhist monk Manbong, displaying his relics and an array of Buddhist artwork. The Kwae Yeon Jae Ceramic Museum offers pottery-making experiences, while the Hoann Museum of Tea Ware provides a delightful journey through the art of making green tea and features relics from over 3,000 years ago. Yeongwol also beckons nature enthusiasts with scenic retreats such as Seogang, Gubongdaesan, Yeonha Falls, and the Naeri Valley.

name: Stourhead House and Garden
description: Though the Stourhead House and Garden date back to the 13th century, the spectacular estate seen today was constructed during the 18th century when Stourhead was purchased by Henry Hoare. Hoare had an elegant Palladian manor erected - one of the first in England - which he and his progeny filled with fine furnishings and a beautiful art collection. The estate's 2,650 acre grounds were also reworked to include an artificial lake, and plenty of Grecco-Roman follies to compliment the classical Palladian architecture. Today, visitors can step into the Hoare family home to marvel at the exquisite interior, with its countless paintings, decadent ornamentation, and refined library. On a pleasant walk through the landscape park, travellers can discover the Temple of Apollo and Grotto, or soak in views of the park from atop the red brick Tower. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/stourhead

name: Cliffs of Moher
description: Running for 14 kilometers, and reaching heights of up to 700 feet, the Cliffs of Moher are one of the most spectacular natural sights in Ireland. Recognized by UNESCO for their ecological importance, nearly 30,000 pairs of birds from 20 species, including Atlantic puffins and razorbills, nest at the cliffs during peak season, with grey seals, porpoises, dolphins, minke whales, basking sharks, and the occasional sunfish plying the waters. A majority of the 1.5+ million people who visit the cliffs stop by the fantastic Visitor's Center to learn about the geology, history, flora and fauna of the cliffs through interactive media displays, or see some unique perspective - such as a video from the underwater caves below the cliffs. If you want to avoid the crowds, there are several more remote access points, and walking trail that works its way along the cliffs.

name: Patzcuaro
description: Patzcuaro has retained its indigenous charm and colonial influence throughout its long history. First founded in the 1320s, the hills of the town are still bejeweled with well-preserved architectural gems. The shimmering lake is the perfect backdrop to colonial-era mansions and brightly-colored adobe facades. Each year, the town becomes a kaleidoscope of color during Day of the Dead celebrations. Local artisans share their creations of brightly colored textiles, carvings and pottery as offerings for friends and relatives that have passed. Food and flowers flow during the festivities and the entire town comes alive. Any time of the year, Patzcuaro brightens any visitor's day.

name: Termas Cacheuta
description: Water parks are always exciting whether you're an adult or a child. Thermal water parks surrounded by mountains? Even better, and we know just the place. Termas Cacheuta Thermal Water Park, a one-hour drive from Mendoza City and overlooked by the Andes mountains, is an excellent spot for both adults and families with children looking for a fun and adventurous way to spend their day. The water park has indoor and outdoor pools filled with thermal water at different temperatures, water slides, lazy river, mud baths and barbecue areas ideal for picnics. The water park has two levels: the upper level is open all year long, but the lower level of pools opens only from 21st September to Easter. Termas Cacheuta can become very crowded during peak season or on the weekends Entry ticket costs about 12 USD/EUR (children under 12 years old free) The park is open every day of the year from 10am to 6pm Seasonal opening times: Summer Season : from 09/21 to Easter the Thermal Water Park is open in its entirety. Winter Season : from Easter to 09/21 only the upper level pools remain open. As an option for adults only, you can visit the nearby Hotel and Spa Termas de Cacheuta and book a half a day spa package which includes access to thermal water stone pools, saunas, and mud bath therapy, complete with a barbecue buffet.

name: Imereti
description: Imereti, the most populous region in Georgia, is teeming with activities and sights to see. Boasting a rich history, it was even an independent kingdom once. To help you navigate its myriad offerings, we've crafted some itinerary suggestions for your visit. As one of the world's oldest wine-producing regions, Imereti offers numerous vineyards to explore. The region is particularly esteemed for its white wines, including Tsolikouri, Tsitska, and Krakhuna. Culinary enthusiasts should take the opportunity to indulge in the local cuisine. Many restaurants serve Imeretian delicacies such as khachapuri featuring a very salty white cheese known as Imeretian cheese. You might also enjoy Chakhokhbili, a tomato-based stew, or Imeretian Kupati, the region's local sausages. Finally, don't miss the chance to immerse yourself in Imereti's stunning natural landscapes. From the mesmerizing Kinchkha Waterfall to the tranquil Gabzaruli Lake, we're confident that the region's natural beauty will captivate you.

name: Alba Iulia
description: One of the oldest settlements in Romania, Alba has been one of the leading wine growing regions since the 1st century AD. During Roman rule, the city served as the region's military and economic center and was rendered a copy of Rome in miniature. The city reached its heydey between 1542 and 1690 when it served as the capital of the independent Principality of Transylvania and seat of the Transylvanian princes. The peasant revolt on February 28, 1785 turned the city into a symbol of justice and freedom. Today, visitors can explore the wide, tree lined boulevards of the Habsburg Citadel - a massive 18th century fortress with baroque elements, or visit the oldest monument in Transylvania - the Roman Catholic Cathedral. The city's rich history is embodied by its regal estates, such as the Apor Palace and the Princely Palace.

name: Hermanus
description: Hermanus is a quiet seaside escape that still honors its fishing tradition. From June through December, Southern Right whales migrate here to mate, making Hermanus one of the best places in the world for whale-watching according to the WWF. You can book a whale watching boat trip, or just keep watch from shore (binoculars recommended). Regardless of the season, the walking trails on the cliffs outside of town offer stunning coastal views, and the chance to see a variety of plant and wildlife. In the town proper, you can visit the Old Harbour Museum to learn about the former whaling industry, or head to the Whale Museum to see a whale skeleton and special audio-visual presentation of whales and dolphins (run twice daily). Of course, as a fishing town, it's a great place to enjoy fresh seafood, complemented by locally-produced wine.

name: Zafra
description: Originally a Muslim settlement, Zafra was captured twice by Christian forces - first in 1229 by Alfonso IX, and then definitively by Ferdinand III. Several of the city's old gates are still standing, each offering a distinct look into the city's past. The Gates of Jerez are typical Andalusian white, while the Arco Del Cubo is a medieval fortification. The city's narrow streets are lined with baroque churches, old-fashioned shops, glassed-in balconies, and traditional houses, all overflowing with flowers. The two plazas, lined with arcades are a pleasant place to relax. The 14th century palace has been converted into a Paradore, or historic hotel.

name: Cheddar Caves and Gorge
description: The Cheddar Caves & Gorge are undoubtedly one of the most spectacular natural sights in all of Britain. The gorge and its 450 foot tall limestone cliffs, were carved out over the course of millions of years by glacial meltwaters, which also formed the Cheddar caves. The UK's most famed showcaves, the 9,000 year old 'Cheddar Man' discovered here in 1903 is the oldest complete skeleton ever found in the UK. The Cheddar complex gives visitors the option to soak in breathtaking views, admire stupendous cave ornaments, or step into the Museum of Prehistory to discover weapons, tools made from flint, bone, antler horn, and bronze, pottery, and the skull of the Cheddar Man himself. There are also multimedia experiences that immerse visitors in the many facets of the Gorge's history and ecology. You can even stop by the gift shop for some cave-aged cheese!

name: Villa del Balbianello
address.addr1: Via Guido Monzino, 1, 22016 Tremezzina CO, Italy
description: In 1785, Cardinal Angelo Maria Durini purchased a 13th century monastery, and built Villa del Balbianello in its place. Over the years, the estate's illustrious owners tailored the estate to suit their tastes, with Count Guido Monzino, leader of the first Italian expedition to summit Mount Everest, filling the interior with artefacts from his expeditions, and adding secret passageways. The villa's groomed grounds and breathtaking views have wowed visitors and Hollywood alike, and make it a popular location for weddings. Inside, the villa's various buildings, visitors will find French and English furnishings from the 17th and 18th centuries, glass paintings, and ethnic sculptures and artefacts from around the world. The upper floor is dedicated to the life of Guido Monzini, and is filled with his belongings, including one of the dogsleds he used to reach the North Pole. The Villa is closed on Mondays and Wednesdays, and from November through March. Please book your tickets in advance at https://ticket.fondoambiente.it/events/villa-del-balbianello/villa-del-balbianello

name: Ciudad Obregon
description: In the heart of Southern Sonora, Ciudad Obregón beckons travelers with its vibrant culture and rich heritage, paying tribute to the Yaqui Indian tribe in all corners of the city. Casa Rosalva, an artistic haven in the city, serves as a platform for contemporary art forms from around the world, where you can delve into the world of art and expression as you roam its galleries. For a deeper understanding of the local culture, the Centre for Popular Cultures offers insight into the various ethnic groups and popular cultures of Southern Sonora. Don't miss the Mercado Municipal, a local market filled with retail spaces and restaurants, and explore the city's vibrant downtown. Nature enthusiasts can unwind in parks and plazas scattered throughout the city. For sports aficionados, watching the hometown team Obregon Yaquis in action is a must, and golf and fishing opportunities abound. Photos by Cnec wiki, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: La Plata
description: Buenos Aires' little sister is well-known for being South America's first planned city. Founded by governor Dardo Roha in 1882, he hired urban planner Pedro Benoit to design the city to be in the shape of a square with a central park and two main diagonal avenues traversing north to south and east to west, giving it its nickname "city of diagonals". As both the city's founder and planner were freemasons, strong freemason symbolism is infused through many aspects of the design, with subtle Italian and German influences present as well. If you're a nature lover, you will delight in a stroll through the city, particularly if you end up at Paseo del Bosque, the largest green space within the city. There, you can treat yourself to the Museo de la Plata, a zoo, an observatory, and numerous botanical gardens. You can even rent a boat! Other notable sites include the Neo-Gothic Catedral de La Plata and architectural marvel Casa Curutchet, which was recently declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Be'er Sheva
description: Be'er Sheva dates back to Biblical times, and was notably where Abraham and his son Isaac lived for many years, and made oaths of non-aggression with the Philistines. Historically, it developed thanks to its wealth of wells, but this original settlement was destroyed and abandoned during the Muslim conquest of the Levant in the 7th century. The present city was established by the Ottomans in the early 1900s to serve as their regional capital, and was the only planned settlement built in Israel under their rule. Today, you'll still find reminders of this period, like the Governor's House, which now houses the Negrev Art Museum, the city's first mosque, and the Turkish railway station built during World War I. There are also a wealth of museums and cultural attractions, ranging from the Israeli Air Force Museum to the Museum of Bedouin Culture. You can even take a tour of Abraham's Well to learn about the father of monotheism and local culture.

name: Constanza
description: Nestled in a valley 1,200 meters (4,000 feet) up in the Cordillera Central, Constanza holds the title of the highest altitude town in the Caribbean. The remote valley was sparsely inhabited, and Constanza itself wasn't founded until 1894. Today, it's a favorite retreat for nature lovers and Dominicans looking to escape the summer heat, with year round temperatures averaging between 5°C-25°C (41°F-77°F). The cozy town center is brimming with bars and restaurants, while the central park is the spot to be for just hanging out. But look outside of town and you'll find farms to tour, and a local version of Christ the Redeemer, which offers views across the valley. Plus, there are four national parks to explore, like the Valle Nuevo National Park, which is the source of some of the country's major rivers, and the humid Ébano Verde Scientific Reserve, which is home to over 80 species of orchids.

name: Comacchio
description: Likely predating the Roman Empire, this little village enjoyed centuries of prosperity thanks to its salt pans and strategic location. It became so successful in the salt trade that rival Venice sacked the city twice between 850 and 950 AD. They're rated internationally important by the Ramsar Convention for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, and offer visitors guided tours to see the flamingo-filled wetlands, as well as their traditional eel fishing techniques. Walking through the picturesque heart of the city feels like you've been transported to a simpler time. Trepponti bridge, spanning canals, offers fantastic photo opportunities. History buffs can step into nearby Museo della Nave Romana to learn about an ancient Roman merchant vessel that was recovered in the lagoon. But for a truly unique experience, visit the La Manifattura dei Marinati museum to learn about Comacchio's eel industry.

name: Orizaba
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: The quaint mountain town of Orizaba features perfectly preserved colonial architecture set against a backdrop of green hills and a snow-capped mountain peak. Orizaba's old city hall El Palacio de Hierro, or The Iron Palace, is an exemplary display of stunning Art Nouveau construction. The building houses various exhibits and cafes. Every nook and cranny is packed with intricate details to make for a stunning piece of architecture and work of art. As for the Orizaba Cathedral, the brown and yellow facade is striking against clear blue skies. Wander the streets or along the river path to get some fresh air before visiting the Museo de Arte del Estado de Veracruz. Inside the museum, you'll find the second largest collection of colorful Diego Rivera works in the country of Mexico. See what there Orizaba has to offer inside and out!

name: Cuautla
description: At the heart of Cuautla is the Zocalo, the city's main square, where a bust of José María Morelos remembers the local hero's prominent role in the Mexican War of Independence. The nearby Ex Convento de San Diego, built in the 16th century by the Dominicans, played an important role in the defense of Cuautla during the war. The Morelos House Museum tells the story of the Mexican War of Independence from Spain, and honors the rebel leader who led the movement. This history is particularly pertinent in Cuautla as it was designated a 'Heroic City' for its efforts in the war. The museum has several rooms displaying archaeological and historical artefacts which give a great insight into this culturally significant time. Next to the museum visitors can take the opportunity to ride a historic steam train - the world's oldest! - which was once used to transport agricultural produce. If all this history puts an ache in your bones, you can have a soak in one of the many nearby hot spring resorts.

name: Guayama
description: Founded by the Spanish in 1736, Guayama sometimes gets written off as an industrial city. But head to the main square and you'll find a rich cultural nucleus. The main landmark is the 19th century Iglesia Católica San Antonio de Padua, the old city hall, historic theaters, and the enchanting Casa Cautiño. This neoclassical abode, ornamented with Puerto Rican flourishes, is now a house-museum filled with 19th century art, sculptures, and furniture made by Puerto Rican craftsmen. For lit-lovers, don't miss the Casa y Museo del Poeta Luis Palés Matos, the former home of the poet who invented Afro-Antillian poetry. Even if you have no interest in history or architecture, there's another reason Guayama is famous throughout Puerto Rico: La Casa de los Pastelillos. Grab some of the largest deep-fried empanadas on the island and dig in right on the white sand beach.
