name: Pano Lefkara
description: Up in the Troodos mountains, Lefkara is a picturesque warren of cobbled streets lined with terracotta-roofed houses. But its allure comes from something much finer: it's been a renowned center for silversmithing and lace weakening for centuries. In fact, according to local legend, Leonardo DaVinci visited in 1481 and bought a lace altar cloth, which he gave to the Milan Cathedral, where it's still on display. Wandering the winding streets, you'll find local women on almost every corner, carefully crafting delicate lace. You can also get a demonstration at the Lefkara Handicraft Centre, the Museum of Traditional Embroidery and Silversmithing, and various workshops around town. There's also a number of historic churches to admire, including the chapel of Archangelos Michail in Kato Lefkara, which has frescoes from the 12th and 15th centuries.

name: Singapore
description: Though it had been settled for centuries, modern Singapore truly began to develop in 1819 when it was made a trading post of the British East India Company. Since then, trade and commerce has been integral to the city-state's identity, and Singapore is now one of the richest countries in the world. This wealth has given the city a certain sheen, while its multicultural inhabitants add the color. Every neighborhood has its own flair, and most importantly to the food-obsessed Singaporeans - its own flavor. This is a city where your food pictures are just as important as any sightseeing, and thanks to the exceptional public transit system, you can easily experience each meal in a different neighborhood. Singapore isn't just modern - it's dedicated to realizing its dream of becoming a 'City in a Garden', with an ever-growing number of 'green' skyscrapers and public gardens. The UNESCO-listed botanical gardens embody this ideal, and are arguably the best in the world.

name: Xilitla
description: Xilitla's position on the steep slopes of the Sierra Gorda has spared it from the worst effects of colonization and industrialization, and it's all the more charming for it. The regional demographics remain mostly indigenous, with the two-fifths of the population speaking a native language (as well as Spanish). Coffee and citrus fruits are the mainstay of the local economy. The mish-mash of architectures combine well with the beautiful tropical forested hillsides surrounding the town, begging for further exploration. But for those just passing through the main draw is the bizarre extensive jungle garden created by the British millionaire and surrealist artist Edward James, one of Mexico's more eccentric immigrants. After escaping the ravages of war-torn Europe in 1940 he wanted to set up something special - Xilitla became the location he would build his "Garden of Eden" filled with Athenian ruins, temples, staircases leading nowhere, gothic windows, and magical pools.

name: Qalhat
description: Qalhat, Oman's first capital, was a bustling medieval city that served as a major port on the Indian Ocean trade network. When Marco Polo visited in the 13th century, he commented on its fine bazaars and beautiful mosque. Spanning 60 hectares, the city was entirely encircled by a fortified wall, though this didn't save it from being sacked and burned by the Portuguese in 1507. Today only one building remains standing. This, however, is a royal mausoleum, built in the 13th century by King Baha al-Din Ayaz for his wife, Bibi Maryam, or perhaps, the other way around. Surrounding this are the foundations of the medieval city, which offer a look into the past - and panoramic views of the sea.

name: Dublin
description: Dublin was founded sometime around the 7th century, after which it was the capital of the Norse Kingdom of Dublin, the principal Irish settlement following the Norman Invasion of Ireland, and the second finest city in the British Empire. This proud status is readily apparent at St. Patrick's Cathedral, the largest in Ireland with a history dating back to the 12th century, and Dublin Castle, where visitors can discover 800 years of Irish history. The city's literary history is equally prestigious with author's including James Joyce and Oscar Wilde helping it earnUNESCO Recognition - in fact, one of the city's most iconic sights is the library at Trinity College. Then, of course, there's Dublin's liquid heritage, with tours of the Guinness Brewery and Jameson Distillery topping the to-do list of every visitor, and the city's countless pubs keeping tourists and locals alike well-lubricated.

name: Annaba
description: Surrounded by mountains, hills, and plains, the coastal city of Annaba was originally established by the Romans as Hippo. But today, many call it the Land of the Jujubes, for the the abundance produced by the fertile fields around the city. Admirers of Moorish architecture would delight in visiting the Saint Augustine basilica (the entrance is free, but it is recommended to take a tour), and WWII enthusiasts have a chance to visit the war cemetery of Bone, a memorial to the British soldiers located just outside the city (free entrance). Of course, you can also see its ancient origins at the ancient Roman ruins at the foot of the basilica. Throughout the city, you'll also find a number of Don't artisan shops where you can get a handmade souvenir. Of course, as a coastal city, you also have a number of beaches where you can just kick back, or walk along Green Main Street, a bustling promenade known for its nightlife.

name: Murchison Falls
description: At Murchison Falls, the White Nile is forced into a rocky gorge less than 10 meters wide, where it drops 43 meters. The power eruption of water is one of the standout attractions in Uganda's famed Murchison Falls National Park. Ernest Hemingway crashed his plane nearby while trying to visit the falls with his wife in 1954, though the British royal family had much more successful visits. In 2019 South Africa's Bonang Power and Energy proposed building a hydropower station on the river, but this was rejected by Uganda as the falls are one of the country's most lucrative tourism sites. So along with getting to enjoy a stunning natural spectacle, your visit to the falls helps protect the entire surrounding ecosystem. Please note that due to the extensive wildlife conservation efforts, the park charges an admission fee upon entry, $40 for adults and $20 for children. For more information, please visit https://www.ugandawildlife.org/

name: Huntington Beach, CA
description: Huntington Beach is inextricably linked with surfing - afterall, it was here that surfing forefathers George Freeth and Duke Kahanamoku pioneered the sport in the early 20th century, century, and the first U.S. Surfing Championship (now summer's Vans U.S. Open of Surfing) was held here in 1959. For a deeper look into how surfing shaped the city, duck-dive into the International Surfing Museum and be sure to stop by Jack's Surfboards to see the Surfing Walk of Fame and Huntington Surf & Sports for the Surfers' Hall of Fame. Even if you don't plan on getting into the lineup, you can watch the action from Huntington's famous, 1,850-foot-long pier, or watch beach-life go by from the oceanfront path that works its way down the nearly 10-mile stretch of sand.

name: Travnik
description: Travnik was the Bosnian capital during the latter part of the Ottoman rule. Today, it's a cultural and historical hub. Nearby Mt. Vlasic is one of the tallest peaks in the country and is an excellent spot for skiing or hiking. Other notable attractions include the Stari Grad Fortress, Sarena Mosque, and the city's historic center. Travnik is known as the most oriental town in Bosnia. The main mosque, Sarena Mosque, is a sight to behold with its beautifully painted walls. The majestic 15th century Stari Grad Fortress is one the best preserved medieval fortified buildings in Bosnia. It provides a spectacular view of the surrounding mountains.

name: Xalapa
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: Xalapa started life from extremely humble beginnings; barely populated at the time of the Spanish conquests it only started to grow when traders came to the area to buy and sell produce. From there it has grown from strength to strength to become a centre of culture and university education, with bustling pedestrian streets, hip nightlife, quality bookstores, great coffee shops. There's an awful lot to do here but pride of place goes to the Archaeological Museum with it's huge array of pre-Hispanic artifacts, and the Francisco Javier Clavijero Botanical Garden, one of the best gardens in Mexico. Of course, you'd be remiss not to stop for some stuffed jalapeños or some other local specialties in the home of the beloved chili.

name: Creil
description: Creil is on land reclaimed from the former Zuiderzee sea and is now home to some of the largest tulip fields in the Netherlands. It is one of Flevoland's ten designated "green villages." This planned community began construction in 1953, and Creil takes its name from a former coastal village and woods that once existed where the IJsselmeer now lies. Today, approximately 1,700 residents call this agricultural community home, where the surrounding landscape transforms each spring into a spectacular patchwork of colorful bulb flowers. The village celebrates this heritage with its annual Bloembollen Vakdagen Flevoland competition between local growers. It is also possible to take helicopter rides over the tulip fields in the spring.

name: Mendocino, CA
description: From a Pomo settlement, Mendocino at first grew exponentially from lumber, but at the turn of the 20th century, it began attracting artists with its ideal location and mild climate. To date, the effect of the artist's hideaway is apparent in almost every facet of the town's culture. For the art connoisseur, you can catch a show almost every night at the Mendocino Theatre Company, or find yourself in the Mendocino film festival, where famed directors and creators of arthouse films alike will be present. For the nature lover, the Mendocino Headlands State Park presents scenic views, nature, and exploration for even the novice hiker.

name: Villach
description: Though the town was heavily bombed by the allies during World War II there's still much of historical and contemporary interest to enjoy. The Villacher Fahrzeugmuseum holds many fascinating antiquities, while the Museum of Doll Art is a must for doll collectors and admirers, some being made on-site. The church of St Jakob has the tallest bell-tower in the region, 94 metres high, and open for climbers who'll be rewarded with superb views. But for more panoramic vistas climb up to Landskron Castle, within easy reach of Villach. The castle was ravaged by fire in the 19th Century and much of it remains a ruin, but is all the more dramatic for that, occupying as it does an almost 700 metre high hill overshadowing the village of St Andra by Lake Ossiachersee. Apart from the tremendous views of the surrounding valleys and mountains the castle hosts regular wild bird displays.Apart from the tremendous views of the surrounding valleys and mountains the castle hosts regular wild bird displays.

name: Beaumaris Castle
description: Started at the end of the 13th century, Beaumaris Castle was the last of Edward I's 'iron ring' of castles in North Wales. Despite never being fully completed because of its exorbitant construction costs, the castle's 'walls within walls' design and its perfect proportions made it one of the most advanced engineering feats of its time, and kept it a relevant military stronghold until the 17th century. Around 1660, a garrison was no longer needed in the region, so the castle was abandoned and fell into ruin. Today, the moat, double ring of walls, and open spaces provide a plenty of places for visitors to explore, with some of the castle's rooms housing historical information to help visitors imagine what it was like several centuries ago.

name: Lake Kawaguchi
description: Lake Kawaguchi is adorned with a hot spring resort town and untouched landscapes of its northern and western shores. Splendid vistas of Mount Fuji await, showcasing its majesty against the backdrop of cherry blossoms in April and autumn hues in November. The lakeside promenade near Kawaguchiko Music Forest is a haven for cherry blossom admirers, while the "Momiji Tunnel" captivates photographers with its maple-lined path along the northern shore. While the lake serves as a base for climbing Mount Fuji, it also presents an array of attractions. Hot spring baths, museums, the Fuji Q amusement park, boat tours, and the ropeway to a nearby mountain summit promise diverse experiences. Art and culture flourish around Lake Kawaguchiko, with museums celebrating kimono design, classical art, musical instruments, and lifelike dolls. The iconic Chureito Pagoda in Arakurayama Sengen Park provides an unforgettable panorama of Mount Fuji, adorned with cherry blossoms in spring and vibrant leaves in autumn.

name: Bastei
description: Standing a staggering 1,000 feet above sea level, the Bastei rock formation towers over the Elbe River. The panoramic views over the Elbe Valley have to be seen to be believed and year-on-year, the Bastei is the most popular viewing point in Saxon Switzerland. Visitors can be as adventuresome or sedate as they choose — there are walking trails for everyone. Some of the rocks are connected by the magnificent sandstone Bastei Bridge built in 1851 to replace the original wooden bridge from 1824, which remains one of the most photogenic attractions in the park. It is difficult to imagine that humans once lived among the wild and rugged nature and signs of how they used to live are still clearly visible. Whether taking a leisurely stroll or a stiff hike, the naturally fragrant air, phenomenal nature with jaw-dropping views and the stunning man-made bridge will make your stop-off one to never forget.

name: Tatton Park
description: Tatton Park dates back to the 15th century when its Old Hall was first built. In 1598 the estate was purchased by Sir Thomas Egerton, Lord Chancellor of England, whose grandson built a stunning neo-Classical manor on a 251,000 acre estate. Tatton Park was owned by the Egertons until 1958, when last Lord Egerton died and left the house to the National Trust. Today, visitors can explore the manor's elegant interiors, admiring the perfect symmetry of the 8000-book library, or the collection of Gillow furniture in the ornate drawing room. Along the way, assistants can shed light on some of the manor's many stories. In the surrounding 50-acre park, visitors can walk through the 19th century fernery (designed by the man behind the Crystal Palace), warm up in the glass houses, or find peace in the tranquil Japanese Garden. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/tatton-park

name: Colle Val d'Elsa
address.addr1: 53034 Colle di Val d'Elsa, Province of Siena, Italy
description: This charming Italian town and commune in Tuscany is renowned for its production of crystal glassware and art, amounting to 15% of the world's total production. But long before its industrial sector became what it is today, Colle di Val d'Elsa was rocked by a turbulent past. Due to its position, close to both Florence and Siena, the town has seen several notable conflicts including a famous battle during the wars of the Guelphs and Ghibellines in 1269, and a siege by Neapolitan troops in 1479. The oldest part of the town is the "colle alta", the higher part, with a well-preserved medieval center. Visitors will enter through the ancient and monumental Porta Nova and following the narrow, winding lanes as they admire the 15th- and 16th-century noble houses and tower houses, making their way to Palazzo Campana, which marks the entry to the oldest part of Colle – the castle.

name: Kobe
description: Intriguing, diverse, and rich in history, Kobe invites you to experience its cultural tapestry and gastronomic wonders. The city's rich history is evident in its architecture, from Western-inspired buildings to the bustling Chinatown. Explore Ikuta Shrine, dating back to 201 AD and popular among young couples seeking blessings of love. Don't miss the lively Nankinmachi, one of Japan's largest Chinatowns, offering an array of tantalizing Chinese cuisine and unique shops. ature enthusiasts will find solace in the beauty of Rokkosan (Mt. Rokko), boasting not only stunning landscapes but also attractions like botanical gardens, observatories, and a music box museum. A visit to the captivating herb garden offers a delightful journey through themed areas adorned with 200 types of herbs and flowers. Indulge in the world-renowned Kobe beef, known for its unparalleled tenderness and flavor. Savor this culinary masterpiece, a must for food enthusiasts.

name: Kota Kinabalu
description: The state capital of Sabah, Kota Kinabalu is the most bustling city in Borneo, with new developments and modern malls keeping pace with the 21st century. However, it's old-world charms are still very much alive amongst the colonial-era houses, and friendly locals. While most people use Kota Kinabalu (or KK as it's commonly called) as a jumping off point for natural excursions, the city's also a great place to experience Borneo's urban jungle. While the city has some specific monuments worth visiting, like the 'floating' City Mosque, ocean-front boardwalk, and an engaging ethnographic village, KK is more about immersing yourself among the locals. Meander around, or just head to the Central Market to see the city's mix of ethnicities come together in an explosion of sights, sounds, and smells. It's also a great place to try some local food - often-times you'll see fishermen selling their catch of the day onsite.

name: Keuka Lake
description: The third-largest Finger Lake, Keuka Lake is unique among its narrow brethren for its distinctive Y shape. This earned it the nickname "The Crooked Lake" among early settlers, but its natural beauty earned it a new moniker: The Lady of the Lakes. Surrounded by forest and vineyard-covered hills, it's an idyllic place to unwind, do a bit of hiking, or take to the water. But relaxing on the shore is really just one of the draws. The surrounding wine region is an attraction in itself, with Dr. Konstantin Frank Vinifera Wine Cellars being New York State's most award-winning winery for 40 years, and the "#1 Winery in the Northeast" according to Wine Report. The Pleasant Valley Wine Company & Great Western Winery is one of the oldest in the Finger Lakes, and according to U.S. Travel & Leisure magazine, Heron Hill Winery has one of the 10 most amazing tasting rooms in the world.

name: Popayan
description: Popayan was established in 1537 by the Spanish conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar, after which it served as an important transfer point for sending gold and other riches back to Spain. While it's since grown into a large, modern city, the historic city center is still a charming jumble of Colonial-era the white-washed buildings. The most beautiful monument in the city is undoubtedly the towering, 18th century San Francisco Church. Along with being an elegant example of Colonial architecture, the church has an ossuary with two mummified bodies (just ask at the entrance). At the town's main square, you can relax with some delicious street-food and admire the city's 16th century cathedral. It's well worth exploring the surrounding area as well, especially if you're hungry - Popayan is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy.

name: Cliveden
address.addr1: Cliveden Rd, Taplow, Maidenhead SL6 0JF, UK
description: Cliveden was first built in the 17th century by the 2nd Duke of Buckingham, supposedly for his mistress, though the current house was built in the 1850s by the architect behind the Palace of Westminster. Cliveden reached new levels of renown in the 20th century thanks to Nancy and Waldorf Astor's lavish parties, which saw everyone from Winston Churchill to Ghandi and Henry Ford. In 1963, John Profumo, Secretary of State for War, was visiting Cliveden when he happened to meet call girl Christine Keeler. The following affair nearly toppled the British government as Keeler was also involved with a Soviet naval attaché. Today, the manor is a luxury hotel that allows visitors to glimpse the decadent interior decor on a guided tour on certain days. The gorgeous gardens cover 180 acres and offer a variety of formal gardens, ranging from a wonderful Japanese Water Garden to a meticulously manicured parterre to the Long Garden, with its colorful flowerbeds, topiaries, and statues. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/cliveden

name: Tangerang
description: Located on the western border of Jakarta, Tangerang is a bustling city known for its industrial and manufacturing prowess - but has a rich cultural and historical life pulsing beneath the surface. Explore its vibrant markets and indulge in the tantalizing flavors of street food from local hawkers. Take a trip to the Thousand Doors Mosque, an ancient structure dating back to the time of the Sultanate of Banten, renowned for its abundance of doors. Art and culture enthusiasts can visit the Textile Museum, housing over 2,000 precious textiles including exquisite batik pieces. Stop by the Jin De Yuan Temple dating back to 1755, with unique architecture, ornate decorations, ancient bells, drums, and Buddhist statues, or head to some of the country's largest malls for some retail therapy. The heart of Tangerang lies in its old town, centered around Pasar Lama (the old market) and Tangerang railway station. This traditional market, with its charming old shops, is famous for its unique cuisine, often prepared by the Chinese Benteng community, whose ancestors have resided here since the Dutch settlement.

name: Safed
description: Safed is believed to have been founded in the 15th century BC or earlier, and between the 6th and 1st centuries BC, was one of five elevated locations where fires were lit to announce the New Moon. The city served as a crusader stronghold and regional capital for centuries, but rose to fame in the 16th century when many Jews from Spain relocated here. Among these were prominent rabbis who made the city a center of Kabbalah. Today, Safed's old town is an enchanting jumble of cobbled streets that hark back to the 16th century. The white-washed houses have their doors and windows painted blue to confuse evil spirits, and the many synagogues are beautifully decorated with large murals. While most of the city is highly Orthodox, the small Artist's Quarter gave birth to many of Israel's most celebrated artists and remains lined with galleries.

name: Karlovy Vary
description: One of the best-known spa towns in the world where some of the most famous figures in European artistic and cultural life, such as Beethoven, Mozart and Casanova have all enjoyed treatment. Today, due to its distinctive architecture, hot springs and popularity with Hollywood celebrities, it is ranked among Europe's elite spa towns. Absorb the atmosphere and the distinct fragrance of a spa town with a walk through the historical center where you can sample water from the healing springs that stand in the shadows of the exquisite colonnades. No visitor should miss the prestigious Grand Hotel Pupp with its world famous façade and regarded as one of the world's best hotels. If you think you've seen it somewhere before then you most likely have — it features in the James Bond film, Casino Royale, among others, and hosts cultural festivals and award shows broadcast across the world.

name: Yeosu
description: Yeosu's allure lies not only in its illustrious past, of famous admirals and stories of war, but in its breathtaking views and local delicacies on offer. It is most associated with Admiral Yi Sun Shin, a celebrated naval commander. The most recent movie about him, "The Admiral: Roaring Currents (명량)"is still the highest grossing film in South Korea, even beating out "Avengers: Endgame". On your visit, indulge in simmering pots of crab stew paired with local Dolsan vegetable sides and savor the taste of the sea. The vibrant teal waters and refreshing salty air create an idyllic coastal ambiance, while striking bridges illuminate the night in radiant hues. At Yi Sun-Sin Square, admire a large replica of the famous turtle ship and a statue of Admiral Yi Sun-Sin at the heart of the plaza. Delight in local delicacies like mugwort ice cream, rice cakes with strawberries, and fresh catches from the lively fish market. Roaming through Yeosu means discovering artistic wonders on Jangdo Island, where local artists showcase their talent in various art installations. In the small port area, find Hamel Lighthouse, adding a touch of charm to the vibrant fishing scene. Embrace the coastal charms and relive the stories of historical heroes in the beautiful seaside town of Yeosu.

name: Pasaje
description: Over the course of its history, Pasaje had to be refounded on three separate occasions before finally settling in its current location on the fertile plain east of the river Jubones in 1800. The city is surrounded by vast banana plantations, and despite its small size, is one of the top producers in Ecuador's banana-making center. The city itself is largely a commercial and agricultural center, meaning the main attractions are its bustling markets, and kitschy church. Get outside of town, however, and you'll find a wealth of natural attractions, and one of the oldest necropolises in South America.

name: Zagreb
description: Zagreb is Croatia's capital and largest city. It's the only city in the country with a population of over one million people. Despite its size, Zagreb has managed to hold on to its old town charisma and welcoming hospitality. The city is located on the slopes of the Medvednica Mountains along the Sava River and is divided into three parts: upper town, lower town, and the post WWII area of Novi Zagreb (New Zagreb). It's also the cultural, economic, and governmental hub of Croatia and is home to the parliament, government, and president. Zagreb has numerous historical monuments and medieval architecture. There are many cafes, museums, galleries, theaters (over twenty), and charming markets to explore throughout the city. It has also been called the "city of museums", with more museums per square foot than any other city in the world.

name: Tumbes
description: Tumbes was originally settled in pre-Incan times by a cultural group of natives called Tumpis, and is believed to have had a population of around 178,000. Under Inca rule, Tumbes and the surrounding area became an important political stronghold, and the Spanish even noted how well-organized the town was when they first arrived. During the colonial period, it was reduced to a small town, and a hotpoint during the border war between Ecuador and Peru in 1940–41. Today, the city rarely sees tourists outside those heading to Ecuador, or looking to explore the nearby nature reserve, but it is oddly alluring for those who take the time to visit. The city's main plaza is dominated by the 18th century St. Nicholas Cathedral, which received a colorful post-Modern makeover to its Baroque facade, and a variety of mosaic-ed buildings are scattered around town. There's also an especially eye-catching statue of Christ that's worth seeing.

name: Derwent Valley Mills
description: In 1772, Richard Arkwright opened the first of his Derwent Valley mills in Cromford. Utilizing his patented water frame and the recently-invented flying shuttle, he was able to able to run the mill non-stop, breaking the work into two twelve-hour shifts. Because rural Cromford didn't have enough people to operate the factory, Arkwright also built housing to attract workers, mostly women and children, the youngest being just 7 years old. This system spread throughout Britain, and reached the US, making Arkwright the richest untitled person in Britain by the time he died in 1792. The mill continued to produce cotton into the mid 19th century before being repurposed and altered. Today, the UNESCO-listed industrial complex gives visitors a glimpse into the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution through its historic buildings, interactive displays, and even a presentation by Sir Richard Arkwright himself.

name: Lachania
description: In the southern part of Rhodes, Greece, lies the picturesque village of Lachania, a hidden gem offering a glimpse into traditional Greek island life. Wandering through Lachania's narrow alleys, visitors are greeted by friendly locals and a laid-back atmosphere that invites exploration at a leisurely pace. The village square, adorned with a quaint church and shaded by olive trees, serves as a focal point where residents gather and visitors can immerse themselves in the local culture. Surrounded by breathtaking landscapes, Lachania offers opportunities for outdoor activities such as hiking and cycling, allowing travelers to discover the natural beauty of the surrounding countryside. Nearby pristine beaches beckon with crystal-clear waters and golden sands, providing a perfect escape for sun-seekers and water enthusiasts alike. History enthusiasts will appreciate Lachania's rich heritage, evident in its well-preserved architecture and archaeological sites. The village is home to ancient ruins and Byzantine churches, offering glimpses into its storied past.

name: Waterloo
description: Though its history dates back to the Middle Ages, Waterloo is synonymous with the pivotal battle that was fought here 200 years ago. The Duke of Wellington and General von Blücher, and their men from the Seventh Coalition, squared off against Napoleon Bonaparte in a last-ditch effort to stop him from reaching Brussels. Their victory over the legendary Napoleon altered European history. Today, visitors can take to the now-bucolic fields where the battle was fought. Dominating it all is the Lion Mound, a hand-built, 40-meter hill topped with a massive bronze lion to commemorate Prince William of Orange, the Dutch crown prince who was wounded in the fight. Visitors who surmount the 226 steps to the top are rewarded with some amazing panoramic views. At the base of the Mound, visitors can learn about the battle though educational videos.

name: Verdun
description: First occupied by Celtic tribesmen around 450 BC, they named the site Virodunum, or 'Strong Fortress'. Throughout its history, the city was hotly-contested, with several confrontations between French and German forces occurring. In the 17th century, the city was fortified by Vauban, and became increasingly militarized through the 19th century. By the outbreak of the eponymous battle, it had perhaps the most advanced fortifications system in France. Today, the town is the epicenter for War Memorials, with Douaumont Ossuary and Fort, Fort Vaux, the Sacred Way, Souville Fort, Thiaumont Fortress, and the city's underground citadel all standing to help visitors understand the War. In the citadel, the miles of tunnels where the soldiers lived now have recreations of scenes from everyday life during the battle. But Verdun also has a rich urban heritage, such as one of Europe's oldest cathedrals, and an impressive art and history museum housed in the 16th-century Princerie mansion.

name: Oxford
description: Settled around 900, Oxford was an important cultural center for medieval England. Not only is it home to the oldest University in the English-speaking world, it was also where the first English constitution was written, and was the birthplace of two English kings. Today, the city is still best known for its University, which is undeniably a cultural highlight - the Bodleian Libraries, Divinity School, and Christ Church College are so magical, they were featured in the Harry Potter movies! For true Potterheads, you can even book a Harry Potter walking tour of the University. With such a rich academic heritage, Oxford also has a multitude of museums, from the eclectic collections of the Ashmolean Museum, to the rotating exhibitions at Modern Art Oxford. If you'd prefer to stay outside, the many towers, domes, and carvings make the 'City of Dreaming Spires' a delight to explore.

name: Pag
description: In recent years, the development of the island's most popular Northern waterfront town Novalja, has brought in tourists from all over the world to revel in Spring Break and other opportunities for fun. But Pag has more to offer than no rest and non stop partying on the boardwalk. In the South there are plenty of chances to sample some of Pag's cheese, visit the Simuni Camping villages, and check out Pag's beautiful mountain ridges. Matching the history of many other Croatia towns, Pag was also under the long time rule of the Venetians. In turn, be sure to visit the Basilica of the Assumption of Mary and seek out the famous lacework in the town of Pag.

name: Vernazza
address.addr1: 19018 Vernazza, Province of La Spezia, Italy
description: Considered the jewel of the UNESCO-listed Cinque Terre, Vernazza is a jumble of pastel buildings around a rocky harbor. Watching over the harbor is the medieval Doria Castle, which originally protected the village from pirates, but now offers fabulous views of the picturesque town. Standing above the cozy cafes, craft shops and wine bars is the beautiful, 14th century Church of Santa Margherita di Antiochia, which is said to be built on the spot where a box containing the bones of Saint Margaret kept returning. While the waterfront deservedly gets the most attention, be it walking, or sunning on the rocks, it's worth taking the time to wander the steep alleyways for the unexpected vistas of the sea that pop up at every turn.

name: Izamal
description: Izamal was originally an ancient Mayan city, and one of their most important religious sites, with a dozen temples dedicated to the creator deity Itzamna and to the Sun god Kinich Ahau. When the Spanish arrived, they built their settlement on top of the Mayan city, but because of the huge amount of work it would take to completely disassemble the monumental pagan structures, they instead built their own religious buildings on top of them. The Convento de San Antonio de Padua covers the Mayan acropolis, with second largest atrio in the Christian world after the Vatican encircling the entire site. The town itself is a charming place to simply amble - nearly all of it buildings have been painted a cheery yellow, and on the outskirts, you'll find several Mayan ruins, including Mexico's most massive pyramid.

name: Tunuyan
description: If you're traveling through the region of Mendoza or the Uco Valley, a mecca for wine connoisseurs, the city of Tunuyán is an excellent place for a little detour. This small city of about 50 thousand inhabitants is located close to the Chilean border and the majestic Andes, hosting tourists attracted to not only wine but rural and extreme sports tourism. While San Martin Avenue and the nearby squares are the heart of the city, Carlos Pellegrini Pedestrian Street is where one would sit down for a cup of coffee – luckily, there are many on the street to choose from. Tunuyán is also a good place for a lunch stop at one of the traditional venues that serve picada, which is an assortment of regional snacks, or parrillada, a mixed grilled meat plate. Of course, you can't go wrong with visiting one of the local wineries, many of them located on the outskirts of the city.

name: Santiago de Cuba
description: Founded in 1514, and first governed by conquistador Hernán Cortés, Santiago de Cuba has long been one of the island's most important cities. It was the capital of Cuba, the focal point of the Spanish-American War, and the starting point of Fidel Castro's communist revolution. With such a rich history, Cuba's second largest city has no shortage of attractions. A great place to start your visit is the Céspedes Park and the Museum of the Historical Cuban Atmosphere, the elegant Nuestra Señora de la Asunción Cathedral, and the Casa Diego Velázquez House nearby. If you love history, there are a number of house museums scattered around the charming historic center, and the Cementerio Santa Ifigenia Graveyard is the final resting place of several local heroes. Or head up to the Castillo de San Pedro de la Roca Castle. This UNESCO World Heritage Site isn't just an impressive fortification - it's also a fantastic viewpoint and informative museum! Santiago de Cuba is also known for its lively music - nearly every Cuban music genre from salsa to son started here, and they continue to pulse through the streets.

name: Londrina
description: Londrina, the "Little London" of southern Brazil, beckons with a rich tapestry of history, culture, and natural beauty. At the forefront of Londrina's allure is the Avenida Higienópolis, the face of the city and a hub of vibrant activity. Chic neighborhoods, residential areas, a yacht club, and striking architecture create a picturesque backdrop for daytime strolls and nighttime excursions. Here, the city comes alive with beautiful people, joggers, and cyclists, transforming every moment into a captivating experience. Londrina's crown jewel, the Igapó Lake, stands as an iconic symbol of the city. A haven for recreation, the lake draws crowds, especially in the summer, offering a perfect setting for walking, cycling, or simply unwinding amidst breathtaking views. With snack options and acai juices available, it's an ideal spot for leisure on lazy Londrina afternoons. Delve into the city's history at the Historical Museum of Londrina, housed in the former train station. A captivating journey spanning over 81 years unfolds, narrating the evolution of this vibrant city. Meanwhile, the serene greenery, clear lake waters, and diverse birdlife create a tranquil atmosphere in parks like those surrounding the cathedral.

name: Puyo
description: Puyo might be small, but as the fastest growing city in Ecuador, the lush Amazonian jungle starts right on the outskirts of town, making it a convenient base to explore this part of the Amazon rainforest. It is home to three major rivers, Pastaza, Puyo, and Bobonaza, so waterfalls are not hard to find in this area. Puyo has a handsome cathedral with a striking interior which is worth a quick visit, and nearby the small but well stocked Museo Etnoarqueológico displays ceramics, artifacts, and models of traditional indigenous homes. Less than 1km north of the city centre is the ethnobotanical park Omaere, where tours taken mostly by indigenous guides educates you in all manner of rainforest life, from native plants to indiginous dwellings to ecological matters. Near the park is an observation platform which affords excellent views of the city, river and Omaere Park.

name: Santiago de Compostela
address.addr1: Santiago de Compostela, A Coruña, Spain
description: In the early 9th century, a hermit saw light shining over a forgotten Roman tomb, revealed to be that of the beloved St. James the Greater. A settlement sprung up around the site, and quickly became one of the most important pilgrimages in Christianity. In the 10th century, the Moors completely destroyed the city, which was completely rebuilt in the following century. The Old Town is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, containing Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, and Neoclassicist architecture. The 11th century cathedral is a masterpiece of Romanesque architecture and houses the Pórtico de la Gloria, a jewel of the medieval sculpture. Its Baroque western façade faces the square of Obradoiro, and is considered one of the world´s most beautiful urban areas. When you're done with the Old Town's winding streets and many monuments, be sure to treat yourself to Galicia's most iconic dish: octopus!

name: Blenheim
description: Blenheim is the principal town in the Marlborough region, which produces 75% of the country's wine. Good wine comes with good food and Blenheim is no different, from great little cafes to fine restaurants to "world famous pies" to choose from. Possibly the town's best attraction is the Omaka Aviation Heritage Centre, which features filmmaker Peter Jackson's personal collection of WWI aircraft and artifacts, and the story of aviation during the Great War brought to life by the famous visual effects studio Weta Workshop. On one of the many sunny days the neat and tidy parks make for great places to relax and maybe have a picnic, from the clocktower adorned Seymour Square, to the Japanese themed Harling Park, or the winding Riverside Park and the chance to dip your feet on a hot day.

name: Rabigh
description: Northwest of Mecca in the historically significant Hejazi region, Rabigh boasts a mesmerizing setting where history and nature converge. A prominent highlight of Rabigh's surroundings is the Red Sea itself, adorned with captivating coral reefs and marine sanctuaries. Immerse yourself in the vibrant marine life and pristine underwater landscapes in the Five Corals Reef, southwest of Rabigh. Meanwhile, the city's culinary offerings are as enticing as its coastal charms. Visitors are treated to the freshest fried or grilled fish, sourced from the day's catch. Quaint shops and specialized restaurants along the main road entice taste buds with local flavors. Rabigh's captivating coastline extends to its beach, a pristine haven adorned with illuminated walkways. Cyclists and exercise enthusiasts find solace here, while the ambiance is completed by the serene presence of date palm trees and the melodic chirping of sea birds.

name: Frutillar
description: In the 19th century, German immigrants settled down on the shores of Lake Llanquihue, establishing the small town of Frutillar. True to their heritage, these immigrants built their homes in the traditional German style, except instead of being surrounded by alps, the half-timbered buildings are watched over by Patagonia's soaring volcanoes. Strolling the tidy streets feels like you're in a museum of German architecture - as embodied by the German Colonial Museum. Explore the garden, machine warehouse, water mill, and furnished main house, and take in the amazing view of the lake and mountains. The other main landmark is the colorful Theater of the Lake, a striking venue jutting out into the water. Aside from the charming architecture, what Frutillar is best known for is its many concerts, culminating in the 10-day-long Semanas Musicales in January and February. These shows are such an integral part of the town's identity that it was even named a UNESCO City of Music!

name: Chartres
description: The ancient town of Chartres predates the Romans, but its heyday came in the Middle Ages when it became a major pilgrimage site after receiving the Sancta Camisa, believed to be the tunic worn by the Mary at the time of Christ's birth, and erecting its UNESCO-listed cathedral. This masterpiece of Gothic architecture was nearly destroyed during WWII, but thanks to Colonel Welborn Barton Griffith, Jr. who snuck behind enemy lines with a single other soldier to confirm the cathedral was clear of enemy troops, it was spared. The Colonel, however, was not so lucky and was killed in action later that day. Today, along with the masterfully-decorated facades, the cathedral is the mecca of stained glass - how its famous 'Chartres blue' was achieved still remains a mystery. Walking the town's picturesque streets, visitors are treated to winding lanes and stairways, lined with half-timbered houses.

name: Kisumu
description: Once an incredibly important trading town, Kisumu suffered a downturn after the collapse of the East African Community, but since it's revival in 2000 the city began to thrive again. The relaxed atmosphere belies the city's size, feeling more like a laid-back town. Attractions are many for the passing visitor, from trips on Lake Victoria in the mornings (too windy in the afternoon), to shopping in the one of the flea (Oile, Kibuye) and art markets (Kisumu Art House, Maasai), or a guided tour of Kisumu Museum which covers the culture of Western Kenya. A little further south the Impala Sanctuary is home to a variety of animals, from the impala themselves to hippos to cheatahs. The food is worth a try too; being by the water fish is a huge part of the diet but many world dishes can be enjoyed here, all with a delightful lakeside twist.

name: Riobamba
description: Situated in the middle of the Andes, Riobamba's historic center is filled with elegant squares, pastel-colored buildings, bustling markets, and cobbled streets. Most of the buildings in the historic centre date back to 1800, giving the city a truly colonial feel. Riobamba is blessed with several beautiful churches. The Cathedral is the only survivor of the 1797 earthquake (and was moved brick-by-brick 20km from the original site). Nearby, you'll also find the pink-domed Basilica and the red brick neo-Gothic Iglesia de la Concepción. If you are lucky enough to be here on a Saturday, the impressive market only a few blocks from the churches, is not to be missed. While exploring the town, you'll also be treated to amazing views of the huge volcano Chimborazo.

name: Nakhon Ratchasima
description: Nakhon Ratchasima, more commonly known as Korat, was founded in the late seventeenth century by King Narai to defend the Ayutthaya Kingdom's border from Laotian or Khmer attack. In 1826, local heroine Thao Suranaree reclaimed the city from King Anouvong's Laotian forces, an act for which she's still revered - her statue in the centre of the city is the single most visited landmark. Nearby is Wat Sala Loi, a temple constructed by Thao and her husband, where a statue of the war heroine stands along clay representations of the life of Buddha, and her ashes are interred. In the old quarter, you'll be able to see the original defensive moats and fortified gates, as well as a wealth of Chinese shrines and old shophouses. As the gateway to Isaan, Korat has a distinctive cuisine blending central and northern flavors, such as som tam Khorat, a Lao/Isaan-style fermented fish on green papaya salad.

name: Formosa
description: Just across the Paraguay River, which forms the Paraguay-Argentina border, lies the relaxed and welcoming city of Formosa. It is a place of wide, tree-lined avenues, well-maintained recreational spaces, and attractive city squares. Famed for it's mild winters, tourists and locals alike can enjoy walks by it's extensive waterfront "Vuelta Fermoza", a route full benches, children's play areas, and plenty of bars and restaurants at which to sample the local cuisine. Three sites of interest you can find just a short walk from the riverfront are the Our Lady of Carmen church (patron saint of Formosa), the informative Craft House (dedicated to the three indiginous cultures of Formosa), and the Juan Pablo Duffard Museum (dedicated to Formosa's history). Just south of Formosa one can enjoy recreational activities such as biking, kayaking, boat rides, bird watching, or relaxing on the beach, at the 62,000 hectare Laguna Oca wetland reserve.

name: Stuttgart
description: No doubt car lovers will immediately head towards the two famous car museums in the city — the Mercedes-Benz Museum and the Porsche Museum. The former combines the history of the company with the development of the automobile alongside world events while the latter is packed with luxury vehicles that even non-car lovers will drool over. For a more sedate side of Stuttgart, there is the wonderful Wilhelma Zoo containing a wide variety of animals set out in different themes. The zoo also incorporates the Botanical Garden with its fascinating plant and flower specimens. A walk in the city center will take you to Palace Square complete with museums, shops, and a vibrant and bustling atmosphere. Remaining in the center, history buffs will appreciate the Old Castle, which houses the 'Everyday Museum' and provides an entrancing walk through history. All in all, Stuttgart has a lot of everything that caters for every traveler's taste.

name: Sant Carles de Peralta
description: The alluring Sant Carles de Paralta, otherwise known as San Carlos, is home to a mix of Ibizan, Spanish and international residents who continue to embrace and cultivate the hippy lifestyle of bygone eras. A communal spirit is evident in the streets, where old farmhouses or "fincas" with no electricity or running water became wholesome homes for people seeking a modest life. Visit the legendary "Bar Anita", where the hippy community would gather to use the only phone booth in the village. Old wooden mailboxes cover its walls and patrons sip on anise-flavored Spanish liquor. Just a 15-minute walk outside of town is Las Dalias, one of the most original hippy markets dating back to the 80's, imbued with vibrant stalls and ivy-covered courtyards and open year-round from February to November on Saturdays. If visiting in the weeks around Patron's Saint Day, on 4 November, watch San Carlos come to life with fantastic fiestas.

name: Monterey, CA
description: A historical wonder, Monterey was a First Nations settlement, then a Spanish Colonial outpost, and finally an American government establishment. California's first constitutional convention happened here, and it was home to the state's first theatre, public building, public library, school, printing press, and newspaper. It was also California's only tax point. Today, you can take in the nicely preserved Spanish architecture, as well as the many educational institutions. Go to the Monterey Bay Aquarium to explore the underwater biome that follows the city's coast. For a delicious seaside experience, head down to the Fisherman's Wharf to try the catch of the day. Monterey is also a city of arts and music, with the the Monterey Jazz Festival and California Roots Music and Arts festival drawing artists from around the country.

description: Built in the 13th century, Hever Castle was converted into a noble manor in the 15th century by Geoffrey Boleyn, whose great-grand daughter Anne Boleyn grew up here before going on to marry King Henry VIII's (and help spark the English Reformation in the process). Today, the castle's interior is a shrine to the Tudor queen, filled with period art, furniture, and Anne's personal belongings, such as her prayer books. Castle's renowned Italian Garden was made at the turn of the 20th century by American millionaire William Waldorf Astor to showcase his statuary, and today, visitors will find statues, fountains, chess pieces carved from golden yew, and a loggia at the lake amongst 4000 roses. Throughout the year, the castle hosts special events, from jousting tournaments to dog shows and Christmas markets.

name: El Tajin Archeological Zone
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: After the fall of Teotihuacan, El Tajin emerged as the dominant trade center of Mesoamerica, exporting everything from obsidian to corn, cacao, and vanilla (the last of which they may have been the first to cultivate). The city enjoyed some 600 years of growth, reaching an estimated 20,000 people at its peak. But in the 13th century, it attracted the attention of (probably) the Aztecs, who raided the city and forced its people into subjugation. While archaeologists have managed to piece together an overview of the city's history, they haven't figured out exactly who built it. The root of the mystery is the unusual art and architecture, which is unique in all of Mesoamerica. Just look at the iconic Pyramid of the Niches, where 365 niches line the 7 stepped terraces, and the intricate stone mosaics and murals found in the palaces at El Tajín Chico. Stop by the ruins in March where you can experience the Cumbre Tajin Festival, which is a cultural nod to the indigenous and local culture, as well as lots of music from around the country.

name: Sibiu
description: Founded in the 12th century by German Saxons, there had probably been a settlement here for many years prior. By the late 1300s the city had become home to 19 registered trade guilds, and more than 40 by the end of the 1500s. The wealth accrued by the guilds allowed for the construction of regal buildings and the fortifications required to protect them. Even today, these robust fortification survive, and visitors can visit 3 15th century towers, or the 16th century Great Tower, where Sibiu's first theatrical performance was staged in 1778. At the heart of the old town, the Great Square is the flanked by the Roman-Catholic church, the city's only Art Nouveau building, and the Brukenthal Palace, which houses one of Romania's most important art collections. A passage beneath the Council Tower connects to the Little Square, which was home to the town's most prestigious master craftsmen.

name: Gitega
description: Gitega, the political and former colonial capital, is the second-largest city in Burundi. For centuries, the king of Burundi was seated in Gitega, which grants the city historical and cultural significance. It's main highlight is the Gitega National Museum, which features an impressive collection of historical and cultural artifacts, including traditional textiles and musical instruments. The city also has a lively marketplace, where visitors can sample local foods and shop for souvenirs. Gishora drum sanctuary, a ten-minute drive from Gitega, offers a unique experience of the whole settlement coming together to perform and play drums for visitors. And with its central location, Gitega makes a great base for exploring other nearby attractions, such as Lake Tanganyika and the Rusizi National Park.

name: Clermont-Ferrand
description: One of the oldest settlements in France, the Gaulish leader who would unite the tribes against the Romans was born nearby. Throughout its long history, the city remained prominent, serving as the base of the First Crusade, and becoming property of the Crown in the 17th century. Today the city has two distinct historic centers: Clermont with the key monuments, Montferrand, which is one of the country's best preserved towns, and perfect for strolling. The city is home to two monumental churches, both of which are worth visiting. The imposing Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption Gothic cathedral, made of black lava stone still has its original stained-glass windows. The Romanesque Notre-Dame-du-Port basilica, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is equally striking, with a exquisitely carved choir, and a crypt with a Black Virgin. In the heart of the city's shopping district, the immense Place de Jaude square a lively space centered around an equestrian statue of Vercingétorix.

name: Church of St. Juan Bautista
address.addr1: Church of St. Juan Bautista, San Juan Chamula
description: The Church of St. Juan Bautista was built in the 16th century when the Spanish arrived and tried to convert the local people to Christianity. Chamulans, however, are fiercely independent, and while the Spanish tried to incorporate indigenous rituals, the locals ultimately appointed their own religious leaders and dropped any pretense of a standard Catholic Mass. Instead, the interior of this unassuming church is blanketed under a carpet of pine needles, and worship usually involves candles, moonshine, and maybe an animal sacrifice lead by a healer. Devotees do pray to the statues of saints lining the walls, but these actually represent Mayan deities, and must live up to local standards - the saints held responsible for allowing the nearby church of San Sebastian to be destroyed had their hands cut off.

name: Magdeburg
description: Though it was founded by Charlemagne in 805, it's Otto the Great, Holy Roman Emperor from 962 who locals revere. Otto, who presented his favourite residence as a gift to his wife Edith, is still beloved by locals today, and is buried within the city's most significant landmark, the Cathedral of St. Mauritius and St. Catherine. Perched on a hilltop and crowned with ornate spires, Germany's first Gothic cathedral can be seen for miles. Right behind the cathedral is the city's oldest building, the Monastery of Our Lady, which now houses an art museum. Nearby, amongst the the contemporary Green Citadel, by Friedensreich Hundertwasser replaced one of the first prefabricated slab buildings in Germany. It's vibrant facade celebrates the beauty and cultural history of the surrounding landmarks while contrasting with the bank and modern austerity.

name: Madrid
description: While the area has been populated since the Paleolithic era, no official settlement existed on the site until an Arab fortress was built along the river in the 9th century. However, it wasn't until King Philip II made Madrid the capital in 1561 that it truly began to flourish, seeing the population grow almost 10-fold in the 16th century. Today, the historic center is known as the "Madrid of Los Austrias" in honor to the Hapsburg monarchs. The fantastic 17th century Plaza Mayor embodies the city's 16th and 17th century splendor. The surrounding area is the aristocratic center, where visitors can find the 17th century Royal Palace, and take a tour through its decadent halls. Along with the vast selection of historic buildings, the city is also home to over 60 museums, which span the entirety of human knowledge. For many, the highlight is the Prado Museum, which is considered one of the world's most important art galleries, while the Reina Sofía National Art Centre is dedicated to contemporary Spanish art and contains works by Picasso, and Salvador Dalí, among others.

name: Mar del Plata
description: Come relax and enjoy the temperate climate in a classic beach destination. Once a luxurious holiday destination, 'Mardel' has become a bustling city that welcomes millions of visitors per year, from around the country and the world. There's plenty to enjoy with its numerous offerings, such as cultural events, a myriad of cuisines, and beautiful historic architecture. It's the perfect balance of a peaceful seaside town and bustling city, and there's something for every taste. You can wander to the coast and take part in a wide variety of nautical activities, or simply admire the view. Within the city's limits, you'll find a variety of pubs, clubs, restaurants, and the centrally located Plaza Colon. Wherever you go or whatever you do, you will always receive the notorious hospitality of its locals, who are delighted to welcome visitors.

name: Kinderdijk
description: The Netherlands are perhaps best known for their wooden clogs, windmills, and being below sea level. Unlike much of the rest of the world, the Dutch utilize these windmills for water-maintenance, otherwise most of the country would be submerged. For over 1000 years, the distinctly Dutch system of dykes, windmills, and pumping stations has been in place. These 18th century windmills create one of the most iconic vistas in the Netherlands. Along with admiring the view, visitors can learn about the windmills history and operation through the two Museum Windmills, and in the Windmill Workshop, a guide explains how the windmills work and are maintained. To check the site's schedule and book your tickets in advance, please visit https://www.kinderdijk.com/

name: Miaoli
description: Miaoli beckons travelers with its vibrant cultural tapestry, scenic beauty, and opportunities to immerse themselves in the traditions and flavors of Hakka culture. It is renowned for its annual display of tung blossoms, which are deeply intertwined with Hakka culture. Typically blooming in April and May, these blossoms transform the streets into a snow-like landscape. In recent years, Miaoli has gained recognition as a slow-living and slow-travel destination, in part due to two of its townships being recognized by Cittaslow, an international movement promoting a leisurely pace of life. The Miaoli Hakka Roundhouse, a cultural exhibition center, tourist hub, performance venue, and DIY art center, stands as a testament to the preservation of Hakka traditions. The city also offers culinary delights at the Miaoli Yingcai Night Market, the largest in the region, where authentic Taiwanese night market experiences can be savored on Fridays, Saturdays, and Wednesdays.

name: Zakinthos City
description: Zakynthos city, the vibrant capital of Zakynthos Island, invites travelers to immerse themselves in its rich history, breathtaking landscapes, and lively atmosphere. Wander through the narrow cobblestone streets of the Old Town, where historic buildings adorned with colorful bougainvillea create a picturesque backdrop. Discover hidden gems around every corner, from quaint cafes and traditional tavernas to boutique shops offering local crafts and souvenirs. No visit to Zakynthos city is complete without exploring its cultural landmarks, including the iconic Solomos Square and the stunning St. Dionysios Church, dedicated to the island's patron saint. Delve into Zakynthos' storied past at the Byzantine Museum and the Museum of Solomos and Eminent Zakynthians, where exhibits showcase the island's artistic heritage and literary legacy. For nature lovers, Zakynthos city serves as a gateway to the island's natural wonders, including the world-famous Navagio Beach, known for its crystal-clear waters and iconic shipwreck. Embark on boat tours to explore hidden coves, sea caves, and marine sanctuaries, or simply relax on the sun-drenched shores of Agios Nikolaos Beach.

name: Getaria
description: While evidence of a Roman village dating back to the 1st century B.C. exists in the area, the village of Getaria was founded between 1180 and 1194 by King Sacnho of Navarre, making it one of the oldest towns in the province. The quaint old town slopes gently downhill toward the small harbour, making for the perfect setting for an afternoon stroll. Today, the village is well-known for its restaurants, seafood, and a local white wine known as Txacolí. Visitors to the town can enjoy the Church of San Salvador, one of the main examples of Gothic style in the area and declared a national monument in 1895; the monument to Elcano, built in 1922 to commemorate the 4th centenary of his journey in 1522; and the observatory of the sea, which offers a stunning view over the beautiful coastline and surrounding ocean. Getaria lends to the perfect blend of nature, history, and culture.

name: Jupiter Artland
description: Jupiter Artland was founded in 1999 by art collectors Robert and Nicky Wilson within the 80 acre estate of the 19th century Bonnington House. The garden is a playful pairing of art and nature with no set routes - visitors instead are encouraged to explore the park in their own way, enjoying the thrill of discovering the singular sculptures spread throughout the park. The mood is set as soon as visitors enter the park with the crafted landscape of Charles Jencks' 'Life Mounds', which isn't meant to just be seen, but experienced. For more information, please visit jupiterartland.org Photo by Steve Hodgson (Flickr.com) under CC BY-SA 2.0

name: Ierapetra
description: Ierapetra, literally "The Sacred Stone", has been the most important town in southern Crete since the days of the Minoans. Today, it's a mecca for sun worshippers, who flock here to enjoy the sunniest and warmest weather in all of Crete. The QualityCoast Awards named Ierapetra one of the top destinations in all of Europe for its pristine beaches, beautiful blue waters, and rich cultural heritage. If you need a break from the beach, start at the 14th-century Fortress of Kales, and then stroll along the waterfront promenade, enjoying the view as you make your way to the small archaeological museum, which is housed in a school built for the town's Turkish children after Crete was liberated from Ottoman rule in 1899. Or, step back from the waterfront and explore the old town, which is dotted with historic churches, an Ottoman mosque, and hidden in an alley, the humble home where Napoleon allegedly stayed on his way to Egypt. Many visitors linger even longer in Ierapetra to make day trips to the protected white sand beaches of Chrysi Island.

name: Ennis
description: Ennis was founded in the 12th century, when the O'Brien dynasty built a royal residence here. In 1240, King Donnchadh O'Brien had a large church built, which he then donated to the Franciscans. While the settlement did well as a religious center, the 18th century Penal Laws proved to be a boon for the town, with Catholics and merchants from Limerick relocating here, establishing it as a thriving market town through the 19th century. Today, history and tradition are still alive and well in Ennis. If you're planning on visiting other sites in County Clare, pay a visit to the free Clare Museum. Housed in a former Sisters of Mercy Convent, the museum details 6000 years of history through an impressive array of artefacts. Nearby is the 13th century Franciscan friary, where you'll find some amazing medieval stonework. Once you've had your fill of history, you can pop into a pub to see why Ennis prides itself as "Ireland's friendliest town".

name: Copala
description: Copala was founded by the Spanish in 1565 as a base for mining the area's rich silver deposits, and named after the mythical city of gold its founded had been searching for in northern Mexico. Mining made Copala one of the region's wealthiest towns in the 19th century, but declining production coupled with declining prices all but destroyed its economy in the 20th century. The town has largely been forgotten by the modern age (it didn't even get electricity until 1979), making it a great place to stroll through the past. The uneven cobbled streets are lined with centuries-old adobe homes, painted in vibrant colors, and often accented by planters overflowing with magenta bougainvillea. Standing on a hilltop overlooking the town is its main landmark: the uniquely asymmetric 18th century church, which is a beautiful example of colonial Baroque architecture.

name: Crater Lake National Park, OR
description: Some 7000 years ago, Mount Mazama violently erupted, destroying itself but creating Crater Lake National Park. Over the centuries, the collapsed caldera filled with water from rain and snow, forming the 1,949-foot-deep lake seen today. This makes it the deepest lake in America, second-deepest in North America, and one of the 10 deepest in the world. The lake's isolation and pure water source also makes it the world's cleanest and clearest large body of water. The main viewpoint is the best place to start to for an amazing vista, but it's far from the only option. You can drive (or join a guided trolly tour) around the lake to take in the spectacle from every angle. There's also plenty of trails that delve into the surrounding old-growth forest. If you want to learn more about the lake's formation and ecology, stop by the Visitor's Center for their exhibits and short film. The park is open year-round, but the many of the roads, trails and facilities close November 1, or after the first major snowfall, whichever comes first.

name: Salerno
description: Settled since around the 9th century BC, the city waxed and waned under the rule of the ancient empires, peaking under the Dukes of Lombard. A renowned center for medieval medical studies, the 10th century Chiesa di San Gregorio honors that tradition with the Museum of the Salerno Medical School. After a textile boom in the 19th century, much of the population was scared off during WW2 in operation Avalanche, only to surge back stronger than ever. Today, it's historic center is littered with medieval churches, like the 11th century Cathedral, which houses a richly decorated interior and plethora of holy relics. Visitors can also enjoy the beautifully terraced Minerva's Garden, or lush community park. Salerno's waterfront promenade is one of the longest in the country, and also one of the most beautiful. High above the city, Arechi Castle offers unparalleled views, and a museum exhibiting archaeological finds from the area.

name: Angkor Wat
description: Angkor Wat was founded by King Suryavarman II in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, made even grander as subsequent kings tried to surpass the buildings of their forebears. The result is a sprawling 162.6 hectare religious complex said to rival anything created by the Greeks or Romans. It's difficult to comprehend the vision and ambition that went into creating Angkor Wat, which stands as a replica of the Hindu universe, bringing visitors back to the creation of being as you walk its counterclockwise course. Along the way, you'll be treated to some of the history's most astonishingly detailed architecture. The exterior of the central temple bears an 800 meter-long series of bas-reliefs depicting historical events and mythological stories, while scattered throughout the complex are over 3000 heavenly nymphs, each totally unique and sporting one of 37 different hairstyles. For more information, please visit http://angkor.com.kh/

name: Segovia
description: Founded by the Celts, the city was conquered by the Romans in the 1st century BC. Around 50 BC, they constructed the city's UNESCO listed aqueduct, which stretches for 813 meters, is considered one of the best preserved aqueducts left in the world. The romantic Alcazar overlooking the city was built under Arab rule in the 12th century. After the reconquest, when Alfonso erected the city walls, it became a favoured noble residence, and the site of Isabella the Catholic's coronation. Today its elegant gardens have been maintained, but now houses the Royal School of Artillery museum. Segovia's 16th century cathedral was the last Gothic cathedral built in Spain. Nicknamed "The Lady of Cathedrals", it's a massive masterpiece of Basque-Castilian Gothic architecture, with 18 ornately decorated chapels. Strewn throughout throughout the city, visitors will find Romanesque churches, Mudejar buildings, and fortified houses.

name: Ravello
description: Dating back to the 5th century, Ravello became an influential town under the rule of the maritime Republic of Amalfi. When the republic went against King Roberto Il Guiscardo in 1081, the town's noblemen refused to accept it. It is said some started calling the town "rebello", rebellious, which is how the name 'Ravello' appeared. Ravello's 11th century Duomo is testament to the prosperity of those years. The simplicity of its white facade is offset by the magnificent 12th century bronze doors, of which Italy only has a few. But Ravello's main draw are its villas. The 13th century Villa Rufolo and its gardens, restored from a state of decay by a Scottish botanist in the 1850s, was Wagner's inspiration for the garden of Klingsor in his opera Parsifal. No less stunning are the gardens of the 11th century Villa Cimbrone. The tree-lined avenues, rose gardens, and wisteria-laden trellises all culminate in what Gore Vidal described as the most beautiful place on the planet: the belvedere. Lined with marble busts and accented with a pseudo-Roman temple, this overlook on a sheer cliff-face gives spectacular views of the Amalfi Coast.

name: Leiden
description: First mentioned in the 9th century, over the centuries the picturesque city of Leiden would grow to be one of the most important in the country. The historic Leiden University, one of the top schools in Europe, and the oldest in the Netherlands, was founded in 1575, and established the city as one of Europe's most prominent academic centers - Einstein himself was a regular professor here. This reputation is further solidified by the city's slew of museum, such as the National Museum of Natural History, where visitors will find everything from fossils and bones to a "treasure chamber" filled with precious gems. The Museum Boorhaave delves even deeper into Leiden's history of science, displaying historic scientific and medical instruments, and even a reconstruction of a Theatrum Anatomicum. Visitors can also opt to simply stroll the city's old town - the second largest in the country - to enjoy the charming canals lined with 17th century houses.

name: Tetouan
description: Tetouan as it stands today dates back to the 15th century when it was re-built and fortified by Ali al-Mandri who had emigrated from the Andalusian city of Granada shortly before the Reconquest. Thousands of Muslims and Jews from Andalucia followed suit, and it's even nicknamed Little Jerusalem by Sephardi Jews. Tetouan's ties to Spain were further strengthened when it was made the capital of the Spanish protectorate of Morocco in 1913. While the medina is one of the smallest in Morocco, it's one of the most complete and unaltered, not to mention distinctive for its Andalusian styling, which has earned it recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Walking through the narrow streets up the hill you're treated to a marriage of Moroccan and Andalusian architecture, with white walls, arabic arches, and even a Catholic church amongst the mosques.

name: Leon
description: Leon is bursting with energy and offers visitors a great combination of historic charm and contemporary entertainment, gastronomy and leisure activities. The rich cultural heritage of the region can be seen first-hand through the Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Light. Built in 1746, this Baroque and Neoclassical structure represents the return of Jesuits into the city. Another beautiful construction, the Expiatorio Cathedral, was built in the 20th century but took so long to finish that locals joked the completion of the building would coincide with the world's end. Luckily, the cathedral stands tall in this lively city. Leon has extensive cycling lanes and plenty of outdoor space to get some fresh air. Before leaving the city, grab some artisan leather goods to remember your trip by.

name: Acadia National Park
description: If you need any convincing on just how beautiful Acadia National Park is, consider this: it was the first National Park east of the Mississippi - putting it up there with Yellowstone and the Grand Canyon (which received its status the same day as Acadia). The rugged coast and surrounding forest have been a popular escape since the 19th century, and remain a destination for nature lovers to this day. There's 158 miles of trails to explore, across coast, woods, and mountains. Experience the power of the sea at the Thunder Hole - a narrow inlet, where the waves from the coming tide explode against the rocky shore. When the waves are rolling, you will get wet. The hike up Cadillac Mountain is another favorite. As the highest point on the Eastern Seaboard, you're treated to spectacular views. Early birds can even catch the sunrise before anyone else in the US!

name: Kufstein
description: Likely dating back to the days of the Roman Empire, Kufstein's position on the River Inn made it an important trade town through the Middle Ages. Its iconic fortress, perched on a 300-foot-tall cliff, dates back to the thirteenth century, with many additions and renovations over the years. This imposing fortification doesn't just provide fantastic views across the town, river, alps in the background - it's also a museum offering a look at medieval life (and the chance to check out secret tunnels and stark prison cells). If you're lucky enough to be visiting at noon or 6:00PM during July or August you'll be able to hear the castle's most famous feature, the outdoor pipe organ, being played. After the castle, it's well worth exploring the charming old town for its cobbled streets and medieval churches. Romerhofgasse is an attraction in itself, its vibrantly decorated buildings housing everything from souvenir shops and restaurants to the world's largest gin gallery.

name: Holasovice
description: This rare example of a Baroque village may be small but provides plenty of food for thought long after leaving. Holašovice was first mentioned in documents in 1263 and three centuries later, was almost wiped out by Bubonic Plague, which today is commemorated by the Plague Column located in the north of the village. Following the end of the Second World War, the German speaking villagers were displaced and the village farms abandoned in a state of disrepair. It remained as a 'ghost village' throughout the communist era until 1990 when it was extensively restored and today has over 140 inhabitants. Visitors can walk through this low-key tranquil hamlet that still remains unspoiled today and experience first hand the feel and architecture of life two-hundred years ago. The village also features a replica Stonehenge built from local stones and positioned on a site selected by psychotronic experts.

name: Soller
description: Nestled among the Tramuntana mountains, Sóller is a captivating Spanish town hailed as one of the country's most enchanting destinations. Archduke Ludwig Salvator of Austria even proclaimed it the island's prettiest town, and once you explore its historic center, you'll understand why. Renowned architect Joan Rubid, a pupil of Gaudí, has left an indelible mark on Sóller's architecture, notably at the neo-Gothic church of San Bartomeu and Banco de Sóller. The town's prosperity burgeoned through the export of oranges and wine to France, shaping its flourishing past and unique character. Delight in a stroll along Sa Lluna, the longest street, where history whispers through open doors revealing private gardens and historic wonders. Immerse yourself in Sóller's modernist essence at Can Prunera, a museum housing precious paintings and showcasing sinuous, nature-inspired shapes. Discover the importance of oranges at Ecovinyassa orchard, where over 18,000 square meters offer a glimpse into orange tree culture amid a special microclimate. Visit the bustling Sóller city market for local products, and savor artisanal ice cream, where orange reigns supreme.

description: The seaport is situated only a few kilometers from the mouth of the river Neretva and sits almost exactly halfway between Split and Dubrovnik. Formally opened in 1945, Ploce is the perfect starting point for tours. A number of summer events such as sporting competitions are also held annually in the town. Nearby Bacina Lakes (approximately 2 km from Ploce) are free to explore, boasting a set of 7 freshwater lakes surrounded by mountains and unspoiled nature. Whether you're admiring nature's beauty or just passing through, Ploce has something for everyone.

name: Guasave
description: Guasave, the seat of the municipality of the same name, has a history tracing back to the pre-Hispanic era. A large pantheon was discovered, along with high quality ceramics and artifacts, suggesting Guasave as the northernmost border of Mesoamerica. The ruins of the San Ignacio temple offer a glimpse into the region's past, along with Pueblo Nuevo de Nio, which preserves the ruins of an unfinished Jesuit mission. Nature enthusiasts will be in heaven at Navachiste bay, an expansive estuary with coves, lagoons, and numerous islands. The waters reap abundant fish species for sport fishing and is also known for its archaeological remains, including petroglyphs, in its surrounding hills and lush vegetation. Visit the Sanctuary of Our Lady of the Rosary, a modern church located in the heart of Guasave that is held in high esteem by the local community, and make sure to try some of the city's delicious fish and shellfish. Dishes such as Zarandeado, aguachiles, ceviche and tamales are deeply ingrained in the local culture.
