name: Viña del Mar
description: Vina del Mar is the top destination in Chile for manicured seaside perfection. The perfect weather does present one problem though - how best to enjoy it. On one hand, you can head oceanside, walk the promenade, sunbathe and swim, grab some fresh seafood for lunch, and perhaps check out the giant flower clock or Wulff Castle, a Romantic seaside manor. The other option is to visit one of Viña del Mar green spaces to see why it's nicknamed The Garden City. The Parque Quinta Vergara was originally the private residence of a 19th century Portuguese businessman, and his Venetian neo-Gothic palace (now an art museum) is still a striking attraction. Even more popular is the National Botanical Garden, a 400 hectare reserve where you can stroll shady paths to see some 3000 species of flora from around the world. Or just feed the ducks at the lagoon.

name: Falun
description: The capital of the ancient medieval Swedish Kingdom of Dalarna County, Falun fits scenically into beautiful valleys and lakes, boasting one of the most significant copper mines in Europe and significant cultural exports. The gorgeous river Faluån flows through the city, with the "mining side" included in the city's World Heritage listing - notable for once producing 70% of all copper in the Western world. You can spend hours exploring the site and learning about the legends of the mine's history, or walk the 1.6km-long trail around the Great Pit. On the other side of the river, the "delightful side" awaits, lined with classical pedestrian streets and small shops selling the world famous Falun sausage "Falukorv". Coated on the wooden houses and bars throughout the town is a deep rust red paint known as "Falu red", created in the town from the iron-rich materials of the mine. It's become an iconic color throughout Sweden and originates right from this charming city.

name: Palmira
description: The third largest city in the region, Palmira is known as the agricultural capital of Colombia, growing coffee, rice, corn, tobacco, and most significantly, sugar cane. In fact, the city is home to the country's most important sugar mills. This not-too-big city doesn't have much in the way of historic monuments, but offers a great place to immerse yourself in "real" everyday Colombian life. Just head to Plaza de Bolivar, grab some street-food, and watch the world go by under the tropical trees before going over to admire the beautiful, red brick cathedral that dominates one end of the plaza.

name: Mijas
description: Founded in by the Tartessians, whose original fortification are still visible in parts of the city's wall, Mijas flourished during the ancient age thanks to its wealth of minerals. Frequent pirate attacks from the 15th to 19th centuries prompted the town to construct the watchtowers that still stand today. For much of the modern era, it was little more than a jumble of shacks, but thanks to the popularity of the Costa del Sol, it's grown into a picturesque 'Pueblo Blanco', creating a setting befitting its rich history. Now, the city's famous Burrito Taxis can bring visitors to the unique oval shaped bull-ring, or the Sanctuary of the Virgin of the Rock, a 15th century chapel excavated in solid rock. Up the hill, the 16th century Church of the Immaculate Conception replaced an old mosque, and uses the Mosque's original towers as belfries.

name: Beziers
description: Occupied since Neolithic times, and officially settled in 575 BC, Béziers is one of the oldest cities in France. Positioned on an important trade-route, it's long been known for its wine, with the city's winegrowers even inventing a container for carrying wine in a ship's hold. In 1209 crusaders massacred nearly the entire city, including the Catholic population, and then burned it down, in the Church's crusade against the Cathar sect. While the original Cathedral was destroyed in the massacre, its 13th century replacement still dominates the town today. From it's hilltop position, it offers stupendous views of the city and the surrounding vineyards. If you wear appropriate clothing, you can also explore the interior, with its rich ornamentation and medieval artwork, as well as the peaceful cloisters. Below the cathedral, the Musée des Beaux Arts exhibits works by Rubens, Delacroix, and several local artists.

name: Blaenavon
description: Towards the end of the 18th century, the little town of Blaenavon put its rich iron deposits to use, and quickly became the world leader in iron production, utilizing cutting edge technologies like coal and steam power. After enjoying this industrial boom, the began to decline, and even an attempt at steel production couldn't save the ironworks, which was finally shuttered in 1904. Today, the 33 square kilometer area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for the role it played in early industrialization. Visitors can head to the Big Pit, home of the National Coal Mining Museum, to learn about the miner's lives and the hard labor they endured. For many living in the UK, overgrown stone furnaces and other imposing structures are the main draw as they were featured in the BBC historic reality show Coal House.

name: Szekesfehervar
description: Founded in 972 by High Prince Géza, who had a small stone castle built, the swampy surroundings protected it during the 13th century Mongol Invasion. Having survived unscathed, the town prospered during the 13th–15th centuries, with several palaces defensive walls being built. This new, regal city became the home of the Hungarian monarchy, seeing 43 kings crowned, and several buried at the now ruined Basilica of St. Stephen. Unfortunately, it didn't fare as well in the following centuries, being sacked by Maximilian I, and falling under Ottoman rule. In the 18th century, under Habsburg rule, the town recovered, and several lavish new buildings erected. Today, visitors can still enjoy the historic old town's Baroque atmosphere, as exemplified by the cathedral, episcopal palace, and city hall. The Black Eagle Pharmacy, with an ornately carved wooden interior is now a museum exhibiting many items accumulated over its 300 years of operation.

name: Matmatat-Al-Qadimal
description: For thousands of years, the Berbers of Matmatat-Al-Qadimal have had a simple solution to escaping the desert heat: make their homes underground. The basic process is to dig a deep circular pit, and then dig underground rooms around the perimeter, leaving the main pit as a courtyard. These unique structures were largely unknown, even to other Tunisians, until the 1960s when severe flooding forced the locals to ask the government for aid. Ten years later, Matmatat was brought to the attention of millions when George Lucas used the Hotel Sidi Driss as Luke Skywalker's home on Tatooine. While the hotel is the best known and easiest to access, the area is dotted with these subterranean settlements, such as nearby Haddej with its underground olive press.

name: Casas Grandes
description: Casas Grandes, also known as Paquimé, stands as a remarkable testament to the rich pre-Columbian history of northwest Chihuahua, Mexico. The city's construction, encompassing about 20% of its potential sprawl, earned it the UNESCO World Heritage Site designation in 1998. Archaeologists believe it evolved from earlier structures, potentially pit houses, built by the Mogollon between 700 and 1200 CE. The cityscape includes platform mounds, expansive plazas, and ball-courts resembling Mesoamerican designs, hinting at its role as a cultural crossroads. Among its ceremonial features are mounds shaped like a feathered serpent and a turkey, possibly dedicated to the god Quetzalcoatl. Despite being only partially excavated, this ancient city offers a profound glimpse into a once-vibrant culture that thrived within its unique environment but mysteriously vanished with the arrival of the Spanish Conquest. The site is open 8:30AM to 7:30PM Monday to Saturday, and 9AM to 7PM on Sunday.

name: Agua Azul Waterfalls
description: The Agua Azul Waterfalls stretch for over a kilometer, showcasing tumbling cascades and pools of bright blue water. The high mineral content in this stretch of the Xanil River has encased the rocks and fallen trees in a thick coating of limestone over time, resulting in elegantly-curved formations. A path works its way along the river bank, treating visitors to beautiful views of the cascades and the dense jungle, culminating in a viewing platform that looks out over the entire stretch of the Agua Azul Waterfalls. Along the way, there are numerous small restaurants where you can stop to enjoy a bite to eat while taking in the view.

name: Caerlaverock Castle
description: The moated, triangular, Caerlaverock Castle was first built in the 13th century, and remained a stronghold of the Maxwell family until its abandonment in the 17th century. In 1300, the castle's formidable defenses allowed 60 men to withstand the entire English army under King Edward I for a considerable time. After being besieged for the last time in 1640, Caerlaverock was partly demolished and abandoned. Though now a ruin, the imposing red sandstone walls still paint an imposing picture particularly for their unique triangular plan. Within the permanent exhibition you can learn about siege warfare - a subject the castle is an expert on. Visitors can also follow the nature trail around the castle moat to the site of an even older fort, or stop by the tea room for some delicious home-baked goods and fresh coffee. Please note: the castle can sometimes close for inclement weather. For more information, please visit historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/caerlaverock-castle/

name: Kampala
description: The vibrant capital of Uganda boasts culture, cuisine, and all kinds of activities! Sprawling but not as crowded as it's capital counterparts, you will feel welcomed by the locals and instantly feel their sense of community. Visit the Uganda National Museum, which is the country's oldest and most impressive collection of artefacts through Africa's history, from fossils to the first printing press in Uganda. Then visit the UNESCO-listed Kasubi Royal Tombs to learn about the Buganda Kingdom history. Holding a huge spiritual significance, this heritage site serves as a resting place to at least four kings. While these two attractions are very popular, there are many more, such as Bahai Temple, the Independence Monument at the Parliament of Uganda, or any of the various markets around the city. Full of fun, excitement, and history, Kampala is a hot destination on the rise.

name: Plock
description: Foreshadowing centuries of strife, Plock started off as a fortified burg in the 10th century. Originally a seat of Masovian bishops, Plock became Poland's capital during the reign of Ladislaus Herman and his son Boleslaus III the Wrymouth, from 1079-1138. Over the following centuries, Plock was attacked and burnt by Lithuanians and Ruthenians several times, and persevered fires and epidemics, the Swedes in the 17th-18th century, the French in 19th century, and the Russian and German armies that robbed and destroyed it during World War II. Each time, Plock rebuilt itself, whether in the form of the 14th century Gothic castle, parish, and fortifications, resplendent romantic manors, or post-war development towards modernity. Visitors can revisit this history by visiting the castle museum, the 12th century cathedral, or gazing down at the city from Tumskie Hill.

description: Embark on a scenic escapade aboard the heritage railway, which winds along a picturesque route from St. Nicholas Abbey to the breathtaking Cherry Tree Hill viewpoint. Ideal for both locals and tourists, this 45-minute train ride offers an immersive experience. Marvel at the panoramic sea vistas as you pause at Cherry Tree Hill, where optional lectures on Barbadian railway history unfold. Here, the manually operated turntable adds an extra touch of authenticity, captivating railway enthusiasts. The journey boasts three captivating stations: St. Nicholas Abbey Station—hub of activity, featuring a shop, catering, and restrooms, Cherry Tree Hill Station, and Croquet Lawn Halt—situated by the estate house and lake, a perfect spot for alighting to explore the rum distillery. Don't miss the chance to explore St. Nicholas Abbey itself, a magnificent Jacobean-style mansion dating back to 1658. Indulge your taste buds at the Terrace Café, savoring homemade delights while overlooking tropical gullies.

name: Seefeld
description: The fresh, crisp mountain air and the views make Seefeld an excellent place to stop by at any time of the year. When exploring the village the legendary pilgrimage church of St. Oswald situated in the market square begs for a visit. The church was the site of the "Miracle of the Host" in the fourteenth-century. Details of the miracle are displayed near the altar in the church. A popular and fun thing to do is to get out of the village and take the Rosshutte, the train that takes visitors up the mountain. Experience the jaw-dropping views of the surrounding nature as the train makes it way up the mountain and stops at the large panoramic restaurant, café, and outdoor seating/activity area. There are not many better or more memorable places to stop for lunch. After all, who could resist a taste of traditional Austrian cuisine in an alpine setting to die for?

name: Morgan's Cave
address.region: Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina
description: Visit Morgan's Cave, where islanders have long whispered tales of the infamous pirate Henry Morgan concealing his ill-gotten riches within this labyrinthine coral cave. This coral cave boasts a series of tunnels leading to a mysterious deep lagoon, providing visitors with an opportunity to immerse themselves in a realm that remains largely untouched due to its challenging access. The cave spans an impressive 35 meters in width and stretches 200 meters in length. Below ground, it connects to the Caribbean Sea, a testament to the enduring influence of time and the patient hand of nature, which has sculpted its unique limestone formations resembling the jaws of a mythical sea creature. Five thematic stations, including The Pirate Museum, Pirate Ship, Coconut Museum, Island Art Museum, and, of course, Morgan's Cave itself, offer visitors an opportunity to delve into the island's captivating past. The cave is open for exploration 9AM to 5:30PM daily. Photo by Aliman5040, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Khao Yai
description: Established in 1962, Khao Yai National Park is the oldest in the country, and at 2168 sq km, the 3rd largest. Despite its size, Khao Yai is one of the most accessible nature experiences in the country. A network of trails and guide options make it easy to get into one of Asia's largest intact monsoon forests and see the the rich variety of wildlife that call Khao Yai home. Here, you have the chance to see wild elephants, monkeys, deer, over 300 species of bird, countless insects, and a single Siamese crocodile. Please note: appropriate clothing and footwear is strongly recommended.

name: Melk
description: Walking Melk today, you can't help but feel like it was some sort of royal bastion. This is largely due to the Abbey, a former palace which dominates the small but perfectly formed town from its rocky bluff. Napoleon strutted his stuff here and the Kaisergang, or Emperor's Gallery, a corridor in the Abbey, is lined with portraits of the Austrian nobility crushed beneath his heel. The highlight of the Abbey however is its baroque church, a controlled chaos of lavishly embellished marble and frescoes, simply drenched in gold. But a close second is the Marmorsaal, or Marble banqueting hall, a magnificent baroque riot of marbled pillars – look out for the gold bewigged caryatids! - and frescoed ceiling by Paul Troger which seems to soar upward vertiginously into infinity. A similarly vertiginous effect is experienced on the tightly circular marble convolutions of the Abbey library stairwell, where you can appreciate why Umberto Eco researched his best-selling novel The Name of the Rose here. While the Abbey cannot – shouldn't – be avoided, the town itself is a delightful place to recover from its profusion of historical and architectural wealth.

name: Talca
description: The capital of Chile's Maule wine-growing region, Talca is overlooked by many travelers, but offers an interesting smorgasbord of Chilean culture. At the main square, you can still find colonial architecture, including the recently-repaired cathedral. Be sure to visit the home of Bernardo O'Higgins block away. O'Higgins signed Chile's Declaration of Independence here before serving as a leader in Chile's War for Independence and then the country's second Supreme Director. The 2,000 objects on display tell the tale of the man and the country. Walking is a popular pastime in the city, so if you want to stretch your legs, hike up to the Cerro De la Virgen viewpoint, or amble through the idyllic University Botanical Gardens where you'll find endangered flora and a farm with 60 animals. Last but not least, if you love wine, visit the Huilquilemu Cultural Village on the outskirts of town. This cluster of 19th century buildings details the winemaking history through antique machinery and a wine cellar - there's also an excellent restaurant!

name: Znojmo
description: To capture a unique snapshot of what Znojmo has to offer, simply take a stroll along the historic medieval city walls that enclose this historic Renaissance-style town with a center brimming with churches, crooked lanes, and endless picturesque nooks and crannies. Almost all the walls are still preserved, and there are various towers and strongholds along the way. The views across the valley through which the River Dyje runs are simply jaw-dropping, no matter the time of the year. The town center, which dates back to the eleventh-century, is easy to navigate on foot. Visitors can choose from a plethora of attractions, whether it be exploring the castle, one of the many churches or the fascinating underground complex of tunnels and cellars that run underneath the town. Of course, few visitors leave Znojmo without sampling and taking away some of the local wines available from one of the many outlets in the town.

name: Mazatlan
description: At first glance, it might seem that Mazatlan is trying to brag - it is a city with over 20 miles of beaches, one of the longest boardwalks in the world, the largest aquarium in Mexico, and the host of the Mazatlan Carnival, considered one of the most important carnivals in the country. But really, Mazatlan is one cool beach town at heart. Visitors will enjoy a stroll along the Malecón (Boardwalk) of Mazatlan where they can gain a view of the city, and especially those with children can visit the aforementioned aquarium, which also houses a botanical garden. The gastronomy of the area will particularly satiate seafood-lovers, as the beach town specializes in ceviches and aguachiles - stop into one of the local restaurants on your boardwalk strut!

name: Invercargill
description: Invercargill is an automotive lover's dream, whether your passion is automobiles, motorcycles, or even history, the shops and museums are among the most impressive. Begin at Bill Richardson Transport World, which is a massive showroom with different sections to display vintage automobiles, motorcycles, and even heavy machinery. An impressive shrine to the motorcycling world and its history is the Classic Motorcycle Mecca, learn about the history and view artifacts from all the best and worst times of cycling's past. Then head over to Dig This, where everyone of all ages can have a chance at operating heavy machinery on this interactive playground. Still can't get enough? Make your way to E Hayes Motorworks Collection, which is a hardware store turned exhibit. You can see classic cars and motorcycles side by side, while you shop for anything you may need (hardware related).

name: Trebinje
description: Trebinje is located in the valley of the Trebisnjica River on the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Croatia. Less overrun by its neighboring cities, Trebinje exudes a warm and hospitable personality. The city's walled old town is still fully intact and one of the few in the country not heavily damaged by war. Today, there are many restaurants and fine wines in Trebinje's old town. The city's most famous landmark is the beautiful Ottoman Arslanagic Bridge with its picture-perfect views. The mid-sized city also has many temples, churches, mosques, markets, and a museum waiting to be explored.

name: Chedworth Roman Villa
description: When the Chedworth Roman Villa was founded in the 2nd century, it was three separate groups of buildings. Over the next 200 years, these buildings were expanded and linked to create an elite dwelling rivalling anything else in Britain. The villa's period of glory was short lived as it was likely destroyed in the 5th century. In 1864, the villa was rediscovered when a gamekeeper was digging for a ferret. Today, visitors can see the spring-fed nymphaeum pool, two separate heated bath houses (one dry and one wet), and the amazing dining room with its marvelous mosaic and heated floors! In the villa museum, visitors will be able to see the Roman coins, jewelry, and figurines unearthed during the site's excavation. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/chedworth-roman-villa

name: Agrigento
description: Founded in the 6th century BC, Agrigento was one of the largest and richest Greek colonies of Magna Graecia. After being sacked by the Carthaginians in 406 BC, the city never fully recovered, and passed under Roman, Vandal, Goth, Byzantine, Arab, and Norman rule in the following centuries. Overlooking the UNESCO-listed Valley of the Temples, modern Agrigento is ringed by unattractive residential towers. However, break through this shell and you'll find the city has managed to preserve some of its historic charms. Walking the via Atenea, you'll be treated to plenty of picturesque buildings and shops selling the city's signature sheep ricotta ice-cream. The city's 11th century Norman Gothic Cathedral presents in interesting amalgam of Arabic, Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque architecture, and houses a museum stocked with rich relics and art. In the Agrigento Regional Archaeological Museum, Grecco-Roman artefacts from the nearby archaeological site, and relics from the even older indigenous civilization are on display.

name: Trabzon
description: Located in the northeastern coast of Turkey, far from the typical tourist tracks, lies the charming city of Trabzon. Its location off the beaten path only amplifies its authentic appeal, with its scenic coastal landscape and lush greenery adding to its allure. Trabzon is steeped in history, being the birthplace of the renowned Ottoman Sultan, Suleiman the Magnificent, and home to a well-regarded local football team. The city is also recognized for its significant exports of hazelnuts and tea. When it comes to sightseeing, Trabzon offers several attractions. The 19th-century Ataturk House, the Hagia Sophia Museum—an epitome of Byzantine architecture—and the vibrant Historical Bedesten Bazaar, where you can immerse yourself in local culture by purchasing crafts, savoring delicacies, and enjoying coffee in traditional cafes, are must-visit spots. Trabzon's culinary scene is dominated by seafood, particularly fried anchovies, and the famous Akçaabat meatballs. And of course, no meal would be complete without pide, a traditional bread that is a staple across Turkey but actually originated from Trabzon. However, to truly experience the spirit of Trabzon, simply take a leisurely stroll through its hilly and mountainous terrain - the rejuvenating walk amidst nature is a treat in itself. Do keep in mind that Trabzon is known for its rainy climate, so plan your outdoor activities accordingly.

name: Sheki
description: Sheki's architectural splendor and its role as a prominent Silk Road trading hub has earned it a place as a renowned UNESCO World Heritage site, standing as a testament to the grandeur of the Sheki Khanate era. Visit the astounding Palace of Shaki Khans, with its exterior and interior adorned with lavish decorations of vibrant glass mosaic windows and intricate Persian patterns. A visit to this ancient palace offers a glimpse into the opulence and elegance of Azerbaijan's past. Delve deeper into Sheki's history within the walls of the Sheki Fortress, holding the Three Saints Church - a unique round-shaped Caucasian Albanian Church. Explore the local craft market where you can purchase handmade silk cloths and other locally crafted souvenirs. To satisfy your taste buds, Sheki is famous for its mouthwatering Azerbaijani sweets, particularly Halva. Designed with patterns reminiscent of Sheki stained glass windows, it's a must-try culinary delight to accompany you on your journey through this captivating city.

name: Lahemaa National Park
description: Situated on the threshold of Lahemaa National Park, Estonia's largest nature reserve, Viru Bog offers easy access to the park's characteristic mix of forest and bog landscapes. Visitors can take the 3.5 km path, or full 6 km long loop, along this nature trail to learn about the bog's flora, former sand dunes, eskers, peat milling field, and heath forest. In the center of the bog-spanning boardwalk, a wooden observation tower provides great views into the bog and natural park beyond.

name: Jeongseon
description: Nestled in Gangwon-do, Jeongseon County has become an increasingly popular travel destination. The county is renowned as the birthplace of "Jeongseon Arirang," a beloved traditional Korean folksong, adding cultural significance to its allure. One of the notable attractions in Jeongseon is the Jeongamsa Temple, founded by Jajang, also known as "Galaesa." Another cultural gem is the Sumano Pagoda, known for its sharpened stone construction. To celebrate the cherished Arirang culture, the county hosts the annual Jeongseon Arirang Festival in October, promoting and preserving the timeless Arirang traditions. The Arirang Museum, operated by the county government, showcases around 600 exhibits related to the famous folksong, offering visitors an immersive cultural experience. Beyond its cultural heritage, Jeongseon provides thrilling adventures at the High 1 Resort, a ski resort located in Gohan-eup. The resort, situated at 1,345 meters, is the highest altitude among Korean ski resorts and offers breathtaking views from its Sky Walk. For an authentic taste of the region, the Jeongseon Five-day Market is a must-visit spot where locals' deep affection for their hometown is palpable.

name: Jozankei Onsen
description: Whether basking in the therapeutic waters, reveling in autumn's brilliance, or exploring mystical temples, Jozankei Onsen promises a year-round escape into Hokkaido's natural and cultural wonders. Established in 1866 by Monk Mizumi Jozan, the spa harnesses the healing powers of its mineral-rich waters, ranging from sodium chloride to sulfur, offering therapeutic benefits for skin conditions, anemia, fatigue, and more. Jozankei is not just a destination for hot spring aficionados but also a place rich in folklore. The town's symbol and guardian, the kappa, a mythical water sprite, adds a whimsical touch. Legend has it that the kappa protects the area, ensuring safety near the waters. Explore the town adorned with fanciful kappa statues, and take home kappa souvenirs as cherished mementos. Surrounded by majestic mountains, Jozankei's fall foliage is a mesmerizing spectacle, making it a prime location for autumn enthusiasts. The vibrant colors typically grace the landscape around mid-October, providing a breathtaking backdrop to the largest onsen town in Hokkaido.

name: Bad Ischl
description: Franz Josef loved the town so much that he visited it every year for 60 years until his death and Bad Ischl quickly became known as the 'Vienna of the Lakes', given that the town sits on the riverside close to the beautiful Mount Katrin. What sets Bad Ischl apart from many other Austrian towns is that the presence of the emperor can still be felt today. Reminders are everywhere, from the portraits adorning buildings, the statue of the emperor and the Viennese-style coffee houses where among the delicious chocolate cake and coffee, photographs of the emperor and his wife abound along with those of the other European royals who would often visit. The ambience coupled with the classical, colorful and graceful architecture of the town still evokes a feel of an imperial age, which in its own unique way, still leaves a lasting impression on all those who stop by this historic spa town.

name: Vouni
description: Vouni is one of the so-called "wine villages" that dot the foothills of the Troodos Mountains. Vouni in particular is one of the most established, and was one of the larges wine producers until the 1990s. Located at an altitude of over 2,500 feet, and bathed in sun, it's no surprise that Vouni is in a perfect location for wine making. Take a stroll through Vouni's cobbled streets, past traditional houses with their signature wooden doors, large windows, narrow balconies, and courtyards. To soak in the local atmosphere, visit the main square and savor a glass of wine at the cafe I Platia. Vouni is fairly small but is home to a few museums such as the Oenological Museum, the Museum of Folk Art, and the Byzantine Museum, an old Olive Mill, historical water reservoirs, and religious and historical monuments. Or, head to one of the several wineries located near the village to really experience its wine-making tradition.

name: Helia Bravo Hollis Botanical Gardens
description: The Helia Bravo Hollis Botanical Gardens are named after Mexico's first certified Biologist and one of the founders of the Mexican Cactus Society, whose contributions to botany were so significant that she's also had six species of cacti named in her honor. The gardens are just one part of the larger Tehuacán Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that's the most biodiverse arid region in North America, and home to members from 70% of the world's flora families. Surrounded by dry hills, the gardens are home to 80 different cactus species, many of which are both endemic and endangered - and strictly protected. Here, you'll not only see the surprising variety of shapes and sizes cacti come in, but you can also learn about the ritualistic, medicinal and nutritional uses for the plants.

name: Mbale Town
description: In the east of Uganda you will find the growing town of Mbale nestled next to one of the highest peaks in East Africa. Booming with educational institutions while maintaining a quaint feel, this town will have the honor of receiving city status in July 2020. A surprising hidden gem of this town is the Nabugoye Synagogue. You can really feel the simplicity and focus on religion by the bare structure of this house of worship. Constructed in the 20th century, this red brick building has been the cornerstone for the Jewish Abayudaya community in Mbale. Services are held in English and Hebrew on Fridays 6pm-8pm and Saturdays at 9am. A perfect place to see how Judaism flourishes in all parts of the world.

name: Alamos
description: Álamos beckons visitors with truly magical experiences, standing as a testament to Mexico's colonial past with its cobblestone streets, colonial houses adorned with white facades, and charming green spaces. Don't miss the awe-inspiring Church of the Immaculate Conception, the graceful Chapel of Zapopan, and the stunning Plaza de Armas, surrounded by majestic arcades and vibrant gardens. As you explore, you'll encounter hidden gems like the Callejón del Beso, where lovers share secret kisses from adjacent balconies, continuing a cherished tradition. But Álamos is more than just a window into the past. It's a town that thrives in the present with its lively arts festivals, including the Festival Cultural "Alfonso Ortíz Tirado," drawing national and international talent. This town's vibrant cultural scene has earned it the moniker "Little Mexican Davos." Visitors can also explore the Museo Costumbrista de Alamos Sonora, which showcases the town's history through a remarkable collection of artifacts, documents, and photographs. Plus, a ride on the little train departing from Plaza de Armas offers a comfortable tour of the town's captivating beauty.

name: Fagernes
description: Fagernes, a small town in the municipality of Nord-Aurdal, is a small artery opening up to the heart of the Valdres region. Kilometers of gravel roads stretch throughout the surrounding areas, perfect for cycling through breathtaking scenery and pasture farms where the scent of local food wafts through the air. Try the famous rømmegrøt, a creamy porridge with cinnamon, sugar, and butter, before visiting the huge open air Valdres Folk Museum situated on the bank of Lake Strandefjorden. Go fishing or boating on the lake, chill out by the waterfront or catch a performance at the Valdres Summer Symphony festival, which attracts classical music enthusiasts from all around the world.

name: Masada
description: Situated on a steep plateau overlooking the Dead Sea, Masada has been fortified since the 1st century BC, originally by Alexander Jannaeus, and later by Herod the Great. The site was etched into the annals of history when a group of nearly 1000 Jews made a desperate last stand against the Romans in 72 CE, choosing death rather than submit to the invaders. While the ruins of the vast palace are impressive, and there's and excellent map-brochure and audio guide, the architectural highlights are the world's best-preserved Roman siege-works. To reach the palace ruins, you can hike up the Roman siege ramp (there's also a cable car if you don't want to walk), and once atop the plateau, you'll see at least one of the eight siege camps and the siege wall if you look down in any direction.

name: San Salvador
description: Founded by the conquistadors in the 16th century atop the region's abandoned tribal capital, San Salvador remained relatively small until the 'Golden Age of Coffee' in the early 20th century. After several tumultuous decades, the city has received a face-lift, and now offers visitors an attractive downtown area. The most unique monument is undoubtedly the Iglesia Rosario. Looking something like an aircraft hangar from the outside, the church interior is illuminated by a rainbow of colors courtesy of the countless stained glass panes covering the building. Nearby, the mid-century Metropolitan Cathedral follows a more traditional design, but it's the tomb of Oscar Romero attracts visitors. San Salvador has some criminally-overlooked museums as well. The Museo David J Guzmanand presents a fascinating exhibition of Mayan artefacts recovered from around Central America, while the "Museo de Arte MARTE has the greatest art collection in the country, and the lavish national palace has been repurposed to house the National Museum.

name: Bombay Sapphire Distillery
description: Housed in an 18th century mill and complimented by a modern glass and steel greenhouse, the Bombay Sapphire Distillery is the promised land for gin lovers. In this beautiful architecture ensemble, visitors will learn about gin's long history, and the artistry that goes into making 'The World's Most Famous Gin'. Discover the 10 botanicals that give Bombay Sapphire its distinctive flavor, and see the cutting-edge distillery in action. Afterwards, enjoy a complimentary cocktail at the bar. Aspiring mixologists can also opt for a Gin Cocktail Masterclass to learn and create cocktails with the resident gin experts. Tickets must be booked in advance. For more information, please visit distillery.bombaysapphire.com

name: Pecs
description: The history of Pecs stretches back over 2,000 years to its first Celtic settlements before it became part of the Roman Empire. Today, the city is well known for its art and culture and is home to the world-famous Zsolnay ceramics and the largest Turkish ruins in Hungary. The fourth-century Necropolis of Sopianae contains a number of underground tombs with incredible murals that depict Christian themes. The site is open to visitors who can also delve deeper into the history of the tombs at the Visitor Center. Among the city's many historic landmarks is the iconic Gazi Kasim Mosque, which is an example of the extensive Turkish and Islamic architecture that flourished when the city was under occupation. Pecs is also situated in the country's warmest wine region, so after sampling the cultural delights of the city then why not relax with a glass of one of the region's must tries — Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Fran, and Merlot.

name: Shizuoka
description: Renowned for its tea production, the Shizuoka Prefecture's heart is the city of Shizuoka, bridging the gap between Tokyo and Nagoya. Once the capital of Suruga Province, its prominence soared when Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate, chose Sumpu Castle as his retirement residence. Shizuoka Prefecture welcomes urbanites seeking a respite from city life. It presents two distinct faces: one cloaked in lush mountains, where tea plantations and forests thrive, and the other defined by the sea's embrace. The Izu Peninsula beckons with its idyllic white-sand beaches, clear waters, and inviting onsen resorts in Atami and Ito. Visitors can immerse themselves in world-class art museums and explore the historic Sunpu Castle, once the abode of Tokugawa Ieyasu.

name: Heraclea Lyncestis
description: Founded by Philip II of Macedon in the middle of the 4th century BC, he named his victory city after the Greek mythological hero Heracles. An important city through antiquity, it was a key stopping point on the Roman road, Via Egnatia, and a Episcopal seat during the early days of Christianity. The city began a gradual decline in the 5th century, thanks in large part to raids from northern tribes. Today, the city is one of the best preserved archaeological sites in Macedonia. Several buildings from the Roman period are visible, such as the baths, theatre - which was used for gladiator fights until the practice was banned. There are also remnants from the Early Christianity years, such as the small and large Basilicas, Episcopal Residence, and necropolis. Also on the grounds is a small museum, which exhibits some of the artefacts uncovered here, and has a nice model illustrating what the city was like at its peak.

name: Coba
description: Founded around the 1st century BC, the Mayan city of Coba was a regional powerhouse thanks to its agricultural holdings. At its peak around 900 AD, the 80 km² settlement was home to an estimated 50,000 inhabitants. While its importance dwindled following a power struggle with Chichén Itzá, Coba remained in use up until the arrival of the Spanish. Today, the excavated parts of the site have revealed the largest network of roads in the Mayan world. These ancient highways connected Coba with other Mayan cities, and all emanate from the central pyramid. The Ixmoja pyramid, located in the Nohuch Mul temple group, is the tallest in the Northern Yucatan at 42 meters (138 feet) high, and offers amazing views of the entire archaeological site for those who brave its steep set of 120 steps.

name: Surakarta
description: From backstreet kampungs and an elegant walled city palace to traditional markets and modern shopping malls, Surakarta will enchant you with its diverse attractions. Situated on the eastern side of the Solo River, the city is bursting with culture, food and history. Visit the magnificent batik museum, where batik clothing is elevated to an art form. For history enthusiasts, the Sangiran Museum of Ancient Man is a must-visit, with the world's largest collection of Homo erectus fossils. A grand Javanese building dating back to 1890 houses the second-oldest museum in Indonesia, the Radya Pustaka Museum, showcasing a valuable collection of local and Dutch literature. Meanwhile, culinary delights await food enthusiasts in vibrant street markets full of roving hawkers. Taste some nasi gudeg, nasi liwet, or indulge in a sweet srabi - rice puddings served on a crispy pancake with banana, jackfruit or chocolate toppings.

name: San Luis Potosi
description: Known by most as an industrial city, San Luis Potosi is a city of surprises. What people may not know is that this city hosts hundreds of classically designed buildings, making it a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Located in the centre of Mexico, San Luis Potosi has historically served as a halfway point between the United States of America and Mexico City. Take a walk down Universidad Street and take in the impressive examples of colonial architecture that this boomtown city has to offer. Each street you pass through, you will find a building that reflects the building trends of each era. Go to the Alameda Theatre and find one of the grandest examples of neo-Moorish architecture that Mexico has to offer. Visit the Sotano de las Golondrinas (Cave of the Swallows) and marvel at the blue and green waterfalls that fame the city. If you want a modern experience, San Luis Potosi offers beautiful examples of post-modern architectures that parades this city as one of the best places to live and work in Mexico!

name: Cesky Krumlov
description: Miraculously escaping the destructive tides of war for over seven centuries, the town's architectural heritage is a harmonious melange of building styles dominated. The facades of painted houses, traditional artisan shops, taverns, and restaurants line a delightful labyrinth of cobbled streets. There's gem after gem to be found in this orange-roofed jewel-box of a town and everyone will have their favorite monument. Standing watch over the fairy-tale village (literally - it's a favorite location for Czech fantasy films) is one of the best-preserved castles in central Europe. Český Krumlov is no static museum piece pickled in amber however, it vibrates with life all year round, with a diverse program of cultural events and festivals celebrating everything from St Wenceslaus to Wine.

name: Jephson Gardens
description: The Jephson Gardens were opened in 1831 as pleasure gardens where the wealthy would go to see and be seen. In 1846, the 'Newbold Pleasure Gardens' were renamed after Dr. Henry Jephson, who had established the town as a spa destination. Ever since, this sprawling green space has been a favourite for locals and visitors who come to enjoy the ornamental fountains and spectacular floral displays, or to play tennis and croquet. Named the "Best Park in Britain" in 2004, the Jephson Gardens provide more than a pleasant walk - visitors can step into a subtropical glass house, or admire the various historic buildings spread throughout the park.

name: Dzibilchaltun
description: Dzibilchaltun was one of the longest-inhabited settlements on the Yucatan peninsula, having been occupied from around 500 BC to the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century.The remains of around 8,000 structures have been found at the site, though only a small portion have been excavated and restored. The most impressive is the Temple of the Seven Dolls, which was found in the 1950s when archaeologists discovered it underneath a later pyramid. Built on a two-tiered platform, the temple has 4 doorways facing the cardinal points, which allow for light from the rising sun to pass straight through the building. There's also a cenote on site where you can enjoy a refreshing swim. In 1958, 30,000 artefacts were found at the bottom of the cenote, many of which are now on display in the nearby museum, where there are also exhibits explaining the daily lives of both ancient and modern Maya.

name: Whangarei
description: Whangarei was once home to the largest Māori Pa - fortified city - in New Zealand. At the Town Basin Māori canoes would congregate as indigenous people used the harbour for transport, before becoming a port for exporting kauri gum, timber and coal after the European settlement. The Whangarei Museum takes you on a journey through time, exhibiting Māori artefacts, photographs of early settlements, military collections and more. Now, the quayside is a hub for international yachting and the marina is peppered with trendy bars and restaurants. The city is known for its vibrant arts culture, evident by the numerous shops and galleries lining the waterside. The Whangarei Art Museum and The Bach Art & Crafts House are popular spots to admire local artists' work. Whangarei Falls is a stunning waterfall just 10 minutes from the city centre; a short walk takes you to the focal point, a 26-metre drop into a plunge pool surrounded by lush trees and greenery.

name: St. Emilion
description: Saint-Emilion is renowned for its Grand Cru wines, making this small town a highlight of every sommelier's pilgrimage. Many of its historic vineyards having existed for centuries, and wine lovers can sample these historic local wines in Saint-Emilion's local bars, cellars, or even chateaus. To add to the experience, the picturesque medieval core is dominated by historic monuments that began sprouting up in the 11th century thanks to the town's position on the Pilgrimage Route to Santiago de Compostela. The stand-out is the monolithic Church with its bell tower, which was partly carved into the living rock in the 12th century, forming the Grotto of Saint Emilion. Visitors can also enjoy the serenity of the medieval monastic catacombs, or the peaceful Collegiate Church with its cloister. Adding to the UNESCO-listed landscape are striking secular monuments such as the massive keep of the Château du Roi and the ruins of the Palais Cardinal.

name: Yongin
description: Home to Everland and Caribbean Bay, the nation's most popular amusement and water parks, Yongin is a playground for thrill-seekers and water lovers alike. But that's not all – the city boasts the grand Korean Folk Village, the largest of its kind, offering a captivating journey through Korean history. Explore the village, where traditional food, captivating performances, and educational craft classes await. Delight in the intricate Korean architecture and immerse yourself in horseback riding or riverboat rides amidst the scenic surroundings. At Everland, explore the zoo, safari, roller coasters and street food, or head to the huge water park at Caribbean Bay. Stop by the small neighborhood of Street Bojeong, where tons of cafes and restaurants are nestled in a picturesque setting. Whether it's the enchanting folklore, adrenaline-pumping rides, or mesmerizing performances, Yongin offers a harmonious blend of cultural heritage and modern entertainment.

name: Eguisheim
description: Settled by the Senones tribe, and made a center for wine-cultivation by the Romans, the village of today didn't develop until the 11th century when the Dukes of Alsace built here a castle here. The village hasn't changed much since the Middle Ages, with its well-preserved half-timbered houses dating back to the town's foundation. The brightly-colored houses are complemented by bursts of blooming flower, which has earned the village the France's highest award for town garden planting. The Rue du Rempart Sud, which follows the town's old moat, now circles the entire medieval center and is a great way to experience the town's charm. In the Place du Chateau, along with with the colorful chateau, church, houses, and fountain visitors will find a family of nesting storks.

name: Bayeux
description: Founded in the 1st century BC, Bayeux was part of the Roman Empire's coastal defense. During the Middle Ages, the town was repeatedly sacked and pillaged, be it by 9th century vikings or 15th century English kings. During the Battle of Normandy, Bayeux was the first city to be liberated, and fortunately saw little damage as most German forces were relocated to Caen. Today, this historic center is still lined by charming stone or timbered-framed houses, watched over by the striking 11th century Bayeux Cathedral. Its modern history is also preserved, with the Memorial Museum of the Battle of Normandy, the Bayeux War Cemetery (the largest of its kind in Normandy), and the Memorial des Reporters all remembering the fallen. But the town's main attraction is undoubtedly the UNESCO-listed Bayeux Tapestry, which depicts the Norman conquest of England through seventy scenes spanning 70 metres (230 ft) of embroidery.

name: Crathes Castle
description: The land on which Crathes Castle stands was given to the Burnett of Leys family by King Robert the Bruce in 1323, along with a coat of arms, and bejewelled ivory hunting horn. Originally a bog fortress, the current castle was built in the 16th century. Walking through Burnett's home, starting with the tower and moving to the country house, you'll find historic furniture paintings and tapestries, and the horn given to the family by King Robert the Bruce, but the real highlight is are the Scottish Renaissance painted ceilings. Then there's the Green Lady's Room, said to be home to the spirit of a girl abused by a mail retainer - a story that may have some fact to it - the skeleton of a young child was found in beneath the hearth stone. The castle gardens are split into eight sections, where you can enjoy everything from a sculpted topiary, to exotic blooms. For more information, please visit nts.org.uk/visit/places/crathes-castle

name: Faenza
description: Dating back to the 2nd century BC, the town prospered producing pottery until the fall of the Roman Empire. Several centuries later, the town began to recuperate, and by the late Middle Ages, many of the town's most notable buildings were constructed. During the Renaissance, the town's glazed earthenware became so popular it became known by the French name for Faenza - faience. Today, the monuments of the town's success are plain to see. A short walk through the old town center offers two piazzas, an early renaissance cathedral, gorgeous fountain and 16th century clock tower. The neoclassical Palazzo Milzetti now serves as a museum to the the city's wealthy heyday. But the main attraction is the International Ceramics Museum, which showcases the town's namesake faience, alongside antique ceramics from all over the world, and contemporary pieces from household names like Picasso.

name: Savonlinna
description: Nestled in the heart of the dazzling Lake Saimaa Lake and enveloped by lush greenery, the old city of Savonlinna. is a charming retreat unspoiled by crowds. Take a leisurely stroll through the Old Town before heading to one of the jewels of Finland: Olavinlinna Castle. Built in the 15th century, it's the northernmost medieval stone castle still standing, and one of Finland's best-preserved bastions. Don't miss out on the opportunity to marvel at the world's largest wooden church, Kerimäki Church, and savor the local delicacy, Lörtsy - a mouth-watering, doughnut-like, half-moon-shaped meat pie topped with a refreshing cucumber salad. Moreover, the burgeoning beer scene in and around Savonlinna provides an excellent chance to sample high-quality local craft beer. While you're down by the water keep your eyes peeled for the Saimaa Ringed Seal, the world's most endangered seal with a population of only about 400.

name: Balatonfuered
description: Balatonfuered's reputation as the capital of Lake Balaton's north shore dates back to 1772 when it was officially declared a spa. The naturally carbonated springs waters that can be drawn from wells here have been attracting visitors from around the world ever since, with Indian Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore coming here for treatment. A beautiful waterfront promenade was named in honor of the poet, offering beautiful views of the lake. Throughout the village itself, you can find 18th and 19th century buildings, including several mansions built by Hungarian nobility. The classicist Lajos Kossuth Spring House is a key stop on any visit, both for its elegant architecture, and for a chance to drink the famous mineral water.

name: Karlskrona
description: Karlskrona is a picturesque town packed with naval heritage, still evident in its impressive architecture that's earned it a listing as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was founded in 1680 by Karl XI, whose statue can be viewed in the famous market square Stortorget - the largest one in Sweden. Neighboring the square are two brilliant baroque churches, Trefaltighetskyrkan and Fredrikskyrkan, the latter of which is one of the most imposing buildings of classical Roman baroque in Sweden. The town's most famous attraction is the UNESCO-listed Naval Port, which is a prime example of a well-preserved 18th-century naval base. The port features several unique buildings, such as the Old Shipyard Crane and the Old Admiralty House. See the centuries-old submarine Hajen and board the submarine HMS Neptun at the Naval Museum, which covers Sweden's history of naval defense from the past 500 years. It also displays a stunning collection of figureheads in Figurehead Hall, which once sat in the bows of Swedish warships. The naval base is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10AM to 4PM and Wednesday from 10AM to 7PM, with a US$7.80 entry fee.

name: Chiayi
description: Nicknamed the "Wood City" due to its historical ties with the forestry industry, Chiayi continues to be a hub for visitors exploring the Alishan National Scenic Area, now a protected conservation area known for its hiking trails and serene natural beauty. The world-famous Alishan Forest Railway and secluded forest trails further enhance its allure, providing a glimpse into the rich mountain culture and ancestral legends of the Tsou indigenous people. The west coast's fishing harbors of Dongshi and Budai offer insights into the oyster industry and coastal ecology. Dongshi Fisherman's Wharf, in particular, has become a popular summer destination. The vast Aogu Wetland Forest Park in Dongshi boasts lush lowland forests, while visitors can embark on fishing raft rides along the Puzi River to explore the coastal fishing industry. In the county's plains area, historical landmarks such as the Tropic of Cancer Monument and centuries-old temples await exploration.

name: Munich
description: Munich - home to the world's oldest brewery and steeped in brewing tradition - welcomes millions of beer lovers each year to delight in the spectacle of Oktoberfest. With beer gardens, Bavar Taverns, and the iconic beer hall, Hofbrauhaus, there is no better place to experience this distinguished event! Come for the beer, stay … for everything else! This city is booming and has been for centuries. Munich is rich in the arts with a multitude of galleries and theaters to discover. You can't miss the grandeur of one of the oldest art galleries in the world, Alte Pinakothek or a show at the admirable Deutsches Theater. In this historical hub, be sure to take it all in at Germany's largest palace, Residenz, or marvel within the halls of the medieval Asam Church. On your way, don't forget to dive into the bustle of Marienplatz; shaded by the New City Hall, here you can enjoy the markets, cafés and local performances at your leisure. If you're looking for a touch of serenity, explore one of the world's largest inner-city parks, the English Garden. Afterwards, you may still have time to catch a game at the Allianz Arena!

name: Mystras
description: The history of Mytras goes back to 1249 when the last Byzantine outpost was conquered by a Frankish prince. He had a fortress built, which was recaptured by the Byzantines. Well positioned, they made it the empire's center in southern Greece. From there, the fortress flourished. It would change rulers on many occasions in the coming centuries until it was finally abandoned in 1834.Today, visitors can admire the surreal views of the surrounding landscape while learning about the structures within the fortress. The stunning Palace of Despots, beautiful Cathedral of Saint Dimitrios, and gorgeous monasteries are all built in the distinct 'Helladic' style, offering a unique opportunity to see this distinctive regional architecture. For more details, please visit: http://odysseus.culture.gr/h/3/eh351.jsp?obj_id=2397.

name: Kavala
description: Continuously inhabited since the 7th century BC, Kavala stayed relatively the same size until a 16th century expansion - a layout which than wasn't changed until the 20th century. The Old Town is still dominated by its 15th century citadel, which offers stupendous views of the harbour below. The cobbled alleys are lined with traditional Byzantine style houses, while cafes and restaurants on the main streets provide scenic stopping points to sit and enjoy some souvlaki and retsina. In the 'New Town', closer to the harbour, the neoclassical mansions and tobacco warehouses are eye-catching reminders of why Kavala was once known as the "Mecca of tobacco". This transformative industry is memorialized at the Tobacco Museum, the walls of which are lined with portraits of tobacco workers.

name: Saitama
description: Saitama Prefecture, nestled in the Greater Tokyo area, offers a unique blend of modernity and historical charm. The Museum of Modern Art, Saitama, known as Momas, dazzles with its architecture and art. Omiya Park, a sprawling expanse, features plum trees, sports facilities, and a free-admission zoo. Its proximity to Tokyo makes Saitama an easily accessible destination for day trips, offering a tranquil escape from the urban hustle and bustle. Saitama is also renowned for its sake, boasting over 35 sake breweries scattered across its cities. While much of Saitama Prefecture is urbanized, the western borders remain untouched havens of natural beauty. The proximity to the rocky, mountainous landscape and the occasional view of Mount Fuji adds to the region's appeal.

name: Davos
description: During the mid-19th century, the town's micro-climate made it a popular destination for the sick and ailing, such as Robert Louis Stevenson, who suffered from tuberculosis. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle also lived here for a while with his sick wife, and wrote an article about skiing on Davos' famous mountain. Today, the town has maintained the natural charms that have made it a destination for so long. In the summer, a funicular brings visitors to the Alpine Botanical Gardens, is home to around 800 different species of plant from all over the world, wonderful views, and even a waterfall. Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, spent the final years of his life here, and the museum dedicated to the artist houses the largest collection of his works in the world.

name: Monkey World Wareham
description: Jim Cronin first opened Monkey World in 1987 to provide a stable home for abused Spanish 'beach chimps'. Photographers used these animals as props, and would often beat and drug them to keep them docile, and kill them once they got too large. Today, Monkey World is home to over 55 rescued chimpanzees from several countries where they were being used in laboratories, as exotic pets, as photographer's props, or as circus animals. Working with foreign governments, Monkey World has also saved 88 capuchin monkeys from a laboratory in Chile, a Bornean orangutan from South Africa, and an orphaned baby Sumatran orangutan from Spain.Along with working to governments from around the world to fight the smuggling of primates, Monkey World also participates in breeding programs to help preserve endangered species. Walking through this 65 hectare park, visitors can learn about the different primates, their past lives, and see how they're recovering. For more information, please visit http://www.monkeyworld.org Photo ©MonkeyWorld

name: Sopron
description: The town sprang to fame in 1989 as the site of the "Pan-European Picnic", when the Iron Curtain between Austria and Hungary was lifted for a few hours to allow hundreds of East German citizens to cross the border, an action that catalyzed the fall of the Eastern Bloc. Modern day Sopron merges past and present, creating a bridge between Hungary and its neighbors. Lying among the charming heritage buildings, churches and museums is the symbol of the city — the Firewatch Tower. The tower was built on Roman ruins and contains the 'Loyalty Gate' built in 1921 in tribute to the occasion when Sopron refused to cede to Austria in the 1900s. Head on up the steps to the tower terrace to check out the panoramic views of the Old Town and the surrounding picturesque lower Alps. The tower includes a visitor center which contains some informative displays on the history of Sopron accompanied by fascinating old paintings and photos.

name: Giethoorn
description: Giethoorn was founded by peat farmers, who harvested the plant-stuff, and created a series of ponds, lakes, and canals in the process. Today, the settlement is often called 'The Venice of Holland' because of its series of canals and bridges. However, this isn't a bustling city, but a charming village where visitors can ride through the canals, under traditional wooden bridges to admire the 18th and 19th century farm houses. For foodies, the town also has a gift for gastronomy, with a slew of excellent water-facing restaurants, including De Lindenhof, which has 2 Michelin stars.

name: Novi Sad
description: Novi Sad, established in the 17th century, is Serbia's second largest city. Its diverse population of Serbs, Hungarians, Croats and Slovaks make the city a highly developed cultural and economic hub. The lively city center has museums, art galleries, and an eclectic cafe and bar scene. Architectural styles include Gothic, Baroque, Art Nouveau, and Neoclassicism. One of Novi Sad's most notable sights is Petrovaradin Fortress. The fortress sits on the right bank of river Danube and provides a home to art studios, a museum, and a hotel. The city is also home to the annual Exit festival, one of Europe's most popular music events.

name: Damajagua
description: Damajagua, also known as the 27 Waterfalls, is one of the most exciting eco adventures in the Dominican Republic. Join a guided excursion up a river ravine cutting through lush jungle before starting your exciting descent that will have you jumping and sliding down waterfalls into pools of refreshing mountain water. The highest jump is about 25 feet, but fortunately there is a staircase to bypass it if you're not ready to take the plunge. Please note: it's highly recommended to wear shorts and closed toe shoes as you'll be hiking up and sliding down rocks. Tour operator policy states this stop isn't appropriate for guests who have had recent surgery (less than 6 months), pregnant women, heart or respiratory conditions, back, neck or knee problems and guests under any medication that carries a warning of any mental or physical impairment.

name: Fondation Monet in Giverny
description: The Fondation of Claude Monet in Giverny preserves the extraordinary legacy of one of Impressionism's greatest masters in the very place where he lived and created for over four decades. This nonprofit organization meticulously maintains Monet's pink-walled house with its color-coded rooms—green doors, a yellow dining room adorned with Japanese prints, and a blue kitchen—all restored using Monet's own palette. The property features two distinct gardens: the geometric flower-filled Clos-Normand and the serene water garden with its iconic Japanese bridge and water lilies that inspired Monet's most famous works. Attracting over 530,000 visitors annually, the estate ranks as Normandy's second most visited site after Mont Saint-Michel. Recognized as a Maison des Illustres, Jardin Remarquable, and monument historique, the foundation opened to the public in 1980 following extensive restoration work funded partly by American philanthropists. Today, visitors can experience firsthand the living canvas that sparked Monet's artistic vision and revolutionary outdoor painting technique. Please check the official website for the most updated opening times, as they are seasonal: https://claudemonetgiverny.fr/

name: Hillsborough Castle and Gardens
description: Hillsborough Castle is an 18th century Georgian country house that was built for the Hill family, the Marquesses of Downshire. ln 1922, the family sold the estate to the British government, which solved their need for a residence for the newly established office of the Governor of Northern Ireland. Since the 1970s, the house has been home to the Secretary of State of Northern Ireland, and also serves as the home of the British Royal family when they visit. On a guided tour, guests are brought through the house's elegantly decorated rooms, including the Throne Room and State Drawing Room. Each is uniquely decorated, adorned with paintings, furnishings, and personal objects accrued by the Royal Family over the years. Surrounding the house are 100 acres of gardens, offering everything from shady woodland trails to manicured formal gardens. The castle and gardens are open from Wednesday to Sunday. Please book your tickets in advance at www.hrp.org.uk

name: Cartagena
description: Cartagena was founded by Pedro de Heredia in 1533. Thanks to its strategic position on the Caribbean coast between the Magdalena and Sinú rivers, it served as Spain's primary port for trade in the New World. In order to defend its interests, the Spanish built an extensive fortification system around the city, which has been preserved to this day. Within the 13 kilometer ring of defensive walls are a jumble of cobbled streets lined with colonial buildings, bursting with color courtesy of bougainvillea and other tropical plants. Sure, there are individual landmarks to seek out, like the beautiful Iglesia de San Pedro Claver, and fascinating Palace of the Inquisition, but the best way to experience the city is to just wander, grabbing some street food as you go. You will want to make sure you wander to the Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas - perhaps the mightiest Spanish fortification outside of Spain.

name: Salento
description: In the heart of Colombia's Coffee Triangle lies Salento, a quaint mountain town with a lively arts scene and welcoming locals. Salento's location has influenced its architecture and culture since Colonial times. Simón Bolívar famously ordered the main road be upgraded after seeing it in poor condition and knowing its strategic importance to the country. Today, visitors to Salento can marvel at the colorful colonial buildings virtually untouched by time along Calle Real, or Royal Road, just off the main plaza. Pop into any restaurant to grab some fresh trout - the region's favorite dish - or swing by a cafe to grab a cup of strong coffee. Afterwards, play a game of Tejo with the locals. Should you fancy unplugging and immersing yourself in nature for the day, just east of town is the beautiful Cocora Valley with its towering wax palms sprouting from the rolling hills.

name: Eger
description: The town's top attraction is the thirteenth-century castle and there are models and drawings in the Bishop's Palace that show the history of the castle. Visitors can also watch a fun 3D film about the castle and Hungary before either taking a tour or simply exploring the castle grounds at their own pace. To get a feel of authentic Hungarian history, then walk along the huge hand-built walls that are hundreds of years old and experience how it must have felt to be under attack all those years ago. The walls provide fantastic views over Eger and excellent photo opportunities. Another popular reason for visiting Eger is that it is famous for its wines, in particular, the 'Bull's Blood', known as Hungary's most recognizable wine. Spare a few minutes to sample this traditional delicacy in either the castle restaurant or one of the many others that can be found in the town.

name: Takasaki
description: Nestled just an hour from Tokyo via shinkansen, Takasaki beckons with hidden treasures and a rich history. Explore Shorinzan Darumaji Temple, where rows of daruma dolls create a unique atmosphere under the eaves of the main building. These papier-mâché dolls symbolize wishes and luck in the city renowned as their birthplace. Gaze upon the towering Byakue Kannon statue, an emblem of serenity overlooking Takasaki. Ascend within for breathtaking city views. Venture to Jomo Sanzan, a trio of famous mountains: Akagi, Myogi, and Haruna. Mt. Haruna boasts a dormant volcano backdrop, with Haruna Shrine radiating spiritual energy. Ikaho Onsen, a premier hot-spring area, invites you to ascend its 365 steps to tranquility. The area's healing waters and scenic views soothe the soul. Shima Onsen mesmerizes with its blue waters, while the streets lead to Sekizenkan Ryokan, an inspiration for "Spirited Away." From serene temples to vibrant traditions, this city paints a picture of timeless beauty and cultural significance.

name: Deia
description: Nestled in the embrace of the Serra de Tramuntana mountains, Deià beckons with its enchanting charm and lush landscapes. The Teix mountain, standing sentinel, casts a majestic shadow over this Mallorcan gem. Deià's allure is not merely rooted in its scenic beauty; it carries the imprints of literary legacy. The illustrious English poet and novelist Robert Graves, captivated by its allure, chose Deià as his abode in 1932. His presence, along with subsequent luminaries like Richard Branson and Princess Diana, has transformed Deià into a cosmopolitan artists' enclave. Today, the village resonates with creativity, boasting art galleries, gift shops, and a rich tapestry of cultural experiences. Beyond its artistic ambiance, Deià reveals a profound connection to nature. Surrounded by the UNESCO-protected Serra de Tramuntana, it invites outdoor enthusiasts to explore its hiking trails and cycling routes. The ancient paths weaving through the hills unveil stunning vistas, including the renowned GR221 Stage 3A, a five-hour trek from Valldemossa to Deià. For a touch of literary history, a visit to Robert Graves' former residence, Can Alluny, now a museum, offers a glimpse into the poet's life. The Archaeological Museum, Es Clot, delves into the island's history, showcasing artifacts from significant local sites.

name: Cape Coast
description: Cape Coast, Ghana, weaves a captivating tapestry of history, vibrant culture, and sun-kissed beaches. Journey back in time at the Cape Coast Castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Explore the poignant yet important stories of the slave trade, and stand where countless souls embarked on a challenging journey. But Cape Coast isn't just a history lesson. Dive into the lively craft markets, overflowing with colorful textiles and handcrafted carvings that tell a story of their own. Indulge in the mouthwatering aroma of sizzling seafood wafting from the harbor front, and lose yourself in the infectious rhythms of live drumming that fill the air. For a touch of tranquility, sink your toes into the golden sands of Coconut Beach, or kayak through the peaceful lagoons. Cape Coast offers a unique blend of historical intrigue, cultural immersion, and relaxation under the warm Ghanaian sun.

name: Dettifoss Waterfall
description: At 100 meters wide and 44 metres tall, Dettifoss Waterfall sees nearly 200 cubic meters of water pour over its edge every second. Dettifoss earned the title of 'Europe's most powerful waterfall' by a simple computation: waterflow times fall height. The unbridled power and raw natural beauty of Dettifoss attracted Ridley Scott, who used it as part of the landscape in Prometheus. Plummeting into a rocky canyon, the falls produce a near-constant mist - perfect fodder for rainbows on sunny days. There are two access roads to the falls - the west bank is a paved road and easy walking trail which will put you in the midst of the falls' mist. The east bank is reached via a slightly more rugged road but is drier and gives you a viewing platform.

name: Sfax
description: Sfax was established in AD 849 on the ruins a Roman city. As a major port, Sfax was its own city-state for centuries before being targeted by the Sicilians, Spanish, Ottomans, and Venetians. When Tunisia became a French protectorate in 1881, this proud city revolted, and the French had to dispatch both ironclad and cannon ships to bombard the city into submission. Today, Tunisia's second largest port is the second most important city in the country, but often passed over by tourists. The historic medina, chock full of souks, is an intoxicating blend of history and modernity where travellers can experience a genuine Tunisian way of life. Sfax's history is proudly presented in the city's excellent museums, be it the Folk Art Museum housed in a lavish 18th century mansion, or the Archaeology Museum in City Hall.

name: Luxor
description: The Sahara Desert is vast. For Ancient Egyptians, their saving grace was the Nile River. Along its banks, their dynasty spanned across millennia. The Great Pyramids of Giza are their crowning creation, and further south lies the revered Luxor and the Valley of the Kings! This archaic mausoleum is home to over 65 tombs across separate exhibits, including the Valleys, the Necropolis, and Deir el-Bahari. Step into the final resting places of Pharaohs like Tutankhamun, Amenhotep II, and the lineage of Ramesses. You can even witness the world's largest open-air museum from above on an exhilarating hot-air balloon ride! Luxor is also marked with grand Temples dedicated to Gods and revered Kings. The Ramesseum, Luxor Temple, and d'Amon Temple are marvelous, yet incomparable to Karnak Temple; the largest sacred building ever constructed. This enormous place of worship has stood the test of time. For over 2000 years, pharaohs added to Karnak, stamping their names and beliefs here, in the form of obelisks, chapels, and statues. Heading south along Sphinx Avenue will take you towards central Luxor, into cultural hotspots like El Souk. This colorful and blossoming market is an enthralling window into authentic Egyptian life and well worth a visit on your trip through the ancient city.
