name: Lugano
description: The shores of Lake Lugano have been settled since the Stone Age, but the Lugano city proper can trace its roots back to around the 9th century. For centuries, warring powers clashed over the city, until it finally fell under Swiss dominion in 1513. Situated on a lakefront, and with a strong Italian history, it's no wonder the town centre has Mediterranean-style squares and arcades, complete with subtropical plants. The city is a treasure-trove for art lovers, with the 16th century Church of Santa Maria degli Angioli filled with fine frescoes by Renaissance masters, while the San Lorenzo Cathedral, with its Lombardy Renaissance facade in the style, contains countless frescoes and Baroque artefacts. For a more contemporary experience, the Museo Cantonale d'Arte exhibits paintings by Klee, Renoir and Degas.

name: Nerja
address.addr1: Plaza Balcón de Europa, 29780 Nerja, Málaga, Spain
description: Positioned at the eastern tip of the Costa del Sol, Nerja boasts nearly 10 miles of powdery beaches, making it a popular destination for beachgoers and watersports. However, its historic town center still feels like a village. The Balcon de Europa is the natural focus of the town and the venue for fiestas. Built on a rocky outcrop, jutting into the sea, it offers spectacular panoramic views of the whole coast. Discover the Nerja caves which are home to the world's largest column and the world's oldest Neanderthal cave paintings. The recent discovery of Roman pottery, Moorish coins, and the presence of an unusual biodiversity have all confirmed that discoveries in the Nerja Caves are seemingly limitless and subject to incredible global speculation.

name: Cognac
address.addr1: 8 Rue de la Richonne, 16100 Cognac, France
description: First mentioned in the 9th century, Cognac first made its fortunes trading salt before it developed its world-famous wine and brandy industries. Today, visitors can explore the old town of this Village of Art and History, enjoying the historic houses and monuments, such as the 12th century Saint-Léger church, the fortified Saint-Jacques gateway, or the noble Valois castle. This noble estate was the birthplace of François I, and now gives visitors a taste of Cognac history through its Renaissance rooms, and, of course, cellars full of the eponymous brandy. For a more detailed look at the city's heritage, the Dupuy d'Angeac mansion exhibits local ceramics, artefacts, and artwork. For those with an unwavering dedication to the famous liquor, the Arts of Cognac museum showcases the brandy's history and production process through everything from stills, to bottles and advertisements. And of course, it's also possible to visit the city's famous cognac houses, such as Hennessy and Rémy Martin.

name: Verdon Gorge - Pont du Galetas
description: Pont du Galetas stands as the quintessential viewpoint overlooking the breathtaking Verdon Gorge in southeastern France's Provence region. This iconic bridge spans the mesmerizing turquoise waters that give the gorge its name—"Verdon," meaning "green" in French, though the striking blue-green hue actually comes from glacial minerals. Formed over 250 million years ago, when ancient seabeds compressed into limestone and were later carved by glaciers, the gorge plunges dramatically to depths of 700 meters. This makes it France's deepest canyon! The bridge serves as more than just a spectacular vantage point; it's the gateway to water adventures, with boat rentals available on both sides—particularly the south side—offering paddleboats, kayaks, and motorboats for exploring the canyon's stunning contours.

name: Wymondham Abbey
description: Wymondham Abbey was founded in 1107 by William d'Aubigny, Butler to King Henry I. Over the centuries this Norman church was enlarged and embellished with its distinctive twin towers and a fine angel roof. Following the dissolution of monasteries in 1538, about half the original building was destroyed. Today, they abbey treats visitors to centuries of religious imagery, from the Norman nave to the 15th century roof, 18th century organ and amazing 20th century gilded altar screen. You'll also find early Tudor terracotta sedilia, a Georgian candelabrum, and carved medieval font with a modern gilded cover. Informative signs and friendly stewards are on hand to shed light on the abbey's long history and many treasures.

name: Burghley House
description: Burghley House was built in the mid-16th century for Sir William Cecil, Lord High Treasurer to Queen Elizabeth I, and has belonged to the family ever since. Today, it stands as one of the finest examples of Elizabethan architecture in the country, with most of the interiors dating from the 18th century. Listed as one of England's 10 'Treasures Houses', many of Burghley's state rooms feature floor-to-ceiling Baroque murals, You'll also find one of the finest private collections of Italian Old Master paintings, both Oriental and European ceramics, as well as furniture and objects d'art from both England and 'The Continent'. You'll also gain some insight into the family, like in the 'Olympic Corridor - a space dedicated to David Cecil, the 6th Marquess and Olympic gold-medal winning hurdler and runner. The surrounding parkland, laid out by the legendary Capability Brown, are alive with colorful flower beds, roaming deer, and contemporary sculptures. For more information, please visit burghley.co.uk

name: Surabaya
description: Surabaya is the second-largest city in Indonesia and boasts mythical stories and historical attractions. The city's prophecy about a battle between a giant white shark and crocodile is said to have foreseen the Mongol Invasion of Java, and has become its symbol, with an iconic statue standing near the entrance of the city zoo. Learn about national history, Surabaya's local economy and the story of Indonesia's popular clove cigarette brands at the House of Sampoerna. Admire Majapahit Hotel, established in 1910, which features elegant colonial architecture and a beautiful garden. The city also boasts cultural landmarks like the Cheng Hoo Mosque, with its pagoda-style architecture and oriental influences, representing the vibrant Chinese population assimilating into Surabayan society. In the wider harbor of Surabaya, the Submarine Monument showcases an actual warcraft used by the Indonesian navy, serving as a symbol of the nation's maritime history. Immerse yourself in the natural beauty of Surabaya at the Ria Kenjeran Beach, located just a short distance from the city center with sandy shores and coastal charm.

name: Verona
description: If you're a fan of Juliet, one must visit the backdrop for the play's most famous love scene - Juliet's balcony. Other than the tale of an ill-fated love, Verona is a destination of art, opera, and urban architecture. Take time to go up the lift to the Lamberti tower and see the sweeping views of the red rooftops. Order some gelato and take a brisk stroll down the infamous shopping avenue, Corso Porta Borsari. The real heartstopper is the entrance to the street. Its gate is called the 'Gate of Borsari' - made with limestone, corinthian capitals, and 2 pediments that predates the 1st century A.D. Abundant in Roman ruins, Verona is full of history, charm, and beauty.

name: Kourion
description: Sprawled across a limestone plateau, Kourion is said to have been founded by Argives in the Late Bronze Age. During antiquity, it was one of the most powerful of Cyprus' city-kingdoms, and thrived until it was destroyed by a massive earthquake in 365 AD. Today, the partially restored archaeological site offers a fantastic opportunity to get up close to ancient architecture in an amazing setting. The centerpiece is the Greco-Roman theater, which was built in the 2nd century BC, extended in the 2nd century AD, and is now used for live performances. East of the theater, the covered remains of the "House of Eustolios" showcase four beautiful 5th century mosaics, and a bathing complex with cold, warm, and hot baths. Elsewhere, you'll find more mosaics to be found at the "House of Achilles" and the "House of the Gladiators", a portico-lined agora, a public bath, Nymphaeum, and an early Christian basilica. Outside the main site, on the road to Paphos, you can stop to see the Temple of Apollo Hylates and a stadium. Because Kourion is mostly exposed, it's recommended to bring a hat and water, especially in the summer.

name: Chambery
description: Closely tied to the House of Savoy, the town was the Savoyard capital from 1295 to 1563, when the capital was moved to Turin, and only became a permanent part of France in 1861. While the Duke's medieval castle is now home to the council offices, a guided to shows visitors some of the highlights, such as the chapel used to house the Turin Shroud, and the 70 famous bells of the 'Great Carillon'. The 13th century Gothic Cathedral has an austere facade, but is home to the largest collection of trompe-l'oeil paintings in Europe. More impressive is the treasury, which houses a 12th century Byzantine diptych. The City Museum of Fine Arts has a large section dedicated to paintings by Italian Renaissance artists, while the Savoy Museum has an excellent collection explaining the long history of Chambery and the Savoy region.

name: Northampton
description: Though the area has been settled since the Bronze Age, Northampton didn't rise to prominence until the 11th century when the Northampton Castle was built, though it's since been completely destroyed. In 1675, the town was devastated by fire, but reemerged as the handsomest in the region, with one of the country's biggest market squares. In the 19th century, Northampton become the footwear capital of England - a tradition honored at the city museum, where you can find everything from remnants of Roman sandals to shoes worn by Queen Victoria and David Beckham. Despite its rapid growth, Northampton also has several historic monuments, such as the 12th century Church of the Holy Sepulchre, one of the only round churches in the country, and the Victorian Gothic guild hall, which is covered with sculptures of English Kings and Queens. Design lovers will want to head straight to 78 Derngate - the only house in England designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh.

name: Shimonoseki
description: Steeped in historical significance, Shimonoseki witnessed pivotal battles in the Kanmon Straits and is home to iconic monuments and stunning vistas. The azure waters beneath the Tsunoshima Bridge, a notable feature of Yamaguchi Prefecture, draw visitors to its captivating beauty. Similarly, the Kanmon Bridge spanning the narrowest part of the straits captivates observers from the bustling Karato Ichiba fish market. Renowned as Japan's primary handler of fugu (blowfish), Shimonoseki embraces this culinary specialty, skillfully prepared in traditional Yamaguchi style. Echoes of the Meiji Period can be seen along the waterfront, while the Akama Shrine commemorates the 12th-century Battle of Dannoura. The Kanmon Bridge, connecting Honshu and Kyushu, spans 1,068 meters and offers panoramic views. With its strategic history and maritime allure, Shimonoseki entices travelers to explore its intriguing past and vibrant present.

name: Black River Gorges National Park
description: Nestled in the heart of Mauritius, Black River Gorges National Park stands as a testament to the island's natural beauty and ecological diversity. At Black River Gorges National Park, lush rainforests blanket the landscape, creating a haven for rare and endemic species of flora and fauna. Towering ebony trees, wild orchids, and vibrant ferns adorn the forest floor, while the melodious songs of native birds fill the air. The park is home to several endangered species, including the Mauritius kestrel, echo parakeet, and pink pigeon, making it a vital conservation area. At the main viewpoint, visitors can marvel at the awe-inspiring sight of the Black River Gorge plunging dramatically into the valley below, creating a spectacle of natural beauty that captivates the senses. The surrounding wilderness teems with life, from the melodious calls of exotic birds echoing through the forest canopy to the elusive creatures that roam the forest floor.

name: Lake Bunyonyi
description: Arguably the most picturesque lake in Uganda, Lake Bunyonyi is the second deepest crater lake in the world. Given the name, "Bunyonyi", meaning "place of many little birds", it will come as no surprise that the lake and its islands are a haven for birdwatchers and nature lovers. Close to the Uganda-Rwanda border, it is a freshwater lake surrounding 29 scattered lush green islands, set within the terraced hillside. The early morning mist gives the lake a mystical, somewhat romantic feel and the views are captivating. Among the islands is "Punishment Island", so-called as it was once used to ship misbehaved individuals where they were left to starve or attempt to swim back to land. Another is Kyahugye Island, the perfect spot for catching a glimpse of wildlife such as zebra and waterbuck. A popular spot for boat rides, canoeing and even swimming in the crystal clear water, Lake Bunyonyi is a sight not to be missed!

name: Dzibanche
description: Dzibanche was inhabited from around 200 BC to the 10th century AD. The earliest use of the Kan emblem glyph appears on one of Dzibanche's staircases, which suggests it was the original seat of the powerful dynasty. The city was also one of the last to create a dated hieroglyphic text, in AD 909. Today, the ruins have only partly been excavated from the jungle, which adds an extra element of discovery to the impressive monuments. The center of the site is a plaza surrounded by temple-pyramids, each of which is named after its distinguishing feature like the carvings of bound captives in the Temple of the Captives, or the ceramics found in Temple of the Owl. Dzibanche literally means "writing on wood" in reference to the Temple Temple of the Lintels, where a wooden support beam with glyphs from the 6th century is still visible.

address.addr1: Trebah Garden, Trebah Garden Trust, Mawnan Smith, Falmouth TR11 5JZ, UK
description: Trebah Garden was created in 1831 when Charles Fox designed himself a pleasure garden, meticulously positioning every tree. During the 20th century, the garden fell into decline, and the D-Day landing on Omaha Beach was launched from Trebah's beach. In 1981, Tony Hibbert and his wife purchased the estate as their retirement home, and dedicated the next quarter of a century to bringing the gardens back to their pre-war splendor. Today, this lush slice of paradise starts with a natural spring, which tumbles into koi pond before gently cascading down to the beach past colorful blooms. Strolling through the garden, visitors will find plants intermingling with huge Australian tree ferns and bamboos groves. In the spring, Trebah is a burst of color as the 100-year-old rhododendrons, magnolias, and camellias bloom, while the 'Hydrangea Valley' fills with delicate puffs of blue and white in the autumn.

name: Powderham Castle
description: The core of Powderham Castle was first built by Sir Philip Courtenay at the end of the 14th century, though it wasn't officially called a castle until the 17th century. A Victorian renovation by Charles Fowler, the architect behind Covent Garden, London repaired damage sustained during the Civil War, and transformed the facade into an idealised medieval castle. The interiors however, are a gorgeous Georgian country house with some revisions made by the family's taste. Case and point is the extraordinary staircase hall, illuminated by a Georgian stained glass skylight, and covered with plasterwork depicting birds, animals, and other motifs celebrating peace and love, though the vibrant blue coloring was a 20th century decor decision. After admiring the stunning rooms, make time to explore the castle grounds where you can admire colorful daffodils, primroses and Devon violets in the woodland garden, or watch Fallow deer graze in the Deer Park. Please note: the castle interior is only accessible on a guided tour. Please visit powderham.co.uk

name: Huamantla
description: The city of Huamantla, remains well-connected to its Spanish Colonial roots. Nothing says this more than its monument to the bull at the gate of the city. This monument is a nod to the age old practice of bull-fighting. Further to this tradition, at the old bullring, a museum is set up with many posters and information about the age, as well as the outfits of the Matadors and the trainers. This is also the city where modern Mexican puppetry came to be. You can visit and learn more about this beloved art at the Rosete Aranda National Puppet Museum. From the 31st of July to the 21st of August is the Huamantla Fair. This is where the city comes alive to show off its age-old crafts and culture. Here, ethical bullfighting takes place, a paella festival is put on and a beauty pageant takes place where they elect a Festival Queen! This is a great opportunity to spend a summer with cultural appreciation.

name: Constanta
description: Founded by Greek colonists in the 6th century BC, legend says that Jason and the Argonauts landed here after finding the Golden Fleece. In 71 BC, the city was conquered by the Romans and thrived until being conquered by the Turks. At the heart of the old town is Ovid Square, dedicated the the famous poet who was exiled here. The bronze statue in his likeness has a twin in his hometown of Sulmona, Italy. Also of Roman origin are the 9,150 square feet of colorful mosaics, which once stretched all the way down to the port. For more ancient history, the National Archaeology Museum has a wealth of Greek and Roman artefacts. The promenade in Tomis Harbour is perfect for those looking for a pleasant seaside walk with the possibility to stop at some of the region's best eateries.

description: Likely of Roman origins, this picturesque town overlooking the waters of Lake Como has long been an important stop for trade and travel between Lombardy and north of the Alps. During the middle ages, the town was encircled by defensive walls, which there is still evidence of today. The historic upper part of town has retained its medieval look, and is lined with shops selling local products, while the Church of Santa Marta houses exquisite artwork dating back to the 16th century. However, the town's main draw is its elegant promenade, which runs along the lakefront. Here visitors are treated to stunning views of the lake and surrounding mountains, as well as the city's scenic architecture.

name: Hamburg
description: Founded as a castle in 808, a settlement quickly, though Vikings, Poles, and the Black Death wreaked havoc on the developing city. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it became a centre of international trade, which elevated it to one of Germany's wealthiest cities. The Speicherstadt district, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was built between 1883 to 1927 and is the largest warehouse district in the world, criss-crossed with canals. The city is also renowned for its nightlife, which isn't something new - the Beatles got their start here, playing almost daily between 1960 and 1962. At the waterfront, visitors will find historic buildings like the famous St. Pauli Piers, as well as supermodern, like the newly opened Elbphilharmonie opera house. The canals aren't the only thing Hamburg has in common with Amsterdam - the city is also home to a Red Light district.

name: Paphos
description: A stone's throw from where Aphrodite is said to have been born from sea foam, Paphos was one of the most important settlements on Cyprus, even serving as the island's capital during the Ptolemeic and Roman eras. But after the city was destroyed by Muslim raiders in 960, it languished until being revitalized by the British occupation in 1878. Today, Paphos is a resort town for sun-lovers with a penchant for history. There are a slew of beaches where you can catch some rays, including Alykes Beach, right downtown, which is surrounded by restaurants, bars, and shops. Or, walk along the harbor to Paphos Fort, a UNESCO-listed bastion, which is watched over by a contemporary statue of Aphrodite, and, in September, the fort serves as the backdrop for the Aphrodite festival. But the standout attraction is undeniably the Kato Paphos Archaeological Park, which boasts some of the most impressive and best-preserved mosaics in the Mediterranean.

name: Timaru
description: While traveling through the South Island, Timaru is a great spot to spend the night or take a day break from the exhausting outdoor activities that New Zealand has to offer. There is a ton to discover including an abundance of museums & galleries, charming parks and relaxing beach walks. One of the town's most popular activities is to walk to the Marine Parade after sundown to watch the adorable little blue penguins return to their burrows for a night's rest. In the Caroline Bay there is the South Beach Coastal track which will provide you with a relaxing walk along the beach where you can watch surfers and look for wildlife such as penguins and seals! If you consider yourself a beer connoisseur, there is also the DB Draught Brewery that you can tour to learn about the past and present methods of brewing beer.

name: Colonia del Sacramento
description: Separated only by a 50 minute ferry ride from Buenos Aires, Colonia del Sacramento was a Portuguese colony with a turbulent history. The town changed hands multiple times between Spain and Portugal, was briefly part of Brazil, and from 1828 part of independent Uruguay. The result is a melting pot of Spanish and Portuguese colonial architecture; the streets of the Barrio Histórico are winding in the Portuguese style, the newer constructions outside the old town follows the usual Spanish grid system. The cobbled streets are full of fascinating things to see. A stone gateway and wooden bridge, which used to service a fortress, leads to avenues adorned with vintage cars (some being used as flower beds). Further up the hill the lighthouse, which rises above the ruined Convent of San Francisco, can be climbed via 111 steps for an unrivaled view of the city and the Río de la Plata.

name: Reutte
description: But this quiet spot is in the Guinness Book of Records for hosting what is the longest pedestrian 'Tibet-style' suspension bridge in the world. Called, somewhat unromantically Highline 179, after Highway 179 above which it passes, it's 406 metres long and connects the ruins of Ehrenburg Castle and the ruins of Fort Claudia either side of a steep-sided valley. The 1.2 metre-wide walkway is made of steel-grating which allows you to see the wooded slopes of the valley below, the valley floor and the highway. With no safety concerns – the bridge is built to hold 500 people at a time – you can go at your own speed and enjoy thrilling views. The two castles are appealing enough in themselves. Fort Claudia, built by the Tyrolean Archduchess Claudia in the mid-1600s played a major role in recapturing Ehrenburg Castle from the invading Swedes. While Ehrenburg's museum offers fascinating insights into the area's history.

name: Burghausen
description: The twelfth-century Burghausen castle complex situated in Oberbayern high above the Salzach River is the longest castle complex in Europe and is still lived in today. The complex stretches an imposing 3000 feet and offers striking views of the picturesque Bavarian countryside from the towers located along the castle walls. The castle features six courtyards in a row, with each courtyard becoming older and more impressive than the last as visitors move through each. Unlike many castles, every part of Burghausen offers views from different perspectives and angles along with vast panoramas of the Salzach River, the nearby town, and the lake, making it the ideal location for keen photographers. Any thoughts of sore feet after the long but enthralling walk are soon washed away by the experience of Burghausen, which is guaranteed to remain in every visitor's memory for a long time.

name: Mainz
description: As well as enjoying fine wines in an authentic atmosphere, Mainz also has a number of other attractions. The majority of these are in walking distance of the Old Town, with its wonderfully restored buildings and vibrant atmosphere. Close by is the 1000-year-old spectacular Mainz Cathedral, one of Germany's oldest, which combines various architectural styles from Romanesque through to Baroque and contains magnificent stained glass and leaded windows. Close to the cathedral in the Market Square is the Guttenberg Museum (Minz is where Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable printing press) and where the first Gutenberg Bible is on display alongside the world's smallest bible and further priceless artifacts. A highlight of the visit is the actual Gutenberg printing press. Mainz is a city best described by its sights and sounds that draws on 2000 years of art, culture and religious history to provide the many travelers that flock there each day with an unforgettable experience.

name: Taba
description: Perched at Egypt's northeastern tip on the Gulf of Aqaba, Taba is framed by turquoise waters and the ochre cliffs of the Sinai Peninsula. Serving as a serene gateway to the Red Sea's natural wonders, the town's pristine beaches and clear waters offer exceptional opportunities for snorkeling and diving, allowing visitors to explore vibrant coral reefs teeming with marine life. History buffs will appreciate a visit to Salah El-Din Castle on Pharaoh's Island, a fortress dating back to the 12th century, offering panoramic views of the sea. For those seeking relaxation and entertainment, Taba Heights provides luxury resorts, casinos, and rejuvenating spa facilities. Whether you're aiming to delve into underwater adventures, explore historical sites, or simply unwind by the sea, Taba caters to a diverse array of interests, ensuring a memorable getaway.

name: Valencia
description: Dating back to 138 BC, Valencia flourished thanks to its port, and was even the capital of Spain from 1936 to 1937. The city's UNESCO-listed "Silk Exchange", embodies its long-running mercantile success. Built in the late 15th century, traders would come from all corners of the Mediterranean to do business in its halls. Within its crenellated-facade are marvelous twisting columns and an incredible vaulted ceiling. The massive Gothic cathedral was originally erected in the 13th to 14th centuries, and received Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical updates made over the centuries. Inside are Renaissance paintings commissioned by Pope Alexander VI, and fascinatingly, in the Chapel of the Holy Chalice, a chalice claimed to have been used by Jesus at the last supper. The city is also famed for its modern architecture, such as City of Arts and Sciences, a 2km complex with everything from an opera house to greenhouse.

name: Arras
description: When Philip II ordered in the 16th century that no building take place in the town of Arras unless the walls are made of stone and brick, with no overhang into the streets, this medieval town began to take on its unique style that it's now known for. Most famous are its two squares, the Main Square and Heroes Square, both of which are encircled by buildings in the town's unique architectural style. Lined with galleries, fine food shops, cafes, and dominated by the Belfry of the Town Hall - named a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005 - Heroes Square is truly the heart of the city and a must-see during your travels in the area. During your stop, be sure to sample the city's sweet speciality, Coeurs d'Arras, a heart-shaped gingerbread cookie.

name: Edradour Distillery
description: Founded in 1825, Edradour Distillery is Perthshire's last original 'farm' distillery. Today, three men are still hand-making the whisky according to the same time-honored traditions established over 150 years ago - even the distillery equipment is from when Edradour first opened! One of the country's smallest distilleries, only 12 casks of whisky are produced a week. One a guided tour of this charming farmhouse distillery, visitors will experience the sights, sounds, and smells of the whisky-making process, and finish the experience with a wee dram or two. For more information, please visit edradour.com

name: Agropoli
description: Settled since Neolithic times, the town gets its name from the Greek 'akropolis', meaning on top. The sea-side cliff was subsequently inhabited by the Romans, Byzantines, and Saracens, before becoming a feudal property in 915. After frequently raids from North Africa in the 16th and 17th centuries, the population dwindled to just a few hundred, before bouncing back to become one of the most vibrant coastal towns in the region. After passing the medieval gate that grants access to the Old Town, visitors are treated with a view of the 16th century Church of Santa Maria di Constantinopoli. Walking through the cobbled streets, visitors eventually reach the Aragonese Castle, which was a 6th century keep enlarged around the 16th century. Along with taking in stupendous views of the coast, visitors can roam the castle grounds and explore its rooms and corridors, which often host art exhibits.

name: Lake George, NY
description: Situated halfway between New York City and Montreal, the Roosevelts, Vanderbilts and the Rockefellers were all frequent visitors to Lake George in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The vacation mansions lining the lakefront soon became known as "Millionaires' Row" - no attempt to hide this brazen show of wealth. Fortunately, you don't have to be a millionaire to appreciate the lake's beauty. The downtown remains small and friendly, and monuments like the Victorian-era Sagamore Hotel offer a bit of history to go with the views. And the 18th century Fort William Henry is a treat for history lovers. Of course, there's plenty of leisurely options too, from lounging on Million Dollar Beach to kayaking and boat rentals. If you're curious to see those exclusive mansions we mentioned, take a tour with the Lake George Steamboat Company.

name: Tupungato
description: Don't be fooled by its small size - the quaint wine and nut capital of Argentina has a lot to offer. Prior to the Spanish settlement back in 1658, the region was populated by the Huarpe ethnic group, who was dispersed through the surrounding mountain ranges. Though few traces of these early settlers remain today, the immigrants who came in the 19th century began a legacy of horticulture and viticulture that has endured to this day. The climate and soil have allowed for the successful cultivation of onions, nuts, potatoes, carrots, and wine, which can be tasted at one of two boutique wineries located in the center of town (these may be visited according to timetable availability). Grab a bite to eat or a cup of coffee on the main avenue, Belgrano, and take a stroll through the serene, adobe-lined downtown, where you can find a statue of General Jose de San Martin - also known as the Liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru - as its centerpiece.

name: Blackburn Cathedral
description: Blackburn Cathedral as it stands today wasn't completed until 1977 when the last piece of stained glass was secured in its modernist lantern tower. However, the cathedral's legacy stretches back over 1000 years, and even some of the building's elements are centuries old. The cathedral nave is actually the 19th century church, while the eight misericords in the north transept date back to the 15th century. Blackburn Cathedral is also home to a fantastic collection of religious artwork, notably the 35 foot 'Healing of the Nation' sculpture on the facade. Throughout the year the cathedral hosts special events ranging like free lunchtime recitals with visiting musicians. For more information, please visit blackburncathedral.com/

name: Kissamos
description: Set deep in a bay between the Gramvousa and Rodopou Peninsulas, Kissamos is a seaside town that has stayed true to its deep roots. The port has been in use since the days of ancient Greece, and flourished under the Romans, who built up villas, baths, a theater, and a fortress. Head to the archeological museum of Kissamos, housed in a historic Venetian manor, to see ancient ceramics, statues, coins, and some excellent mosaics. From there, follow the delightful Skalidi street through the old town, browsing the small shops of local tradesmen in the traditional buildings. Follow this down to the fishing port and sit at one of the tavarnas. Kissamos is an agricultural center for the region, so be sure to try the local brandy-like dry red wine. From here, head towards the main port to see the 10th century Ioannis Damialis church built into the rock face, and pass through a tunnel to the beautiful Damiali beach.

name: Riquewihr
description: Dating back to the ancient Romans, Riquewihr flourished as a fortified village in the Middle Ages, and miraculously escaped World War II unscathed. Now listed as one of the 'most beautiful villages of France', the village looks much as it did in the 17th century, complete with fortified walls, colorful half timbered houses, and lots of flowers. On Rue du General de Gaulle, the main street, visitors can stop at the Tourist Office for a map. However many of the most interesting buildings are on the same street. Attractions not on the main street include the 13th century Dolder tower, part of the town's original fortifications. In front of the Dolder is 'the fountain of gauging', which was used to check the capacity of wine barrels. The Thieves Tower is pentagonal on the outside and square on the inside, and still has a torture chamber inside.

name: Vendome
description: Founded by the Gauls, the current city of Vendôme grew up around a Dark Age feudal castle. Never restored or renovated, the ruins are now encompassed by a large park. Walking through Vendôme's historic district, visitors are treated to beautiful historic houses, and bridges criss-crossing the canals of the Loire River, a charm epitomized by romantic Ronsard park with its bridge and its lavoir, or Saint-Martin square and its old houses. The 11th century Abbey of the Trinity retained its original Romanesque tower, while the church facade received a Flamboyant Gothic make-over. The abbey's other buildings contain the cloisters, and the town Museum.

name: Nice
description: Surprises are in store for everyone throughout the city of Nice. The stunning seaside city has a dazzling old town, plenty of markets and shops, and convenient connections to neighboring Monaco. For art lovers, a trek to the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art is definitely on the list for the best collection of avant-garde. Or if Matisse is more your taste, Nice is also home to the painter Henri Matisse and his museum. This city is made for relaxing and gazing off into the sea. After having had an espresso, taken some photos of Castle Hill, and partaking in a bike tour along the Promenade des Anglais, Nice will leave you breathless and fond of wonderful memories.

name: Souillac
description: Nestled along the southern coast of Mauritius, Souillac exudes a captivating blend of natural beauty, cultural richness, and historical significance. Souillac is renowned for its stunning coastline, where rugged cliffs meet the azure waters of the Indian Ocean, creating a picturesque backdrop for leisurely strolls and breathtaking sunsets. The iconic Gris Gris cliffs, with their dramatic viewpoints and crashing waves, are a highlight for nature enthusiasts and photographers alike. Beyond its natural splendor, Souillac boasts a rich history that reflects Mauritius' diverse heritage. Visitors can explore historical landmarks such as the Robert Edward Hart Memorial Museum, housed in a colonial-era building, which showcases artifacts and exhibits detailing the island's past. The village also offers a glimpse into Mauritius' maritime legacy, with the famous Souillac Maritime Museum providing insight into the island's seafaring history and the importance of the ocean to local culture and livelihoods. For those seeking cultural immersion, Souillac hosts vibrant markets where locals sell fresh produce, handicrafts, and traditional delicacies, providing a taste of authentic Mauritian life. Visitors can also indulge in culinary delights at seaside eateries, savoring fresh seafood and Creole specialties while soaking in the laid-back coastal ambiance.

name: Grand Baie
description: Grand Baie, nestled on the northern coast of Mauritius, is a vibrant coastal town renowned for its picturesque beaches, azure waters, and bustling atmosphere. Visitors can indulge in a plethora of aquatic adventures such as snorkeling, diving, sailing, and windsurfing in the crystal-clear waters of the Indian Ocean. The nearby islands of Coin de Mire and Île Plate provide excellent opportunities for day trips and exploration. Beyond its pristine beaches, Grand Baie boasts a lively and vibrant atmosphere. The town is dotted with charming cafes, restaurants, bars, and boutiques, offering visitors a taste of Mauritian culture and cuisine. The local market is a treasure trove of souvenirs, handicrafts, and local delicacies, providing a vibrant sensory experience. For those seeking relaxation and rejuvenation, Grand Baie offers luxurious spas and wellness retreats where visitors can unwind amidst stunning coastal scenery. Additionally, the town serves as a gateway to the scenic hinterland, with opportunities for hiking, horseback riding, and exploring lush tropical forests. Grand Baie truly encapsulates the essence of tropical paradise, offering visitors a delightful blend of sun, sea, culture, and adventure.

name: Tula Toltec Archaeological Ruins
description: Tula began as a small urban settlement in the 7th century, but by its peak around the 900 or 1000, had grown to the largest and most powerful city in Mesoamerica. However, the city's dominion didn't last long, with the site being largely abandoned by the 12th century, and its pyramids and temples burned, leaving behind a small community of indigenous craftsmen who continued to inhabit the ruins through the colonial era. While little more than foundations remain of the residential neighborhood, two pyramids still dominate the site. The Pyramid of Quetzalcoatl stands in front of the ruined palace, and is unique in Mesoamerica because it is topped by four 4-metre-high basalt columns carved into Toltec warriors. Allow yourself 30 minutes for the on-site museum to see artefacts like ceramics, jewelry, metalwork, and stone figures from Tula and other ancient civilizations throughout Mexico.

name: Sant Rafel de sa Creu
description: San Rafael sits at a crossroads halfway between Ibiza and San Antonio and hosts a rich cultural milieu in its humble villagery. It has been declared a "Zona de Interes Artesanal", meaning an area of artisanal interest, due to work of renowned potters in the area. Visit sites of interest such as the Icardi ceramic workshop to browse beautiful, locally made pottery, and make sure you catch the San Rafael Handicraft Show held every Thursday in the Summer with over 50 stalls of handcrafted goods and gastronomic products. See the silhouette of Dalt Vila on the horizon and the luxurious yachts and cruise ships lined at the harbor down below from the Church of San Rafael in the Plaza de Joan Marí Cardona. Claiming world's largest super club, "Privilege", San Rafael is considered a clubbing epicenter of the world - come dusk, the village is beset with twinkling lights and electrifying aerial shows.

name: Wadi Mujib
description: Measuring 1 kilometer deep and 4 kilometers wide, Wadi Mujib runs 70 kilometers, from the Desert Hwy to the Dead Sea. This stunning chasm isn't just significant for its scale - it's said Moses walked through the wadi, which served as the historic boundary between the ancient Amorites and Moabites. The wadi is the centerpiece of the Mujib Biosphere Reserve - a UNESCO protected area that covers 212 square kilometers of rugged landscape and is home to some of the region's most precious species like the Syrian Wolf and Caracal mountain cat. The reserve is criss-crossed with a network of hiking trails of varying difficulty. If you don't mind getting wet, the 2km Siq Trail will having you hiking upriver (in chest deep water at times) between soaring walls of banded rock, culminating in a waterfall with a large pool where you can swim.

name: Chuncheon
description: Chuncheon is the capital of Gangwon Province and has become a popular destination for tourists, thanks in part to its appearance in the beloved Korean drama "Winter Sonata." The city's allure lies in its scenic landscapes, historic temples, vibrant festivals, and delectable local cuisine. Namiseom Island, located in the Han River, captivates visitors with its serene ambiance and maple-lined roads that burst into a mesmerizing display of autumn colors, and attracts fans especially from across East Asia for its appearance in the famous Korean drama. For a glimpse into the region's Buddhist history, the Cheongpyeongsa Temple offers a serene retreat surrounded by breathtaking natural beauty. Having stood since the 10th century, the temple bears witness to centuries of worship. Chuncheon also pays tribute to the international contribution during the Korean War, with the Memorial Hall for Ethiopian Veterans in the Korean War honoring the soldiers from 16 nations, including a battalion from Ethiopia, who fought alongside South Korean troops in the conflict.

name: Cambridge
description: Established as a city in the 1st century, Cambridge is known around the world for its illustrious university, which was founded in 1209. Today, it's the 4th oldest surviving university in the world, and encompasses 31 constituent colleges, which are a key part of this university town's identity. In fact, the city's most famous landmark is probably the Chapel at King's College - a masterpiece of Perpendicular Gothic architecture with the world's largest fan vaulted ceiling and a rood screen purchased by Henry VIII in celebration of his marriage to Anne Boleyn, which is now the finest piece of Italian decor in the country. As these historic colleges are situated next to each other along the banks of the River Cam, 'punting' down the river in a gondola is a great way to soak them in, along with the city's other sights, such as the Bridge of Sighs - Queen Victoria's favourite spot in the city.

name: House on the Hill Toy Museum
address.addr1: Castle visitor center, Lower Street, Stansted Mountfitchet CM24 8SP, United Kingdom
address.city: House on the Hill Toy Museum
description: The House on the Hill Toy Museum is all the collection of one man: Alan Goldsmith. Born during World War II, a time when Britain had to make many sacrifices for the war effort, Alan got his very first toy when he was 7 years old. This magic moment sparked a lifelong passion in the man, who has since accrued another 70,000 toys and playthings. Part nostalgia trip, part pop-culture chronicle, a visit to the museum is sure to produce plenty of 'Wow, I used to have one of those!', 'Wow, I wished I had one of those!', and 'Wow, what is that!?'s. Along with teddy bears and children's books, are life sized models, movie and music memorabilia, and oddities like an 'electrically assisted pedal cycle' from the 80s. For more information, please visit http://www.stanstedtoymuseum.com/

name: Thirlestane Castle
description: Founded as a fort in the 13th century, Thirlestane Castle as it stands today was built by the Maitland family starting in 1590, when John Maitland, Chancellor to James VI of Scotland, erected a large keep. His grandson, named Secretary of State for Scotland in 1660, commissioned renowned architect Sir William Bruce to create a manor where he could conduct affairs of state. The quiet of the 19th century allowed the Maitlands to add two more large extensions to the castle to use it as a country mansion. Today, the Maitlands welcome visitors into their family home to share in its rich history and many treasures. In the Entrance Hall, you'll find weapons dating back to the 18th century, while the stately dining room houses one of Scotland's largest family portrait collections. Throughout the house, you'll also find exquisite 17th century plasterwork, and fine furnishings. For more information, please visit http://thirlestanecastle.co.uk/ Photos: Phil Wilkinson

name: Dead Sea
description: At 431m below sea level, the Dead Sea is the lowest point on earth, and being about 10 times saltier than the ocean, is one of the world's saltiest bodies of water. The salts and minerals here made have been used for their skin-friendly properties for thousands of years, and the sea was the site of one of the world's first health resorts - made for King Herod the Great in the 1st century BC. Since then, its super-saline waters have attracted visitors from around the world who come for both their health, and to experience the extra buoyancy - swimming is actually quite difficult because you float. While floating is fun, don't drink the water! The Dead Sea is lined with resorts and spas, and paying the little extra to visit one of the private beaches is well worth it, if just for having a shower to rinse off with!

name: Gwangju
description: Known as the breadbasket of Korea and the starting point of the pro-democracy movement, Gwangju attracts numerous visitors each year with its cultural allure and signature events like the Gwangju World Kimchi Festival. Gwangju's fame extends beyond its historical significance and culinary treasures. It boasts being the hometown of renowned national idols like J-Hope (BTS), Yunho (TVXQ), Seungri (BigBang), and Suzy. The city's artistic charm shines through numerous cafes, street paintings, and delightful flower beds adorning the sidewalks, creating a sweet and romantic ambiance for visitors to relish. The Gwangju National Museum, featuring traditional Korean architecture, houses two floors displaying precious artifacts that offer insights into the nation's rich history. For shopping enthusiasts, Chungjang-ro Street, known as the Myeong-dong of Gwangju, forms a bustling shopping complex, with fashion and beauty stores alongside enticing restaurants. Nature appreciators flock to Sajik Park and Observatory, renowned for its cherry blossom festival and observation tower. From the observatory, visitors can use binoculars to admire the breathtaking panoramic views of the entire city.

name: San Jose de Gracia
description: San Jose de Gracia is a town in the Mexican state of Aguascalientes, home to a number of historical and cultural attractions, including the Cristo Roto (Broken Christ), the Boca del Túnel Adventure Park, and the ruins of the old town that was flooded when the Plutarco Elias Calles Dam was built. After tragedy struck the town, a massive statue of Christ missing his right arm and leg was built, and is one of the most visited monuments in all of Mexico. For thrill-seekers, the Boca del Túnel Adventure Park is a great place to go for adrenaline-pumping activities like horseback riding, biking, and rappelling. The park is also home to a beautiful lagoon and rock formations, making it a great place to go for a hike or simply relax and enjoy the scenery. In addition to its historical and cultural attractions, San Jose de Gracia is also home to a number of delicious traditional dishes, such as pacholas, a preparation in which beef is ground in a metate and then mixed with chili and spices. If you're looking for a charming town with a rich history and culture, then San Jose de Gracia will deliver.

name: Cenote Cristalino
description: Conveniently located between Tulum and Playa del Carmen, Cenote Cristalino is a lesser known gem among the Yucatan's innumerable cenotes. This natural sinkhole is open to the sky, making it look like a natural swimming hole surrounded by lush jungle. However, one look at the crystal-clear water and you'll know how it gets its name. Relatively shallow, the cenote is filled with curious fish, which makes it great for snorkeling, or just a refreshing dip. And you can just dangle your feet in for a natural fish spa. Since it's less popular than other sinkholes, but still with amenities like toilets and showers, it's a great option for those looking to sneak in a day at the (natural) pool without hordes of other people.

name: Bukhara
description: Step into a bygone era where turquoise domes pierce the sky and the iconic Kalyan Minaret, the city's tallest landmark, casts a watchful gaze. Imagine wandering through the Poi Kalyan complex, a breathtaking masterpiece where the Kalyan Minaret, a soaring tower adorned with intricate brickwork, stands sentinel. Adjacent, the grand Kalyan Mosque and revered Miri Arab Madrasa (Islamic school) whisper stories of sultans and scholars. Each intricate tile and soaring arch transports you to a world of bygone splendor. Bukhara isn't just a museum city; it's a vibrant hub where the past and present collide. Haggle for treasures at the Lyabi Hauz market, a labyrinth brimming with handcrafted souvenirs, glistening carpets, and the heady aroma of spices. Savor steaming bowls of plov (national rice dish) enjoyed alongside locals under the shade of ancient chinar trees. Delve deeper into Bukhara's soul at the Nadir Divan-Begi Madrasa, a stunning exemplar of 17th-century Timurid architecture. Ascend the Ark citadel, a formidable fortress that has witnessed centuries of power struggles.

name: Sisteron
description: Settled since around 2000 BC, Sisteron is combines natural beauty with a rich history. Nestled on the banks of the Durance river between two cliffs, the town is dominated by its imposing 11th century citadel. Remodelled in the 13th, 16th, and 19th centuries, the strategically located fort is now home to a museum devoted to Napoleon, as well as an exhibition of horse-drawn carriages. In the charming historic center, visitors can explore the narrow streets, punctuated by petite squares and picturesque fountains. The 12th century Romanesque cathedral is one of the largest in Provence, and its interior is accented by some magnificent gilded artwork. Nearby the Musée Terre et Temps, housed in an old chapel, explores the concept of time through its collection of rare and unusual objects, ranging from meteorites to a water clock with automata.

name: Gyor
description: It's won a European award for the protection of its historic heritage, notably the reconstruction of its Baroque centre. Churches, palaces, museums, characteristic corner-balconies and narrow lanes, are all charmingly vivid reminders of the town's long and varied history. The Bishop's Cathedral on Káptalan Hill, though having a beautiful exterior, houses some fascinating sacred objects within. Outstandingly, the reliquary of Ladislaus I, containing the skull of Hungary's revered eleventh-century saint-king. Gyor also possesses perhaps the most beautiful Baroque square in Hungary, Bécsi kapu tér (Vienna Gate Square), with every house a historic building. Following Király utca, a street full of Gyor's signature Baroque-style bay windows, brings you to the city's main square since the fourteenth century, Széchenyi Square. This is also chockful of Baroque buildings, and once the site of the Roman town Arrabona. The seventeenth-century Baroque Benedictine Church is well-worth exploring, if only for the ceiling pictures of the sanctuary and nave painted by Paul Troger.

name: Caprarola
description: Setting the trend for palace boulevards 100 years before Louis XIV made the Champs-Élysées, Caprarola is a picturesque medieval village bisected by a long, straight road leading right up to a massive villa. In 1504, Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, the future Pope Paul III, acquired an estate at Caprarola, and had a pentagonal fortress made on the site. It was the Pope's grandson, Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, who would refine the structure into one of the finest examples of Renaissance architecture. Today, the casino and its gardens is one of the homes of the Italian President, while the main villa is an unmissable museum for fans of Renaissance art and architecture. At five stories tall, with a Colosseum-like center courtyard, the many marble and fresco-filled rooms are still as imposing as they were first intended to be.

name: Saluzzo
description: Located on a hill, and originally enclosed by a double ring of walls, much of Saluzzo's 15th century old town remains intact. A series of cobbled streets, steep staircases, churches and elegant palaces reward visitors who explore the old city center. The Piazza Castello, with its historic fountain, dominated by the 14th century Mole di Castiglia castle. Built in 1270 by the Marquis Tommaso I at the summit of the village, even criminals were able to experience the city's rich history, as the castle was used as a prison from the early 19th century until 1992. Of course no trip to Italy would be complete without sampling some local cuisine, and the local cheeses, such as "paglierine", aren't to be missed.

name: Meknes
description: Founded in the 11th century as a military settlement, Meknes rose to prominence in the late 17th century when Sultan Moulay Ismaïl made it the imperial capital of Morocco. He transformed it into an impressive stronghold with high walls with grand gates protecting a Spanish-Moorish style city. While today it's overshadowed by neighbors like Fez, its UNESCO-listed medina offers some of the finest historical monuments in the country without the mass of crowds that clog other cities. A sign of its former stature, the main imperial gate, known as the Bab El Mansour, was built using materials from palaces taken during Ismail's sack of Marrakesh. While impressive the gate doesn't hold a candle to the incomparable craftsmanship at Ismail's tomb. Then there's the the king's cavernous fortified granary, which could house 12,000 horses, mosques dating back to the 12th century, and plenty of other sites to discover in its winding alleys.

name: Kakopetria
description: Hugging the foothills of the Troodos mountains, Kakopetria is one of Cyprus' most enchanting villages. Greenery proliferates thanks to the higher altitude, combined with the two rivers that converge in the heart of the village. The narrow streets of the old town are a timeless delight, with traditional wooden balconies and plants and flowers enticing you to explore every nook and cranny. Aside from just enjoying the village's quaint aesthetic, there are a few landmarks you can seek out, from historic churches adorned with 16th century frescoes to old water mills and even a small park with a waterfall. After you've finished exploring the village make sure to save time to visit the church of Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis (St. Nicholas of the Roof) a few kilometers away. Founded in the 11th, this Byzantine church is covered with murals from the 11th to 17th centuries, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Toledo
description: Settled since pre-Roman times, the city has held an important position for every major empire of the past 2000 years, including being the seat of supreme power under Charles V. Toledo's harmonious cultural history is what makes it such a unique attraction today. Here, visitors can see the Santa María la Blanca, the oldest remaining synagogue in Europe, before heading to see the military museum in a 10th century Moorish fortress. Perhaps even more impressive than the hilltop citadel is the city's cathedral - the second largest in Spain. Built during the 13th century, many consider it Spain's finest example of High Gothic style. Inside, the Cathedral is practically its own museum with an altarpiece by El Greco and its own gallery exhibiting works by the likes of Rubens, Van Dyck, and, of course El Greco.

name: Cancun
description: Connecting their empire from Mexico to Belize and Honduras, the Mayans built Ka'an Ku'um. Remnants of this vital trading post can be explored throughout Cancun's archeological sites, the most prominent being El Meco and El Rey. Today Cancún is known for much more than what it used to be. The glorious island, fascinatingly shaped like the number 7, and its partnering city have blossomed into a pillar of modern international tourism. An inspiration for coastal hotspots worldwide, Isla Cancun, is lined with magnificent hotels, restaurants, and even the odd golf course to experience! Up and down the shorefront, you'll find pristine beaches, each claiming to be Mexico's finest. Some are peaceful paradises offering a moment of relaxation amongst nature, while others adorn exotic beach clubs, open 'til dawn, and adventurous activities to take part in! Take a boat or jet ski and tour the coastline through the natural paradise of Nichupte Lagoon and into canals of mangrove forests. Delve into the Caribbean Sea and snorkel through one of the world's largest coral reefs, or dive deeper to witness the beauty of the Underwater Museum of Art. If you're really lucky, you'll spot a wonder of the animal kingdom, a colossal Whale shark!

name: Guaranda
description: Guaranda is a small city located in the Andes mountains in central Ecuador, known for its daily and weekly markets, and its carnival festivities in the month of February. If you visit during carnival season expect to see traditional dancing, bright and bold costumes dressing the local participants and food and drink being served out of homes and street stalls. There's music blaring through the streets and live trumpets and drums adding to the energetic atmosphere - but be warned, water fights are part of the carnival tradition so prepare to get wet! The Parque Simon Bolivar is the central square in the city and houses the Cathedral of San Pedro with its impressive towers and stained glass windows. From Guaranda it is impossible to miss the grand monument of the El Indio Guaranga, a 5 meter high sculpture sitting on a hilltop a few kilometers in the distance.

name: San Miniato
description: The probability of burning calories as one meanders the hilly city of San Miniato is a perfect excuse to do nothing but dine while there. Besides the opportunity to see the amazing views of the rolling hills in Tuscany, one should find San Miniato's infamous white truffle. Eating well is a known favorite pastime in Italy. After you've taken a trip to see the reconstructed medieval fortress tower, Torre di Frederico II, snack on some local artichokes, cinta senese, and raw milk at the Mercato della Terra di San Miniato. Explore all the churches and museums that this well preserved little town has to offer.

name: Sirmione
description: Wedged at the end of a finger-thin peninsula, Sirmione has been a resort destination since the 1st century BC, when rich families from Verona began building villas on the lake shore. The town's aggressive position also made it a military stronghold for almost the entirety of modern history, with a garrison occupying the castle into the 19th century. To this day, you can still explore the ruins of a Roman villa, and the town itself is dominated by one of Italy's best-preserved medieval castles, complete with a rare port fortification. turn attracting writers for the past 2000 years. Poet Gaius Valerius Catullus had a villa here in the 1st century, Alfred Tennyson, Giosuè Carducci wrote about it, and Ezra Pound and James Joyce met in Sirmione. If you're thinking that there must be something in the water that's attracting so many writers, you'd be right - Sirmione natural hot springs!

name: Atlixco
description: In the picturesque city of Atlixco you cannot miss the breathtaking backdrop provided by the neighbouring Popocatepetl volcano. The cloud of smoke emanating from its peak lends a mystical and somewhat enchanting feel to the city, captivating visitors day in and day out. The Cerro de San Miguel mountain is one of Atlixco's main landmarks, providing a spectacular panoramic lookout for views across the city and beyond. The city centres around its main square, Zócalo de Atlixco, with many restaurants and cafes and, most notably, beautiful, immaculately maintained gardens filled with the most colourful and attractive floral displays. The square is also home to the former convent of Carmen, a church built in the late 1600's, and Atlixco has many other beautiful churches well worth a visit for their impressive baroque-style architecture. The city is most famous for its flower production - if you're visiting on a Saturday, be sure to check out the weekend market for a stunning selection!

name: Paraty
description: Paraty became a booming port after gold was discovered in the mountains of Minas Gerais in the late 17th century. However, pirates preyed on the gold-laden ships leaving for Rio de Janeiro, and Paraty was left by the wayside after a safer overland route was established. Fortunately, the wealth of colonial buildings funded by the gold rush have been well-preserved. Wander the cobbled streets of the historic center, where the white-washed buildings are punctuated by pops of color on their doors and latticed windows. While exploring, be sure to stop for some local cachaça! If you're curious about Brazil's national liquor, you can even tour one of the cachaça distilleries. But the charming old town is just half of why Paraty is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The beautiful surroundings are actually endangered "Atlantic Rainforest", and the nearby Parque Nacional da Serra da Bocaina offers some fantastic hiking opportunities.

name: Marbella
description: Having been home to Phoenicians, Romans, and Visigoths, the town rose in prominence under Moorish rule, eventually becoming their most important coastal possession. Even today, their presence can be felt in the city, be it the tower from their 9th century citadel, or the Arab kings who still own property here. The prestigious Puerto Banús is the waterfront strip, which welcomes some of the most luxurious yachts into the world, to allow their owners access to the luxury developments, and premium business. At the heart of the nearby historic city center is Renaissance Plaza de Los Naranjos, which is flanked by stately buildings such as the 16th century City Hall and 17th century Chief Magistrate's Office. There are also remnants of Roman rule, such as the Paleochristian basilica of Vega del Mar, the baths of Guadalmina, or the villa of Río Verde.

name: Porec
description: Porec is a small town on the west coast of Istria dating back to Roman times. It's a culturally and historically rich town, making it an ideal tourist and family destination. The main sight of Porec is the 6th century Euphrasian Basilica. The basilica is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its gorgeous gold mosaics. The Romanesque architecture, Venetian Gothic palaces, preserved stone houses, and narrow streets all add to Porec's old town charm. There are also many open-air bars and cafes, quaint shops, and seafood restaurants to explore.

name: Surin
description: Founded during the Khmer era, Surin's cultural heritage stems from the Suay or Kuay ethnic groups. These peoples were talented elephant trainers - a tradition that's still a key part of the city's identity. Today, two festivals see elephants parade through the streets. The first comes in the mid-May, when monks-to-be, dressed in decorative silks, ride across the Mun River on elephants. In the 3rd week of November, the Surin Elephant Roundup sees elephants roaming the streets, performing in everything from beauty contests to battle reenactments. The rest of the year, visitors can admire the city's pretty temples, like the distinctive red city pillar shrine. At the Queen Sirikit Sericulture Centre, educational tours preserve Thai silk industry's heritage, detailing the full silk-making process, right down to the care of silkworms. While in town, be sure to pick up some "Mai", a dried lotus seed snack, named one of the 50 Best Gourmet Souvenirs by Condé Nast Traveller.

name: Hveragerdi
description: Hveragerdi and the nearby Reykjadalur Valley are part of the Hengill geothermal area - a vast volcanic system that provides most of Reykjavik's hot water and electricity. Hiking through Reykjadalur (literally "Steam Valley"), you're treated to a variety of geothermal features including steam vents and bubbling mud cauldrons, with a gorgeous waterfall thrown in for good measure. But the main attraction is bathing in the so-called "hot river". This stream is naturally heated by the hot springs that feed it, making it a popular destination for daytrips from the capital. After about an hour-long hike, you reach the wooden boardwalk with partitioned changing zones that marks the bathing area (many of the other springs aren't suitable for bathing - pay attention to the signs!). After you've changed into your bathing suit, hop in and enjoy the valley's natural beauty while bathing in a heated river - just don't forget a towel!

name: Chur
description: Dating back to around 3500 BC, Chur's location made it a prime target for invasion, with the Romans, Ostrogoths, Francs, Magyars, Saracens, and Holy Roman Empire all having controlled it at one point. The town also has been particularly prone to fire, having had several major fires over the years, on of which burnt down everything but a church and bishop's residence. The city's long history offers a unique mixture of ancient and contemporary. The scenic old town, with its car-free cobbled streets, gives visitors a taste of traditional Swiss architecture. Parts of the cathedral date back to the 5th century, while most of the structure is from the 12th century. The Church of St. Luzi was first mentioned in 821 when the relics of St. Luzius were removed from the church. Or experience Swiss modernity in the Giger Bar, designed by H. R. Giger himself, or cubist art gallery.

name: Bamberg
description: Narrow passageways, medieval and baroque buildings coupled with a dash of romance contribute to the modern day treasure that is Bamberg. The town's long tradition of beer brewing complements the bustling street cafes and antique shops and can boast a total of nine breweries offering 50 different types of beer, all served in the town's traditional brewery pubs and beer gardens. However, it's not only beer aficionados who love Bamberg. The town that Henry, Duke of Bavaria attempted to make a second Rome 1000 years ago, is now a thriving arts and cultural center dating back over ten centuries and famed for its many different facets. With everything close to the Old Town, visitors can sample the unique cultural atmosphere, buildings, gardens and shops within an historical environment. Whatever your taste, you will be sure to find it in the eclectic work of art that is modern day Bamberg.

name: Linares
description: Linares is a picturesque colonial city founded in 1712 known for its well-preserved historic architecture, vibrant culture, and delicious cuisine. Explore the Plaza de Armas de Linares - a meeting place for the Linares locals lined with emblematic buildings and green trees. At the Cathedral of San Felipe Apóstol, built 1770, witness the fusion of baroque and neoclassical elements and admire the oil paintings inside. Stop to take photos at the Casino de Linares - a historical casino that still functions for members of the club, known for its pistachio green facade and white details clearly inspired by the Paris Opera House. Beyond its historic attractions, Linares is also renowned for its warm hospitality and delicious food. Sample a variety of regional specialties, including cabrito (roast goat), machacado (dried beef), and carne seca (dried beef jerky).

name: Colonia Suiza
description: Discover the enchanting charm of Colonia Suiza, a quaint mountain village nestled just outside Bariloche. As you wander through the picturesque streets, you'll encounter chalet-style architecture, a testament to the enduring Swiss influence. The Colonia Suiza Market, held on Wednesdays and Sundays, beckons with local handicrafts, regional jams, and the aroma of the famous Curanto—a traditional Patagonian dish. Don't miss the serene shores of Lake Moreno, accessible through a tree-lined path, where you can bask in the summer sun and cool off in the pristine waters. For family-friendly adventures, Aldea Duende offers a whimsical theme park experience, weaving through native forests with miniature goblin statues scattered throughout. Embark on a culinary journey at the Berlina brewery, just blocks away from Colonia Suiza's entrance, where craft beers and regional delicacies await. Dive into the region's rich past at the Museum Los Viejos Colonos, housed in Marcelo Goye's residence, showcasing family trees, vintage photographs, and historical artifacts.

name: Joinville
description: Joinville, nestled in the southern state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, welcomes you with a rich blend of German heritage and Brazilian warmth. Immerse yourself in the vibrant festivals that define Joinville, including the renowned Joinville Dance Festival and the blossoming beauty of the Joinville Flower Festival. Beyond the festivities, uncover the city's history at landmarks like the National Museum of Immigration and Colonization, showcasing the resilience and stories of European settlers. For nature enthusiasts, Boa Vista Hill offers breathtaking views of Joinville, perfect for an early morning hike or a tranquil sunset picnic. Discover the diverse wildlife at Joinville Zoo, where over 2,000 animals, including endangered species, find sanctuary. Explore the city's roots at the Municipal Market, savoring local cuisine and collecting unique souvenirs. Wander the pedestrian-only Rua das Palmeiras, lined with palm trees dating back to 1873, capturing the essence of Joinville's charm.

name: Petra
description: Settled as early as 9,000 BC, Petra was made the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom sometime around the 4th century BC. Over the following years, the city flourished as a trade hub, reaching a population of 20,000 by 100 AD. As trade took to the seas, the city declined, and though several Byzantine churches were built here, it was abandoned by the early Islamic era, and only used by nomads until its rediscovery in 1812. Today, the network of temples, tombs, and churches hand-hewn into the cliff are a breathtaking sight, blending raw-beauty and human artisanship. And though not as glamorous, the city's water system is a feat of engineering. While the most iconic building, the treasury, is the first thing visitors see after walking through the 1.2-kilometre-long gorge to reach the city, Petra covers nearly 100 square miles, and can easily take a few days to fully explore.

name: Barcelos
description: According to a 13th century legend, a pilgrim passing through Barcelos was wrongly accused of theft and sentenced to death by hanging. He was spared when the roasted rooster the judge was about to eat got up and crowed. Ever since, the brightly painted ceramic roosters have been sold throughout Portugal as symbols of luck. If your schedule allows, Barcelos' huge square hosts one of the largest open-air markets in Europe on Thursday mornings.. Of course, there's plenty to see every day of the week, including the 18th-century Nossa Senhora do Terço Church on the north side of the square, which houses beautifully decorated panels tiles and gilded wood in its plain exterior. In the town's old quarter, historic buildings abound, such as the Parish Church, and the ruins of a palace belonging to the Dukes of Bragança, which now houses an open-air archaeological museum.

name: Timisoara
description: As the largest city in western Romania, Timisoara has been influenced by many cultures. It was used as a crossroads fortress by the Romans, conquered by the Turkish armies in 1552, and came under Austrian rule for two centuries in the early 18th century. Its eventful past has left its mark in Timisoara, and influences from many cultures can be seen in neighbourhoods throughout the city. Settled on the northern bank of the Bega River, the charm of this city lies in its distinct architectural character and vibrant cultural life. Often referred to as "Little Vienna," Timisoara is home to year-round musical and theatrical performances, art galleries, and museums. It was also the first European city (second in the world only to New York City) to use electricity to illuminate its public streets.

name: Barber
description: In the northern reaches of Curaçao, the town of Barber unveils its unique charm every Sunday morning, when the Marshe di Barber transforms the local market hall into a bustling food haven. The town is strategically located inland from the north coast, near the major road junction southeast of Christoffelberg. It shares borders with neighboring settlements like San Hyronimo, Santa Cruz, Soto, and Ascencion. Barber boasts not only a lively market scene but also significant historical and natural attractions. The oldest tree in Curaçao, a Ceiba pentandra or silk cotton tree, stands as a testament to the town's enduring legacy. This remarkable tree, claimed by some to be 800 years old, is a centerpiece in Barber's landscape. Delving into the town's history, the Kas di Pal'i Maishi serves as an open-air museum, providing insights into the living conditions of slaves. As visitors explore the Hofi Pastor Nature Reserve on the outskirts of Barber, they encounter a small yet captivating botanical garden with native flora and fauna, complemented by walking trails that offer a glimpse of the town's natural beauty.

name: Honfleur
description: First mentioned in the 11th century, within 100 years Honfleur had developed into the key point for trade between Rouen and England. Over the centuries, the seafaring town flourished, becoming one of the principal French slave-trade ports. Honfleur is even where Samuel de Champlain set off from to found Quebec. The French Revolution and the continental blockade halted the town's growth, leaving it frozen in time. Visitors can walk through the ancient port, admiring the traditional fisherman's houses. Built with wood or slate, these distinctively narrow structures can reach up to seven stories and now house boutiques and art galleries. The maritime influence is obvious in the 15th century St Catherine's church, where the wooden construction and arched ceiling give the impression of being inside an overturned ship. Next door is a museum dedicated to the work of Eugène Boudin, the Honfleur-born painter who initiated Claude Monet into open-air painting.

name: Al Wajh
description: Al Wajh, a captivating coastal city nestled by the Red Sea, boasts unspoiled beaches and a rich historical tapestry. Visitors to Al Wajh are treated to a seafood feast sourced from its thriving fishing industry, savored in the traditional Arab manner – seated cross-legged on floor cushions. The city's array of mosques, characterized by exquisite architecture, showcases its spiritual heritage. Al Wajh Castle, erected during the 1870s, has transitioned from fortification to a museum, narrating the town's evolution. The museum's apex offers an arresting vista of the port. Al Wajh's shoreline allure is epitomized by beachside parks, a haven for relaxation and family recreation. Al Wajh Corniche Park, gracing the coast, beckons with idyllic picnic spots. Al Hashrah Beach invites quick swims and tranquil contemplation. With its portside charm, Al Wajh unfolds its splendor through stunning beaches and shorefront parks. The Corniche Park, a stage for breathtaking sunsets, offers an array of family-friendly activities.

name: Kenilworth Castle
description: Founded in the 12th century around a mighty Norman tower, Kenilworth Castle was steadily enlarged and refined up until the 17th century. Its mighty fortifications allowed it to weather the longest siege in English history, and made it a base of operations during the War of the Roses, but the castle's most noteworthy role in history had to do with love, not war. In the 16th century. Queen Elizabeth I gave the castle to John Dudley, who transformed the castle into a Renaissance palace. When the renovations were completed, Dudley threw one of the most spectacular parties in English history for his beloved Queen, complete with mock battles, jousting, and all manner of sensory extravagance. After having been destroyed during the English Civil War, only 2 of the castle's buildings remained habitable. Along with exploring the ruins, visitors can step into the Gatehouse to discover Elizabethan rooms, and a particularly intriguing portrait of Queen Elizabeth. For more information, including the event schedule, please visit english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/kenilworth-castle

name: Hestercombe Gardens
description: Spread out over 50 acres, the Hestercombe Gardens were first laid out in the 18th century, as a Georgian landscape complete with ponds, a grand cascade, a Gothic alcove, and follies. In the 1870s, a Victorian formal parterre was added by Henry Hall, and the early 20th century saw Gertrude Jekyll and Edwin Lutyens lay out an Arts and Crafts style Edwardian garden, renowned for its attention to detail and bold patterns. Today, the Hestercombe Gardens provide a unique opportunity to experience three different eras of garden design in one place. On a single walk, visitors can enjoy colorful flower-beds, woodland paths, lakeside views, classical temples, and tumbling cascades. Afterwards you can step into the historic house to admire the contemporary art exhibition, or if you're feeling hungry, stop by the Stables Cafe, or tuck into an elegant three-course lunch at the Column Room Restaurant. For more information, please visit hestercombe.com

name: Clonmacnoise
description: Founded as a simple wooden church by Saint Ciaran in the mid-6th century, Clonmacnoise had established itself as one of the most important monasteries in Ireland by the 9th century. Along with attracting scholars from around Europe, a secular community developed around it, with its craftsmen producing some of the finest metal and stonework seen in Ireland. Just a century later, the community fell into decline, and in 1552 it was finally ruined after having been looted by the English garrison at Athlone. Today, the remains of the Clonmacnoise Cathedral, Temple Doolin, Temple Hurpan, and Temple Melaghlin preserve this rich history with a round tower and picturesque cemetery keeping watch over the ruins. At the on-site Visitor Centre, you can learn more about the fascinating history of Clonmacnoise and marvel at the historic artefacts on display, including the 9th-century Cross of the Scriptures.
