name: Loja
description: Founded in 1548, by Field Marshal Alonso de Mercadillo and one of the oldest cities in Ecuador, the city was fortified due to its proximity to gold areas and served as a departure point for the Amazon basin. In addition, Loja is unique because it is the first city in Ecuador to be wired for electric power by an advanced hydroelectric dam that was completed in the 1890s. Take a stroll through the streets and pop into various music and salsa clubs, and gaze upon local artworks; massive painted tile murals and frescoes. Additionally, there are various monuments, churches, and beautiful structures which will keep you busy for various hours.

name: Puerto Varas
description: Puerto Varas was founded by German immigrants on the shores of Lake Llanquihue in the 19th century. Unsurprisingly, Puerto Varas has become a destination for both its beautiful surroundings and its German heritage. Start your visit at the Sacred Heart of Jesus Church, which was modeled after the Marienkirche Church in Germany's Black Forest. From here, head down to the waterfront for the sweeping views of the lake and twin volcanoes beyond. Follow the waterfront walk south to the Museo Pablo Fierro to see works by the artist, as well as historic artifacts from the region, or head north to the La Puntilla mirador for the best views in town. If you have a sweet tooth, Puerto Varas is famous for its traditional German cakes, and even has a Kuchen Day celebration on the first Saturday of February. You also have plenty of options for other German snacks in the many shops, restaurants and cafes.

name: Vercelli
description: Fist settle by the Libici tribe in pre-Roman times, after the fall of the Roman empire, the town fell under Lombard control. Over the centuries control shifted between noble houses and European empires until 1704, when it shared the destiny of the Savoy domains. A regional artistic center, it was one of the stops on the Via Francigena connecting Canterbury to Rome. Today, visitors can enjoy the city's artistic and religious history in its many churches and museums. The 13th century Basilica di Sant'Andrea is a masterpiece of Gothic-Romanesque architecture, with a unique facade made of several types of stone, and serene cloister sequestered inside. The gothic theme continues inside, with artwork including the 14th century funerary monument of abbot Thomas Gallus, a Lombard fresco, and a 15th-century painted crucifix. The Borgogna Museum exhibits the region's most important artwork from the Renaissance to the 1800s.

name: Peschici
description: This picturesque villages can trace its roots back to a Slavic group who built a castle on the ruins of a farmhouse in 970. By 1023, a Slavic community had established itself around the fort. The castle was destroyed by Venetian troops in the 13th century, but rebuilt by Frederick II of Swabia. Today, this medieval castle still guards the bay, offering visitors great views of the coast, and a firsthand look at medieval torture devices in its museum. The nearby Bridge Tower grants access to the maze of white-washed buildings, alleyways, and stairways carved into the hillside. Within the city center, panoramic viewpoints offer breathtaking vistas of the Aleppo pine tree-lined coast, dotted with watchtowers.

name: Paseo del Viejo Oeste
description: In 1971, the first major production, "Hate on the Prairies" featuring Sidney Portier and Harry Belafone was filmed at the iconic Paseo del Viejo Oeste and marked the beginning of its cinematic legacy. Transformed into a theme park for more than a decade, Paseo del Viejo Oeste offers you a chance to immerse yourself in the Old West. The park features restaurants, souvenir shops, wagon rides, horse rentals and the opportunity to don cowboy attire for memorable photographs. A spectacular show channeling tropes of the Wild West allows visitors to participate and create their own movie experience. Walk where legendary movie stars have walked, including John Wayne, Kirk Douglas, Anthony Quinn and Jack Nicholson. Observe remnants of the permanent sets and take a nostalgic journey into the Wild West era. Paseo del Viejo Oeste is open Monday to Sunday from 11AM to 7PM with shows performed Saturdays and Sundays at 1:30PM, 3:30PM and 5:30PM. Prices are subject to change.

name: Ravenna
description: Once serving as the capital of the Western Roman Empire, Ravenna has long been a special place for its proximity to the Adriatic and its collection of art. As a capital for several kingdoms, the city kept many of its gems well preserved over the centuries. The intricate designs and lavish features in many of the mosaics have won the heart of many. A major point of interest is the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, a Roman building filled with mosaics praised by UNESCO experts as the most "artistically perfect". Basilica di Sant'Apollinare Nuovo and many monuments in Ravenna have been deemed unique and timeless. So much so, in fact, that Ravenna has 8 sites featured on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Although Ravenna is an inland city, it is connected to the Adriatic by the Candiano Canal which has much beauty to offer. The coast of Ravenna has 9 seaside resorts, giving you a perfect place to rest after exploring this ancient city of art.

name: Pazin
description: Due to its strategic position, Pazin has garnered the attention of empires for centuries, passing between the Holy Roman Empire, the Austrians and Italians before becoming part of Yugoslavia, and ultimately the independent country of Croatia. After 600 years, Pazin's castle was reconstructed in the 16th century, which is the façade we see today. Housed inside is the Istrian Ethnographic Museum, which houses historic and cultural items such as peasants' outfits and agricultural equipment. The castle's unique position above a 100m chasm was the inspiration for Jules Verne's 'Mathias Sandorf'.

name: Esztergom
description: Visitors approaching from the direction of the Danube are greeted with the sight of the spectacular Esztergom Basilica rising high above the town from the hilltop overlooking the city. The vision of the reflection of the Basilica in the waters of the Danube is an experience that visitors never forget as they approach the largest church in Hungary and the third largest in Europe. The colossal dome measures over 230 feet high and can be seen from miles around. The interior is no less impressive, housing the richest ecclesiastical collection in Hungary and the red and white marble Bakócz Chapel with its Italian Renaissance stone-carving and sculptures. For the more venturesome, the 400 stone steps leading up to the cupola at the top of the building are well worth the climb to check out the dazzling views over a city steeped in history with its baroque churches, medieval fortresses, city walls, and Turkish bastions from bygone eras. PLEASE NOTE: The Basilica is under heavy reconstruction until late autumn 2025, and all features may not be visible.

name: Rize
description: Rize, the capital city of the province by the same name, is notable for its tea production, a beverage just as honored by Turks as coffee. The region's fertile conditions are perfect for growing tea leaves; what's more, its mountainous landscapes, rushing rivers, and lush green plateaus make it a haven for nature enthusiasts.In the city itself, don't miss the opportunity to visit the medieval Rize Castle. Make sure to also stop by one of the local tea gardens, known as 'Çay Bahçesi' in Turkish. These hidden gems are scattered throughout the cities and towns, and are places where people from all walks of life come together. Rize is also renowned for producing some of the best dairy and honey products in Turkey, which can serve as gifts for your loved ones. Despite its charms, the city remains largely untouched by foreign tourists, so if you're in search of an authentic Turkish experience, Rize is an ideal destination. Travellers often comment on the warmth of the local people, who are not frequently exposed to foreign tourists and are thus extraordinarily hospitable. Coincidentally, Rize is the hometown of Turkey's President, which you won't forgest about because of the frequent display of his portraits all around the city. Please note, as Rize is one of Turkey's rainiest regions, it is important to stay informed about the weather conditions during your visit.

name: Zell am See
description: The town has its very own `home mountain,' the Schmittenhohe, reached by hiking trails from the town centre. Further afield is the famous Kitzsteinhorn glacier, Austria's very first glacier ski region, and still a favourite with skiers and snowboarders, and also home to Gipfelwelt 3000, a complex at the summit. At over 3,000 feet above sea-level the views are utterly stunning, especially aided by viewing platforms with views of the valley, Lake Zell, and the seemingly endless chain of Alpine mountains. The National Park Gallery is full of fascinating information on the region's natural wonders, both geological and technological, while `Cinema 3000` runs `Kitzsteinhorn - The Nature' a documentary film shown on an 8-metre wide screen. Zell am See itself is not to be neglected, and there are many charming nooks and corners in this historic town. St. Hippolyte's Church with its ornate parapet resting on carved columns of precious marble is one such.

name: Memphis, TN
description: When it was founded in the 19th century, Memphis was one of the Deep South's major cotton markets and slave brokers. A hundred years later, it became synonymous with the Civil Rights Movement. Both faces of the city's African American history are preserved at the Slave Haven Underground Railroad Museum and the National Civil Rights Museum, which is housed in the Lorraine Motel where Dr. Martin Luther King was assassinated in 1968. Then there's Memphis' other great legacy: music. Head over to Beale Street to immerse yourself in the birthplace of Blues and Jazz, and catch a show at one of the countless venues. Over at Graceland, Elvis Presley's home, you'll find the world's largest Elvis museum, with everything from his private jet to costumes to fully furnished rooms. And if you're ever hungry, just have some BBQ. Memphis' slow cooked meats are so good that they hold the World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest here every May as part of a month-long festival.

name: Ventura, CA
description: Formerly a Spanish Colonial settlement, Ventura is now one of the best places to escape the hustle of LA and unwind with beautiful sea, surf and sun. The Spanish-influenced architecture is still one of the city's defining features, and the 18th century Mission San Buenaventura undeniably charming. But the beautiful buildings are really just a bonus. Its the beach that has Los Angelites, celebrities, and sun-lovers clamoring for Ventura. From the beach to the pier to the many surfbreaks and a seemingly endless array of parks, you'll have no shortage of recreation and fun in this village-like city.

name: Baden
description: The mineral springs are an integral part of Baden's identity - its name literally means 'baths' in German. It was "Aquae Helveticae" to the Romans, and a relaxing escape for the likes of Goethe, Nietzsche, and Dürrenmatt. Even today, the icon of the city is the unique thermal bath building designed by Mario Botta, which is both a meeting place, and visitor attraction. Elsewhere in the car-free old town, visitors will find the remains of the medieval Stein Castle, historic municipal buildings, and in the Langmatt Foundation, one of Switzerland's finest art collections. There's even a Swiss Children's Museum, covering 300 years of the world of children.

name: Yufuincho Kawakami
description: Yufuin, once a town in Ōita District, Ōita Prefecture, is now a district in the city of Yufu. Visiting it is like stepping into a Ghibli cartoon, so if you're a fan, don't skip this location! Yufuin is renowned for its idyllic vistas, exquisite traditional Japanese architecture, and soothing onsens (hot springs). There are several onsens in Yufuin to choose from depending on one's budget, but experiencing one is a must for those wanting a quintessential Japanese experience. If an onsen isn't on your agenda, consider the tranquil Kinrin Lake, Yufuin Stained Glass Museum, or the delightful Floral Village, a haven of souvenir shops and cafes adorned with flowers. Along the main road and Yunotubo Street, you can discover cozy cafes, craft shops, and eateries serving traditional Japanese dishes, all set against the backdrop of the town's picturesque rural landscapes.

name: Vung Tau
description: In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Vung Tau cape was a swampland used by European traders as an anchorage. Ever since, it has been inextricably tied to the sea - be it as a pirate base, or launching point for the 'boat people' fleeing Communism. Today, the city and it's long stretch of beach is a popular weekend escape for sun-seekers. If you don't want to get your feet wet, Vung Tau's wide boulevards are lined with colonial-era buildings, and a surprisingly varied restaurant and bar scene caters to the many expats and oil and gas workers. While Buddhism dominates Vietnam, the most noteworthy monument here is the 28-meter-tall statue of Jesus standing on a hilltop overlooking the sea and city. On another hill overlooking the beach stands the French Colonial Governor's summer house. Known as the 'White Villa', the manor now exhibits hundreds of artefacts from Cau Islet-Con Dao.

description: Originally an indigenous settlement, Santa Catarina Juquila became one of the most popular pilgrimage sites in Mexico after word spread about its miraculous Madonna. The 15th century statue of the Virgen de Juquila, survived a fire in 1633 that destroyed the rest of the village, and since then has been drawing faithful to ask for a miracle in exchange for promising to visit. The 30cm-tall statue is housed in a wedding cake of a church, backed by the rugged foothills of the Sierra Madre del Sur.

name: English Harbour
description: Nestled on the southern tip of Antigua, English Harbour is a captivating blend of maritime heritage and modern boating allure. With its deep, protected bays, English Harbour has become a haven for boaters, offering safe moorage and an electrifying maritime atmosphere. The legacy of its British Royal Navy history is still palpable as you wander through the charming streets of English Harbour Town. The town's bustling energy, infused with the presence of luxury yachts and sailing crews, creates a unique fusion of past and present. Among the crown jewels of English Harbour is Nelson's Dockyard, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that pays homage to Admiral Horatio Nelson. Once a vital naval dockyard, this historic landmark now houses restored colonial buildings transformed into shops, restaurants, and bars. Beyond its maritime allure, English Harbour offers a gastronomic adventure. Dockyard Drive is lined with an array of restaurants offering diverse cuisines, many of which highlight the bounty of local seafood. Whether you're savoring a meal by the water's edge or exploring the vibrant local scene, English Harbour promises an unforgettable experience.

name: San Francisco de Campeche
description: Spanish conquistadors founded San Francisco de Campeche in 1540 on the site of the Maya city of Can Peche. The city's location on the Yucatán Peninsula made it an important part of the trade routes between Spain and the New World, which in turn made it a target for pirates. To combat the corsairs, the city was guarded by defensive walls and watched over by forts, which took advantage of the hilly terrain. The most prominent of these is the 18th century San José el Alto, which is a prime example of military architecture, and houses an excellent museum dedicated to underwater archaeology. Campeche's historic center is the last walled city in the Americas alongside Montreal, and its bastions, colorful buildings, and well-preserved mansions, and preserve a picture-perfect slice of the colonial era.

name: Jerusalem
description: Settled since the Bronze Age, Jerusalem was made the capital of the united kingdom of Israel by King David, and was where his son, King Solomon, built the First Temple. Centuries later, the prophet Muhammed ascended to heaven here, and Jesus Christ was crucified just outside the city. These key events have made Jerusalem one of the most revered places on Earth to a third of the world's population. The Western Wall marks the last remaining piece of the ancient Jewish Temple compound, and is the single holiest site in that religion. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre encompasses the two holiest in Christianity: the site where Jesus was crucified and Christ's empty tomb. For Muslims, the stunning, 8th century Al-Aqsa Mosque is the third holiest site after Mecca and Medina. And the iconic Dome of the Rock is revered by both religions as where God created the world. These, and the 220 other historic monuments envelop the city in an air of multicultural awe.

name: Yumka
description: Opened in 1993, the Yumka ecological reserve is home to 946 animals from 80 different species. Along with Tabasco's indigenous jungle residents like howler monkeys, jaguars, and toucans, a trolley through the savanna section allows visitors to see elephants, giraffes, zebras and hippos. A separate Asian section is home to Eastern species including axis deer, antelope, buffalo, and gaur - the world's largest ox species. Along with these open-air areas, the aviary and reptile enclosures offer visitors the opportunity to see flighty and elusive species up close.

name: Meissen
description: Due to its prime location along the River Elbe, Meissen has always been a town of high importance. Built in 1741, Albrechtsburg castle was the first castle in Germany to be built solely for residential use (as opposed to military). Therefore great care was taken with the aesthetic design, resulting in the stunning architecture seen today. In 1710, the first European hard-paste porcelain manufacturer was established at the castle, growing in prominence and finesse until Meissen Porcelain became a much sought-after and well-renowned style of design. Meissen Cathedral resides on the same hill as Albrechtsburg castle, providing a fitting neighbor for the palace. Its gothic design perfectly complements the castle while remaining impressive in its own right.

name: Jonkoping
description: Whether you would like to visit museums, beautiful 17th century churches or spend your time in the great outdoors, Jonkoping is a definite must in your travels through Sweden. You can escape the city life along the beaches of the vast Lake Vattern, while still having the luxury of cafes and restaurants nearby. Along the beaches are opportunities for hiking, canoeing, sailing or even motorized boating in this environmentally friendly atmosphere. One of the rarities you will find in Jonkoping is one of three matchstick museums in the entire world. The birthplace of the safety match is Jankoping!

name: San Cristobal
description: Unlike many places in Mexico, San Cristobal wasn't the site of a pre-Hispanic city. Instead, it began as a military fort founded by the conquistador Diego de Mazariegos in 1528. From then, it quickly grew into a thriving settlement, and served as the state capital until 1892. The historic heart of the city is a network of cobbled streets lined with colorful houses and beautiful colonial buildings. The airy main plaza is watched over by the clementine Cathedral, which was visited by Pope Francis in 2016. The city's most beautiful building, however, is the nearby 17th century Templo Santo Domingo - a church and former convent with a stupendous Baroque facade and equally ornate gilded interior. While these bits of eye-candy stand out as individual sights, the true essence of San Cristobal comes from its primarily indigenous population whose influence can be seen in everything from hand-made ponchos to liquor and cuisine.

name: Buraydah
description: The capital of Qassim province, Buraydah, is a rapidly growing city and an emerging tourist hotspot, located in the middle of the country. Known as an agricultural hub, Buraydah has earned the nickname "the city of dates" due to its high-quality production of the fruit. The city's surroundings offer a charming glimpse of country life with farms and orchards, while the city itself is a modern hub with various tourist attractions. Here, you'll find museums such as the Buraydah Museum and the Aloqilat Museum, which showcase the history of the city and the region, a number of parks including the lush King Khalid Park and Garden, and landmarks like the Buraydah Water Tower, which has a viewpoint. Entertainment centers, shopping malls, and dining options abound in Buraydah as well. Lastly, thanks to its climate, the city is renowned not only for its date production but also for the cultivation of palm trees and various citrus fruits, such as oranges and lemons.

name: Aregua
description: Set atop a hill, Aregua takes its name from the indigenous inhabitants that established the area before Spanish colonization and loosely translates to 'those from above'. Follow Avenida del Lago, or Lake Avenue, to get a bird's eye view of the town. This historical route starts at the hilltop church of Iglesia de La Candelaria and runs down to the banks of the Lake Ypacarai. On the way down, don't miss Cerro Coi! This unique hillside rock formation is known to exist in only two other countries. Get a taste of the local craftsman culture in town by visiting one of the many art galleries and then purchase some traditional pottery pieces. In addition to the arts, Aregua is known for its strawberry production and hosts annual festivals showcasing the fruit. Sink your teeth into something sweet before exploring the rest of this lakeside gem.

name: Poitiers
description: Dating back to the Romans, the provincial town used to be one of the major cities in western Gaul. While not much remains from the Roman settlement, the city is home to one of the oldest churches in Europe. The fourth century Baptistry, is decorated with some of the earliest murals in France, and houses a small archaeological museum. In the Middle Ages, the city began to flourish again, with several landmarks being built. The 11th century Notre Dame la Grande, with its ornately decorated facade, is one of the finest examples of western French Romanesque architecture. 100 years later, King Henry II had a Gothic cathedral erected, which has beautiful stained glass windows. Near the historic town center, with its half-timbered houses and cozy cafes, is the Musée Sainte Croix, which exhibits historic and archaeological artefacts, alongside a collection of mostly French paintings and sculpture from the 19th and 20th centuries, including works by Rodin, Bonnard and Sisley.

name: Melrose Abbey
description: Founded by King David I of Scotland in 1136, Melrose Abbey's roots date back to a 7th century monastery where St. Cuthbert was trained. Over the centuries, the Melrose grew to become Scotland's premier abbey, but its position on a main road made it subject to frequent English attacks. After being severely damaged on two occasions in the 14th century, the abbey never fully recovered, and was reduced to a parish church by the time it was assaulted by Oliver Cromwell during the English Civil War. Today, visitors can admire the elegant architecture, which is primarily from the 15th century, and filled with unusual sculptures including hobgoblins, ladle-bearing cooks, and a bagpipe playing pig. In the Commendator's House, visitors can examine artefacts unearthed during excavations, and a commemorative stone plaque in the grounds marks burial place Robert the Bruce's heart. For more information, please visit historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/melrose-abbey/

name: Tuguegarao
description: Tuguegarao was founded in 1604 as a mission center, and by 1841 had grown to become the provincial capital. During World War II, the city was the target of heavy Allied bombing as it was being used as a base and airfield by the Japanese. While this destroyed most of the city, some historic buildings survived, including the 18th century Sts. Peter and Paul Metropolitan Cathedral. The church's red-brick facade is regarded as one of the most beautiful in the Philippines, and even has a photograph hanging in Vatican City. Even older is the St. Hyacinth Church, which dates back to the city's founding in 1604, though it's had to be rebuilt on a few occasions. History and culture lovers will want to pay a visit to the Cagayan Provincial Museum and Historical Research Center, which exhibits everything from ethnographic artefacts to fossils - there's even an extensive exhibition on the discovery of Callao Man.

name: Norrkoping
description: First mentioned in 1283, Norrkoping has been a thriving commercial and industrial hub for centuries. From weapons to ships to textiles, the city's long industrial heritage earned it the nickname "Sweden's Manchester". The unique Arbetets Museum, situated in an old textile mill on a river island, focuses on industry and work in Sweden, with special focus on the social and environmental impact of industry. Walking the riverside, you'll find plenty of other historic buildings that preserve Norrkoping's industrial heritage, but head to Himmelstalund to the west of the city center, and you'll be able to see a very different history. Here, you'll find over 1600 petroglyphs depicting boats and hunting scenes that date back around 3,500 years. In recent years, Norrkoping has enjoyed a cultural revival, and is now boasts some excellent art museums, and a growing gastronomic scene.

name: George
description: George began as a humble timber-supply-base by the Dutch East India Company in 1776, though the town proper wasn't officially established until 1811. Today, it's the commercial hub of the famed Garden Route, though still maintains its small-town atmosphere thanks to the wide streets and traditional white buildings. George's central landmark is known as the 'Slave Tree' - an ancient English Oak so named for chain embedded in its trunk, which has been named a national monument. George is also home to the only botanical gardens on the Garden Route, which preserves the diverse but threatened flora of the Cape Floristic Region - a UNESCO-listed biome. For many visitors however, the main attraction is the range of championship golf courses.

name: Telc
description: Founded as a royal water fort in the 13th century to monitor the busy merchant routes between Bohemia, Moravia and Austria, Telc enjoyed great prosperity up through the 18th century. After a fire in the 14th century destroyed the town, it was rebuilt in stone, with the locals trying to one-up each other with increasingly elaborate homes. To this day, Telc's main square is lined with some of the country's most elaborate Renaissance and Baroque buildings. While the amazing facades get most of the attention, the houses are all connected by a maze of underground tunnels, which you can explore on a guided (Czech language only) tour. The gorgeous Old Town leads up to the elegant Renaissance castle and Gothic cathedral of St. James. If you're looking for the best vantage of the picturesque town, you can climb to the top of the tower.

name: Odense
description: Named after Odin, Odense's is one of the oldest cities in Denmark, first mentioned in 988. While Odense was relatively important through the Middle Ages, it was the modern age that put the city on the map, becoming a thriving industrial center in the 18th century, and thanks to Hans Christian Andersen, a cultural one as well. Today, the city is filled with whimsical references to the renowned author such as his silhouette in the pedestrian lights, but the best place to learn about him is in his ancestral home, which is now a museum. Here visitors will find artefacts documenting his life, and of course, his stories. But the city has much more to offer, such as Denmark's best zoo, or the 19th century Funen village, which brings rural traditions to life.

name: Valladolid
description: The capital of of Castile and León didn't rise to prominence until 1072, when Count Pedro Ansúrez built a palace, and two churches here. Afterwards, it skyrocketed in size and stature, becoming the venue King Fernando and Queen Isabel's wedding, and hosting Magellan, Christopher Colombus, and Miguel de Cervantes, the latter two having house-museums in the city today. The unfinished Cathedral would have been the largest church in Europe, but after resources ran dry, it's only half its intended size. The structure exhibits several architectural styles, a magnificent reredos from 1562, and houses the impressive Diocesan Museum. The esteemed University's Baroque façade is decorated with various academic symbols, while the Santa Cruz College is one of Spain's finest Renaissance structure, and houses a valuable library.

name: Muyil
description: Inhabited from around 350 BC to 1500 AD, Muyil was one of the earliest and longest-inhabited Mayan settlements on the Yucatan Peninsula's eastern coast. Situated along the Sian Ka'an lagoon, Muyil lay on the Caribbean trade route and was believed to have strong ties to the powerful city-state of Coba. Like many other Mayan settlements, Muyil was abandoned following the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century. While only a portion of the site has been excavated, the buildings here offer a succinct survey of Mayan architecture.The most impressive structure is the 15 meter tall Castillo. This five tiered pyramid was built in the steep-sided Guatemalan style, and sits atop two temples. While Muyil itself isn't that large, it sits in the UNESCO-listed Sian Ka'an Biosphere Preserve, and visitors can extend their visit to explore the mangroves, or climb an observation tower to gaze out over the lagoon.

name: Franschhoek
description: Franschhoek was settled by French Huguenot refugees in the late 17th century. Known as 'the French Corner', their farms have since grown into renowned wineries, while still preserving their traditional Cape Dutch houses. Wine-lovers won't want to miss the Franschhoek Wine Tram. This hop-on hop-off tour, brings you through the heart of the Franschhoek Valley, allowing you to hop off at points of interest to enjoy beautiful views, fine wines, and the valley's history. Much of the village is made up of unspoiled Cape Dutch architecture, providing a pleasant atmosphere to walk and shop. And when you get hungry, you can stop to enjoy the town's exceptional gastronomic scene. Be it a lunch from locally grown produce, or dinner at a world-class restaurant (you'll need advance reservation for these, of course).

name: Modena
description: Modena is an automotive town filled with factories of some of the biggest names in the car industry: Maserati, De Tomaso, Pagnini, and Ferrari, to name a few. Besides its long-standing history with cars, Modena is also known for its food. The town is a major protector of authentic flavor. As the birthplace of balsamic vinegar, one could easily stumble upon unknown hidden restaurants with some of the most amazing food in the world. The art and architecture in Modena are unrivaled and a delight for lovers and artists alike. Discover the civic museums at the Palazzo dei Musei and be humbled in the Church of San Giovanni Battista and Sant'Agostino. Admire the wonders of Palazzo Ducale, the Duomo di Modena, and the Villa San Donnino. Don't forget to tour the Enzo Ferrari Museum, too!

name: Cuernavaca
description: Cuernavaca blossoms through every season with warm weather and cool mountain breezes nourishing both plants and people all year round. The picturesque streets of the City of Eternal Spring are filled with fragrant African tulips, lilies and jasmine. Standing above the flowering trees are beautifully preserved buildings that house restaurants, shops and residences. The Cuernavaca Cathedral, the former convent of La Asuncion and UNESCO-listed site, is the city's main church and features multiple chapels built at different periods throughout history. Palacio de Cortés is said to be the most representative building of Cuernavaca and is one of the oldest colonial-style civil structures in the Americas. From the first Aztec emperor to Spanish conquistadors until today, many have been drawn to the land for its undisputed beauty and heritage.

address.addr1: Lungotevere degli Anguillara, 12, 00153 Roma RM, Italy
description: According to Roman mythology, Rome was founded by Romulus in 753 BC after killing his brother Remus over a dispute on which hill their city should be built on. Called the "Eternal City" for its long history, and the "City of Seven Hills", Rome's nicknames give a clue what to expect. Now home to nearly 3 million people, the Eternal City's long history is well-preserved in its many monuments and museums. Head to the UNESCO-listed city center to find most of Rome's most iconic monuments, like the Colosseum, Foro Romano, and Palatino. Along with its many ancient monuments, Rome was a major Renaissance center and the birthplace of the Baroque style and Neoclassicism. The Trevi Fountain, Sistine Chapel with Michaelangelo's famous ceiling, and Saint Peter's Basilica are all masterpieces. Save time for Rome's museums, like the Vatican Museums, the Musei Capitolini, the Borghese Gallery, and the Palazzo Barberini Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica to see the works of Masters up close.

name: Ruins Chacchoben
description: The Mayan settlement of Chacchoben was established around 200 BC, with most of the buildings seen today dating from the 8th century. Chacchoben wasn't officially reported to the Mexican government until 1972 when Dr. Peter Harrison spotted a series of hills in the otherwise flat forest while flying past in a helicopter, and realized that these were likely temples buried by time. Today, two large pyramids have been excavated and restored, with palapa roofs protecting some buildings where the original red paint is still visible. Much of the site belongs to the jungle, and following the circular path through the palms and hardwoods, you'll spot the remains of stairways, courtyards, and other buildings beneath the roots, and maybe some spider monkeys in the branches!

name: Agros
description: Built in a natural amphitheater in the Troodos mountains, Agros is one of the best places in Cyprus to immerse yourself in rural life. Famous for its roses, rosewater, cured meats, marmalades, and sweets, and the many workshops are open to visitors to see their traditional production techniques. Aside from the many treats to indulge in, Argos is also known for its many historic churches. Chief among these is the Church of Panagia Eleousa, which was built on the site of the medieval monastery the village formed around. Nearby, the Museum Fragoulides is dedicated to one of Cyprus' pioneering modern artists, Solomos Fragoulides.

name: Birmingham
description: Established around the 6th century, Birmingham was one of the poorest settlements in the region until it was allowed to hold a market in the 12th century. After this, it became a major trade center, and experienced explosive growth during the Industrial Revolution. Today, Birmingham is the second largest city in the UK, with the culture to match. Stroll along the formerly-seedy canals, which are now lined with shops and restaurants, before heading to the Jewellery Quarter to be dazzled by its glittering goods. The 'Bull Ring' has been the commercial heart of the city since it hosted Birmingham's first market in the Middle Ages, and is now the busiest shopping center in the UK, thanks in large part to the metal-plated Selfridges building. The city also offers a variety of museums, ranging from the National Trusts' 'Back to Back' workingman's museum, to the quirky Coffin Works. For fans of 'Peaky Blinders', there's even a walking tour that sheds light on the darker side of the city's history.

name: Lydford Gorge
address.addr1: National Trust - Lydford Gorge, Okehampton EX20 4BH, UK
description: Appreciated for its natural splendor and beauty for centuries, the Lydford Gorge's dramatic landscape also made it the perfect hideout for a gang of 17th century sheep rustlers. Today, this stunning site is owned by the National Trust, and offers a variety of pleasant walking paths. The full circuit is 3 miles, and takes about 2 hours, but this is the only way to experience the gorge's most famous formations. At one end, the Whitelady Waterfall', the tallest in the region, falls 30 meters into a pool surrounded by lush greenery. At the other end, the Devil's Cauldron roars and bubbles as water rushes past its potholes. Please note some areas can be quite steep and slippery, so sturdy footwear is recommended.

name: Vardzia
description: Vardzia, an intriguing village in Georgia, is renowned for its 12th-century cave and tunnel system etched into a cliffside. The cave complex, towering up to 19 stories high, ranks among Georgia's most striking ancient cave towns. Today, remnants of a throne room, a church, a wine cellar, and a bell tower can still be observed in the complex network of caves and tunnels. The Church of the Dormition stands as the most striking portion of the site, notable for its paintings, impressive archways, and suspended bells. Spending several hours exploring the cave city of Vardzia allows for a leisurely journey through its every corner. If time is scarce, an hour-long visit will suffice for a one-way walk through the main caves and churches before returning to the parking lot. Situated off the beaten path, Vardzia may not offer mass tourism luxuries, but its authenticity significantly enhances the travel experience.

name: Town of Krk
description: The Town of Krk is one of the oldest cities in the Adriatic Sea with the birth of its protective walls dating back to the first century BC. With more than two thousand years of history, Krk's most prominent tourist attractions are their 3 sacred churches rooted in Roman, Franciscan, and Benedictine history. The Gothic Church of St. Francis in Krk nicknamed the 'Little Vatican', is a sacred site that must be explored. If it's solitude you seek, along the coast line one will find plenty of hidden coves and pristine private beaches. Outside of the city there are lush camping grounds and a wealth of recreational facilities.

description: The glacial lake is located in the Julian Alps in Northwestern Slovenia, where it adjoins the town of Bled. This beautiful emerald-green lake has been ranked many times as one of the top 10 most beautiful lakes in the world. A 17th-century Baroque church sits on a small fairytale island in the middle of the lake, giving it a truly magnificent view. A pleasant 6-kilometer walk around the lake can be completed in about an hour for a magnificent look into this picture-perfect destination.

name: Parnu
description: First founded in the 13th century, Pärnu had to be completely refounded after it was destroyed in 1600. An important harbour and trade town, the city started to make to transition to resort town in the 19th century when its mud baths began to grow in popularity. Today, visitors flock to enjoy 'the best sun in Estonia' on Pärnu's white sand beaches, are walk along the seafront promenade. While the city's famous mud-baths were closed following the Soviet occupation, the neo-Classical building was reopened in 2014, allowing visitors to once again enjoy this historically relaxing experience. Visitors can also enjoy this charming mix of historic architecture in the city's old town, such as the original fortified gate, the 18th century Baroque architecture in Estonia, St. Catherine's Church, which is one of the finest examples of Baroque architecture in the country, or the eye-catching red steeple of the St. Elisabeth Church.

name: Mayfield Lavender Farm
description: In the 18th and 19th centuries, the area around Mayfield had a booming lavender industry. In 2006, the Mayfield Lavender Farm was set up on the site of one of these Victorian-era fields to help revive the area's historic industry. Stretching for 25 acres, two varieties of English lavender are grown, harvested, and distilled into oil here. and this organic lavender field Lavender is a 25-acre organic lavender field on an original Victorian site situated on the North Surrey Downs. Two varieties of English lavender are grown on the chalky soil; flowers are harvested and distilled to produce lavender oil. Visitors can also join the a 'bee safari' to learn about beekeeping and taste some fresh lavender honey. After enjoying the sights and scents (and snapping countless photos, visitors can let the experience soak in at the alfresco teashop. The farm is only open from June until September. For more information, please visit www.mayfieldlavender.com/

name: Afula
description: The first record of the ancient city of Afula dates back to the 19th century BC when it was listed as an enemy of the Egyptian empire by Pharaoh Thutmose III. The site remained inhabited through the 13th century, being mentioned in the Hebrew Bible as the ancient Israelite town of Ofel, and archaeological excavations revealing Persian, Roman, Byzantine, Crusader, and Ayyubid ruins and artefacts. Near the city center, the ancient mound, known as Tel 'Afula, is topped by a fortified Crusader tower, which has visible Roman sarcophagi in its defensive walls. On the outskirts of town, the Well of Harod is was mentioned in the Book of Judges, and today this historic landmark sits at the center of a pleasant park.

name: Salamanca
description: With a booming industry coupled with a quiet colonial atmosphere, Salamanca has experienced rapid growth in recent years and welcomes more visitors with each passing season. People from across the country now call this city home and they've brought their regional cuisines and customs with them. Salamanca has become a culinary melting pot and is a foodie's delight. Throughout the city, you'll find restaurants serving up anything from carnitas from Michoacán to enchiladas from just around the corner. Grab some prickly pear cactus with green chili sauce before hitting the road. You're sure to get your fill!

name: Trujillo
description: Before being founded as one of the first Spanish cities in the Americas, the area around Trujillo had been settled by indigenous tribes for thousands of years. Having led Peru to independence, and served as the country's capital on two occasions, Truijillos historic center has a wealth of colonial architecture. There are a surprising number of historic churches to admire, though the vibrant cathedral on the Plaza de Armas is arguably the most impressive. Several of the historic mansions have been preserved, and offer a glimpse into the Colonial and Republic eras. The problem with visiting Trujillo is that along with the pretty city center, two of Peru's best archaeological sites are nearby. Chan Chan was the Chimu capital and the largest pre-Columbian city in the Americas, and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The temples of the Sun and Moon are even better preserved, and claim the superlative of the country's largest pyramid.

name: Barranquilla
description: Within a century of being recognized as a town, Barranquilla grew to be the country's principal port and second-largest city. A melting pot of cultures, the city's diverse population gave birth to the country's largest carnival - a UNESCO-listed affair that sees a dizzying variety of costumes and music parade through the streets. The rest of the year, Barranquilla receives few visitors, meaning it will just be you and the locals in the many great bars and restaurants. The Plaza de San Nicolás is dominated by the vibrant, 18th-century St. Nicolas Church and is lined with cafes and restaurants where you can watch the world go by. Gabriel Garcia Marquez used to meet with a group of like-minded writers and philosophers at the restaurant-bar La Cueva, which still holds live performances and readings. Garcia Marquez even has a section among the varied exhibits at the unique Museo del Caribe. If you really want to surround yourself with the ocean, head to Puerto Mocho Beach. This beach marks the beginning of a causeway that offers 360-degree views of the water!

name: San Sebastian
description: While the area around the city has been settled since 24,000 BC, San Sebastian proper owes its founding to a medieval monastery. Despite its long history, most of what stands today dates from the 19th century or later, thanks to British and Portuguese troops razing the city after retaking it from Napoleonic forces in 1813. Buildings such as the lavish Hotel Maria Cristina and belle époque spa perched over the shoreline make the city a treasure-trove for fans of 19th and early 20th century architecture. The picturesque buildings lining the Parte Vieja, the city's old town, are home to guesthouses, boutiques, and pintxos (Basque tapas) bars. With more Michelin-star restaurants per capita than anywhere in the world, the city is a culinary treat, and favourite for foodies like Anthony Bourdain.

name: Salto del Nogal
description: Salto del Nogal spills 105 meters down a craggy brown rock face and crashes into an iridescent green pool to offer visitors a cool retreat at the end of a dusty trail. After a challenging 45-minute hike uphill, the mist from the tumbling falls and breeze from the canyon are welcome treats. The hike back down the hill is another 30 minutes. The trail can be a bit of a challenge so it's recommended to be in good physical shape. Be sure to wear sturdy shoes and bring plenty of water to stay hydrated!

name: Utrecht
description: Though settled since the Bronze Age, Utrecht's founding is generally credited to the Romans in 50 BC. An important trading post throughout the Middle Ages, Utrecht developed an ingenious canal system, where goods could be unloaded and stored at water level, while elevated pedestrian walkways were left unimpeded. Today, the store-houses are now shops and cafes, giving visitors a quiet and secluded place to relax while walking along the canals. Utrecht is also home to the tallest belfry in the Netherlands.The 14th century Dom Tower was part of a long-gone cathedral, and now offers visitors a hand reference point for exploring the old town, and amazing views over the city for those who scale its 465 steps.

name: Izmir
description: One of the oldest settlements in the Mediterranean Basin, Izmir's strategic position made it an important trade center for much of recorded history. Izmir was so important as a port that the entire Gediz River was redirected in the late 19th century to save the gulf from silting over. Despite the obvious pride taken in the city, it was all but razed to the ground during the Turkish War of Independence. Despite this tragedy, the port city has a laid-back atmosphere and plenty of hidden gems for history lovers. The ancient Agora, built by order Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and the Corinthian colonnade are eye-catching, but it's the vaulted basilica basement chambers and cisterns that you don't want to miss. Then there's the 17th century Kemeralti market, a neighborhood with winding alleys and broad squares where you can get a bit of history while sampling local specialties.

name: Puerto de la Cruz
description: Since the late 19th century, Puerto de la Cruz has attracted genteel members of the European upper class and accommodated famous travelers and writers such as William Wilde. Where Victorian ladies once bathed in its spas, modern-day tourists are now drawn to its stylish surrounds of leisure. Dotted with gardens, terraces, swimming pools, bars, and restaurants, the Lago Martiáenez leisure complex has everything you need for a laidback getaway. You can't visit Puerto de la Cruz without seeing one of the biggest attractions of the Canary Islands - the Loro Parque zoo. From €28, explore the world's largest indoor penguin exhibition, longest shark tunnel, and most extensive parrot collection. Check out the local street art scene to the left of Plaza del Charco and, once you've worked up an appetite, enjoy a host of international cuisines - from German-style bread to traditional Canarian dishes.

name: Huye
description: Located in the south of Rwanda, Huye is a charming city known for its rich history and culture. Several museums showcase the country's past, present and future, with the Ethnographic Museum being a key highlight. Enjoy the elegant modern exterior and browse traditional artifacts and antique monochrome photographs from Rwanda's pre-colonial past. Stop by the Cathedral of Butare, the largest in all of Rwanda, and hear the soulful, uplifting voices of the gospel choir within the red-brick building that dominates the landscape. For a deeply moving and emotional experience, visit the Murami Genocide Memorial Centre for a guide around the site at which thousands of Tutsis were massacred by Hutus in the Rwandan genocide. Understand the entrenched history of the country while admiring its rich culture in the city of Huye.

name: Postojna Cave
description: Postojna is a 24,120m long cave in southwestern Slovenia, making it the second longest cave in the country. The cave is a 24-kilometer network of passages, galleries, and chambers. Begin your visit aboard the cave train, which takes you on a 2-kilometer ride deep into the caves. After the ride, you'll go comfortably on foot to explore more of the caves. Electric lighting allows you to take in all the splendor of the towering limestone formations. Guided tours are available and last approx. 1.5 hours. Audio guides are also available in 15 different languages.

name: Zadar
description: Zadar is located in the heart of the Croatian Adriatic and is Croatia's 5th largest city. It was founded in the 1st Century BC by the Romans and has been ruled by many since. Today, the peaceful town is rich in preserved cultural monuments from the Roman period and Middle Ages. The historic old town is set on a small peninsula surrounded by fortress walls. There are many Roman ruins, medieval churches, museums, art installations, and cafes. St. Donatus' Church, built in the 9th century, is the most famous medieval basilica and a trademark of the city. Walk along the marble stone walkways while enjoying the beauty and rich history of this charming Mediterranean town.

name: Evora
description: Inside the 14th-century walls, the narrow, winding streets take visitors past the ancient city's striking architectural works. The elaborate medieval cathedral and cloisters, 16th century bone chapel, and ancient columns of the Templo Romano and Roman baths are all protected in this UNESCO World Heritage Site. While admiring the picturesque town square, you'd never suspect it was once the site of some rather gruesome scenes courtesy of the Inquisition. The Chapel of Bones, filled with the remains of 5000 bodies, is a 16th century monument made to give people a peaceful place to reflect on life and death. With such a long history in a limited space, it's easy to walk between examples of Romanesque, Gothic, Manueline, Renaissance, and Baroque architecture in one of the most-livable cities in Portugal.

name: Khao Sok
description: Khao Sok National Park covers and area of 739 sq km, including the 165 sq km Cheow Lan Lake, Though it's not the largest park in the world, the rainforest it protects is an estimated 160 million years old, and estimated to contain over 5% of the world's species. At Cheow Lan Lake, visitors can hire a longtail boat to head out onto the water and admire the soaring mountains and swirling mists that surround in. Alternatively, there are a network of trails heading into the forest, where you may spot bears, tapirs, gibbons, wild elephants, and maybe even a tiger, along with some 300 bird species and 38 bat varieties. In order to go more than 3km into the forest, a guide is required, which is also the only way to see the endangered Rafflesia kerrii- one of the world's largest and smelliest flowers.

name: Dana Point, CA
description: Tucked away between San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente, Dana Point Harbor is the city that Orange County (thankfully) forgot. Often called the only romantic spot left on the coast, the harbor area is lined with small shops and restaurants, and paths along the port offer a pleasant place for a stroll. At the far end of Dana Point, you can pay a visit to the Pilgrim, a replica of the famous 19th century brig immortalized by the classic book Two Years Before the Mast, and Steven Spielberg's Amistad. Next to the Pilgrim is the family-friendly "Baby Beach", complete with a roped off swimming area for kids and a lifeguard on hand (just check the water quality beforehand - it can stagnate). For a great view of the coast, especially with a picnic, head up to one of the lookout points on the bluffs behind the beach.

name: Es Castell
description: The charming town of Es Castell has a long and fascinating history dating back to the 16th Century. The town was originally called Georgetown when it was developed during the British occupation in the 18th Century. When the Spanish reclaimed the island in 1782, its name was changed to Villacarlos and it wasn't until 1985 that the town became known as Es Castell. You can see the influence of the town's colonial past in the Georgian architecture dotted around, most noticeably in the main square. Here you can find a strikingly red-painted Town Hall next to the equally dramatic Military Museum of Menorca where you can learn about the island's military history. Two harbors offer scenic strolls along their promenades, where you can find many restaurants and bars, some of which are built inside caves! Perfect for scenic sunset views, sit back, relax, and enjoy the picturesque sea views while trying some tapas or fresh seafood.

name: Nicosia
description: Nicosia offers a unique experience that you'll only find in a handful of other cities: it's split between two countries! The southern half of Nicosia belongs to the Republic of Cyprus, while North Nicosia is the capital of the UN-unrecognized Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. On both sides of the border, it's steeped in history and culture, with landmarks that showcase its Venetian, Byzantine, and Ottoman heritage. From the 16th century Venetian Walls that encircle the Old Town to the 17th century Church of Archangelos Michail and 16th century Büyük Han, which now doubles as an artisan market, Nicosia's history is proudly preserved. For a pick-me-up, stop by Haratsi, an almost-century-old coffee shop. For contemporary Cypriot art, visit the Diachroniki Gallery, showcasing the work of local artists and those inspired by the island. Modernist fans also won't want to miss Eleftheria Square, a futuristic public space designed by the late Zaha Hadid. An important note: don't forget to bring your passport if you want to visit both the southern and northern parts of the city!

name: Galway
description: The city of Galway grew around a 12th century fortification built by the King of Connacht. During the Middle Ages, it was Ireland's principal port for trade with Spain and France, and was even visited by Christopher Columbus in 1477. In the 17th century, the city's fortunes turned, and a string of misplaced alliances saw it besieged and captured on several occasions, which, coupled with the potato famine, left it debilitated until the late 20th century. Today, the city is littered with reminders of its rich history, like the 15th century Spanish Arch - a section of the medieval walls that protected moored Spanish ships. Another section of the medieval walls has been incorporated into the Eyre Square Centre shopping mall, while Ireland's finest town castle is now an AIB bank. The city itself is abuzz with buskers and street performers, which makes for some great entertainment as you seek out some of Galway's famed fresh seafood.

name: Campo Real Vinícola
description: Nestled in the breathtakingly high altitudes of over 7 thousand feet above sea level, Zacatecas, the birthplace of these unique vineyards, stands as one of the few states in Mexico untouched by a major river's flow. With an annual rainfall that barely makes a dent, the area's climate is as harsh as it gets for viticulture. The high elevation prompts dramatic diurnal temperature fluctuations, so Vinicola Campo Real also contends with the threat of frost damage as winter temperatures can plummet to 20 degrees Fahrenheit. Yet, despite these challenges, the winery thrives, and it's not just about surviving against the odds - it's about excellence. The meticulously tended vineyards produce some of Mexico's most esteemed wines, instilling immense pride in the locals. Visitors consistently applaud not only the sublime taste of the wine, but also the friendly staff and the stunning setting. The unanimous verdict is that a visit to Vinicola Campo Real is a must for any wine lover, promising an enriching journey into the heart of Mexico's high-altitude winemaking. To plan your visit, navigate to the site's website at https://www.vinostierraadentro.net/inicio.

name: Ica
description: On the edge of the world's driest desert, Ica is more than just a base for exploring the surrounding area's wonders. Ica is central to South America's oldest vineyards and Vista Alegre Winery is only 10 minutes from the city. It's a traditional winery which is also dedicated to the production of pisco. You can still view vine processing techniques practiced in colonial times. Closer to home there's a number of interesting sites to enjoy. St. Jerome Cathedral, constructed in the 18th century, renovated in 1814, was heavily damaged in the 2007 earthquake. Thankfully it has been repaired and you can view it's neoclassical exterior and Baroque interior. Another of Ica's temples that was ruined by the earthquake is the Sanctuary of the Lord of Luren, the patron saint of the city. Repairs were finally enacted in 2016, this neoclassical phoenix can be enjoyed today during the hours of mass.

description: In 1998, Peter Jackson spotted the Alexander Farm just outside the town of Matamata during an aerial search for film locations for The Lord of the Rings. Saying the area was "like a slice of ancient England", the pastoral farmland was transformed into the Shire, and appeared in the Lord of the Rings Trilogy as well as the Hobbit. Today, a guided tour of the set transports visitors to the Shire and the magic of Middle Earth. While walking past (and into) you'll see Hobbit Holes™ you'll learn about how the movie magic was made - like making the hobbit holes in different sizes depending on the perspective needed. After seeing the most famous locations, you'll end your tour at the Green Dragon™ Inn and an exclusive Hobbit™ Southfarthing™ beverage. On Sunday, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, you can also sign up for an evening banquet tour to see Hobbiton at sunset, before feasting on traditional Hobbit fayre. Bookings must be made well in advance at www.hobbitontours.com

name: Potosi
description: Founded by the Spanish in 1545 as a mining town, during the second half of the 16th century Potosi produced an estimated 60% the silver mined in the entire world. This fabulous wealth bestowed Potosi with grand architecture, and even birthed an extant Spanish expression: valer un Potosí ("to be worth a Potosí"). It also claimed an estimated 8 million lives. When silver production dropped off, Potosi fell into decline. Head to the UNESCO-listed historic center to see the Baroque cathedral and government buildings lining the central plaza. From there, explore the winding streets to find the ornate Church of San Lorenzo and the Convent of Santa Teresa. The lavish, 16th century Casa de la Moneda ("House of Money") is another highlight, both for its architecture and the local history within. If you're especially brave, you can take a guided tour of the mines, to see the grueling conditions Potosi's miners work in just to scrape by. This is not a simple sightseeing tour - you will be brought into an active mine. It can be dangerous and disturbing, but also enlightening. Please research more to make sure you are up for it.

name: Pamplona
description: Founded by Roman General Pompey in 75 BC, Pamplona prospered through the centuries, eventually establishing itself as the seat of the Kingdom of Pamplona. Today, the city's "hamlets" have preserved its medieval origins. One of the best places to experience the city's rich history is at the Plaza Consistorial square, which is home to the Baroque 18th century Town Hall, 13th century Gothic church, and the city's oldest building, the 13th century Cámara de Comptos. However, the heart of the city would have to be the tree-lined castle square. Surrounded by 18th century buildings, the area is dominated by the Neo-Classical Palace of Navarre. Book a tour in advance to see the Baroque throne room, the Chapel's altarpiece, and a portrait of King Felipe VII painted by Goya.

name: Santa Fe
description: Santa Fé played a significant role in the Spanish history. Being founded by Catholic Kings at the end of 15th century, its historical roots cannot be missed. At first, the town served as a military camp, housing the army that would go on to besiege Arab-ruled Granada. The town's military roots are still evident in the fortified walls surrounding the city center. Having established itself as a safe have, Santa Fé hosted Christopher Columbus when he came to sign the agreement to finance his voyage to East Indies, which would eventually lead him to discovering the New World. This historical legacy is carried over by several sights you can visit and admire in the town. The gorgeous Hermitage of Cristo de la Salud from the 15th century, the town's central church or the medieval gates provide visitors with a timeline of Santa Fé's history.

name: Petrovac
description: Petrovac is surrounded by olive groves and pine forests and has 650m of stunning sandy beach. This small town, dating back to the Roman times, is devoted to tourism. Petrovac has a wide range of cafes, bars, and restaurants for visitors to enjoy. The 16th century Venetian Castello Fortress, situated on a coastal cliff, is one of the symbols of the town. It offers a stunning view of the clear water and pebble beaches. With over 300 sunny day per year, it's no wonder why this calm resort town was chosen as a favorite getaway spot.

name: Tepic
description: Tepic's main plaza is the home of the ornate Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception which serves as a gathering point for members of this tight-knit community. Many of the town's residents are part of Nayarit's indigenous population, with Tepic having the second largest indigenous population in the state. Traditional clothing is often worn by the Huicholes which pops against the green of the surrounding hills and lush gardens of the main square. Feast your eyes on the vibrant scenery. Not many leave Tepic without trying the local specialties: tejuino (a fermented corn drink) and guamuchil (a small white fruit).

name: New Plymouth
description: New Plymouth is an incredible city to visit not just for its wide range of activities and attractions, but also for its nearby geographical beauty. This town holds a coastal walkway, a free zoo, an art gallery, and a massive park with a free light festival. If you travel a bit outside the city, you can find yourself upon an ancient volcano known as Paritutu Rock. If you're up for it, you can brave the gnarly climb of 100 metres of an almost vertical ascent; but don't worry, there is a rope there to help you. Making it to the top will reward you of the views of the Sugar Loaf Islands, the bustling city, a glimpse of the famous Surf Highway.

name: Gudauri
description: The Gudauri ski resort is situated in the Greater Caucasus Mountain Range. Imagine hiking or gliding down expansive slopes surrounded by towering peaks—some of Europe's highest—and all at a stone's throw from Tbilisi. Gudauri is more than just an idyllic winter wonderland; it's an adrenaline-fueled playground offering snowmobile rides, paragliding, and cable car adventures. The little ones are not left behind, with an array of child-friendly options. If you're not into sports, fear not: you can opt to rejuvenate your senses in one of several spas, luxuriating in treatments or unwinding in a steamy sauna. Your palate is not forgotten either. Explore an assortment of eateries serving Georgian cuisine alongside a variety of international flavors. With that said, in Gudauri, the magic exists not only during the ski season but year-round. So embark on this enchanting escape and let Gudauri capture your heart, one adventure at a time.

name: Siana
description: Siana, a picturesque village situated in the enchanting Greek Islands, offers visitors a serene retreat amidst breathtaking landscapes and authentic island culture. Perched on the slopes of Mount Akramitis, Siana boasts stunning panoramic views of the surrounding countryside and the shimmering Aegean Sea. The village is renowned for its traditional architecture, with whitewashed houses adorned with vibrant bougainvillea flowers, creating a postcard-perfect setting. Visitors to Siana can immerse themselves in the rich local culture by exploring its narrow cobblestone streets, lined with quaint tavernas and cozy cafes serving delectable Greek cuisine and locally-produced wines. The village is particularly famous for its production of thyme honey, which is harvested from the fragrant wildflowers that carpet the nearby hillsides. Nature enthusiasts will find plenty to explore in the vicinity of Siana, with hiking trails leading to scenic viewpoints and hidden waterfalls. The nearby Seven Springs offers a refreshing escape, with verdant forests and gushing streams providing a tranquil oasis.

name: Limerick
description: Officially founded in 812, it was the Normans who produced most of Limerick's landmarks when they redesigned it in the end of the12th century. Most notable of these is King John's Castle, a robust fortification that weathered five sieges in the 17th century. Not just one of the best-preserved Norman castles in the country, recent restorations have bequeathed it with an excellent museum detailing the city's history. Another Norman relic, and the oldest building in the city, is St. Mary's Cathedral. Founded in 1168, the 14th century Gothic tower is the highest in Ireland, and the church walls still bear the marks of when defenders sharpened their swords on its walls during the Siege of Limerick. It's well worth joining a guided tour to learn more about the history of the building and the Irish heartland. If you need a pick-me-up, stop by a pub for an Irish coffee - the drink is said to have been invented nearby.

name: Cala d'Or
description: Nestled on Mallorca's radiant east coast, Cala d'Or, or 'Golden Bay,' unveils a captivating haven for sun-seekers. The resort unfolds like a tapestry of exquisite coves, each with its unique character—Cala Ferrera, Cala Esmeralda, Cala Serena, Cala Gran, and Cala Llonga. These former fishing harbors have metamorphosed into contemporary marinas, connected by a charming mini train for seamless exploration. Tastefully developed in compliance with stringent regulations, Cala d'Or boasts whitewashed Ibiza-style buildings that add a touch of elegance. Divided into distinct areas, the resort caters to diverse tastes, whether one seeks the thrill of sailing, diving into azure waters, or relishing wine in waterfront bars. For those yearning for tranquility, the main marina and town center offer an array of delightful restaurants. The allure of Cala d'Or extends to its enchanting beaches, such as the picturesque Cala Gran, with its turquoise shallows and golden sands hugged by pine forests. For a more secluded escape, Cala Varques, a locals' favorite, beckons with its golden stretch and pristine setting.

name: Ioannina
description: Founded in the 6th century, Ioannina flourished under both the Byzantine period, when many wealthy families came fleeing the sack of Constantinople, and the Ottomans when it was an epicenter of the modern Greek Enlightenment. The city's wealthy and aristocratic heritage stemmed the colloquialism "to live like the Pasha in Ioannina". Today, the influence of Ali Pasha can be felt throughout the city. The city's 6th century castle guards the Fetiche Mosque, where visitors can learn about the city's influential ruler, and see the graves of Ali Pasa and his first wife. Visitors can also take a ferry to the lake island where Ali Pasha was assassinated, which, along with a quiet village, houses a museum dedicated to the visionary leader. The city is also renowned for its gastronomy, so visitors would be remiss not to try the local specialties, such as frog's legs, sugary pastries, and perhaps the world's only alcohol-free liqueur.

name: Prato
description: First known as the textile centre of Italy, Prato has so much more to offer than just locally produced fabrics. Prato is the third largest city in Central Italy after Rome and Florence and is about 40 minutes North-West of the latter. Situated along the Bisenzio river at the foot of Monte Retaia, Prato is a city composed of impressive architecture, culture, and history. Visitors can enjoy the countless palaces and castles in the area, and explore the narrow streets of this lesser-known Italian city. Prato is also home to many museums and other cultural monuments, including the Filippo Lippi frescoes in the Cathedral of Santo Stefano, which have recently been restored. Situated in an area proven to have been inhabited since Paleolithic times, the list of sites worth visiting in Prato is almost equal in length to the areas fascinating history.

name: Kabale
description: Kabale is the main centre of activity for the entire of south-west Uganda, a focal point for most economic and transport operations. Indeed it has been since colonial times when, in 1913, it was set up as the administrative headquarters of the Kigezi district. Kept cool due to it's 2000 metre altitude, Kabale is a vibrant town with it's overflowing bars and vigorous night clubs. A little earlier in the evening you can try the local beverage, such as "enturire" (a mixture of water, sorghum and honey fermented together)" or "muramba" (a mixture of sorghum and water), and if you're a lover of pork there are many places where you can taste the way the locals make it. For a little culture, check out the Home Of Edirisa, a small museum containing a replica of a traditional Bukiga homestead made from sticks and papyrus.

name: Trogir
description: The medieval town and harbor of Trogir sits on a tiny island in central Dalmatia enclosed by medieval walls. The old town has many intact buildings from the 13th and 15th centuries with an impressive collection of Romanesque and Renaissance architecture. The narrow, marble-lined hidden streets lead visitors around the old town to reveal restaurants, shops, galleries, and cafes. The Cathedral of St. Lovro, Town Hall, and thousand-year-old Monastery of St. Nicholas are sights that can't be missed. Wander the spacious seafront promenade to revel in the medieval beauty and natural surroundings of the stone city of Trogir.

name: Paihia
description: Originally established as a Christian mission, modern Paihia is the gateway to the amazing Bay of Islands, a collection of sparsely populated islands perfect for quiet walks surrounded by nature, or relaxing on one it's golden sandy beaches, serviced by a variety of fast ferries. You can also catch a boat across to Russell, the former capital of New Zealand and home to some of the nation's oldest collection of buildings. Heading a little inland a short walk to the wide Haruru Falls is rewarded with a large lagoon perfect for peaceful reflection, and maybe even a picnic. Many people come to visit the historic Waitangi Treaty Grounds, where New Zealand came under the rule of the British Crown and the Maori people were given rights as British subjects. Written in both English and Maori, the Treaty of Waitangi was signed by native tribal chiefs and British officials.

name: Ingapirca
description: Located in the Ecuadorian Andes, Ingapirca has a high elevation and serves as a perfect place to hike and discover the history of an ancient civilization. The most famous part of these Incan ruins is El Temple del Sol, which directly translates to "The Temple of the Sun". This structure was used by the very advanced Incan society for not only calendar purposes, but also religious practices, serving as a monumental part of their civilization. With a combination of both Incan and Canari architecture, this site symbolizes the opposing ideologies of both cultures; The Incan sun worshippers and the Canari moon worshippers. On your way to the location, you will pass through beautiful country towns where indeginous people inhabit, and find yourself arriving in an incredible UNESCO world heritage site, giving a glimpse into its incredible ancient history.

name: Polesden Lacey
description: Though a house has stood on the site since the 14th century, the core of today's Polesden Lacey was built in 1824. In the early 20th century, the Regency-style home was expanded into a beautiful Edwardian manor that Queen Elizabeth and George VI enjoyed for 2 weeks during their honeymoon. Today, a tour of the interior gives visitors a taste of Edwardian opulence in rooms designed by the same architects responsible for the Ritz. The wood panelling and fine carvings in the Central Hall were originally the reredos in London's St Matthew's Church, while the extravagant saloon, with its gilted panelling, was taken its entirety from an Italian palazzo. Visitors can also enjoy a stroll through the estate's breathtaking grounds, where you can bask in the beauty of the Edwardian rose garden, relax in the fragrant lavender garden, soak in the wildflowers and orchids of the upper sunk garden. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/polesden-lacey

name: Wellington
description: "Windy" Wellington has a long-standing cafe culture, and more recently a wider culinary excellence is prominent here, which makes wandering the quirky Cuba Street or the waterfront from the Railway Station to Oriental Bay a pleasure when great refreshment is just around the corner. In terms of culture look no further than the world-leading Te Papa (Our Place) museum, where ever-changing exhibitions cover all aspects of New Zealand life, past and present, bicultural, and cleverly portrayed. There are excellent tours to be had, such as the nation's parliament or the Weta Workshop visual effects studio (Lord of the Rings). For stunning views and the Botanic Garden ride the historic cable car from Lambton Quay to Cable Car Lookout.

name: Phicardou
description: Located in the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus, Fikardou is known for its well-preserved traditional architecture, including stone houses with red-tiled roofs and narrow streets. The village was founded by dissident groups from the nearby coastal towns who were forced out of their homes by anti-pagan regulations and foreign invasions. Deserted in the 19th century, its houses, built mainly in the 18th century, are a prime example of folk architecture, and are now recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site. The tiny church of Apostles Petros and Pavlos is the center of the village, as well as the busy Taverna Yianakos that serves traditional Cypriot food like slow-cooked lamb. To learn more about the history of the village and region, visit the Local Rural Museum, located in two renovated houses. You can also simply walk around the village on its cobbled streets and beautiful rural nature, taking in the view of the surrounding mountains.

name: Teide National Park
description: Journey to Tiede, the most visited national park in Europe that welcomes over 3 million people a year. In the jaw-dropping surrounds of the park is Mount Tiede, described by UNESCO and NASA as the third-tallest volcanic structure in the world - and it looks as breathtaking as it sounds. Covered in a snowy peak and jagged with petrified lava, the behemoth reaches an impressive height of 7,500 meters. Purchase a cable car ride to reach a lookout point with stunning views, or book a guided walk at the national park office to ensure you do Tiede right. Feast your eyes on flora and fauna endemic to the area such as the Tenerife lizard, Tenerife gecko and the Corsican mouflon. Count yourself lucky if you spot the "red bugloss" blooming in spring, amongst the magnificent mise en scene of Tiede National Park.
