name: Ganja
description: Deriving from the Persian word for "treasure", Ganja blends ancient mosques, hammams, and red-brick architecture with examples of Socialist Classicism and modern elements that magnify its fascinating history. Witness the Imamzadeh mosque and mausoleum complex, a spiritual center with roots in the 8th century, and the Nizami mausoleum, honoring the renowned Azerbaijani poet from the 12th century. The Juma Mosque, a marvel built in 1606 features red bricks and a striking white dome which can be visited during Ramadan. Art enthusiasts can take a visit to the Nizami Ganjavi Museum, filled with 542 exhibits including original manuscripts of Khamsa, or visit the unique Bottle House, a structure constructed using over 50,000 glass bottles. Despite its ancient history, Ganja was designated as the European Youth Capital in 2016, showcasing the vibrant and youthful energy that weaves into trendy cafes and art spaces in the city center.

name: Abengourou
description: Unveiling the heart of eastern Côte d'Ivoire, Abengourou isn't just a town; it's a captivating tapestry woven with rich cultural heritage, breathtaking natural beauty, and a touch of adventure. Beyond the market's allure, Abengourou offers a glimpse into the past. Visit the King's Palace, a majestic residence adorned with intricate carvings, whispering tales of the powerful Anyi royalty. Learn about the fascinating traditions of the region at the Musée National du Costume, where captivating displays showcase the vibrant attire reflecting the Anyi identity. Escape to Lac de Kossou, a shimmering reservoir fringed with lush greenery. Take a boat tour and spot a kaleidoscope of birdlife flitting through the papyrus reeds, or simply relax on the shore and soak in the tranquility of this natural paradise. For the adventurous soul, Abengourou offers a gateway to exploration. Hike through Comoé National Park, a sprawling reserve teeming with diverse wildlife, from majestic elephants to playful monkeys. Kayak down the rushing waters of the Bandama River, surrounded by breathtaking scenery. Photo by: Adou.atta, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ortisei
description: Beginning as a Roman style church in the 13th century, San Giacomo was remodeled multiple times over the years until finally reaching the Gothic style seen today. Those who make the hike up to this church dedicated to St. Jacob, the patron saint of travelers and pilgrims, are rewarded with awe-inspiring views of the surrounding valley, with the Dolomites standing starkly in the background. The interior is richly decorated with Gothic frescoes that date back to the late 15th century, wall paintings from the late 1500s, and locally carved reproductions of the original baroque statues, which are now in the Gardenese Museum in Ortisei.

name: Mosta
description: Mosta is one of the largest towns on the island of Malta, surrounded by the villages of Naxxar, Rabat, Burmarrad and Lija. The most stunning landmark in the town is the Rotunda, a grand basilica constructed by Mosta's parishioners. It boasts the world's third-largest unsupported dome and houses a replica of a German bombshell that famously pierced the dome during World War II without detonating upon impact. Visit on the 15th of August for Mosta's famous parish feast of the Assumption that draws locals and tourists for vibrant festivities and traditions. For aviation enthusiasts, the Malta Aviation Museum is a must-visit. Located on the outskirts of Mosta, the museum showcases exhibits with a spacious hangar dedicated to the Air Battle of Malta. Art enthusiasts can stop by the Farmhouse of the Marquis Mallia Tabone for a scenic farmhouse overlooking the valley of Wied il-Ghasel, holding exhibitions throughout the year. Its rich heritage and captivating attractions makes Mosta a delightful experience in Malta's northern region.

name: Lopburi
description: Lopburi is one of the oldest and most important cities in Thailand, having been founded in the 7th century, and made the country's second capital in the 17th. While Lopburi has an array of palaces and temples from the Khmer and Ayuthaya empires, it's the monkeys that make this city truly unique - they roam the streets, hang from the powerlines, and generally run the town. The Khmer-era Phra Prang Sam Yod is known as the Monkey Temple for the mischievous macaques that live on the temple grounds. It's the perfect place to see monkeys climbing all over ancient ruins, just hold onto your belongings - they're bold enough to steal the hat off your head. At San Phra Kan you'll find a centuries-old statue of Shiva topped with an Ayutthaya-period Buddha head, and at 10:00 or 16:00 this is also where city officials feed the monkeys, turning the yard into a fuzzy feeding frenzy.

name: Virpazar
description: First mentioned as 'Vir' in 1242, the Turks capitalized on the strategic location, erecting the still-standing Besac castle on the hill overlooking the village. After the Turks were expelled in the 18th century, the town became the most important trading post in the country, even adding 'pazar' (marketplace) to its name. The sleepy village is famous for being the site of the country's first uprising against Axis invaders during WWII, an event memorialized by a massive stone monument. The town is arranged as a circle, centered around the wide, tree-shaded square. Most days vendors are selling local products, such as wines and brandy, while Fridays sees a full-fledged market. A short walk brings visitors to the 15th century Besac Castle, which was also used as a police station and Italian stronghold. A climb to the top of the citadel rewards visitors with a view of the town, surrounding flood-plains, and wonderful natural scenery.

name: El Cerrito
description: El Cerrito was first settled by the little-known Chupícuaro culture around 300 BCE, but it was the Toltecs who elevated it into an important religious center. The city flourished under the Toltecs until 1200 CE, when their society collapsed, leaving it in the hands of small tribal communities for the following centuries. What sets El Cerrito apart from most other Mesoamerican pyramids are the ruins of a grand colonial manor, built in 1887 on what the owner thought was a small hill. Excavations revealed not just the Toltec pyramid, but a number of artifacts, including sculptures of the Chupícuaro's fertility goddess. Along the pyramid with its strange crown, there's a small museum showcasing artifacts from El Cerrito's long history. Opening hours for the archaeological site and museum are from 9:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. from Tuesday to Friday and 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekends, but they don't always follow these.

name: Kuala Belait
description: Kuala Belait, known as KB by the locals, exudes a charming small-town atmosphere, with its popular boulevard lined with cozy cafes and restaurants. Visit the Kampong Pandan Mosque, one of the country's largest mosques, surrounded by scenic lawns, jogging paths, and a serene lake. Stop by the Menara Cendera Kenangan, a towering beacon that offers panoramic views of the Belait District, or take a wander past the Sungai Belait riverside where crocodiles and exotic birds take refuge. For history and culture enthusiasts, the Belait Museum provides insights into the district's heritage and the discovery of the oil and gas industry, while the nearby Silver Jubilee Park offers a tranquil spot for picnics or beach visits. A stroll along Jalan pretty, adorned with colorful buildings, charming bakeries, and sidewalk plants, provides a delightful experience that leads to the Belait riverfront. Kuala Belait may be a lesser-known destination, but its simplicity, natural beauty, and cultural treasures make it a worthwhile visit.

name: Tartu
description: Founded in the 5th century, Tartu grew to be an important trade center and regional capital in the late Middle Ages. After capturing the town in 1625, Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus founded Tartu University 7 years later. Today, the University's large student population imbues a youthful passion to Tartu's charming streets - a sentiment memorialized by a statue of kissing students in the heart of the town square. Exploring the compact city center, visitors are treated to an array of eye-catching architecture, from the University's classicist ensemble, to districts of quaint wooden buildings. At the Estonian National Museum, the most modern museum in the Baltic and Scandinavia, visitors can learn about the country's history in a 350-metre-long glass ramp rising from the runway of a former soviet airfield. The AHHAA Science Center is equally large and modern, filled with hands-on exhibits and workshops, where visitors can experience the joy of discovery.

name: Tarnow
description: Founded around the 12th century, the entire city was privately owned until 1787. It was in the 16th century, under the eye of Jan Tarnowski that the city was restyled, earning it the nickname the 'Pearl of the Polish Renaissance'. In the Old Town, visitors can see the glorious Cathedral, a scenic market square, and castle-esque Town Hall. The city isn't just a quiet artist's pallette, Tarnów's citizens were among the first to join the Polish legions in WWI, and was the first Polish city to reclaim independence. On August 28th, 1939 German terrorists detonated a bomb in the city's train station, which some historians consider the official start of World War II. The war decimated Tarnów's Jewish population, which made up nearly half the city. Today, all that is left of the Jewish community are related to the former ghetto.

name: Prague
description: According to legend, Prague was founded in the 8th century when the duchess Libuše stood atop a rocky cliff overlooking the Vltava and prophesied: "I see a great city whose glory will touch the stars!". In the 14th century, Charles IV Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia personally elevated Prague into an imperial capital. Charles himself designed the layout of Nové Město, laid the first stone of the Charles Bridge, and founded Charles University. Over the following centuries, Prague experienced its fair share of ups and downs, not to mention a few defenestrations, but was spared the devastation that befell many European cities. Every visitor's first stop should be the Old Town Square, for the beautiful Baroque buildings lining it, and the famed astronomical clock on the Old Town Hall. From here, you can easily reach the world famous Charles Bridge, and make your way up to expansive castle complex.

name: Higuey
description: Originally a Taino indian chiefdom, Higüey was subjugated by the Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León in 1503, and the Spanish settlement founded in 1505. The town's parish church was perhaps the first Marian shrine in the Americas, which has cemented Higüey as a place of pilgrimage. Even today, the city's main attraction is the modernist Basilica of La Altagracia. Crowned by a concrete tower, the brutalist structure belies the church's historical significance. Inside, the elaborate shrine of the Virgin Mary, houses a magnificent altar and painting that has been on display in Higüey since 1571. Nearby, the Museo de La Altagracia displays art, artifacts, and vestments covering the church's history. The other main attraction is the artisan market, the Plaza Higüeyana, which is a great place to pick up your DR souvenir while supporting local craftsmen.

name: Unaizah
description: Positioned in the heart of Central Arabia, within the historical region of Najd and the extended expanse of the Wadi al-Rummah, Unaizah embodies both antiquity and beauty. Encompassed by the alluring Al-Ghamis Sands to the north and west, Unaizah stands as a captivating oasis adorned with approximately 500,000 date palms, celebrated as the creators of the world's finest dates. Esteemed scientists and historians assert that Unaizah's roots stretch back centuries before the rise of Islam, with references in poetic verses by pre-Islamic Arabian luminaries like Imru' al-Qais. Revered as the "Paris of Najd," Unaizah has garnered attention across the centuries, retaining its Najdi architectural heritage. Notably, the Al Bassam House, an architectural masterpiece constructed from mud in the traditional Najdi style, showcases the city's rich legacy. As a crossroads for vital trade and caravan routes, Unaizah's historical significance shines. Caravans, laden with goods, embarked from Unaizah along arduous routes to Kuwait, Riyadh, Medina, Makkah, and even to distant lands like Egypt, Syria, and Iraq.

name: Sincelejo
description: Built on the site of a small indigenous settlement, Sincelejo at first failed after the Spanish founded it in the 16th century, and was reestablished in 1775. Since then, Sincelejo has grown to become the department capital, subsisting primarily on agriculture and cattle. The cattle industry is so important to the city, that every January it hosts a massive bullfighting festival. Outside the bullring, things are much quieter- as you'd expect from a city known for it hammocks. The heart of the city is Santander Park, which was inaugurated right after Sincelejo was founded. The large open park was the site of Sincelejo's bullfights until 1946, and is watched over by its most beautiful building: the 19th century cathedral of San Francisco de Asis.

name: Koblenz
description: First established as a Roman outpost in 8 BC, the city celebrated its 2000th anniversary in 1992. With the fall of the Roman Empire, the city fell to the Franks and became a royal seat. Its strategic position made it a desirable target for the French up until the 20th century. The Basilica of St. Castor, Koblenz' oldest church, dates back to the early 9th century, and was an important meeting place for emperors and kings. Right next door is the Ludwigmuseum, a modern art museum, complete with giant metal thumb, housed in an ancient building made by the Teutonic Knights. When you're done with the Picassos, right behind the museum is the German Corner, a monumental space jutting out into the rivers' confluence. The most scenic view is offered by a cable-car ride over the Rhine to the massive Ehrenbreitstein Fortress, a UNESCO heritage sight built in 1817.

name: Gordes
description: Gordes grew around an 11th century castle, gradually spilling down the mountainside in several levels as the town grew. Today, the town is still quintessentially 'Provincial', and just the view of it from across the valley makes it worth visiting. A charming maze of cobbled alleys, Gordes' main landmark is its mountaintop chateau - a 16th century update to the original medieval fort. Today, this imposing monument hosts art exhibitions, and houses the Tourist Office, where you can get a map of the town. In the quiet square nearby, you'll find the town fountain - Gordes' only source of water until 1956. The Palais Saint Firmin is also worth seeking out to delve into its subterranean halls, cisterns, stairways, and even olive mills. Gordes rewards simply exploring, with the labyrinth of cobbled lanes allowing visitors to get lost in its charms.

name: Tzintzuntzan
description: Tzintzuntzan was first settled around the 12th century, and by the 15th, had grown to become the capital of the region's most formidable empire. For nearly a century, they held off invasions led by some of the Aztecs' most notable emperors, and until the arrival of the Spanish in 1520, had never seen a military defeat. After the Conquest, however, their bustling capital of 30,000 was largely abandoned, and was instead used by Vasco de Quiroga as his first base in the region. Today, only the ceremonial center remains of the indigenous city, where 5 stepped pyramids gaze out over Lake Pátzcuaro, while the onsite museum exhibits artefacts uncovered at the site. In the modern town, two churches and a monastery stand as charming reminders of its colonial history. Pay close attention to the monastery's masonry - much of the stone came from the nearby pyramids, with some engraved with indigenous symbols.

name: Copenhagen
description: Starting as a humble Viking fishing village, Copenhagen became the capital of Denmark in the early 15th century, and has remained one of the most important settlements in Scandinavia ever since. The multi-faceted city can be hard to describe as anything other than "cool". Among the colorful historic buildings and royal palaces that dot the the greenest urban center in the world, you'll find a mouth-watering food scene with 15 Michelin-starred restaurants, including Noma, voted the best in the world on three occasions, not to mention the painfully-cool streetwear labels, world-famous furniture and lighting, and hand-made ceramics and glassware. Then there are the wealth of museums ranging from Viking artefacts to Danish chairs in a Baroque hospital to the largest collection Egyptian sculpture in northern Europe, and Scandinavia's finest collection of Islamic art. And who can forget Tivoli, the endearing amusement park said to have inspired Disney World?

name: Lascaux
description: Some 20,000 years ago, prehistoric man adorned the walls of Lascaux with hundreds of colorful paintings. A testament to the talents of our ancient ancestors, after his visit to the cave Picasso allegedly said 'we have invented nothing'. Shortly after being opened to the public, it became apparent that the very presence of people was severely damaging the paintings, so it was closed to visitors. Today, there are two museums where visitors experience the beauty and history of the caves. The original, known as Lascaux II is the original reproduction, filled with identical copies of the horses, buffalo, and other animals depicted in the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Lascaux IV, a cutting-edge museum opened in 2016, houses not only a replica of the Lascaux cave, but also interactive workshops and immersive technology which put the cave into the context of human history.

name: Sulmona
description: Settled by the Romans, this ancient town was the birthplace of the poet Ovid, who has a statue in the main square.. Sulmona is set in the 3rd century. While a massive earthquake struck the town in 1706, many historic buildings survived. The town's main street, is lined with palaces, churches, shops, and cafés. The 11th-century Cathedral, built on the site of a Roman temple, had to be reconstructed after the 1706 earthquake. Now in the Baroque style, elements from its long history have been maintained, such as 15th-century sarcophagi, a Byzantine relief with Virgin and Child, and the original Romanesque crypt. The early Renaissance Palazzo Annunziata survived the earthquake of 1706, and now houses a museum exhibiting the city's Roman history through a series of artifacts. The candied almonds often given out at weddings are a local specialty known as confetti, and are often transformed into sugary flowers and bouquets.

name: Domodossola
description: First settled by the Romans, the town was destined to be an important religious sout when its name means 'capital with the main church of the area'. Napoleon's 1805 undertaking to build a road across Simplon pass, and the opening of the railway a century later made this historic border town a junction between Italy and Switzerland. In the medieval town centre, the Piazza Mercato is lined with historic buildings, such as the Teatro Galletti. The 14th century Palazzo Silva, ornamented with local marble, is now a museum displaying Etruscan and Roman artefacts, as well as fragments of Egyptian mummies. However, if you can only see one thing in Domodossola, make it the Sacro Monte del Calvario. Built by Capuchin monks in 1657, the 12 chapels of this baroque complex illustrate the Passion of Christ.

name: Dolceaqua
description: Crossing the curved bridge and entering the narrow, cobbled streets of Dolceacqua feels like stepping back in time. The stone faces of the multi-story buildings, with unique, cavernous between here feel like they're guarding against modernity itself. As you make your way uphill to the 11th century castle, the rustic architecture, shops selling locally produced regional specialties, and healthy sprinkling of churches small shrines, might just make you forget what year it is. A trip to the of the hill rewards visitors with a unique angle of the village, the famous bridge, and the rolling hills of the Italian countryside.

name: Kotor
description: The feeling of charm and romance lingers in the Venetian palace and every cobblestoned street in Kotor. The buildings of this town have been stuck in the middle ages and the walls that protect the city still stand tall today. Cafe's line up side by side with live music restaurants and museums in this ancient town of Kotor. Situated in the Kotor bay next to Lovcen mountain, Kotor is most famous for its creation of the best sailors, traders, and artists. Otherwise, one should take a trip to the Kampana Tower, Kotor Fortress, and the Churches of St Nicholas and St Luke.

name: Parras de la Fuente
description: Green vineyards and cypress trees will fold you into an oasis in the otherwise scorching surrounds of Parras de la Fuente. Spaniards who founded the town at the end of the 16th century realized the area's climate was perfect for vines and ushered in a longstanding winemaking tradition. The oldest winery on the continent, Casa Madero, calls Parras de la Fuente home. Visit in August for the jubilant Grape and Wine Fair, with cultural events, wine and brand tastings, Coahuilan snacks and symbolic grape-stomping. The village itself has an air of old charm and contains several historic landmarks including the Church of Madero, which appears in the right quarter of the city's coat of arms. The Church occupies almost the entire summit of the Sombreretillo hill and is a great architectural symbol of the city, with 360-degree views of the vast Coahuila desert from the top.

name: Yolombo
description: To the north east of Medellin, you will find the tiny municipality of Yolombo. Even though it is a sleepy area of the region it is home to a beautiful church, known as Iglesia de San Lorenzo. Still an operating Catholic church, it is now part of the Girardota diocese, but it was not always. Created in 1680 it was apart of the Popayan diocese, until it was moved to become a part of the diocese in Bogota. 200 years later it was handed off to the Antioquia diocese. Then, as forty years passed it was transferred to the diocese of Medellin and finally in 1988 it found its home in the diocese of Girardota. These changes meant moving, reconstruction, and revival of the church, but it always remained a comforting place of worship for parishioners.

name: Passau
description: Settled since the 2nd century BC, Passau thrived thanks to its position at the confluence of 3 rivers. The city grew rich trading Bohemian salt, reaching its pinnacle as the largest bishopric in the Holy Roman Empire. Following a massive fire in the 17th century, much of the city was rebuilt in the Baroque style, and has remained essentially the same ever since. Today, the Old Town is a maze of narrow passages and alleys between beautiful buildings. Within one of the area's most striking houses you'll find the Museum of Modern Art, which hosts some unusual touring exhibitions. At the heart of the Old Town is St. Steven's Cathedral, which, along with incredibly ornate ornamentation, is home to the world's largest organ. Since the 13th century, the Veste Oberhaus fortress has watched over Passau, and now provides stupendous views of the city below, and a museum exhibiting everything from archaeological finds to medieval weaponry and Gothic painted panels in one of Europe's largest preserved castle complexes.

name: Gijon
description: Dating back to the Roman empire, Gijon remained a relatively humble fishing village until the 16th century, when the Catholic monarchs decided to transform it into a port. This point-of-access allowed the city to enjoy a boom during the Age of Enlightenment, primarily thanks to Gaspar Melchor de Jovellanos, who has an entire plaza and museum dedicated to him. The city's historic quarter starts on the hilltop and works its way down to the headland. Here, visitors can catch a glimpse at the city's Roman origins, such as the remains of ancient walls, and the hippocaust for the baths. The most elegant place in the city would have to be the Plaza del Marqués. Looking onto the marina, it is faced by the Palace of Revillagigedo and the Collegiate Church of San Juan Bautista, which now hosts modern art exhibitions.

name: Tampere
description: Located on a strip of land between two lakes, Tampere is a walkable, relaxed city with scenic views and old, industrial red-brick buildings in the city center which have been converted into restaurants, cafes, museums and shops. But it's not the history that's made Tampere the top destination amongst Finns. No, they flock here for the saunas! The sauna is so important to Finnish culture that it's inscribed on the the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List, and Tampere has over 50 public saunas to choose from! Try Rajaportti, Finland's oldest public sauna, Rauhaniemi or Suomensaaren. If you're looking for a unique sauna, Saunaravintola Kuuma is a good choice because it also has a restaurant. But prepare yourself: swimsuits are banned in the hot rooms. If you're visiting with kids, Tampere has a great amusement park, Särkänniemi. Finally, of course, let's not forget about food! After sweating it out in the sauna, head to Tampere Market Hall or Laukontori Market Square for some black sausage with lingonberry jam.

name: Lakeland, FL
description: Though it might have only been settled 1875, Lakeland, FL has quickly grown into a pleasant retreat from nearby Tampa. A mining boom town for much of its history, the city has also preserved its past, and is home to over eight historic districts! Head to the the legendary Historic and Antiques district for antiques dealers, specialty shops, art galleries, and museums lining the picturesque streets. If you're a modern architecture lover, don't miss the Florida Southern College campus to see the largest collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture. For a bit more history and culture, the Polk Museum of Art is one of the best in the state. Of course, for a city named Lakeland, the waterfront is the main attraction, and the beautiful Frances Langford Promenade delivers in spades!

name: Caceres
description: Since Pre-Roman times, Cáceres has been an important trading town and political center. Even today remnants of its Roman, Arab, Jewish and Christian inhabitantscan be found within the walled city. Access is granted through the arch of La Estrella, which was built in the 18th century to replace the earlier gate. In the mediaeval centre, the numerous palaces and noble mansions are easily identified by their family crests. Several of these ring the Plaza de Santa María square, including a 12th-century Moorish tower, which houses the Tourist Department. Perhaps the most striking is the 15th century Palace of Los Golfines de Abajo, with a striking 6th-century Renaissance façade, and Gothic, Mudejar, and Plateresque embellishments. The 15th century cathedral of Santa María has an image of 'the Black Christ' - according to legend, any who dared to look at or touch the figure would die.

name: Loches
description: The town of Loches sprung up around a 6th century monastery that was founded here by St. Ours. Towering above the town, Loches' citadel is still surrounded by its 12th century ramparts, protecting a medieval old-town filled with historic monuments, such as the Royal Lodgings' of Charles VII, where Joan of Arc came to persuade Charles to go to Reims to be crowned King of France. In the palace visitors will find the tomb of Agnes Sorrel, who was renowned for setting a trend of semi-nudity in the Court of Charles VII. Dominating the citadel is the 10th century donjon, one of the oldest in France. In the lower town are excellent example of Renaissance architecture, such as the 16th century Tour Saint-Antoine. The nearby Town Hall and Hotel Nau, with its 3 storeys of Italian loggias, are also highlights.

name: Punta del Diablo
description: This small Uruguayan village is known specifically for the white sand beaches which (during the high season) are lined with open bars and are very popular for surfing. Dune boarding is also quite a popular alternative to surfing, an activity which is similar to snowboarding but done on the sand dunes. At Los Botes (Fisherman's Beach) visitors have been known to join the locals around beach fires playing guitars and singing songs. While on the beach in the summer months, it is very common to see whales along Uruguay's shore! You can also easily make friends in Punta del Diablo, as both stray and owned dogs, who love people, freely roam the town in search of camaraderie. If you are in town early enough, you can witness the beautifully colorful sunrises which will surely start your day off right. Nearby is also the Santa Teresa fort, which can be a perfect alternative to the beach. This Portuguese fortress dates back to 1762, and was captured by the Spanish in 1793 after many hard fought battles.

name: Graaff-Reinet
description: Founded in 1786 by Cornelius Jacob van de Graaff, Graaff-Reinet is the fourth oldest town in South Africa. Built in the heart of the arid Karoo region, the flat sandy plains are broken up by the lush mountains of the surrounding Camdeboo Park. The town itself is charmingly well-preserved, its sleepy streets lined with historic Karoo-style homes. Parsonage Street, is lined with restored buildings, and ends with the Reinet House, named after the first governor's wife, Cornelia Reinet. Now a museum dedicated to its inhabitants, the garden is home to the world's largest living grape vines, which were planted in 1870. Meanwhile, on Stretch's Court, you'll find the Karoo cottages that were once the homes of labourers and emancipated slaves. Then there's the 19th century Groot Kirk, an elegant and imposing building that's downright opulent y Dutch Reform standards.

name: Dundee
description: Founded around the 11th century, Dundee thrived as a port and trade center, transitioning from wool to textiles like linen and jute, and in more recent years, microelectronics for companies like Timex. While many travellers pass the city over, it's one of Britain's cultural hubs. Dundee was the first city in Britain to be named a UNESCO City of Design, and is home to the only V&A museum outside of London (and only design museum in Britain outside the V&A). Just walking along the city's historic waterfront, you'll find the modern V&A, Industrial-era buildings, and the RS Discovery, the ship that took Robert Falcon Scott and Ernest Shackleton on their first journey to the Antarctic. Today, she's back in the city, docked near the Tay Bridge, and one of the finest attractions in Scotland. Berthed just down the river, you'll also find the HMS Unicorn - the world's 6th oldest ship still afloat.

name: Sozopol
description: Founded in the 7th century BC by Greek colonists, seaside Sozopol grew into an important trade and naval center, keeping strong ties with Greece. Known as Apollonia for the temple dedicated to Apollo, and the giant colossus of the god that once stood here, during the early years of Christianity the religion had to make a concerted effort to establish itself in the city still dedicated to the pagan god. To this end, relics of St. John the Baptist were brought to the city in an attempt to overshadow the cult of Apollo. Today, the quiet cobbled streets of the old town still harken back to the city's past, with charming wooden houses nestled next to historic monuments. In the archaeological museum, visitors will find artefacts from the prehistoric, Thracian, Greek, Roman, and Bulgarian history.

name: Ceske Budejovice
description: Founded in the 13th century by King Ottokar II of Bohemia as a way to increase the royal presence in the homeland of the influential House of Rosenberg, České Budějovice has since grown to one of the country's largest settlements. Renowned for its beer, the city was once the imperial brewery for the Holy Roman Emperor himself. For those looking to get a taste of this tradition, it's possible to tour the modern Budweiser Budvar Brewery, more commonly known as 'Czech Budweiser', though reservations are required at least 2 days in advance. The Old Town is home to one of the largest squares in Europe, measuring a full hectare. For the best view, climb the the 16th century Black Tower for sweeping views across the square. The charming Town Hall, decorated with murals and bronze gargoyles, marks the hour with a tune from it's glockenspiel-like bells, making it a great place to relax with a lager.

name: Altea
description: Likely an Iberian settlement which was supplanted by Greek colonists, the town's name likely stems from the Greek 'Althaia', which translates into "I Cure". The original site is still inhabited today in the form of a small village surrounded by cypress trees. During the 18th century, an agricultural, commercial, and fishing boom brought the population up to around 5000. This development fostered growth, and brought this city-by-the-sea to the attention of European vacationers in the 19th century. Before hitting the 6 km stretch of beach, visitors should walk through charming old town. The white-washed houses provide the perfect backdrop for flower-filled planters, and views of the cerulean sea below. Scattered through the narrow cobbled streets are bars and restaurants where you can relax with some tapas and sangria.

description: Plitvice Lakes National Park is Croatia's most popular attraction. The park covers an area of 300 square kilometers and is surrounded by dense forests. Deer, wolves, bears, owls, eagles, and rare species inhabit the woodland surroundings. Wooden plank pathways lead visitors through paths to the spectacular natural lakes and waterfalls. Veliki Splat Waterfall, the highest waterfall in Croatia (100 ft.) can also be found in the park. The waters of Plitvice Lakes bear distinctive colors, ranging from turquoise blue to gray or green. Plitvice Lakes is a must-see attraction for walkers, hikers, and nature lovers to discover the real beauty of Croatia. Please note: tickets MUST be booked at least 2 days in advance. The tickets are for a set entrance time. For more information, please visit np-plitvicka-jezera.hr/en/

name: Edzna Archaeological Zone
description: Edzná was first settled around 400 BC, though it didn't develop into a major city until the 3rd century AD. Despite being inhabited up until 1500, the reasons for its decline and abandonment remain a mystery. The impressive heart of the city is the group of religious builds at its center, dominated by a large pyramid. Known as "The Sun Point", Edzna's 5-tier pyramid is decorated with glyphs and stucco on every step, and topped with a temple that provides a view of the whole city. Next to this is the Small Acropolis, which stands only 8 meters high and is topped with three buildings. The acropoles overlook the Temple of the Masks, which is named for the two small masks depicting the Sunrise God and Sunset God on the east and west corners of its foundation. Across from the acropolis is the imposing, 135-meter-long palace, which still has four large rooms standing atop its monumental staircase.

name: Magdalena de Kino
description: Discover the magical city of Magdalena de Kino, named after the pioneering Roman Catholic missionary and explorer, Father Eusebio Francisco Kino, who left an indelible mark in the area and across the border in Arizona. Wander through the city's charming streets, where stone buildings adorned with intricate engravings narrate the history of Mexico. Visit the Temple of Santa María Magdalena, home to an image of San Francisco Xavier, an important historical figure for both Sonora and Arizona. The city boasts sites that commemorate Father Kino's legacy, including the Grave of Father Kino and the Father Kino Museum. The museum showcases a treasure trove of indigenous cultural objects, photographs, weaponry, and clothing. For those seeking a spiritual experience, the annual celebration of San Francisco Javier is a grand fiesta and religious event, during which pilgrims from far and wide gather for traditional dances, music, and regional foods as they honor this revered figure.

name: Camecuaro Lake
description: Lying in the Lago de Camécuaro National Park, Lake Camecuaro is small but packed with natural beauty. The lush vegetation and beautifully reflective waters, make this lake uniquely stunning and perfect for a relaxing afternoon. Take a colorful boat ride, or sit amongst the rooted trees that provide a cooling shade, which provides the perfect relief on a hot summer day. In the shadiest parts of the lake you can see how the beautiful blue shades of water create an almost mirror-like reflection, see if you can capture it!

name: Belgrade
description: Belgrade is the capital and largest city in Serbia. It lies at the confluence of the Sava and Danube Rivers on the Balkan peninsula. Part of former Yugoslavia, it's a capital with gritty resilience and soul. The old Belgrade Fortress, constructed by the Romans in the 6th century, is one of the world's oldest strongholds and a must-see sight. There are many cafes, restaurants, cathedrals, museums, and theaters to freely explore. Belgrade is also famous for its ample nightlife and many hidden bars and clubs. The diverse, dynamic city offers a rich history and a modern culture scene that visitors of all ages can enjoy.

name: Cuevas del Drach
description: Discover the enchanting depths of Europe's vast subterranean wonder at Cuevas del Drach, a mesmerizing cave complex nestled along the east coast near Porto Cristo. Measuring an impressive 1,200 meters in length and 25 meters in depth, the tour winds through an underground spectacle adorned with magnificent stalactites and stalagmites, illuminated to perfection to enhance your experience. The highlight of your journey awaits at an expansive cavernous lake, fittingly named after Martel, where visitors are treated to a unique classical concert. Seated aboard a boat, the musicians create a captivating symphony in this natural concert hall, adding an unforgettable auditory dimension to your subterranean adventure. Don't miss the opportunity to explore the interconnected Black Cave, White Cave, Cave of Luis Salvador, and Cave of the French, vital components of the region's rich heritage. The caves maintain a consistent temperature of around 18°C throughout the year, creating a comfortable environment for your hour-long exploration and musical interlude. Ticket prices, at €16.00 for adults and €9.00 for children (2-12 years), offer access to staggered visits to avoid overcrowding, with varying entry times depending on the season.

name: Veliko Tarnovo
description: The hilltops overlooking an idyllic river-bend have been settled since around 3,000 BC. In the 12th century, after two local brothers battled the Byzantine Empire, the establishing the Second Bulgarian Empire, and made Veliko Tarnovo its capital. Today, visitors can still walk along the medieval parapets of Tsaravets Fortress to the top of the hill, where they are rewarded with stunning views of the city and its river-bend, and modernist murals in the Church of the Ascension. A walk through the Old Town fully immerses visitors in the town's rich history, exemplified by the 19th century Bulgarian Revivalist architecture. The city's Archaeological Museum houses the region's history from prehistoric times through the Middle Ages, including one of the world's oldest gold treasures, which dates from the 4th millennium BC.

name: Bautzen
description: Perched on a hilltop overlooking the Spree River, Bautzen is permanently posing for pictures and is home to some spectacular architecture, including The Reichenturm, one of the steepest leaning towers north of the Alps. Behind its charming façade, Bautzen offers a rich history for those who desire to delve deeper. The first written evidence of the town dates back to 1002AD, and the first recorded battle only 13 years later, which kicked-off a long history of military importance, including battles in the Napoleonic Wars and World War II. During Nazi occupation Bautzen housed a subcamp of the Groß-Rosen concentration camp, and after the division of Germany, was infamous throughout East German for its penitentiaries. Bautzen I was an official prison, nicknamed Gelbes Elend ("Yellow Misery"), whereas the secret Bautzen II was used for prisoners of conscience. Today, Bautzen I is still in use, and Bautzen II serves as a memorial.

name: Chordeleg
description: For those who enjoy immaculate, quaint towns to escape from the hustle and bustle of the city, Chordeleg is the place for you. This charming town is famous for its jewelry production, a nod to which you can see in the giant earrings hanging from the street lamp posts. The craftsmen of Chordeleg are specifically skilled in filigree, the art of rolling silver into a wire-thin strand and manipulating each piece by twisting it into a complex design. The result is a beautiful, delicate piece of jewellery, be it earrings, rings, a necklace or other decorative accessories. The streets lining the town square are filled with silver stores run by local artisans, where you can often see them crafting their goods for sale while you shop. The prices are great and bartering is expected, so don't be afraid to ask for a bargain!

name: Tivat
description: This stunning waterfront development project opened in 2009 on the coast of Tivat, Montenegro. It lies in the Bay of Kotor, the deepest natural harbor in southern Europe. The glamorous marina houses tremendous yachts and a year-round village. The walled city of churches, alleys, and squares features over 50 retail stores, fancy boutiques, restaurants, bars, and cafes for the public to enjoy. A destination in itself, Porto Montenegro is becoming one of the up-and-coming hot spots in Montenegro.

name: Saint Jovan Bigorski Monastery
description: Founded in the 11th century, the Saint Jovan Bigorski Monastery was destroyed, rebuilt, and renovated several times over its 1000 year history. Today, this peaceful respite still houses a monastic community, who welcome visitors to enjoy their hospitality, and their monastery's rich heritage. The monastery church, filled with colorful frescoes, is dominated by a 19th century wooden iconostasis. Intricately carved by local artist artists, it depicts over 700 tiny figures and is considered one of the finest in the world. In the monastery reliquary, visitors will find not only the forearm of St. John, but also relics from several saints, including Lazarus of Bethany, Saint Nicholas, and Saint Barbara, and part of the Holy Cross. The monastery also houses the miraculous 11th century icon of St. John, around which it was founded.

name: Ramon Lopez Velarde House & Interactive Museum
address.addr1: Museo Interactivo Casa Ramón López Velarde
address.city: Ramon Lopez Velarde House & Interactive Museum
description: Ramón López Velarde is celebrated for his renowned contributions to Mexican literature at The Ramón López Velarde House & Interactive Museum. The museum is located in the very house where the writer was born and spent his early years, making for an authentic and moving experience. Move through the large living room, kitchen, and patio, past furniture that recreates the poet's room, along with photographs of his family and writings of the poet. A library with texts used by López Velarde when he studied law is also contained within the museum. Sensors that activate narrations, smells, sound, and audiovisual makes the museum a more immersive experience for visitors. The Ramón López Velarde House & Interactive Museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10AM to 5PM, with an admission fee of USD $1. Photo by Danaeef1294, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Arequipa
description: Located in a lush valley that has been inhabited since the days of nomadic hunter-gatherers, the city of Arequipa was founded by the Spanish in 1540. Thanks to its strategic location on a trade route, Arequipa grew to become the region's commercial and political center, which in turn resulted in a wealth of beautiful buildings. The sprawling historic center is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site for its beautiful Baroque monuments, and the hundreds of traditional houses, which still lie on the original Spanish layout. Architectural highlights include the massive the vast Cathedral Basilica of Arequipa backed by El Misti, and the sprawling Monasterio de Santa Catalina. Taking up a whole city block, this multi-colored monastery is one of the country's most captivating colonial buildings. To delve even deeper into the area's history, head to the Museo Santuarios Andinos, to learn about the mummy known as the "Inca Ice Maiden".

name: Oslob
description: For years, the little town of Oslob was pretty much off the radar of tourists. But centuries ago it was an important Spanish outpost. Today, the Municipal Heritage Park preserves the remains of a late-18th century watchtower, and the unfinished walls of what would have been a barracks. These marshal reminders flank the picturesque Church of the Immaculate Conception. Constructed from cut coral stone between 1830 and 1848, the church interior was gutted by a fire in 2008, though its icons were miraculously spared. While the Heritage Park offers some fascinating insights into the town's past, Oslob has been attracting visitors from around the world for a very different reason - swimming with whale sharks! About 10 kilometers away, the fishermen of Tan‑awan hand-feed these gentle giants to keep them coming back for tourists. For early-risers (it's best to arrive at 11AM), seeing the world's largest fish up close is surely an unmissable experience.

name: Loviisa
description: When Loviisa was founded in 1745, it was a fortress town on the Russian border, guarded by not one, but two bastions. Over the years, it's also been known as a spa town, and in the 20th century, home to Finland's first nuclear power plant. Despite its more recent industrial development, Loviisa's Old Town still epitomizes the charm of rural Finland. The streets are still lined with painted wood houses, many of which open their doors to guests during the "Historical Houses of Loviisa" event in August. The 17th century annex of Degerby Farm, which are some of the oldest wooden buildings in Finland are a particular highlight. Then there's the charming red brick church, and the Commandant's House museum. You can also walk the ruins of the Loviisa fortress, or take a ferry (15EUR return ticket) to Svartholma fortress. If you need to stretch your legs further, follow the Myllyharju nature trail for some breathtaking views of the Gulf of Finland.

name: Shuakhevi
description: Nestled in the mountainous republic of Ajara, the quaint town of Shuakhevi is one of Georgia's many hidden gems waiting to be discovered. Veiled amidst the mountains, the Shuakhevi area is home to the remnants of a medieval castle and arched bridges, steeped in history and mystery. Not far from the town, the Black Lake offers a serene and picturesque retreat. The surrounding wilderness is an embodiment of Georgian nature at its finest, hosting an array of wildlife including deer, wild boar, hedgehogs, hares, foxes, bears, badgers, and numerous bird species. The region is recognized for its tobacco cultivation, adding to its rich, local heritage. However, the true stars of Shuakhevi are its friendly inhabitants and the organic local cuisine, both of which you won't want to miss during your visit.

name: Beppu
description: Beppu, located in Ōita Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, Japan, is renowned as the king of hot springs. Nestled amid mountains and highlands, the city's western region boasts scenic spots such as the Yufugawa Canyon and Aso Kujū National Park. Beppu is most famous for its geothermal wonders: it houses eight major geothermal hot spots, often dubbed the "eight hells of Beppu". These springs are too hot for bathing, but the surrounding facilities have earned the nickname 'Samurai Spa'. Known as 'onsen' in Japanese, each of these hot spring stations offers modern pools, as well as traditional ryokan accommodations with excellent bathing facilities. Beppu doesn't stop at typical hot springs; it also provides sand and foot baths. A notable spot is the "Beppu Kaihin Sunayu, Ashiyu" or "Beppu marine beach sand bath and foot bath". Beyond its baths, Beppu has a rich history in bamboo crafts, making them a perfect souvenir from the city.

name: Bernal
description: Bernal was founded in the 1642 a stones throw away from the towering rock monolith known as the Peña de Bernal. Decidedly provincial, the quiet town is centered around the Moorish influenced Castillo, around which are numerous charming churches and colorful buildings. The streets are an enchanting place to wander, filled with photo ops and delicious street food, sweet stores, and artisanal workshops, but the main draw is the Peña. At over 1000 feet tall, it's the 3rd largest rock monolith in the world, which locals say has mystical powers that imbue them with extra longevity (the town is rumored to be home to more centenarians than anywhere else in Mexico). Nature and adventure lovers can take the demanding hike to the top, or sign up for an adrenaline-inducing climbing and rappelling session (add another 90-120 minutes to your stop if you'd like to summit the Peña de Bernal).

name: Bardejov
description: Bardejov has one of the most beautifully preserved town centers in the country with the cobbled main square and Baroque buildings. Standing alone in the middle of the square is the Old Town Hall, which contains the town museum. This is where visitors can learn more of the town's history and check out the visual evidence of how little the town square has changed over the last 100 years. Visitors will be surprised to discover that for an attractive town with such a whimsical ambience, Bardejov has quiet a dark side to its history. However, the dominant building in the square is the Church of St. Egidus, which with its Gothic-revival interior, huge main altar and eleven smaller winged altars on either side of the highly detailed pews makes it difficult to know what aspect to focus on first. For amazing views of the town then the climb up the spiral staircase to the top of the tower is more than worth the effort.

name: Aoraki Mount Cook Village
description: At the end of a stunning drive up a valley and past the turquoise waters of Lake Pukaki is the awe-inspiring Aoraki Mount Cook National Park. There are many amazing walks from Mount Cook Village and not all of them require huge amounts of fitness. For an easy route take the track to Tasman Lake, which is constantly full of mini icebergs, or the steeper Hooker Valley track, which takes you past the eponymous lake - both of which will take you to the foot of Mount Cook itself. Mount Cook is where the first man to conquer Everest, Sir Edmund Hillary, trained for his expedition. A short but sharp climb up to Red Tarns makes for a great view over the village, while a climb up the Mueller Hut Route, as far as Sealy Tarns Viewpoint, offers unsurpassed views towards Mount Sefton and it's constantly creaking glaciers.

name: Regensburg
description: Dating back to pre-Roman times, Regensburg was one of the most important cities in the region for centuries, sitting on key trade routes, and serving as the starting point of Christianization of the Czechs. Reminders of the city's medieval golden days abound in the UNESCO-listed Old Town. Covering nearly 200 hectares and 1500 buildings, the historic city center is reached by crossing the 13th century stone bridge that made Regensburg wealthy. Near the foot of the bridge you'll find one of the city's most unassuming but important landmarks: the Sausage Kitchen, which has been serving its signature wursts and mustard since 1146. Nearby, St. Peter's Cathedral is considered the premier Gothic monument in Bavaria, famed for both its architecture and the heavenly voices of its Boys' Choir. Meander through the picturesque Old Town for a few minutes, and you'll reach the Thurn und Taxis Castle. A 13th century Benedictine monastery that was converted into a residential palace, it's bigger than Buckingham Palace, and offers a unique blend of architectural styles, such as the 11th century Basilica with a lavish Rococo makeover.

name: Termoli
description: This idyllic stretch of coast has been settled since pre-historic times, and played host to Roman villas, but the first documentation of the city standing today came in the 10th century. For centuries, the town stayed ensconced within its fortified walls. Though it began to decay, it wasn't until 1770 that the Kings of Naples gave the villagers permission to 1770. Today, the historic old town has been well restored with many houses painted in pleasant pastels. Home to many small squares and tiny alleys, including one of the narrowest in Europe, the central square is home to a 12th century cathedral, which houses the relics of the two city's patron saints.Part of an earlier basilica from the 11th century has been found under the edifice.The promontory's prominent castle was erected in the 11th century with renovations made under the rule of Frederick II.

name: Calixtlahuaca
description: Regularly passed up by tourists, the ruins of the ancient city of Calixtlahuaca are a remarkable demonstration of early life in the region that are sure to please history buffs and curious learners alike. Temples, private quarters and various outposts were constructed and across the valley floor but subsequently destroyed and rebuilt by Aztec forces. Locals were forced to abandon their homes and move elsewhere. Today, visitors can see what remains of communities that have long since left. Be sure to check out Building 3 which is said to be a temple created by the Serpent Cult of Calixtlahuaca. Be sure to double-check the opening hours before your visit so you can get the most out of your visit.

name: Six Flags Great Adventure
description: Are you ready for your Six Flags Great Adventure?! The New Jersey branch of one of America's best-known amusement park chains promises an adventure for the whole family! Packed with thrilling roller coasters, adrenaline junkies will feel right at home. Batman, Green Lantern, the Justice League and more will take you on exhilarating rides at mind-boggling speeds if you dare, while Bugs Bunny, Daffy and Porky Pig come to the little ones' rescue with far more subdued experiences. Then go wild on a drive through the wild safari to see over 1,200 animals including elephants, giraffes and lions. They even have a venue putting on live shows! And with plenty of restaurants and casual dining available, you won't go hungry - maybe save your appetite for after the rides, though!

name: Cascavel
description: Nestled in the heart of Paraná, Brazil, Cascavel beckons with its modern charm and meticulously planned development. Discover the city's heartbeat at Cascavel's Lake, a 5-kilometer haven for a healthy lifestyle. Adorned with wild animals like monkeys, birds, and the iconic capybaras, this urban oasis offers a serene escape. The old church on the lake's edge, while not open for visitation, adds historical charm to this natural sanctuary. Stroll through the city's heart at Avenida Brasil, where popular and upscale stores converge. The renovated Calçadão encapsulates the essence of Cascavel, featuring landmarks like Catedral Nossa Senhora Aparecida and the Central Park Towers. Immerse yourself in the spiritual ambiance of the city's largest Catholic Temple. The modern architectural marvel of Nossa Senhora Aparecida Cathedral, with its colossal cross sculpture and golden altar, invites contemplation and awe.

name: Trinidad
description: Trinidad was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in 1514 as the Spanish crown's third village in Cuba. Through the 18th and 19th centuries it was an important center for the sugar trade, and even today, its economy still relies on agriculture, though of a more combustible leafy variety. You'll want to start your visit at the Plaza Mayor, the heart of the city and where the restoration that earned Trinidad its UNESCO status began. Here, you'll find not just the obligatory church, but also colonial mansions (there are 50 around town!) that have been transformed into museums. Then set off down the cobbled streets, where colorful houses offer plenty of photo opportunities. Just a few blocks from the Plaza Mayor, the Palacio Cantero is now home to the Municipal History Museum, displaying Cuba's finest collection of colonial furniture.

name: Cesis
description: In the early 13th century, German crusaders known as the Livonian Brothers of the Sword blazed a trail into pagan Latvia and built a hilltop fort as their stronghold. Shortly after, a marketplace and church were built, creating the foundations of Cesis. Today, the cobbled streets and historic buildings make the town one of the cutest in the country, which is presided over by the 12th century St. John's Church - one of Latvia's oldest and largest medieval monuments. At the heart of the village visitors will still find the ruins of the medieval castle, which is now the centerpiece of the town's beautiful park. In the 18th century 'New Castle', visitors can admire elegant rooms while learning about the town's history.

name: Lublin
description: For centuries Lublin was a leading centre of Jewish scholarship in Poland, but suffered greatly under the Nazi regime. Due to its large and noticeable Jewish population, Lublin became a target of severe Nazi repressions and Jewish residents were forcibly removed to Lublin Ghetto, one mile outside the city. The majority of the ghetto inmates were deported to the Bełżec extermination camp and very few survived the war. Despite such atrocities, architecturally Lublin survived the war mostly intact meaning it can now boast one of the most authentic and ornamental old towns in Poland. A highlight of the old town is Lublin Castle; one oldest and best preserved Royal residencies. The castle now houses the Lublin Museum but its attractive façade hides a dark past. Used as a prison from 1831 to 1954, inmates were often Polish Resistance fighters.

name: Nuoro
description: Nuoro is the proud, rugged heart of Sardinia. In fact, the region is called "Barbagia" because when the local "barbarians" forced back the Romans. This remote hilltop town was most noted for banditry until the 19th century when several renowned artists, including poet Sebastiano Satta, novelist Salvatore Satta, sculptor Francesco Ciusa and Nobel Prize-winning author Grazia Deledda were born here. Thanks to these personalities, Nuoro boasts some of the island's most important museums, like the Museo MAN, Sardinia's best modern art museum, the Museo Cuisa, as well as ethnographic and archaeological museums detailing the region's history. Or you can just wander the Rione Santu Predu, the historic artist's district, which still looks much as it did in the 19th century. No matter what, try to track down su filindeu, a pasta half as thick as angel hair that only two women know how to make. It's sometimes available at Al Ciusa and Il Refugio.

name: Chillan
description: Chillán can trace its roots back to 1580 when it was founded by the conquistador Martín Ruiz de Gamboa. But a slew of catastrophic earthquakes, including one in 2010, leveld most of the city's historic monuments. What did endure, however, was trade. Historically Chillán was an important marketplace where Mapuches, Pehuenches, Mestizos, and Criollos brought their goods, and today, that tradition lives on in the Feria de Chillán. In this sprawling market, you'll find everything from huaso clothing, knitwear and blankets, baskets, pottery, and even caged birds and fruit and vegetables. After you've found yourself a good souvenir (or maybe just a Chilean sausage), head to Chillán's other most noteworthy landmark: its modernist cathedral. Built in the 1940s after the original cathedral was destroyed by the great earthquake of 1939, this half-cylinder with its 10 arches was designed to represent hands in prayer.

name: STEAM Museum of the Great Western Railway

address.city: STEAM Museum of the Great Western Railway
description: The STEAM Museum of the Great Western Railway is dedicated to what was the world's most advanced railway system when it opened in 1835. The museum is housed in part of the old Swindon Works, which produced the train cars for the GWR, and was one of the largest in the world during its prime. Here visitors won't just see historic locomotives, but learn about the people who built, operated, and travelled the Great Western Railway through hands on activities - visitors can drive a train simulator or operate the rail switches. Oftentimes there are former railway employees on hand to offer some personal insights into the exhibits! For more information, please visit steam-museum.org.uk Photo by Murgatroyd49 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Murgatroyd49) under CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Sizergh Castle
description: Home to the Strickland family since the 13th century, Sizergh Castle has gradually been expanded into a romantic mansion. While the oldest part of the castle is a 14th century Solar Tower, it's the intricate Elizabethan woodwork that steals the show. Along with having some of the country's most ornate oak overmantels, and a unique collection of portraits, the castle's distinctive Inlaid Chamber entices visitors up four flights of stairs to behold stunning panels inlaid with English Poplar and "Bog" Oak, and the original state bed and stained glass. For those with mobility issues, a replica of the panel is displayed on the ground floor. In the beautiful grounds surrounding the manor you'll find quiet walking trails, colorful wildflowers, wonderful water gardens, and the National Trust's largest limestone rock garden. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/sizergh

name: Quevedo
description: An important trade and agricultural centre, Quevedo is the hub of Ecuador with every major highway, including the Pan-American, passing through it. The city has a strong artistic and cultural feel to it, and this is evident in Central Park, a blend of modern architectural styles and natural features. By the river the attractive Quevedo Boardwalk leads to the Quevedo Bridge, which is impressively lit-up in blue at night, and the Crystal Palace where exhibitions are shown year round. The 8 hectare Quevedo Zoo is highly regarded and a great source of natural, cultural, and educational recreation. Quevedo's biggest pull is it's amazing food culture. The city is blessed with an abundance of top-class restaurants offering quality dining experiences. Although international cuisine is readily available, trying some of the local meal choices is a must - liver steak, fish buns, bocaschico stew and encebollado - a fish stew served with banana chips are all menu items that should be experienced.

name: Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve
description: The Monarch butterfly congregates in the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, 100 km north-west of Mexico City. They settle in clusters on the branches of oyamel fir trees, arriving in early November as they flee the winter cold of North America. A 45 minute steep hike from Santuario Rosario sees you arrive at the viewing point, at an altitude of over 3,000 metres. From afar it's easy to mistake the trees as rotting, covered in old, dead leaves. Look a little closer and you'll see these are sleeping butterflies, nestled together with closed wings exposing a greyish colour as they weigh down and bend the branches they cling to. As the sun shines the butterflies begin to fly, revealing the distinctive bright orange and black Monarch pattern as they spread their wings and flutter in crowds of thousands in the sky. The beating of their wings in such volume mimics the sound of gently falling rain. An impressive sight not to be missed!

name: Sankt Johann im Pongau
description: Its picturesque setting allows beautiful views of the surrounding mountains and the Salzach Valley, and many peaceful strolls can be had along various trails around the town. The Liechtensteinklamm, a narrow gorge, is the star natural attraction of the area. Around 4 kilometres long and around 300 metres deep, the gorge is comfortably accessible by wooden walkways allowing you to immerse yorself in this natural wonder formed by mountain streams over thousands of years. The town itself has no lack of man-made attractions. The Pongauer Dom or Cathedral, named in honour of St. John the Baptist, is one of the most significant Gothic churches in Austria. The original church was destroyed in the town fire of 1855 but has been rebuilt. This two-spired parish church looks out majestically over the valley, its interior equally majestic with wooden Gothic sculptures and a number of Late-Gothic figures among Neo-Gothic altars.

name: Cienfuegos
description: Founded by the French in 1819 as a resort town, Cienfuegos is Cuba's newest, and arguably most unique city. The city center was arranged in a perfect grid of streets and avenues, with most of the buildings done up in the Neoclassical style. This clean, modern, and spacious atmosphere earned Cienfuegos the nickname "The Pearl of the South", as well as recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Wandering the easy-to-navigate downtown, you'll find plenty of elegant buildings to admire, like the Cienfuegos Cathedral, Government Palace, and Ferrer Palace. Head down to Punta Gorda to walk along the waterfront boulevard lined with pretty houses and plenty of casa particulares if you need a hearty home cooked meal. Just outside of town, the 97 hectare botanical gardens are home to over 2000 species of plants and a pleasant place to stroll, while the Jagua Fort predates Cienfuego and is an excellent example of Spanish military architecture.

name: Dana Village
description: Perched on the edge of a large canyon, the little town of Dana is a well-preserved slice of 19th century life. While the historic buildings and narrow alleys are charming, the real draw here is the Dana Biosphere Reserve, which covers 308 square kilometres, and is the largest in the country. Ranging in altitude from 1700m near Dana, to 50m below sea level in Wadi Araba, the biosphere is home to 600 species of plant, 180 species of bird, and over 45 mammal species - including 25 endangered. The reserve is lined with hiking trails, offering everything from a short jaunt to a full-day trek and a variety of difficulty levels (though many require a guide to be arranged in advance). If you don't feel like working up a sweat, you can also relax at the viewpoint near the village and just admire the amazing scenery.

name: Essaouira
description: As one of the best anchorages on Morocco's Atlantic Coast, Essaouira has served as a port since prehistory. The current city, however, was built in the 18th century by Mohammed III, who brought in several European architects. Today, the medina is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its well-preserved blend of European and Moroccan architecture, particularly the Vauban-inspired sea-fort. Walking the canon-lined ramparts, you are treated to both rich history and unparalleled views of the Atlantic. While you're still by the sea, be sure to stop by the fishing port where you'll find the town's famed 'blue boats' and a market where you can enjoy fresh-caught fish grilled right in front of you. In the winding alleys of the medina, you'll see traditional Moroccan architecture, complete with colorful doors and windows. What sets Essaouira apart is its old Jewish quarter - a crumbling reminder that nearly half the city was Jewish at one point.

name: Antwerp
description: Settled since around the 5th century, Antwerp has had its fair share of ups and downs, thanks in large part to its important port. Napoleon had hoped to make it the finest in Europe, while during World War II, the Germans fired more V-2 rockets at it than every other target combined. In 1609 Rubens established his atelier in the city, which now exhibits his work. Along with the Rubens Antwerp's old town is filled with centuries of historic architecture - from the Medieval castle to the Gothic cathedral to Baroque palaces all within walking distance of each other. Visitors can also take a trip to the city's hip side: made a fashion capital by a group of local designers in the 80s, visitors can learn about Antwerp's fashion heritage at MoMu. Scattered throughout the city are bold works of modern architecture, such as the Museum by the Stream, which revitalized the dockside area.

name: Santiago
description: Santiago was founded as a small rural settlement in the 16th century. In the past few decades, the city's convenient location halfway between Panama City and the Costa Rican border has allowed it to flourish as a trade and commerce hub. For travellers, this makes it a great waypoint to stop, stretch your legs, and recharge at one of the local restaurants. While Santiago doesn't have much in the way of monuments, its historic cathedral is worth a visit.

name: Walt Disney World Resort
description: Walt Disney World has served over fifty years of fantasy, fun, and adventure, cementing itself as one of the most beloved amusement parks on the planet. With over 25,000 acres of water parks, hotels, golf courses, resorts, rides, and even a shopping centre, Disney World is nothing short of a memory-maker for you and your family. Go to the Magic Kingdom, where you can get the original Disney experience. For nature-filled fun, the Animal Kingdom is a great place to put your explorer hats on, and observe the hundreds of live animals that cavort the grounds. For thrill-seekers, the Twilight Zone Tower of Terror is sure to have your heart skip a beat. Sit (or slide) back and relax, at Disney's Blizzard Beach, or travel the world, and experience the future at Epcot.

name: Cachi
description: Thanks to its signature white buildings, Cachi is without a doubt one of the most recognizable places in Argentina. Even getting to the village is an adventure in itself, due to the epic narrow serpentine road which lies through a mountain range – a job for experienced drivers only. Once you arrive in Cachi, you won't want to miss exploring its streets to gaze on the well-preserved colonial architecture, and walking around the town's main square, Plaza 9 De Julio. Cachi is home to one of the best archeological museums in the country, Museo Pío Pablo Díaz, where visitors can learn about the pre-Hispanic history of the region (open every day except Monday, and the entrance fee is only about 0,5 EUR, descriptions are comprehensive but in Spanish only so it is recommended to take a tour; it is recommended to verify opening hours in advance). Next, explore the Saint Joseph Church, built in the mid-18th century (pay attention to the ceilings and confessional, built with the wood of the Cordon cactus). Lastly, expand your palette and try goat stew (or llama stew, if you're brave enough) and, of course, empanadas, paired with a glass of wine. Important note: it is not recommended to visit Cachi during bad weather, especially during or right after heavy rain.

name: Pontevedra
description: In the 1500s, Pontevedra was the capital of Galicia, and an important port. In fact, Christopher Columbus' flagship was built here, and many locals believe Columbus was actually a Pontevedran nobleman who faked his own death and took on a new identity. Many of the city's squares and and streets in are named after traditional trades, such as the 'Praza da Leña', or 'firewood square'. Here visitors will find a classic 'cruceiro', elegant houses with granite arches, and the Pontevedra Museum. The 18th century Peregrina Chapel may not be the city's oldest church, but this baroque church has an unusual rounded façade and is an important part of the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. In a region famous for its seafood, it would a shame not to take a siesta and sample the mouth-watering offerings from a local eatery or the famous food market.

name: Reindeer of La Cruz
description: No one knows where it came from - a larger-than-life sculpture of a reindeer, made of sticks and twigs, hanging out on the Mexican coast. Was it crafted by a local artist looking for a festive twist to his locale? Or perhaps an homesick expatriate from the cold, snowy North? Whatever the reason, the marina of La Cruz is blessed each day by this quirky homage to the holidays. The sculpture is mounted on wheels, so often it can be found in different locations along the marina's beach front. What better opportunity to stretch your legs than with a stroll along the lovely marina and a taste of local public artwork?

name: Otuzco
description: Settled since the dawn of civilization, Otuzco has seen indigenous culture blend with Spanish, making for a predominantly mestizo population in this city. Backed by the soaring Andes, the narrow streets are lined with elevated houses with wide doors and tiled roofs; the city square dominated by a distinctive Baroque cathedral constructed from grey volcanic stone. The city is known as Peru's Faith Capital, and every December, thousands of pilgrims walk the 73km from Trujillo, ascending from sea level to Otuzco's 2641m altitude to pray to the Virgen de la Puerta in a week-long festival.

name: Viseu
description: High in the Beira Alta hills, Viseu is a medieval city that's been an important crossroads since Roman times. In fact, the Romans had a 40 square hectare compound in the city to house their garrison. The cathedral at the town's apex dates back to the 13th century, though restoration and remodeling blended the architectural styles, putting Medieval alongside Manueline and Baroque. Next to the cathedral, is the Grão Vasco Museum, which showcases the works of Vasco Fernandes, Portugal's finest Renaissance painter as well as a collection of carved, painted baroque figurines and other religious objects. The square at the heart of the historical city centre is lined with cafés and restaurants and backed by the cathedral walls - a perfect place to relax and enjoy the city's signature Dão wine.

name: Ollantaytambo
description: Formerly the Incan Emperor's royal estate, Ollantaytambo is probably the longest continuously inhabited settlement in South America. Located in the Sacred Valley, this is the only place where the Incas gained victory against the Spanish conquistadors, albeit briefly. Still to this day there are a scattering of original Incan houses, as well as aqueducts from this time. The old town in particular is unique in Preu, built over 500 years ago and inhabited to this day by Incas. The jewel in the valley is certainly the ruins of the temple/fortress of Ollantaytambo. Books or personal guides are available in the market below and both will give you a good overview of the architectural and religious significance of each structure. The Temple of the Sun is particularly impressive with it's 50-ton monoliths and sun calendars. The view of the town and the valley from the ruins is especially stunning.

name: Monument Valley, AZ
description: Once upon a time, Monument Valley was a flat basin, but over the past 50 million years, wind and water have peeled away the layers of earth, revealing the dramatic rock formations seen today. Since first being featured on film in the 1930s, they've come to be the collective image of the American Southwest in pop culture. You can easily view the world-famous panorama of the Mitten Buttes and Merrick Butte from the Visitor's Center, but it's well worth joining a guided tour from Navajo tour operators to see these mythical formations up close. Monument Valley is no less stunning at night, when they're illuminated by countless stars and the pastel swirl of the Milky Way. About one mile from the visitor center you'll find a collective of Navajo vendors selling arts, crafts, native food, and souvenirs at roadside stands. You can purchase your admission or book a tour at https://navajonationparks.org/tribal-parks/monument-valley/
