name: Dresden
description: Viewed from the Elbe, Dresden's skyline is dominated by the spires, domes, and towers of the city's stately buildings. This picturesque view makes it difficult to imagine the horrors of the firestorm that engulfed Dresden when close to four tons of bombs were dropped on it. Although many of the buildings were destroyed, their treasures had been hidden away during the war, meaning they can be viewed today in the rebuilt city, which now stands as a tribute to peace and reconciliation. Modern day Dresden is lush and green, rich in culture, art and history. It's a paradise for culture vultures who can explore the museums and palaces, while architecture buffs can marvel at the variety of architecture on display.

name: Banyalbufar
description: Nestled amid the majestic peaks of the Tramuntana mountain range, Banyalbufar emerges as a hidden gem on Mallorca's western coastline. Scattered farms and vineyards ascend the surrounding peaks, creating a picturesque landscape that captivates travelers seeking the island's hidden treasures. As you wind through the village streets and historic agricultural systems, the allure of Banyalbufar unfolds. The working fishing port of Es Port de Canonge beckons, offering a glimpse into local maritime life, while nearby coves and beaches, including Cala Banyalbufar, Es Corral Fals, and Son Bunyola, provide tranquil spots for sunbathing and swimming. The journey to Banyalbufar itself is a visual feast, with breathtaking views along winding roads that cascade down to the coast, revealing mountain peaks and dramatic rock formations. Explore the charming town center, discover a pretty waterfall, and marvel at the historic Torre de Ses Animes, a tower built in the 16th century to guard against pirate attacks. For outdoor enthusiasts, well-marked hiking routes lead from the village to the fishing port of Es Port de Canoge, offering a perfect blend of nature and history. The area's appeal extends to food and wine lovers, who can savor local delights at shops, vineyards, and restaurants.

name: Onomichi
description: Onomichi is a dreamy coastal town that overlooks the Seto Inland Sea, located in Hiroshima Prefecture. Serving as a port in the Middle Ages and facilitating foreign trade, these days Onomichi attracts visitors with its scenic slopes, where many of the town's attractions are situated. For example, Onomichi's Temple Walk takes visitors up and down the slopes as it leads past the route's 25 temples. Onomichi is also the starting point of the Shimanami Kaido, Japan's most famous cycling route. Several renowned Japanese writers were born here, and the town honors them with the Path of Literature. Due to the town's unique geography, it is often used as a filming location for movies. Japanese cinema enthusiasts might recognize Onomichi from a film or two! Lastly, don't forget to try the local varieties of ramen and okonomiyaki at one of the town's excellent izakayas.

name: El Quelite
description: Stepping into El Quelite feels like stepping back in time, as cobblestone streets resound with the rhythmic clop-clop of horses' hooves instead of the rumble of cars. Houses and buildings are adorned in tropical colors of azure, ochre and coral, while vibrant hibiscus and bougainvillea add bursts of color and cacti gracefully emerge from terracotta rooftops. Beyond the welcome arch, a sculpture of a man skillfully balancing a solid rubber ball on his hip pays homage to the ancient game of Ulama, which has been played in the region since 1000 BC. Anchoring El Quelite is the 19th-century Cathedral of Our Lady of Guadalupe and its surrounding plaza of shady respite, where children play games and adults engage in leisurely conversations. Head down the main street to explore colorful shops and galleries brimming with clothing, art, shoes, local candies and pastries, then take a short uphill walk to the Capilla a San Judas Tadeo chapel for stunning panoramic views of the town.

name: Napier
description: After much of the area was leveled in the 1931 Hawke's Bay earthquake, the town of Napier was quickly restored and buildings were erected in the popular Art Deco style. Today, visitors can meander the streets and take in the sights in one of the best-preserved Art Deco towns in the world. Don't miss the Art Deco Festival if you're travelling through the area in February. Take a guided walking tour any day of the year (except Christmas Day)! After gazing up at the exemplary edifices, look down on the city from the city's Viewing Platform. Stay on level ground and snap a photo in front of one of the many murals painted on the sea walls surrounding the city. Before leaving, make sure to visit one of the most photographed statues in the country: Pania of the Reef on the Marine Parade.

name: Mestia
description: Mestia, a picturesque village in Georgia's Upper Svaneti region, is one of the most beautiful locations amidst the majesty of the Caucasus Mountains. Enveloped by soaring, snow-dusted peaks, Mestia offers outdoor enthusiasts a myriad of exhilarating hiking routes, premier skiing resorts, and just great views to enjoy. As a well-facilitated tourist destination, Mestia ensures your comfort while immersing you in its authenticity. Many buildings in Mestia maintained their original design, especially the Svan towers. These towering stone structures, built by the indigenous Svan people, served as fortresses against invaders since the 9th century. While nature is the show-stopper with its stunning landscapes, there's more to discover: you can opt to visit the old town, where each cobblestone street tells a tale, or sit down to enjoy hearty Georgian food. Either way, this enchanting destination is trusted by thousands of visitors exploring what the Svaneti region has to offer.

name: Coronel Oviedo
description: Founded as a quiet agricultural community in the 18th century, Coronel Oviedo has been discovering new life as a center for the arts, film and music. In the early 2000s, the growing city increased its arts programs for the children, and this initiative has since attracted creatives from around the country. It's now a hub for local filmmakers who use the city's unassuming facades as the backdrop for their contemporary stories. The city also has had an increased focus on music with a philharmonic orchestra located in the city along with traditional music and folkloric ballet. Its central location allows the city to take influences from all corners of the country, further influencing its rising status. Take advantage of its cultural offerings and visit its museums, theatres, concert halls and public spaces to get a slice of authentic Paraguayan life.

name: Kong Lor Cave
description: The Kong Lor Cave is one of Southeast Asia's geological wonders - a 7 kilometer long subterranean network formed by the Nam Hin Bun River cutting its way through an entire mountain. Local villagers still use the cave as a shortcut when transporting goods, and believe the emerald-green pool in one of the recesses is sacred. Visitors can enjoy a ride through the tunnels, some of which are narrow passages, some towering chambers, with a local boatman. Along the way, they often pull ashore, giving the opportunity to spelunk on foot.

name: Lampang
description: Founded by the Mon in the 7th century, Lampang is known throughout Thailand for its charm. Nicknamed 'the horse carriage city', Lampang is the only city in Thailand that still offers horse carriage rides, making for a singular way to tour the city. However, many of Lampang's landmark's are best experienced up close. Wat Phra Kaeo Don Tao is one of the city's dearest temples - once home to the Emerald Buddha, visitors will still find plenty of treasures here, including an impressive chedi, a reclining Buddha statue, and a museum of Lanna-era relics and artifacts. At Wat Phra Chedi Sao Lang you'll find 20 chedi in its courtyard, and a 15th-century solid gold Buddha image in the temple. If you get hungry, be sure to stop to try the delicious, traditional Lanna food, and definitely make time to experience the Walking Street Market if your in town on a weekend!

name: Xabia
description: Xàbia, known as Jávea in Spanish, occupies a spectacular Mediterranean setting in the Marina Alta comarca of Alicante province. This coastal town attracts Spanish and European visitors who appreciate its position between two protective rocky headlands. They create a natural harbor and a diverse landscape. The central Platja de L'arenal provides classic beach resort amenities with its sandy shoreline attracting sunbathers and surfers. The adjacent promenade offers numerous shops, bars, restaurants, and ice cream vendors. If you like hiking, the Montgó mountain provides cooler weather above the coastal heat. Port de Xàbia presents a contrasting experience with its network of narrow traditional streets and wilder coastline character, particularly appealing during quieter morning hours.

name: Athens
description: A Mediterranean Megalopolis, Greece's Capital is one of the world's oldest cities and a testament to the Ancient Greeks. Athens was idolized by Romans, Byzantines, and Ottomans alike; follow in their footsteps, into this labyrinth of charming streets, and it's easy to see why the city is so revered. Pre-Christian monuments adorn the age-old streetscape. Starting in the heart of the city, you'll find the Temple of Hephaestus and the Ancient Agora of Athens. Then pass Areopagus Hill and walk among the icons of the Acropolis and its crowning jewel, the Parthenon. Beyond them, a cluster of foregone deities are heralded in the Zappeion Garden, with Temples to Zeus, Apollo, and Kronos. Exploring this timeworn garden, you will pass landmarks like the Monument to the Unknown Soldier and the Kallimarmaro, a 4th-century B.C. stadium that hosted the first modern Olympics. The park ends on a street of museums, featuring the Benaki Museum, the Museum of Cycladic Art, and the Byzantine and Christian Museum. Close by is Plaka; a quaint, cobblestoned neighborhood, encrusted with beautiful boutiques, traditional cafés, and family-run tavernas. Finally, like the legends of Mount Olympus, gaze in the wonderment of Athens from atop Mount Lycabettus.

name: Banten City
description: Banten City has been a prosperous town since its 16th century connection to the famous maritime Silk Road. Once renowned as the most important port city of the Hinduist Kingdom of Sunda, engaging in trade with Sumatra and the Maldives, it now offers captivating historical experiences for visitors. Old Banten, north of Serang city, holds the remains of the ancient walled port city of Banten. Visitors often come to pay their respects and offer prayers at the graves of Sultan Maulana Hasanuddin and his descendants, as well as visit the impressive Great Mosque, both of which serve as reminders of the sultanate's former glory. For those interested in delving further into the city's heritage, the Benteng Heritage Museum offers a captivating experience. Housed in a traditional Peranakan Chinese building dating back to 1684, it is one of the oldest historic structures in Tangerang. Banten City stands as a vibrant testament to its rich past, offering a glimpse into the region's historical significance and cultural treasures.

name: Yangsan
description: With its blend of cultural treasures, thrilling attractions, and natural wonders, Yangsan offers a multifaceted experience for all who venture to explore this enchanting city. At the south of Jiuqi Mountain, lies the renowned Tongdu Temple, one of Korea's three famous temples. The temple's fame stems from housing the real body relics of Bodhisattvas, resulting in a unique absence of Buddha statues. Surrounded by a lush forest, the temple boasts over 70 buildings of various sizes, showcasing cultural relics and picturesque landscapes. For thrill-seekers, Tongdu Paradise, situated between Gajisan Provincial Park and Tongdu Temple, is a playground featuring an array of amusement facilities. This spot gained popularity when it was featured in the drama "My Love From the Star." The Yangsan Tower offers an amazing panoramic view of the city, making it a must-visit attraction for budget travelers, as it has no entrance fee. From the top, everyone can admire the fantastic landscape that Yangsan has to offer. History and culture enthusiasts will find delight in exploring the Yangsan City Museum, which opened in 2013. The museum showcases various cultural items from the Yangsan area, providing visitors with a comprehensive understanding of the city's heritage.

name: White Desert
description: The White Desert formed over centuries, erosion and sandstorms slowly carving into chalk outcrops, forming natural sculptures. The landscape is littered with formations with names like "mushroom", "ice-cream cone," "the Monolith", and "Inselberg". The most famous is the "chicken and atomic bomb" - a two-piece formation that looks exactly as promised. Around these formations, the sands are sprinkled with quartz and pyrite and the occasional small fossil. During sunrise and sunset the white stones take on rosy hues, while the entire desert is given a ghostly glow under the light of the full moon.

name: Gifu
description: Gifu promises an enriching journey off the beaten path, situated strategically in Japan's central region. Historically, the city played a pivotal role in the country's history, attracting notable figures such as Oda Nobunaga during the Sengoku period. Delve into Gifu's rich heritage at the Gifu City Museum of History, where the area's evolution unfolds from ancient times to the present, offering insights into life during Oda Nobunaga's era. Embrace the allure of Gifu Castle perched on Mt. Kinka, granting breathtaking panoramic views of the city and the Nagaragawa River. This meticulously reconstructed castle pays homage to its 16th-century predecessor and is surrounded by a tapestry of shrines, temples, and museums. Discover the remarkable Buddha statue at the base of Mt. Kinka, erected to honor earthquake victims. This monumental structure and the adjoining temple echo the grandeur of Nara and Kamakura's great Buddhas.

name: Chaves
description: Situated on the fertile banks of the Tâmega river, only 10km away from the Spanish border, this ancient town is steeped in history. The fantastically maintained Roman Bridge was reputedly built by enslaved locals towards the end of the 1st century. Commanding such an important position, the town developed as a fortified settlement with two forts, and with good reason - it was attacked by every empire that had an interest in Portugal. To protect as many of its medieval residents as possible, the houses were built tall and thin, with balconies that grow successively larger than the one below. The main square is dominated by a 14th century keep which now contains a military museum. Flanking the square are two of the town's characteristically humble churches. Visitors sore from travelling should bring a swimsuit - the town's natural springs are some of the hottest in Europe, reaching over 70ºC.

name: Al Hofuf
description: Renowned for its prolific date production, Al-Hofuf boasts rich cultural heritage and striking natural landscapes. Graced with an array of attractions, Al-Hofuf showcases mosques, palaces, ancient architectural marvels, and vibrant markets, presenting a tapestry of history and modernity. The city's allure extends to its recreational offerings, with King Fahd Park and Lake Al Asfar inviting relaxation amid scenic gardens and serene waters. Springs like Ain Al-Khudood and renowned hotels such as Bonis Hotel and Layali Al Sharq Hotel cater to diverse preferences. Al-Hofuf's essence lies in its rural charm, as lush orchards and palm oases beckon visitors to unwind and experience the tranquility of its surroundings. Al-Hofuf serves as the core of Al-Ahsa, boasting the world's largest oasis, Jebel Al-Qarah, and significant historical landmarks. Though the city itself doesn't reveal ancient remnants due to urbanization, it is believed to have ties to the ancient land of Dilmun referenced in Mesopotamian texts.

name: Saintes
description: The first Roman capital of Aquitaine, Saintes has enjoyed 2,000 years of being an important regional hub, leaving it rife with landmarks representing its Gallo-Roman, Medieval and Classical heritage. On the East bank of the river, visitors will find a Roman triumphal arch, Archaeological museum, and the 11th century Abbaye aux Dames. The facade of the abbey's 12th century church is particularly beautiful with carvings representing various Biblical stories ornamenting the entrance. One the West bank, the old town is filled with houses from the 17th to the 19th centuries. Dominating this part of town, the Cathedral of Saint-Pierre was founded in the 12th century, with extensive 15th to 17th century renovations. Following the Valley of the Arenas brings visitors to the best preserved Roman amphitheatre in western France. The UNESCO-listed Church of Saint-Eutrope dates from the 12th century, and has an exceptional crypt - almost an entire subterranean church on its own.

name: Besancon
description: While first mentioned in 58 BC by Julius Caesar, this picturesque bend in the Doubs River has been settled since at least 1500 BC. The city's strategic position has made it an important military, political, and trade hub over the centuries. Watching over the city is its UNESCO-listed Citadel. Designed by Vauban, this feat of 17th century military engineering is now home to several museums and a zoo. In the heart of the city, the 11th century St. Jean cathedral, houses one of Renaissance master Fra Bartolomeo's great works, as well as a 19th century astronomic clock, a beautiful testament to the city's watchmaking industry. Nearby is the 2nd century Porte Noire triumphal arch. The city has an exceptional selection of museums, such as the Musée des Beaux Arts, which was established in 1694, and the Museum of Time, which covers both the city's history, and the history of watch-making.

name: Torun
description: With its picture-perfect setting on the Vistula River and much of the medieval city walls still remaining, Torun is one of those towns that visitors just love to wander around. The old town is chock-full of exquisite medieval buildings, statues, restaurants, café bars as well as the charming town hall, which along with the everyday hustle and bustle, simply oozes atmosphere. Take a walk around the cobblestone streets and immerse yourself in the charm of this medieval market town. Besides the incredible architecture and buildings, Torun can also boast that it is the birthplace of Copernicus (the astronomer who placed the sun, rather than the earth, at the center of the universe) who has his own statue in the town and a university named in his honor. The town is also famous throughout Poland for its gingerbread, made there since the thirteenth-century and a treat every visitor should try.

name: Omis
description: This small Central Dalmatian town and harbor is protected by large cliffs. It came into prosperity through piracy and was once home to the most feared sailors on the Adriatic. Today, Omis is an adventure lover's paradise. Visitors can enjoy free climbing, canyoning, rafting, and ziplining. There are also many beautiful beaches of all kinds throughout the town. Omis is very historic and has 9 churches and 2 fortresses. The 13th century fortress Mirabella stands just outside the city center and was once used as a shelter for pirates. Whether you're searching for beauty, tranquility, or a taste of pirate culture, Omis is sure to provide.

name: Kylemore Abbey
description: Built in 1868, Kylemore Abbey was originally the family home of Mitchell Henry, a wealthy English doctor, who moved to Ireland after visiting on his honeymoon. Henry eventually sold the estate to the Duke and Dutchess of Manchester, who in turn were forced to sell it to pay off their gambling debts. The buyers were an order of Benedictine Nuns from Ypres, Belgium, who had been bombed out of their abbey during World War I and rescued by the men of the 8th Battalion of the Royal Munster Fusiliers. Today, the nuns invite visitors to experience the beautifully restored rooms, learn about their fascinating story, and admire the neo-Gothic architecture of the abbey and its church. On the expansive grounds, you'll find plenty of pleasant walking trails, and the incomparable Victorian Walled Garden - the largest of its kind in Ireland. For more information, please visit www.kylemoreabbey.com

name: Bologna
description: Bologna is the capital of the Emilia-Romagna region and dates back to almost a thousand years B.C. A center of university life, Bologna is also home to the oldest university in Europe. The city has a rich culinary history with many creamy pasta sauces and hearty meat dishes. When visiting Bologna, you'll notice plenty of arcaded streets. The town center is one of the best preserved in Europe. Piazza Maggiore, the heart of the city, is lively and entertaining with many outdoor dining and drinking establishments. It's surrounded by the Basilica of San Petronio, the city hall building, and the Neptune fountain (among other buildings). Don't forget to check out the Asinelli Tower, the city's largest tower. This slightly leaning tower is actually larger than the famous Leaning Tower of Pisa and can be reached to the top in 498 steps. After enjoying some Italian cuisine, stroll along city's arcaded streets and explore all that Bologna has to offer.

name: Tours
description: An important settlement since Gallic times, under the Roman empire the city became an important metropolis, and was home to one of the five largest amphitheatres in the empire. In the 4th century, the city's bishop was St. Martin, a connection which made it a major centre in the Middle Ages. Today, this rich medieval history is still preserved by the beautiful 12th to 15th century half-timbered houses in the historic center. The city's cathedral received a 15th century Flamboyant Gothic makeover, covering every inch of the exterior with ornate ornamentation. Inside, along with a beautiful organ and vibrant stained glass windows, visitors can see the tombs of the children of Charles VIII. Next door are the cloisters of La Psalette, one of 85 National Monuments in France, which feature elaborate stonework in an impressive mix of architectural styles.

name: Safi
description: One of Morocco's oldest cities, Safi is believed to have been founded by the Carthaginian Hanno in the 5th or 6th century BC. Safi was one of Morocco's most important ports up until the 18th century, when Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah banned foreign trade in all ports except his newly built city of Mogador. Today, it's Morocco's main sardine fishing port and a hub for textiles and ceramics. Being off most tourist routes, Safi's fortified medina provides a pleasant place to experience traditional Morocco without the suffocating crowds of better known destinations. Wandering the twisting alleys, you'll vibrant blue doors and windows, local ceramic shops, and historic monuments like the remains of the 16th-century Cathédrale Portugaise. At the waterfront, you'll find the 16th century Portuguese fort, which offers great views of the coast and medina. 500 meters offshore, the Kechla was a prison until 1990, but now serves as a ceramics market.

name: Schaffhausen
description: First mentioned in the 11th century, Schaffhausen was a city state, and even minted its own coins. It owes its success to the impassible Rheinfall waterfall - shippers would need to unload their goods in Schaffhausen to bypass the falls. Dominating the town is the 16th century Munot fortress, which provided great views of the town and surrounding landscape. In the car-free Old Town, visitors can wander the cobbled streets, admiring the oriel windows and lavishly painted facades from the Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque periods. Near the river, visitors can stop by the IWC museum, where Schaffhausen's most prestigious local business exhibits over 230 of their legendary watches, walking visitors through their history and development.

name: Noto
description: Founded in pre-Roman times, Noto was decimated by an earthquake in 1693, and as such was completely rebuilt in a new position. Expertly planned on a modern grid, and built in the beautiful Baroque style, the city was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its historic urban plan and rich architecture. Of the city's many beautiful churches, the Cathedral is without a doubt the most impressive. Visitors are given plenty of time to admire its elaborate Baroque facade as you work your way up the monumental staircase. The interior is an elegant white with pops of opulent ornamentation. Nicknamed 'the stone garden' for its many richly ornamented buildings, Noto's beauty is best experienced by simply walking around, discovering its many fountains, plazas, and many hidden details.

name: Todi
description: According to legend, the beautiful hilltop town of Todi was built by Hercules, though archaeological evidence points to the Umbri people settling here in about the 8th century BC. Between then and 217 BC, it was a fortified Etruscan city, the walls from which can still be seen today. When the Romans conquered the city, it expanded and a new set of walls were erected. The city expanded again in 1244, and new quarters were enclosed in a new circle of walls. The heart of the city, the Piazza del Popolo, is surrounded by historical buildings. The 12th century cathedral, built on a temple to Apollo is famous for its long flight of stairs and classic Romanesque facade. The town's three major palaces, built between the 13th-14th centuries, are not only marvellous examples of medieval architecture, they host a slew of museums.

name: Sigiriya
description: Step into the mesmerizing realm of Sigiriya, the famed "Lion Rock". This ancient stone fortress, nestled in the central Matale District of Sri Lanka, unfolds a tale of royalty, artistry, and architectural marvels. Chronicles reveal that King Kasyapa (477-495 AD) transformed this once forested hill into a regal capital. He adorned it with frescoes and a grand palace accessible solely through an imposing lion gateway. The name "Sigiriya," or Lion Rock, derives from this awe-inspiring structure. Surrounded by the remnants of vast reservoirs and meticulously designed gardens, it's an unparalleled testament to ancient landscaped beauty. At the heart of Sigiriya is the Lion staircase, a remarkable tile-covered walkway that emerges from the open mouth of a magnificent beast. This intricate masterpiece, constructed with brick and timber, leads to the palace garden atop the rock. Its climb is accessible to adventurers of all ages and fitness levels, inviting you to unravel the secrets of an ancient world perched upon a rock.

name: Ciudad Delicias
description: In the state of Chihuahua, Delicias is a gem of agricultural production, gastronomy and natural history. Informally known as the "breadbasket" of the state, its major crop production includes pecans, chile, cotton, tomato, onion and peanuts - all of which and more can be found at the vibrant Morelos and Juarez open air farm markets. Try some traditional "queso Chihuahua", a mild and buttery cheese available in braids, balls or rounds. Visit the Sotol Factory where the renowned Sotol drink is distilled using the plant of the same name. Similar to mezcal, it is smooth and mellow with a warming finish and is known as the traditional drink of Chihuahua. You may even pick up some tesgüino - a type of beer made from malted corn that originated in the Sierra Madre valleys. While sipping on your drink, head to the Teatro de Delicias and admire the murals designed by one of Mexico's renowned painters, Aarón Piña Mora. Meanwhile, the Chihuahua Desert Museum and Paleontology Museum offer fascinating ecogeographic and natural history exhibits for the science buffs.

name: Sremski Karlovci
description: Starting as a Roman fort, the picture-perfect town of Sremski Karlovaci became a major cultural and spiritual center in the 18th century, leaving behind a legacy of beautiful Baroque buildings. These are best exemplified by the town's religious edifices, such as the St Nicholas Orthodox cathedral, built in 1758, which is filled with art and fine woodwork, while the stately Orthodox Theological Seminary - the second of its kind in the world. In the heart of town, the magnificent Four Lions fountain embodies the town's charms - it's said that anyone who drinks from the fountain will return to Karlovci to be married. At the southern end of town, the charming yellow Chapel of Peace marks the spot where the the Austrians and Turks signed the 1699 Peace Treaty. Once you've had your fill of architecture, be sure to pay a visit to one of the local wine cellars for a taste of local culture.

name: Besalu
description: In the Middle Ages, Besalu was the capital of its own independent state - major economic and political hub, where Jews and Christians lived in harmony for centuries. Even during the anti-Semetic pogroms at the end of the 1500s, it's believed the Jews of Besalu were allowed to flee without bloodshed. Today, it stands frozen in time, greeting visitors with a 12th century fortified bridge, which grants access to the quiet network of cobbled streets. After admiring the medieval Cornellà residence, with its Romanesque arcaded gallery, and the many Romanesque churches, visitors have the unique opportunity to visit Besalu's historic Jewish quarter. Most notable is the 12th century mikvé, a bath used for ritual ablutions, which is the oldest of its kind and one of only five left in the country. And of course, in such a traditional setting, Besalu is the perfect place to site down, and enjoy some traditional cuisine in a charming setting.

name: Cadiz
description: Spain's oldest city, and likely the oldest in Western Europe, Cadiz is a sun-soaked explosion of history and culture. Famous for its 10-day-long Carnival every February, the city is filled with delights year round. History lovers won't want to miss the Gadir Archaeological Site - a singular 9th century BC settlement where you can see two streets and eight homes, as well as everyday tools used by the Phoenician settlers. In the Old Town's jumbled streets you'll stumble on buildings in a slew of architectural styles, but the crown jewel is undoubtedly the 18th century cathedral and its mish-mash of architectural styles. If you need a break, stop by one of the city's many seafood restaurants for some tapas and sherry before heading to the Castle of San Sebastián at the very end of the isthmus. Only accessible by a stone causeway, the fort offers great views of the city.

name: Podgorica
description: Building off the remains of an ancient Roman settlement, Slavic tribes established a riverfront village that would be the basis of modern day Podgorica. First mentioned by name in the 14th century, it fell into Ottoman hands only 100 years later. By the end of the 15th century, the Turks had fortified the city, with towers, gates, and defensive ramparts that give the appearance of an oriental military city. In World War II, the city was bombed over 70 times, razing most of it. Scattered among the modern buildings are the ancient Roman Duklja ruins and Ribnica Bridge, and an Ottoman clock tower built just before the fall of the empire. The most striking modern landmark is the new Cathedral, where every inch of the interior is decorated in traditional Serbian Orthodox style.

name: Cenote Chaak Tun
description: The surreal subterranean scene at Cenote Chaak Tun makes it easy to see why the Mayans believed cenotes were entrances to the underworld. A boardwalk through the jungle leads visitors to the crystal clear waters of the first cenote, where you can stop to cool off. A short walk further through the tropical forest, and the path leads to a small opening in the earth, with a spiral staircase descending into its depths. Once underground, an opening in the cavern ceiling is the only source of natural light, which baths a small, tree-covered island. Around this is the cenotes vast cavern, where a wealth of stalactites and other cave formations are illuminated by limited artificial lighting, leaving some dark corners to add to the cenote's mystique. Please note: tickets are not included. Entrance is with a guided tour, which costs $40. You can book in advance for a discount at https://chaaktun.com.mx/

name: Baeza
description: Settled since Roman times, and a once booming Moorish capital, this provincial town's lasting rise to fame came thanks to a handful of families, rich from grain-growing, and cloth and leather production. In the 16th century, these wealthy local nobles hired major architects of the era to redesign their town in the en-vogue Italian style. When the local economy collapsed in the 17th century, few newer structures were built, preserving the town's Renaissance legacy that earned it a place on the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Marquessa de Jabalquinto palace has an elaborate Isabelline front with a Moorish influence, and is right next to the 16th century cathedral. While it features Baeza's signature painted iron screens, it has a hidden attraction in the form of a huge silver custodia cunningly placed behind a painting of St Peter, which whirls aside for a small donation.

name: Auxerre
description: Settled on a main road that's existed since pre-Roman times, the Auxerre flourished on the banks of the River Yonne. Filled with half-timbered houses, this City of Art and History's historic center is a 67-hectare preserved area, divided into distinct neighborhoods. The beautiful La Marine district, nestled on the banks of the Yonne, lies at the foot of the oldest monument in Auxerre: the Benedictine Abbey of St. Germain. Founded in the 5th century, its Carolingian crypt is decorated with the oldest known murals in France. Nearby stands the Gothic Cathedral of St. Stephen, with its ornately-decorated asymmetric façade and superb stained glass windows. In its 11th-century Romanesque crypt is a magnificent fresco of Christ on horseback. Among the picturesque half-timbered houses, Renaissance homes, and Art Deco buildings of the L'Horloge district is the 15th century Clock Tower, built in the on the remains of a Gallo-Roman castrum.

name: Exconvento de Calpan
description: From a distance, Exconvento de Calpan is a starkly beautiful structure with a refined and elegant facade but the walls reveal a more detailed picture up closer inspecting. Built in 1548 by Franciscan friars, the stunning Plateresque details display intricate reliefs and stories made with ancient materials and methods that hint to the indigenous origins of the location. The interior of the structure features a single nave with rounded arches and stained glass. The rich history has earned Exconvento de Calpan a place on the UNESCO Cultural Heritage list.

name: Punta Arenas
description: Despite being used since the 16th century, Punta Arenas didn't develop until 1840 when it became became the primary port for exporting Costa Rica's coffee in the Pacific. It was also the country's largest fishing port at one point, and it continues to be a great source for fresh seafood. Strolling the waterfront promenade, you'll find plenty of sodas (traditional eateries), where you can dine like a local while looking out over the water. If you need to cool off, try the city's signature churchhills - a concoction of shaved ice and ice cream. As a working Tico city, things are pretty laid back, but if you still need somewhere cool and calm to collect yourself, you can always pop into the neo-Romanesque cathedral.

name: Yanbu
description: Yanbu, also known as Yambu or Yenbo, stands as a captivating city with a history spanning over 2,500 years, once serving as a vital point along the spice and incense route connecting Yemen to Egypt and the Mediterranean. Beyond its economic prominence, Yanbu enchants with its natural harbor, boasting unspoiled coral reefs and captivating Red Sea vistas. This aquatic haven invites water enthusiasts for scuba diving, fishing, and birdwatching. Three distinct regions define Yanbu: Yanbu Al-Bahr, the northern hub; Yanbu Al-Nakhl, featuring villages and farms; and Yanbu Al-Sina'iya, an industrial area with modern housing and amenities. Tourists and history enthusiasts revel in the city's attractions, including the recently renovated house of T.E. Lawrence, famed as Lawrence of Arabia. Additionally, Yanbu Waterfront, a burgeoning project, entices visitors with a 12-kilometer stretch for leisurely strolls, jogging, and sightseeing, offering gardens, marinas, hotels, and even islands.

name: Teruel
description: While the area has been settled since pre-history, Teruel proper didn't get its start until 1171, when Alfonso II founded the city. Within a few centuries, it became a fortified border town, at the edge of the Muslim kingdom of Valencia, which strongly influenced the Christian city. This cultural melding culminated in the UNESCO listed, 12th century Cathedral, which features outstanding ceramic decorations on its square tower. Inside, the cathedral's richly decorated Mudejar coffered ceiling is one of the most important in the country. Also on the UNESCO list is the tower of San Salvador, with its brick façade, double set of arches and elaborate tiled decoration. Also preserving the city's Mudejar aesthetic are the tower of the 14th century church of San Martín, and San Pedro. Within San Pedro are 2 sarcophagi, which hold the mummified remains of Diego and Isabel, a pair of ill-fated 13th century lovers

name: Vicenza
description: Settled around 300 BC, the growing Roman presence eventually assimilated the original Paleo-Veneti inhabitants, and by 157 BC the city was a Roman centre. After the fall of Rome, it faced a tumultuous several centuries, being destroyed, sacked and dominated as they tried to navigate Italian politics. By the 16th century, it was one of the most downtrodden cities of the Veneto, but Andrea Palladio revitalized it, leaving many outstanding palaces and villas. Among his greatest achievements is the Olympic theatre, widely considered the first modern covered theatre. The arch-faced Basilica Palladiana shows one of the first examples of what have come to be known as the Palladian window. So great was Palladio's influence that the city even has a Palladio museum housed inside a Palladio palace. If you ever tire of his works, the city's many parks churches offer beautiful and quiet spaces to escape to.

name: Roskilde
description: Roskilde was founded by Harald Bluetooth in the 980s, and developed into a major trade hub that served as the country's capital from the 11th century until 1443. The city's UNESCO-listed Gothic cathedral was the very first building in the "Brick Gothic" style, and is even more culturally significant as it houses the tombs of generations of Danish monarchs, as well as important Vikings including Harold Bluetooth and Sweyn Forkbeard. Next to the cathedral is the Baroque Roskilde Palace, which served as the bishop's residence, and now houses the Museum of Contemporary Art. The city's Viking heritage is proudly displayed at the Viking Ship Museum, which exhibits the well-preserved remains of five 11th-century ships, as well as fully functional recreations. Despite its historic importance, Roskilde is best known for hosting one of the largest music festivals in Europe, which inspired the excellent Ragnarock Museum where rock and pop history have been transformed into interactive exhibits.

name: Ex Convento de Tecali
description: The Ex Convento de Tecali was built in the 16th century by Franciscan monks as an important religious center. Sparing little expense, the complex was one of the finest examples of Renaissance architecture in the region. While it has since fallen into disrepair, there's still more than a glimmer of its golden days. Visitors are first greeted with a view of the towering bell tower and the intricate facade before passing through the remains of the original wooden door to the grass-covered floor of the roofless, column lined building. The romantic blend of beauty and decay is especially popular among photographers - particularly at sunset.

name: Jajce
description: The small town of Jajce is very historic and rich in culture. It has been home to medieval kings and Ottoman governors, to name a few. The Old Town has many medieval and Ottoman-style buildings which highlights its diverse past. The town itself is compact, making it easy to wander the historic sights. The Jajce fortress, built in the mid-14th century, is a medieval fort overlooking the city. It's the perfect site for history lovers. Jajce is famous for its Turkish wooden water mills situated on the Pliva River. The Pliva Falls themselves are also a sight to behold. The 20 meter waterfall is unique in the fact that it decorates the center of town. Whether searching for history or nature, you're sure to find it in Jajce!

name: Alnwick Castle
description: Built around 1096, Alnwick Castle has been inhabited by the same family since the 13th century. Over the years, the castle was expanded and remodelled to suit its owners' needs and tastes, and today is the second largest inhabited castle in the country. Of the many lords who have called Alnwick home, Harry "Hotspur" Percy is the best known, being immortalized by Shakespeare's Henry IV, and a giant statue on the castle grounds. Today, the Duke and his family still live in part of the castle, but visitors can tour some of the sumptuous rooms, or see special exhibitions in the towers, including the family's archaeological collection, the story of the local volunteer soldiers raised to repel Napoleon, and the Regimental Museum of the Royal Northumberland Fusiliers. What's attracting many visitors these days is the castle's role as Hogwarts in the first two Harry Potter films - the castle even hosts 'broomstick training' sessions in the summer on the very spot Harry had his first lesson.

name: Varazdin
description: Varazdin is quaint and inexpensive, remaining virtually unspoiled by mass tourism. It offers a historic core and Baroque architecture, including 11 churches, 3 monasteries, and a cathedral. Make sure to stop in the Main Square and Old Castle. The well-preserved castle contains a museum that highlights the town's history of artifacts, paintings, and period rooms.

name: Huancavelica
description: Huancavelica is a small city surrounded by mountains and packed with beautiful churches, recognised for their distinguished silver-plated altars. The oldest, Iglesia de Santa Ana, dates back to the 16th century and is famous for its statues made in Italy. Many of the cities churches are open daily from 5-7 PM. The city plays host to several annual festivals where you can be entertained by traditional dancing and ceremonies and party with the locals over traditional food and drink. The Plaza de Armas, despite being the hub of the town in the historic centre, is somewhat serene, most likely due to vehicle access being prohibited. Street vendors line the streets daily selling handcrafted artisan products, and on a Sunday sellers come from out-of-town villages for a larger fair. For a little history, the Museo Direccion Regional de Cultura Huancavelica showcases ceramics, textiles and even MUMMIES!

name: Khujand
description: Khujand, a radiant gem in Tajikistan's crown, beckons travelers with its rich history, vibrant culture, and picturesque landscapes. Wander through Khujand's bustling bazaars, where the scents of spices and freshly baked bread mingle in the air, and merchants offer an array of colorful textiles, handmade crafts, and exotic fruits. History buffs will find themselves enthralled by the city's numerous landmarks, including the imposing Khujand Fortress, which has stood as a sentinel overlooking the city for centuries. Immerse yourself in Khujand's cultural tapestry as you explore its array of museums, art galleries, and performance venues. Discover the legacy of the revered Persian scholar and philosopher, Avicenna, at the Museum of Regional Studies, or marvel at the intricate designs of traditional Tajik crafts at the Arbob Cultural Palace.

name: Jinja
description: A small floating sign claims that the waters here are the true source of the Nile. This deceivingly innocuous sign stands as the only reminder of an incredibly tumultuous debate that raged during the Age of Explorers. In the 19th century John Hanning Speke claimed to have found the source of the Nile in Jinja. This claim would lead to a furious debate back in Britain that would turn friend into enemy and consume the scientific community. This conflict would only end with the mysterious death of Speke before a public debate on the matter. Jinja is no stranger to death as it is also the final resting place for a large contingency of European and African soldiers who perished during the first and second world wars. Despite, it's somewhat morbid past, Jinja is now a center of adventure. Come and get your adrenaline pumping while rafting on the rapids, kayaking on calmer waters or riding quad bikes through gorgeous terrain.

name: Rosario
description: Birthplace of revolutionary Che Guevara and footballer Lionel Messi, Argentina's third largest city is rich in culture, neoclassical architecture, and possesses a vibrant nightlife. It is widely regarded as the most liberal and tolerant city in the country. This bike-friendly city boasts a huge array of things to do and see, more than just walks along the 15km of lovely Paraná riverfront. The Monumento Nacional a la Bandera celebrates the creator of the nation's flag, and panoramic views of the city can be seen from the top of the tower section. Museo Histórico Provincial, located in the middle of Parque Independencia (where you can paddle on the park's lakes), has excellent exhibits from religious displays to indigenous artifacts, and a fascinating section on mate (the local herbal drink). Also worth a look is the Cathedral. The sombre facade of the Basilica Our Lady of Rosario belies the marble-adorned stunning interior.

name: Cordoba
description: Founded by the Romans for its strategic location, it became such an important port city that they named it the capital of Hispania Ulterior. Today, their mighty bridge still stands, alluding to the historic landmarks awaiting visitors in the city. Even the status of a Roman capital was eclipsed when the city became the capital of the Moorish kingdom of El-Andalus. The height of Islamic sophistication, it was during this time that the massive Mezquita mosque was erected. Even the reconquering Christians in 1236 were so awed by its beauty that they left it standing, building their cathedral amongst its arches and columns. Today, the mosque still stands as one of the world's greatest Islamic buildings, with the ornate church creating an extraordinary architectural fusion. From the mosque, the the narrow streets of the old Jewish and Muslim quarters offer row upon row of historic buildings and hidden gems.

name: Gouda
description: Starting as a fortified castle built by the Van der Goude family, the town of Gouda became an important trade center in the 13th century when a series of canals were dug to connect the town to the Rhine river. During this time, Gouda acquired a monopoly on cheese trading, and this is the origin of gouda cheese's name - it was traditionally traded in the city. On Thursday mornings, between April and August, farmers and merchants still negotiate for golden wheels the old fashioned way- at the Gouda cheese market. Visitors can also head to the Weigh House to learn more about the cheese's history. Dominating Gouda's historic center is the UNESCO-listed Sint Janskerk church, the largest in Holland, and famous for its 16th century stained glass windows. Gouda's 15th century City Hall is another of its beautiful monuments, with mechanical dolls that come to life two minutes past every hour and half hour.

name: Erawan
description: Covering 550 square kilometers, Erawan National Park and is best known for the beautifully blue pools under its tiered waterfall. Named after the legendary Hindu elephant, Erawan Falls has three easily accessible tiers, which are also the most crowded. If you're in better shape, and have the time, the 2km trek to the upper tiers is recommended - at the fourth tier there is a natural rock slide, while level six has the fewest visitors. Along the way, you're likely to see macaques (who will snatch unattended belongings). If you decide to go for a swim, the fish are nibbly! For more information, please visit thainationalparks.com/erawan-national-park

name: Yogyakarta City
description: Yogyakarta is a vibrant and culturally rich destination in Indonesia, and being the only city still ruled by a monarchy, holds great significance as a center for classical Javanese fine arts and culture. Home to the influential Mataram kingdom in the 16th and 17th centuries and considered the cradle of civilisation on Java along with Solo, it has an abundance of museums to immerse yourself in its rich history. Spend time at the living museum of The Kraton, the Sultan's Palace, and the renowned Alun Alun. Witness the artistry of silversmiths and indulge in shopping along Malioboro road, before going for a dip at one of the beautiful beaches such as Parangtritis, Indrayanti, Pok Tunggal or Siung. Culinary enthusiasts will be delighted by Yogyakarta's offerings, including the iconic Gudeg, a traditional Javanese dish, and the popular Bakpia, a flavorful snack perfect for souvenirs. You can even immerse yourself in the authentic daily life of the locals, learning traditional skills such as weaving and dancing, at some of the tourism villages.

name: Mafra National Palace
address.addr1: Terreiro D. João V, 2640 Mafra, Portugal
description: King John V made a vow to build a convent if his wife Queen Mariana gave him offspring. The birth of his first daughter prompted the construction of what was initially planned as a relatively small project. However, once gold from the Portuguese colony of Brazil began to arrive by the boatload, King John V changed his plans, and announced the construction of a sumptuous palace. Filling an impressive 40 000 square metres, it remains one of the largest royal palaces in Portugal. The imposing façade of the palace runs for 220 m, and faces the town of Mafra. At each end stands a square tower and in the centre, a magnificent church built in marble. It is hard not to get lost in the beauty and grandeur of this monumental structure, and is a must-see stop for travellers in the area.

name: Valdivia
description: Founded in 1552, Valdivia was once the southernmost city in the Spanish Empire and one of the most fortified cities of the New World. In the mid-19th century, Valdivia was the main port of entry for German immigrants who reshaped the city's identity, making it a hub for beer, sausages, and Old World culture. In 1960 Valdivia was devastated by the strongest earthquake ever recorded, with floods from the resulting tsunami turning pastures and parts of the city into permanent wetlands, which are now protected areas. The best place to start a visit to Valdivia is the riverside market, where you can enjoy the view of the and feed the local sea lions and pelicans. You can also hop on a cruise to tour the many ruined forts if you're staying longer (tours are about 5 hours). From here, head to General Lagos St. to admire the German-style houses and maybe grab a sausage. For beer lovers and Bavariaphiles, head to the Cervecería Kunstmann on the outskirts to learn about brewing history and sip a sudsy cerveza.

name: Sint Willibrordus
description: Nestled 12 miles northwest of Willemstad, the capital of Curaçao, lies the picturesque village of Sint Willibrordus, known locally as Williwood. The cheeky "Williwood" sign, mimicking California's iconic Hollywood sign, stands proudly on a modest hill, overlooking a barren soccer field. While it initially began as a lighthearted endeavor, the sign swiftly captured hearts and, in 2011, the town officially embraced its newfound fame. Sint Willibrordus boasts a grand Roman Catholic church, a neo-Gothic masterpiece dating back to the 1880s. Designed by architect Evert Margry, the church stands as a testament to the village's rich history. Nearby, visitors can explore the remnants of the Rif St. Marie salt pan, one of the island's oldest plantations, now adorned by resident flamingos. As tourists flock to Williwood, they discover a village that has seamlessly blended its historic charm with newfound vibrancy.

name: Calvi
description: The port of Calvi has been bustling since Roman times and takes its name from "Calvus" - the "bald" rock upon which its impressive citadel is built. The 13th century fortress opens up to charming cobblestoned streets, with the towering Cathédrale Saint Jean–Baptiste at the highest point within it, overlooking the Mediterranean sea. The architecturally significant city is reputedly the original birthplace of explorer Christopher Columbus when it was part of the Genoese empire and holds history at every turn - from the Corsican polyphonic singing concerts you might encounter in the cathedral to the aging promenades. In modern times, Calvi has become a capital of culture in Corsica, with music festivals sending lively sound across the harbor in the summertime. For nature lovers, a pine forest stretches along six kilometers of beach, bordering the bay. Take yourself through the maze of gelato and coffee shop-lined streets in Calvi's charming citadel.

name: Hardwick Park
description: Hardwick Park has its roots in the 18th century when businessman John Burdon began to develop the grounds. Not only did he extend the lake, he added 40 acres of ornamental features including an artificial river, temples, grottoes, and follies. While the park wasn't maintained particularly well in the following centuries, the garden still retains its core 18th century design. Today, a walk through the park combines the natural beauty of the lake and woodland with historic buildings and statues. At the visitor center you can learn about the park's history, and its extensive restoration through interactive displays.The park also puts on a variety of events throughout the year.

name: Caernarfon Castle
description: Built in the 13th century by Edward I as a royal palace and military fortress, Caernarfon Castle was part of the kings 'Iron Ring' of castles in Wales. This show of force used around 90% of the nation's income, partly because he brought in the masters of the day, such as the lauded military architect Jacques de Saint-Georges d'Espéranche from Savoy, and the same artists who decorated Westminster Hall. The castle was even equipped with cutting-edge comforts like bathrooms, toilets, and running water. It's because Edward's son was born here that England's next-in-line to the throne is the Prince of Wales. The castle was in use up until the English Civil War in the 17th century, after which it was abandoned until conservation efforts began in the 19th century. Today, the castle still dominates the small town of Caernarfon. Visitors are free to explore the castle's grounds and halls, and even scale the towers where you'll be rewarded with stupendous views, and some historic exhibitions.

name: Lowther Castle
description: Lowther Castle has been occupied by the same family since 1150 - admittedly in several different buildings. The current castle was commissioned in 1806 by the 1st Earl of Lonsdale, and designed by the architect Robert Smirke - the man responsible for great civic buildings like the British Museum in London. However, the 5th Earl's unrestrained spending depleted the family fortune and the estate was abandoned - its roof was stripped to avoid paying taxes, and the castle's decorations and fixtures right down to the door knobs were sold off to repay outstanding debts. Today, the shell of the magnificent manor still stands, its 365 room replaced by charming gardens. The surrounding grounds are also slowly being reclaimed, not just for gardens, but outdoor activities including England's largest wooden playground. In the new stable gallery, The Story of Lowther exhibition recounts the castle's history in relationship to its times. For more information, please visit lowthercastle.org

name: Ulsan
description: Ulsan boasts not only a thriving industrial hub, but also offers scenic views and serene attractions. Daewangam Park, with its picturesque sea views and pine trees, creates a tranquil atmosphere for visitors. In the southern side of the Gaji Mountain range, the Seoknamsa Temple stands among the four major Buddhist temples in Gajisan Provincial Park. Rebuilt multiple times since its establishment in 824 A.D., it showcases 30 buildings and a stunning Three-story Pagoda, a symbol of protection from foreign invasions. Beyond its industrial prowess, Ulsan unveils a rich history dating back to prehistoric times, evident through various archaeological sites. The city's rapid development, from a center of heavy industry during the Japanese colonial period to its present status, is an intriguing journey to explore. With its breathtaking coastline, picturesque parks, and vibrant local cuisine, Ulsan combines industrial progress with natural beauty and cultural heritage.

name: Tacna
description: In one of the southern-most parts of Peru, Tacna is known for its role in Peru's independence and the War of the Pacific. During the War of the Pacific, Tacna was occupied by Chile for 50 years, always resisting Chilean propaganda. Finally, In 1929, the Peruvian nationalists prevailed and the Treaty of Lima was signed. This treaty allowed Tacna to remain a part of Peru, a great victory for the people of Tacna. The main attractions of this city revolve around monuments dedicated to the war and Peruvian's independence - this is Peru's most patriotic city, after all. Before leaving, stop by the Cathedral de Tacna, a lovely colonial structure in the center of town. You'll arrive there via the Paseo Civico, which is a relaxing promenade decorated with lush shrubbery and many places to sit and enjoy the afternoon!

name: Manama
description: Situated in the Persian Gulf, Manama has long been a significant trading hub and symbol of Arab affluence, with a tantalizing mix of expansive malls and daring skyscrapers combined with signs of its trading past. Manama's Souq stands as a testament to this, offering an authentic glimpse into the ambiance of an ancient bazaar. Its narrow streets and alleyways emanate from the iconic Bab Al Bahrain, captivating visitors with its vibrant energy and diverse culinary scene that's putting Manama on the map as a food lover's haven. The National Museum, Beit Al Quran, presents an impressive journey through Bahrain's history, showcasing archaeological artifacts, the Hall of Graves and exhibits on the Tylos and Islamic periods. Admire the evolution of ancient Qurans over the centuries at Beit Al Quran, and see the magnificent Al Fatih Mosque towering over the landscape and paying homage to the founder of modern Bahrain.

description: Now standing as testimony to man's inhumanity to man, Auschwitz is a major part of history that many people feel compelled to visit and pay their respects to those who died there. Both sections of the camp, Auschwitz I and the much larger outlying camp at Birkenau (Auschwitz II) have been preserved and are open for visitors, who are free to find their own way around or arrange a tour. Auschwitz I consists of a cinema showing a fifteen-minute film on the history and horrors of the camp followed by the barracks, each containing displays relating to life in the camp. Auschwitz II-Birkenau is vast and is where the main gas chambers and crematorium were situated (Birkenau was the site of most of the killings and not Auschwitz 1) and has mainly been left as the Nazis left it, with many of the buildings dynamited flat or burnt down. Please note: as tickets often sell out quickly you should book in advance at http://auschwitz.org/en/visiting/

name: Konya
description: Founded by the Hittites around 1500 BC, Konya is one of the longest continuously inhabited cities in Turkey. In the 12th and 13th centuries it flourished as the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate. During this time, the mystic Mevlana Celaleddin-i Rumi founded the Mevlevi Order, or as they're called in the West, the Whirling Dervishes. Today, Mevlana's green-tiled mausoleum is the city's central monument. The 13th century building is a beautiful example of traditional architecture, and contains a museum with exhibits on Mevlana, mysticism, and his sect. The Alaeddin Mosque, built atop the city's citadel in 1221, commands Konya's skyline and serves as a reminder of the city's religious dedication. To one side of the mosque are the remains of the Seljuk Imperial Palace. Near the palace you can visit the late-13th century Karatay Madrasah, which is now a museum displaying beautiful Seljuk-era artifacts.

name: San Pedro de Atacama
description: San Pedro de Atacama is a Chilean town, situated in the lovely heart of the Atacama desert. It was once part of Bolivia before being claimed by Chile, but prior to that its first inhabitants were the Atacamenos, an indigenous population native to the surrounding areas. The climate is dry and mild, and the town and surrounding areas are jam-packed with things to do. Exploring the ethereal natural landscapes is easy, whether you choose to rent a board and go sandboarding in the Valley of Death just 2km outside the city, or take a guided tour of the most notable sites around. If you're feeling ambitious, you can rent a bicycle and traverse the terrain yourself. The town itself is actually quite small, lined with cobbled streets and adobe houses. But you can find some small delights here, such as a colonial church and markets filled with local crafts and delicacies. Those interested in its pre-Columbian history should visit the R.P. Gustavo Le Paige Archeological Museum, where you can find pottery, baskets and ceramics made by the Atacamenos.

name: Aix-en-Provence
description: Founded in 123 BC by the Roman consul Sextius Calvinus, by the 4th century AD, it had became a bustling metropolis. In the centuries following the fall of Rome, the town was repeatedly plundered and conquered, not fully developing until the 12th century, even though it was the capital of Provence. Under the houses of Barcelona, Aragon and Anjou, it became an artistic centre - a tradition that carried on for centuries, with artists like Granet and Cezanne calling it home. Today, visitors can explore the city's art museum's, such as the Art Centre housed in a palatial 18th century hotel, or the Granet where visitors can find work from Picasso and Cezanne. Of course, you can always enjoy the oh-so-French feeling of stopping at a cafe after walk down the scenic Le Cours Mirabeau boulevard to the famous roundabout fountain.

name: Cudillero
description: Some legends say Cudillero was founded by the Vikings. While we cannot confirm these claims, what we can say is Cudillero has been doubted as one of the prettiest villages in Spain. This teeny tiny fishing settlement is off limits to cars and exploring has to be done on foot - the way it should be. Cudillero's charm is built on unique colorful architecture and narrow streets. Each fishing boat in the harbor has to correspond with its color to the house's color where its owner and fisherman lives. All this of this has a background of beautiful turquoise water of the Atlantic Ocean. So, when you visit, you get to enjoy off the beaten track way of life mixed with beautiful views. Have a nice walk around the village, soak into the experience and possibly treat yourself with a great cup of coffee in one of the local cafés.

name: Dijon
description: Inhabited since the Neolithic era, Dijon was rather inconsequential until the 11th century when it became the seat of the Dukes of Burgundy. Over the next four centuries, it developed into a thriving hub of art, learning, and science, not to mention staggering wealth and power. The UNESCO-listed town center is filled with charming half-timbered houses with polychromatic roofs, and impressive reminders of Dijon's Renaissance-era wealth. Visitors can tour the Palais des Ducs de Bourgogne to admire beautiful architecture from the 14th to 18th centuries, as well as the art and artifacts in the exceptional fine arts museum. Those who brave the climb up the "Tour de Philippe le Bon" are rewarded with an impressive view of Dijon. The 13th century Church of Notre Dame, has an unusual flat facade lined with 51 gargoyles. Though Dijon's imposing Gothic Cathedral is a few hundred years more recent, the crypt is one of France's oldest Christian sanctuaries still open to the public.

name: Salisbury Cathedral and Magna Carta
description: Construction Salisbury Cathedral began in 1220 under the supervision of Elias of Dereham, and the main sections were completed in just 38 years. Elias was present at Runnymede in 1215, and was given the task of distributing copies of the Magna Carta around England, so he understandably brought one to his home parish. Today, Salisbury's is the best-preserved of the four surviving original copies, and its history is brought to life by a fascinating interactive exhibition. The cathedral's tower and spire were completed in 1320, and great pains have been taken to keep them standing - after Lincoln Cathedral's spire collapsed in 1549, Salisbury's became the tallest in the country. It's in this tower that visitors will find the world's oldest mechanical clock, which dates from 1386. Not only does Salisbury have the tallest tower in the UK, it also has the largest cloister in Britain. For more information, please visit salisburycathedral.org.uk

name: Fresnillo
description: Fresnillo has a rich history and was once a prosperous silver mining town. With such mineral wealth, the mines of the town were worked constantly beginning in the late 1600s. Mine shafts were dug over 50 meters into the earth which eventually led to flooding and sent the town into economic crisis. Around the time of collapse, the Iglesia de la Purificación was built. This church has seen historic times of despair and violence and a number of bullet holes in the tower can still be seen today! Silver is still mined in the town but agriculture has also become a major player for Fresnillo's residents. Each year, the town sees religious pilgrimages and welcomes tourists during all seasons.

name: Duba
description: Duba, often referred to as a pit-stop on the coastal highway, reveals its maritime significance through its bustling port, which connects Tabuk Province to Egypt and Jordan via ferries. Visitors are drawn to the iconic King Abdulaziz Fort, a historic testament to the past. Constructed in 1933 during the reign of King Abdulaziz, the fort's mud-brick walls stand as a preserved memory of a simpler era. Beyond its historic treasures, Duba boasts the enchanting Duba Gulf as a backdrop to its lively fish market. A stroll through this authentic Arabian marketplace offers a vibrant experience, showcasing the region's maritime soul. However, Duba's true allure rests in its picturesque coastline and tranquil beaches, where the views of the Red Sea captivate visitors. For a leisurely escape, Duba presents its own serene public park, inviting families and visitors to enjoy leisurely strolls and picnics by the sea. With its charming beaches, historical landmarks, and warm Arabian hospitality, Duba encapsulates the essence of the Red Sea coast and offers a glimpse into Saudi Arabia's coastal treasures.

name: Malcesine
description: The ancient harbor town of Malcesine is situated between lake waters and the gigantic mountain ridge of Monte Baldo. This small picturesque town is the perfect spot to unwind for an hour or two or partake in thrilling water sport activities. Stroll through the medieval cobblestone streets while enjoying the village's many ice cream parlors, cafes, and boutiques. Malcesine's main attraction is the Castello Scaligero, a historic castle dating back to the 13th century. Another notable attraction is the 15th century Palazzo dei Capitani, the former headquarters of Venetian rulers of the area. Today, the building serves as the village library. Don't forget to check out the cable-car as well! The slowly rotating cable-car up the Monte Baldo mountains is a great way soak up 360 degree views of Malcesine and the surrounding areas.

name: Insurgency Museum
description: The Insurgency Museum, situated in the historic Hacienda de San Blas, stands as a commemoration of the significant events that unfolded during Mexico's quest for freedom. Established in 1967, its walls are adorned with mesmerizing murals by Alfredo Flores Zermeno, vividly portraying the cultural, political, and social milestones spanning two centuries from 1810 to 2010. Be enthralled by the immersive experience, designed to give you a thorough understanding of the insurgency's history within the walls of a visually stunning building. Nestled within the serene and picturesque surroundings of Pabellón de Hidalgo, it provides an ideal setting for reflection and contemplation, and has been honored with UNESCO's prestigious designation as a Heritage of Humanity. As the first museum of its kind in the state, The Insurgency Museum holds a special place in Mexican history. Photo by Isacdaavid, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chautla Hacienda
description: Built on an enormous flat of farmland northwest of Puebla, this colonial Chautla Hacienda has seen many changes throughout the centuries. The hacienda was first built to process the natural resources of the area and stimulate the economy, the main production was the farming of grain, which created jobs and eventually created the basis of the economy at the time. In the 19th century, it was bought by an Englishman, named Thomas Gillow, who later passed it on to his son. Who, while maintaining the production of grain and wheat, sought to modernize the hacienda. He introduced early electricity and even built the first hydroelectric power plant on the estate. He also built one of the property's most iconic structures, "El Castillo" (The Castle), which overlooks the dam on the property. Today the hacienda is a cultural center where you can spend the day, learning about colonial history and wandering the expansive grounds.

name: Miri
description: Miri is the second-largest city in the state of Sarawak, situated near the border of Brunei. Visitors to Miri are spoiled for choice when it comes to attractions and activities, beyond the natural attractions that surround the city. Miri's thriving economy, driven by offshore oil, has contributed to its modern and vibrant atmosphere. From the iconic Unity Tower and Pustaka Miri to the fascinating Petroleum Museum, there are plenty of cultural and historical sites to explore. For panoramic views of the city, a trip to Canada Hill is a must. The San Ching Tian Temple and the beautiful Esplanade Beach at Luak Bay offer serene and picturesque settings. Miri is also renowned for hosting one of Sarawak's biggest events, the Borneo Jazz festival, showcasing the best of international jazz talent every May. For shopping enthusiasts, explore the variety of malls and take advantage of the affordable prices in the city. With its blend of modernity, natural beauty, and cultural richness, Miri offers a unique experience for travelers.

name: Chimbote
description: Perched on Peru's west coast in Ferrol Bay, Chimbote was one of the world's biggest fishing towns after more than 30 fish factories opened in the 1970s. Unfortunately, overfishing has weakened the fish economy, but you can still see many fishing boats floating in the bay as you take an evening stroll along the boardwalk. Still recovering from the crash of the fishing business, this small town has not lost it's charm, try the ceviche and walk along the boardwalk as the views of the bay are one of a kind!

name: Locarno
description: Situated on a river delta and sheltered by the Alps, Locarno has been a holiday destination since the days of the Roman Empire. In the early 1900s, beautiful belle epoch hotels were built to accommodate the new influx of tourism. However, what brought the city to the world stage was the signing of the so-called "Locarno Treaty" in 1925, which Locarno the nickname the "Town of Peace". Just off the palm-lined lakefront, the "Piazza Grande" is lined with charming old houses, cafes and restaurants, and is transformed into an open air cinema every August for the International Film Festival. The Renaissance-era Old Town fans out from the square, culminating in the 13th century Castello Visconteo, which houses the Municipal and Archeological Museum. High above the city, the 15th century Santuario della Madonna del Sasso offers superb views and a richly decorated interior.

name: Padangbai
description: The vast majority of travellers who make it to Padangbai are just passing through, as it runs the ferry connecting Bali with Lombok. Outside of the ferry service, the town is still very much traditional fishing village at heart that caters to divers and snorkelers. Scattered around the town are several temples, including the 11th century Pura Silayukti. Set on a headland, visitors can walk along the beach and then take a short path to reach one of Bali's oldest temples, which was once home to the great Hindu sage Empu Kuturan. A testament to the town's identity, if you're looking for something to eat, fresh grilled fish is usually one of the cheapest options!

Since then, over 40 buildings from around Wales were collected and rebuilt on the castle grounds to present 500 years of Welsh history. Stroll the castle's formal gardens, peek into a medieval church, or visit a Victorian school to learn how people in Wales have lived, worked, and played over the centuries. Special workshops bring the history to life as craftsmen demonstrate traditional techniques, such as the wood whittling wiles of one of Wales' last clogmakers. For more information, please visit museum.wales/stfagans

description: According to Roman legend, the Cascate del Murino were formed after Jupiter threw a lightning bolt at Saturn, but missed and hit the ground. Today, the picturesque springs, which tumble past an old mill in a series of pools and cascades are a free, natural spa popular among locals. A great photo-op, visitors who bring their own towels and bathing suits can hop into the 100 F therapeutic waters any time of year. There's even a bar where you can buy drinks, sandwiches, and snacks.

name: Ixmiquilpan
description: Ixmiquilpan was founded in 1550 by a group of Augustinian monks who were accompanying Spanish soldiers scouting the area. They began by building the church and monastery of San Miguel Arcángel, which remains the heart of the city. The monastery and church are beautiful examples of the heavy "fortress"-like buildings with intricate plateresque details favored by the Augustinians. But, they were built using forced indigenous labor, which caused tension with the artists working on the church. The result is a series of murals depicting scenes from indigenous Otomí mythology like Jaguar knights, eagle knights, coyote warriors, and other fighters locked in battle instead of your typical Biblical scenes. In the 16th century, indigenous iconography was forbidden by the Spanish, making these murals all the more intriguing.

name: Bonifacio
description: Rising majestically from the turquoise waters of the Mediterranean Sea, cliff-top Bonifacio weaves ancient history into its coastal charm. Reported to be the mythical site of Odysseus' encounter with man-eating giants, the city itself grew around a 9th century fortress. Explore the nooks and crannies of the 9th century Genoese citadel before taking on the 187 steps of Escalier du Roi d'Aragon - a dramatic staircase carved into the southern cliff face. Gaze out to uninterrupted sea views from the marine cemetery, with village-like rows of houses where ship-wrecked sailors lay to rest. A descent to the Old Town will envelop you in brasseries, cafes, bars, boutiques and piazzas - and further down, the harbor's seafood eateries beckon. Take a boat ride out from the harbor to gain a vantage point of the uniquely shelved limestone cliffs. Left untouched by bustling tourist seasons, Bonifacio's reefs and the neighboring Lavezzi islands boast colorful marine life and unforgettable aquamarine waters that will leave you feeling like you've stumbled upon a secret.
