name: Cartagena
description: One of the best harbours in Western Europe, the city has been settled since at least the 3rd century BC. Today, it offers visitors a wide range of attractions from various stages of its history. At the historic harbour, visitors can still see the 18th century sea wall built by Charles III, and the prototype of the world's first submarine, and visit the Naval Museum or National Museum of Underwater Archaeology for more maritime history. The city has a slew of Roman sites such as the 1st century Roman theatre, which is considered one of the most important in Spain, with a museum for the artefacts found on the site. There's also the remains of the old forum, which still has its luxurious marble floors, and the adjoining Roman baths. For something more recent, the city also offers some gorgeous modernist buildings, such as the Belle Époque town hall.

name: Strasbourg
description: From a Roman military outpost, Strasbourg has grown into one of the most beautiful and important European cities. Known as one of the four de facto capitals of the European Union, it was the first city in the world to have an entire district classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Petit France, accessed by crossing a 14th century fortified bridge, is filled with charming half-timbered houses dating back to the 1500s. Criss-crossed by waterways, weirs, and locks, this lost-in-time district is also a great place to sample classic Alsatian fare like tarte flambée. Strasbourg's standout monument is its towering sandstone cathedral. Begun in the 12th century in the Romanesque style, it evolved into one of the most spectacular examples of Gothic architecture - not to mention holding the title of tallest building in the world until 1874. From the impossibly delicate facade to the monumental organ played by Mozart, every aspect of the cathedral is sublime.

name: Durham Castle and Cathedral
description: Durham Castle and Cathedral were built at the end of the 11th century under the orders of William the Conqueror to house the relics of St. Cuthbert, as well as defend the northern borders of England. The site's innovative architecture foreshadowed the Gothic style, and stands as a monument to the power of the prince-bishops of Durham, who resided here until the complex was donated to the University of Durham. Today, the Cathedral is considered the one of Britain's finest monuments, and it's easy to see why with its perfect proportion, and elegant architecture, which still house the relics of Saint Cuthbert. The serene cloisters are of particular interest for pop-culture fans - they were featured in Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. Across the green, visitors can take a guided tour of the castle, which is still used as a very Potter-esque student residence. Stepping into the Great Hall it's hard not to expect letter-bearing owls to fly in.

name: Fukuoka
description: Fukuoka, Kyushu's largest city and one of Japan's most populous urban centers, holds a significant place due to its proximity to the Asian mainland. An important harbor city since ancient times, it was even chosen as the landing point for Mongol invasion forces in the 13th century. Divided into Hakata and Tenjin districts, it offers a blend of historical charm and urban vibrancy. The city is renowned for its affordable and delicious cuisine, including tonkotsu ramen and the local specialty, goma saba. The Hakata Dontaku Festival during Golden Week and the Hakata Gion Yamakasa in July are notable highlights, attracting millions of attendees each year. Dazaifu Tenmangu, an ancient shrine, preserves the legacy of scholar and politician Michizane Sugawara, with a spectacular plum blossom display in spring. The city's manageable size allows easy exploration of nearby mountains, beaches, and attractions like Fukuoka Tower.

name: Cajamarca
description: Those seeking a taste of ancient Inca civilization will find most of the historical gems outside the actual city of Cajamarca in nearby archaeological sites and excavations. However, the city itself stands up as the site of the historic battle between the Inca Emperor Atahualpa and Spanish conquistadors, making it a bastion of Peru's most important historical turning points. Visitors will appreciate the colonial architecture of the city's various cathedrals, and the adventurous will try the traditional local food (guinea pig on the menu!). And if you happen to be here in February, you can participate in Carnaval - the most raucous and celebratory festival of the year, all month long!

name: Mare Anglaise
description: Mare Anglaise in Seychelles beckons travelers to discover a coastal haven where tranquility meets tropical allure. With its ivory-white sands and inviting cerulean waters, Mare Anglaise offers an idyllic retreat for sun-seekers. The gentle waves create a soothing melody as visitors stroll along the shoreline, absorbing the breathtaking vistas of the Indian Ocean. This coastal haven is perfect for those seeking both relaxation and a connection with nature. Mare Anglaise is renowned for its stunning coral reefs, making it a haven for snorkelers and divers eager to explore the vibrant marine life beneath the surface. The crystalline waters reveal a kaleidoscope of colors, with coral gardens teeming with tropical fish and other mesmerizing sea creatures.The surrounding area boasts lush landscapes and verdant hills, inviting adventurers to embark on scenic hikes and nature walks. Discover the unique flora and fauna that thrive in this island paradise, with the Morne Seychellois National Park nearby providing opportunities for immersive exploration.

name: Ciudad Victoria
description: Named after Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico, Ciudad showcases rich cultural heritage with an abundance of green spaces and attractions. The Metropolitan Cathedral, an iconic religious structure with a striking neoclassical facade, stands as one of the most important architectural gems in Ciudad Victoria. The Tamatan Zoo offers a delightful escape into nature, while the Juarez Market immerses visitors in a bustling hub of local flavors and craftsmanship. For those seeking relaxation and outdoor enjoyment, Parque Bicentenario provides a serene setting to unwind. Meanwhile, the Museo Tamux will take you on a captivating journey through the history and culture of Tamaulipas, featuring exhibits on indigenous heritage, the Spanish conquest, and the state's development. If visiting in October, enjoy the Tamaulipas International Festival, where musical and cultural events take center stage—and all year 'round, don't pass up the opportunity to sample some savory grilled meats or thick corn tortillas.

name: Lviv
description: Established in the 13th century, Lviv's had a rough history, being conquered by everyone for the Mongols to the Swedes and Poles. Through it all, the locals adhered to their Ukrainian identity, with the city playing a key role in the fight for Ukrainian independence from the Soviet Union. This resistance helped the city retain its old-world charm, steadfastly denying the Soviet-aesthetic. In the UNESCO-protected Rynok Square, visitors will find 400 years of architectural history, and 4 fountains, presided over by the 19th century town hall. Visitors who brave climbing the stairs to the top of the town hall are rewarded with the best view in the city. The beautiful building next door is now the main branch of the Lviv History Museum, where visitors will find thousands of artefacts from the city's long history, and an exceptionally charming cafe. Proving the city is still Ukraine's cultural capital, visitors can head to the Dzyga art gallery for contemporary art exhibition by

name: Ba Ho Waterfalls
description: The Ba Ho Waterfalls provide a great alternative activity for those needing a break from the beach. Literally meaning 'three-pool stream' in Vietnamese, a half-hour hike through the forest with a bit of boulder hopping brings visitors to the first pool. Here, you can relax on the rocks, and take a dip in the cool water to refresh. More adventurous visitors might want to try for the 2nd and 3rd pools, which require some climbing to reach, but are even more impressive, and less crowded. Please note: this stop is not recommended for people with mobility issues.

name: Herrenchiemsee
description: Only accessible by ferry, this island retreat was built more as a 'Temple to Fame' rather than a residence. As expected of the man known as 'Bavaria's fairytale king', the stunning interior is pure extravagance, boasting the most opulent of décor. While you'll pass through room after decadently-decorated room, nothing can truly prepare you for the sight that is the Great Hall of Mirrors, an amazing 1,000 feet 'tunnel of light' that runs the entire length of the garden and is an almost perfect copy of the Galerie des Glaces in Versailles. Once you have your breath back from this show of affluence, come back down to earth with a visit to the Ludwig II Museum that contains fascinating artifacts from the reign of one of history's more eccentric characters, and humble yourself at the Augustinian canon seminary with its abbey buildings. Default stop time is for the ferry ride and tour - if you'd like to linger a little longer, just add some time!

name: Mantua
description: Mantova lies in the southeastern part of the Region of Lombardy. It stands on the banks of the River Mincio and is surrounded by three lakes: Lago Superiore, Lago di Mezzo, and Lago Inferiore. The city was founded in 2000 BC and attracts visitors interested in history, art, and architecture. Mantova's old town area became a World Heritage Site in 2008 based on its Renaissance architecture. The charming alleyways are lined with arcades, handmade crafts, and local wine and cheese stands. One of Mantova's most notable monuments is the beautiful palace Palazzo Te, or Tea Palace. Designed by Giulio Romano in Renaissance style, the Tea Palace features a number of exquisite frescoes. Today, it's home to the city's Civic Museum. Another imposing monument is the Ducal Palace. Once used as a residence of the powerful Gonzaga family, the palace is a huge complex made up of over 500 rooms, including buildings, courtyards, and gardens. The little gem known as Mantova attracts visitors eager to explore Renaissance architecture and palaces.

name: Santa Marta
description: Santa Marta was founded by the Spanish in 1525, making it their first settlement in Colombia, and the second oldest in South America. The city's importance to the Spanish made it a target for English and Dutch pirates, who ravaged the colonial town over the centuries. Today, it's a rough-at-the-edges port city that's a popular retreat for Comlobian holiday makers. For the average tourist, the main draw is the old city center, where the colorful colonial buildings have an authentic "lived in" vibe. The Catedral de Santa Marta in particular is worth seeking out as it's considered the oldest cathedral on the continent, and was the resting place of Simón Bolívar before his remains were sent back to Venezuela. You should also seek out the Museo del Oro Tairona in the old customs house. This free museum has a well curated collection detailing the history of the region's four indigenous groups complete with English descriptions.

name: Wroclaw
description: Did you know the Mongols invaded Poland? In 1241 Wroclaw was abandoned, becoming a casualty of the First Mongol Invasion of Poland. Rampaging Mongols not-withstanding, Wroclaw's absorbed Bohemian, Austrian, and Prussian influences over its long history, making for a unique architectural and cultural make-up, culminating in Rynek, its magnificent market square. Spanning the Odra River, over 12 islands, with 130 bridges and riverside parks, Wroclaw begs to be explored. For lovers of Gothic architecture, the beautifully preserved Cathedral Island can't be missed.

name: Padua
description: The picturesque city of Padova blends art, culture, nature, and spirituality in a unique mix. There are many churches, canals, and daily markets to explore. Padova's largest tourist attraction is the Scrovegni Chapel (Cappella degli Scrovegni). This chapel is home to priceless frescoes by Giotto, considered one of the greatest artworks of all time. This is just one of eight buildings with masterwork 14th-century frescoes that make up Padua's UNESCO World Heritage Site. Another acclaimed attraction is The Basilica of St. Anthony of Padua. The basilica, dating back to 1232, is filled with magnificent art and is one of Christianity's most popular shrines. The town center is lovely to explore and has many historic arcaded streets to wander. Parks and gardens are also plentiful. With all that, it's clear that Padova (perhaps northern Italy's oldest city) is worth a second glance.

name: Chacahua Lagoons National Park
description: Just off the Oaxaca coast, the Chacahua Lagoons National Park has blessedly remained off the radar of most tourists. Only reachable by boat, a tiny village supports the handful of visitors who come for the laid-back atmosphere, beginner-friendly surf, lagoons, and mangroves. Take either a direct boat (around 45-60 min for 200-600 pesos per person) or go local on a boat and colectivo truck (35 minutes and around 100 pesos per person) from El Zapotalito to Chacahua. At the main beach, you can rent a surfboard or sign up for lessons. For calmer waters, walk down to the estuary and jump off the sandbank into the river and float into the sea. Or, if you prefer, extend your visit for a few hours and hire a local boat for a sightseeing tour of the mangroves and lagoon. Since Chacahua is still a fishing village, it's also a great place to fill up on all the seafood you can handle!

name: Jauja
description: Back in the 1500's, before Lima took the title, Jauja served as the capital of Spanish Peru. It's known as the "Land of Cockaigne", a mythical paradisaical place where you can live without having to work. When the Spanish arrived to Jauja they thought they had found utopia in this idyllic small city! It maintains its charm today as an immaculate town just off the beaten tourist track. If you're there on a Sunday or Wednesday, don't miss the famous weekly markets to get your hands on local handicrafts for low prices. Regardless of what day you're in town, don't miss the Baroque Juaja Cathedral and the Gothic Capilla Cristo Pobre church, and for an insight into the pre-Incan Xauxa culture, there's an archaeological museum and a fossil museum in town. Or, just outside of town enjoy a boat ride around Laguna de Paca before tucking into some local cuisine at one of the surrounding lakeside restaurants.

name: Ba Na Hills
description: Built around an early 20th century French hilltop resort, the Ba Na Hills is one of Vietnam's most ambitious projects. Accessed by a record-breaking cable car, visitors are treated to fantastic views of rich forests and the distant coast en-route to a whimsical recreation of a medieval French village, complete with cobbled streets and half-timbered houses. While strolling, make sure you don't miss the instagram-famous 'hand bridge'. Thrill seekers will want to try out the Alpine Coaster, which lets you fulfill your need for speed while catching some fantastic views, or head indoors, where the drop tower provides panoramic vistas through a glass dome before dropping you 95 feet into a cave inspired by Jules Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth and Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. For more information, please visit banahills.sunworld.vn

name: Dickenson Bay
description: Considered one of Antigua's most beloved beaches, Dickenson Bay's allure captures the hearts of both tourists and locals who frequent its shores. Situated in the northwest region of the island within St. John's Parish, this beach is known for its inviting white sands, calm waters, and the delightful array of restaurants, beach bars, and water sports facilities. Among the options for dining in the vicinity, the Beach Restaurant and Bar stands out, offering not only nourishing meals and snacks but also cooling cocktails to combat the tropical heat. Dickenson Bay boasts renowned accommodations like Sandals Grande Antigua Resort and Siboney Beach Club, as well as attractions like Ana's Restaurant and Art Gallery and Coconut Grove. As you savor your fare, the splendid views include nearby uninhabited islands and a vibrant coral reef, inviting exploration below the waves.

name: Masaya Volcano
description: The Masaya Volcano is the centerpiece of Nicaragua's oldest and largest National Park. The still-active volcano is the result of an even larger prehistoric volcano that collapsed on itself during an eruption thousands of years ago. This also formed a second volcano and five major craters within the park. After entering the park, you can first stop at the visitors center, where you can learn about the park's history, natural ecology, and of course, the area's volcanoes. From here you can head up to the main attraction - the volcano crater (for safety reasons, only one is open to the public). For the viewing platform on the rocky rim, you can gaze across an other-worldly landscape, and down into the famed 'lava lake'. If you happen to visit around sunset (between 5:00-8:00 PM), you're treated to a completely different experience, with the red glow of lava below, and the stars twinkling above.

name: Villarrica
description: From Flocking Pilgrims to Portugese Bandits, Villarica has had a lasting appeal throughout its long history. Moved seven times to stay standing, today it is still regarded by many as Paraguay's second most important city after the capital Asuncion. A blend of native traditions and heavy European immigration has created a melting pot from which many of the country's premier academics and cultural icons have emerged. Begin your journey at the Plaza de los Héroes to see the architectural jewel that is the City's main theatre and then explore the many parks and churches this walkable city has to offer.

name: Kerak
description: The rocky spur on which Kerak Castle stands has been fortified since Biblical times when it was a city in the kingdom of Moab. The vast fortification seen today was built by the Crusaders in the 12th century as the center of Transjordan and their most important fortress on the King's Highway between Jerusalem and Aqaba. After having withstood several sieges, the castle finally fell to Saladin in 1189 and was expanded under Mamluk rule. Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt nearly destroyed the castle castle while capturing it in 1840. Today, Kerak Castle is an excellent example of medieval military architecture, and the Crusader and Arab elements are clearly distinguished - the former used dark volcanic tufa, and the later, white limestone. Visitors enter the castle through the Ottoman Gate, after which you can wander its courtyards and battlements and delve into its vaulted passageways (a flashlight is recommended). Tucked away in the lower part of the castle is a small Archaeological Museum, where you can learn more about the site.

name: Bayamo
description: Founded in 1513, Bayamo was the third Spanish city in Cuba. While it thrived in its early years as an inland port, specializing in trading contraband in the Antilles, it cemented itself in history as an insurgent stronghold in Cuba's war for independence - a position that saw much of the city reduced to ash from arson in 1869. Today, things are more tranquil, with life revolving around Parque Céspedes, one of the largest and leafiest plazas in Cuba. At its center is a large statue of Carlos Manuel de Céspedes, the leader of Bayamo's insurgency. His house borders the north side of the park and is now a museum dedicated to the local hero. From here, walk a block to the Plaza del Himno to see the charming Iglesia Parroquial del Santísima Salvador, another survivor of the 1869 fire, where you'll find a mural of Céspedes above the altar. Transportation here is unique if you'd like to travel around the city - nearly half the residents rely on horse-drawn-carts, many of which operate like buses.

name: Dover Castle
address.addr1: Castle Hill Rd, Dover CT16 1HU, UK
description: First built as a Roman fort in the 1st century, Dover Castle as it stands today took shape under the auspices of King Henry II, who replaced the wooden fort that had stood on the site with a stone great hall surrounded by a curtain wall. Over the centuries, further expansions and modifications were made to the castle, including secret tunnels and gun batteries, allowing it to remain in use until 1958. Today, visitors can experience the different eras of the castle's history in its many exhibition areas. In the Great Tower, the lavish lifestyle of Henry II's medieval court comes to life through an ambitious recreation of the medieval rooms, and on select dates, the characters of the court themselves. Visitors can also delve into the secret tunnels to see the WWII underground hospital, and learn about Operation Dynamo, the greatest rescue operation in history. For more information, please visit http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/dover-castle/

name: Jecheon
description: Jecheon is nestled in North Chungcheong Province, with alluring garden complexes and pristine lakes. Jecheon's allure is enhanced by the pristine waters of Uirimji Reservoir and Cheongpung Lake, which mirror the azure sky and the majestic Woraksan, Sobaeksan, and Chiaksan mountains. These serene waters beckon adventure enthusiasts with opportunities for paragliding, kayaking, and zip-lining, all set amidst the breathtaking landscape. In the vicinity of Jecheon Hyanggyo Confucian School, the quaint Gyodong Minhwa Village showcases a vivid display of local artistry. Local artists have adorned the town with vibrant paintings, infusing it with colors and turning it into a captivating tourist site. The artwork encompasses themes of scholastic achievement, long life, eternity, hope, success, and more, offering a delightful glimpse into Korean folk traditions. Visitors can immerse themselves further in the traditional craftwork, as local workshops sell folk painting-inspired handicrafts, pottery, and even offer minwha fan-making and baking minwha-inspired cookies.

name: Copiapo
description: Copiapó, situated in northern Chile, stands as the capital of Copiapó Province and the Atacama Region. The town is steeped in mining heritage, notably commemorated by a bronze statue of Juan Godoy, the discoverer of the Chañarcillo silver mines during the 19th century. The Copiapó-Caldera railway line, established in 1850, holds the distinction of being South America's first. The city attracts visitors with its stark desert landscapes and indigenous landmarks, such as the Inca cemetery and the Museo Regional de Atacama, which offers insights into the region's natural history, human heritage, and mineral wealth. The museum showcases a diverse range of artifacts, from ancient indigenous pottery to weaponry from the War of the Pacific. Additionally, it pays tribute to the resilience of the 'Los 33' miners who were successfully rescued after being trapped underground for 69 days in 2010. Copiapó, with its mining legacy, desert allure, and rich history, beckons travelers to explore its unique blend of culture and natural wonders.

name: Miskolc
description: Lillafured became an attractive tourist destination in the 1930s and a center for those seeking healing and relaxation. Today, the pre-war ambience of Lillafured Palace has been retained and sits comfortably in the twenty-first century in one of Hungary's most beautiful locations. The pleasant walks around the palace in the hanging gardens make for a peaceful and memorable experience of the beauty of nature. Close by in Miskolc is the Cave Bath of Miskolctapolca, a "lake bath" channeled by water out of hard bath stone over thousands of years. It is a unique experience to swim in passages thousands of years old surrounded by nature in water known for its recuperative powers. The network stretches over three miles while the basins inside and outside the cave enable visitors to relax and enjoy the sounds, fragrances and the unique atmosphere of the only bath cave of this type in Europe.

name: Cosala
description: Cosalá, a small city in the state of Sinaloa, captures the essence of a bygone era where ghosts of a thriving mining town and trade center linger in the urban landscape. The historical downtown area, characterized by its irregular geomorphic design, will enchant you with its charming streets and unexpected corners that unveil beautiful sights at every turn. The architecture made of beams, reeds, bamboo roofs, mud and tiles seamlessly integrates with the natural surroundings. Plaza de Armas boasts an 1800's gazebo, and horse-drawn carriages roll across the cobblestone taking tourists around the city. The plaza is home to vendors selling refreshing juices, homemade candies, and typical Cosalá gastronomy such as sweet breads and dulce de leche. Visit the magnificent 18th-century Santa Ursula Temple for an iconic example of colonial-era Sinaloa Catholic architecture, with hidden tunnels connecting it to neighboring homes. With ghost stories and sightings still passing through the town, Cosalá truly brings the past to life. Photo by E. Ruvarey under CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Durnstein
description: Durnstein first sprang to fame back in the tenth century when Richard the Lionheart was imprisoned in Durnstein Castle by Leopold V after tearing up the Austrian flag and refusing to share his spoils of war. His petulance earned him a year in the castle dungeon until a ransom was paid for his release. The castle ruins still remain intact and after a short hike, these romantic remnants offer panoramic views of the natural and cultural sites that line the Wachau Valley. The landscape is marked with natural beauty such as the old vineyards that when coupled with the warm climate, create an unforgettably picturesque scene that lives long in the memory. After strolling the medieval streets and passageways, what better way to refresh yourself than with a glass or two of the excellent local wine at one of the cozy taverns or shaded garden restaurants that populate the landscape.

name: Bouake
description: Plunge into the vibrant heart of Côte d'Ivoire at Bouaké, a captivating city where history, culture, and modern energy collide. Imagine yourself strolling along the historic Rue Houphouët-Boigny, lined with colonial-era buildings adorned with intricate balconies and colorful facades. Picture yourself stopping at a charming cafe, sipping on a refreshing glass of Bissap juice and soaking in the contagious energy of the city. Every corner whispers tales of Bouaké's rich past, from its role as a French colonial hub to its vibrant art scene. Explore the bustling Marche du Centre, a sensory explosion of sights and sounds. Amidst the stalls overflowing with fresh produce and local crafts, discover hidden gems – innovative artwork by talented Ivorian artists. As the sun dips below the horizon, Bouaké transforms into a vibrant tapestry of twinkling lights and lively music. Catch a performance at a local "maquis," where pulsating rhythms and energetic dance moves. Photo by: Gilly Zed, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chefchaouen
description: Chefchaouen was founded in the 15th century as a fortress to fend off the Portuguese invasion of Morocco. A century later, it welcomed Muslims and Jews from Andalusia who had to flee Spanish persecution during the Reconquest. At some point in the 20th century, the traditional buildings of the medina were painted a vibrant sky blue. One explanation for the decision is that blue keeps mosquitos away, while another theory is that it was introduced by Jews fleeing Hitler in the 1930s with the blue serving as a reminder of heaven and God's power. The most cynical is that the decision was made in the 1970s simply to attract tourists. Regardless of the reason, the winding alleys and traditional buildings rendered in a brilliant blue are undeniably entrancing. Add to that the traditional handicrafts and cuisine not found elsewhere in the country and you're in for an unforgettable experience, and countless photos if you ever need a reminder.

name: Navojoa
description: Step into the past and immerse yourself in the rich heritage of Navojoa, filled to the brim with local museums and historical sites. The Regional Museum of the Mayo, housed in a historic building that once served as the region's railroad headquarters, showcases vivid static displays that narrate the history, culture, and traditions of the Mayo people. Visit the Hu-Tezzo museum, which mirrors the caverns discovered in the region and features prehistoric paintings and petroglyphs, offering a glimpse into the lives of early inhabitants. Explore the city's vibrant municipal market, the Mercado Municipal, where you can shop and savor traditional Mexican cuisine. Stroll through Plaza Cinco de Mayo and witness the newly renovated concert shell with enchanting backstage murals. This plaza is a starting point for monument walks and offers a tranquil space to observe the lively spirit of Navojoa's residents. Photo by Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

name: Piura
description: Also called the "Ciudad del eterno calor" or "The city of eternal heat," it's no wonder many visitors to Piura flock to the closest beaches to cool off from the inland desert landscape. But that doesn't mean the city itself is lacking! On the contrary - as the third city the Spanish founded when they settled South America in the sixteenth century, Piura is known for its depth of "mestizo" or mixed culture, bringing together Indigenous, Spanish, African, and Chinese influences. You'll be sure to find a fascinating variety of food (such as local dish Seco de Chavelo), dance, and architecture. Don't forget to stop by the historical park Plaza de Armas, which has hosted many military parades over the years, and check in to the Piura Cathedral for a precious example of colonial history.

name: Trebon Lake Area
description: While Třeboň may lack the large tourist numbers associated with larger towns and cities, it more than makes up for this with the historic and natural charms that greet visitors as they turn each corner. The town center displays a captivating mix of Baroque and Renaissance buildings and is surrounded by a variety of parks leading to delightful and relaxing walks without having to leave the city. Visitors can stroll around the large sixteenth-century carp ponds and experience nature as it was intended. The town is no less admirable with its fourteenth-century Renaissance chateau set alongside an English-style flower park. After exploring the town's squares, monuments, and religious sites, including the Schwarzenberg Mausoleum and the Augustinian Monastery, visitors may wish to relax and watch the world go by as they sample a quiet drink or two served on the terrace of the town's famed Regent brewery.

name: Etretat
description: The little fishing village of Etretat became the go-to destination for well-to-do Parisians at the end of the 19th century when getting some sea air was all the rage. An avalanche of attention followed, with painters including Monet and Eugène Boudin immortalizing its beautiful white cliffs on canvas. Guy de Maupassant spent most of his childhood here, and Maurice Leblanc chose the Hollow Needle as the hiding place of Arsène Lupin's (France's most famous fictional gentleman thief). It's no wonder that Etretat has been a destination for over a century - just look at the soaring white cliffs and their stunning formations. During low tide you can even walk through one via the "manhole". While the town's continued popularity means there's no shortage of modern hotels, you can still find a slew of extravagant 19th century villas, and a unique early 20th century covered market.

name: Bolsover Castle
description: Built in the 17th century on the site of a medieval castle, Bolsover Castle was captured and slighted by Parliamentarians during the English Civil War. Within a few decades, the castle was returned to good order, and ultimately became a seat of the Dukes of Portland. After enjoying the stupendous views from the castle battlements, visitors can step into the riding house for an introductory exhibition, where intriguing facts about Bolsover Castle are revealed. Within the castle, a labyrinth of rooms and halls showcase elaborate wall art, exquisitely carved marble fireplaces, and stunning painted ceilings. The 'Little Castle' has no ropes or barriers, and encourages visitors to take a hands on approach and enjoy the reproduction furniture. The lavish lifestyle of Sir William Cavendish is revealed in the 17th-century style 'cabinets of curiosity'. The castle's indoor Riding School, one of only four classical dressage schools left in the world, also puts on regular shows of cavalier horsemanship and training demonstrations. For more information, please visit english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/bolsover-castle

name: Tauranga
description: Picturesque Tauranga is one of New Zealand's fastest growing cities and for good reason. In addition to being a hub for international trade, business and shopping, this beach getaway boasts glistening turquoise waters and endless beaches that are perfect for water sports such as kayaking, diving, paddle boarding and surfing. During your visit and after taking a dip, take a stroll through one of the many parks that dot the city. Visit the popular Tauranga Art Gallery or schedule a tour of the historic mission house known as The Elms. Still haven't had your fill? Look into a dolphin-watching tour or charter a fishing boat (and taste the fruits of your labor later). Whether you're looking to relax or be reinvigorated, Tauranga has something in store.

name: Manuel Antonio National Park
description: Manuel Antonio National Park was established in 1972 through local conservation efforts. It is Costa Rica's most visited natural sanctuary despite being one of its smallest. Spanning just 1,983 hectares of land and 25,634 hectares of marine area, this Pacific coastal gem attracts millions with its perfect blend of pristine white-sand beaches, rocky islands, and lush tropical forests. The park features four stunning beaches, Manuel Antonio, Espadilla Sur, Tesoro, and Playita, which are connected by accessible hiking trails that wind through habitats supporting remarkable biodiversity. 109 mammal species and 184 bird species call Manuel Antonio National Park home. Visitors routinely encounter three-toed and two-toed sloths, three monkey species (howler, squirrel, and capuchin), iguanas, coatis, and numerous birds, including toucans and parakeets. The park's thoughtfully designed infrastructure, including bioclimatic visitor centers and universal access facilities, balances human enjoyment with environmental protection. Please note that with daily visitor limits of 600 people, early arrival is recommended during peak season.

name: Copán
description: The Mayan city of Copan was first settled around 2000 BC as a small village. Little is known about the pre-Classical settlement, but around the 5th century AD, it began its rise to becoming a major city state. Despite its importance, with an estimated 20,000 inhabitants at its peak, Copan collapsed in the 10th century and was left abandoned. Today, the ruins are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, standing as an exceptional example of Mayan architecture. Apart from the impressive architecture, what really sets Copan apart from other Mayan ruins are its exceptional carvings. One monumental staircase is marked with over 1,250 individual glyphs, making it the longest known Mayan inscription, while other buildings are ornamented with intricate friezes. There's even a museum on site where you can learn more about the city and see the more delicate artefacts. While you can roam the ruins yourself, it's highly recommended to sign up for a guided tour to better understand what you're seeing and gain access to more of the site.

name: Anse Boileau
description: Anse Boileau in Seychelles invites you to indulge in the serene beauty of an unspoiled tropical paradise. With its powdery white sand and crystal-clear turquoise waters, Anse Boileau beckons sun-seekers to bask in the idyllic Seychellois sunshine. The gentle waves create a soothing soundtrack as you stroll along the shoreline, feeling the soft, warm sand beneath your feet. Nature enthusiasts will be enchanted by the verdant surroundings of Anse Boileau. The nearby Montagne Posée offers a picturesque hiking trail, rewarding adventurers with panoramic views of the village, the Indian Ocean, and the lush hillsides. The dense vegetation surrounding the village is home to a variety of endemic flora and fauna, creating an immersive experience for those eager to explore the Seychelles' unique biodiversity. The charming village exudes a relaxed vibe, providing a delightful escape for those seeking tranquility and a taste of local life.

name: Chattanooga, TN
description: Beginning as a Cherokee settlement, Chattanooga quickly grew into a trade center and industrial hub. In the 21st century, it reinvented itself as one of the most progressive in the south. The pride of Chattanooga is the Tennessee Aquarium, which has both fresh and saltwater sections. You'll be able to see and touch creatures from around the world, and not just aquatic ones! If one of the best aquariums in the US doesn't do it for you, how about a stroll through one of the many waterfront parks? Just a short walk from the aquarium, the Walnut Street Bridge is the longest pedestrian bridge in the world! Then there's the vibrant Bluff View Art District, where you'll find some of the city's best museums and eateries. If you didn't visit it on your trip in to Chattanooga, be sure to take the Lookout Mountain Incline Railway from the historic St. Elmo's neighborhood!

name: Weimar
description: Back in the eighteenth and nineteenth-centuries, Weimar was regarded as the cultural center of Europe with Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, Bach, Liszt and Lucas Cranach all deciding that this post-World War I symbol of liberal democracy was the place to be. Nowadays, the city is often described as a "park with a town attached to it" and this becomes clear after a walk through romantic Park an der IIm, which contains Goethe's Garden House along with a host of other monuments from the 'Age of Enlightenment.' It is rare to find a public park that is so vividly green and breathtaking in the middle of a city. The river dissects it with plenty of bridges and benches to take a rest on and admire the cultural treasures that seem to be everywhere. Park an der IIm is such a unique part of the city and is a must-see if you like parks…and even if you don't!

name: Vigo
description: Centered in one of the finest natural ports in the world, which has been utilized since Roman time, Vigo now claims to be the largest fishing port in the world. Overlooking the city is the 17th century Castro Fortress, which was intended to protect the city from invaders, but proved lacking. The historic Cidade Vella, is centered around the old maritime quarter of O Berbés, near the port. Here, among the network of tiny streets is the Collegiate Church of Santa María. Built in the Neoclassical in style, it stands on the rubble of a Gothic church burned down by the pirate Francis Drake. But if you only do one thing in Vigo, make sure you visit the unmissable Pedra market, just north of the church. A fascinating experience, the famed ostreiras, or female oyster sellers, offer visitors fresh Galician oysters to slurp on the spot.

name: Ferrara
description: Situated in the Emilia-Romagna region of Italy lies the remarkable cultural landscape of Ferrara. The Este family governed here for three centuries and can be thanked for the city's unique blend of medieval and Renaissance. Although Ferrara suffered damage during WWII, its historical core remains intact. Today, the center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its breathtaking beauty and its important place in Italy's art and culture. The winding cobblestone streets and wide range of museums, art galleries, busy shops, and cafes make Ferrara a can't-miss destination. One of the city's most important monuments is Castello Estense. This moated castle, built in 1385, served as the stronghold and residence of the Este family. The many castle rooms, including dungeons and prison cells, are a sight to see. Another noteworthy sight is Ferrara's Cathedral, built in 1135. This cathedral is a shining example of Romanesque and Gothic architecture. Wander the city sights while taking in all the splendor that is Ferrara.

name: Xpujil
description: Today, Xpujil is a quiet village that's a popular home base for tourists looking to explore the famous Mayan ruins dot the region. Many visitors, however, don't know that Xpujil itself was once a thriving Mayan settlement with ruins of its own. Inhabited between the 4th and 13th centuries, most of the structures here are typical of the Classic Río Bec architectural style, including their use of "false" temples, which have no feasible function. However, the dully named "Structure 1" is unique in the region for its three-tower construction, rather than the usual two.

name: Ankara
description: Settled since the Bronze Age, Ankara was overshadowed by the various other urban centers that dominated Turkey's history. This all changed in the 1920s when Mustafa Kemal Atatürk led the anti-Allied resistance from Ankara, and made it the capital of Turkey. While most tourists pass the city over, writing it off as a modern development, it offers some fascinating cultural sites if you know where to look. The hilltop citadel has some elements dating back to the 7th century, and is surrounded by the Old Town, which is filled with traditional buildings and is slowly being restored to be more tourist friendly. There are also several Roman ruins scattered around the city, including baths and a theatre, but the most significant is the Monumentum Ancyranum, where the most complete record of Emperor Augustus' life and deeds was discovered. Those with an interest in history and culture won't want to miss the exceptional Museum of Anatolian Civilisations.

name: San Cristobal de La Laguna
description: The 15th century colonial city of San Cristóbal de La Laguna - with its founding square, Upper, and Lower Town - was harmoniously designed according to philosophical principles and has influenced famed locations around the world such as Old Havana in Cuba. Its historical center, filled with leafy courtyards and brightly coloured buildings, earned its reputation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. Walk through the array of historical buildings such as Teatro Leal and House of the Marquises of Torrehermossa, and catch a glimpse of the incorrupt body of Mary of Jesus de León y Delgado in the Monastery of St. Catherine. You might even sense the lingering spirit of Cataline Lercarco haunting the Museum of the History of Tenerife. San Cristóbal de La Laguna is a marvel of architectural varieties, from the neoclassical, neo-gothic and baroque stylings of the early 1900's La Laguna Cathedral to the beautiful courtyard of the 16th century Church and Former Convent of St Augustine.

name: Tuxtla Gutierrez
description: The site of a Pre-Columbian settlement, today's Tuxtla Gutierrez was likely founded in 1560 when Dominican monks established a community for the dispersed Zoques around the Saint Mark's Cathedral. Today, the 16th century church is still the spiritual heart of the bustling capital, which marks the hours with chimes accompanied by figures of the apostles. The Zoológico Miguel Alvarez del Toro Zoo is said to be one of the best zoos of its kind in Latin America, and exhibits, studies, protects, and preserves local species. In total, the zoo is home to 1,400 animals from 220 species, including jaguars, tapirs, macaws, howler monkeys, and quetzals. The Regional Museum of Anthropology and History is one of the best in Mexico, covering both pre- and post-Spanish history, with the state's only paleontological museum standing next door.

name: Monschau
description: Dating back to the 12th century, Monschau rose to prominence in the 18th century thanks to its booming textile industry. Though the textile industry diminished in the 1900s, it left the town with a wealth of historic buildings. Today, the historic town center looks much as it did 300 years ago, its cobbled lanes lined with rows of half-timbered houses bearing flower-filled window boxes. The 18th century Red House is the town's standout landmark. Built by the textile-industrialist Scheibler family, the red-brick facade stands out from the surrounding half-timbered houses, and the interior is a lavish display of Rococo, Louis XVI, and Empire-style decor. Of the many amazing furnishings, the highlight is the self-supporting oak staircase which features elaborate carvings depicting the various stages of textile production. To get a real taste of local culture, heade to the 150-year-old Felsenkeller Brewery & Museum, or the local mustard mill.

name: Aktun Chen
description: Aktun Chen might not be the largest eco-park in Mexico, but it offers a wide variety of activities for nature lovers. The main attraction is the park's 5-million year old cave, which is filled with such stunning stalactites and stalagmites, bizarre columns, and cascading curtains that National Geographic named it one of the 10 Best Underground Walkways in the World. Afterwards, you can swim with the fishes in the bright blue waters of the park's underground cenote. Above ground, the large eco-park is home to a variety of local flora and fauna including adorable spider monkeys, Coatimundis, Kinkajous, and Tall Tail deer, while the exhilarating zip line lets you fly through the jungle like one of the park's many tropical birds.

name: Taif
description: Taif's moderate climate and enchanting mountain resorts make it a sought-after destination for both locals and tourists seeking respite from the scorching Arabian summers. Taif is affectionately referred to as the "City of the Roses" due to the fragrant and unique flowers that flourish in its fertile valleys. Visitors are spoiled for choice when it comes to attractions. The Taif Cable Cars offer breathtaking views of the city, while the awe-inspiring Al Wahbah Crater, a geological marvel, leaves visitors in awe. The Qantara Mosque, adorned with Abbasid-inspired architecture, stands as a testament to the region's historical significance. Shubra Palace, once a royal residence for King Abdulaziz, has transformed into a museum offering insights into the area's history. The striking Al-Kaaki Palace, characterized by juniper wood, granite stone, and intricate glasswork, showcases the artistic fusion of various architectural influences. With its scenic beauty, cultural festivals, and historical treasures, Taif beckons as an irresistible blend of history and modernity, waiting to be explored and admired by all who venture to this remarkable city.

name: Providence, RI
description: Founded by Roger Williams in 1636, Providence grew into one of the first thirteen colonies and subsequently played an integral role in the American Revolution. The vibrant coastal city has since developed into New England's third most populous metropolis. The Downtown area spans three rivers, and between May and November, hosts Providence's signature "WaterFire" - a series of lit braziers in the river. There are still vestiges of Providence's history, such as the "Mile of History" on Benefit Street. One of the standouts here is the 18th century John Brown House, which offers a glimpse into life in the 1700s. The Roger Williams Park, which includes a zoo and Museum of Natural History, is another favorite for visitors and locals alike. And if art is your thing, the RISD Museum of Art is one of the largest and best in the US, with exhibits covering everything from Ancient Egypt to Andy Warhol.

name: Basildon Park
description: Basildon Park built towards the end of the 18th century in the elegant Palladian style, with fine neo-Classical furnishings. The house frequently changed owners over the years, and by the 20th century was all but derelict. In fact, after a failed attempt to dismantle the building and move it to the US, it was stripped of its furnishings (much of the dining room is now in the Waldorf Astoria) and abandoned. In the 1950s, the Lord and Lady Iliffe purchased the estate, and spent years restoring it, scouring the country for 18th century fittings to create their home. Today, the house decor is a fabulous mix of old and new, where visitors can admire the delicate original plasterwork and staircase and 18th century furniture alongside a large collection of seashells, and a fully-stocked 1950s kitchen. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/basildon-park

name: Toyama
description: Toyama, where tradition meets contemporary charm, promises a unique Japanese adventure that unveils a rich cultural tapestry. The city's waterfront promenade, Mirato Mirari 21, has undergone a transformative makeover, inviting visitors to enjoy enchanting evenings by the water. Sports enthusiasts can revel in the excitement as Yokohama hosts major Japanese teams in football, rugby, and baseball matches. Culinary aficionados will relish Toyama's diverse restaurant scene, while nightlife comes alive on the vibrant Noge Street. The Toyama Glass Art Museum, housed within the architecturally striking Toyama Kirari complex, showcases captivating glass art. This modern museum offers a budget-friendly artistic journey, complete with a souvenir shop and a cozy café. Himi Banya-gai beckons seafood lovers with its bustling harbor market and natural hot spring facility, providing a feast for both the senses and health. Toyama Castle Ruin Park invites exploration with reconstructed castle remnants and a tranquil moat. Amidst the urban bustle, this park thrives with nature and hosts a mesmerizing cherry blossom spectacle.

name: Warsaw
description: Founded in the 13th century, Warsaw became the capital of Poland in 1596 when King Sigismund III Vasa moved his court from Kraków. However, to say the city's had a turbulent history would be an understatement: it's been sacked by the Swedes and Transylvanians, withstood the full force of the Red Army, and was nearly annihilated during World War II. Warsaw, however, rose from the ashes more vibrant than ever. The UNESCO-listed historic center was one of the most ambitious restoration projects in history, and now stands in all its colorful 18th century glory. At the Warsaw Uprising Museum, you can learn about the bloody battle that caused the deaths of as many as 300,000 Varsovians and the city's destruction, while the POLIN museum is dedicated to the history of Polish Jews. However, the city's museum's aren't all so sobering - you learn about the legacies of Chopin and Marie Curie, or test the laws of nature at the groundbreaking Copernicus Science Center.

name: Greenwich
description: Maritime Greenwich grew around the 16th century Palace of Placentia, and over the years grew to become the nation's scientific and maritime centre. The 17th century Royal Observatory played a vital role in navigational developments like longitude, and of course, set the world's time standard, and now houses a fascinating museum, and London's only planetarium. Visitors can also head to the National Maritime Museum, the world's largest on the subject, to learn about the island nation's legendary seafaring history, including heroes like Admiral Nelson. To complete the experience, step aboard the famous Cutty Sark, the world's last tea clipper, and the fastest ship in the world back in its day, to see what life at sea was like in the 19th century. The 17th century 'Queens House' was built for Anne of Denmark, and is considered one of the most important landmarks in all of Britain as it was the country's first classical building, and now houses a sumptuous art museum.

name: Paestum
address.addr1: Via Magna Graecia, 918, 84047 Paestum SA, Italy
description: Founded by the Greeks in 600 BC, the city was conquered by the Romans in 273 BC. However, the fall of the Empire, malaria outbreaks, and raids by the Saracens eventually forced the population to abandon the city. Today, the archaeological site is home to three of the world's best-preserved Greek temples, most notably the large Temple of Hera, which was once thought to be dedicated to Neptune. The Temple of Ceres, which is actually dedicated to the Athena, was transformed into a Christian church in the middle ages, and still houses three tombs. The museum is filled with smaller and more delicate archaeological finds, including ceramics, daily paraphernalia, and even frescoes such as the iconic Tomb of the Diver funerary fresco.

name: Huajuapan
description: An ancient Mayan settlement, Huajuapan went under Spanish Colonial rule to become an agrarian viceregal territory. Near the present day town is a hill known as the Cerro de las Minas, the site of an ancient Mixteca settlement. Here, you will find a museum containing relics liek pottery and valuables once owned by the indigenous population that inhabited the site. In the city itself is a quaint plaza overlooked by the Cathedral of Our Lady of Guadalupe. The plaza is lined with trees, botanical gardens and kiosks for the people's leisure. Once you go out of the city, you will find Las Campanas, which is a cluster of calcite rocks that drip water creating a great sightseeing attraction.

name: San Antonio Oeste
description: Divided into three distinct localities, the heart of San Antonio Oeste, located on the western shore of the bay, exudes a quiet elegance. Notable landmarks, such as the neo-classical Municipality and the neo-baroque Church, add character to the town's modest yet inviting architecture. The harbor section, characterized by picturesque old wooden houses, provides a glimpse into the town's maritime heritage, creating a nostalgic ambiance. The beaches of San Antonio Oeste emerge as the main attractions, offering a quieter alternative to the bustling Las Grutas. With diverse landscapes, from rocky shores with interesting formations to sandy stretches with stunning views, these beaches provide a serene escape for visitors. Playa El Fuerte, located to the south, boasts sandy expanses and scenic views of the coastal landmark, El Fuerte. Beyond its coastal allure, San Antonio Oeste is a haven for culinary enthusiasts. Charming restaurants, both in the town itself and in San Antonio Este, serve delightful fish specialties, inviting visitors to savor the maritime richness of the region.

name: Bohemian Switzerland
description: The artist Ludwig Richter set up his easel in this land of weirdly weathered rocks and medieval robber-baron hideouts while Carl von Weber set his famous opera Der Freischütz in one of its towns. There are some beautiful spots to just linger in, such as the pretty village of Jetřichovice in the Děčín district with its baroque church, though for a more active approach try the village of Tiské (Tisa) in the Elbe Mountains. Tiské gives its name to the Tiské Stěny, the 'Tisa Walls' one of the most captivating natural formations in the area. Rising to the north of the village to a height of over 600 meters, these sandstone walls enclose a whole labyrinthine sandstone city. Rock towers and needles, honeycombs, gates, windows, and whatever your imagination can sculpt out of the sandstone as you walk through a dense network of narrow gorges and ravines. But don't worry, the robber-barons have long since been captured. Most of them anyway.

name: Vejle
description: From its buildings, street art, landmarks and indoor and outdoor exhibits, Vejle is a city proudly enshrined in art. While mostly known for art, Vejle has everything to offer from outdoors, vibrant city life, shopping, family friendly outings, gourmet food and history. Named Denmark's best shopping town, you can find a unique and welcoming shopping experience from design shops, antiques to home decor with plenty of chances to stop for a break at its many cafes. If the outdoors are your more your thing, you will not be disappointed. In the Vejle outdoors you can experience everything from cycling tours, canoeing, fishing, camping and other exciting adventures in the country's scenic downs.

name: Monteriggioni
description: Dominating a hilltop in the rich Tuscan lowlands, this walled city was built by the Sienese at the beginning of the 13th century to defend the Cassia Road, and the cities of the Val d'Elsa and Staggia. Today, the walls are still in almost their original condition, the only changes being when the towers were lowered in the 16th century, and in 1921, 3 of the towers were lowered to the same level as the walls. Today, visitors are still able to walk the walls, and a combined ticket includes access to the interactive Armoury museum. The Romea Gate opens up into the main Piazza di Roma, which was originally used as a large vegetable garden that provided food when the town came under siege. Facing the square is the Romanesque Church of Santa Maria Assunta, which is as old as the town itself.

name: Port Royal
description: Port Royal was once a hub of English commerce in the New World, infamous for its devil-may-care atmosphere and home sweet home to pirates, prostitutes, and opportunist Englishmen. This notorious city was even ruled by the ultimate pirate, sir Henry Morgan, later lieutenant governor of Jamaica. As if struck by divine retribution, it was wrecked by hurricanes and fires, a powerful earthquake sinking a good chunk of the city underwater. What was left of Port Royal served as a Royal Navy Dockyard until almost completely destroyed by another earthquakes in 1907. Today, most of the 17th-century city rests beneath 40 feet of water, and what is left on the surface is a small fishing village. The underwater city has been a subject of interest to archeologists from around the world and is often compared to Pompeii for its archaeological significance. One of the top attractions in Port Royal includes the Port Royal Maritime Museum, which showcases the history of the notorious pirate city, Fort Charles, a 17th-century military fortification with sweeping views of the Caribbean Sea, and the nearby Giddy House, an artillery storage house.

name: Chania
description: Chania, Crete's second-largest city, is also its most enchanting. It can trace its history back to the Neolithic era, but it was the Venetians and Ottomans who shaped the Old Town into the . The city's multicultural heritage is on proud display in the old harbor, where you can see Venetian shipyards (which now house an excellent maritime museum), a 17th century Ottoman mosque, and a 9th century Egyptian lighthouse. Step back from the water into the Old Town's warren of narrow streets and alleys, you'll find the colorful houses punctuated by Byzantine and Minoan ruins, Renaissance churches, Venetian fortified walls, Turkish baths, and a centuries-old municipal market. Add in some fascinating museums and excellent eateries, and it's easy to see why Chania has become Crete's top destination.

name: Tiberias
description: Founded in around 20 CE, Tiberias is said to have been built on the site of the ancient Israelite village of Rakkath. Around 150 CE, the Jewish court settled here and cemented Tiberias as the Jewish political center in the Land of Israel. While much of the modern city is marred by architectural eyesores from the 1970s, this Galilee resort town is still dotted with reminders of its rich past. Most notably, the Hammat Tiberias National Park preserves the ancient spa that was so famous that Roman Emperor Trajan had a coin minted in its honor. Death is also a big draw in Tiberias, with the Old Cemetery offering both Jewish and Muslim sections, and the Tomb of Meir Ba'al Hanes standing as one of Judaism's holiest sites. There are also medieval churches, and remnants of Muslim rule, like the citadel that dominates the beach.

name: Valldemossa
description: Nestled in the Tramuntana mountains, just a short drive from Palma de Mallorca, Valldemossa beckons with its enchanting charm and captivating cultural tapestry. Valldemossa gained fame as the winter haven for Polish composer Frédéric Chopin and French writer George Sand in 1838/9. Their stay in the monastery, now a museum, adds a touch of romantic allure to this mountain retreat. Explore the Real Cartuja, a Royal Carthusian Monastery, where Chopin's original piano resides in cell number four, and immerse yourself in the town's unique history. Costa Nord, a cultural center founded by Hollywood actor Michael Douglas, adds a contemporary touch to Valldemossa's cultural landscape. Discover the island's only saint, Santa Catalina Thomas, in the peaceful surroundings of Sant Bartomeu's church. For outdoor enthusiasts, Valldemossa is an ideal base for exploring the Tramuntana mountains. Hike to Puig des Teix for breathtaking vistas or stroll through the town's cobblestone streets, filled with shops and boutiques. Indulge in Valldemossa's famous Cocas de Potatas biscuits and explore the vibrant Sunday market.

name: Cascada El Salto de Eyipantla
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: Cascada El Salto de Eyipantla is a monstrous waterfall in Los Tuxtlas and, according to legend, is home to the ancient Aztec God of Rain. The powerful falls crash into a roaring river below to create quite a dramatic scene. The falls are impressive in their own right but many choose to visit the location where Mel Gibson's epic adventure Apocalypto once filmed. Steps lead visitors down to the bottom of the falls so you won't have to take the 50 meter plunge. There is also a viewing platform at the top of the falls for a bird's eye view of the churning waters below.

name: Tenom
description: Tenom combines natural beauty, cultural heritage, and endless cups of flavorful coffee, making it a must-visit for travelers seeking an authentic experience in the heart of Sabah. Its fertile land has made it an agricultural hub, with rubber being the primary crop. Soybeans, maize, vegetables, and cocoa also contribute to the local economy, with Tenom coffee gaining popularity as a renowned local specialty. Yit Foh Coffee Factory, founded in 1960, offers a taste of Tenom's finest roasted Robusta coffee, prepared using traditional methods. Fatt Choi Coffee Factory is another notable establishment to visit, providing a fascinating glimpse into the coffee production process. For a unique experience, hop on the North Borneo Railway, which has been transporting crops from Pangi to Tenom since the 1900s. The vintage train journey offers picturesque views of the Padas River, paddy fields, rainforests, and rubber plantations, immersing visitors in the nostalgic charm of the past. The Tenom Orchid Centre offers a glimpse into the stunning world of orchids, while the Murut Cultural Centre provides insights into the indigenous heritage of the region. Cycling enthusiasts can explore the Melalap paddy fields, capturing stunning photos against the backdrop of the vast fields and enjoying the romantic atmosphere.

name: Palmerston North
description: Home to one of New Zealand's largest educational institutions, Massey University, the cultural standing of Palmerston North is nothing to sniff at. Not only is there the university, but a bounty of theater and music venues, as well as the Te Manawa Art Museum and National Rugby Museum, inform the city's vibe as a quietly thriving artistic hub. If you need to stretch your legs, there are a diverse range of scenic walks, such as the Manawatu Riverside Walkway. And certainly do not miss "The Square" at the very center of the city: a green haven, and great jumping-off point to explore the surrounding area.

name: Capernaum
description: Established in the 2nd century BC on the main trade route connecting Damascus and Egypt, Capernaum flourished until the 11th century when it was abandoned. The city plays prominently in the Bible, being cited in all 4 gospels as the home of the Disciple Matthew, and where Jesus lived after leaving Nazareth and worked many of his healing miracles. The ruins of the 3rd century Ancient Synagogue stand atop the original synagogue where Jesus gave the Sermon on the Bread of Life, and performed several miracles. Nearby are the foundations of the home of St. Peter, said to be where Jesus resided while in Capernaum, which became a place of worship after Jesus' death, and is now protected under a glass floor in a modern Franciscan church.

name: Little Petra
description: Little Petra is believed to have been built during the 1st century as a suburb of the famous Nabatean capital, as both an agricultural and residential center, and stopping point for traders on the Silk Road. Like its big sister, Little Petra was abandoned after the decline of the Nabataeans, and used only as a camp by Bedouin nomads until its excavation in the mid-20th century. Reached by a sun-blocking canyon, this free destination offers visitors a more immersive experience than Petra - you can explore the site freely. One of the most unique sights is a dining room discovered in 2010 that has Hellenistic-style frescoes considered to surpass even those at Herculaneum in Italy. It's also worth taking a little time to visit the nearby archaeological site of Beidha - a neolithic settlement dating back to the 11th millennium BC.

name: Montgomery, AL
description: From the seat of the Confederacy to being the birthplace of the Civil Rights Movement, Montgomery, Alabama is an ongoing tale of struggle, perseverance, and beauty. If you are interested in American history, this city is the place to be. Visit the Rosa Parks Library and Museum, where you can learn of the courageous woman who sparked the Civil Rights Movement. For a more comprehensive lesson, head to the Civil Rights Movement Memorial, which marks the pivotal turning point of the last century. If you love the 1920s, go straight to the Scott & Zelda Fitzgerald Home and Museum to learn about the glamorous tale of the 20th century's most starstruck lovers, as well as their life works! If you like jazz, catch a show at the Sous La Terre Blues and Jazz Club for some soulful sounds.

name: Helen, GA
description: Helen, GA was founded as a logging town in the early 20th century. But as that industry fell into decline, the town had a creative solution: to reinvent itself as a Bavarian-themed tourist attraction. Since 1969, all buildings have been required to follow an alpine theme, right down to the fast-food chains. The cobbled streets along the Chattahoochee River are lined with colorful buildings that look like they've been transplanted from some tiny German village. The shops and restaurants specialize in Bavarian fare, so you can grab a pretzel and sausage with a mug of beer while you explore. There are over 200 specialty and import shops selling everything from handmade candles and glass to cuckoo clocks and quilts so you can get a German souvenir without ever leaving Georgia.

name: Bacharach
description: But why struggle? This historically significant little town has as much to offer as several other Valley towns rolled into one. On a 520 foot crag sits Castle Stahleck, of unknown foundation, though we know it was occupied in the late 11th Century. The emblematic Werner Chapel, a still poetically potent Romantic ruin, is probably the most evocative piece of High Gothic architecture in the area, while the Market Tower is an impressive survivor of the ten which were once part of the town walls. The market place itself is one of the best places to sample a few of the many delightful and lovingly preserved half-timbered houses in the town, such as the 'Old House' and the Kurpfalzische Munze, a gold and silver coin mint in the middle ages. Bacharach's charm seeps underground too. It can be sipped in the form of home-grown wines in the old brick-arched wine cellar of the Winery Stahl.

name: Tbilisi
description: Established in the fifth century AD, Tbilisi has a rich history, having been the capital for numerous Georgian kingdoms and republics. Tbilisi is distinctively Georgian being the heart of the country, yet its cultural fabric is richly woven with influences from a myriad of cultures, creating a captivating blend of diversity within its authenticity. Its abundance of attractions is too vast to enumerate, but there are a few standout sights that should not be missed. For one, explore old town and the city's street art. The city's identity is also shaped by its numerous churches and cathedrals, including the Holy Trinity Cathedral and St. Nikoloz Church. Next, take a cable car ride from Rike Park to the Narikala Fortress or check out Mother of Georgia monument for panoramic city views. Don't forget to walk across the iconic Bridge of Peace, a striking contrast to the traditional cityscape. Tbilisi, which translates to 'warm place' in Georgian, is named for its numerous sulfurous hot springs, which are well worth a visit. Lastly, no trip to Tbilisi is complete without immersing yourself in the culinary delights of Georgia. Sample quintessential dishes such as khachapuri and khinkali, and wash it down with fine Georgian wine.

name: Bolgheri
description: First mentioned in 1075, when its boundaries were being drawn, the town grew around the 11th century castle. Sitting on a hilltop, the brick bastion dominates the surrounding farmland, and it's easy to see why it was attacked on several occasions, and has been owned by the Della Gherardesca family since the 13th century. Today, it's still the first thing that emerges from the 5 kilometer long cypress boulevard made famous by Carducci's "Davanti San Guido". Nearby, the Church of Saints James and Christopher is the oldest building in the area and has maintained its medieval essence, even after its 1902 renovations. Of course, no visit to this charming village is complete without stopping to sample its world-famous wine, such as the Super Tuscan Sassicaia, which is considered one of the finest red wines in Italy.

name: Chichen Itza
description: First settled in the 5th century, Chichen Itza became the most powerful city in the Yucatan around 1000AD after it was conquered by the Toltecs. This blending of Mayan and Toltec cultures made Chichen Itza one of the most diverse ancient cities in Mesoamerica, a tradition that was preserved in its art and architecture. The most famous monument is, of course, the 30 meter high pyramid, with its serpent-headed staircase. If you're visiting around the equinox (or come for the night show), you'll see how the corners of the pyramid were carefully constructed to create a serpent-like shadow on the sides of the staircase. But the pyramid is just one part of this once-great city - nearby you'll find the Great Ball Court, the Skull Wall, and multiple temples. And in the group of buildings to the south, a stellar observatory. Then there's the older Puuc-style neighborhood, with monuments like the Temple of the Panels and the Temple of the Deer.

name: Concepcion
description: Concepcion began as a humble fort, but quickly grew into one of Chile's most important cities. Briefly serving as the capital of the Kingdom of Chile, the Chilean declaration of Independence took place here, and Concepción elites dominated Chilean politics through the 19th century. Today, the bustling port is known for its just-as-busy cultural scene. Many of Chile's top rock bands get their start here, and at the Casa del Arte, you'll find the second largest art collection in the country. History is also alive and well. The Natural History Museum is a great place to learn about Chilean prehistory. Or for something a little more recent, board the Huáscar for a hands-on history lesson on the Chilean fight for independence. And, while the center of Concepcion sits back from the water, if you want something a little more peaceful (or just love seafood), head to Caleta Lenga. This tiny beach town is known for its tranquility, and dense number of great restaurants.

name: Jesus Maria
description: Nestled just four kilometers north of Estancia de La Caroya, Jesús María's origins are intertwined with the Royal Road to the viceroyalty's capital, shaping its development over the centuries. Evolving from barracks into brick and stone constructions, the estate's architecture reflects a unique blend of monastic and mercantile influences. The estate's church, characterized by a simple façade and a distinctive vaulted aisle, houses a significant central dome adorned with native American-inspired reliefs. The venue's viticulture prowess gained global recognition, with Lagrimilla, an exquisite wine, becoming the first American wine tasted at Philip V's royal table in Madrid. The museum showcases the original wine-making basement and a diverse collection of archaeological finds, religious artifacts, and Jesuit treasures. Annually, the city comes alive during the Festival Nacional de la Doma y el Folclore, a ten-day celebration since 1966, attracting over 200,000 attendees from around the world.

name: La Loma
address.region: Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina
description: Nestled atop a small hill to the north of the island, this quaint town offers a mesmerizing panorama of San Andrés and the picturesque Caribbean Sea. It's a place where the true essence of island life is preserved. The inhabitants, descendants of Afro-Caribbean slaves who migrated from Jamaica and neighboring islands, have created a vibrant and unique community. Here, English and Creole are the primary languages, and walking its charming streets feels like stepping into a colonial past. The iconic Baptist Church, built in 1844 and reconstructed in 1896 after a storm, stands as a testament to the island's architectural heritage. However, the true gem of La Loma is the viewpoint at the town's edge, a place the locals consider magical. From this vantage point, visitors are treated to breathtaking vistas of the "seven-colored sea," with its mesmerizing shades of blue and green. Take a leisurely stroll through this vibrant village, appreciate the colorful houses, and immerse yourself in the melodious sounds of Caribbean music.

name: Augsburg
description: Augsburg was home to the Fuggers, bankers to the Hapsburgs and the Papacy, who left a still-living mark in the shape of the 'Fuggerei', the world's oldest social housing area. Originally founded for the city's poor in 1516 this charming complex still operates on the same virtually rent-free principle. It's open to visitors, and both the original and modern apartments can be viewed; there's also a small museum dedicated to its philanthropic founders. Also unique to Augsburg is a UNESCO-listed system of canals and water towers dating back to the 14th century, which continue to supply the city with water. The city is also renowned for its wealth of Rococo monuments (so much so that it was called the Augsburg style in Germany), and while there's much to marvel at in Augsburg Cathedral, such as the oldest stained glass windows in Germany, the standout of which is the City Hall and its decadent Golden Hall where you'll find fabulously pompous portals, coffered ceiling, and murals.

name: Abydos
description: Abydos has been inhabited by the rulers of Egypt since before the days of the Pharaohs, and was used up until the 4th century BC and the arrival of the Ptolemaic dynasty. During its heyday, it was the center of the Cult of Osiris, and a major pilgrimage site for Egyptians. Today, Abydos is considered one of the most important archaeological sites in the country for its ancient temples, and royal necropolis, though much of the city is now buried beneath a modern highrise. The main attraction is the Temple of Seti I, which is an unusual L-shape rather than the regular rectangle. Within this imposing building are some stunning carvings, many of which are still beautifully colored, and the pièce de résistance: a list of almost all the pharaohs that ruled Egypt. Nearby, you'll find the smaller Temple of Ramesses II, and an elegant temple that was devoted to the beloved Queen Nefertari.

description: Right away, you can tell that the Santuario de la Virgen de Schoenstatt isn't your typical Mexican church - the whitewashed walls and steeply sloping roof have a distinctively alpine feel to them. That's because the church was built by the members of the Schoenstatt Movement, which was founded by Father Joseph Kentenich while he was interred at the Dachau concentration camp. After the war, his views of spreading a sense of community caught on, and today, the Schöenstatt Movement has a presence in 42 countries. Though only built in 1980, the Santuario de la Virgen de Schoenstatt has become a pillar of the local community, holding events and weddings to help the faithful live according to their morals. But even for non-believers, the charming church and its quiet gardens filled with local species offer a place to find serenity.

name: Jerash
description: The area around Jerash has been settled since the Neolithic Age, but its Alexander the Great who's credited with founding the city of today. After being absorbed by the Roman Empire, Jerash flourished, and continued to grow until the 8th century when it was devastated by an earthquake. Today, the ruins of the Roman city are considered some of the largest and best-preserved outside of Italy. Walking down the city's colonnaded main street, you'll be treated to exceptionally ornamented monuments like a large Nymphaeum fountain, a Forum lined with 160 Ionic columns, and two theatres. The 3000 seat south theatre is still used for concerts and performances to this day! The city terminates at Hadrian's Arch, which was built in 129 in honor of the Emperor's visit, behind which is the hippodrome where chariots raced for up to 15,000 spectators. It's also worth visiting the Jerash Archaeological Museum to see the many artefacts uncovered over the 200 years of excavations.
