name: Fussen
description: If you think you've seen this castle somewhere before, then you have — it's the real life castle that was the model for the castle featured in Sleeping Beauty, used in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang and inspired Disney to create his Magic Kingdom. Even the location of the castle is simply breathtaking, as it sits at the top of a beautiful gorge in the Bavarian Alps. Built by Ludwig II between 1869 and 1886, the interior of the castle is every bit as awe-inspiring as the outside and reflects his obsession with Wagner, his preoccupation with medieval royalty and his retreat into fantasy. Central to the castle is opera and the works of Wagner, which Ludwig intended to be a shrine to his close friend. Although some rooms were never finished, Neuschwanstein remains the ultimate visitor experience for those looking to come face-to-face with a genuine fairytale castle.

name: Iznik
description: Settled since at least the 4th century BC, Iznik played a key role in shaping the Christian church through the councils held here. In the 14th century it was the capital for the growing Ottoman Empire, and by the 16th century had established itself as a world center for pottery. While war and weather have taken their toll on the city, this tentative UNESCO site is still considered a 'living museum' for its historical and cultural value. Amongst the tile shops and sleepy you'll still find plenty of historic monuments. The 6th century Hagia Sophia hosted the Second Council of Nicaea before being converted into a mosque in the 14th century, and today offers a fascinating blend of Christian and Muslim architecture. The 14th century Green Mosque was built for Çandarli Hayreddin Pasa, the first Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire. His Mausoleum is also located in town and filled with 18 sarcophagi.

name: Visegrad
description: Not long after its founding in the 15th century, Višegrad was conquered by the Ottoman Empire and remained under their rule until 1878 when Austria-Hungary took control. The narrow gauge train line constructed under the Austro-Hungarians at the turn of the 20th century was one of the most expensive railways in the world at the time. Today, it's part of the Šargan Eight heritage railway line, which was facilitated by Serbian film director Emir Kusturica. However, Višegrad is best known for Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge, a UNESCO world heritage site built under Ottoman occupation in the 1570s. Nobel laureate Ivo Andrić popularized the site in his novel The Bridge on the Drina. Andrić's work was so influential that they constructed a tourist site called Andrić Grad (Andrić's Town) near the bridge, which gives visitors an Adriatic style escape in the Balkans.

name: Petra
description: Petra's claim to fame lies in being the birthplace of Fray Junipero Serra, a revered missionary whose legacy extends to the founding of California. Wander the historic streets adorned with majolica tiles, exploring Serra's birth home, the Sant Pere Church, and the baptistery where his journey began. Rich agricultural heritage weaves through Petra's tapestry, evident in the grand Sant Pere Church and scattered windmills paying homage to the town's cereal crops. Explore the well-kept streets, revealing historic buildings like the convent of Sant Bernardí and the iconic Escoles Velles. Immerse yourself in Petra's history at the Fray Junípero Serra Museum, offering a glimpse into the life of this Californian pioneer. Wander the squares—Plaza de Beat Ramón Llull and Plaza de Fra Juníper Serra—where local eateries beckon with culinary delights. Escape to the Ermita de Bonany, a small church atop a hill, for solitude and breathtaking panoramas. Petra's natural landscape beckons hikers and cyclists, with trails leading to the scenic Puig de Bonany. Petra's dining scene is a blend of local authenticity and global flair. Es Celler captures Mallorcan traditions, while Can Salom and C'an Oms offer delectable dishes in charming settings.

name: Avila
description: Founded in the 11th century to protect the Spanish territories from the Moors, Avila's 3 meter thick walls are punctuated by 87 semi-circular towers and nine gates, and is the best preserved medieval bastion in the country. The eastern apse of Avila's cathedral forms part of the town walls, and is half church, half fortress. The church's earlier Romanesque parts are made of a red-and-white "blood" limestone, while the Gothic sections are pure white. These mixed materials continues inside, and is accented by stunning stained glass and Renaissance art. Among the city's many churches, the 12th century Basilica of San Vicente pioneered the Gothic style in Spain, and houses the Cenotaph of the Holy Brothers Martyrs, considered one of the most important works of Romanesque sculptures in Spain. If all the walking has built up your appetite, try the Chuletón de Ávila, a T-bone steak from indigenous beef.

name: Punta Cometa
description: According to local legend, Punta Cometa was used as an indigenous ceremonial center, used for healing ceremonies, astrology, and as a hiding place for Aztec gold. The remnants of a stone wall with an abundance of traditional healing herbs confirm that this rocky peninsula indeed held some importance to the Aztecs. After the 20-minute hike to the point, it's easy to see why they were so mystified by Punta Cometa. As the most southwestern point in all of Mexico, the 180-degree views of the Pacific, especially at sunset, are unparalleled. There are two paths leading out to the point - to the right will take you on a more winding track, while the center is a more direct route. Both do have some rougher sections, so footwear more robust than flip flops is recommended.

name: Cantona
description: Every year 4 ½ million people flock to Teotihuacan to see the extensive city remains and queue for up to 3-hours to climb it's Pyramid Of The Sun. Cantona, on the other hand, was a city almost as big as Teotihuacan, covered in small pyramids, and with the magnificently pointy Pico de Orizaba volcano looming in the background, it has the superior view. It's half the price and there is hardly anybody there - truly a hidden gem of Mexico, belying it's vast nature. At its height, Cantona had around 80,000 people living there. Every section of the city was connected with paved walkways, there were at least 24 ball courts present (more than any other site discovered), and its main avenue stretched over ½km long. Unlike its better-known contemporary there is an undiscovered story surrounding Cantona, given it was mysteriously abandoned 500 years before the arrival of the Spanish.

name: Gaeta
description: Founded as an Ionian colony, Gaeta has been an important military and trade port since its inception, hosting everything from a Roman fort to a NATO naval base. Centuries of success have endowed the city with a wealth of historic monuments, such as the imposing 12th century Aragonese castle, which dominates the old town. The 11th century Cathedral of Saint Erasmus, crowned by a 12 century Arab-Norman tower, houses some stupendous works of art, such as a 13th century Easter candle. The 14th century Church of SS. Annunziata is another highlight, thanks in large part to its ceiling of gilded carved wood. At the Gaeta Archeological Museum, visitors will find artefacts dating back to Roman times, and an art gallery with works from the Renaissance and Baroque ages. If you get hungry while exploring, be sure to try the city's signature 'tiella', a baked pocket sandwich traditionally filled with seafood.

name: Riga
description: An important port since antiquity, the charming cobbled streets of Riga's UNESCO-listed Old Town have over 500 monuments, representing every style from Gothic to Art Nouveau. These are all represented in Riga's Cathedral, the largest medieval building in the Baltics, which also houses the fascinating Museum of the History of Riga and Navigation in its serene 13th century cloister. The 'Three Brothers' gives another overview of the city's long history - these three adjoined houses were built in the 15th, 16th, and 17th centuries, and now house the Museum of Architecture. Just north of the Old Town is the Art Nouveau district, one of the world's richest collections of the style. Fans of the style should head to the Art Nouveau Museum, which is home to one of the most impressive staircases in Europe. For a taste of Riga's cosmopolitan energy, the Central Market is the largest in Europe, housed in 5 beautiful WWI Zeppelin hangers.

name: Huarmey
description: The seaside town of Huarmey looks like any small fishing village at first glance. A smattering of houses, and string of sandy beaches nestle against the rocky coast and its cold waters, with surfers and beachgoers looking to get away from it all being the only regular tourists. However, in recent years, the town has proven to be an archaeological goldmine. A few kilometers outside of town, the remains of 200 people were found on a secluded beach. Dating from 1350 AD, they were blindfolded, bound, and stabbed in the heart as part of a giant human sacrifice - likely by the powerful Chimu people in celebration of conquering the valley. Meanwhile, a few kilometers inland, the stepped pyramid known as Huarmey Castle was an important ceremonial center for the Wari people between the 7th and 9th centuries, and burial site that has given archaeologists a glimpse into the daily lives of nobles.

name: Bucaramanga
description: Though it dates back to 1622, Bucaramanga remained a relatively small settlement until the 19th century when it began attracting German merchants and adventurers. Today, it's one of Colombia's largest cities, and the most successful - with the highest per capita GDP in the country. With over 160 parks, Bucaramanga is aptly nicknamed "The City of Parks" and "Colombia's Beautiful City". For visitors, this makes it a great city where you can relax and recharge, particularly by strolling its green spaces. The most important park in the city is arguably Parque Santander, which is surrounded by economic or historically significant buildings like the elegant Sagrada Familia Cathedral. The best park in the city, however, is the 19 acre Eloy Valenzuela Botanical Gardens, where you can see 3,500 species of native flora while walking its well-maintained trails.

name: Santa Clara
description: From a small inland settlement, Santa Clara has grown into one of Cuba's largest and most historically important cities. It was here that Che Guevara led the decisive battle against dictator Fulgencio Batista y Zaldívar, winning Cuba for Fidel Castro. One of Che's boldest actions during the battle was derailing a train of enemy reinforcements, an action now memorialized by a giant statue. After he was executed in Bolivia, Che and 16 of his fallen comrades were brought back to Santa Clara and interred in a mausoleum. Right next to the mausoleum is a museum detailing Che's life. While Che is a big name here, he's not the only local hero. Head to the Parque Vidal to see a statue of Marta Abreu, the "benefactress" of the city, and some elegant buildings like the Santa Clara Libre, Teatro La Caridad, and the former city hall. Be sure to visit Calle Independencia for a local shopping experience.

name: Wollaton Hall and Gardens
description: Sir Francis Willoughby used nearly all of his resources constructing Wollaton Hall in the 1580s, creating a prodigy house to rival those of royal courtiers. In the 17th and 18th centuries, the interiors were remodelled, though the exquisite Elizabethan facade was left largely untouched. Since 1926 the estate has been owned by Nottingham Council and houses the city's Natural History Museum. Included in the 750,000 object collection are fossils, minerals, shells, taxidermy, and jars preserving more delicate animals in 'spirit'. On a guided tour, visitors can also learn about the manor's history and inhabitants while visiting the well-preserved Prospect Room, roof walkway, and underground Tudor Kitchen and Admiral's Bath. The surrounding 500 acres of gardens and parkland aren't just a popular place for visitors to walk - they attract herds of red and fallow deer. For more information, please visit wollatonhall.org.uk

name: Uruapan
description: Founded in 1533, Uruapan (lit: "Eternal Spring") was named in recognition of the Cupatitzio River that flows through the city. The park is a tropical escape from the hustle and bustle of town, as birds and butterflies fill the trees as ice-cold water cascades over rocks and down waterfalls. In the city, visit La Huatapera Handicrafts Museum, an ex-hospital from the 1500's, for an insight into the city's rich culture. Casa Angosta, otherwise known as The World's Narrowest House at just 1.42 metres wide, is home to an entire family and an unusual sight to see during your time in Uruapan. And did you know that Uruapan is the avocado capital of the world?! The city made it into the Guinness Book of World Records for creating the largest batch of guacamole, producing almost 1,300 kgs using one ton of avocados!

name: Yeoju
description: Yeoju holds great importance in the nation's history, preserving the legacy of past rulers and making significant contributions to contemporary South Korean ceramics. Partnered with the neighboring city of Icheon, it hosts the esteemed World Ceramic Exposition annually. The region also takes great pride in producing high-quality rice, sweet potatoes, and yellow melons. The Namhan River gracefully flows through Yeoju, enhancing its natural beauty. Notably, the city boasts two UNESCO World Heritage sites: the royal tombs of King Sejong and King Hyojong. One of Yeoju's unique attractions is "The Phone," the world's first and only phone museum, exploring Alexander G. Bell's initial invention to the latest smartphones. For nature enthusiasts, the Hwanghaksan Arboretum stands as a picturesque destination to revel in the tranquility and beauty of nature. The arboretum houses 14 distinct gardens, each dedicated to various ecological and functional plant categories, including wetland, stone, mountain fruit, and more.

name: Valenca
description: Dating back to Roman times, there's still a Roman milestone marking the XLII mile of the road connecting Braga to Tui inside the city's fortified walls. During the 12th century, King Sancho I ordered the stronghold populated, naming it Contrasta, meaning "village opposed to another", in this case, the Spanish town of Tui. In the 13th century, King Afonso III changed its name to Valença. The successfully resisted multiple sieges by both Spanish and French forces. Today, a walk along the expansive series of fortifications shows visitors just why the city was such an effective defence, while its streets offer well preserved architecture dating back to the 12th century. The Romanesque Church of St. Mary combines simple architecture with ornate baroque ornamentation. For the best view of the city, visitors are encourage to take a short trip across the Eiffel Tower inspired bridge to Tui.

name: Barichara
description: Barichara began as a humble chapel and handful of houses that were built near the site where the Virgin Mary appeared on a limestone rock in 1702. By the end of the century, a full-fledged village had grown around the site, dominated by a cathedral built from the same yellow sandstone that the Virgin Mary appeared on. Inside, you'll find colorful tiled floors, a remarkable wood and bamboo ceiling, and opulent gilded altar piece. While the Cathedral is the main monument in town, you'll want to wander the cobbled streets, past the whitewashed houses with their red tile roofs and colorful accents to really see why it's named "Colombia's Most Beautiful Village". While the entire region is famous in Colombia for its cuisine, Barichara is a stand-out for foodies looking to try traditional dishes, which can range from sun-dried steak and grilled goat to fried, giant ants, which are best described as something between peanuts and popcorn.

name: Quedlinburg
description: The town owes much of its historic importance to the Saxonian-Ottonian rulers, founders of the first German state. It was the royal residence of 10th century King Henry 1st, out of whose private chapel the Collegiate Church of St. Servatius rose to its present prominence towering on the steep sandstone of the castle hill above the town. The church contains the Quedlinburg Treasure, a gorgeous collection of golden chests, religious manuscripts, ivory grooming items and crystal glassware. The medieval town plan is very apparent as you walk the streets, both within the city walls and outside in the 'new town.' It's the half-timbered buildings in the old town's cobbled streets which turn a stroll into a peripatetic time-trip back to the medieval period, Breite Stresse, leading north out of Market Square is a particular delight. The Square itself is lined with excellent examples of medieval and renaissance buildings.

name: Brindisi
description: First settled as a Greek colony, the city was conquered by the Romans in the 3rd century BC. They worked to capitalize on the site's natural harbour, developing it into a major maritime base, which would later be used by Venetian merchants. The end point on their Via Appia road, its marker column still stands. This important port was well-defended, and is still watched over by the Red Castle and Swabian Castle, which is a venue for major cultural events. The 12th century Church of San Giovanni al Sepolcro has a finely-decorated marble portal, and the city's many other medieval churches, such as the geometric Santa Maria del Casale with its 14th century frescoes, all have their own unique charms. Next to the cathedral, the 13th century Portico of the Templars was actually a bishop's palace and now houses the Museo Ribezzo archaeological museum.

name: Osogovo Monastery
description: Built in the 12th century, nothing remains of the original church. What stands today is a smaller church from the 14th century, while the larger structure is from the 19th. Dimitar Andonov Papradishki's vibrant frescoes on the larger church are fascinating for their unusual imagery, such as flying, disembodied heads, and a particularly pleased-looking Satan. Inside, the masterfully crafted iconostasis houses some valuable icons likely painted by Hristo Dimitrov. Water from the spring next to the church is believed to have healing properties. After the last monk died in 1967, the monastery became a pilgrimage site and peaceful respite, which becomes home to an art colony and an architecture school during the summer.

name: Colima
description: Colima is a tranquil retreat for those looking to escape hectic city life. Despite being the capital of the state, Colima is not the most popular tourist destination in the area but is sure to delight those that venture off the beaten path. The city's residents adhere to a slower pace of life and rest and relaxation are sure to come easy to any visitors. A walk down to the main square demonstrates why Colima is known as the City of Palms. Towering trees, gurgling fountains and cool breezes practically beg visitors to slow down and take a deep breath. Walk the gardens of Jardin Libertad and admire the well-preserved colonial buildings. When you're hungry, try a traditional meal made from corn, local fruits, pork or seafood

name: Vitoria
description: Vitoria was founded by the Portuguese as the Espírito Santo state capital 1551, but didn't really prosper until the 20th century. Now, it's one of the best places to live in Brazil. You have a number of serene beaches (as with most other cities in Brazil, check the water quality report before swimming) and green spaces to enjoy. Parque Pedra da Cebola, with its manicured gardens crowned by a strange rock formation, and Vale Botanical Park are perennial favorites. Or hike to the top of Morro do Moreno for some fantastic views of the coast. For a bit of history, head to the "Centro" district. While a bit tired, the Old Town has some gems, like the 16th century Palácio Anchieta, which now serves as a government building and offers tours. And while technically in Vila Velha, the once can't-miss monument is the 16th century Convento da Penha. Molded to a rocky outcrop, you get amazing panoramic views, historic architecture, and beautiful decor all in one place.

name: Cartago
description: As the first successful settlement in the country, Cartago served as the capital of the Viceroyalty of Costa Rica for 250 years. The most stunning reminder of this status is the beautiful, blue-grey Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles. The church is a local pilgrimage site because of the miraculous Black Madonna displayed on the main altar. It is said that in 1639 a young local girl found the blackened Virgin Mary statue and brought it home, only for it to reappear in its original location the next morning. Also worth visiting are the ruins of Santiago Apóstol Parish in the central park, a beautiful centrepiece for a wonderful public area. Just outside the city is The Lankaster Botanical Gardens, a must-see for plant lovers. If you need a bit to eat, stop by the Cartago Central Market for local cuisine and fresh produce.

name: Budapest
description: Often dubbed the 'Paris of the East', this 2000 year-old city's long history has left it rich in historic buildings. The most noticeable is Castle Hill, where the Royal Palace, Sándor Palace, and high-Gothic Matthias Church dominate the skyline, offering beautiful architecture and unparalleled views of the city. Budapest's neo-Gothic Parliament, the largest building in Hungary, allows visitors to book a tour of the interior in advance. Once inside, visitors can admire the opulent decor, such as a staircase decorated with 25 kg of gold. Saint Stephen's Basilica, has the Holy Right Hand of the founder of Hungary, King Saint Stephen, on display. No visit to Budapest is complete without a stop at The New York Cafe, considered 'the most beautiful cafe in the world,' where guests can enjoy a coffee or upscale meal in a breathtaking Rococo hall.

name: Uluwatu
description: The heart of Uluwatu is its temple, which is believed to have been established 1000 years ago by the revered monk Mpu Kunturan, who founded several other temples on the island, though another local legend attributes the temple to the priest Danghyang Nirartha. Within the temple you can find a 10th century winged gate, a brahmin statue admiring the view of the Indian Ocean, and even a Megalithic coffin. What made Uluwatu an international destination is the beach below the cliff. Discovered by surfers in 1971, Uluwatu is now one of the most famous breaks in Bali. Even if you don't plan on paddling out, visitors can hang on the beach, grab a snack from one of the many garungs, or explore the dramatic ins and outs of the rocky coastline.

name: Ice Village
address.addr1: Ice Village 星野リゾート トマム アイスヴィレッジ
description: Tomamu Ice Village is a testament to locals of Hokkaido transforming frigid nights into joyous celebration. Climb to the observatory overlooking the entire Ice Village, then descend on the thrilling ice slide. Glide gracefully on the naturally formed skating rink, rent skates, and create fantastic memories on ice. Explore the Ice Sweets Shop, where milk gelato is slowly frozen on an ice plate, or savor hot-chocolate-dipped ice cream bars at 550 yen each. The Ice Bakery & Cafe offers 15 varieties of ice breads, heated on the spot for a freshly-baked treat. Indulge in hot cheese fondue at the Ice Bar and discover the brand new Original Gin made with Tomamu's snowmelt. Beyond delightful treats, immerse yourself in various domes featuring an Ice Musical Instrument Shop and a Snow-themed Ice General Store with Hokkaido artist-crafted goods. Engage in craft-making at the Ice Atelier, sculpting your own ice glasses or creating a snow crystal keychain. Visit from December 10, 2023, to March 14, 2024, between 5PM and 10PM, with an admission fee of 600 yen, and let the Ice Village captivate your senses in this unforgettable Hokkaido retreat.

name: Strbske Pleso Mountain Lake
address.addr1: Štrbské Pleso, 059 85 Vysoké Tatry-Štrbské Pleso, Slovakia
description: Štrbské Pleso is one of the best go-to destinations for all fun outdoor activities in Slovakia. Skiing is the major sport of the region, as it offers multiple ski lifts and slopes. But during any time of year, it is more than a mountain; it is a resort, a lake, and a town. Štrbské Pleso's origins began as a hunting lodge owned by a noble family that later opened it up to tourists. With the advancement of railroad technology, this resort gradually expanded in size and attractions. It is the starting point for popular hikes including to Kriváň and Rysy, as well as a great place to relax and unwind. Less than a 20km drive from the international airport of Poprad, Strbske is a beautiful resort with much to offer.

name: Loch Ness and Urquhart Castle
description: Loch Ness & Urquhart Castle are one of the most popular destinations in Scotland thanks in large part to the legendary monster that dwells beneath the lake's waters. While the earliest mention of a monster at Loch Ness dates back to the 6th century, Nessie wasn't brought to international attention until 1933. Decades of obsession have never turned up any conclusive results, but explanations for the monster range from tree trunks to a bathing circus elephant to a Greenland shark. And while you probably won't see the beast, a boat trip on the lake is made more exciting by the legend. Overlooking the lake, the sprawling Urquhart Castle is one of the largest in Scotland, where visitors can enjoy a guided tour, or simply roam the ruins, to appreciate this majestic medieval castle, and great views of the Loch Ness.

name: Vang Vieng
description: Though it's been settled since the 14th century, Vang Vieng isn't a historical attraction. Instead, this riverside city is a contemporary basecamp for exploring the region's famed karst mountains. A party hotspot for backpackers during the 1990s, things have since mellowed out, and the town center is gradually becoming more refined, with better restaurants, shops, and accommodations emerging to cater to their new clientele. However, the famed river tubing experience is still the main activity in town, though it's now a much more relaxed affair, with a focus on sitting back, and soaking in the lush surrounding (though there's still a few bars you can stop at along the way).

name: Bovec
description: Bovec is a small mountain town near Triglav National Park. It's a haven for nature lovers and adrenaline junkies alike. Bovec is the perfect place to escape city life. Visitors find themselves enchanted by charming waterfalls, caves, and crystal clear waters. The stunning nature also makes Bovec the ideal spot for outdoor activity. Sports such as hiking, cycling, rafting, kayaking, or skiing at Bovec Kanin (Slovenia's highest ski resort) are in high demand. If you prefer a more relaxed atmosphere, the charming city center is filled with many restaurants and bars to enjoy.

name: Tende
description: With prehistoric rock carvings alluding to an ancient origin, it's unclear when Tende was initially settled, though the oldest record dates back to the 7th century. The village had a particularly tumultuous recorded history, being fought over by French and Italian powers, finally becoming a part of France in 1947. Today, this isolated town is notable for being largely preserved-but-unpolished, its multi-story medieval houses showing centuries of wear. Wandering the narrow streets and alleys you'll find fine such as carvings and frescoes on cracked facades, giving Tende a tangible 'Old World' feel. The town clocktower exemplifies this living history - the structure is the last remnant of a medieval castle destroyed by Napoleon that was repurposed to house a clock. Tende's main monument is the 16th century Collegiale Church of Notre-Dame, with its beautiful baroque facade, and remarkably decorated interior.

name: Knole
description: Knole manor as it stands today was constructed in the 15th century as an archbishop's residence, with additions made in the 16th, and 17th centuries when it became the property of the Lord High Treasurer Thomas Sackville. It's Sackville's renovations that the estate is known for today, for it has remained essentially unchanged, and still stands as a 'monument to private greed.' While the 7th Baron Sackville and his family still live in Knole's private apartments, the manor's formal spaces belong to the National Trust, meaning visitors can experience its historic grandeur. In the rich showrooms, visitors will find lavish furnishings and rich artwork from the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries that have been carefully conserved in their original states. Once home to Vita Sackville-West, author and former lover to Virginia Woolf, a unique audioguided tour reveals the lives of Knole's women. Visitors can also enjoy a walk through the manor's deer park, walled garden, and medieval orchard. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/knole

name: Conwy Castle
address.addr1: Rose Hill St, Conwy LL32 8AY, UK
description: In the 13th century, Edward I built a series of imposing castles in Northern Wales to cement his authority in the region. Along with the formidable fortification, Edward also had the English colony of Conwy surrounded by a defensive wall. Abandoned in the 17th century, the castle fell into ruin, though its attracted atmosphere attracted artists. Today, visitors can scale the castle's towers to for stunning views of the quaint historic center of Conwy and its town wall, explore the inner and outer wards with their many rooms, and roam the ramparts of the wall and its 21 towers that still guard the town. While in Conwy visitors can also enjoy some traditional Welsh cuisine, and see the smallest house in Britain, which is only 3.05m x 1.83m.

name: Husavik
description: Settled by the Swedish Viking Garðar Svavarsson around 870, Húsavík is the oldest town in Iceland. It's known as the country's whale-watching capital thanks to the 23 species of cetacean, including the Blue Whale, that can be spotted in the bay. At the Whale Museum, you'll learn about whales, marine ecosystems, and man's impact on them - and see skeletons from 9 different species in the gallery. For those looking to learn more about Iceland in general, head to the Museum House at Húsavík, which houses a maritime museum, natural history museum, folk museum, district archives, photograph archives, and an art gallery. Finally, the Exploration Museum covers the entirety of man's endeavors, including a monument honoring the Apollo astronauts who trained around Húsavík. The town's main landmark is the charming gingerbread church, built in 1907, which is unique in Iceland for not having a pulpit. And of course, being Iceland, you can bathe in geothermally heated sea water.

name: Bolzano
address.addr1: 39100 Bolzano, Province of Bolzano - South Tyrol, Italy
description: Bolzano is the capital city of the province of South Tyrol. The lively Italian town is situated in a valley surrounded by charming green mountains. Bolzano has Austrian flair and a Germanic character, combining Italian, German, and Ladin cultures harmoniously. The walkable, cosmopolitan city has many churches, museums, and castles to discover. It's also home to three cable cars for a peak at stunning panoramic views. Additionally, Bolzano's surrounding vineyards also make it the ideal stop for wine tasting.

name: Zacapoaxtla
description: An ancient agrarian town, Zacapoaxtla is famous for its fight against the French. Nicknamed 'The City of 25 April" for the historic battle the townsfolk fought in, this city has a lot to offer for its legacy. Head the the Plaza de la Constitucion to see two historic churches side-by-side. At the larger Church of San Pedro Apostol, you can gain an in-depth look into the religious devotion people practice in this city, as well as a step into the past life in colonial Mexico. For a look at a more natural side of the city, visit its two waterfalls, the Cascada La Gloria and the huge Cascada Velo de Novia. Both waterfalls have unique features of their own and make for great photo opportunities. For a great view above, visit the Cerro del Tomaquilo, where you can admire Zacapoaxtla's answer to the Christ the Redeemer monument in Brazil.

Built in 1956, this architectural masterpiece is a 70 foot tall structure jutting out of the red rocks! Other than spiritual pursuits, you can explore the town itself with the Tlaquepaque Arts and Shopping Village, where you can learn about the region's First Nations community. For scenic lookouts, educational opportunities and a chance to get active, Sedona is a great point of interest.

name: Castro Urdiales
description: A Roman colony was first established in the area in 74 AD, most likely to take advantage of the abundance of iron in the area. In was in 1163, however, that the town of Castro Urdiales first received its municipal charter. The town benefited greatly from its strategic location, at a crossroads in the trade route between northern Europe and Castile. It was destroyed by the French in 1813, but was quickly rebuilt and fortified. Visitors to Castro Urdiales can enjoy El Faro Castle, a 13th century pentagonal fortress; the Church of Santa María de la Asunción, a Gothic basilica church with 3 naves, built under the protection of King Alfonso VIII of Castile in the 13th century; the palace, castle-observatory, and Ocharan gardens, dating back to the early 20th century; the 16th-century city hall, and the Roman milestone, opposite the church of Santa María, dating back to 61 and marking the distance to Pisoraca.

name: Venice
description: Likely founded by Roman refugees, the island city of Venice has developed into one of the most iconic cities in the world. The narrow streets, romantic canals, and impressive historical buildings all add to its grandeur. The heart of Venice is the Piazza San Marco, which is surrounded by impressive buildings and dominated by the imposing bell tower and Saint Mark's Basilica. It's the perfect spot to enjoy Venice's scenery, as well as the many cafes, shops, and live music. As the gondola is the symbol of the city, it's an absolute must to float down the canals and experience the beauty of Venice by boat! You'll pass by many churches and palaces, lively squares, museums, and shops along the way. Take some time to explore this one-of-a-kind city; even the smallest building can contain works by some of the history's most renowned artists including Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto, and Veronese.

name: Uji
description: Nestled between the historic hubs of Kyoto and Nara, Uji is a captivating small city with a rich cultural heritage. During the Fujiwara clan's reign in the Heian Period, Byodoin Temple and Ujigami Shrine, Japan's oldest surviving shrine, were erected, enhancing Uji's cultural prominence. Notable attractions include the Uji Tea Festival held at Koshoji Temple in October, Tsuen, Japan's oldest tea shop since 1160, and the ancient Ujigami Shrine with its curved roof. The crown jewel, Byodoin Temple, founded in 1052, enshrines a gilded Amida Buddha, its Phoenix Hall adorned with twin phoenixes symbolizing protection. The temple's museum hosts guided tours revealing replicas of its original vibrant wall paintings. Strolling along the Uji River or cruising its waters unveils the town's romantic essence, with Uji Bridge acclaimed for its role in "The Tale of Genji." This picturesque town, featured in the 11th-century masterpiece "The Tale of Genji," charms visitors with tea fields, riverside allure, and sacred sites, making it a sought-after day-trip destination from Kyoto.

name: Dingli
description: Dingli is a picturesque village renowned for its magnificent cliffs that overlook the sparkling Mediterranean Sea. The village offers uninterrupted sea vistas on one side and a charming old town with traditional townhouses on the other, within easy reach of major attractions like the medieval city of Mdina. Visit the awe-inspiring Dingli Cliffs that stretch for over two kilometers from Bahrija to Mungar, featuring sharp pathways that lead down to the sea. Along the way, catch glimpses of Filfla, a small uninhabited islet. Perched on the edge of the cliffs is the St Mary Magdalene Chapel, marking the highest point in Malta with panoramic views of the coastal landscape. After enjoying scenic walking trails by the cliffs, stop by The Cliffs Interpretation Center for information about the cliff's geological significance, and indulge in local specialties in the restaurant area, infused with wild edible plants like nettles, borage and wild asparagus.

name: Port Royal Golf Course
description: Port Royal Golf Course, perched on the shorefront of Southampton Parish, is not only a favorite among locals but has also earned the admiration of gold legend Jack Nicklaus himself. The 18-hole course presents an invigorating challenge to gold enthusiasts, with doglegs and brisk ocean winds adding a touch of complexity to each swing. The Bermuda Open Championship graces this course annually, a testament to its caliber. Among its splendid holes, the 16th stands as the signature gem—an iconic par-three poised precariously on cliffs overlooking the vast Atlantic expanse. To conquer this hole demands near perfection. A driving range with captivating ocean vistas and varying practice distances caters to players of all levels. Port Royal Golf Course welcomes golfers daily from 7AM to 6PM. To secure your tee time and bask in the Port Royal experience, visit the official website: www.portroyalgolfcourse.com.

name: Puy du Fou
description: Puy du Fou was founded in 1977 when French politician Philippe de Villiers was still a student. Starting with the original show "Cinéscénie", the amusement park has grown to include 26 spectacular shows and become of of the most popular theme parks in France. The park's buildings span French history, from a medieval fort to early 20th century village, and the dramatic shows go back even further. Visitors can take a seat in a Gallo-Roman stadium to see gladiators, witness a Viking ship full of warriors magically rise from a lake, or witness the Knights of the Round Table meet with Merlin and King Arthur. However, the mainstay is still the night-time Cinéscénie, which sees 1,200 actors take to the world's largest stage to reenact 700 years of the area's history...with the aid of 800 fireworks. For more information, please visit puydufou.com/fr

name: Walltown Crags - Hadrian's Wall
address.addr1: Walltown Crags - Hadrian's Wall, United Kingdom
description: The Walltown Crags section of Hadrian's Wall was built around the 2nd century to mark the Northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. This particular section made the most of the area's rocky outcrops, incorporating them into the wall, and using them as another layer of defense. Today, the Walltown Crags are one of the best preserved and scenic places to view Hadrian's Wall. After a short hike, visitors are treated to stunning views of the wall that inspired 'The Wall' in Game of Thrones. In some sections, the wall is still 2.2 meters tall - an amazing feat considering its 2000 years old. There are also the remains of two 'mile castles', and two turrets. The Walltown Turret is particularly interesting because it was built as a freestanding structure, suggesting it predates the wall. A history-filled amble through the countryside is topped off by the local residents - grazing farm animals.

name: Ocotlan
description: Situated at the shores of Lake Chapala, Ocotlan is the gatekeeper to the Chapala resort area, but offers some attractive attractions of its own. Founded in 1530, this is a city of religious significance. There are two cathedrals that line the main plaza. Ocotla houses the church of La Purisima (The Most Pure), which is one of the oldest buildings in the state of Jalisco, with an altar made of gold. The church of Nuestro Senor de Misericordia (Our Merciful Lord), was built in the 1800s after a large earthquake flattened the city, where an apparition of Jesus Christ was seen the following Sunday.

name: Taoyuan
description: Taoyuan, with its dynamic urban life, cultural treasures, and natural wonders, beckons travelers to explore its multifaceted identity, making it an intriguing destination in Taiwan. The Northern Cross-Island Highway offers scenic delights, while the Chiang Kai-Shek and Chiang Ching-Kuo Cultural Park attracts millions of visitors annually. The city takes pride in preserving its Hakka culture, military communities, rustic areas, trails, bikeways, and local industries, offering a fascinating blend of heritage and innovation. Daxi Old Street, with its historic architecture and delectable snacks, provides a glimpse into the past and delights the senses with Taiwanese treats like dried tofu, moonlight cake, and peanut candy. Xinnan Old Street, also known as Zhongshan Old Street, offers a contrasting experience to the bustle of Daxi. This quiet residential area once housed affluent merchants. Strolling along its red brick arcades and admiring ornate carvings on old arches transports visitors to a bygone era.

name: Schladming
description: A small town in the center of Austria, Schladming has gained popularity amongst tourists for their killer mountains and access to freshly untouched snow. With a large and attractive ski resort highlighting its 'red'; and 'black'; slopes for its more competitive crowd, in 2013 Schladming was the location for the FIS Alpine World Ski Championships. But there is just as much fun in the summer! With romantic views from the mountains, it is also very popular to hike and bike through the nature of Schladming. From gourmet food, cafe's and restaurants, there is plenty of time to eat, relax, tour, and experience Schladming's magical moments.

name: León
description: Leon was first established in 1524 by the conquistador Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, though the present city is located a few miles from the original site. Leon served as the capital of Nicaragua through colonial times, and with the founding of the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua, it also became the country's intellectual capital. These students helped form the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN), which led the revolt against the US-backed Somoza dictatorship in the 1970s. For those looking to learn more about Leon's liberal history, you can stop by the Museo Historico de la Revolución. Leon has several colonial-era churches, but the main landmark is its Baroque cathedral, which offers the best views in town from for those who pay the $3 to visit the roof. For those who really want to immerse themselves in the city's history and culture, Hokano Adventures offers a Revolution Tour, which will take you to the cities main sights, and give more detailed context to what you're seeing.

name: Tropic of Cancer Beach
description: Unveiled on the shores of George Town, Tropic of Cancer Beach beckons with a touch of the extraordinary. Imagine sinking your toes into the powder-soft sand, the gentle waves lapping at your feet like a soothing whisper. The Bahamian sunshine bathes the beach in a warm glow, inviting you to unwind and embrace the tranquility. Unlike the lively energy of some Bahamian beaches, Tropic of Cancer Beach offers a serene escape, a perfect sanctuary for those seeking peace and seclusion. A vibrant underwater world awaits just offshore. Rent snorkeling gear and discover a kaleidoscope of colorful fish flitting through coral reefs teeming with life. For the adventurous, stand-up paddleboarding offers a unique way to explore the coastline, granting panoramic views of the beach's secluded beauty.

name: Tupiza
description: Surrounded by strange red rock formations baked under the sweltering sun, the little town of Tupiza still has that rugged air often associated with the American Wild West. Immerse yourself in authentic Bolivian life in the thriving market, where locals go to buy fresh meat and vegetables. But Tupiza's main attraction is the amazing natural surroundings. Hike (or take a tour on horseback) through the rugged landscape. Hike to the top of Cerro de la Cruz for a sweeping panorama of the inhospitable hills, or head to the Valle de los Machos, Puerta del Diablo, or Cañon del Inca to wander the desert landscape (it's hot so bring plenty of water). To really live out your Wild West fantasies, you can even join a horseback tour to the site where Butch Cassidy and the SUndance Kid were shot down by Bolivian police.

name: Le Mans
address.addr1: Vieux Chemin du Mans, 72100 Le Mans, France
description: Le Mans was the birthplace of the Plantagenet dynasty, the house who ruled England from 1154 until the death of Richard III in the War of the Roses in 1485. While the city is famous for the 24-hour race it hosts every June, its old town looks like it's stopped in time. The palace where Henry II was born is now the town hall, and its cobbled streets have set the stage for films such as "The Man in the Iron Mask", and the "Three Musketeers". In the summer the old town hosts a free sound and light show five nights a week, adding even more magic to the medieval atmosphere.

name: Pelekas
description: Perched atop a verdant hill on the enchanting Greek island, Pelekas captivates visitors with its picturesque charm and breathtaking vistas. Pelekas entices adventurers with its idyllic setting overlooking the azure waters of the Ionian Sea, providing panoramic views of the sun-kissed coastline and dramatic sunsets that paint the sky in hues of orange and pink. Its tranquil ambiance and traditional architecture create a timeless atmosphere, inviting exploration and relaxation alike. Steeped in history, Pelekas boasts ancient roots dating back to antiquity, evidenced by its well-preserved landmarks and archaeological sites. Wander through its narrow cobblestone streets lined with charming tavernas, cafes, and souvenir shops, where the warm hospitality of the locals enhances the allure of this coastal gem. Nature enthusiasts will delight in the surrounding landscapes, as Pelekas is surrounded by lush olive groves and verdant hillsides, ideal for leisurely hikes and scenic strolls. The nearby beaches beckon sun-seekers and water lovers with their golden sands and crystal-clear waters, offering opportunities for swimming, snorkeling, and sunbathing.

name: Anghiari
description: Overlooking the Tiber River, this charming hilltop village likely began as a Roman vineyard, as as evidenced by the wine cellar uncovered in the Palazzo Pretorio. Thanks to its strategic position and fortified walsl, the town played an important role in the Middle Ages, with the flat valley below setting the scene for the famous Battle of Anghiari in 1440, which was commemorated in Florence with a fresco by Leonardo da Vinci. Unfortunately, the painting deteriorated due to Da Vinci's experimental technique, though Anghiari has a museum dedicated to the battle and the artwork. At its center, the Palazzo Taglieschi houses to the Museo Statale, which exhibits holds important art such as a colorful wooden Madonna by Jacopo della Quercia, and a sixteenth-century table organ.

name: Bitola
description: Founded by Phillip II of Macedon in the 4th century BC, Bitola is Macedonia's oldest, and second largest city, but its preserved reminders from when it was ruled by the Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Slavs, and Ottomans. On the outskirts of town, you'll find the remains of Heraclea Lyncestis, the original city founded by Philip II of Macedon, and later built upon by the Romans and Byzantines. Walking atop the ruined walls, you'll see staples like baths, temples, and an early Christian church, but the real highlight are the incredibly well-preserved mosaics. In the sleepy Magnolia Square, you'll be able to see the 17th century Clock Tower, 16th century Yeni Mosque, and and the 18th century Church St. Dimitrija with its amazing carved and gilded iconostasis. It's also worth wandering the Stara Čaršija, the old Turkish Bazaar, where you'll find traditional crafts and an authentic food market.

name: Lima
description: Founded by the Spanish in the 16th century, Lima has since grown into Peru's political capital, as well as its financial, commercial, and cultural focalpoint, and the 3rd largest city in the Americas. Despite its size, Lima's historic center is well-preserved, and has earned UNESCO recognition for its colonial architecture, which is well-represented by the many elegant churches. Many of the country's most precious historic artefacts are housed in Lima's museums, so it's well-worth taking some time to get some more insights into those famous archaeological sites. If you're looking for something more lively, the districts of Miraflores and Barranco are alive with music and street-art, while the Barrio Chino (Chinatown) is the best place to experience Chifa - Peru's famous Chinese fusion cuisine.

name: Yamoussoukro
description: Journey to the heart of Côte d'Ivoire and discover the captivating allure of Yamoussoukro, a city that blends modern marvels with rich cultural heritage. See the city from the awe-inspiring Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, the world's largest church. Admire its majestic white facade and intricate stained-glass windows, a testament to the country's faith and artistic expression. Immerse yourself in the lively atmosphere of Place Jean-Paul II, the city's central square, where locals gather to chat, vendors showcase their wares, and the energy pulsates with an infectious rhythm. But Yamoussoukro isn't just about grand structures and bustling squares; it's a haven for culture enthusiasts. Delve into the vibrant history of the Côte d'Ivoire at the National Museum, where ancient artifacts and captivating exhibits whisper tales of the country's past. Explore the bustling Marche du Centre, a sensory overload of sights, sounds, and smells.

name: Arcos de la Frontera
address.addr1: 11630 Arcos de la Frontera, Cádiz, Spain
description: Declared a national monument in 1962 because of its breathtaking beauty, the tangle of cobbled streets of Arcos de la Frontera lead up to 11th century Moorish castle. Unfortunately the castle is not open to the public, so can only be appreciated from afar. But worry not, the rest of the old town is flush with fine landmarks. Calle Nueva was the castle moat until the 1755 Lisbon earthquake collapsed a stretch of wall. The Iglesia de San Pedro, is a Renaissance church built into a 14th century fortress and combines Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque styles in its tower and facade. The 17th century Convento de las Mercedarias Descalzas is the only remaining cloistered convent in Arcos. If you have a sweet tooth, its nuns make and sell homemade sweets.

name: Geneva
description: Geneva's modern, polished facade belies a history stretching back to the ancient Gauls. Situated on the shores of Europe's largest alpine lake, the symbol of the city is the "Jet d'eau" – a fountain shooting a jet of water 140-meters into the air, within view of many of the most upscale hotels and many restaurants. On the left-hand shore, the Old Town is dominated by St. Peter's Cathedral. Founded in 1160, the Romanesque-turned-Gothic structure was given a neo-classical facade in the 18th century. Along with the rich religious trappings, visitors can also see the archaeological dig site in the basement, or climb the tower for stupendous views of the city. The entire country is synonymous with watches, and the Patek Philippe Museum is sure to make even the most seasoned horologist green with envy.

name: Le Puy-en-Velay
description: The early history of Le Puy-en-Velay is lost in legends of saints and apostles, but it was certainly the most popular pilgrimage destination in France during the Middle Ages. Charlemagne came twice, followed by a slew of other notable figures over the centuries, from Kings to Dukes, to Joan of Arc's mother. Over the years, the Notre-Dame-de-France cathedral, was expanded and rebuilt, and today, this UNESCO World Heritage Site reflects every architectural style from the 5th to 15th centuries. The Romanesque style facade has distinctive Eastern and Spanish-Moorish influences in its striped arches. Walking the old town, you'll find plenty of pretty houses, but the other main sights are on the basalt cones overlooking the town. The taller is topped with a monumental statue of Notre-Dame de France, made from captured cannons in the 19th century. On the smaller is the 10th century chapel of Saint Michel de l'Aiguilhe - perhaps the most picturesque medieval chapel in France.

name: Medulin
description: The area around Medulin has been settled for thousands of years, but the town's current roots date back to Roman times, when the population started forming closely-built settlements. The town proper is a former fishing village, so fans of seafood should tuck into some local specialties like cuttlefish risotto. The St. Agnes Church, with its white facade is unique in Istrian architecture for its twin bell towers. For visitors who want to see some of the area's rich history, the green peninsula at the heart of Medulin bay houses the remains of a Roman villa, thought to have belonged to Emperor Constantine the Great, and other ancient ruins, with signs along the way to educate visitors.

name: Drogheda
description: Founded by the Normans in the 12th century, Drogheda quickly rose in prominence, often hosting Irish Parliament in the 15th and 16th centuries. This status made it the target of several sieges, most notably, when Oliver Cromwell massacred both the Royalist garrison and the civilian population in 1649. In the 19th century, it developed into a major center for the brewing and distilling industry, hosting companies ranging from Jameson Whiskey to Coca-Cola. Today, there are still reminders of the town's rich history, including St. Lawrence's Gate, a remnant of the medieval town wall, and Magdalen's Tower, a splendid medieval belfry. The main attraction is St. Peter's Church, an 18th century Gothic Revival structure that houses the National Shrine to St. Oliver Plunkett. Here, you'll find the mummified head of the 17th century martyr, along with other relics, and even the door from the prison in which he was held.

name: Cosenza
description: Cosenza is one of the most ancient cities in Calabria, and its rich history is apparent everywhere you look. The city's old quarter is has been touted as one of the most beautiful in all of Italy, and it's easy to see why while exploring its charming steep and narrow streets. Cosenza's exquisite 12th century cathedral and the 11th-century castle are just two of the dominating landmarks. The city's rich history is also preserved in its exceptional museums, where visitors can look at everything from ancient artefacts to classic art. Of course, there's also an almost endless number for great cafes for visitors to take a break, and soak in some authentic Italian flavour.

name: Lubeck
description: This fascinating and enchanting city has many corners to explore and most visitors begin at the Old Town, which is surrounded by water with seven towers and five churches that bring over 1,000 years of history to life. The whole town is UNESCO protected as the Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Neo-Classical buildings, narrow alleyways and streets, churches and abbeys, merchant houses and fortifications form a remarkable whole. A jewel of brick-Gothic architecture, the Church of St. Mary, is Lubeck's finest ecclesiastical building and the inspiration for at least 70 other churches around the Baltic. The church sits at the highest point of the town and its brick-vaulted roof, which is the highest in the world, is a remarkable feat of architecture. Of course, no visitor should miss out on tasting and appreciating a delicacy that the city is world renowned for — Lubeck Marzipan, which has been around to tempt visitors ever since almonds were first ground into paste.

name: Freiburg im Breisgau
description: Renowned for its sunshine, Freiburg has much to offer, whether strolling around the historic old town to learn about the culture and history of the city or simply watching the world go by in one of the many cafes and cozy pubs. The main attraction in the town is the Gothic sandstone cathedral, built in 1330 with a tower that soars 380 feet into the sky. This huge landmark is famous for its incredible detail, from the amazing gargoyles on the outside to the intricate stained glass windows on the inside. For jaw-dropping views of the city, then the climb to the top of the bell tower provides excellent photo opportunities. If all that climbing gives you an appetite then maybe browse the market outside the cathedral and surrender to the temptation of the delicious aromas that permeate the square. Among many other items, the market offers the opportunity to snack on authentic and mouth-watering German sausages.

name: Rastoke
description: The watermill village of Rastoke is the historic city center of Slunj in Croatia. Often referred to as 'the small lakes of Plitvice', it's a place where the crystal clear waters of river Slunjcica criss-crosses into the Korana river. The peaceful village has many well-preserved mills and waterfalls of different sizes. Although Rastoke was one of the hardest hit regions during the 1990's conflict, it has undergone a successful restoration program under the direction of the government. Visitors can hike the pine forests and explores the nearby canyons and caves or simply relax at one of the town's waterfront cafes.

name: Masca
description: In the mountains of the Teno Rural Park, the jaw-dropping scenery of Masca will enchant you with its scattered white houses and cypress-lined mountainsides. The tiny town of under 100 inhabitants whispers legendary stories of pirates hiding in the valley and holds ancient history. Masca was one of the last dwellings of the aboriginal people of the Canary islands - Guanches - until the land was seized in the 15th century by Spanish conquistadors. Learn about the town's eerie past at the Masca Museum before enjoying the spectacular view from the Plaza de Masca. Try some of the signature cactus food and drinks from a Canarian restaurant and head to Masca's small Church of the Immaculate Conception, picturesque with its white volcanic stone. Masca is known for its famous hike, taking you through gorgeous gorges and down the ravine to Masca Beach. It's a long and physically demanding hike, but the otherworldly panoramas can be viewed from the carpark near the main town.

name: Garachico
description: Once a prosperous port connecting Europe, Africa and the Americas, Garachico's dramatic history of plagues, fires and a volcanic eruption in 1706 has melded its unique coastal character over the centuries. Striking blue waters encircle obsidian rock where lava once flowed, while colonial-style churches and medieval buildings perch atop the land. In the central Plaza de la Libertad, white, blue, orange and yellow houses welcome you to a quintessentially Spanish square. Take a walk to the Parque de la Puerta de Tierra, a green oasis where the old archway leading to Garachico's 16th century trading port still stands. The Piscinas Naturales de El Caletón are a must-see assortment of large rock pools arranged by a volcanic inlet, popular during the summer months for paddling. Admire the spectacular views of the La Cutala cliffs and Roque de Garachico, the formidable islet and official Natural Monument from which this city derives its name.

name: Fayoum
description: 100 kilometers southwest of Cairo's chaotic metropolis, the Faiyum Oasis offers a peaceful retreat. Nourished by the Bahr Yussef canal, a branch of the Nile that has transformed this once-arid basin into a lush agricultural region. The oasis is home to the city of Faiyum, which is renowned for its bustling bazaars, historic mosques, and distinctive waterwheels as symbols of the area's agricultural traditions. Notable sites include the Qaitbay Mosque and the nearby archaeological remains of Crocodilopolis, an ancient center of worship for the crocodile god Sobek. Hike along Lake Qarun, a large saltwater lake, and Wadi El-Rayan nature preserve, home to Egypt's largest waterfalls. Also nearby is the UNESCO World Heritage site Wadi Al-Hitan, famed for its early whale fossils. Whether you're interested in history, nature, or local culture, Faiyum offers a diverse array of experiences that reflect Egypt's timeless allure.

name: Granada
description: Inhabited since at least 500 BC, Granada has been the region's political center for the entirety of recorded history, and has the monuments to prove it. Next to the grand 16th century cathedral, you'll find the beautiful carved alabaster tombs of Isabella I and Ferdinand II, the monarchs responsible for finally driving the Moors out of Spain, and backing Christopher Columbus on his voyage to the New World. There's also still vestiges of the city's Moorish heritage. The Old Town follows its original layout, and there's some amazingly well preserved monuments including a bathhouse with reclaimed Roman capitals and the Corral del Carbón, a 13th century warehouse and shelter for merchants. To experience the roots of the city's flamenco tradition, pay a visit to the Sacromonte neighborhood with its 16th century cave dwellings. Granada's crown jewel, however, is the Alhambra. With its impossibly intricate details, this 14th century fortress-turned-palace is perhaps the single finest piece of Moorish architecture (tickets MUST be purchased in advance at https://www.alhambra-patronato.es/).

name: El Yunque - Angelito Trail
address.addr1: El Yunque National Forest, puerto rico
description: Covering 28,000 acres of land on the slopes of the Sierra de Luquillo mountains, El Yunque National Forest is the only tropical rainforest in the United States National Forest System. Some areas of these jungled mountains receive over 20 feet of rainfall a year, creating a lush ecosystem with four distinct forests climbing the slopes. A number of hiking trails wind through the jungle, showcasing the rugged scenery and biodiversity of the mountains held holy by the Taino. For some fun in nature, the El Angelito trail is just a half mile long and brings you to a jungle lagoon you can dive into. For more intrepid hikers looking to see more of El Yunque's ecosystem, the challenging 0.8-mile Mount Britton trail will have you climbing pathways through the Sierra Palm and into the cloud forest. At the end, you'll be rewarded with some amazing views from atop a 1930s lookout tower. You can adjust your stop time according to the hiking trail you plan to take. Please note: face masks are required at all times in the park. It's strongly recommended to reserve your visit in advance through https://www.recreation.gov/camping/gateways/14487. The park doesn't guarantee walk-in availability. For more information, please visit https://www.fs.usda.gov/elyunque

name: Valley of the Kings
description: Situated under the pyramidal shadow of Al Qurn mountain, the Valley of the Kings served as the burial site for the pharaohs of the New Kingdom. Between 1550 and 1069 BC 63 magnificent royal tombs were built here. Over the years, many of these were stripped of their treasures, but in 1922, it was the site of one of the greatest archaeological discoveries of all time: the untouched tomb of King Tut. Today, authorities keep a rotation of 18 tombs open to the public in an attempt to protect them from damage. While, King Tut's tomb is neither the oldest or grandest, it remains the most popular - perhaps because it still houses the boy king's mummy and gilded sarcophagus. For those looking to see the mummies and many treasures that once filled the tombs, be sure to visit the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza Pyramids.

name: Bosa
description: Bosa as it stands today was founded in 1112 by the noble Malaspina family just 2½ km from the site of an ancient Phoenecian settlement. Even today, Bosa's most notable (and unmissable) landmark is the 12th century castle. While little more than the walls remain, the views across the colorful town following the river to the sea are worth the trip alone. The Romanesque church with its 14th century frescoes is an added bonus. But Bossa's real draw is the old town, with a patchwork of pastel colored houses rising from the riverfront. Just wander the narrow pedestrian-only streets, taking in the charms, and stopping at a cafe or restaurant as the mood strikes. There's also a few museums in town, like the Museo Casa Deriu, which showcases local arts and crafts in a stately 19th century building, and the Museo delle Conce in a 19th century tannery, which offers insights on how the town's famous tanneries worked.

name: Imola
address.addr1: 40026 Imola, Metropolitan City of Bologna, Italy
description: Situated along the river Santerno about 50 km southeast of Bologna, Imola has been under Roman, barbarian, Papal, and Austrian rule at various points throughout history. One of its most prominent historic sites is Rocco Sforzesca, or Sforza Castle. First built in the 14th century on the remains of a pre-existing 11th-century tower, the fortress has primarily served as a residence and prison, and is now home to a museum consisting of over 600 pieces dating from the 14th to 20th centuries. Formula One racing fans will also know Imola as the home of the famous Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dineo Ferrari, named after the late founder of Ferrari and his son, and the former venue of the Formula One San Marino Grand Prix.

name: Hiroshima
description: Many are familiar with Hiroshima's tragic past – it was the first city to suffer a nuclear weapon attack when an atomic bomb was dropped during WWII, killing thousands of people within seconds and destroying two-thirds of the city. Since then, Hiroshima has been rebuilt and is now a modern metropolis that has over a million inhabitants. Despite its resurgence, the city remains deeply connected to its history, drawing numerous visitors who come to pay their respects. A primary destination for visitors is the Atomic Bomb Dome, an enduring symbol of the city. Adjacent to it is the Peace Memorial Park, dotted with memorials and sculptures, and housing a memorial museum. Other points of interest include the Hiroshima Peace Poster Exhibition and gallery, and Hiroshima Castle, originally constructed in the 16th century, destroyed by the bomb, and rebuilt in the 1960s. Many may not know that Hiroshima also boasts a rich culinary scene, hence, trying local specialties, such as okonomiyaki, is a must.

name: Uppsala
description: Uppsala is one of Sweden's oldest cities, and the thrum of history and culture can be felt walking its lushly decorated, spire-filled streets. Scandinavia's largest cathedral, the Uppsala Cathedral, carves a striking shape into the city's skyline and recalls a grand royal past. King Gustav Vasa is buried there and it has been the site of many coronations until the 19th century. Guided walks atop the castle roof are available where you can view the sprawling cityscape of Uppsala from above. The city is also home to Uppsala University, the oldest university in Sweden. The bustling student life makes Uppsala a vibrant cultural center, boasting the past residence of famed Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus. Take a walk through his floral haven at the Linnaean Gardens of Uppsala, perfect for a summertime stroll. Visit the Gustavianum museum, part of the university, to learn more about Swedish history and culture, and sample some fine Swedish cuisine at one of the many renowned restaurants in town.

name: Casablanca
description: Settled by Berber tribesmen around the 7th century, Casablanca as it stands today is rooted in the work of Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah, who rebuilt the town following a devastating earthquake in 1755. After becoming a French colony in the early 20th century, Casablanca rapidly expanded, and today it's one of the largest financial centers in Africa. Known thanks to the classic film, most visitors still bypass Casablanca in favor of more tourism-focused locals. But the city offers visitors a great mix of architecture and culture, including Art Deco buildings from the colonial era, a historic medina complete with bustling souk, and a scenic waterfront promenade. However, the city's proudest monument is the massive Hassan II Mosque. Traditional architecture on a grand scale, the city is so proud of its mosque that outsiders are allowed in on guided tours! Just be sure to dress conservatively.

name: Wernigerode
description: Located in the foothills of the Hraz region, its origins are lost in the distant past, with the first written record being the appointment of a count in the 12th century. The narrow streets of the old town are lined with Germany's iconic half-timbered houses, with the Gothic town hall's timbered facade dating back to 1498. Now, it is a popular gateway to Northern Germany's most mountainous region, and is part of the 'German Timber Frame Road', a route through Germany meant to preserve the cultural heritage of the variety of half-timber styles. Overlooking the town is the 19th century Wernigerode Castle, which was built on the foundations of a much older medieval castle. Visitors can tour the lavish interior, and enjoy panoramic views of the city and Brocken Mountain beyond.

name: Lacock
description: Recorded in the Domesday Book, Lacock hasn't changed much over the centuries. In 1944, the Talbot family, who'd owned the town for centuries, donated the entire estate to the National Trust. Since then, the village has been kept free of signs of modernity, meaning there are no telephone poles or electric street lights. Most of the town's houses are from the 18th century or earlier, with the oldest predating the 13th century abbey. The upstairs of the beautiful building has been preserved as it was when it was inhabited by William Henry Fox Talbot, the man who invented photography in 1835. They abbey's historic cloisters and rooms were featured in Harry Potter, and visitors might recognize the room where Harry found the Mirror of Erised, and Professor Quirrell's classroom. Wandering the town, visitors can also admire the 14th-century St Cyriac's Church and tithe barn, and see the Home where Harry Potter's parents lived.

name: Arezzo
description: Thanks to its strategic position, Arezzo has been a thriving settlement from nearly 3000 years. Unfortunately, this also made it a target for Allied bombing during World War II, which destroyed large swaths of the city. Despite this, the city is still rich with historic monuments for visitors to enjoy. Visitors can stop by the 13th century Church of San Francesco, which houses the exceptional Early Renaissance 'Legend of the True Cross' fresco cycle by Piero della Francesca, or step into the 16th century Casa del Vasari, which is lavishly decorated by the owner himself. The gently sloping Piazza Grande is surrounded by historic buildings, such as the unique Chiesa di Santa Maria della Pieve, and the Grand Art Gallery, and hosts Italy's most famous antique fair the first weekend of every month.

name: Mycenae
description: Homer's Iliad tells us a tale about the most powerful king in ancient Greece - Agamemnon, who ruled from his magnificent fortress, Mycenae. Homer described the structure's grandeur, and according to archaeological findings, Homer was right. Today, visitors can admire the fortress' gates, graves, and walls, along with the Treasure of Atreus, which contains possibly the most impressive and well-preserved Mycenaean tombs. For more details and history of this stunning site, please check out: http://odysseus.culture.gr/h/3/eh352.jsp?obj_id=2573.

name: Vienne
description: Once the capital of a Gallic tribe, after the area was conquered by the Romans, this ideal riverside location was made into a provincial capital. Even today, this City of Art and History's rich heritage is preserved in its many monuments. Two ancient Roman monuments are still standing: the 1st century BC Temple of Augustus, and the huge 1st-century AD Théâtre Antique, which was one of the largest in Gaul, while Gallo-Roman archaeological remains can be found in the Garden of Cybele. Visitors can also discover the city's beautiful medieval heritage by strolling through narrow lanes to it many monuments. The Romanesque Gothic Saint-Maurice Cathedral has some beautiful Flamboyant portals and colored roof, while Flemish tapestries adorn the interior. At the Romanesque Saint-André-le-Bas Church, visitors can take a peaceful walk through the cloisters, decorated with carved capitals.

name: Godafoss Waterfall
description: With a height of 12 meters, the Godafoss Waterfall might not be the largest waterfall in Iceland, but the 30-meter-wide cascade pouring into a river basin is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful. The falls are made even more fascinating by their unusual history. Iceland's original settlers in the 9th and 10th centuries followed the Old Norse religion - you know, the one worshiping gods like Thor, Odin, Loki, and Freya. However, around 1000, it became evident that Norway would retake the land if the country remained pagan. The decision was left to the Ásatrú priest (or goði) Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði. For the good of the people, he chose to make the country's official religion Christianity. To mark his decision, he went home, collected his Norse idols, and threw them over the falls.

name: Bursa
description: First settled in 5200 BC, Bursa was made the first capital of the Ottoman Empire in 1326. While it was only capital for a few decades, Bursa remained the empire's spiritual and commercial center until Constantinople was conquered in 1453. Today, Bursa is Turkey's 4th largest city, though it's still possible to see the civic center the capital grew around. Bursa's largest mosque, Ulu Cami, was built in 1400 under Sultan Bayezid I, and is filled with 192 monumental wall inscriptions by the famous calligraphers of the day. The Green Mosque, built by Mehmet I in 1419 illustrates the next phase of Ottoman architecture, and exhibits some stunning calligraphic carvings, not to mention its namesake green tiles. Also on the grounds is the 'Green Tomb' - the final resting place of Sultan Mehmet I. If you're after a pleasant stroll, there's no better place than the Muradiye Complex with its park, cemetery, and intricately ornamented 15th century mosque.

name: Rothenburg ob der Tauber
description: Seeing Rothenburg ob der Tauber's forty-two gates and towers etched against the unspoiled countryside from a distance, you'd swear you were looking at the Fifteenth Century through field glasses. Inside, the town's almost completely intact walls and carefully-preserved half-timbered houses truly do bring visitors back in time. But the past isn't all pretty buildings. Stop by the Medieval Crime Museum to see the horrific reality of medieval correctional methods lovingly detailed in the vaults. A whole department is dedicated to witchcraft and witch-hunting in Bavaria. Back in the light of day, the Town Hall Tower beckons with its fine views of the town and the idyllic surrounding countryside. A walk around those intact town walls is also a temptation to fully surrender to.

name: Gullfoss
description: Fed by a glacial river, Gullfoss waterfall makes its 32 meter tumble in two stages. The first, is an 11 meter 'staircase', while the second is a 21 drop into a rocky crevice. Running 2.5 kilometers perpendicular to the falls, this canyon is Gullfoss' picturesque defining feature. During the summer, around 140 cubic meters of water surge over the falls every second, making the Gullfoss the highest volume waterfall in Europe. In the early 20th century, an English businessman wanted to harness this natural power and build a hydroelectric plant at the falls. He likely would have gotten away with it if it weren't for Sigríður Tómasdóttir, who fought fiercely to preserve the falls, walking the 100 kilometers to Reykjavík on many occasions, and even threatening to throw herself over the falls should construction begin. Today, she's considered Iceland's first environmentalist, and has a small monument at Gullfoss.

name: Braga
description: Home to more than thirty churches, Braga has been the religious capital of Portugal since the 12th century. Thanks to wealthy archbishops, an architectural overhaul beginning in the 16th century transformed the city from a medieval town to a baroque wonderland, earning it the nickname "the Rome of Portugal." Speaking of Rome, the city's last remaining Roman relic is the Fountain of the Idol, a Celtic rune covered shrine from the 1st century that was once part of an ancient temple complex. Perhaps most iconic is the hilltop Bom Jesus do Monte. Completed in 1811, the baroque basilica is accessed by a winding staircase lined with grottoes, fountains and gardens known as the Sacred Way. From the cathedral's hilltop, visitors are rewarded with a sprawling view of Braga. Nearby is Braga's other hilltop church, the 19th century Santuário do Sameiro, a neoclassical monument with wide, open grounds.
