name: Soomaa National Park
description: Covering over 390 square kilometers of land, Soomaa National Park is a vast spectacle of nature and an icon of Estonia. It was created in 1993 to protect the high-elevation bogs, grasslands covering floodplains, forests transformed by water saturation, and rivers with winding courses. Rich meadows cover the riverbanks and are home to approximately 200 species of flora, with the eye-catching and mist-filled swamp forests that surround the site giving a mythological look to the landscape. For fans of bird-watching, Soomaa National Park has one of the most representative compositions of bird species in all of Estonia including the golden eagle and Eurasian whimbrel. Visit in autumn to see the show-stopping migration of around 2,000 Bewick's swans flocking to the park. Head to the Sooma National Park Visitor Center for comprehensive guides to the nature and hiking trails and explore the park's wetlands and waterways by canoeing. If you're visiting in winter, walk over the stunning frozen wetlands and connect with the area's nature and history.

name: Nuuksio National Park
description: Just 20 miles from downtown Helsinki, Nuuksio National Park spans 53 square kilometers of forests and lakes. Eight hiking trails for both beginners and experienced offer plenty of options to experience Finland's pristine natural beauty. Start your visit at the Haltia Center, where you can check out all the possible routes, distances, and difficulty levels for each trail before setting out. All of the trails are well marked, no need to worry about getting lost. One of the most popular trails is the one that leads to Haukkalampi, a small lake with a refreshment area (usually open during the summer). From Haukkalampi, there are other trails to choose from, giving you a wealth of opportunities to enjoy the fresh air and maybe spot one of the endangered species that call the park home. There's a large population of Siberian flying squirrels, the emblem of the park, which are especially exciting to see gliding from tree to tree!

name: Babbacombe Model Village
description: Babbacombe Model Village was opened in 1963 by Tom Dobbins, who had previously opened another model village in Southport. While the village is entirely fictional, there are quite a few recognizable UK landmarks, including Stonehenge and The Shard. Along with traditional scenes of canals and cul-de-sacs, the village has a few surprises in store, like super-heroes and a fire-breathing dragon. Be sure to keep an eye out for very British puns like Ivor Faggot Butcher and Terry Bull Gardening Service, Decorators. There's also a 4D theatre, which has screens special themed short films for the holidays. For more information, please visit model-village.co.uk

name: Frascati
address.addr1: 00044 Frascati, Metropolitan City of Rome, Italy
description: While the village of Frascati wasn't officially founded until around the 7th century, the area has been a getaway since the 1st century BC, when the senator Lucullus built a holiday villa here. In the surrounding hills, the eponymous wine, known as the 'Golden Wine' in Rome, has been produced since the days of the Republic. The town is one of several historic hilltowns near Rome known collectively as the Castelli Romani, which are known for their wine. Romans will often drive here just for an evening of fresh air, food and wine. Famous for its villas, built from the 16th century onwards, many are still privately owned and closed to the public. Fortunately, the Villa Aldobrandini's grounds are open to the public, and is the only Papal garden not owned by the state. Here, great views, and a massive neo-Classical 'Water Temple' await.

name: Atlatlahucan
description: Atlatlahucan is a small town with a long history of conquests and cultural changes. Once forced to pay tribute to the Aztec sovereign, the city pretty much ignored any mandates set by the Spanish after their conquest, which prompted the Crown to dispatch Augustine friars to convert the locals. They erected the Monastery of San Mateo Atlatahucan around 1570, and today it stands as UNESCO World Heritage Site for both its beautiful architecture and its cultural significance. A wide stone path cuts through the colorful town of Atlatlahucan and leads directly to striking stone monastery. Every detail of the building is immaculately preserved which is sure to impress any visitor. This city's rich history can be felt through streets and witnessed through its magnificent architecture.

name: Brasov
description: Founded by the Teutonic Knights in 1211 on an ancient Dacian settlement, and redeveloped by the Saxons as one of their seven walled citadels, Brasov's location at the intersection of trade routes allowed Saxon merchants to obtain considerable wealth during their reign. To protect their hub, the city's fortifications were continually expanded, with each of its several towers maintained by a different craft guild. While it was an important industrial center during communism, and even renamed 'The City of Stalin', its historic center has managed to retain its medieval charm. The 'Black Church', named after the fire damaged that blackened its walls, is the largest hall church east of Vienna. Inside, along with many Gothic embellishments, visitors will find the largest organ in Eastern Europe. Behind it, the Town Hall Square is lined with colorful baroque buildings, all centered on the 15th century Town Hall, which now houses the local museum.

name: Rwamagana
description: Rwamagana is the capital of the Rwamagana District and means "place of a hundred things", with an abundance of popular attractions. In the city itself, a main market, secondary school and conference center make up the urban expanse. The drawcard of the city is its Parish Church, a grand piece of artwork that stands proudly in red-bricked neo-classical style. Established in 1919, the church was designed and built by Dutch-born Peter Johannes Josephus van Heeswijk who was spreading Catholicism through the African Mission. The whole structure consists of one main building and a bell tower, and is a striking scene against the blue skies and dusty cobblestoned promenade. The church has been active over the last 100 years and has introduced many initiatives such as the support of needy students at schools and work with the charity Caritas. name: Da Nang
description: Founded by the Chams at the end of the 2nd century, Da Nang has since grown to become the 4th largest city in Vietnam. The 30 kilometer stretch of coast, centered around the famed My Khe or Lang Co Beaches has always been Da Nang's main draw, and now the Han waterfront is lined with modernists highrises, and an ever-improving restaurant scene. In the bustling downtown, one of the main sights is the famed 'dragon bridge', which is the longest in the country at 666 meters. If you need a break from the crowds, you can head to the beautifully manicured Phap Lam Pagoda, or to the Lady Buddha Da Nang, the tallest Buddha statue in Vietnam. If you have, or plan on visiting any of the ancient Cham temples, be sure visit the Cham Museum Da Nang, which exhibits hundreds of statues from the 7th to the 15th centuries.

name: Grasse
description: Dating back to the Middle Ages, the hilltop town of Grasse became the perfume capital of the world after it began manufacturing perfumed gloves in the 16th century. Today, Grasse's perfumeries are responsible for ⅔ of French production and the historic Fragonard, Galimard, Molinard manufacturers provide free guided tours. For those who want to delve even deeper into the perfume tradition, the International Perfumery Museum trace's perfume's 3000-year history, even offering a perfume-plant-conservatory garden. Even if perfumes aren't your passion, Grasse has one of the largest and best-preserved old towns in Provence. The main thoroughfares are painted in pastel orange to lighten the narrow streets, but duck into an alley and you'll find an authentic Provence where laundry is hung out to dry from original unpainted houses. The single most important historical monument is the 12th century Cathedral Notre-Dame-de-Puy where you'll find stark Romanesque architecture, Baroque ornamentation, and three paintings by Rubens.

name: Milan
description: One of the most popular shopping destinations with Prada, Gucci, and Fendi all in tow, is Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. Named after the kingdom of Italy's first king, this galleria is one of the oldest shopping malls in the world, standing 4 stories tall, adorned in Gothic style, and a unique iron and glass roof. The Galleria connects two of Milan's most famous landmarks: the Teatro Alla Scala and The Duomo. This intricate Duomo took over 600 years to complete and is full of detail including a sundial adorned with astrological signs on the marble floor. After one is done marveling at the duomo, and rubbing your heel for good luck in the galleria, make sure you see some of the many masterpieces Milan has to offer including the infamous painting of the Last Supper at Milan's Santa Maria delle Grazie.

name: Fukuyama
description: As Hiroshima Prefecture's second most populous city, Fukuyama offers an array of captivating attractions that showcase its cultural heritage. Centrally located around Fukuyama Station and adjacent to Fukuyama Castle, the city's heart exudes historical charm. Tomonoura, a quaint port town to the south, captures the essence of old-fashioned fishing communities with its tranquil ambiance. Tomonoura's past as a bustling port town echoes through its streets, which are lined with reminders of its maritime history. Venture southwest to discover Shinshoji Temple, a serene haven nestled in lush forested grounds. This Rinzai Zen temple provides visitors with a Zen experience through meditation classes, tea houses, and a museum gallery showcasing the artwork of Zen master Hakuin. Fukuyama's allure goes beyond its historical sites. With its proximity to the Seto Inland Sea, Fukuyama boasts a stunning coastal landscape that adds to its charm. Whether exploring its historical treasures or embracing the tranquil beauty of the sea, Fukuyama promises an enriching and memorable experience for all who visit.

name: Las Labradas Archaeological Site
description: Located on the Pacific coastline of Northwestern Mexico, the Las Labradas Archaeological Zone is a remarkable testament to a long-extinct culture. It is known for its impressive 1200-foot stretch of basalt rock formations, etched with enigmatic carvings that the ocean waves continually wash over. This site, found in the Southern Sinaloa region within the unique Meseta de Cacaxtla Flora and Fauna Protection Area. Las Labradas is celebrated for having the highest concentration of engraved stone drawings in Mexico, and it is uniquely positioned within a coastal tide zone, making it the only such site globally. The countless inscriptions, which remain largely undeciphered to this day, likely form an ideographic system. Originating in pre-Mexican times, the designs are diverse and complex, with stylized human representations, animal motifs, concentric circles, spirals, crosses, and abstract figures. Some of these engravings are believed to be up to 4500 years old, further adding to the site's profound historical significance which secured the site a spot in UNESCO's World Heritage list. name: Al Jubail
description: Jubail is on the map as the largest civil engineering project globally, but it offers so much more beyond that. Along with producing 2743.6MW of electricity and 800,000 m3 of water daily, and contributing around 7% to the nation's Gross Domestic Product, Jubail has a rich historical background. The Old Town originated as a modest fishing village until 1975, and the whole city's roots can be traced back centuries to the ancient Dilmun civilisation who were renowned for their maritime trade and commerce. Despite its harsh desert climate, Jubail has transformed itself into a modern, livable city. Visit the vibrant marketplace known as the International Market, along with several malls such as Fanateer Mall, Galleria Mall and Jubal Center Mall. Fanateer Beach is one of the city's top destinations, with palm-lined walkways providing an ideal setting for a leisurely stroll. Corniche Jubail is a must-visit spot, with a 2.5 kilometer-long promenade for joggers, runners, and playgrounds for children, all while providing breathtaking views of the Arabian Gulf.

name: Valle de Bravo
description: You can't help but be won over by the charm and beauty of the lakeside Valle de Bravo. The view from the municipal harbor across the lake to the wooded hills on the far shore is to die for. It's no wonder that it is classed as one of Mexico's "Magical Towns". A cliff the looms above the town, providing a fantastic panorama. On the cobbled streets below, the main plaza is the best place to soak in Valle de Bravo's old-world atmosphere. The plaza features the impressive 17th century Parish of Saint Francis of Asisi, whose main bell was cast during the Mexican Revolution. The Jardín Central next door often has live music, and is a great place to gab some street food. Tucked away nearby, the charming Temple of Santa María Ahuacatlán is often overlooked, but well worth a visit for both its elegant architecture and the unusual Black Christ on its main altar.

name: Pasto
description: Founded in the 16th century, Pasto has served as the regional administrative, cultural, and religious center since colonial times, and was nicknamed "The Theological City of Colombia". Today, the city center still has some beautiful colonial buildings, like the Iglesia de San Juan Bautista, with its gold-crusted interior, the beautiful blue and white Iglesia San Felipe, and several other colonial churches. Throughout Colombia, the city is famous for its Blacks and Whites Carnival in early January. This multi-day festival is a raucous riot of color, and recognized by UNESCO for its celebration of the region's diversity. If you're not in town for the celebration, you can always check out the Carnival Museum to see traditional costumes and floats, and learn about the carnival's history and traditions. On the outskirts of town, you'll find the Casa Museo Taminango - a 17th century manor that's been converted into a museum exhibiting traditional folk artefacts.

name: Hughenden Manor
address.addr1: Valley Rd, High Wycombe HP14 4LA, UK
description: Built at the end of the 18th century, Hughenden Manor received an eclectic Victorian remodelling when it became home to Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli. Architect Edward Buckton Lamb 'dramatised' the house with Gothic references, including juxtaposing brickwork, stepped battlements, and unusual window pediments. Today, the manor provides a look into the lives of Disraeli and his wife Mary Anne, like his beloved library and study, her boudoir, and exhibitions showcasing his lasting impact on British policies, and exotic mannerisms. There's even a display of gifts Queen Victoria bequeathed to her favourite Prime Minister. During WWII, the house was a classified map-making base - a secret not uncovered until 60 years later when a house volunteer overheard a man telling his grandson he'd been stationed here. After a decade of research, the manor cellars now have an exhibit of the role 'Hillside' played in supporting bomber command - earning it a spot on Hitler's list of top targets. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/hughenden

name: Budva
description: Known to rival Miami for its exuberant nightlife, the people of Budva know how to let loose. After you admire the hundreds of people lounging on the beach and partaking in various watersports, be sure to wander to the Venetian built stone walls. Meander under the stoned archways that covers much of the Old Town, known to the locals as "Stari Grad". Budva's Stari Grad lies on a small peninsula with narrow windy streets that slyly reveal it's age. Settled since the 5th century BC, Budva's sandy colored buildings delivers its exquisite charm with its most popular attractions: the tomb of writer Stjepan Ljubisa, the Santa Maria in Punta, the Citadel, and the ruins of a Roman-era necropolis.

name: Ciudad del Carmen
description: Before the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century, Ciudad del Carmen was an important bridge between the Aztec and Mayan civilizations in Mesoamerica. During the colonial era, pirates used it as a base of attack against the Spanish until 1717 when it was finally taken by the Spaniards. For much of the modern age, it was a small fishing village, but in the late 1970s oil was discovered, and the city experienced a period of growth. In the 1980s, the longest bridges in Mexico was built to connect the island to the mainland - a trip previously only managed by boat. Despite the 20th century build-up, the city still has a few reminders of its past, such as the preserved narrow streets around the old Calle del Comercio, and the 18th century Baroque Cathedral. The small museum housed in the old Victoriano Nieves Céspedes Hospital building is also worth a visit, exhibiting both Mayan and pirate artefacts.

name: Pachuca
description: Pachuca began as a Spanish silver mining town in the 16th century, with the precious or attracting a larger population of English immigrants. It was these English (mostly Cornish) immigrants who established the Pachuca Athletic Club in 1900, which gave rise to C.F. Pachuca - one of Mexico's most successful professional clubs. While Pachuca eats and breathes football, the Cornish were also responsible for the city's other main landmark: the Monumental Clock of Pachuca, which was inaugurated on 15 September 1910 in celebration of the Centennial of Mexico's Independence. Around town you'll also find vestiges from its days as a wealthy mining town,like the Asunción Church, the Cajas Reales, where miners paid a 20% share of their extractions to the Spanish Crown, the Baroque Church and ex monastery of San Francisco, which now also houses a photography museum. While walking around, be sure to get a pastes - a Mexican twist on the Cornish pastie.

name: Santa Agnes de Corona
description: Santa Agnès de Corona is known best for its striking surrounds of orange, lemon and almond trees that bloom spectacularly in January and February. The Pla de Corona winds around the village, an extensive red earth hiking trail lined by blossoming trees. Spend your time in Santa Agnès de Corona fully immersed in nature, or take a visit to the parish church, beautiful in its simplicity. Directly in front of the church is "Can Cosmi", a famous restaurant known throughout Ibiza for its mouth-watering tortillas. Sit on the terrace, let the sun hit your face, and hear the chatter of local residents who frequent the beloved spot. Take the road to the left and see signs leading to the magnificent Las Puertos del Cielo, or "Heaven's doors". The steep cliffs, covered with green pine, is a sight to behold in this hidden gem of Ibiza.

name: Pitigliano
description: Pitigliano was first carved from the volcanic stone cliffs around the 6th century BC. 1000 years later, Jews fleeing Rome settled in the town, and lived here until the World War II, when the town helped its Jewish population escape Fascist persecution. Today, visitors can step into the historic Jewish quarter to see the striking 16th century synagogue, the peaceful Jewish Cemetery, an old butcher's shop, women's baths, and a cellar used for producing kosher wine. Visitors can even join a walking tour to explore the system of tunnels that connect the town's many cellars. There are also plenty of medieval monuments to discover, from the 14th century castle, the original town wall and gates, and the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, which received an elaborate Baroque remodelling. The town is also renowned for its wine, so be sure to take a break, and appreciate a glass in this historic setting.

name: Ventspils
description: One of the oldest ports in Latvia, Ventspils' ice-free harbour made it a major military and trade port. In the 20th century, the Soviets built an oil pipeline to the city, making it into the USSR's lead crude oil exporter. This boon from oil and shipping has allowed the city to focus on urban beautification projects. The riverfront promenade provides a well-groomed space to watch the constant flow of traffic on the river, and hunt down the city's whimsical cow statues. Near the waterfront, the medieval Ventspils castle has been transformed into a museum that preserves 10,000 years of history though its collection of tools, jewellery, documents and costumes. At the Open-Air Maritime Museum, visitors can see the city's sea-faring history, both in the exhibition hall, and the historic fishing boats and fishermen's cabins around it. Visitors can also hop on a the 1916 train that connected the coastal villages here until the 1950s.

name: Mayapan
description: Founded after the fall of Chichen Itza, Mayapan was the capital of the Maya from the 13th through the 15th centuries. With over 4,000 buildings within the city walls, and even more outside, it was home to an estimated 15,000 people. The city, and much of the Mayan Empire, fell in 1441, after a powerful noble led a revolt and sacked and burned Mayapan. Today, the ruins preserve the final hours of a once-great empire. Like any city, the most important buildings are located in the center. For Mayapan, this means religious, government and administrative buildings, and the homes of nobles. However, the buildings here reflect the empire's already weakened status - many of the buildings copy those found in Chichen Itza, such as the main pyramid and the "Caracol", but were constructed on a smaller scale with inferior ornamentation.

name: Tlaxcala
description: Tlaxcala prides itself on its lovely old town, with buildings constructed from the colonial era in shades of burnt orange, gold, and salmon. Walking around town you can sense the colonial era still hanging in the air. These beautifully colored buildings are most prominently displayed at the Plaza de la Constitución, the main square. Then stroll around the town to discover the other historic buildings that show a creative use of color and design. Such as, the Baroque styled San José parish church, which has bright orange walls decorated with blue and white tiles. Then take a history lesson at the Royal Indian Chapel. Which was built for the nobility of the indigenous people of Tlaxcala, and although it was once destroyed by a fire in the 18th century, you can still visit the ruins and reflect on the centuries old history of Tlaxcala.

name: Vallarta Zoo
description: Situated in the Mismaloya mountains and surrounded by lush forest, the Vallarta Zoo is home to a ark-full of wild animals and welcomes curious visitors from all over looking for a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Upon paying the entry fee (Adults: 10 USD, Children 2-10: 5 USD), you will receive a bag of goodies to feed the animals. Trained personnel share educational tidbits and assist guests in feeding carrots, seeds and other tasty treats to the zoo's residents. Want to get up close and personal with a big cat? Packages are available for purchase so you can hold a baby cub. Prices range from 50-85 USD for this extra opportunity.

name: Piriapolis
description: Built right up to the sea, Piriapolis is of course known for its beaches, gorgeous promenades, and spectacular views. The city provides excellent opportunities to experience nightlife or get some delicious seafood at its many restaurants. You can visit an old Spanish look-out point used to monitor enemy ships approaching, which is now enshrined as a fountain with wonderful panoramic views. If your lucky you could even catch a live band performing! Don't miss the picture-perfect Piria's castle, which was used to practice a religion that was a combination of Christianity and mysticism. If it's views you like, make the hike up San Antonio Hill, the stunning backdrop has made it a popular place for proposals.

name: Pleiku
description: The capital of Vietnam's least populated province, Pleiku served as an American and South Vietnamese base during the Vietnam war. When they withdrew from the city, the South Vietnamese set it ablaze, leaving the Soviet Union to rebuild it the following decade. Though it's usually passed over for prettier pastures, Pleiku offers a taste of the same highlands culture, like the famed pho kho, or if you're feeling more adventurous, bun cua (vermicelli noodles with broth from ground freshwater crab), or braised escargot. Around 2km from the city center, the Minh Thanh pagoda is likely the city's architectural highlight. The large pagoda with its intricate details and daring dragon roof accents is surrounded by a beautifully verdant garden. After passing the huge doors inlaid with reliefs of the four heavenly kings, you'll find the main hall ornamented with over 3,000 statues, including four 8-meter-tall depictions of Thousand-armed and Thousand-eyed Avalokiteshvara.

name: Villa La Angostura
description: Villa La Angostura beckons with its enchanting charm, with each building adorned with logs and expansive windows, inviting you to step into a world where nature and architecture dance in perfect harmony. Whether blanketed in winter snow or bathed in the warmth of summer, this haven offers a myriad of experiences. Bayo Hill's ski center boasts dry, compact snow on 20 miles of runs, ensuring a perfect stay for winter enthusiasts. In the warmer months, traverse the Fuegian forests, discovering trails adorned with streams, rivers, and cascades like Inacayal and Río Bonito. The town is a gateway to natural wonders, with Arrayanes National Park and Nahuel Huapi National Park showcasing the region's rich biodiversity. Engage in sport fishing, kayaking, windsurfing, or sailing, and relax on the serene beaches of Brava, Mansa, and Bahía Manzano. For history buffs, explore the pioneer road, discovering ancient constructions that narrate the village's past. There is so much to do in Villa La Angostura, so be sure to adjust your stop time accordingly.

name: Omodos
description: Like many of the other villages in the Troodos mountains, Omodos is a picturesque jumble of historic houses built around a monastery. But at Omodos, residents have turned their traditions into an attraction. Wandering its cobbled streets, you'll find countless shops and wineries offering the famous local wine (many with free samples), arkatena bread, pretzels, and other snacks, while other vendors showcase intricate narrow-knit lace, jewelry and handicrafts. If you need something more substantial, there's a wealth of tavernas to choose from where you can take in the atmosphere and a traditional meal. If the glut of goods has you feeling repentant, head to the 18th century Timios Stavros Monastery. Inside you'll find a wealth of art and artifacts including a piece of the true cross, the rope used to tie Jesus to the cross, relics from multiple saints, as well as a Museum of Byzantine art, Museum of national struggle for the liberation of Cyprus, and a Museum of narrow-knit lace.

name: Blenheim Palace
description: Built in the early 18th century as a reward for John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough for his military triumphs during the War of the Spanish Succession, Blenheim Palace was designed by Sir John Vanbrugh in the rare and short-lived English Baroque style. Today, the palace reflects the lives of the generations of Churchills who have inhabited it. Visitors can marvel at the rich decorations within the stately rooms, including ornate stucco work, period furniture, eclectic artwork, and even a functioning pipe organ in the library. The noble setting is supplemented by a variety of exhibits ranging from period costumes to interactive multimedia installations, with a special exhibition dedicated to Sir Winston Churchill. The palace is surrounded by over 2000 acres of extraordinary parkland, with magnificently manicured formal gardens, the Great Lake, and ancient trees. Visitors can even take a buggy tour of the grounds!

name: Nazca
description: While the geoglyphs get all the attention, the city of Nazca should be considered the archaeological capital. Built by the Spanish on an indigenous settlement, the arid desert area and parts of the city still rely on a system of ingenious aqueducts that could have been made by the Nazca as early as the 6th century. Just outside the city, there's also the overlooked Paredones archaeological site, which served as an administrative center and is an interesting example of the organization behind the empire's expansion. Of course, if you're here, the Nazca Lines are also on your itinerary, so it's worth paying a visit to the Maria Reiche Museum, which is dedicated to the German scientist who brought international attention to the geoglyphs, or the Museo Antonini, which exhibits Nazca artefacts.

name: Saint Paul
description: Nestled on the picturesque western coast of Réunion, Saint Paul embodies the essence of island charm and natural beauty. At the heart of Saint Paul lies its bustling market, where the air is filled with the aromas of exotic spices, tropical fruits, and freshly caught seafood. Here, visitors can immerse themselves in the lively atmosphere, browsing stalls overflowing with local crafts, souvenirs, and traditional Creole delicacies. Beyond the market, Saint Paul boasts a fascinating history that dates back to the island's colonial era. The town's historic buildings and landmarks, including the iconic Saint Paul Church and the Maison Serveaux, offer glimpses into its storied past and architectural heritage. For nature enthusiasts, Saint Paul offers access to some of Réunion's most breathtaking landscapes. The rugged coastline beckons adventurers with its dramatic cliffs, pristine beaches, and crystal-clear waters, perfect for swimming, snorkeling, and surfing. Venturing inland, visitors can discover the lush greenery of the island's interior, with verdant forests, cascading waterfalls, and awe-inspiring mountain peaks waiting to be explored. Nearby attractions such as the Cap Noir viewpoint and the Trou de Fer waterfall offer unforgettable experiences and panoramic vistas of the island's natural wonders.

name: Lund
description: Settled by the Danes in the early 11th century, Lund was the seat of the largest archbishopric in all of Europe through the Middle Ages. The 11th century cathedral reflects this status, and is considered the finest piece of Romanesque architecture in the country, with a wealth of medieval art and architecture, including an astronomical clock from 1380. The entire historic quarter next to the cathedral is now an open air museum, where you can walk down cobbled streets, and step into some of the larger historic building which now serve as museums and galleries. This eventually gives way to Lund's university-run botanical garden, which has its roots in the 17th century and has 7,000 species of flora in its eight-hectare grounds, including 200 kept in a greenhouse. The unique Museum of Sketches for Public Art showcases preliminary sketches and models by over 1,000 artists from 30 different countries, offering a glimpse into the creative process.

name: Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex
description: Opened in 1962, the Kennedy Space Centre is a true testament to the innovations of humanity. The technology that got man on the moon, and that we use every day is all thanks to NASA and this space center. You can visit the space centre, where you can arrange a bus tour of the spaceport. Or join the Shuttle Launch Experience to learn about the mechanics of space travel while the simulation blasts you off into space. And see if you have what it takes to become an astronaut by trying the astronaut training experiences, including a Mars base simulator! Look at the very spacecraft that first got us into space. For more information, please visit https://www.kennedyspacecenter.com/

name: Brno
description: At the first sign of summer, the city transforms itself into a scene of lively street cafes, outdoor restaurants and street performers that make any visit that bit more memorable. The compact nature of the city means that restaurants, malls, museums, and galleries are all close at hand and the center can easily be viewed on foot or by taking a ride on one of the many trams that run both through and around the city center. Experience the delightful mix of cultures that make up Brno, a city that went unknown to most travelers for so long but emerged from the shadow of Prague in the 1990s. Take a tip from the locals and 'look up' when taking a stroll through the center in order to truly appreciate the beauty of the architecture where functionalist and gothic often combine to create the perfect blend of old and new.

name: Badajoz
description: Built by the Moors in 875 over an existing Visigoth settlement, the area was disputed between Spain and Portugal for several centuries. While not much remains of the ancient Roman and Visigoth structures, there are some stunning examples of Moorish and medieval architecture. Overlooking the city is the ancient Moorish citadel of Alcazaba, which dates almost to the city's founding. Down the hill, the vibrant Plaza Alta is home to the city's oldest houses and. For a more ornate example of Moorish architecture, La Giralda is almost an exact copy of the Giralda de Seville, and shouldn't be missed, even if it's a commercial space. The 16th century Puerta Palmas is a unique fortified gate with two towers, which served as a royal prison until the end of the 19th century.

name: El Jem
description: El Jem was founded 2000 years ago as the Roman city of Thysdrus - itself built atop a former Punic settlement. At the time, the city enjoyed a less arid climate and grew wealthy as an important center for olive oil production. By the early 3rd century, it was second only to Carthage in terms of wealth and power. Today El Jem is a small town, still surrounded by age-old olive groves, dominated by its Roman Colosseum. With a seating capacity of 35,000, it is eclipsed only by the Colosseum in Rome. As one of the largest and best-preserved Roman buildings in the world, visitors can explore from the upper decks to the subterranean tunnels where they kept the gladiators and beasts for an immersive look into the might of this legendary empire.

description: Built in 1841, the Ouse Valley Viaduct spans a 1500 foot stretch of river lowlands. Though it's 10-stories tall at its highest point, the viaduct is a perfect blend of graceful design and economic restraint. The bridge's 37 arches were constructed using over 11 million bricks, a number that would have been exponentially higher had the builders not had the ingenious idea to hollow out the piers between the arches. Along with saving money and materials, this design element creates an Escher-esque illusion of stretching to infinity. There are also a number of walking trails that weave through the lowlands, but as the area is usually pretty wet, appropriate footwear is recommended.

name: Nymans Gardens and House
address.addr1: Nymans, Staplefield Lane, Handcross RH17 6EB, UK
description: The Nymans Gardens and House seen today began to develop in the late 19th century when Ludwig Ernest Wilhelm Leonard Messel purchased the 600 acre Nymans Estate. Ludwig's son replaced the house with a picturesque manor blending Gothic and Tudor styles, and continued to expand the gardens. In 1947, the manor was devastated by a fire, and only a portion of the house rebuilt afterwards - the rest was left as a ruin. Today, visitors can walk the estate's renowned gardens, which offer peaks of the manor through the blooms, hedges and topiaries. Inside the manor itself, visitors will find historic furniture, Flemish tapestries, and family photos, arranged just as they were when the Nymans lived here.

description: Hidden away in the depths of the forest in Veracruz State, lies the Cascada de Texolo. This waterfall is 80 feet of pristine beauty. With the smooth water falling almost gracefully into the water below. You can walk over the gorge with a bridge that connects the rainforest together. What is notable about this waterfall is that it has been shot for a number of films, including the classic "Romancing the Stone". There are other waterfalls including the Mascada de la Monja, to add to your adventure, and to spend more time in Veracruz State's natural wonders.

name: Scilla
description: Scilla is an unusual combination of a rustic village and a seaside resort. The more modern Marina Grande, which runs along Scilla's pleasant beach, is the more recent development, filled with bars and restaurants catering to visitors and beach-goers. High above the town, the medieval Castello Ruffo provides stupendous views of the town below, Sicily, the Calabrian coast, and even the Aeolian Islands on a clear day. Also exhibited in the fort is the town's last luntre, a traditional local boat used for fishing for swordfish. On the other side of the headland, visitors will find the ancient fishing settlement where colorful cottages are built right up to the waters. Named one of the 'Most Beautiful Villages in Italy', visitors can still get a taste of authentic Italy here, especially if the fishing fleet is returning with a fresh swordfish. The symbol of the town, fresh swordfish is naturally at the top of every restaurant menu.

name: Semarang
description: Semarang offers a wealth of captivating experiences for visitors, with its strategic location making it a vibrant melting pot of cultures including Chinese, Indian Arab and European influences throughout. Exploring the Chinese quarters and the historic Dutch commercial district reveals the rich tapestry of cultural heritage that defines Semerang, including a series of well-preserved old buildings in the Kota Lama that harken back to the city's European commercial history. The city is also known as "Lumpia City", owing to its famous culinary delight, lumpia - a spring roll with delicate pastry. Stop by the Sam Poo Kong temple dating back to the 16th century, and if you visit during the sixth month of the lunar calendar, a procession of Admiral Cheng Ho's statue from Tay Kak Sie temple to Sam Poo Kong is a highly anticipated festival event.

name: Pocheon
description: Nestled in the scenic landscapes of the far northeastern region of Gyeonggi province, Pocheon beckons visitors with its serene charm and captivating attractions. One of Pocheon's highlights is its abundant spring water spots, particularly in Sanbuk-myeon, Yeongbuk-myeon, Ildong-myeon, and Hwahyeo-myeon. These natural wonders have been thoughtfully developed to attract tourists seeking relaxation and tranquility. Among these gems is the Korea National Arboretum, renowned as the expansive Gwangneung Arboretum. A sanctuary for biodiversity, it proudly shelters the rare white-bellied black woodpeckers and houses the Gwangneung Forest Museum and Gwangneung Forest Beach. For those with an artistic spirit, the Pocheon Art Valley offers an enchanting experience. Originally a quarry, it has transformed into a captivating culture and arts space, featuring a lake surrounded by intriguingly shaped rocks. K-drama enthusiasts might recognize the picturesque quarry backdrop from famous shows such as "The Legend of the Blue Sea" and "Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo."

name: Hyde Park, NY
description: As New York City became increasingly industrialized in the 19th century, the upper-class took flight, seeking refuge in places like Hyde Park. Among the illustrious names that took up residence in Hyde Park: the Vanderbilts, the richest family in the world who kickstarted America's consolidation as a world power. Designed by the esteemed McKim, Mead & White architecture firm, you can stroll the pleasant park around the the Beaux-Arts, but you'll want to take a tour of the manor to see the Vanderbilts' decadent lifestyle. Even the Vanderbilts play second to Hyde Park's best known resident: President Franklin D. Roosevelt. FDR was born and lived at his estate, Springwood. Take a tour of the interior to see how FDR lived and learn more about the life of the beloved president. Then visit the museum or presidential library, or stroll through the gardens where you'll find the graves of FDR and his wife, Eleanor. And speaking of Eleanor, her home of Val-Kill is only about 2 miles away and is also open to visit!

name: Teguise
description: Nestled in the sun-soaked heart of Lanzarote, Teguise is a captivating town that whispers tales of history, culture, and natural beauty. Wander through the historic center and marvel at the architectural splendor of centuries-old landmarks. The Church of Our Lady of Guadalupe stands as a testament to Teguise's rich past, while the Castillo de Santa Bárbara offers panoramic views that stretch across the island's volcanic landscape. Art lovers will find solace in the local galleries and the renowned Timple Museum, which celebrates the island's musical heritage. Every Sunday, Teguise transforms into a bustling market town, hosting one of the largest and most vibrant markets in the Canary Islands. Stroll through stalls brimming with handcrafted goods, local delicacies, and artisan crafts, all while soaking in the lively atmosphere and the melodies of traditional Canarian music.

name: Natural History Museum at Tring
description: The Natural History Museum was founded in 1889 to showcase the private collection of eccentric zoologist Walter Rothschild. After his death, the building and collection were gifted to the nation. Today, over 4000 specimens are on display in the elegant Victorian building. Visitors can stroll the halls to discover creatures from around the world, from polar bears to pythons. There are also extinct animals like the Tasmanian Tiger and great auk, hybrid animals, and an unusual dog collection documenting the effects of selective breeding in creating tiny Russian lapdogs and racing greyhounds. Throughout the year, special themed exhibition showcase specimens not normally on display, and activities and workshops immerse visitors in the natural world. For more information, please visit nhm.ac.uk/visit/tring Photos: © Trustees of the Natural History Museum, London [2018]. All rights reserved.

name: Okayama
description: Gardens bloom, legends thrive, and modernity intertwines with the echoes of history in Okayama. At the heart of Okayama lies the famed Korakuen Garden, gracing the land as one of Japan's top three landscape gardens alongside Kenrokuen and Kairakuen. Just across, Okayama Castle holds court, with its iconic black walls earning it the nickname "Crow Castle." It's a testament to history, having been rebuilt in 1966 after World War II's ravages. Legends thrive here too, as Okayama serves as the backdrop for the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy. His legacy weaves through the streets, offering glimpses of the heroic narrative. Kurashiki Bikan Historical Area speaks to Okayama's merchant town past, showcasing traditional homes and vibrant market stalls. Meanwhile, Setonaikai National Park's beauty unveils itself at every turn, inviting you to savor the breeze and panoramic sea views.

address.addr1: San Juan de los Lagos, Jalisco
description: The city of San Juan de los Lagos is unassuming at first glance. Sunny and warm, with a typical spread of religious institutions. But one among them stands out - the Basilica, which houses a shrine to the "Virgen de San Juan de los Lagos." The virgin itself is but a small figure standing just 38 centimeters tall and brought to San Juan in the early 1500s. A miracle ascribed to its power in the early 1600s has since provided the figure with a world-wide reputation of divinity. Nowadays, the tourism which it brings each year to the Basilica of San Juan de los Lagos is the main bolster of the city's economy, with total tourism draws amounting to 7-9 million pilgrims per year. Make like the pilgrims to pay your respects, or favor the town's less-crowded offerings of chapels and markets.

name: Seria
description: It was in Seria that Brunei's first commercial onshore oilfield was discovered in 1929. The small city offers unique attractions, with the Seria Mosque standing as a prominent landmark. The Oil and Gas Discovery Centre provides insights into the industry, while the seafront park features static nodding donkeys, symbolic of the oil extraction process. Visit the Billionth Barrel Monument, commemorating the extraction of the billionth barrel of onshore oil, accompanied by state plaques depicting scenes from the industry. While strolling along the streets surrounding the bus station, you'll notice the donkeys and storage tanks that dot the landscape. A giant food court awaits, offering opportunities to savor local flavors. Seria's charm extends beyond its oil industry, as nature enthusiasts may spot hornbills—fascinating birds native to the area.

name: Landsberg am Lech
description: Landsberg am Lech burnt to the ground in the 13th Century, shortly after being granted its town charter. but, rebuilt, went on to weather the wars, pestilences, and economic upsets of the ensuing centuries, growing in the process. Of its three districts the Old Town is the best place to enjoy evidence of that growth. Much of the town's 15th Century fortifications are still extant, such as the Bayertor Gate, the largest late Gothic gate in southern Germany, with a superb viewing platform. The Hauptplatz is full of majestic patrician houses and home to the much-loved Maria Fountain, along with the Town Hall, the town's prettiest secular building, with its richly decorated stucco facade and frescoed banqueting hall. Some of the best glass paintings in Germany can be found in the 15th Century Church of St. Mary while the Holy Cross Church has a truly splendid interior blooming with rich Baroque and Rococo decorations.

name: Packwood House
description: Packwood House was first built as a timber-framed farmhouse for the Fetherston family in the late 16th-century. In the early 20th century, the house came into the possession of Graham Baron Ash, the son of a Birmingham industrialist, the restored and extended the building, stripping away Georgian and Victorian-era additions to create an asymmetrical structure in the Tudor style. An aesthete and fine art connoisseur, Ash filled his home with a fine collection of 16th to 18th century tapestries and textiles, 16th and 17th century furniture, and countless other fine fittings, such as the Jacobean panelling and chimneypieces, much of which he installed. Outside, the manor's sprawling gardens, dating back to 1650, are a monument in themselves. The famous Yew Garden has one of the world's largest collections of yew trees, while the herbaceous Carolean Garden provides stupendous views from its 17th century brick gazebos. For more information, please visit nationaltrust.org.uk/packwood-house

name: Singaraja
description: Singaraja was the Dutch colonial capital of Bali, and remains a key administrative center to this day. Singaraja's wide treelined streets still have a distinctively colonial feel to them, and the city is one of the few places in Bali where you can still find traces of Dutch rule, as well as Chinese and Islamic influences. At the 17th century Puri Singaraja Royal Palace, you can admire beautiful Balinese art and architecture on a guided tour while learning about the royal family (who still live there). Another relic from the city's rich past is the Ling Gwan Kiong Chinese Buddhist temples, a colorful ensemble from 1873 that's still in use today. It's also worth strolling through the surrounding seaport area where you'll find historic warehouses and plenty of places to stop for some local food.

name: Qingjing Farm
description: Nestled over 5,000 feet above sea level, Cingjing Farm graces the picturesque mountaintop town of Cingjing (alternatively spelled Qingjing) in Ren'ai Township. Visitors flock to this attraction to enjoy breathtaking mountain vistas, interact with farm animals, or go horse riding, among other things. Qingjing Farm consists of three areas: the Green Green Grasslands, the Great Nature Theater Ecological Area, and the Guanshan Pastoral Area. A sea of sheep grazes the pastures here, easily visible without venturing far. If you're with kids, don't miss the daily sheep shearing show at the outdoor amphitheater. Additionally, the farm's European-inspired architecture is sure to catch your eye. Operating hours run from 8 am to 5 pm. Entrance tickets, valid for a day, are priced at NT$160 on weekdays and NT$200 on weekends, special holidays, and during winter or summer breaks. Please note that entrance tickets and third-party attractions must be purchased separately.

name: Iguazu Falls Brazil
description: Nestled on the border between Brazil and Argentina, the Iguazu Falls stand as the largest waterfall system globally, a mesmerizing spectacle of natural grandeur. Divided by the Iguazu River, the falls offer a unique duality – 20% on the Brazilian side and 80% on the Argentinean side, each with its own distinctive charm. Embark on a dual-country adventure, exploring the Brazilian side from Foz do Iguaçu first. A convenient public bus takes you to the Iguazu National Park, offering panoramic views and optional nature hikes along the Iguaçu River. The Brazilian side unfolds a 5.6-mile network of walkways, granting panoramic views of the falls. Stand spellbound as the Devil's Throat steals the show, a U-shaped cascade creating a misty curtain. Marvel at the immense power of Iguazu, where First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, upon seeing it, famously remarked, "Poor Niagara!" Whether navigating the intricate walkways or taking optional hikes, each moment resonates with the legend of a deity, immortalized in the name "Iguazu" – a fusion of Guarani words for water and big. As you stand on the walkway, surrounded by the cascading mist and endless falls, the sheer force and beauty of Iguazu Falls become an unforgettable testament to nature's majesty.

name: La Noria de San Antonio
description: La Noria is just northeast of Mazatlan and provides a quintessential Mexican experience, with its rich history dating back to 1565 when it was established as a mining outpost. Browse the many traditional crafts, including pottery making and various forms of leatherwork such as saddles, sandals and belts. For a taste of authentic Mexican cuisine, a visit to El Habal Ranch is a must. Here, you can indulge in traditional dishes amidst a rustic Mexican country environment, before heading to the picturesque Parroquia San Antonio de Padua La Noria Catholic church. Known for its whimsical yellow structure, it provides a serene backdrop for contemplation and a glimpse into the village's religious heritage. Enjoy the stunning natural landscapes, traditional craftsmanship and culinary delights this mountain village has to offer.

name: IWM Duxford
description: The International War Museum in Duxford has deep roots in aviation - it was established as a World War I aerodrome, and its renowned pilots were the first to receive the Spitfire and Typhoon fighters during World War II. On D-Day, the base launched every available fighter to assist with the invasion at Normandy. Duxford continued to serve as a RAF base until 1961, and was reopened as the International War Museum in 1977. Today, the site is home to a vast collection of aircraft, tanks, military vehicles, and naval exhibits. Along with iconic British aircraft like the Spitfire and Lancaster, visitors will also find an entire American collection, which includes the famed SR-71 Blackbird and A-10 Thunderbolt, and fascinating exhibitions covering everything from the Burma Campaign to aircraft restoration. Visitors can even step inside some of the larger aircraft, or watch (and hear) historic fighters fly by - there's even the opportunity to take a flight yourself! For more information please visit www.iwm.org.uk

name: Kew Gardens
address.addr1: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Richmond TW9 3AB, UK
description: Established in 1759, Kew Gardens was shaped by some of the world's most internationally renowned landscape architects as they reworked, rebuilt, and expanded the landscape and its buildings to house the world's largest botanical collection. Today, over 30,000 different plant species grow in the gardens, while the herbarium has over seven million preserved specimens. Among the many areas visitors can experience are an oak forest, world of high-alpine flora, the water-lily house, while the Temperate House is the largest surviving Victorian glasshouse. Other landmark buildings include a 50 meter tall 18th century pagoda, and the 17th century Kew Palace - the smallest royal palace in Britain. More than just a beautiful park, Kew Gardens have been contributing to preservation and study since their inception, having helped spread the rubber tree outside of South America, and today hold the world's largest seed bank.

name: Motovun
description: Motovun was built in the 13th century and exudes a strong Venetian influence. Today, the small town (home to about 500 inhabitants) offers a number of galleries, boutiques, bars, and restaurants. Motovun's main square is the only flat place in the whole town and houses a colorful church. The leading highlight of the village is a enchanting panoramic view of the Istrian valleys. Motovun also has exceptional Croatian wines made from the grapes of surrounding vineyards and many black truffle infused dishes. Whether visitors are searching for old town charm or exquisite cuisine, they're sure to find it in Motovun.

name: Canazei
description: Canazei is becoming increasingly more dependent on winter and summer tourism. It's most known for being one of the main hubs of the Dolomiti ski area, with 3 areas of access. Due to its climate and location, many sport-activities are popular in the area. Downhill and cross-country skiing, a snow park, bike park, and a swimming pool are all available to enjoy. Canazei also boasts wellness centers and pubs and bars to experience true ski nightlife. Additionally, various traditional festivals are held throughout the year for local and travelers alike.

name: Sansepolcro
description: According to legend, Sansepolcro was founded by two monks returning from the Holy Land brought a stone from the Holy Sepulcher back with them, and built a chapel to house the relic. This eventually grew into a true community that became an important trading town during the Middle Ages. To this day the town is dominated by the fortress the Medici family had erected to protect their asset. The original chapel has since been replaced by the Romanesque cathedral, which houses artwork by the renowned regional artist Della Francesca. At the Museo Civico, visitors can see his most renowned work, the Resurrection, which Aldous Huxley considered the most beautiful painting in the world. Of course with the many striking stone palaces, the town is worth taking time to explore.

name: Ulcinj
description: This ancient seaport has been passed between empires for 2000 years, and today is mostly populated by Albanians. Famous for the 12km long Long Beach, the lengthiest in Montenegro, the city also has plenty to offer visitors who want to keep out of the water. The beachfront Sailors' Mosque was constructed by the Moors in the 14th century, presumably as a place for their merchants to pray. Nearby Pasha's mosque was made using materials stolen from Venetian merchants as retribution for a Venetian attack on the town, and is home to the only Turkish bath in Montenegro. On a hill overlooking the bay is the Old Town, protected by massive stone walls, parts of which are from the original Illyrian fortification. A true pirate town, visitors can still see the slave market where Ulcinj pirates ransomed villa owners captured in their coastal raids.

name: Portobelo
description: Portobelo was founded by Spanish explorer Francisco Velarde y Mercado in 1597. Between the 16th and 18th centuries, it served as one of Spain's most important port in Central America, exporting Peruvian gold and treasures from the far east back to Europe. So important was the port that Sir Francis Drake was buried in a lead coffin near Portobelo Bay though his body has yet to be found. Though English privateers managed to raze the town multiple times, the Spanish continued to maintain fortifications in the bay, and along the coast - a defensive network now recognized by UNESCO for their pragmatic and creative genius. The colorful fishing town actually has two Spanish forts - Fuerte Santiago, with nearly 10 foot-thick cut coral walls, watchtowers, artillery sheds, and officers' headquarters, and the larger Fuerte San Jeronimo, with its 18 cannons, and still-standing watchtowers and officers' quarters.

name: Parque Natural de Ses Salines
description: Sant Jordi de ses Salines is the closest village to the airport in Ibiza, in close vicinity to the thrumming nightlife of other hotspots but far enough to escape it all. Its prime location in the Natural Park lends it access to three of the most famous beaches of Ibiza - Playa d'en Bossa, Es Cavallet and Salinas. The village is emanated by a spiritual feel with the presence of an imposing 15th century church, built for workers of the Salinera. The urban center buzzes with bars and restaurants that quickly get packed, while a second-hand flea market bustles in the old horse racing hippodrome. Browse through books, Indian jewelry, local food products and clothing as the jubilant beat of bongo drums rouse excitement in the markets. On Saturday evenings from July to August, enjoy a classic film with Spanish subtitles in the village square for free, while sipping on a digestif.

name: Antigua
description: Founded in the 16th century, Antigua served as Guatemala's capital until it was destroyed by a massive earthquake in 1773. Following the earthquake Antigua was rebuilt, developing its own, more resilient Baroque style, but kept its original Renaissance layout. Today, the city is recognized by UNESCO as being one of the earliest and best-preserved examples of city planning in Latin America, and for the slew of monuments and ruins that preserve early Spanish culture, and the importance of the Church during the colonial era. In fact, of the many gorgeous churches in the city (just take a look at the Cathedral), Antigua's main landmark is a Baroque arch, which is actually a covered bridge for nuns to travel between parts of their convent. The other central attraction is the lively mercado, where you'll find everything from fresh fruit to traditional handicrafts offered in the vibrantly colored stalls.

name: Monaco
description: Overlooking the pristine blue waters of the Mediterranean, this small city-state is steeped in 700 years of Grimaldi royal history. The Palais Princier, former home of Princess Grace and current home of her son, Prince Albert II, is at the top of the cliff-bound, medieval Monaco-Ville, better known as Monte Carlo. The famous Monte Carlo Casino, an opulent example of Belle Époque architecture, is a must visit – both for its extravagance, and that of its guests. The casino is so successful in fact that in 1869, the principality stopped collecting income tax from its residents, which has made Monaco not only a playground for the rich, but also a favored place for them to live.

name: Vila Real
description: Founded by King Denis, this literal Royal Town housed more members of the royal family in the Middle Ages than anywhere except Lisbon. The villas scattered throughout the city still bear their family Coats of Arms. The most iconic is perhaps the regal Palacio do Mateus. Used as a holiday home by the royal family during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, it's considered one of the finest villas in Europe. The grounds are free to roam, allowing visitors to soak in the striking Baroque facade, and impressive garden with its cedar tunnel. Visitors can also book a tour in advance to walk through the imposing interior and marvel at the macabre collection of fragments of holy martyrs and confessors. Within the city itself, the fifteenth century Gothic cathedral, the Baroque Igreja de Sao Pedro, with its gilded ceiling, and the Baroque Capela Nova, with its jaw-dropping facade shouldn't be missed.

name: Levoca
description: First mentioned in 1249, shortly after Germans resettled the area following the Mongol invasion, this medieval village's strategic trading position made it a center for commerce. The town began to decline during the anti-Habsburg uprisings in the 17th century. In 1700 the town mayor was murdered, and his arm cut off, embalmed, and preserved in the town after being injured by a local nobleman during a hunt. Today, things have quieted down, and the Renaissance town hall now houses a museum on local history. The metal cage outside is from the 16th century, and was used to publicly humiliate miscreants. Next door, the 14th century St. James church houses an ornately carved, 18.6 meter, late Gothic altar - the tallest in the world.

name: San Cosme y Damian
description: Fifty kilometers west of Encarnación, by the Parana River, the mission of San Cosme and Damián is the only Jesuit church in Paraguay that still offers services. During colonial times this mission was the main focus of astronomy in the whole of South America; it's importance in astronomical research was such that its works were released in Europe. The Jesuits built telescopes and quadrants for such a purpose, and there is still an astonishingly precise sundial at the site. The church, restored in 1977 after a fire, is named after twin saintly brothers that were believed to be protecting the native Guarani people against the diseases introduced by the European colonists. It features images of religious value, including it's two saints and various wooden statues. A visit to this site may include a film about native Guaraní cosmology and the chance to get a glimpse of the sun though their helioscope.

name: Kranjska Gora - Zelenci Lake
description: Kranjska Gora is located in the breathtaking Sava Dolinka Valley, close to Austrian and Italian borders. It's a town most famous for its winter sports. The quaint town hosts annual World Cup competitions at its famous ski resort. The resort is the perfect spot for visitors of all ages to enjoy winter sports such as skiing, ice skating, and tobogganing. The town of Kranjska Gora itself is popular year round and has many lively cafes, shops, and bars. Travelers are free to use the walking trails or go hiking or cycling. There are also swimming pools/spas for those who prefer relaxation. It's truly a town full of charm and culture for every season.

name: Azogues
description: Less than an hour from Cuenca, the provincial capital of Azogues feels like a big city without the pressure. It's famous for producing Panama hats, many of which wind up for sale in Cuentes, and hat houses can be found throughout the city, many of which are happy to give visitors a glimpse into the production process of these Ecuadorian icons. Azogues' main attraction is the colorful San Francisco de la Virgen de las Nubes Church perched on a hill overlooking the city. Along with beautiful stained glass windows and an opulent altar, the church offers fantastic views of the countryside. Surprisingly, the church is also a great place to shop, with numerous stalls offering handicrafts and even small animals - the nuns have one of their own, selling embroidery, knitting and other hand-crafted items.

name: Ciudad Rodrigo
description: Settled since antiquity, the only reminder of the Roman presence are three columns from a temple, which have been part of the city's coat of arms since the Middle Ages. During the 11th century, the town was rebuilt and repopulated, while the fortified walls were added a century later. Construction of The Cathedral of Saint Mary began at the end of the Middle Ages, but took two centuries to complete, and combines neoclassical facade with Gothic flourishes. It was embellished with a clock tower in the 18th century. The city's castle was constructed in the 14th century, and now houses an upscale hotel. Scattered throughout the town are landmarks from the 15th and 16th centuries - a time when the city flourished thanks to its relationship with Portugal. Perhaps the most representative is the town square, which showcases the 16th century city hall and plateresque Casa del Marques de Cerralbo.

name: Buckfast Abbey
description: Founded as a Benedictine monastery in 1018, the original Buckfast Abbey was reduced to ruins following the dissolution of monasteries in the 16th century. In the 1880s Benedictine monks purchased the site, and spent the next several decades rebuilding an abbey in the medieval style. Today, visitors can admire the abbey's rich decorations while learning about its long history with the help of some modern installations. The Abbey is self-sustaining with a farm for vegetables, bees, pigs, and cattle. There's also a shop on site selling the abbey's products which include honey beeswax, fudge, and the famous tonic wine. Made according to a French recipe, the caffeine in the wine was meant to give the monks a pick-me-up, though local hooligans use it as fuel for their antics. For more information, please visit buckfast.org.uk

name: Dozza
description: Every two years, famous national and international artists flock to Dozza for its Festival of the Painted Wall, where they paint the town red, and blue, and yellow, with awe-inspiring works on the houses and buildings. Visitors can begin their visit to Dozza by strolling through the streets of the town to take in the beauty of these works on their way to the famous Rocca di Dozza castle. The fortress is home to the Rocca di Dozza museum, which consists of an art gallery, a medieval and renaissance fortress, as well as two residences: one from the renaissance period and another from the eighteenth century. Located in the cellars beneath the fortress, visitors can end their stop in Dozza with a glass of wine at the Enoteca Regionale Emilia Romagna, an enoteca and wine bar dedicated to the oenological products of the region.

name: Rustaq
description: Settled since pre-Islam times, Rustaq briefly served as Oman's capital in the 17th century. Today the town remains an important regional center watched over by one of Oman's largest and most impressive forts. First built in the 13th century, the Rustaq Fort offers amazing views of the surrounding area, and some interesting artefacts in its museum. The other famous historical landmark is the 18th century Al Hazm Castle, which is an outstanding example of the intricate Omani Islamic architecture of the time. At the heart of town, you'll find a verdant green hotspring, which feeds into private baths where you can relax your feet. Bait al Garbi, a 200-year-old house, has been restored and repurposed into a museum exhibition historical heirlooms ranging from books, swords, and ancient coins to the family's collection of perfumes, bags, and trinkets.

name: Lanciano
description: According to legend, the Lanciano was founded in 1181 BC by Solimus, a Trojan refugee, though archaeological findings show that the area was settled in the 5th millennium BC. Over the centuries, Lanciano grew in importance, until in the 16th century, when the Turkish threat and the loss of its status in the Kingdom of Naples. Today, many monuments from its heydey still stand to delight visitors with their history, including the majestic city walls from the 11th century. Filled with historic churches, the 12th century Church of Santa Maria Maggiore is one of the most important in the region. The masterfully decorated main facade was reconstructed in the 14th century, when the bell-tower was also added. However, the Church of San Francesco is perhaps the most famous. Here, a doubtful monk had his wine and bread miraculously transformed into blood and flesh, which is on display in a reliquary.

name: Castillo de Teayo
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: The contemporary settlement of Castillo de Teayo developed around an ancient pyramid, with its name meaning "on the stone turtle" in the Huastec language. The site served as a pivotal location between the expanding Aztec civilization from central Mexico and the Huaxtec Maya of the central Gulf of Mexico coast. Gaze in awe at the synthesis of Aztec influences with Huaxtec materials in its architectural style. The pyramid plaza houses stone sculptures portraying gods, animals, and human figures, which are exhibited in the museum on-site. Visit the museum for a showcase of pre-Hispanic objects from the Veracruz northern region, providing insights into inhabitants of the Castillo de Teayo. Among the notable stone sculptures is the "Stone of Corn", an enormous monolith discovered near the Teayo temple. Uncover this and more at the incredible Castillo de Teayo.

name: Cirebon
description: Known as the "Shrimp City", Cirebon boasts a prominent role in fishery and visitors are encouraged to savor the delicious shrimp delicacies for which the city is famous. Straddling the border between West and Central Java, Cirebon's heritage incorporates Sundanese and Javanese cultures, as well as Arab and Chinese traditions. Palace buildings and Islamic graves are adorned with ancient Ming porcelain plates, and the batik cloths bear strong Chinese influences. The Keraton Kasepuhan Cirebon, the most magnificent palace in Cirebon stands as a testament to the city's rich history, having been built in 1529 and showcasing red brick walls made of Java. Its gates resemble those found in Balinese temples, making for a stunning aesthetic display. Nature enthusiasts can find respite in the Siwalk Tourist Park, a sprawling 175-hectare area with lush green rice fields and rolling hills, packed with outdoor activities.

When looking at the local Catholic church with the mountains in the background, one is reminded by the sheer size of the surroundings. If you want a piece of true natural beauty, Theft should be high on your list of priorities.

name: Santiago de Querétaro
description: Following a boom in the 1990s, Santiago de Queretaro has consistently been celebrated as Mexico's fastest growing city. Thanks to an infrastructure project of epic proportions, the city is well-connected in the transportation front as well as the pedestrian front. Walking through the UNESCO World Heritage Site that is the city centre, you will see one of the most impressive examples of Baroque architecture in North America. Take a stroll along the immaculately maintained aqueduct. Wine lovers can join in on the fun as Santiago de Queretaro is the second largest wine producer in Mexicos after Baja California! This city's extensive past as well as its optimistic future will be sure to facilitate an educational and enjoyable travel experience.

name: Neum
description: The town of Neum is situated along Bosnia and Herzegovina's Adriatic coastline and is surrounded by steep hills and sandy beaches. Neum's Mediterranean weather allows for long, warm summers and short winters. The town starting becoming an attractive tourist destination in the 1950's. Today, Neum attracts visitors with its beautiful coast, sunny weather, and affordable prices. There are many new and renovated hostels in the area and ample seafood restaurants. The crystal-clear blue sea is ideal for swimming, scuba diving, and snorkeling and keeps an average temperature of 32 degrees celsius in summer.

name: Lausanne
description: Originally a Celtic settlement, Lausanne is now the second-largest city on Lake Geneva. Its historic old town is largely car free and filled beautiful monuments, such as the 13th century cathedral. Considered the most impressive piece of early-Gothic architecture in the country, every day since 1405, a lookout has called out the hour 10 PM to 2 AM. The city is also home to some exceptional museums, such as the Art Brut museum in Beaulieu Castle, the Olympic Museum, which provides and overview of the Games' history, and the charming Fondation de l'Hermitage, every-changing art exhibition breath new life into the classic 19th century villa.

name: Zug
description: Said to have been founding in the early 13th century by the Counts of Kyburg, archaeological evidence shows the area has been settled since 14,000 BC. It was after World War II that the town lowered its tax rates and became a popular haven for businesses. This influx of well-to-dos has given the town a subtle polish, such as the timbered Art Museum being able to exhibit works by Kandinsky, Mondrian and Eliasson. The town's historic center has been preserved in all its Gothic glory, with its Late Gothic town hall, erected in 1505, and 16th century church of St. Oswald, with the 52-meter-high Zyt Tower dominating the skyline. Dating back to the town's founding, the large clock was added in 1574. Right below this is an astronomical clock which indicates the week, the phase of the moon, the month and the leap year.

name: Plasencia
description: Sitting in a scenic loop of the Rio Jerte, Plasencia is surrounded by 12th century walls, which incorporated seventy towers, eight gates, and an Alcazar. While the Alcazar no longer stands, most of the walls remain - though much of it is used as the back walls of houses. The city has a unique conjoined cathedral. The older, Romanesque, Vieja contains a museum with works by Ribera, while the 'New Cathedral' is a Gothic edifice from the 16th century that was left unfinished. The 15th century Convent of San Vincente Ferrer was built in the old Jewish quarter on the site of a Jewish and has a breathtaking cloister with Mudejar ceiling. For peace and quiet, the Palace of Mirabel has a lovely patio and garden, as well as a collection of Roman busts and altar stones.

name: Glasgow
description: Begin your journey in this vibrant city at its very heart, at George Square, surrounded by impressive Victorian architecture and bustling with life. A short stroll away, the Glasgow Cathedral stands as a testament to the city's medieval roots, offering a serene escape with its stunning Gothic design and peaceful Necropolis. Art enthusiasts will find their haven in the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, home to an eclectic collection ranging from natural history to Renaissance masterpieces. Nearby, the Riverside Museum, designed by the legendary Zaha Hadid, showcases the city's rich transport heritage with its striking modern architecture. Glasgow's West End is a trendy area filled with bohemian charm. Explore the cobbled streets of Ashton Lane, brimming with cozy cafes, eclectic bars, and boutique shops. Don't miss the University of Glasgow, where the majestic cloisters and Gothic towers evoke the grandeur of Hogwarts. The city's music scene is legendary, with venues like the Barrowland Ballroom and King Tut's Wah Wah Hut hosting world-renowned acts and emerging talents. For a taste of local culture, visit the vibrant Merchant City, known for its lively markets, stylish restaurants, and historic buildings.

name: Bucerias
description: Renowned for its stunning beaches, delectable cuisine, bustling markets and vibrant art galleries, Bucerias captures the essence of a quintessential Mexican experience. Immerse yourself in the vibrant atmosphere of the town's colorful markets, with the Flea Market, situated in the heart of downtown, beckoning visitors with its fresh produce stalls and local handicrafts. Visit some of the most breathtaking stretches of shoreline in all of Mexico on the sandy shores of Bucerias and spend some time basking in the sun's warm embrace, before satisfying your appetite with the mouthwatering fish tacos at El Rinconcito de Ensenada. Tucked away just a block from the beach, this hidden gem promises an authentic Mexican culinary experience with its fresh and flavorful seafood delights. Whether you're seeking relaxation or adventure, Buceriass has something to capture your heart.

name: Huasca de Ocampo
description: Between the 1760s the 1780s, Count Pedro Romero de Terreros had established the town of Huasca de Ocampo as the centre of the region's mining operations. He built four major haciendas (large economic estates) which, coupled with other operations in Pachuca and Real del Monte, made him the richest man in the world. Romero's death in 1781 saw operations fall into poor management; by 1810 the lands were mostly used for agriculture. Little has changed in Huasca de Ocampo in the centuries since, so it was ripe to become one of Mexico's "Pueblos Mágicos", or Magic Towns. Cobbled streets run between the pretty colonial-era houses, and the pace of life is extremely sedate. The old haciendas have become beautiful complexes of architecture and nature, so much so film crews flock there (such as Mask of Zoro).

name: Road Town
description: Immerse yourself in the vibrant heart of the British Virgin Islands at Road Town, Tortola's beguiling capital city. The warm Caribbean breeze carries the aroma of fresh seafood wafting from inviting restaurants, while friendly locals greet you with a smile. Explore a treasure trove of duty-free shops, brimming with luxury brands and unique island crafts, the perfect opportunity to discover a special souvenir. Immerse yourself in the island's rich history at the National Museum of the Virgin Islands, where captivating exhibits and artifacts unveil stories of pirates, sugar plantations, and the resilient spirit of the BVI people. Beyond the shops and museums, Road Town offers a taste of island life. Mingle with friendly locals at lively bars and restaurants, savoring fresh, locally-sourced cuisine and swaying to the rhythm of reggae music.
