name: Trapani
description: Trapani was founded by the ancient Elymians as a port, and thrived under the many empires that ruled Sicily, sitting at the heart of a powerful Mediterranean trading network, and serving as the Spanish's launching point for their conquest of Sicily. Today, the varied influences are visible in the Arab-influenced architecture, ancient buildings, and marvelous monuments and churches. At the Pepoli Regional Museum, housed in a 14th century convent, visitors can learn about the city's long history through its artistic heritage. Nextdoor, the 14th century Sanctuary of the Annunziata was the largest of its age, and has some exceptional Baroque interior ornamentation, particularly its altars. Trapani's Cathedral is even more impressive, with its Gothic portal and decadent Baroque decor. Trapani's also a favourite home base for exploring the many nearby islands, including the Egadi archipelago, which is part of the largest protected marine area in Europe.

name: Lamanai
description: Lamanai was first settled around 1500 BC as a small agricultural community, and by the time it was abandoned in 1680 had developed into a major Mayan metropolis. Unlike most Mayan cities that are centered around large ceremonial plazas, Lamanai was built in a linear fashion along the banks of the New River and the New River Lagoon. After being abandoned, the site was reclaimed by the jungle, and only around 5% has been investigated. But the excavated and partially excavated have revealed a treasure trove of Mayan art, architecture, and artefacts. Many of the major structures bear larger-than-life carvings, such as the 2-meter-tall face of the Maya Sun God on the Temple of the Mask, and the heavily-eroded forms at the base of the 33-meter-tall High Temple. Before exploring the complex, i's worth stopping by the small museum at the entrance to learn more about the site and examine the intricate pottery and jewelry uncovered at the site. Access to the Lamanai ruins is by boat up the New River from Orange Walk

Lay out in the sun with the view of the turquoise waters you will later swim in for a relaxing seaside excursion. Boasting two state parks, you can visit the St. Andrews State Park for some scuba diving, and reed exploring in the offshore coast! For sunset, go to the Camp Helen State Park to get an unparalleled view of the Gulf! For a spot of shopping, head on over to the Shopping Pier Park Mall to get an exclusive deal on the best brands without losing sight of the water!

name: Ovalle
description: Known for its wine production and serving as a vital center for commerce and transportation, Ovalle is a delightful destination, especially during the warm and dry summer season. The Museo del Limarí showcases the cultural and natural heritage of the Limarí Province, featuring fossils, minerals, and archaeological treasures. Nature enthusiasts will appreciate the Bosque Encantado, a nature reserve boasting lush forests and pristine waterfalls, perfect for hiking, birdwatching, and picnicking. The Iglesia San Vicente Ferrer, a national monument, stands as a testament to architectural beauty, constructed in the neo-Renaissance style in 1867. The heart of the city, Plaza de Armas, combines Spanish colonial and modern architecture, offering a lovely setting to relax under large trees, admire the fountain, and explore cobblestone alleys. Casa Museo Fray Jorge, once a Franciscan convent, now houses exhibits highlighting the region's natural and cultural heritage, including thousand-year-old mummies found on its grounds.

name: Rabat
description: Rabat was once part of the ancient Roman city of Melite and is adorned with historical and cultural treasures. The village is home to the Apostolic Nunciature of the Holy See to the Republic of Malta, making it a religiously significant destination. You may recognise Rabat's beautiful scenery from Stephen Spielberg's 2005 film "Munich" and Eric Carson's 1988 "Black Eagle". Visit the Catacombs of St. Paul and St. Agatha, used in Roman times as burial grounds located outside the city walls. The town also boasts the Domvs Romanva, a site that preserves the remains of a valuable townhouse featuring impressive mosaics that rival those found in Pompeii and Sicily. Stop by Casa Bernard, a 16th-century palace, which epitomizes Rabat's charm with its exquisite architecture, antique furniture and paintings. With the proliferation of historic buildings, newly developed areas such as Tal-Virtu and Ghajn Qajjet build after the Second World War also bring a modern side to the beautiful Maltese town.

name: Huacachina
description: The tiny village of Huacachina owes its existence to a small blue lagoon, for there's just sand in every other direction. Extremely popular with both Peruvian and international tourists, Huacachina is the ideal destination for adventures and relaxation. Head to the desert and ride dune buggies, sand board, and take a walk all over the golden dunes that surround the town. Or, you can relax throughout the town at the lagoon or one of the local swimming pools. The unbelievable views are the perfect backdrop for rest and relaxation. And, don't forget to try the local drink, a pisco sour, as you watch the sunset over the dunes.

name: Wonju
description: Wonju is the most populous city in Gangwon Province and offers a blend of natural beauty and vibrant cultural treasures. One of the must-visit places in Wonju is the Hanji Theme Park, a cultural space dedicated to traditional Korean printing methods and Hanji, handmade paper made from mulberry tree bark. Visitors can immerse themselves in the history of this art form and take part in short classes to create souvenirs to cherish. For adventure seekers, the Sogeumsan Suspension Bridge Trail presents an exhilarating challenge. After a rigorous hike uphill, visitors can tread across the 200-meter-long suspension bridge, providing stunning views of the surrounding landscape. For a culinary adventure, Jungang Market delights visitors with a wide array of authentic Korean delicacies and foreign foods prepared expertly. From traditional Korean donuts to unique snacks and savory treats, the market caters to diverse tastes.

name: Trieste
description: At one time, Trieste was part of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Today, the city is the capital and largest city of the Friuli Venezia Giulia region. Trieste is isolated from the rest of the Italian peninsula, with the Slovenian border just a few miles away. The cosmopolitan city has a lively culture that combines Italian, Austrian, and Slovenian roots. The main square, Piazza Unita d'Italia, is surrounded by palaces, city hall, a fountain, and a statue. Many bars and cafes can be found in the open space of the main square. The city is also home to the Trieste Cathedral and several museums and theaters. Visitors enjoy the calm, quiet atmosphere of this underestimated strip of land.

name: Iten
description: With more champion long-distance marathoners hailing from Iten than any other place in the world, runners flock to this Kenyan town to uncover the secret to what it takes to be a global competitor. Ask any local and they'll tell you it's no mystery why so many Olympic medalists come from (and train in!) this town in the Rift Valley. The combination of clean air, a high altitude and miles and miles of hilly dirt roads culminate to produce the perfect training ground. Many distance runnings have placed Iten at the top of their running bucket list - why not put it on yours? Drop in and witness world class athletes in action.

name: Le Port
description: Located on the northwest coast of Réunion Island, Le Port beckons travelers with its unique blend of historical charm and vibrant maritime atmosphere. Le Port boasts a fascinating history intertwined with its maritime roots, reflecting the island's past as a crucial stop along maritime trade routes. Visitors can stroll through the historic quarters adorned with colonial-era architecture, offering glimpses into the town's bygone era. For nature enthusiasts, Le Port offers picturesque landscapes, with stunning views of the Indian Ocean and rugged coastlines. The nearby Cap Bernard offers panoramic vistas of the coastline, perfect for capturing breathtaking sunsets or simply immersing oneself in the beauty of nature. Beyond its natural beauty and historical charm, Le Port is a lively hub of activity. The waterfront bustles with fishermen hauling in their catch of the day, while colorful boats bob gently in the harbor. Visitors can wander through bustling markets, sampling local delicacies and soaking up the vibrant atmosphere.

name: Pebble Beach, CA
description: A former old Hollywood getaway, Pebble Beach is a scenic town at the last frontiers of the Pacific Coast. With a high price-point and an even higher natural value, this town is awash with surfing, golf and recreational opportunities. Surfers flock here, especially when the swell is up - sometimes reaching 60 feet! If you are a golfer, choose one of Pebble Beach's seven 18-hole golf courses. Or hit the 9-hole course, if you want a more intimate experience. If you want to just take in the views, visit the iconic Lone Cypress, the town's most iconic point.

name: Ancud
description: Ancud was founded by the Spanish in 1778 as a "city-fort" to serve as the capital of Chiloé archipelago and guard Patagonia against foreign powers. The city held true to its purpose and remained the last stronghold of the Spaniards in the Americas, serving as the seat of their government-in-exile until 1826. Today, this bustling fishing port is the perfect place to prepare for exploring Chiloé and its UNESCO-listed churches. At the small Churches of Chiloé Museum, you'll get an introduction to these wooden wonders, including cutaway models and displays demonstrating their nailless construction. Fort San Antonio, offers a look at Ancud's colonial origins, and great views of the bay from the well-preserved battery. If shopping is more your thing, the Feria Rural y Artesanal is a great place to pick up local handicrafts or for a seafood lunch. From September to March it's also possible to arrange an excursion to the nearby Pingüineras de Puñihuil penguin colony (you'll want to extend your stop to at least 4 hours).

name: Monteria
description: Founded by the Spanish in 1777, Monteria moved to its present location after the original settlement was destroyed by natives in 1803. With a river port connected to the Caribbean Sea, Monteria has grown to become one of the 10 largest cities in the country. There isn't much in the way of sights, but head to the Parque Simon Bolivar, and you'll find an open air market offering handicrafts and street-food, and perhaps the prettiest building in the city: the elegant, white Catedral de San Jeronimo. If you're shopping for souvenirs, keep an eye out for the city's signature Sombrero Vueltiao, a patterned hat that's one of Colombia's national symbols - the more flexible it is, the higher quality. Alternatively, you can head to the Ronda del Sinú on the banks of the River Sinú for a stroll through the largest lineal park in Latin America, where monkeys and iguanas roam free and multiple restaurants offer laid-back dining options.

name: Memmingen
description: Founded by the Romans, during the Middle Ages, Memmingen was an important trade center, sitting at the crossroads of two important trade route. The town flourished through the centuries, seeing a slew of lavish homes and monuments sprout up, much of which has survived the test of time. Exploring its charming historic center visitors will see a variety of different architectural styles and influences from its long history. The Gothic St. Martin's church is one of the oldest in the region with a stunning 500-year old choir. Visitors can also relax at the Marketplatz square, dominated by the beautiful Renaissance town hall, which has an attached museum. Visitors can also walk along nearly 2 kilometers of the medieval walls, punctuated by gates and towers, or stroll the canal before stopping at one of the many quaint cafes or restaurants.

name: Orient
description: Orient weaves a narrative of remoteness, inviting travelers to embrace its authenticity, whether exploring its medieval houses or embarking on scenic hikes through the Tramuntana. For cycling enthusiasts, Orient offers a picturesque hub, seamlessly blending cycling with ventures to nearby attractions like Alaró market and the Alaró Castle climb. Hiking enthusiasts find solace in the embrace of Coanegra stream, the Puig de l'Ofre, and the Cúber reservoir, promising nature's splendor. Dining options abound, offering authentic Mallorcan flavors, and a selection of rural retreats and converted olive mills beckon those seeking tranquility. Orient's quaint streets, crowned by the Sant Jordi church and old school, invite leisurely strolls, with the public washhouses offering glimpses into the hamlet's past. Venturing beyond, Orient unveils natural wonders like Salt des Freu, a captivating waterfall nestled in a forest oasis. The trail to Castell d'Alaró promises panoramic vistas, with a historic castle offering a scenic perch for refreshments.

name: Makarska
description: Makarska's location between the rocky foothills of the Biokovo mountains and Adriatic sets the perfect conditions for fun and entertainment. With the Biokovo mountain's protection, the Makarska Riviera receives mild winters, cool breezes, and long warm summer nights. Along the shore there tons of restaurants and cafes to relax and admire the crystal blue waters. There also many beaches secluded by pine trees to give way for those who crave a more intimate and private area. Once you've finished watching the locals jet ski make sure to visit the old town, the markets and stands, as well as the Franciscan monastery. If you have time, the monastery hosts an exquisite contemporary mosaic and a delicate shell museum. As a center for culture and education, there is a little bit of everything for everyone at Makarska.

name: Malindi
description: A paradisiacal Kenyan port town on the Indian Ocean coast, Malindi is a laid-back tropical haven for lovers of pristine beaches, glorious sunshine and fresh, mouth-watering seafood! Laden with historical sights, Malindi is rich in Swahili and European history. The House of Columns is a Swahili structure operating as a museum showcasing ever changing temporary exhibitions with themes such as marine life and tribal history and culture. The Vasco da Gama Pillar is one of the most iconic sights in Malindi, though not for its aesthetics but rather what it represents; an age of exploration, installed in the late 1400's by Portugese explorer, Vasco da Gama. European influence continued as many Scicilian's settled in Malindi in the 1970's, and the coastal town remains popular as a destination with Italian tourists today. Malindi is also home to Africa's oldest marine park, home to coral reefs, sea urchins and many other species of sea life in the crystal clear waters.

name: Devil's Bridge and Indian Town NP
address.city: Devil's Bridge and Indian Town NP
description: Carved by the relentless crashing of waves over millennia, Devil's Bridge showcases dramatic geysers and blowholes that shoot water and spray into the air. Its tragic history is intertwined with the stories of enslaved Africans seeking escape from the horrors of slavery, leading to its ominous moniker. Devil's Bridge offers a captivating display of the Atlantic's raw energy and the harsh beauty of the coastline. Adjacent to Devil's Bridge, Indian Town National Park holds the title of Antigua's oldest and most diverse park. Encompassing lush rainforest-covered hills and significant historic sites, the park is a sanctuary of natural beauty and cultural heritage. The area's lagoon serves as a habitat for West Indian Manatees and a haven for migratory and resident bird species. Indian Town's historical importance is deeply embedded in the park's fabric, with connections to indigenous cultures and even pirate lore. This cultural treasure is a beloved spot for both locals and tourists, providing opportunities for activities like hiking, birdwatching, and kayaking.

name: Stresa
description: Stresa started out as a tiny fishing town and took off as a tourist resort in the 20th century. Today, Stresa has a lakefront promenade, botanical gardens, churches, and local markets to enjoy. The small town of 5,000 residents provides awe-inspiring views overlooking the islands. Take a trip on the Mottarone Cable Car for a mesmerizing panoramic ride to Mount Mottarone. Don't forget to also check out Parco della Villa Pallavicino, a zoological park with a collection of deer, zebras, llamas, and more. The Villa Taranto Gardens, a botanical garden, is also a great attraction and hosts a collection of plants and flowers from all over the world. Gallivant along the promenade for some great views of the Borromean islands. You'll come across statues, monuments, and public gardens along the way.

name: Leuven
description: It's said the red and white on Leuven's coat of arms represents the blood-stained shores of the river Dyle after King Arnulf of Carinthia defeated a Viking army here in 891. Many of the city's main landmarks were built in the 15th century, such as the amazing Town Hall, which is covered in statues of local historical figures. Across the square, stands the the imposing 15th century St. Peter's Church, which, thanks to its UNESCO-listed bell-towers, was the tallest building in the world when it was built. Inside, visitors will find exceptional artwork dating back to the 15th century, the highlight of which is Dirk Bouts' famous painting of the last supper. The city's other UNESCO World Heritage Site is the unusual Groot Begijnhof, a neighborhood built in the 13th century expressly for religious women. Most of the beautiful red-brick buildings in this idyllic quarter were built in the 16th and 17th centuries. Then, of course, there's the Stella Artois brewery - a landmark in its own right for beer lovers, which offers visitors with fascinating two-hour tour. You'll want to increase your stop time to 150 minutes and book tickets in advance at https://www.breweryvisits.com

name: Machala
description: Founded by the Spanish in the 16th century, Machala's seaside position and fertile surroundings allowed it to grow into one of the country's chief agricultural and shipping centers. Bananas, in particular play a major role in the city's economy where they're known locally as "green gold". During the third week of September, the city celebrates all things banana during the World Banana Fair, and the fruit features prominently in its public art, like the Monumento al Bananero (the Banana Picker). While Machala is seen more as a transit hub than a real destination, its coast is lined with sandy beaches where visitors can relax and soak up the sun and a boat or canoe trip to the Isla del Amor, is a little-known treat for nature lovers, thanks to its amazing abundance of birdlife.

name: Coimbra
description: Coimbra's long history is visible by the Roman Cryptoporticus on display in the town's Museu Machado de Castro. When the Moors conquered the city in the early 8th century, it served as a trading center for almost three hundred years – today's Arco de Almedina gateway marks the entrance to a former Moorish medina. Shortly after the Christian Reconquista of 1064, Coimbra became the country's capital. During this time, the Sé Velha was built, along with the Convento de Santa Cruz. The Universidade de Coimbra opened its doors in 1290, and is reputed to be the second oldest university in the world, producing many nationally and globally acclaimed academics. Immerse yourself in medieval houses "sobrado" cascading down a hillside on the east bank of the Rio Mondego: it's a multicoloured collage of buildings spanning nearly a millennium.

name: Ciutadella
description: Situated on the west coast of Menorca is the stunning city of Ciutadella. Founded by the Carthaginians, the city has a long history of being ruled by many empires, from the Caliphate of Cordoba to the Byzantine Empire. Ciutadella was the island's capital until the British occupation when the capital moved to Mahon. Wander the charming historic streets admiring the golden stone architecture and browsing the street market stalls for local artisan crafts. Eventually, you will reach the heart of the city, Es Born, where you can find the captivating Cathedral of Santa Maria, constructed in the 14th century in a Catalan-Gothic style. Head down to the waterfront harbor to stroll amongst the cafes and restaurants and admire the sparkling sea views. At sunset the harbor buzzes with life; now is your chance to sample some local seafood and a famous Pomada, a gin cocktail unique to Menorca, while watching the sunset.

name: Patras
description: Settled since 3000 BC, the capital of western Greece has been a cosmopolitan center for thousands of years. History lovers can stroll the cobbled streets of Patras' old town, where stunning neoclassical mansions make way to a medieval castle with origins in the 6th century. The remains of the Roman Odeon, and the Orthodox church of Saint Andrew (who was crucified here) tell a tale of the city's history from different eras. Another of the city's landmarks watches over the beautiful views of the port - the Patras lighthouse. Exploring can be exhausting, thankfully Patras has a good answer for this issue: take a break at a local café or restaurant to try some of the delicious local dishes.

name: Stavanger
description: Stavanger is a city rich in history, cultural and natural beauty, officially founded in 1125 after the completion of the iconic Stavanger Cathedral. Explore Gamle Stavanger, the oldest part of the city, where picturesque white-painted wooden houses line the streets, galleries and handicraft shops. Don't miss the vibrant Øvre Holmegate, also known as Fargegata, where you'll find a street adorned in a rainbow of colors, offering delightful cafes, boutiques and galleries. Works from the renowned Nuart festival are scattered throughout the city, so join an art walk and encounter impressive murals and tiny artistic treasures tucked away in unexpected corners. The discovery of oil transformed Norway, and the Norwegian Petroleum Museum offers an immersive experience into the country's most significant industry. Or, step into the innovative Viking House, where virtual reality transports you to the Viking Age. Afterwards, pick up a hot drink from one of six local coffee roasters in Stavangers and savor the flavors of locally produced delights.

name: Pisac
description: Tucked away on a mountain ridge in Peru's Sacred Valley, the Písac ruins are a masterpiece of engineering and spirituality. This well-preserved archaeological site, a strategic Inca stronghold, cascades down steep slopes with precision-cut agricultural terraces, ceremonial baths, and the iconic Intihuatana ("sun stone")—an astronomical altar honoring the sun god. Visitors should note that there is an entrance fee, and because of uneven terrain, sturdy shoes are recommended. Below, in the town of Písac, the vibrant markets are the perfect place to pick up souvenirs on your way to Cuzco, where prices may be a bit higher. Here, local artisans display a colorful array of handcrafted goods, from alpaca wool textiles to intricate jewelry. A visit to Písac seamlessly combines the exploration of ancient archaeological wonders with the lively ambiance of Andean commerce.

name: Jardin
description: This almost untouched colonial town just south of Medellin provides a colorful sanctuary in the middle of lush jungle surroundings. Sip on a traditional cup of 'tinto', a heavily sweetened Colombian coffee, as you enjoy people watching in the main plaza. Throughout the town and surrounding areas, you are able to view various magnificent tropical birds- see if you can spot the 'Andean cock-of-the-rock'! In the middle of the town, the Basilica of the Immaculate conception is not to be missed. This neo-Gothic church is a marvel to the town, built in 1872, it can be seen from almost anywhere in the town. One of the splendors of Jardin is La Cueva del Esplendor, a 3 hour hike (or shorter by horse ride) to a cave just outside the town, that includes a beautiful waterfall streaming through the cave's roof. Or you can take a very unique cable car from one end of the town to the other, in a wooden gondola operated by a mechanical pulley system- not for the faint of heart!

name: Astorga
description: Astorga was founded by the Romans in 14 BC, and relics of their empire have been collected in a theme park where sections of a basilica, baths, mansions and part of the sewerage system are exhibited. During the Middle Ages, the city was an important stopping point for pilgrims on their way to Santiago de Compostela. Passing through the Puerta del Sol, the fortified area is dominated by the Cathedral, which took 200 years to complete. As such, its art and architecture exhibits Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements. To commemorate the city's important role for pilgrims, the Bishops Palace, a Neogothic work by Antoni Gaudí, now houses the Pilgrimage Museum where visitors will find religious artifacts from around the 11th-17th centuries. In 1528, after Hernán Cortés brought Cacaoback to Spain, Astorga became the birthplace of European chocolate. The Chocolate Museum exhibits the evolution of chocolate production, and lets visitors sample chocolate from around the world.

name: Kokand
description: Unveiling the veil of history, Kokand, Uzbekistan, enchants with its legacy as a bygone silk road giant. Imagine strolling through the magnificent Khudonazar Khan Palace, its intricate tilework and soaring arches whispering tales of a bygone era. Explore the Rishtan Museum, a treasure trove of artifacts that bring the city's rich history to life. Witness traditional silk production firsthand, the rhythmic clatter of looms a testament to a craft honed for centuries. Kokand isn't just a history buff's paradise; it's a feast for the senses. Delve into the labyrinthine corridors of Chorgon Bazaar, where mountains of spices fill the air with an intoxicating aroma. Sample steaming bowls of hand-pulled lagman noodles, a local favorite, and savor the unique blend of flavors that defines Uzbek cuisine.

name: Dubrovnik
description: Dubrovnik lies in the heart of Europe on the Adriatic and is often referred to as Croatia's most beautiful town. The breathtaking views of the pristine, crystal-clear Adriatic Sea is reason enough to pay this town a visit. An impressive Middle Age city wall surrounds the entire city. The 1970 meters of white stone dates back to the 11th century and served to protect Dubrovnik from threats. Today visitors can explore the ancient city walls for themselves. The city's pedestrianized old town has narrow stone walkways and features a stunning amount of architecture including: churches, monasteries, museums, and fountains. There is also a vast amount of livelihood, with many seafood restaurants and cafes and bars featuring live music. The Dubrovnik cable car takes visitors to the top of Srd hill for a fantastic view of the old town and the Adriatic Sea. On a clear day, you can see up to 60km away.

name: Yagul
description: First settled around 500 BC, Yagul lies a short distance from where man first began domesticating plants, making the transition from hunter-gatherer to farmer. Around 500 AD, more elaborate residential, civic and ceremonial structures were erected, with the ruins seen today mostly being built between the 8th and 10th centuries when Yagul was the capital of a city-state. While pyramids and temples are the main draw at most archaeological sites, Yagul is best known for its decorated underground tombs. Above these, the Palacio de los Seis Patios showcases a labyrinthine network of rooms and walls, which were originally plastered and painted red. While Yagul only had around 6,000 residents at its peak, it boasts the second largest ballcourt in Mesoamerica after Chichén Itzá. It's also worth hiking up the hill behind the site, both for the ruins of a pre-Columbian fortress and the panoramic views.

name: San Luis
description: Founded at the end of the 16th century, San Luis is located in the foothills of the Sierras Grandes in an area known Punta de los Venados (Deer Point) part of the Sierras Grandes); hence the nickname for locals – puntanos. The historic center is still dotted with colonial buildings, which are easy to find if you start your visit at Pringles Square, named in honor of local hero Juan Pascual Pringles, who fought for Argentinian independence. The park is dominated by the Neoclassical San Luis Cathedral, and its twin bell towers serve as an easy-to-spot reference point for your explorations. There are several museums worthwhile museums, like the History Museum or Dora Ochoa de Masramón Provincial Museum, where you can learn more about the city and region. The Park of the Nations and Cenetary Park are popular destinations to seek refuge and a breath of cool air on a hot day. Gambling is legal in San Luis, and visitors can try their luck in any of the local casinos.

name: Saint-Leu
description: Nestled along the scenic western coast of Réunion, Saint-Leu beckons travelers with its captivating blend of natural beauty, cultural heritage, and adrenaline-pumping adventures. Saint-Leu's pristine beaches, such as the legendary Kelonia Beach, offer idyllic settings for sunbathing, swimming, and indulging in water sports like surfing, snorkeling, and stand-up paddleboarding. Thrill-seekers can also embark on unforgettable paragliding adventures, soaring above the coastline for breathtaking panoramic views. Beyond its coastal splendor, Saint-Leu boasts a rich cultural tapestry waiting to be explored. Visitors can wander through the vibrant streets, discovering charming Creole architecture, colorful markets, and quaint cafés serving up local delicacies. The town's lively atmosphere and warm hospitality reflect the unique fusion of French, African, Indian, and Chinese influences that define Réunion's cultural identity. For those seeking a deeper connection with nature, Saint-Leu offers enchanting hiking trails that wind through lush rainforests and dramatic gorges. One of the most popular routes leads to the iconic Pointe au Sel, where travelers can witness mesmerizing sunsets over the Indian Ocean.

name: Joshua Tree, CA
description: Joshua Tree National Park spans nearly 800,000 acres, covering parts of the Mojave and Colorado Deserts. Between the two, you'll find everything from rocky moonscapes to prickly cactus gardens, and, of course, the park's namesake Joshua Trees. The .6-mile Indian Cave Nature Trail is maybe the best option to see the Joshua Trees. Surrounded by boulder formations, keep your eyes open for bighorn sheep and desert tortoises. The half-mile Arch Rock Trail is a favorite for dramatic formations, with the 30-foot-tall Arch Rock being the standout. The Cholla Cactus Garden is another of the park's most popular trails, showcasing one of the world's densest concentrations of the Cholla cactus on its 0.25-mile loop. Cottonwood Springs showcases just how precious water in the desert is, with tall palms thriving in the arid landscape. Not only is this one of the best trails for wildlife spotting, but it has an interesting human history as well. For more information, please visit www.nps.gov/jotr/index.htm

name: Honda
description: Honda was founded by the Spanish in 1539 on the banks of the Magdalena River. Up through the early 20th century, the Magdalena was the only connection between the Caribbean and Bogotá, and as the chief river port, Honda flourished. With the rise of planes, trains, and automobiles, the Honda stagnated, and today is a working town that has preserved its turn-of-the-century character. Compared to Colombia's other Heritage Towns, Honda's historic center has a more "lived-in" feel, and you'll likely see cracked concrete among the colorful facades while exploring its cobbled streets. The narrow Calle de las Trampas is the most famous, but there are plenty of other picturesque alleys to discover in the old town. The heart of Honda is its main square and colonial-era cathedral, but this is second fiddle to la Plaza de Mercado, the town's covered market, which is nicknamed "The Parthenon of Honda" for its 148-column arcade.

name: Rosenheim
description: The entire city center is renowned for its historical charm and is fully pedestrianized, making it easy to get around and admire the breathtaking architecture, cozy cafes, restaurants, and the stores that cater to every taste. Feel the true spirit of Bavaria by heading on up to the Old Town to see the churches, historic buildings, lovingly restored townhouses, and the museums. These are centered around Max-Josefs-Platz, the square where visitors can while away the hours in a comfortable atmosphere exploring what the locals call 'the parlour of the city' with its wide arches, pastel-colored buildings and amazing eighteenth-century artwork and decorations. The friendly shops, friendly people and the inviting terraces that tempt visitors to take a seat and watch the world go by all add to the special ambience that surrounds Rosenheim. It will come as no surprise to visitors to hear that the city's motto is "We live and work where others spend their vacation".

name: Rab
description: The most notable beach is called Paradise Beach; it's clear and shallow waters make it ideal for children. The beach that is most well known is called Sahara Beach for its nudism. Rab pioneered nudism on its beaches after the arrival of its most famous guests then King: Edward VIII and his lover Wallis Simpson. In the beautiful main square one could find the plaque commemorating the day the couple whisked into town. But beyond gossip, Rab is steeped in beautiful red-roofed houses, hidden coves, and the Kalifront Forest. Tour the forest or grab an oar, Rab has plenty to offer.

name: Ein Gedi
description: Covering 14 square kilometers on the eastern edge of the Judean Desert, the Ein Gedi Nature Reserve is one of the most diverse and most popular natural attractions in Israel. Several hiking trails wind their way through the reserve, offering everything from easy, half-hour walks to full-day treks. The most popular are those that go through Wadi David, which leads up to David's waterfall through a beautiful, plant-filled river gorge, which contrasts with the surrounding rocky landscape inhabited by hyraxes and ibexis. Dedicated hikers can extend their visit by another 4 hours for a more challenging hike to the "upper section" where you'll pass the beautiful Dodim's Cave and other swimming holes before reaching the Ein Gedi Spring.

description: Traditional houses with quirky chimneys line the narrow streets of San Agustín, where a gently sloping hill and 18th century church forms the centerpiece of this authentic village. It's one of the best-preserved villages in Ibiza and simply oozes rusticism. Explore the old farmhouses or "finca" dotted around the village, and walk through the fields of grapevines that produce a hearty red wine. Find yourself a table at "Can Berri Vell", set inside a 17th century peasant house and known as one of the most romantic restaurants in Ibiza. Visit from the 28th of August for a week-long celebration of Saint Augustine, where a traditional Ibiza folk dance will be performed followed by a nighttime concert. A short distance away are the pristine beaches of Cala Comte and Cala Bassa.

name: Lake Myvatn
description: Lake Myvatn formed about 2300 years ago following a massive volcanic eruption. Its name literally translates to 'Midge Lake', for the dense swarms of the insects found here during the summer. These in turn support a wide variety of waterfowl, including thirteen species of ducks, and many other rare birds, making the lake a favourite destination for bird lovers. For many, it's the lake's volcanic features that are the highlight for many visitors. Iceland is famous for its hot spring baths, and the Myvatn Nature Baths offer a less-crowded but equally-beautiful alternative to the popular Blue Lagoon. Also near the lake are the Hverarond sulphur springs, which, while a bit smelly, create an interestingly colored, bubbling landscape. The dramatic rock formations of Dimmuborgir resemble a natural fortress, and served as the wildling camp in Game of Thrones. Near the lake, the Grjótagjá geothermal cave was also featured in Game of Thrones as Jon Snow and Ygritte's love nest.

name: Sai Yok
description: The Sai Yok National Park is known throughout Thailand for its picturesque waterfalls. After King Rama V visited in 1888, his brother Prince Niris compose a song about the beauty of the falls, which cemented them in the Thai consciousness. The park is home to a variety of wildlife including elephants, monkeys, deer, and even the world's smallest mammal - the Kittis Hog-Nosed Bat, which you might come across on you jungle trek. Unlike many national parks, Sai Yok has clearly marked trails that don't require visitors to be accompanied by a guide. The park is also riddled with caves, some of which are within easy reach of the park visitors center, making for a quick way to get your fill of bats and stalactites - just remember to take a flashlight with you if you're planning on exploring them as they're unlit.

name: Slavonice
description: Founded in the 13th century, this sleepy border town flourished during the Middle Ages when it sat on the route between Prague and Vienna. During the 14th century, Slavonice refined its urban design, creating two squares lined with houses and shops creating a convenient commerce center for its inhabitants. During the Renaissance, many facades were remodelled to incorporate frescoes and fine carvings, and are some of the oldest examples of the technique in the country. In Horní Square, several of the well-preserved buildings are open to the public. Along with the beautiful houses, Slavonice offers visitors some particularly unusual attractions. The first is a tour of the medieval tunnels that run under the town. The other is the Muzeum Samorostů, which is perhaps the world's most unusual museum, dedicated to unusually shaped wood found in the forest.

name: Eze
description: Settled as early as 2000 BC, Eze's long history saw it controlled by the Greeks, Romans, Moors, French, and Turks. In 1706 Louis XIV destroyed the town's fortified walls during the War of Spanish Succession, but it wasn't until 1860 that the town's residents unanimously voted to become a part of France. Today, Eze is one of the gems of the French Riviera, offering stupendous views of the Cote d'Azur from its mountaintop perch. The town's narrow lanes wind between medieval stone houses that are now how to charming cafes, boutiques, and galleries. You can even sip a coffee on the terrace of the terrace of a medieval chateau. At the very top of the village, the ruins of a medieval castle are now surrounded by an exotic garden filled with cacti and sculptures, and the best views in town.

name: Pisa
description: Pisa, located in the Tuscan region of Italy, has more than 20 historic churches and several medieval palaces. This university town is renowned for its art and architectural treasures. Pisa has a lively street life and a vibrant cafe/bar scene. The famous Piazza dei Miracoli, or Miracles Square, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and contains the city's most notorious sights. Its most famous, The Leaning Tower of Pisa, is a tilted bell tower that came to be as a result of poor construction. Today, tourists flock to the Leaning Tower for a glance at the unique structure. Feel free to climb the 300 steps to the top for a spectacular view of town. Another acclaimed monument is the Duomo Pisa, or the Pisa Cathedral. The medieval Roman Catholic cathedral, founded in 1064, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Pisa's architectural gems. The Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta in Pisa Romanesque style, is also a notable sight worth exploring. The remarkably ornate and rich history of the city make Pisa a must-see tourist destination.

name: El Rosario
description: Once a prosperous mining town, El Rosario reigned as the wealthiest settlement in Northwest Mexico for nearly 250 years. The town holds significance as the birthplace of Lola Beltrán, a world-renowned Mexican singer. In her honor, a small museum in the town exhibits her gowns and other personal items. Make sure to visit the town church, constructed between 1731 and 1759 and home to a mesmerizing Baroque-style gilded altar that showcases intricate craftsmanship. The architectural splendor alone played a pivotal role in El Rosario's recognition as a Pueblos Mágico and makes visiting the town worthwhile. If visiting in May, don't miss the Spring Festival from 1 May to 10 May - one of the oldest festivals in Mexico that showcases the town's vibrant spirit and heritage. Browse the pottery, furniture and leather goods that the local economy thrives on and enjoy authentic Mexican food in the center.

name: Tehuacan
description: The city of Tehuacan was founded by the Spanish in the 15th century, but its roots reach much deeper - around 4000 BC. It was in the nearby La Mesa Archaeological Zone that maize was first domesticated, and pottery made for the first time. Scattered among the stunning desert scenery are hundreds of little-understood buildings, artefacts from which are displayed in the onsite museum. The surrounding desert is part of the UNESCO-listed Tehuacan-Cuicatlán Biosphere Reserve - the most biodiverse arid zone in North America. Some 70% of worldwide flora families are represented here, many of which are both endemic and endangered, and can be seen either by hiking the reserve or in the Helia Bravo Hollis Botanical garden. In the city proper, the main attraction is the 16th century Ex-Convent of San Francisco, which preserves the historic periods through its art and architecture, though the natural history exhibited at the Museum of Mineralogy is also worth a look.

name: Chinandega
description: Chinandega was a small settlement during the colonial era, being described as a 'piece of paradise' in 1613. The fertile lands surrounding the city, and its role as a commercial hub allowed Chinandega to flourish - it even served as the capital of the fleeting Federal Republic of Central America. Despite earthquakes, hurricanes, and political strife, the city has managed to preserve its roots. In colonial tradition, it's centered around the Neo-Romanesque Our Lady Santa Ana Church. Rebuilt following an earthquake in 1885, the Antigueño-style doors on the north and south flanks of the church are from an older building. Chinandega doesn't protect its colonial buildings by law like other Nicaraguan cities, but there are still quite a few other colonial-style churches and buildings scattered around. The city has a small, but excellent archaeological museum with an extensive collection of pre-Columbian artefacts.

name: Kafar Kanna
description: Though predominantly Muslim today, the ancient town of Kafar Kanna played an important part in both Jewish and Christian history. It is (likely) here that Jesus performed his first miracle: turning water into wine at a wedding feast after the bridegroom's supply ran out. There are two 19th century churches in town that claim ties to the miracle. The Catholic "Wedding Church" is the traditionally accepted site of the miracle, and preserves the ruins of a Byzantine basilica in its basement. The nearby Greek Orthodox church of St. George lays claim to two stone jars believed by Greek Orthodox followers to be the very vessels in which Jesus performed the miracle of the wine.

name: Zugspitze
description: The Zugspitze is also home to three glaciers and Germany highest ski resort, which is also a popular attraction for non-skiers. Trips to the top can be made in the comfort of a cable car. This exciting mode of transport allows visitors to marvel at the astounding views of the lake below before reaching the summit and experiencing the remarkable 360º panoramas. Look down on Germany and Austria as you feast your eyes on over 400 mountain peaks that lie in the line of vision. There is also more to Zugspitze than meets the eye, for example, the museum at the top that gives a fascinating insight into the history of Germany's most famous mountain. There is also Germany's highest church and an igloo village to peruse. When ready, then stop off for a warming coffee, a delicious hot chocolate or even lunch in one of the excellent mountaintop restaurants.

name: Quetzaltenango
description: Quetzaltenango was a pre-Columbian settlement that was originally known as Xelajú before being conquered by the Spanish and their native allies, who renamed it Quetzaltenango. After Central America gained independence from Spain in the 1820s, it served as the capital of the short-lived Central American Confederation, and enjoyed a period of prosperity in the late 19th and early 20th century thanks to a boom in coffee production. Despite being Guatemala's second-largest city, Quetzaltenango has a well-preserved colonial center with a charming hodgepodge of classical, neoclassical, and Italian Renaissance style building. The squat Ermita de la Concepcion has a beautiful Baroque facade and houses the the oldest altarpieces in Central America and the first effigy of the Virgin Mary brought from Europe. The Espiritu Santo Cathedral is also worth a stop - the newer structure has preserved the intricate facade of the original 16th century parish church.

name: Sines
description: With artefacts pointing to Punic and Visigoth settlement, Sines has been an important port town since antiquity. As the city had already existed for centuries, the 15th century fort was made to fit into the existing layout, giving it its compact shape. Sines' most famous son, Vasco da Gama, was born in the castle, and has a statue standing near one of the towers. Also in the castle complex is the Museu de Sines, which focuses on the town's long history, showcasing Visigothic masonry discovered during excavations at the castle, and the Treasure of Gaio, a Punic necklace and earrings interred with a wealthy woman around the 3rd century BC.

It is famous for its chocolate manufacturing industry, as well as beautiful beaches for sunbathing and swimming. Brightly colored houses line the white-stone-paved walkways, apparently painted brightly to attract their fishermen back to the right shoreline after being out at sea. It's a small but lively town with bars and restaurants offering local seafood, wines, and of course, chocolate.

name: My Son
description: The ancient city of My Son flourished between the 4th and 13th centuries as the capital of the Champa Kingdom. Over its 900-year history, over 70 temples and numerous stele were erected, though US carpet bombing during the Vietnam War destroyed much of the site. The longest inhabited archaeological site in Indochina, My Son is the preeminent Hindu temple complex in all of Southeast Asia. Among the 17 surviving temples, all but one were built from red brick using still-not-fully-understood construction techniques. The beautiful architecture is further accented by intricate carvings made directly into the brick facade, as well as striking sculptures of Hindu deities. More delicate and at-risk statues from the site are housed at the nearby My Son museum, which is a great source of information for those who'd like to learn more about the art and architecture of the complex and gain a better understanding of Cham culture in general.

name: Ajijic
description: Originally occupied by nomadic Indian tribes and later inhabited by the Spanish, Ajijic has been influenced throughout history by people drawn to its picturesque location along the hilly north shore of Lake Chapala. Today, the lakeside getaway draws visitors looking for perfect weather, monthly cultural festivals and an endless array of shops and restaurants. Ajijic has a long history of art and local artists continue to create striking murals and sculptures around the city. Be sure to check out El Muro de las Calaveras (The Wall of Skulls) by local Efrén González which memorializes those who have died. Patrons pay their respects by placing candles between the clay faces in remembrance of Ajijic residents. If you happen to arrive on a Wednesday evening, you might be able to visit a local farmers market to grab some local treats or crafts.

name: Tlacotalpan
address.region: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
description: Tlacotalpan is one of the most unique cities in Latin America, starting from its build. A completely checkerboarded city, Tlacotalpan has immaculately and extremely selective and organized city planning. It is a port city by a river set back slightly from the ocean. Its organizational structure is apparent when looking at the quarters. There are two distinct sections with the Spanish Quarter being one and the Native Quarter being the other. With a public and commercial sector dividing the two to bring them together as one harmonic city. This makes it extremely easy to navigate the city. The city's Spanish architecture is built of Southern, Arabic inspired Andalusian architecture, while the Native sector is built up in the Caribbean style with beautiful red roofs, arches and colourful facades. This perfect attention towards the city and great care taken has led the city to gain UNESCO World Heritage status.

name: Monsanto
description: On the hillside of the Mount Monsanto, the earliest traces of man in this area date back to the stone age. The town has a positively Flintstone-ian feel to it, incorporating natural granite boulders and caves into the construction of the local houses. Visitors will be transported back in time as they stroll through the narrow streets and alleyways, admiring the truly surreal setting. Climbing up the mountain, visitors can also visit the ruins of the Castle of Monsanto, a 12th-century medieval castle that overlooks the surrounding nearby town and village. One-of-a-kind architecture and enthralling vistas are just a few of the things waiting for you in this fascinating little village.

name: Santander
description: First settled by the Romans, Santander as it stands today wasn't mentioned until the 11th century. Since then it's been closely tied with the sea, playing an important role in trade with the New World. In the 19th century it became a popular destination for beach-goers, who still flock to its long, sandy beaches. On weekends, visitors can tour King Alfonso XIII summer residence with a distinctly English flair. In 1941, a major fire destroyed much of the city's medieval center, though the massive cathedral survived. Bordering on austere, it was built during the transition from Romanesque to Gothic architecture. In the crypt, which was the original church, a glass floor exhibits the remains of the original Roman settlement. At the Sardinero, the city's main beach, visitors can walk the promenade lined with belle epoch hotels, restaurants, and a famous casino, and stop for some of the city's famous seafood.

name: Chesterton Windmill
description: Built around 1632, the Chesterton Windmill was likely designed by Sir Edward Peyto, Lord of the Chesterton Manor House, with assistance from John Stone, a pupil of Inigo Jones. A mathematician and astrologer, some argue that the windmill was originally an observatory, though local records show it has always been a windmill - making it the oldest tower mill in England to still have its working parts. In 1910 the it stopped functioning as a mill, and after having been restored in 1970, the Chesterton Windmill has been a subject for aspiring artists, and beautiful backdrop for a walk through the English countryside.

name: Kristianstad
description: Kristianstad is a city renowned for its natural beauty and historical center, dotted with copper beech trees, beautifully proportioned squares and gridded streets lining the river. It was founded in 1614 by King Christian IV of Denmark, who set out to make it the most beautiful city in the south, establishing many stunning monuments such as the grandiose Heliga Trefaldighetskyrkan church. Visit the spiraled goliath and explore the Tivoliparken or "English park", with a fine Art Nouveau theater at its center. Most notably, the naturum Vattenriket visitor center is a must-see to learn about the natural world of the 100,000 ha wetlands that make up two-thirds of the municipality. A diverse range of flora and fauna inhabit Kristianstad's wetlands, seasonally flooded grasslands, leafy forests, and sandy arable land. Access the 21 designated visitor sites for free in April, May, June, September and October, with specific opening hours available on the website: https://vattenriket.kristianstad.se/naturum/besok/.

name: Gelsenkirchen
description: Nestled in the heart of North Rhine-Westphalia, Gelsenkirchen is a vibrant city that seamlessly blends its rich industrial heritage with modern cultural flair. Arena AufSchalke has proudly hosted prestigious UEFA soccer matches in 2004 and 2024, as well as thrilling FIFA World Cup games in 2006, cementing its status as a premier sports venue. Beyond its sporting prowess, Gelsenkirchen is a magnet for music lovers, drawing world-class acts to its stages. The iconic Taylor Swift graced the city with her presence during her highly anticipated Eras Tour in 2024, captivating audiences and adding to the city's allure as a top destination for concerts and live performances. But Gelsenkirchen offers more than just a stellar event calendar. Visitors can explore a city rich in cultural and historical treasures. The local museums and art galleries provide a fascinating glimpse into the region's past and artistic endeavors. Meanwhile, the beautifully maintained parks and green spaces offer a tranquil retreat for those looking to unwind amidst nature.

name: Metz
description: Founded as a Celtic oppidum 3,000 years ago, Metz was a major cultural center throughout history. Today, this rich cultural heritage is spread throughout the city. Visitors can explore the cobbled streets of Sainte-Croix hill, where you'll find mansions and monuments such as the the Récollets Cloister and Trinitarian Church. In the 18th century Iles district, the elegant opera-theatre is the oldest to still active in France. In other districts, visitors can find the 4th century Church of St. Pierre-aux-Nonnains, one of the oldest in France, and the 13th century Cathedral of St. Stephen, one of Europe's tallest Gothic cathedrals. The stained glass windows are so large, it earned the nickname "The Good Lord's Lantern". Meanwhile, the new Centre Pompidou-Metz has been exhibiting some of the world's best modern and contemporary art since 2010.

name: Nairobi
description: A unique city in all fronts, Nairobi has become a defining factor in what it means to be in Africa. People from all races, tribes, and origins have congregated in this city nestled in the foothills of the great East African plains. Currently undergoing a boom, Nairobi facilitates all the comforts of a modern city, but with a traditional twist. Find yourself a great deal at the Maasai Market, which takes place at the Galleria Mall. You will find all kinds of local trinkets, and an opportunity to test your bargaining skills. Visit the Karen Blixen Museum, home to the Danish author of Out of Africa. The savannah is never too far away, as the Nairobi National Park is just a short way off the beaten path. You will never be disappointed by the natural wonders and cosmopolitan atmosphere.

name: Perast
description: The quaint town of Perast is preceded by two islands located in the Bay of Kotor. It offers breathtaking views and an ancient, old town feel. The bayside village has a population of less than 400 people and just one single seaside road. Despite its small size, Perast is home to 16 preserved palaces and 19 churches. With its Venetian inspired architecture and untouched romantic charm, Perast is the perfect bayside haven to unwind.

name: Oradea
description: Dating back to 1113, this border town was passed between various empires of the centuries, though its fortress put up a gallant resistance. Much of the town was destroyed by a large fire in 1836 and rebuilt in the then-trendy Secession style. Flush with richly decorated facades of pale pink, blue, green and white, making it a haven for fans of Art Nouveau architecture. The Black Eagle Palace, built in the early 20th century, houses a glass-roofed art nouveau shopping arcade between its two main buildings. Tuesday through Sunday, the City Hall offers the best view of the city from the three observation decks in its 170 foot tall. Its four clocks are operated by a 'mother clock' mechanism made by a local watchmaker. Seven distinct architectural styles are visible in the main square: Baroque, Classical, Eclectic, Historicist, Secession, Romantic and neo- Romanian.

name: Villa Carlos Paz
description: The enchanting city of Villa Carlos Paz captivates visitors with its pristine lake, rolling hills, and pulsating nightlife. The city unfolds a tapestry of attractions, ranging from the hilltop marvel of El Cerro de la Cruz, offering panoramic views accessible by cable car or hike, to the sprawling Dique San Roque, a reservoir inviting fishing and water sports against a backdrop of majestic mountains. Teatro Luxor, a historic theater, stages a vibrant array of concerts and performances. Paseo de las Artes, an arts and crafts market, invites weekend strolls amid live music and street performers. Parroquia Nuestra Señora del Carmen, a Gothic-style church, stands as a testament to the city's architectural charm. Culinary delights in Villa Carlos Paz are a feast for the senses. Indulge in the iconic Argentine barbecue, Asado, or savor Chorizo a la pomarola, a delectable sausage dish. Adventurers find solace in the mountainous landscapes, accessed through chairlifts and offering an array of activities from archery to scenic train rides.

name: Pilsen
description: First mentioned in the 10th century, Pilsen has been one of the most important cities in the Czech Republic since being named a 'Royal City' in 1295. However, the city's claim to international fame came in 1842 when Bavarian brewer Josef Groll created the world's first blond lager: Pilsner Urquell. Today, the factory attracts visitors from around the world who want to see how it's made, and drink from the frothy source. The tour ends with a sample of unfiltered beer in the cool cellars. Tours must be booked in advance at https://www.prazdrojvisit.cz/en/tours/. While Pilsen is best known for its lager, as a 1000-year-old city, it has its fair share of historic landmarks. The 14th century Cathedral of St. Bartholomew has the tallest church tower in the Czech Republic, and unlike most churches in Europe, remains essentially unchanged. Pilsen's Republic Square was once the largest in Europe, and the many Baroque and Renaissance style buildings that line it make for a perfect backdrop to sit and sip a Pilsner Urquell. If, however, you're looking for an under-the-radar activity, join the hour-long tour of the Pilsen underground - a network of tunnels dating back to the 14th century that played a key part in the city's history.

name: Cuenca
description: Founded in 1557 on the site on an indigenous settlement, Cuenca has grown from a valley village to the third largest city in the country. Over this time, its historic center stuck to its original Spanish colonial plan, with some of its buildings receiving 19th century makeovers courtesy of wealth from exports like quinine and straw hats. Cuanca's main square is the best place to experience its architectural beauty. At one side, you'll find the "Old Cathedral" - an elegant 16th century building that serves as the Museum for Religious Art. Opposite this is the "New Cathedral", which was begun in 1885 but took 90 years to complete. One of the largest churches in South America, visitors a free to explore its cavernous interior, and can even climb to its blue-domed roof. For even better views, you can head to the Turi Viewpoint on the hill overlooking the city.

name: Samarkand
description: Located in the heart of Uzbekistan, Samarkand emerges as an enchanting tapestry woven from centuries of history, culture, and architectural splendor. With origins dating back over two and a half millennia, Samarkand has been a crossroads of civilizations, a melting pot where East meets West, and a vibrant center of trade along the historic Silk Road. Its illustrious past is etched into the intricate mosaics, towering minarets, and majestic domes that adorn its skyline. Step into the bustling bazaars, where the air is filled with the aroma of exotic spices and the sound of merchants haggling. Lose yourself in the labyrinthine streets of the Old Town, where every alleyway holds a tale of bygone eras. Marvel at the grandeur of Registan Square, an architectural masterpiece adorned with three stunning madrasahs that stand as testament to the city's scholarly legacy. Venture further to explore the celestial beauty of the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, the serene tranquility of the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis, and the imposing grandeur of the Gur-e-Amir Mausoleum, where the great conqueror Tamerlane rests in eternal slumber.

name: Minca
description: Sitting 600 meters up in the Sierra Nevadas, the little mountain village of Minca is surrounded by lush cloud forest that has been listed as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1980. The incredibly fertile soil has allowed organic coffee farms and cocoa plantations to flourish, and the dense surrounding forest is home to an incredible variety of birdlife. Depending on where your interests lie, you can head to La Victoria to tour one of Colombia's oldest coffee farms, or learn about some of the finest cacao in the world. A few farms, like the El Paraiso de Tuki B&B Cafe y Cacao Farm even grow both coffee and cacao. Of course, you could just set out into the cloud forest to try to spot some of the rare species that call the area home as you make your way to the picturesque Marinka waterfalls. If you'd like to experience all of these, we'd recommend extending your stop by 2 hours per activity.

name: Sparta
description: When Paris of Troy abducted Menelaus of Sparta's wife Helen, his fate was sealed. Not even the mighty Achilles could save him from the might of Sparta. The Trojan War is undoubtedly among the best known stories from Greek mythology, though the city of Sparta itself hasn't garnered much attention in modern history. Its stunning neoclassical buildings tell of a peaceful more recent history, which has allowed the city to focus on its groves of lemon, orange, and olive trees. The local cuisine is something Spartans are deservedly proud. Try local Sýglina - smoked pork with local herbs, or Rafiólia - pies of flaky pastry. The city did not forget about its history, with the local archaeological exhibits artefacts from its ancient past. And so, we can calmly say - this is Sparta.

name: Daloa
description: Daloa isn't just a bustling city in western Côte d'Ivoire; it's a captivating tapestry woven with rich cultural heritage, a vibrant modern pulse, and a touch of adventure. Immerse yourself in the infectious rhythm of the city at a local "maquis," a vibrant restaurant serving up mouthwatering Ivorian cuisine. Savor dishes like "attiéké" (fermented cassava) with grilled fish or succulent "alloco" (fried plantains), each bite bursting with authentic flavors. As the evening unfolds, the city transforms into a tapestry of twinkling lights and lively music. Catch a performance at a local bar, where pulsating rhythms and energetic dance moves will leave you breathless. Beyond the urban buzz, Daloa offers a gateway to exploration. Escape to the nearby Lake Bandama, a shimmering expanse of water teeming with birdlife. Take a boat trip and spot majestic hippopotamuses basking in the sun or playful monkeys swinging through the trees along the shore. Hike through the lush surrounding hills, where hidden waterfalls cascade down moss-covered rocks, creating a scene straight out of a fairytale.

name: Barcelona
description: Crossing the mouths of River Besós and Llobregat, Barcelona is a sightseer's delight. With mesmerizing landmarks on every corner, start at the Magic Fountain of Montjuïc, a beautiful gateway into the birthplace of Barça. Standing boldly in the backdrop of this wondrous display is Montjuïc. With museums, galleries, botanic gardens, and castles, there's a lot to explore atop this hill of history! From here, head along the harbor, past the towering Columbus Column, and into the Gothic Quarter. Within, you'll find some of the city's oldest icons like the historical Roman Walls and beautiful Barcelona Cathedral. Stroll along the winding streets and you will soon find yourself along the iconic boulevard Las Ramblas, full of restaurants, street artists, and shops. At the top of Las Ramblas, you will find the lively Plaça de Catalunya in the city's heart which leads onto the tree-lined avenue of Passeig de Gracia, famously housing the extraordinary architecture of Antoni Gaudi. Both former residences that Gaudi renovated, Casa Batlló and Casa Milá, are located here. Now they are UNESCO World Heritage Sites open to the public and completely dedicated to their designer. Barcelona really was Gaudi's grand workshop. From Casa Milá, you can continue North, to beautiful Parc Guell, where his vibrant mosaics and enchanting designs are all around. Or follow Calle de Provença, for the climax of your trip and Gaudi's most famous masterpiece, La Sagrada Familia!

name: Pacentro
description: While the village dates back to the 9th century, it was the 14th century that still dominates the hilltop that provided protection for the village to grow. Today, two of the original four towers still stand, granting visitors great views of the surrounding valley - exactly what they were built for. The Piazza del Popolo, is home to the 17th century Chiesa Madre, with its large bell tower. Within the sedate, Mannerist facade, astounding Baroque stucco adorns the ceiling, as well as a baroque pulpit and confessionals, carved from solid walnut. The church also serves as a sanctuary for the relics of San Crescenzo, a Roman Legionnaire who converted to Christianity. Around the Piazza are a number of 16-19th century palaces and mansions, and ancient streets filled with and splendid views. While the village is well known for its beauty, it's perhaps best known for being the home of Madonna's paternal grandparents.

name: Ivrea
address.addr1: 10015 Ivrea, Metropolitan City of Turin, Italy
description: Founded as a Roman outpost around 100BC, Ivrea was a Ducal seat under the Lombards, and throughout the middle ages was involved with some of the most prominent figures in Italy, being fought over by the King of Italy, the Holy Roman Emperor, various bishops, the marquisate of Monferrato, and the House of Savoy. Monuments from the city's early days still abound, such as the 14th century castle, 10th century Bishop's Palace, or the ancient Cathedral, which houses a Roman sarcophagus in its crypt. While the Old Town is beautiful, Ivrea also offers a unique modern attraction in the UNESCO-listed Open Air Museum of Modern Architecture. In the 1930s through the '60s, Adriano Olivetti brought in the best architects in Italy to develop an urban utopia for the workers of his typewriter company. Adriano believed he could reinvest his profits for both world-class industrial production and benefit the whole of whole society.

name: Jardines de Mexico
description: The Jardines de Mexico is the largest flower garden in the world; a truly magical place designed to awaken your senses and explore the natural world through plants. Seven immaculately designed gardens have been harmoniously curated to take you on a journey of exploration through nature. The Japanese garden features bamboo architecture, rocks, waterfalls and a pagoda symbolising ancient Buddhist culture. The Tropical garden is a jungle oasis of prehistoric plants, and the Labyrinth of Senses is most mystical of all. Designed to lead you to find yourself this fantastical maze of green tunnels is filled with excitement and surprises, nature and art. There is an educational space for children (and big kids!) designed to develop an awareness of the senses through interactive workshops, learning and participation in the environment. A butterfly observatory and insects pavilion are just a couple of examples of the adventures that await your little ones!

name: Gothenburg
description: Designed and built by Dutch allies, Gothenburg was originally a heavily fortified trader's tax haven for the Netherlands. Today, Sweden's second largest city, and Scandinavia's largest port, is home to major industrial players such as Volvo, several high-profile universities, and Sweden's hippest culture.Trams, wide canals, and neoclassical architecture can be enjoyed on Gothenburg's chilled out streets. Attractions are many in this vibrant city. Röda Sten Konsthall displays contemporary and edgy art pieces in a wide variety of mediums. The Haga district, the first built by the Dutch, contains a host of cobbled streets lined with cafes and small shops. The three-story timber houses in this area are particularly charming. For the thrill-seekers Liseberg amusement park contains Europe's highest freefall tower (116m), but close by is Sweden's best museum for kids, Universeum. A humid rainforest is home to tropical birds and marmosets, and next door a hands-on science exhibition will thrill the children.

name: Punakaiki
description: The main attraction in this tiny village could be considered a world wonder. The pancake rocks are renowned as being an amazing site, especially during high tide. The pancake rocks were made over thousands of years by the layering of sediments and components of the ocean floor, then eroded away by rain and wind to eventually create the flat layered stone you can see today. During high tide you can observe that when the ocean swells, the water and air are compressed through the shafts within the rocks creating a geyser-like effect, the site is truly breathtaking. Take the easy walk up to the view point where you can see this attraction in full swing!

name: Solden
description: Around 3200 BCE, people began immigrating to the Ötztal Valley, as is evidenced by the famous Ötzi, the Iceman, who lived between the Neolithic and Bronze Age. Since then, Solden has been bountious for farmers, skiers and archaeologists. As a ski resort, it's a winter hotspot, and the population sometimes quadruples with eager skiers, but the summer is also a great time to visit. Sölden is Austria's first resort to have three mountain peaks beyond 3,000 m- called the BIG 3 - which are easily accessible by ski lifts. From the BIG 3, you are offered panoramic views of the Alpine scenery. Visitors from all over come to see these panoramic views and compare them to scenes from James Bond's Spectre, which was shot here. Drive along the 15 km Ötztaler Glacier Road, the second highest paved road in Europe, for breathtaking views from every curve of the road.

name: The Tank Museum Bovington
address.addr1: Linsay Rd, Bovington, Wareham BH20 6JG, UK
description: It's said the Tank Museum at Bovington was started in 1923 when Rudyard Kipling suggested that these vehicles should be saved for posterity, so a shed was requisitioned to house the collection. Over the years, more vehicles were added to the collection as the came out of service, and the museum officially opened in 1947. Today, the museum houses nearly 300 vehicles from 26 countries. The well-laid-out exhibitions showcase the evolution of armoured warfare, immerse visitors in the trenches of WWI, and tells the stories of the first 'tankers'. The museum also hosts temporary exhibitions and special events, such as taking Tiger 131, the world's only operational Tiger I tanks, out for a spin. For more information, please visit http://www.tankmuseum.org

name: La Spezia
description: Since the days of the Roman Empire La Spezia has been one of the region's most important ports and trade centers. It's also home to Italy's largest naval base. Many travelers overlook that it also has an atmospheric Old Town and is a great base for exploring the surrounding area. Walking the narrow lanes, it's still possible to see architectural elements ranging from engraved 14th century portals to double lancet windows, baroque pediments, and embellishments often seen on Renaissance palaces. The Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta offers a survey of changing architectural styles as it took 600 years to fully complete. For a more nuanced look at Italian history, head to the 13th century San Giorgio Castle, which has an archaeological museum with artefacts dating back to the Copper Age. The Naval Technical Museum offers fascinating insights into Italian naval history with fantastic displays like cannons, dive suits, model ships, and control panels from battleships.

name: Matagalpa
description: Despite being one of the largest and most important cities in Nicaragua, Matagalpa has maintained its laid-back village atmosphere. After gold was was discovered around Matagalpa in 1840, prospectors from around the world flocked to the city for their chance at fortune. One German couple, Ludwig Elster and his wife Katharina Braun, are credited with planting the first coffee trees in the area - a crop that's now the region's bread-and-butter (supplemented with chocolate and tobacco). While wandering the city, you can't not stop to enjoy a life-altering cup of joe, or heavenly local chocolate. Along the way, you're sure to pass the local cowboys, or musicians musicians playing Polkas and Mazurcas on guitar, trumpet, violin and accordion. These aren't ploys for tourists, but genuine expressions of local culture. Adding to the city's lost-in-time feel are its historic buildings, such as the 19th century cathedral and the other nearby churches.

name: Huaraz
description: One of the biggest towns in the Peruvina Andes and the biggest tourist destination in the Ancash region, Huarez is the perfect place for your inner adventurer. Most visitors come to take advantage of the many outdoor activities offered in Huascaran National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Because most people come to Huaraz for activities outside the city, it's tourist-friendly without being packed with tourists. You can lounge at the Plaza de Armas and admire the elegant church, duck into the Regional Museum of Ancash to learn about local history, or shop for handicrafts in the market without the press of people found in cities like Cuzco. To warm yourself up for your Andean adventure, and to enjoy the the best view in town, climb up to Mirador Rataquenua, where you can see Huaraz below, and the surrounding Andes.

name: Moroto Town
description: A blossoming town, you'll feel at home as the locals are community driven and love interactions with their neighbors. It feels almost like a slow town, with everyone running into friends and catching up with them, not a care in the world. Step into this thriving community's world and experience all there is to see and do in Moroto Town! Check out the Karamoja Museum, which gives a rich history into life before man, you see fossils that are over 3 million years old as well as teeth from the oldest known fossil monkey! Or, visit the Manyattas, which are the traditional homes of the Karamojong. Eco friendly and mostly made of mud, it was a cool place to be during the sweltering hot days. A mix of culture and relaxation, it will certainly be hard to Leave Moroto Town.

name: Kabah
description: Kabah has been inhabited since the 3rd century BC, with most of the structures seen today dating from the 7th century to 11th centuries AD. Once the second largest Mayan settlement in the region after Uxmal, Kabah relied on an intricate water catchment system since there are no cenotes nearby. Like most other Puuc Maya settlements, there are a number of pyramids, temples, and houses with decorative friezes and lintels, many of which depict either the city leaders or the god Chaac. The standout structure here is the aptly-named "Palace of the Masks", the facade of which is entirely covered with decorative masks depicting a Mayan deity. This repetitive pattern is almost unique in the Mayan world where buildings would usually only have a decorative frieze above plain walls.
